The runner's BTN5 press keeps its one meaning (close a lap) and is *read* as the corral return, which stands that window's bell lap down; BTN5 grew no third tier and the §350 grammar is untouched. Two consequences fall out and both are deliberate: at most one loop is counted per bell window, so a fat-fingered second press at hour 30 cannot inflate the scored number; and the count is therefore "bells this run closed a loop on", which for a runner still in the race is their loop count.

**The loop's length is learned, not configured.** A five-button watch is a poor place to enter 6706 metres, and events differ. The runner runs loop 1; from loop 2 the mean of the loops closed so far *is* the loop, and the projected return margin comes off it plus the live pace. Loop 1 has no margin and says `--` rather than guessing, as does a runner with no live pace — the [`cutoff_eta`](../custom_watch/quality_standards.md) rule that a stale input withholds the number instead of dressing it up. In the corral the margin is absent entirely rather than zero: `0:00` there would read as "you only just made it" when the honest statement is that there is nothing left to project.

**The refusal: the watch never declares a runner in or out.** It would be easy — the bell passed, no return was marked, so call it. It would also be a lie in the one place a lie is unforgivable. The corral is the race director's, the timing mat is theirs, and a runner who crossed the line at 59:58 without reaching for a button has not been eliminated by their watch's opinion. So there is no `DNF` verdict, no elimination banner, and no "you will not make it" claim anywhere in the mode — only the margin, the countdown, and the count, each withheld when its inputs are missing. The app's own `is_dnf` modelling stays where it belongs: with whoever ran the race.

**Arming lives on the watch, in the settings menu, idle-only.** No `SET1` field and no version bump: a backyard runner arms this at a start line in a field, and the menu is exactly the §351 surface for a setting a runner changes without a phone. It persists in a spare `CFG1` flag bit with no companion "set" bit — disarmed is the default, so a clear bit already says what an unset choice would, and every pre-§372 record decodes as a watch that is not in a backyard. Idle-only is not a limitation but the point: arming re-points the auto-lap, so a run has to be wholly inside the mode or wholly outside it. The sixth row cost the §351 press bound nothing, because it went in at the ring's far seat — a 6-ring's cursor distances are `[0,1,2,3,2,1]` against the 5-ring's `[0,1,2,2,1]`, so **every pre-existing row keeps its exact cost** and the new 5-press maximum belongs to the one row touched once per race. Six rows also fill the panel exactly, so a seventh needs a layout rather than a push, and a test pins that.

**The whistles ride the existing alert slot.** `Alert::BackyardBell(min)` goes through the same `AlertEngine` as everything else — one banner at a time, TTL 8 s — as a **drop-not-queue** arm, the milestone rule: a `3 MIN` banner read at 1:40 is a lie about the clock, and the page carries the live countdown anyway. It sits one rung under the zone ceiling and above pace, fuel and milestones, because missing the bell ends the race outright with nothing left to correct afterwards. It is deliberately *not* gated on `Recording`: the runner the whistle is most for is the one auto-paused in the corral with sixty seconds left.

**Rung.** Host-tested (24 tests over the core, plus recorder, face, alert and menu coverage) and build-verified for `thumbv7em-none-eabihf` across the default, `ble` and sim feature sets. **Not sim-verified, and cannot be today**: every NMEA fixture carries a few minutes of clock, so no Renode scenario can reach a bell at all — the first thing owed is a fixture that can. The bench checklist item in [`quality_standards.md`](../custom_watch/quality_standards.md) names what only hardware settles, including the uptime-extrapolation drift between fixes, which is an open value.

## 373. Sleep-station mode computes the nap from the race, refuses to guess at it, and does not claim to wake anyone

**Date:** 2026-07-30

The 200-mile racer's question at 3 a.m. is not "what time is it" but "how long can I sleep and still make the next cut-off". The roadmap listed the wedge as a tier-2 item on the grounds that both halves were already on the wrist; they are. `cutoff_eta::next_cutoff_eta` picks the nearest cut-off ahead and returns `margin_s` = *(limit − elapsed) − (time still needed to cover the remaining distance)*, which is the nap budget before a safety reserve. `sleep_station` therefore adds no cut-off maths at all: it calls that same function once, with a different pace, and subtracts a reserve. Everything worth recording is in the three decisions around that subtraction.

**The budget is its own countdown, so there is no nap timer.** The race clock keeps running through a pause (the same call `alerts` makes for the time alert), so a budget recomputed each tick falls one second per second while the runner sleeps. That removes an entire feature: no nap to arm, no nap state to persist, no nap state to recover after a reboot, and no new button edge in a press grammar five other in-flight surfaces already share. A runner lies down; the number on the wrist is what is left. A test pins the 1:1 fall.

**Every term can be unknown, and an unknown term withholds the number.** `cutoff_eta` returns `Unknown` on a stale fix rather than a plausible ETA, and a sleep budget is that projection minus a reserve, so it inherits the refusal whole rather than papering over it: `SleepStatus::Unknown` renders `--`. Four states, not two, because the three ways of having no number are different instructions — `NoCutoff` (nothing bounds the nap; **not** "sleep freely"), `NoBudget` (computed, and the answer is none), `Unknown` (a term is missing, and the page says which class of missing by splitting on whether a pace exists at all). A limit already passed resolves to `NoBudget` even with no pace, because "do not lie down" is knowable there and reporting it as unknown would leave the runner to guess. The hero keeps a measured `0` and a refused `--` visibly apart: merging them would let a runner read "no time to sleep" as "the watch does not know" and lie down anyway.

**Every rounding leans toward waking early, because the asymmetry is total.** A runner woken early loses sleep; a runner woken late loses the race. So: the projection takes the *slower* of the run's moving pace (what the cut-off page uses) and its race pace including every stop so far — moving pace alone ignores the aid stations that will keep happening, race pace alone flatters a runner coming apart at hour 40; the budget floors to whole minutes rather than rounding; and a sub-minute budget settles to `NoBudget` rather than displaying a `0` that reads as a broken page. The leg ahead may also be steeper than the ground behind — the projection is flat-pace, like the cut-off ETA's — which is a reason the reserve exists, not a reason to grade the budget on terrain the runner has not walked.

**The reserve is floor-plus-proportional because it absorbs two errors of different shapes.** `SLEEP_RESERVE_FLOOR_S` is `CUTOFF_TIGHT_S`, reused rather than invented: the product has already decided a cut-off made by under half an hour is not comfortable, so a nap must not eat margin the rest of the product treats as spoken for, and the floor also covers the fixed cost of a stop — getting up, shoes back on, a refill — which does not scale with the leg. `SLEEP_RESERVE_FRACTION` is 0.25 of the time still needed, because the dominant error is that post-nap pace is slower than the pace it was projected from, and *that* error does scale: the same slip costs five minutes on a twenty-minute leg and ninety on a six-hour one. A fixed reserve is useless on one and absurd on the other. The fraction is **a judgement call, not a measurement** — no post-sleep degradation corpus exists here — and is registered as derived-not-measured in `quality_standards.md` beside the battery projections.

**Nothing wakes the runner, and the page says so in words.** The tier-1 BOM has no vibration motor and no buzzer; every alert in this firmware is display-only. An alarm was refused outright rather than approximated: any arm added to `alerts` would fire silently onto a screen a sleeping runner cannot see, creating the *appearance* of a wake without the function — which is precisely the oversleep this feature exists to prevent. The honest tier-1 wake mechanism is a crew member reading the wrist, and the page carries `WATCH CANNOT WAKE YOU` on row 7 unconditionally, through the empty states too, because it describes the device rather than the data. Making it a real alarm needs the tier-2 haptic channel; until then, the notice is the feature's most important line, not its disclaimer.

The page seats directly after `CutoffEta` — it is that page's margin less a reserve, so `TIGHT` is one tap from what `TIGHT` costs in sleep, and the two appear and vanish together off one projection. Host-tested only (22 core, 4 face, 2 recorder); nothing here can be bench-verified, since no hardware exists.

## 374. Auto-lap is a chosen trigger with a closed catalogue, and its time axis banks on moving time — an elapsed-clock auto-lap manufactures empty laps

**Date:** 2026-07-30 · **Scope:** `apps/custom_watch` (research-tier)

The tier-1 recorder's auto-lap was a constant — `AUTO_LAP_DISTANCE_M = 1000.0`, applied to every run by every runner. The roadmap row "Auto-lap / manual lap / auto-pause" counted it as built, but a lap trigger nobody can change is not the feature: an ultra runner wants it off, a US runner wants miles, a treadmill session wants time.

**The trigger is a closed catalogue, not an arbitrary value.** `watch_core::auto_lap::AutoLap` names eight rungs — `Off`, 1 km, 1 mi, 5 km, 5 mi, and 5 / 10 / 30 minutes — and nothing else. The obvious alternative (a `u32` of metres on the wire, Garmin's own model) was refused for a reason specific to this device: the flash lap budget is 64 records (`run_store::MAX_STORED_LAPS`), so a 1 km trigger already loses laps past 64 km and an open field would let a runner set 50 m and exhaust the whole budget inside 3.2 km with nothing telling them. The coarse rungs exist to keep a 100 km run inside the store, and `Off` exists so a runner can spend those 64 records on splits they choose by hand. A closed catalogue also costs one byte on the `SET1` wire and three bits in the `CFG1` flags byte, which is what let the trigger survive a power cycle with no config-record version bump.

**Each rung names its own unit; the watch has no unit preference to derive one from.** Every render surface on the device is metric today, and adding a global km/mi preference is a much larger change than this row. So the mile rungs are explicit rungs, and the side that *does* hold `preferred_unit` — the phone — is the side that picks which rung to push. This is not a deferral of the unit preference; it is the honest placement of it.

**The auto-pause interaction, which is the load-bearing decision here.** Paused time counts toward nothing on either axis:

- *Distance* is structural. Distance only accrues on a fix the acceptance filter takes as real movement, so a runner standing at an aid station accrues none and closes no lap however long they stand there.
- *Time* is a choice. The budget is **moving** time — the same axis the fuel arms bank on (§ 214) and the axis auto-pause exists to define — not the elapsed clock. An elapsed-clock auto-lap turns a 40-minute sleep-station stop into eight zero-distance laps at the 5-minute rung, and on a 64-record budget those empty laps *displace real ones*. That is a data-integrity failure, not a cosmetic one: the runner loses splits they ran to laps they slept through.

This deliberately differs from the § 332 **time alert**, which banks on elapsed on purpose ("the clock a race is scored against"). The difference is what the two produce. An alert is transient and its cost is one banner; a lap is a persisted record that evicts another. The infinite-empty-lap case is pinned by a test that runs both an armed distance rung and an armed time rung through an hour of sub-threshold GPS jitter plus 3600 ticks and asserts the lap counter never moves.

A **manual** BTN5 lap while paused still closes, unchanged since § 350 — that is a runner's deliberate act, not an automatic one, and it still resets the countdown on whichever axis is armed.

**Where the setting lives, and where it deliberately does not.** The trigger reaches the watch on the `SET1` frame, which took the version bump v6's saturation assert existed to force: both presence bytes were full, so `flags3` arrives with **version 7** exactly as `flags2` arrived with version 2. `decode` accepts v1–v7 side by side and the frozen v6 golden vector is pinned as still decoding with an absent trigger — a phone that has not shipped the encoder leaves whatever the watch already holds standing rather than resetting a race's splits to a default. The byte travels raw and the rung guard runs in `settings_apply`, beside the race-phase preset's, so a garbage byte costs its own field and never the frame around it.

It is **not** a § 351 idle-settings-menu row, and the reason is what the setting *is*, not what the menu costs. The menu holds the levers a runner needs **without a phone** — GNSS mode, hide-empty, profile, re-zero, medical ID — and the auto-lap trigger is not one of them: it is chosen once before a race, on a keyboard, in the same sitting where the runner picks km or miles, and a wrist row would only duplicate a phone surface. This is the same call `pages` got ("33 checkboxes do not belong on five buttons").

**This paragraph originally rested on the menu's five-item press budget, and that argument no longer holds — recorded rather than quietly dropped.** § 372 landed a sixth row (BACKYARD) in the same integration, for a setting that genuinely cannot be a phone one: a runner arms backyard mode at a start line in a field. Six rows put the farthest three cursor steps out. Recomputed rather than assumed: a 6-ring's step distances from the cursor's home are `[0,1,2,3,2,1]` against the 5-ring's `[0,1,2,2,1]`, and BACKYARD went in at index 3 — the far point — so **every pre-existing row keeps its exact cost** and only the new one costs 5. The mid-race ≤ 4 bound therefore holds; what the paragraph above can no longer say is that the menu is *sized* at five. Auto-lap's exclusion survives intact, because it never depended on the budget — but an ADR may not keep citing a bound its own PR spent.

**It persists, because the failure it prevents is specific.** `CFG1`'s flags byte takes the trigger the way it took hide-empty (§ 351) and the activity profile (§ 353) — a set marker plus three bits — so pre-§374 records read as "no stored trigger" and the record needs no version bump. Without it, a battery pull at hour 60 of a 100-miler silently puts the rest of the race back on 1 km laps and spends the lap store on splits the runner had turned off. Bit 7 is the last one free: the next persisted setting owes a `CONFIG_VERSION` bump and a wider record.

**The Lap page names the trigger** beside the last split (`LAST 4:58    1KM`, or `OFF`). A setting that changes what a page counts, on a page with no way to see it, reads as a broken lap counter rather than a choice.

**Still owed:** the phone-side encoder. `watch_settings.dart` still emits v7's predecessor, so the field is on the wire and honoured by the firmware but not yet reachable from the app — a single optional field plus its golden-vector bytes, on both twins. Nothing here is bench-verified; § 82 outranks all of it.

**That debt was paid on 2026-07-31, at v8 rather than v7** — recorded here because the paragraph above names a version the encoder skipped. By the time the phone caught up, § 376's storm threshold had taken `flags3` bit 1, so `watch_settings.dart` and its iOS twin went straight to the current version; a v7 frame is now something only the firmware's decoder will ever see. The trigger crosses as a `WatchAutoLap` enum whose declaration order IS the wire discriminant — the `WatchRacePhasePreset` drill, and the same reason: a reorder re-points every trigger already pushed. Nothing about the rung guard moved: the byte still travels raw and `settings_apply` still refuses one that names no rung. The bench claim is unchanged — § 82 still outranks all of it.

## 375. A countdown timer and a stopwatch are honest on a watch with no buzzer; an alarm and a find-my-phone are not

**Date:** 2026-07-30

The roadmap's daily-smartwatch section carried one row — "Alarms / timer / stopwatch / find-my-phone — trivial; ship opportunistically" — that bundled four features on the assumption they were all the same size. Two of them are. The other two cannot be built honestly at tier 1, and the reason is the same constraint in both cases, so the row is split rather than ticked.

**The constraint.** The tier-1 BOM has no vibration motor and no buzzer. Every alert in this firmware is display-only, which `alerts.rs` has said in its own module doc since [§ 214](#214-tier-1-on-run-alerts-anchor-their-fuel-cadence-to-fuel_plans-defaults-bank-on-moving-time-and-share-one-display-slot), and which the roadmap's sleep-station wedge already records from the other direction ("needs the tier-2 haptic channel to actually wake anyone"). A screen cannot interrupt someone who is not looking at it.

**Refused: the alarm.** An alarm is not a clock with a threshold — it is a promise to interrupt you at a time you have chosen *not* to watch. There is no way to keep that promise here, and a scheduled-time face that fired a silent banner would look exactly like an alarm to a runner setting it before a nap and would fail exactly when they were relying on it. The word therefore appears nowhere on the device: not on a page, not on a settings row, not on a banner (the expiry banner reads `! TIME UP`, not `! ALARM`). This is a **T2 item gated on the haptic channel**, not a trivial one skipped for effort, and the roadmap now says so.

**Refused: find-my-phone.** The watch is a GATT peripheral ([§ 210](#210-tier-1-ble-s140-softdevice-is-a-compile-verified-feature-gated-build--mutually-exclusive-with-the-sim-off-by-default), [§ 211](#211-owner-override-build-the-full-watchphonesupabase-run-sync-vertical-now-despite-the-tier-2-gate)). The phone connects to it; every characteristic is something the phone reads, writes, or subscribes to, and the phone-side code (`WatchIngestQueue`, `sim_watch_link.dart`) is a pure consumer with no ring handler and no background-execution contract. Making the watch ring the phone needs a new characteristic, new phone-side code, and background-audio permissions on both mobile platforms. And § 210 is explicit that the SoftDevice path can never be sim-verified and there is no dev kit — so a feature whose entire value is *it makes a noise somewhere else* would ship at build-verified and stay there indefinitely. Nothing was stubbed; a characteristic that compiles and has never made a sound is worse than an absent feature, because the roadmap would read as though the capability existed.

**Built: one instrument, not two.** `watch_core::timers` is a single state machine whose preset ladder starts at zero, and zero *is* the stopwatch — with nothing to count down to it counts up. That is why there is no mode switch and no second key. The eleven rungs are durations this repo already names: 1/3/5 min for an aid-station turnaround, 10 through 90 for the documented 20-90 minute sleep-station nap, and 60 min for the backyard-ultra bell the backyard-mode wedge is built around. The ladder is clamped, not wrapping, per § 351's no-teleport rule, and it is **refused once armed** — moving the target under a running countdown would silently shift an expiry the runner is already timing against.

**The honesty decision that falls out: an expired countdown counts up past zero.** A kitchen timer may freeze at 0:00 because its beep told you when. This one cannot tell you, so the only part of a missed expiry that survives being missed is *how long ago*, and the page answers it — `+2:14`. Freezing at zero would throw that away and leave a stopped clock on the wrist.

**Where it lives, and what it cost.** The expiry rides the *existing* alert slot rather than a second banner path: a new `Alert::TimerDone` at the milestone rung, **dropped rather than queued** when the slot is busy (the Timer page carries the overrun, so nothing recoverable is lost) and below fuel, because § 214 says a gel is the one reminder that must never be dropped. It is not gated on `Recording` — a countdown set at an aid station is running precisely while the recorder is paused. Because the alert engine is a run surface, an expiry while idle raises no banner at all; the instrument stays correct and simply makes no claim it cannot keep.

The button cost is **one press on a key that was dead**: idle BTN2 opens a modal, the same dead-key repurposing § 291 gave idle BTN4 and § 351 gave idle BTN5, and the last one the § 350 grammar had. A modal rather than a tap/hold split because "idle gestures are duration-stable" is a stated navigation invariant. Inside, every key is spatially true to what it shows — BTN1 the START verb it carries everywhere, BTN2/BTN3 the vertical pair moving the one value up and down (the settings menu's cursor pair, repurposed because this modal has no list to walk), BTN4 exit on the § 81 BACK slot where the settings menu already puts it, BTN5 reset. Reset is refused while running, so a brushed sleeve cannot zero a live timing.

The page cost is the 38th built-in, and it moves **no published press-cost ceiling**: recomputing § 289's BFS at 38 gives symmetric worst 7 (unchanged, it steps at 44) and forward-only worst 10 (unchanged, it steps at 42); only the linear-walk worst grows, 18 → 19, and the averages move 4.0541 → 4.0789 / 5.2432 → 5.3421 / 9.2432 → 9.5000. With the four composed-screen seats the full mask is 42, still inside the 7-press ceiling — but the margin is now one page rather than two, which is the real cost and is recorded rather than rounded away. The page is data-presence gated on the instrument being *armed*, so a watch whose owner never opens the modal walks exactly the cycle it walked before.

**Two things deliberately not built.** The timer is not shown on the idle home face: that face is minute-resolution precisely so a resting clock flushes zero SPI lines, and a second-resolution row would make an idle wrist redraw every second for a feature the runner can check with one press. And the modal closes after 30 s of inactivity like the settings menu, for the same reason (it covers the home clock) — so an idle timer is *consulted*, not *watched*. The place it is watched is the run view, where the 1 Hz redraw is already paid for.
## 376. Storm detection trends a sea-level-reduced pressure against GPS altitude, and says nothing at all when it cannot

**Date:** 2026-07-31

The roadmap's "Weather / storm alerts" row has read *partial: baro-driven storm detection is cheap ([`vision.md`](../custom_watch/vision.md) req #7) and worth it; full forecast sync is deferred* since the parity backlog was written, and nothing had been built. The word "cheap" was doing a lot of work in that line, and this entry is mostly about what it was hiding.

**The problem is not detecting a falling barometer. It is that climbing looks identical.** An approaching front moves station pressure a few hectopascals over hours. Five hundred metres of ascent moves it ~57 hPa in forty minutes. A watch that trended raw station pressure — which is what "cheap" imagines — would announce a storm on every col of a mountain ultra and clear it on every descent: a warning generated entirely by the runner's own legs, on the one device whose stated discipline is that it never fabricates.

**The separation is a pressure reduction, and its altitude has to come from somewhere else.** `elevation::sea_level_pa` is the exact inverse of `altitude_m` and shares its constants: given a pressure and the altitude it was taken at, it returns the sea-level-equivalent pressure that implies. Climbing moves the station pressure and the altitude together, so the reduced value does not move; a front moves the pressure alone, so it does. That only works while the altitude is *independent* of the pressure. Feed back a baro-derived altitude and the reduction returns the reference it was derived against — exactly, on every sample, with the weather divided out. A host test pins that (`a_baro_derived_altitude_reduces_back_to_the_reference_it_came_from`), and the sim reproduces it as a *falsification*: with the tracker mutated to take the baro altitude, the still atmosphere reads a suspiciously exact `+0.00 hPa` at the ISA reference and the scripted front never arrives at all.

So the reference is the **GPS receiver's** altitude, narrowed through the same `elevation::plausible_gps` window the vert filter refuses to pull its bias toward.

**Not the complementary filter's corrected altitude, which is the tempting reuse and is exactly wrong.** `VertAccumulator` already publishes a smooth, GPS-referenced altitude, and reaching for it is the obvious move. That altitude is `HPF(baro) + LPF(gps)`, crossing over at `GPS_PULL` per *fix*. Reduce against it and the error term is `HPF(weather)` — the very signal being measured, suppressed by precisely the filter that makes the altitude smooth. In Expedition mode a fix lands once a minute, so the crossover sits near a hundred minutes and would swallow most of a three-hour trend. The filter is right for vert (its job is to remove weather) and wrong for weather (whose job is to keep it). The two look like the same number and are opposite tools.

**Trading that smoothness away costs noise, and two averages pay for it.** A receiver altitude carries ~±15 m, which is ~1.8 hPa of reduction error — comparable to the storm signal itself. Samples are averaged into five-minute buckets, each requiring three corroborated readings before it banks at all (one un-averaged reduction carries more error than the thing being measured), and the tendency is a **least-squares slope over every banked bucket in the window** rather than a difference of its two endpoints. An endpoint difference stakes the whole verdict on two samples; one bad altitude at either end moves it by more than the threshold.

**What it refuses to say, which is the half that matters.** No corroborated GPS altitude within two minutes and the answer is `NoReference` — not a trend computed off the last good reference, and emphatically not one read off raw station pressure. Under canopy, in a canyon, or with the receiver in backup mode, the watch cannot tell a front from a climb, and the honest report of that is that it does not know. Less than a third of the window banked and the answer is `Building`, because a tendency extrapolated from a fraction of its window amplifies its own residual by the reciprocal of that fraction. Both refusals still carry the *absolute* reduced pressure where it is known, since that half is real from the first corroborated reading — a working barometer must not read as a broken one.

**The numbers are chosen, not measured, and are registered as such.** Three hours because that is the synoptic pressure-tendency interval every barometric convention is quoted over; 4.0 hPa because that is what the mainstream outdoor watches ship as their storm-alarm default. Nothing in this repository has watched a real front cross a real barometer, so both join `quality_standards.md`'s derived-not-measured register. The latch releases at half the opening fall — the same open-wide / close-narrow asymmetry [§ 359](#359-climb-detection-is-hysteretic-on-both-edges-and-the-crest-ahead-is-a-separate-answer-from-the-climb-underfoot)'s 20 m / 10 m pair uses — so a trend hovering on the boundary cannot flap the word on the page.

**Where the alert sits, and why.** Between pace and fuel, in the **re-queued** class. It is the first arm on `alerts.rs` about the world rather than the runner, and the placement follows from *when* the thing it warns of arrives: a zone excursion, a corral bell and a pace drift all want a decision inside seconds, so a front measured over three hours yields to all three. But it fires perhaps once in a race and there is no later reminder, so it takes fuel's never-dropped rule ([§ 214](#214-tier-1-on-run-alerts-anchor-their-fuel-cadence-to-fuel_plans-defaults-bank-on-moving-time-and-share-one-display-slot)) and leads that class — a missed gel is re-offered a cadence later, a missed front is not. It is off by default, once per front, and there is **no cooldown constant beside it**: unlike a BPM crossing a zone boundary the signal is already hysteretic and moves over hours, so a second timer would guard nothing. Only a *measured* recovery re-arms it, so a canyon that withdraws the trend cannot turn one front into two banners. The pending banner and the arming both survive a run boundary, because the sky did not reset when the runner pressed stop.

**The page states the measurement and names the limit.** Hero is the signed change over the window — signed always, because the sign *is* the reading — with the trend word, the absolute reduced pressure, and the span the fit actually covers (a tendency over 55 minutes and one over three hours are different claims, and the window thins whenever the reference lapses). The closing row reads `TENDENCY NOT FORECAST`, in the register [§ 373](#373-sleep-station-mode-computes-the-nap-from-the-race-refuses-to-guess-at-it-and-does-not-claim-to-wake-anyone)'s `WATCH CANNOT WAKE YOU` established: a word like STORM invites a runner to read a forecast off it, and there is no forecast on this device — only what the barometer has already done.

**Refused: a runner-tunable threshold.** Garmin offers 2–6 mb and it would have been three more lines. The 4 hPa centre is a constant nobody here has validated against a real front, and letting a runner tune a number whose centre is unverified is guessing twice. The wire field carries a threshold so the capability exists the moment the bench has something to tune against, and the phone-side control that would expose it is deliberately not built. Also refused, and for the older reason: **forecast sync stays deferred**, which is what keeps this feature honest — the watch reports a measurement it took, never a prediction someone else made.

**The wire cost is a version bump nothing about the layout required.** `SET1` v7's `flags3` had six free bits, so the storm threshold could have ridden one silently. It does not, because an unknown presence bit is how `decode` tells a corrupt push from a newer one, and that only holds while a version names exactly one field set — so v8 it is, the frozen v7 golden vector keeps decoding, and a v7-stamped frame carrying the v8 bit is refused whole. One field, two sinks, and the second only on an arm: the alert engine takes the on/off, the tracker takes the threshold its own plausibility guard vets, and a disarm leaves the page classifying at whatever it had, because switching a banner off is not a recalibration.

**The page cost is the 41st built-in, and it moves no published ceiling.** Re-running § 289's BFS at 41 gives symmetric worst **7** and forward-only worst **10** — both unchanged, since the symmetric one stepped at 44 and the forward one at 42 — with the averages moving 4.25 → 4.2927, 5.55 → 5.6585 and 10.0 → 10.2439. With the four composed-screen seats the ring is 45, past the 7→8 step at 44 that [§ 364](#364-a-composed-screens-empty-slot-shows-its-unfed-class-and-the-cycle-flash-radio-and-phone-rails-land-with-it) already recorded, and 45 does not step it again. The page's presence bit is "a reduced pressure can be stated", so an indoor or reference-less watch never meets it.

**Sim-verified**, for exactly what the scenario names: the tracker withholds a tendency until a third of its window is banked, reads a still atmosphere as `Steady` inside 0.5 hPa, reaches `Storm` past the armed threshold under a scripted sea-level fall, raises exactly one banner for it, and the page enters the cycle and renders. Verified to fail as well as pass (the circular-reference mutation above). What it cannot assert is the climb-versus-front separation itself — the firmware's altitude reference comes from the NMEA fixture, which the harness cannot ramp independently of the barometer, so an in-sim "climb" is a baro ramp against a flat GPS altitude, which *is* weather as far as any correct implementation can tell. That separation stays host-tested. And § 82 is unchanged: nothing here has executed on silicon.

## 377. The watch's privacy gap was half the size the roadmap claimed, and `privacy.rs` staying unwired is the correct answer, not the outstanding work

**Date:** 2026-07-31

The roadmap's "Privacy posture for the watch" bullet read: *"Watch records GPS, HR, biometrics. The rest of the product takes data minimization + retention + export seriously; the watch inherits nothing yet."* Read against the code, "nothing" is wrong in both directions — some of it was already right and undocumented, and the part everyone would reach for first is a thing that must **not** be built. The inventory, the rules, and the deferred items now live in [`docs/custom_watch/privacy.md`](../custom_watch/privacy.md); this entry records the three judgements behind it.

**Already right, and now written down rather than accidental.** The GATT data plane has been fail-closed against unpaired peers since [§ 285](#285-run-store-v2-byte-15-becomes-a-record-tag-laps-interleave-with-points-and-a-full-slot-decimates-instead-of-truncating-the-threkir-gatt-service-is-encrypted-only-with-one-persisted-bond) — all seven characteristics carry `security = "justworks"`, so run tracks and config pushes never cross an unencrypted link. The ICE card is deliberately readable without authentication, and its exposure is bounded to exactly that: it is a face on the display, never a characteristic, never in the run blob, and its hand-written `defmt::Format` prints `blank`/`set` and never a field. And a watch-synced run inherits export, deletion and zone-clipping **for free**, because it lands through `runFromWatchPayload` → `api.saveRun` as an ordinary `runs` row with an ordinary Storage blob. No new table means the Art 20 export guard already covers it and `delete-account`'s bucket drain already reaches it. The rule that falls out is for the future, not for today: any data class the watch invents later must arrive with an owner FK and a cascade or an explicit drain.

**`privacy.rs` is dormant on purpose, and wiring it would be the bug.** The port has zero callers, which reads as an unfinished job and is not one. [§ 33](#33-privacy-zones-live-in-user_settings-clipping-is-client-side-nearby-leak-is-a-known-v1-gap) makes clipping a **read-time, viewer-keyed** transform precisely because a write-time clip is destructive — a runner who later turns a zone off can never recover the trace it ate — so the durable track is stored raw and `clip_track_for_user` runs when the viewer is not the owner. The phone recorder evaluates no zones at all. The watch's only egress is to the one phone it is bonded to, which is its owner's, so a watch that stores and syncs a raw track is *consistent with* the model; clipping there would mutilate the run before its owner had ever seen it. Two facts pin it: `WatchSettings` carries no zone list, so the device cannot learn where home is even if something wanted to clip, and § 370 already drew the boundary from the other side — a course pushed to a non-owner's wrist is clipped, because "the radio is just another way out of the app". The trigger that earns `privacy.rs` a call site is tier-2 live spectator tracking, where forwarding `link::status_frame` turns a 1 Hz position stream into a **broadcast to non-owners** — and § 33's `live_run_pings` precedent is explicit that a broadcast drops in-zone fixes *at the source*, because a downstream filter cannot unsend. On that path the watch is the source. Keeping the dormant port is therefore cheaper than deleting it.

**The real gap was the log stream, and it is fixed.** `gps.rs` logged latitude and longitude on every published fix, so the defmt/RTT stream reconstructed the whole run; `hr.rs` logged raw bpm change-gated, which is a biometric time series; `hr_strap.rs` logged the strap's BLE address, a stable identifier following one wearer. A defmt stream is not a private channel — it goes wherever the cable, the CI artifact or the bug report goes — and the repo already treats this class as a real finding for its server tiers (`/audit/pii-in-logs`), a sweep whose scope had never included this firmware. A stock build now logs fix *quality* (speed, satellites) and pulse *presence*, which is what those chains are actually debugged against. The values sit behind `log-personal-data`, **default off**, following the crate's existing invertible-feature convention. `bin/watch-sim.sh` enables it and nothing else does: the sim's coordinates are the synthetic `bench_jog` rectangle with no wearer behind them, and `sim/ci_smoke.py` asserts on the logged fix and BPM, so the sim-verified rails are untouched rather than weakened to accommodate the fix. The bench build keeps it off — `bin/watch-flash.sh` forwards cargo args, so debugging position maths on your own wrist is a deliberate opt-in.

**What is deliberately still owed, and why it is not in this change.** The largest gap is that **no wearer can erase their own data from the device**: there is no factory reset, no clear-all-runs, and no wipe. `Waypoints::clear()` exists with no caller; the ICE card can be cleared only by a phone push; the bond and the run slots cannot be cleared at all. A lost, stolen or resold watch cannot be sanitised by the person who wore it. The primitives are all present and this is tier-1-sized work, but the affordance is a settings-menu row plus a destructive-action confirm, which moves the menu's row count and therefore the published press-cost model in [`navigation.md`](../custom_watch/navigation.md) — it is a navigation change as much as a privacy one, and it belongs in that lane. Separately and deliberately **not** done: erasing a run when the phone marks it synced. `mark_synced_if_complete` fires when the phone has *pulled* the bytes, but the phone then queues them to disk and uploads later, retrying across sign-ins; a pull is not durability, and erasing at pull would delete the only surviving copy of a run whose upload had not landed. Preferring a synced run as the eviction victim is the right strength. Retention on the device is otherwise a **capacity** bound and not a clock — four run slots, eight waypoints, newest-wins — and `SlotDir::forget` drops a directory entry rather than bytes; the doc says so plainly rather than implying a policy exists.

**Rung: build-verified.** `clippy -D warnings` clean for `thumbv7em-none-eabihf` across the default, sim, `ble`, and `ble,log-personal-data` feature sets; `cargo fmt --all --check` clean; the 2365 host tests unchanged, since the change is confined to `app/`, which host tests exclude. **Nothing here is bench-verified — no hardware exists**, and per § 210 the BLE encryption this posture leans on can never be sim-verified either. This entry describes a research prototype with zero users; it is an inventory and a set of rules, **not a compliance claim**.

## 378. The watch gets a factory erase on the settings menu's far seat, guarded by the stop's two-press window, and it erases a flash *range* rather than a list of records

**Date:** 2026-07-31

[§ 377](#377-the-watchs-privacy-gap-was-half-the-size-the-roadmap-claimed-and-privacyrs-staying-unwired-is-the-correct-answer-not-the-outstanding-work) named the largest gap on [`privacy.md`](../custom_watch/privacy.md) and left it open: **no wearer could erase their own data from the device.** No factory reset, no clear-all-runs, no wipe; `Waypoints::clear()` had zero callers; the ICE card could be cleared only by a *phone* push, and the run slots and the BLE bond could not be cleared at all. A lost, stolen, or handed-on watch could not be sanitised by the person who had been wearing it. This closes it, on the device alone, which is the whole point — the wearer this is for does not have a phone to hand.

**The affordance is a seventh settings row, and where it sits is a computed answer, not a taste one.** § 351's real budget was never the row count but that no row a runner reaches for *mid-race* costs more than 4 presses, and § 372 kept that intact by seating BACKYARD at the 6-ring's far point. [`navigation.md`](../custom_watch/navigation.md) then predicted that "a seventh item would raise an existing row's cost". **That prediction was wrong, and it was wrong for an instructive reason: it assumed appending.** On a wrapping ring the cursor distance to index `k` is `min(k, n-k)`, so a 6-ring's distances are `[0,1,2,3,2,1]` — one far seat — while a 7-ring's are `[0,1,2,3,3,2,1]` — **two**. A seventh row can therefore take the *second* far seat without displacing the one already sitting on the first. Appending is the one placement that would have raised two rows' costs (RE-ZERO 2→3, MEDICAL ID 1→2), and it is also the *cheapest* seat on a wrapping ring — one BTN2 press from the cursor's home — which is precisely wrong for a wipe. ERASE goes in at **index 4**: every pre-existing row keeps its exact cursor distance (verified by a test that computes both rings from `ITEMS` rather than restating them), the value rows stay contiguous above the action rows, and the erase lands on the hardest seat in the menu to reach by accident. It costs 5 presses to arm and 6 to complete, against BACKYARD's 5 and every mid-race row's ≤ 4.

**The layout change § 372 predicted did have to happen, and it spends the last slack.** Six rows filled the 9-row panel exactly under a legend, a title and a blank spacer, so `MENU_TOP_ROW` moves 3 → 2 and the spacer is gone; `MENU_TOP_ROW + MENU_ITEMS == ROWS` is still pinned by a test. The list stays legible because every item row is indented two cells behind its cursor marker while the title is flush left, so the indentation does the separating the blank row did. An **eighth** row has nothing left to reclaim and needs § 333's row-scrolling window ported from the grid — stated here so the next person reads a design rather than rediscovering a wall.

**The confirm is the stop guard's, deliberately, and a hold was refused.** An erase is the second irreversible action on this device and the first already taught the runner a two-press dwell, so `erase::EraseGuard` is `StopGuard`'s shape and `ERASE_CONFIRM_WINDOW_S` *is* `STOP_CONFIRM_WINDOW_S` rather than a second number to learn. The other guarded-destructive idiom here is hold-to-open (the page grid's 0.5 s), and it cannot be used: the settings menu is an idle surface and **idle gestures are duration-stable** is a pinned navigation invariant — § 375 declined to split BTN2 by duration for exactly this reason, and a duration split inside an idle modal would be the first gesture to break it. So: right on the row arms, a second right inside the window wipes, and **every other press cancels** — a cursor step, a left press, the exit, the menu closing, or the window lapsing. The arm borrows the menu's single deadline slot while it is live (4 s beats 30 s), so it lapses *visibly*: the row goes back to `FACTORY ERASE` under the runner's thumb rather than standing as a prompt for a press that would now only re-arm. Both presses that resolve an arm change meaning — BTN1 stops being "edit right" and BTN4 stops being a bare exit — so § 337 says both must be read, and the legend row is **replaced** with `B1 ERASE    B4 CANCEL` rather than appended to. That is also what stops the arm being missed: one changed row of nine can be walked past, a changed chrome row cannot.

**What it clears, and the argument for each.** Run slots, waypoints, and the config record are the payload and need no argument. Three do.

- **The ICE card — cleared.** It is the only *third-party* personal data on the device: a next-of-kin's name and phone number, belonging to someone who never consented to anything and cannot be asked what the next holder should know. It is also special-category health data. The case against is real — a medic reads this off a collapsed runner — but it resolves cleanly: the erase is a six-press, confirmed, idle-only act nobody performs before a race by accident; the card is phone-authored and re-pushable in one action, so the recovery cost is one push against an unbounded exposure; and a wipe that left the medical record would make the wipe a lie, which is worse than no wipe at all, because a runner who believes they sanitised the watch stops checking.
- **The BLE bond — cleared.** The strongest case of the three, and the least obvious. A bond is not a stale record, it is a **live credential**: a watch that keeps it lets the previous owner's phone re-encrypt and read the *new* owner's runs and live position. Worse, `BondRecord` carries the peer's IRK, which resolves that phone's random addresses forever — so leaving it defeats the previous owner's own address privacy permanently, and is strictly worse than leaving a run behind. Re-pairing costs one phone-side action and loses nothing, since the runs are gone anyway. The framing settles it: this is a *factory erase*, one action with one meaning, not a "clear my runs" that happens to keep the link. If a runs-only clear is ever wanted it is a second row and it should be argued on its own.
- **The pushed course and workout — cleared.** RAM-only, so they die at the next power cycle regardless, but they are drawn on pages a next holder would page straight to, and a course is *where the runner planned to be*.

**The recorder is replaced whole rather than cleared field by field, and that is the same rule the flash side follows.** `plan_factory_erase` returns a *range* — the config page abuts the run region, so the wipe is one contiguous span rather than a list of records a later record could be left off — and its test checks every published record offset and every slot against that range rather than against a copy of the arithmetic. `Event::Erase` does the RAM analogue with `Recorder::new()`, taking the waypoints, the pushed max and resting HR, the pacer goal, the gear, the roadbook and fuel plan, the curated page mask, the auto-lap rung and the backyard arm in one line. **Erase by default, not by allowlist**: a personal field added to either side next year is covered without anyone remembering to extend a list. Safe only because the menu is idle-only, so there is never a live run to throw away — which is also why the erase arm sits in the idle branch of the record task's select rather than as a `try_changed` at the loop head: that branch has no ticker, and in Expedition mode the next fix is a minute away, which is a minute of a marked stash and a medical ID still on the panel of a watch its owner was told is erased.

**It erases bytes, not directory entries.** `SlotDir::forget` drops a slot's entry and leaves the blob where it was written — right for a failed write, wrong for a wipe. The adversary a factory erase exists for is whoever holds the device next, and nothing in this workspace enables APPROTECT, so a debug probe reads exactly what the directory was hiding. Stated precisely, because the claim invites over-reading: the erase returns every address the firmware wrote to `0xFF`, and this store addresses pages directly with no wear-levelling or copy-back layer to leave a shadow copy elsewhere. It is **not** a claim against charge-remnant recovery on a decapped die, and it does nothing about a probe attached *before* the erase — that is encryption at rest, which tier 1 does not have and `privacy.md` still lists as deferred.

**What it deliberately does not clear.** The **timezone offset** stays: a UTC offset is shared by a continent rather than identifying anyone, it is RAM-only and dies at the power cycle the erase is a prelude to, and `Watch::clear()` does not wake receivers — so writing `0` would be the only propagating option and would make the home clock claim `LOCAL` while showing UTC. A false label is worse than a retained offset. A **live BLE connection** is not torn down: the durable bond is gone, so the next boot has no peer, and the only window is until power-cycle, during which the wearer is holding the watch. Tearing a SoftDevice link down from the button task would need a new `ble`-only seam that can be neither host- nor sim-verified (§ 210), which is the one subsystem this project holds to build-verified-only. The **compiled-in sim course** survives, correctly: it is a fixture, not the runner's data.

**The erase is the one action row that stays open**, where RE-ZERO and MEDICAL ID both close and hand the screen to something that answers. Here the menu *is* the answer: `GNSS MODE` back at its default rung, `PROFILE` back to `--`, `BACKYARD` back to `OFF`, all on the screen the runner pressed from. That is § 351's own confirmation rule ("the row re-rendering with the new value is the confirmation") applied to a whole menu, and it says more than a six-character banner could. It also needs no new `HeroBand` variant or banner precedence, which a transient idle banner would have.

**Rung: host-tested and sim-verified, and specifically not more.** 11 new host tests (2407 → 2418, 0 failed) over the guard's arm / confirm / expiry / cancel / clock-skew behaviour, the row's placement cost against the 6-ring, the armed rendering, and the erase range's coverage of every record offset and slot. `cargo fmt --all --check` clean; `clippy -D warnings` clean for `thumbv7em-none-eabihf` on the workspace default, `-p app --no-default-features --features ble`, and the sim feature set. The `idle` Renode scenario walks it: one press arms and changes the panel, stepping off the row and back leaves the next press arming again rather than confirming, and only the second adjacent press wipes — after which the GNSS mode falls back from the `Expedition ~220h` the scenario itself walked the ladder to, down to `Performance 1s ~110h`. **What the sim does not earn is the part that matters most**: Renode's flash is plain memory behind an SVD-derived NVMC model that answers `READY` and swallows the `ERASEPAGE` write, so the firmware reports a success over an emulator that changed no byte. **That four run slots and a config page actually read back `0xFF`, and that a re-paired phone is genuinely a re-pair, are bench items** ([`quality_standards.md`](../custom_watch/quality_standards.md) step 7) — and the bond half can never be sim-verified at all (§ 210). Nothing here is bench-verified, because no hardware exists.

## 379. The app stores are the distribution channel — a website APK is Play's own artifact, and iOS has no such door

**Date:** 2026-07-31

The question was whether the marketing site should hand out the app directly, on the reasoning that Settings already carries an update button so a downloaded build could keep itself current. The reasoning is inverted: that button *is* the store.

**The update button is Google Play.** `settings_licenses_screen.dart`'s `defaultCheckUpdate` wraps `in_app_update`, which is Play Core's `AppUpdateManager` — it asks Play whether a newer version of `com.threkir.app` is available for *this installation*, and Play performs the download and install. Play has no record of an installation it did not make, so on a sideloaded build the check throws and the L4 catch fails closed to `LicenseUpdateStatus.unavailable`; the screen hides the row rather than surfacing an error. The failure banner already says where the update lives. A direct download therefore does not give a user *easier* updates, it gives them *none* — they are frozen at whatever they downloaded until they think to come back. Every distribution channel needs an update channel, and the only one built is the store's.

**iOS is not a choice we get to make.** There is no supported way to hand a general user an `.ipa` from a website. Ad Hoc distribution caps at 100 devices a year and needs each device's UDID registered in advance. TestFlight is a beta channel — builds expire after 90 days, external testers sit behind a review, and it tops out at 10,000 — useful before launch, not a distribution route. The Apple Developer Enterprise Program is for an organisation's own employees, and Apple revokes certificates used to distribute publicly. The EU's DMA opened Web Distribution in iOS 17.4, but it demands notarization, an EU-established entity, two continuous years of Developer Program membership in good standing, and an app that saw over a million first annual installs in the EU the previous year. None of those describe us. **The site's iOS affordance is a link to the App Store**, and during beta a public TestFlight link — nothing else is on the table, so nothing else gets designed for.

**The Android signing key is a one-shot decision, and it is already made: Google holds it.** Android identity is `applicationId` plus signing certificate. Same package name under a different certificate is not an update — the install fails `INSTALL_FAILED_UPDATE_INCOMPATIBLE` and the user must uninstall to switch channels, taking the local run store and any queued unsynced runs with it. That is the failure this entry exists to prevent. We ship an `.aab` signed with an upload key and let Play App Signing re-sign with a distribution key that never leaves Google (`apps/mobile_android/deployment.md § Signing setup`). Play does allow an enrolling developer to supply their own app signing key instead, which would let CI produce a Play-compatible APK directly — **rejected**, because an upload key that is lost is resettable through a multi-day Play Console flow while a self-held *app signing* key that is lost ends the listing's ability to ever update again. Trading a recoverable failure for an unrecoverable one to save a download is a bad trade.

**So a website APK is not built, it is fetched.** Because Google holds the distribution key, no artifact this repo's CI produces can ever carry the signature an installed Play build expects — the note in `docs/ops/releasing.md` about a locally-built release APK installing as a second app is the same fact seen from the developer's side. The only signature-compatible artifact is **the universal APK Play itself generates**, downloaded from the Play Console's App Bundle Explorer for the release in question and hosted as-is. Doing it that way buys the property that matters: the certificate matches by construction, so a user who sideloads and later installs from Play gets an in-place upgrade with their data intact and Play adopts the app from then on. The sideload becomes an on-ramp rather than a cul-de-sac. Any other artifact makes the two channels permanently separate apps that happen to share an icon.

**A direct APK is a secondary channel, deliberately.** It serves pre-release testers, de-Googled Android devices, and regions where Play is awkward. It is not the headline call to action, because a channel with no update path should not be the one most users take, and because Google is phasing in developer verification for sideloaded apps on certified Android devices through 2026 — sideloading survives, but as a registered-developer route, and betting the acquisition funnel on it would be betting on someone else's policy.

**Purchases do not cross the channel boundary, and entitlements do.** Play Billing exists only for apps installed from Play, StoreKit only for App Store installs. A sideloaded build has no billing service, so `purchases_flutter` cannot complete a purchase there at all — the site APK is structurally a free-tier build. Entitlements are the other way around: RevenueCat resolves them against the app user id, so identifying by the Supabase user means someone who subscribed on Play keeps Pro in a sideloaded build, because that read is a server call rather than a store call. Buying is store-bound; *having bought* is not. Adding a Stripe web-checkout path to close the gap would split billing across two systems with different renewal and refund semantics, and is not proposed here.

**What is explicitly not built.** Self-update for a sideloaded build. It would need a version-manifest endpoint, an APK download, the `REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES` permission, and a system-installer hand-off the user confirms each time — and Play's Device and Network Abuse policy forbids an app distributed *through Play* from updating itself by any mechanism other than Play. That makes it a product flavour, not a feature: the Play build must not contain the self-updater. There are no product flavours today (one `applicationId`, one build, per `apps/mobile_android/deployment.md`), so this is real work behind a real policy line, and it stays unbuilt until the sideload channel has users who justify it.

## 380. Falling behind the next cutoff raises a banner — once per excursion, re-armed only by a measured recovery

**Date:** 2026-07-31

The CUT page has projected on/tight/behind at the next cutoff since § 215, but the verdict lived only on that page: a runner parked on Pace or Climb learned they were missing the race's own clock only if they happened to page past. The five-persona UX hunt (2026-07-31, `reviews/persona-watch-*-uxhunt.md`) flagged it as the highest-severity alert gap, so `watch_core::alerts` grows a `CutoffBehind` arm: when [`CutoffEtaStatus`] falls to `Behind` the engine raises `! CUTOFF` — carrying nothing, because the margin and the still-sufficient pace are on the CUT page and the banner's job is to send the runner there. Three placements were decided, not defaulted. **Rank:** it leads the re-queued class (above storm, below zone/bell/pace) — like storm there is no later reminder, but the cutoff arrives sooner than the front; it stays *below* the correct-it-now trio because it is a projection off recent pace, not the race director's clock. **Hysteresis:** once per excursion, re-armed only by a MEASURED `On`/`Tight` — `Unknown` neither fires nor re-arms, storm's canyon rule pointed the other way: a stale fix is the watch losing sight of the runner, not the runner catching up, and re-arming on it would turn one canyon into two banners. **Lifetime:** unlike the storm pair it is cleared at the run boundary — a cutoff is a property of the run's course, not of the world between runs. There is no arming setting: cutoff legs on the pushed course are the opt-in, and a course without them never fires.

**Amended 2026-08-01:** the "leads the re-queued class" claim above was true when written and is now stale — § 381 inserted off-course *above* cutoff the same day, and the shipped order is off-course → cutoff → storm → eat → drink. Cutoff leads everything below off-course; § 381's wording is the accurate one. Recorded rather than edited in place so the ranking's history stays legible.

## 381. The off-course verdict leaves the Nav page — and its release is the engine's one affirmation

**Date:** 2026-07-31

The 40 m / 20 m off-course hysteresis has rendered a steady `OFF COURSE` band over the Nav page's map panel since the course work landed, but only there: a runner parked on GAP or Climb in fog learned about a wrong turn by paging to Nav or not at all — two of the five persona hunts (2026-07-31) surfaced it independently, and `app/src/tasks/nav.rs`'s `warn!` reaches nobody on a wrist. The verdict now rides the recorder like the turn cue already does (`Snapshot::nav_off_course`, fed beside `set_route_position`) and `watch_core::alerts` edge-detects it into two banners. `! OFF CRS` (the `CRS1` frame's own abbreviation — the full phrase overflows the ten-cell band) fires once per excursion and leads the re-queued class, above cutoff: every unseen minute banks wrong-way distance, and a wrong turn invalidates the cutoff math anyway. Its release fires `ON COURSE` — the engine's one affirmation and the one banner without the `!` prefix, because on this face `!` means *act* and an all-clear asks for nothing; it sits in the dropped class (a stale all-clear after the runner drifted off again is a lie the Nav page would contradict) but leads it, ahead of the milestones. The snapshot field is tri-state: `None` (no course, no projection yet) clears the edge detector silently, so a course swap or a lost projection is absence of knowledge — it neither fires the affirmation nor leaves a stale excursion armed against a freshly-pushed course. The Nav page's own steady band is unchanged; the banners are for the other forty pages.

## 382. The waypoint hold answers on the screen that asked — a wrapping counter per outcome, not the store's count

**Date:** 2026-07-31

§ 357's BTN5 hold persisted the mark and said nothing: success was a flash write plus a defmt line, and a refused mark (no position anchor yet) was indistinguishable on the wrist from a hold that didn't register — the navigator persona hunt (2026-07-31) ranked it the worst feedback gap on the device. The recorder now carries two wrapping event counters in the snapshot, `waypoint_mark_seq` and `waypoint_refuse_seq`, and the alert engine edge-detects them into `WPT SAVED` (an affirmation, un-`!`-prefixed like `ON COURSE`) and `! NO FIX` (the cause, not the failure — the fix is to wait for one). Counters and not [`Snapshot::waypoint_count`], because the eight-slot newest-wins store saturates: the ninth mark changes the count not at all and must still be answered. They take the workout edges' precedence — blocked only by a zone banner or the corral whistle, displacing fuel (which re-queues) — because the runner is looking at the screen at exactly the moment they held the button; a blocked one is dropped, not owed, since a confirmation shown late confirms the wrong thing. The engine baselines both counters on the first sample of a run instead of firing, so marks banked before this run (or before a reboot restored the store) can't replay as a banner at the start line.

## 383. The standing fuel-overdue marker clears on a held Fuel page, not a fly-by

**Date:** 2026-07-31

§ 346's always-visible fuel-overdue tag exists because a heads-down runner misses the 8 s banner — but the tag treated `page == Fuel` on any frame as the acknowledgement, so ordinary ring-paging (one second over the Fuel page on the way to Nav) silently defeated the one backstop built for exactly that miss; the desert persona hunt (2026-07-31) ranked it the surface's worst safety-UX defect. The acknowledgement is now a **dwell**: `alerts::FuelAckDwell` (pure, display-side, host-tested like the tracker it feeds) reports the runner attending to fuel only once the Fuel page has been the current page for `FUEL_ACK_DWELL_S = 3` continuous seconds, and leaving the page resets the clock — three fly-bys are three misses, not an acknowledgement. Three seconds because the alternatives were worse: no button on the run view is free to be a confirm key (§ 350 spent them all), and a longer dwell starts punishing the runner who genuinely stopped to read their carry-out. The ui task's frames are event-driven rather than periodic, so the dwell measures against the frame clock and a late frame simply reads the threshold as already met.

## 384. The Fuel page's carry-out runs on the runner's pushed cadence, inverted through the units the reminders reduced through

**Date:** 2026-07-31

`SET1` v4 put the fuel cadences on the wire and the alert engine honoured them, but the Fuel page's carry-out math still built its plan from the temperate defaults (60 g/hr, 500 ml/hr) — a desert runner who tightened their drink cadence got faster reminders and an unchanged carry-out, two surfaces describing two different plans. The recorder now mirrors the same pushed intervals (`Recorder::set_fuel_intervals`, the engine's zero-is-ignored guard shape) and `fuel_snapshot` derives its hourly rates by **inverting the exact reduction** `alerts` used forward: one gel (`GEL_CARBS_G` = 25 g) per eat interval, one sip (`SIP_FLUID_ML` = 125 ml, newly named so the two directions share the constant) per drink interval. Inversion rather than a second pair of wire fields because it keeps one source of truth — the cadence — and makes disagreement between the reminders and the plan structurally impossible. The `heat_factor` half of the desert finding stays deliberately unbuilt: § 376's shape (no runner-facing threshold controls) and the § 24 rule both point the same way, and a runner raising their fluid cadence over `SET1` achieves the same outcome through the field that already exists. The sim's shortened bench cadences (30/45 s) are deliberately NOT mirrored into the recorder — they are harness arming for the alert rail, and a 15 L/hr Fuel page would be the sim lying about the product.

## 385. A signal void announces itself — and the pair lives in the dropped class, because the AUTO tag is the persistent truth

**Date:** 2026-07-31

§ 367 made a fix drought auto-pause the recorder and flip the corner tag to `AUTO` — but a tag is a state, not an event, and a heads-down runner reads it minutes and a kilometre of unrecorded moving later; the ultra persona hunt (2026-07-31) ranked the silence its #3 finding. The engine now edge-detects [`Snapshot::signal_lost`] into `! GPS LOST` and its release into `GPS BACK` (an affirmation, un-`!`-prefixed like `ON COURSE`). Both sit at the head of the **dropped** class rather than the re-queued one, deliberately: the tag carries the persistent truth on every run page, so a banner the slot swallows loses only the announcement — and a stale `GPS LOST` shown after the fixes returned would be the banner lying about the tag beside it. The edge detector is a plain bool, not the tri-state the off-course pair needed: `signal_lost` is always meaningful during a run and false at the start line, so there is no absence-of-knowledge state to model.

## 386. GAP joins the metric catalogue at byte 39 — and the phone's catalogue catches up to storm's 38

**Date:** 2026-07-31

The vert persona hunt's top finding: no surface on the watch puts live grade-adjusted pace in the 32x48 face — the Pace page's hero is the whole-run average with GAP demoted to an 8 px row, and `face::Metric` had no `Gap` variant, so a runner could not even compose it. Rather than re-heroing a shipped page (the PACE page's hero should be pace) or adding a 42nd built-in, GAP takes the § 364 route: `Metric::Gap` lands at wire byte 39 with the pace hero idiom (`M:SS`, `/KM`, `NeedDistance` when unfed), and a composed screen is how it reaches a hero slot — exactly what composed screens exist for. Closing the loop exposed a live wire drift: `StormDelta = 38` had landed firmware-side with the 2026-07-31 storm batch while the phone's `WatchMetric` catalogue still ended at 37, so a storm-delta slot was compose-able on no phone and the Dart wire-contract test pinned the stale count as correct. Both entries land together on both twins (with the six-locale editor labels), and the byte-map guards on each side now pin 39.

## 387. The page grid's name row carries a position counter — and the name wins the row when both cannot fit

**Date:** 2026-07-31

§ 333 turned the full-to-the-cell grid into a scrolling window, which took away the one thing a full grid gave for free: where you are in the list. The cursor row now reads `DASHBOARD        1/45` — the counter is the cursor's seat in the *enabled* ring, so a filtered mask shrinks both numbers honestly. It sits on the name row and not the legend row above it, because that row's staticness is a deliberate repaint invariant (it can never redraw, whatever the cursor). Two page names (`ELEVATION PROFILE`, `ADAPTIVE RE-PLAN`) cannot leave the counter its five cells plus a gap; there the name wins and the counter drops — the counter is orientation, the name is what the runner is about to jump to, and truncating the name to keep the number would invert that priority.

## 388. The nav panel labels its auto-zoom state — and only that state

**Date:** 2026-07-31

The § 350-era nav panel silently switches between two transforms an order of magnitude apart in metres-per-pixel: whole-course fit, and the runner-centred ~1.2 km auto-zoom window a long course forces. Nothing on the panel said which one a visible fork was being read through — the navigator persona's "is that fork 100 m or 2 km away" finding. `NavPanel` now exposes the `windowed` decision (host-tested with the rest of `nav_map`) and the render layer draws a 1x `ZOOM` label at the panel's bottom-right when it is set, after the polyline so the word survives a dense breadcrumb. Only the zoomed state is labelled: whole-course is the default the panel has always meant, and a label on both states is a label on neither.

## 389. A held GAP carries `~` on the text rows — and never in a hero, because the numeral face drops glyphs it lacks

**Date:** 2026-07-31

The GAP estimator's power-hike hold (§ 24-ported from the mobile field) shows the last above-gate effort-pace for up to ten sub-gate updates so a headwall crawl reads its recent effort instead of `--:--` — but the face rendered the held value indistinguishably from a live sample, so ten updates of yesterday's pace could pass as now. The snapshot now carries `gap_held` (read off the estimator *after* the same tick's sampling call — struct literals evaluate in source order, and the flag describes that call's answer) and the two GAP text rows (the Pace glance's `GAP  4:52~ /KM`, the Dashboard's `NOW/GAP` pair) mark a held value with a trailing `~`, the race predictor's own approximate glyph. The mark deliberately never reaches a hero band: the 32x48 numeral face has no `~` and silently renders glyphs it lacks as nothing — the § 364 bug class — so a "marked" hero would read as an unmarked one, which is worse than no mark.

**Amended 2026-08-01 — the rationale above is wrong, and it cost us a bug.** A `~` can never reach the numeral face to be dropped, because both hero paths gate on the glyph set *before* choosing a face: `numeral_hero` (`ui_frame.rs:117`) is true only when every byte is in `NUMERAL_GLYPHS` (`0123456789:-.+`), and `slot_band` / `hero_band` fall back to `TextHero` otherwise — where the 8x16 font covers printable ASCII 32..=126, `~` (126) included and inked. So marking a hero **demotes it in size**; it never silently drops the glyph. "Never in a hero" remains defensible as a *legibility* preference, but not as glyph-safety, and stated as glyph-safety it reads as a correctness constraint that must not be touched. It duly steered a later reviewer away from a real honesty bug: the composed data screens SC1–SC4 render GAP through `metric_hero`, which carried no mark at all, so a held estimate passed as live on every slot — including slot 0, the largest placement and a `Single` layout's only one. That is now marked (§ 411), accepting the size demotion on the grounds that a held number at full size that reads as live is wrong, whereas a smaller one is merely smaller. The root cause of the miss was neither doc nor code but a test bound: three catalogue-walking guards in `face.rs` — among them `every_value_a_slot_can_hold_lands_in_a_face_that_can_draw_it`, the guard for exactly this class — were hard-coded `1..=37u8` while the catalogue had reached 39, silently exempting `storm_delta` and `gap`. They now derive the set from `Metric::from_byte`, as does the sibling bound in `screens.rs`.

## 390. The nav position marker gets a one-pixel cleared halo — a fork must not swallow the runner

**Date:** 2026-07-31

The position marker was a 5 px cross drawn with the same 1-bit ink as the course polyline, and the place a navigator most needs it — a fork — is exactly where course segments converge on the runner's position and the cross melts into the line-work. `draw_nav_panel` now clears a one-pixel ring around the cross before inking it, clipped to the panel band so the halo can't blank the title or GPS rows beside it. A cleared ring is the only contrast a 1-bit reflective panel has to spend; it costs nothing on open trail (clearing blank pixels) and buys the marker back at every junction.

## 391. Sim scenarios that need a quiet alert slot drop the canned course — `--no-alerts` cannot silence data-driven arms

**Date:** 2026-07-31

The `storm` scenario failed on PR #656 and the failure was structural, not flaky: its "one front, one banner" and bannerless-dump assertions rest on `--no-alerts` leaving the alert slot empty, but the § 380/§ 381 cutoff and off-course arms alert on **data presence** — the canned `sim-course`'s legs and cutoff schedule — not on any sim setter, so `--no-alerts` cannot reach them. bench_jog leaves the course every lap, and each workout edge that displaced the OffCourse banner re-queued it, a handoff chain in which `record: alert cleared` never fires. The fix is scenario isolation, not engine damping: `bin/watch-sim.sh` grows `--no-course` (drops the `sim-course` feature) and the `storm` + `workout` scenarios take it — neither asserts anything the course feeds. The engine's re-queue semantics stay: on hardware, a runner off course during a workout *should* keep being told, and the `alerts`/`pages`/`terrain` scenarios still exercise the full chain with the course loaded.

## 392. The nav task gates its fixes on physical plausibility — a multipath teleport must not touch the off-course latch

**Date:** 2026-07-31

The recorder has always rejected a fix implying an impossible speed before it could move the track, but the nav task consumed the raw fix channel unguarded — so one canyon-bounce position 500 m off the trail could fire `! OFF CRS` (since § 381, on every page at once) or, worse, clear a live alert while the runner stood exactly as lost as they were. `nav_project::FixGate` now fronts the projection with the recorder's own throttled-mode rule: the ceiling is `MAX_SPEED_MPS × dt` from the last *accepted* fix, a rejected outlier never moves the anchor, and a genuine relocation (a signal void crossed on foot) self-heals as `dt` grows the ceiling past any real displacement. A zero `dt` is a timestamp duplicate and fails closed. The gate deliberately survives a course swap — it judges the position stream, not the projection, and the runner did not teleport because the phone pushed a new route. The 40 m/20 m hysteresis stays what it always was: protection against *jitter*, which this gate does not touch.

## 393. The fuel cadence gets the plausibility bound every other arm already had — and it lands at the push seam, not the setter

**Date:** 2026-07-31

Distance, time, pace, QNH and timezone pushes all pass a plausibility window before they can arm anything; the fuel drink/eat cadence — the arm that *re-queues itself forever* — decoded a raw `u32` off the wire with only a zero-check. A one-second interval would win the alert slot's arbitration nearly every tick and starve the GPS-lost, off-course and cutoff banners for the whole race. The bound (60 s to 4 h, per arm) lives in `settings_apply`'s fan-out rather than `AlertEngine::set_fuel_intervals`, because the bench sim legitimately arms 30/45 s cadences through that setter so a reminder fires within a bench run — the seam guards the *phone*, not the caller. Out-of-range drops rather than clamps: a clamp invents a cadence the runner never chose and chirps it all race, a drop leaves the last truthful state standing; and a bad arm costs only itself — its sibling still lands.

## 394. The GAP hold budget scales with the GNSS fix interval — ten ticks of a frozen speed is not ten seconds of evidence

**Date:** 2026-07-31

The § 389 power-hike hold spent `GAP_HOLD_WINDOW` (ten) sub-gate updates before blanking, but the updates are the UI's 1 Hz ticks while the speed they judge freezes for a whole fix interval — 60 s in Expedition, the mode built for exactly the multi-day efforts where the hold matters. The budget exhausted ~10 s into every gap and GAP blanked for the remaining ~50 s of a genuine headwall crawl, defeating the mechanism's whole purpose. `gap_hold_ticks(fix_interval_s) = GAP_HOLD_WINDOW + (fix_interval_s − 1)`: at 1 Hz the term vanishes and the historical ten ticks are preserved bit-for-bit; at 60 s the hold now spans one full inter-fix gap plus the original grace past the next fix that could refresh or retire it. The cadence rides the existing `Recorder::set_fix_interval_s` seam and survives the estimator's reset — it is device config, not run state. The § 389 honesty mark is untouched: a held value still says `~` for the whole held span, and a genuine stop (a fix at ≤ walk floor) still blanks at once.

## 395. The breadcrumb thins by shape, not by index parity — a switchback apex must survive its own halving

**Date:** 2026-07-31

TrackBack's buffer halved by keeping `points[0, 2, 4…]`, and pure index parity knows nothing about geometry: on a switchbacked climb it could drop the apex vertices and render a straight chord across the terrain the switchback exists to avoid — on the one page a benighted runner is told to trust. `Trackback::thin` now reduces through `route_simplify`'s priority-DP engine (`simplify_to_budget`, the same budgeted Douglas-Peucker the § 370 course cap uses, generalised over a deviation metric so the breadcrumb's planar metre offsets and the course's geographic points share one loop), with a widest-gap midpoint fallback when a featureless straight gives the geometry no signal — so the halving contract (exact count, doubled nominal spacing, unchanged trigger cadence) holds everywhere. On the hairpin fixture the parity chord measured ~19 m of cross-track error; the shape-aware thin stays under 2 m and keeps every detected apex.

## 396. The factory erase names the unsynced runs it would take — a settings reset and irrecoverable race data do not share one shrug

**Date:** 2026-07-31

§ 378's `ERASE ALL?` confirm guarded the wipe with the stop's two-press window but never said that "all" includes finished runs the phone has not pulled — conflating a settings reset with permanent race-data loss under one undifferentiated prompt. While armed with `N > 0` unsynced runs, the menu's title row now yields to `N RUNS NOT SYNCED`; with everything synced (or nothing stored) the prompt is byte-identical to before, because a warning that always shows is a warning nobody reads. The stake rides the *title* row since the armed item row's cells cannot carry both the count and the commit key (§ 337 forbids dropping the key), and replacing a chrome row is already how this arm announces itself. The count comes from a new `SlotDir::unsynced_count()` (finished and not yet pulled — a live checkpoint and a synced slot are both excluded), published change-gated from every directory mutation path. No third press was added.

## 397. The zones and pace pages say whether their over-effort alert ever armed — a phone-only arm needs an on-watch witness

**Date:** 2026-07-31

The zone-ceiling and pace-band alerts arm exclusively from a `SET1` push and defaulted to off, and no surface said which state the watch was in — so a phone-less runner (this device's stated norm) could race a hundred miles believing an alert stood guard that was never armed.
