The engine's *validated* arms now mirror into the snapshot (`Recorder::set_alert_arms`, fed from the engine's own getters at the settings fan-out, never from wire values — one owner, no second interpretation) and the pages that own the metrics render them: the Zones page's label row carries `CEIL Z4` / `CEIL --` in its slack cells, the Pace glance's label row `BAND ON` / `BAND --` ending clear of the state tag's seat. Armed pace shows `ON` rather than the corridor: the row has nine free cells, and a bare range with no word naming it reads as a second pace. `--` rather than a reason line because these are absent *values* inside fed rows — the unfed vocabulary's own boundary — and the arm's only cure is the phone either way.

## 398. The Nav page trades its info row for a back-to-course bearing while alerting — the marker has left the panel by the time the latch trips

**Date:** 2026-07-31

The whole-course fit keeps 2 px of margin and the off-course latch trips at 40 m, so going off far enough to alarm reliably pushes the position marker off the fitted panel — the map loses the runner at the exact moment the runner most needs it, and `NavStatus` carried nothing directional to fall back on. The projection already computes the perpendicular foot on the course, so `project_fix` now stamps `back_to_course_deg` — the absolute great-circle bearing from the fix toward that snapped point, through the same `initial_bearing_deg` + 16-wind sectors the Waypoint and Back-to-start BRG rows render, so the three pages speak one compass (tier 1 has no magnetometer; absolute winds are what a stopped, lost runner can act on). While the latch alerts, the Nav info row becomes `BACK TO CRS W 120M`; quiet, it keeps the along/off pair, because when the runner is on course the map is the story. The bearing gates on the trackback's 5 m stability floor — under it the projection foot wobbles with GPS jitter and a bearing would be noise dressed as guidance. `marker_px`'s refusal to clamp stays: an edge-pinned marker lies about where the runner is, a bearing does not.

## 399. An eviction that takes an unsynced run says so — a banner at the loss, a standing row at the pressure before it

**Date:** 2026-07-31

`SlotDir::victim`'s all-unsynced fallback evicted the oldest finished run with a defmt warn as its only witness — invisible on a phone-less multi-day race, where losing a banked run is losing the race's record. Two surfaces now carry it. The banner: eviction is detected *before* the reservation (`next_write_evicts_unsynced()` — the reservation's own entry is finished-and-unsynced, so no after-the-fact count can see the victim), rides `Snapshot::run_lost_seq` through the § 382 wrapping-counter seam, and fires `! RUN LOST` once per eviction in the re-queued class's bottom rung — below off-course / cutoff / CRS FAIL / storm, which all still have a decision to make, above fuel only because a reminder comes round again and a lost run never does. A stop-time commit's eviction lands after the engine reset and is deliberately adopted silently at the next start: the between-runs story belongs to the second surface. The row: at three of four slots unsynced — the point where a new run's second checkpoint *must* evict, pinned by `three_unsynced_runs_are_one_start_from_a_loss` — the idle home face carries `N RUNS NOT SYNCED`, rendered by the same `erase_stake_row` the § 396 prompt uses (one vocabulary, no third copy), with the § 331 RECOVERED marker's restraint: a standing tag, never a modal, retired the moment a phone pull drains the store.

## 400. A rejected course push raises `! CRS FAIL` — the watch is still navigating the OLD course, and only a banner can say so

**Date:** 2026-07-31

A phone re-pushes a corrected course mid-race; it fails CRC or decode; the ble task warned into defmt and left `state::COURSE` untouched — so the runner navigates a course they believe they replaced, with the Nav page cheerfully rendering the stale line. All three failure sites (short chunk, rejected reassembly, decode fail) now bump a reconnect-surviving counter published on `state::COURSE_REJECTS`, mirrored into the snapshot and fired by the engine once per rejection with None-baseline adoption. Precedence sits between cutoff and storm: a cutoff is the race being lost *now*, a stale course gets expensive at the next fork — minutes away, sooner than a front. A successful push stays silent; the Nav page already re-announces the loaded course, and a confirmation banner would teach runners to wait for one that failure also never showed.

## 401. Bond *formation* is gated by two handlers, not one — and `advertise_pairable` stays, because in this crate it is not an on-air property

**Date:** 2026-08-01

An audit found the GATT data plane correctly fail-closed after bonding while nothing gated forming a bond: `can_bond` returned `true` unconditionally and the advertise loop always called `advertise_pairable`, so any central in radio range could Just-Works-pair at any moment for the life of the device, read every stored run (the wearer's location history), write settings/course/workout, and evict the owner's bond. Gating `can_bond` alone is **not sufficient**, which is the non-obvious half: `security = "justworks"` is Mode 1 Level 2 (`nrf-softdevice` `types.rs`, `(1, 2)`), and a bond-less just-works pairing still reaches Level 2 — the stranger would have read everything and merely failed to persist a bond. So the fix is two handlers: `can_bond` refuses a second durable bond, and `request_mitm_protection` returns true once bonded, naming a `mitm=1` + `io_caps=None` combination Just Works cannot satisfy, which is what actually refuses the procedure. The refusal is signalled out of SoftDevice event context and the central dropped from task context, the same split `BOND_SAVED`/`bond_persist` already uses. **`advertise_pairable` is deliberately retained**: `advertise_connectable` and `advertise_pairable` delegate to the same `advertise_inner` with the same advertisement bytes and differ *only* in attaching the security handler (`peripheral.rs:322` vs `:333`), and that handler is what serves `BLE_GAP_EVT_SEC_INFO_REQUEST`'s LTK lookup (`gap.rs:258-266`) — dropping it would change nothing an attacker sees while locking out the owner's own phone. FACTORY ERASE (§ 378) is therefore now a **security** control, not only a privacy one: `plan_factory_erase` starts at `CONFIG_OFFSET` so `BND1` goes with the runs, which is what makes refusing a second bond safe to ship. This **corrects § 285**, whose "no MITM protection during the one-time pairing" framing described a setup window that did not exist — the window was the device's whole life — and whose "a new pairing replaces the old bond" recorded a takeover as if it were a feature. A "forget phone" / time-boxed pairing settings row is the nicer affordance and is **not** built: it costs a menu row under § 351's press-cost model, and erase already answers the lost-phone case. Build-verified only; pairing behaviour is bench-only and can never be sim-verified (no S140 under Renode, § 210).

## 402. The BLE run manifest is rebuilt on a store generation counter, not once a second

**Date:** 2026-08-01

The per-connection stream loop rebuilt the manifest every 1 Hz tick — taking the flash-store mutex, contending with the record task's commit and checkpoint writes — and refreshed the GATT value whether or not the phone had ever subscribed, even though the manifest only changes when a run finishes, is evicted, or is synced. The store now carries a generation counter bumped on entry to `commit`/`checkpoint`, in `mark_synced_if_complete`'s hit branch, and in `factory_erase`; the loop rebuilds only when the generation moved, plus once on connect (hoisted above the ticker, so a read inside the first second is correct where previously the first publish was at t=1 s). Bumping on *entry* deliberately over-approximates, so a future early return cannot leave a stale manifest published. One honest cost: the manifest header's uptime anchor is now the value at the last rebuild, so within a quiet connection it can lag and under-age a run — the same direction `SlotDir::manifest_at` already documents for a run recovered across a power cycle, and which the phone's footer fallback already handles.

## 403. Every settings frame the watch accepts carries a checksum — v1 and v2 stop decoding

**Date:** 2026-08-01

§ 319 added a mandatory CRC at `SET1` v3 but left v1 and v2 decodable for an un-upgraded phone, so `decode`'s `has_crc` was `false` on those two arms and a bit-flip in `max_hr` or a pacer goal was applied as truth. Post-bonding write access is already the security boundary (§ 401), so this was a reliability hole rather than a new capability — but the deployed fleet is zero watches and the phone has emitted v3+ for months, so there is no compatibility debt to honour and the arms are withdrawn, mirroring the reasoning `course_store.rs` already records for its own format. Every surviving version is now checksummed, which collapses `has_crc` out of the version table entirely. Two findings fell out of the conversion and are the reason it is recorded here rather than treated as a chore: a first cut of the rejection tests **passed with v1 decoding restored**, because an unsealed legacy frame is refused by the now-mandatory CRC regardless of the version gate — so the tests were re-cut against CRC-*sealed* legacy frames, leaving the version byte as the only defect, which is also the exact shape of the bypass; and `unknown_flags2_bit_is_rejected` was passing **vacuously**, its v8-stamped header rejected on length before reaching the flags2 check, now re-stamped v4 with a must-decode control so it cannot regress to vacuous.

## 404. Alert arms are evaluated in ladder order, and an arm's `outranked` set must name everything above it

**Date:** 2026-08-01

`AlertEngine::on_update` called `take_slot` from five blocks in source order Zone → Pace → Workout → Waypoint → Backyard whistle, while three of those arms named `BackyardBell` in their own `outranked` match — a check that reads `self.active` as it stood *before* the whistle block runs, so it could not see a whistle arriving later in the same tick. The blocks are now ordered to match the documented ladder (zone → whistle → workout → waypoint → pace), which makes the existing checks correct for free; the whistle stays outside the `RecordState::Recording` gate, between the two gated blocks, and keeps its `else` seq-reset. **Only Pace actually lost an alert**, which is the part worth recording: Workout and Waypoint advance their seq tracker *before* the `outranked` check, so a blocked edge is consumed either way — "dropped, not owed", exactly as their comments say — whereas Pace banks `pace_armed = false` and the cooldown while `take_slot` re-queues only fuel/storm/cutoff/off-course, so the excursion was gone. The reorder *required* one logic change: pace's `outranked` gains `WaypointMarked | WaypointNoFix`, proven necessary by deleting the variants and watching a waypoint confirmation — dropped-not-owed and unrecoverable — get overwritten by an excursion that can come back. The general rule the doc ladder now states: an arm's `outranked` set must name every arm above it, and evaluation order is load-bearing, not incidental.

## 405. Course segment geometry is cached at build time — cache what costs a libm call, derive what does not

**Date:** 2026-08-01

`Course::project_biased` ran on every published fix and, per segment, recomputed a full haversine for the segment length and a `cos_lat` — both functions of the course's fixed points — plus a second great-circle haversine for the perpendicular offset. At 255 segments that is 3,825 double-precision libm calls per fix, of which 2,040 were course-invariant; `Course::build` already computed each segment length once for `total_m` and threw it away. `build` now caches `seg_len_m` and `seg_cos_lat`, and the offset is the Euclidean norm in the projection's own planar frame — no less accurate than a great-circle distance to a point located by that same planar approximation. Per-fix libm calls fall 3,825 → 255 (the remaining 255 are `sqrt`, so the offset half is zero *trig*, not zero calls). `bx`/`by` are deliberately **not** cached: deriving them from `seg_cos_lat` costs no libm call, and caching would add 12.2 KiB across the three concurrent course copies for no transcendental saving — hence the rule in the title. The cost is real and accepted: `size_of::<Course>()` goes 4,632 → 8,784 B, ×3 concurrent holders ≈ +12.5 KiB steady of 256 KiB, pinned by a compile-time size assert so the next field is a deliberate decision. `segment`, `t`, `along_m` and the snapped point stay bit-identical; only `off_m` moves, by under a millimetre at realistic offsets, five orders below the 20 m off-course hysteresis, and no test tolerance was loosened. One behavioural difference: a foot clamping to a vertex two segments share used to tie exactly and now ties approximately, so `Projection::segment` can pick the later segment — read nowhere outside the module's own tests.

## 406. Local metre-frame math goes to `f32`, but a bearing never does — cancellation, not precision, is the limit

**Date:** 2026-08-01

The firmware targets `thumbv7em-none-eabihf`, and the Cortex-M4F FPU is single-precision only, so every `f64` op is software-emulated (confirmed by compiling: `f64` division emits `bl __aeabi_ddiv`, `f32` emits `vdiv.f32`). Absolute lat/lon needs `f64`; once a value is in a local metre-scale frame, `f32`'s relative precision is sub-millimetre against a GPS noise floor of metres. So `haversine_metres` gains an `f32` **sibling** rather than changing in place — twelve-plus phone-fed batch callers have no per-fix cost to save — and `record.rs`'s `segment_distance_m` and `trackback`'s separation/distance math adopt it, replacing a hand-rolled Newton `sqrt` whose iteration count scaled the wrong way (7 for a 4 m hop, 13 for a 240 m Expedition hop): 74–110 soft-float calls per accepted fix become 9, worst-case in the mode chosen for battery. The line that matters is **structural, not magnitude**: haversine differences the coordinates *before* any transcendental, so `f32` is safe; `initial_bearing_deg` computes `cos φ₁ sin φ₂ − sin φ₁ cos φ₂ cos Δλ`, subtracting two nearly-equal O(1) products *after* the trig, so on a short hop the true difference (~1e-8) sits below `f32`'s absolute error on either term. Measured, that returned **43.21° where the answer is 45.00°** — a 1.8° error at the 5 m heading gate. It stays `f64`, with a test that fails by that margin if anyone retries. A breadcrumb projection was also declined rather than widen an exact inclusive test bound by 4 µm.

## 407. The phone link change-gates its frames behind a slow beacon; the settings pipe deliberately still reads one byte at a time

**Date:** 2026-08-01

`phone::run` was the one task the README's "no gratuitous wakers" discipline never reached: a bare 1 Hz ticker writing a full status frame unconditionally, with no change gate and no listener check, in the default build that tier-1 bring-up and the Renode sim both use. It now gates on the data having changed, with a 30 s unconditional heartbeat as a liveness beacon. The 1 Hz ticker is **kept as the gate's sampling clock** rather than replaced by an event wait, because `ci_smoke.py` asserts `uptime_s` is strictly increasing and the frame's clock has one-second resolution — an event-driven wait would emit two frames with the same stamp. Honest sizing: idle is ~900 writes/hour, not the 3,600 the tick rate suggests, because GPS de-rates to a 4 s fix when idle; the real win is a multi-day Expedition run, ~3,600 → ~120/hour. The sibling burst-read was **declined on evidence**: `gps.rs`'s doc advertises burst reads, but `UarteRx::read` resolves only when the buffer is full and returns `Result<(), Error>` with no count (embassy-nrf 0.10.0 `uarte.rs:694`), so a read cancelled by the gap timer — which is every frame, since `SET1` is not a multiple of 32 — cannot report how many bytes landed, and a burst buffer would silently truncate almost every push. NMEA tolerates that loss because the stream tops the buffer up and the parser resyncs on `$`; a settings frame does not. The durable fix is `read_until_idle` on the `split_with_idle` receiver, which needs a spare TIMER and two PPI channels supplied where the UARTE is built.

## 408. Every state watch the UI renders needs a wait-tree arm unless a companion signal provably fires with it

**Date:** 2026-08-01

`ui::screen_task` documents itself as re-rendering when a state watch changes and otherwise sleeping, and every watch it reads had a `.changed()` arm in the select tree — except `state::ICE` and `state::COURSE`, drained only by a top-of-loop `try_changed()`. For `TIMER`/`TIMER_MENU`/`PROFILE`/`SCREENS` that pattern is provably safe because every path that changes them also fires `state::INTERACTION` or moves the recorder snapshot, both of which are in the tree; ICE and COURSE have no such companion, because a phone-pushed `WatchSettings` frame can carry an ICE card — or a `CRS1` course — with no other field set. So both could sit unrendered for up to `TICK_IDLE` (30 s): the medical-ID face whose whole purpose is a stranger reading the wrist, and the nav map, which also owed a `panel_cache.invalidate()`. Both now have arms, added by **widening the innermost `select` rather than nesting a level**, so no existing arm's `Either` index moves and the mutually incompatible yield types make a misbinding a compile error. `invalidate()` still fires exactly once per change: `poll_changed` advances its seen-marker only in the `Poll::Ready` branch (embassy-sync 0.8.0 `watch.rs:170-184`), so a future dropped while `Pending` leaves the marker untouched and the next `try_changed()` sees it. `state::IDLE_VIEW` is verified safe and deliberately untouched — its only mutation is the BTN4 face walk, which stamps `INTERACTION` in the same tick.

## 409. An undroppable record reserves footer space — one give-up, one log line

**Date:** 2026-08-01

`push_point_bounded` reserved room for the 20-byte footer, but `push_lap`, `push_step` and `push_workout` checked only their own record-count budgets, so any one of them could leave the staging buffer with fewer than `FOOTER_LEN` free bytes. Consequence, deterministic on the stop path: a run that reaches the 253-record cap with a workout armed runs `flush_workout` and then `commit_run` with no intervening thin, the first step record takes the buffer from 4,064 to 4,080 of 4,096, and `finalize`'s footer write fails — discarding **the whole blob**, not one point. A single lap press followed by stop does the same. The three pushes moved onto the capacity-bearing `impl` (there is nothing to reserve against on the generic `ByteSink` one) and now share `has_record_room`, checked *before* their budget so the app's attribution is exact rather than approximate. `checkpoint_blob` and `finalize` need no bound of their own: with every record push holding the reserve, `len <= N - FOOTER_LEN` after any push, which is now pinned at the boundary instead of asserted in a comment that was false. The same commit split `PushOutcome::Dropped` into `Decimated` and `Exhausted` so a genuinely full sink warns while routine decimation stays silent — the rule in the title, and the convention `push_lap`/`push_step_result` already followed. `Exhausted` is separately proven unreachable under today's budgets (129 undroppable records = 2,116 of 4,096 bytes) by a structural assert plus a flood test, so a future budget change fails in CI rather than quietly truncating a shipped watch's track.

## 410. The watch's GATT table is the source of truth, and the phone client transcribes it under test

**Date:** 2026-08-01

The phone's `reactive_ble_watch_transport.dart` had its first three characteristic UUIDs shifted by one against the firmware: it read the run manifest from `..e1` (the live-status `frame`) and wrote chunk requests to `..e2` (`run_manifest`, read+notify, no write property), so **watch→phone run sync could not have worked at all**. Everything from `settings` (`..e4`) onward was aligned, which is the signature of `frame` being inserted ahead of the sync characteristics without the client following. Nothing caught it because this path has never run on hardware and cannot be simulated (§ 210). The client is aligned to the firmware, which is the authority on its own GATT table, and the two-constant chunk shape collapses to one: `run_chunk` at `..e3` is a single write+notify characteristic — the phone writes a `ChunkRequest`, the watch notifies the slice back — as `ble_sync.rs`'s doc and § 211(d) both already said, so modelling it as separate request and data UUIDs was the error that let the pair drift. A test now transcribes all seven rows with `ble.rs` named as source of truth, asserts the manifest constant `isNot` the frame UUID so the specific regression is named rather than merely excluded, and asserts all six characteristics sit on distinct handles. That test is a transcription, not an enforcement: nothing makes the two languages agree at build time, and a generator or shared fixture is the durable answer if this drifts again.

## 411. A held GAP is marked on the composed screens too — the size demotion is the price, and the guard now walks the catalogue

**Date:** 2026-08-01

§ 389 marked a held GAP on the Pace and Dashboard text rows and excluded heroes on a rationale that turned out to be false (see its amendment). The composed data screens SC1–SC4 render every metric through `metric_hero`, whose `Metric::Gap` arm carried no mark, so a held estimate read as a live sample on all three slots — worst on slot 0, the largest placement and the only slot a `Single` layout has. The mark is now applied in that arm, which reaches exactly the composed screens (`Metric::Gap` is the hero metric of no built-in page, so `screen_slots` is its only caller). The consequence is a **size demotion, not a dropped glyph**: `slot_band`/`hero_band` gate on `numeral_hero` before choosing a face, so a value carrying `~` renders in the 8x16 text face instead of the 32x48 numerals. That trade is deliberate — a held number at full size that reads as live is wrong, whereas a smaller one is merely smaller — and it is pinned in both directions, so a future edit cannot reinstate a numeral face over a marked value. The honest general rule this leaves: `gap_held` is the only hold flag on `Snapshot` that coexists with a *rendered* value; every other staleness path withholds the number instead (`cutoff_snapshot`/`sleep_snapshot` pass `stale` into the projection, which returns `Unknown` and renders `--` with a reason), which is the pattern to prefer for anything new. The reason this survived § 389 is worth more than the fix: three catalogue-walking guards were hard-coded `1..=37u8` against a catalogue that had reached 39, so `storm_delta` and `gap` were exempt from the very guard written to catch a value no face can draw. Those guards, and the sibling bound in `screens.rs`, now derive the metric set from `Metric::from_byte`, so a new metric is covered by adding its byte with no test ceiling to remember.

## 412. The heading freshness budget scales with the GNSS cadence — an Expedition arrow was blank 83% of the time

**Date:** 2026-08-01

`HEADING_STALE_S` was a fixed 10 s while the selected GNSS mode decides how often a heading can refresh at all — 1 s in Performance, 15 s in Balanced, 60 s in Expedition. So in Expedition the arrow expired after 10 s and could not refresh for another 50: blank **83% of the time**, in the mode a multi-day ultra runner picks for battery, on the Back-to-start page whose entire job is un-losing a lost runner. The same fixed window silently blanked the Waypoint page's HDG row too. The budget is now `HEADING_STALE_S + (fix_interval_s - 1)` — 10 / 24 / 69 s — the **additive** shape this codebase had already settled on twice, in `face.rs`'s `stale_after_s` and (upstream) `gap_hold_ticks`, reached independently here and then cross-checked against both. The multiple is deliberately **1, not 2**: one full inter-fix gap is exactly the span during which no update can arrive, whereas a second gap of slack would let a pre-switchback arrow keep pointing down the old leg, and a bearing that is confidently wrong about *direction* is worse than a pace that is stale about *effort* (§ 406 measured how much sharper bearing math is). The floor keeps Performance at its existing 10 s rather than an absurdly tight 1. `reset()` preserves the interval — it is device configuration, not run state — mirroring the same choice upstream made for `GapEstimator`. The trade accepted is **fresh-but-coarse over nothing**: in Expedition the runner *cannot* obtain a fresher heading, since the cadence is their own battery choice, so blanking the arrow gives them no information they didn't have. That leaves the honesty half owed rather than done: an age of up to ~60 s should be *disclosed* on the row the way § 389 marks a held GAP, and the row lives in `back_to_start_glance` — a follow-up, not a claim. One residual is recorded rather than fixed: a ~0.5 m/s power-hiker in Performance needs ~10 s to clear `HEADING_MIN_SEP_M`, so the floor is borderline there; widening for it would be inventing past the idiom. Since the two budgets now differ only in their base constant (both 10), they should collapse into one shared helper when the trees reconcile.

## 413. The phone reduces an over-cap roadbook cut-offs-first, and refuses rather than drop one

**Date:** 2026-08-01

The `RBK1` frame carries 16 checkpoints and 16 cut-off legs, and the firmware refuses an over-cap frame outright rather than truncating — so the reduction is the phone's job, which is also the only place there is a runner to tell. `watch_roadbook.dart`'s `watchRoadbookFromRoadbook` makes three choices worth recording. **(a) Cut-offs are never reduced.** The watch's CutoffEta page projects a live arrival against *the next* cut-off, so a dropped one does not merely lose a row — it makes the page confidently wrong about which limit is coming, which is strictly worse than having no schedule. A route whose cut-offs plus the schedule's end exceed the checkpoint cap is therefore **refused** with the count and the cap named, not trimmed. The cap is generous in practice: a 240-mile race has ~16 aid stations and far fewer timed barriers, UTMB ~10 barrières. **(b) The remaining checkpoint budget is filled by farthest-point sampling on distance-along-route**, seeded from the start line, after the schedule's end and every cut-off-bearing checkpoint are reserved. Even index-sampling — the obvious cheap rule, and what `capCoursePoints` does for the course polyline — would clump wherever the aid stations clump and leave the longest stretches of the race unscheduled, which is the exact thing a crew sheet exists to prevent; farthest-point sampling minimises the longest unscheduled gap instead. The synthetic start row is dropped first and always: it is 0 m / 0 s, which the watch knows the instant a run begins, and `Pacer::set_schedule` already skips a leading `(0, 0)` by construction. **(c) Wire collisions are collapsed before any selection**, higher-ranked stop winning (cut-off > finish > refill). Two markers can legitimately share a position — an aid station that *is* the barrier is normal on a mountain ultra — and the checkpoint curve is fed to `Pacer::set_schedule`, which requires strictly increasing distance *and* time and **silently rejects a non-monotonic schedule whole**, degrading the virtual partner back to even pace with no indication on the wrist. Collapsing on the rounded wire units (not the doubles) is what makes that guarantee hold, and it stops a duplicate from eating a slot. Per-checkpoint `legDistanceM` is recomputed against the previous *surviving* checkpoint so the pushed legs still sum to the course. One honest gap remains: the route-detail push has no start clock, so a clock-only cut-off cannot resolve into a limit — the result counts those and the banner reports them rather than letting a cut-off quietly fail to reach the watch. A runner-chosen goal time and start clock (the crew sheet already collects both) is the natural next step; the push currently uses the crew sheet's own opening default so the two surfaces at least agree.

## 414. The track-thinned notice leaves its page — and it is the bottom rung of the re-queued class

**Date:** 2026-08-01

When a run fills a flash slot, `run_store`'s decimation thins the track and the wrist shows `! TRACK 1/k RES` — on the **Distance page only**, row 7. Every other must-not-miss condition was deliberately promoted to a cross-page banner (§ 380 cutoff, § 381 off-course, § 399 run-lost, § 400 course-rejected), and this one is about the fidelity of the record the runner is creating, which cannot be recovered afterwards. The tempting counter-argument was § 367's signal-void reasoning — the page carries the truth, so a swallowed banner loses only the announcement — and it fails on inspection: the `AUTO` tag rides the shared state tag on *every* page, whereas this row occupies one row of forty-one pages. One row is not a backstop. It joins the **re-queued** class rather than the dropped one (it carries no factor, so it cannot go stale while queued) at the bottom rung, under `RunLost`: both are irreversible and ask for no decision, so the ordering is what was lost — a whole race gone forever outranks a run kept at half fidelity — and it leads the fuel reminders on § 399's own argument, that a gel comes round again a cadence later while a halving is announced once or never. **Hysteresis:** every *increase* re-fires, with no cooldown, because each doubling requires the slot to fill again and so the events are geometrically spaced, self-rate-limiting to at most the eight steps a `u8` can name; a *fall* is only `Recorder::start`'s reset and is never announced, because a stored track never regains resolution. **Lifetime:** cleared at the run boundary — decimation is a property of this run's slot, more clearly run-scoped than § 380's cutoff, and the next run stages into its own slot at full resolution. The banner is `! TRK RES`, 9 glyphs: the 2× band caps at `TEXT_COLS / 2` = 10, which is also `Banner`'s capacity, so `! TRACK RES` at 11 would have been silently truncated.

**Amendment to § 399:** its "the re-queued class's bottom rung" now describes `TrackThinned`, not `RunLost`. Shipped order is off-course → cutoff → course-rejected → storm → run-lost → track-thinned → eat → drink. Recorded rather than edited in place so the ranking's history stays legible.

## 415. One staleness-budget shape, two baselines kept apart on purpose

**Date:** 2026-08-01

Three modules had independently grown the same sum — a base window plus one full inter-fix gap — and § 412 recorded that they should collapse once the trees reconciled. They now share `stale_budget::for_cadence(base_at_1hz, fix_interval_s)`: `trackback`'s heading budget (base `HEADING_STALE_S`), `grade_adjusted_pace`'s GAP hold (base `GAP_HOLD_WINDOW`, § 394) and `face`'s GPS-signal budget (base `STALE_AFTER_S`), the last of which was also the only one using raw rather than saturating arithmetic. It lives in its own small module because no caller owns it and `gnss_cadence` is explicitly scoped to which fixes the `gps` task forwards, not to how long a derived value stays trustworthy; it is unit-agnostic, since GAP counts snapshot ticks and TrackBack counts seconds. **The three base constants deliberately stay separate even though all three are small and two are identical today** — how long a held pace stays meaningful, how long a bearing does, and how long a missing fix may pass unremarked are independent decisions, and § 406 measured bearing math to be far the most error-sensitive of them; one shared constant would silently couple three choices that must stay free to move apart. `face`'s `run_active` gate stays outside the shape: it selects which *surface* is being rendered — an idle face keeps the tight budget so a genuinely lost signal still flags in seconds — which is a rendering concern, not a cadence one. All three ladders are unchanged and pinned as literals.

## 416. The GATT table is enforced across languages, not transcribed

**Date:** 2026-08-01

§ 410 fixed a shifted characteristic UUID that made watch→phone run sync impossible, and closed it with a Dart test transcribing the firmware's table — a snapshot, which cannot catch the firmware moving a row underneath it. `scripts/check_watch_ble_uuids.mjs` now parses both sources and compares: the `#[characteristic(uuid = …)]` attributes in `app/src/tasks/ble.rs` paired with the **field identifier that follows each one** (not positionally, so a reordered table still reads its names correctly), against the Dart `Uuid.parse` constants. Only the name→name pairing lives in the script; every UUID comes from a file. Three edge rules, each chosen rather than defaulted: a firmware row the phone deliberately does not consume (`frame`) is listed and passes, **but a Dart constant pointing at one is a hard failure**, because that is precisely § 410's shape; a new firmware characteristic with no Dart counterpart is a **warning, not a failure**, so the watch stays free to grow its table without a mobile change — the client discovers by UUID, not by index, which is what made § 410's shift a bug rather than a benign mismatch; and **either parse reading zero rows is a loud error**, so the guard cannot pass vacuously. It proved itself immediately: the `RBK1` work added `..e8` and the guard warned, then went green when the phone claimed it.

## 417. The mode row shows the fix cadence, because no honest qualifier for the battery hours fits

**Date:** 2026-08-01

The idle face and the settings menu rendered `EST 110H` / `EST 220H` from `GnssMode::battery_est_h`. Those hours are a projection for **tier-2 hardware that does not exist**, and they already assume a receiver power-down this firmware schedules but has never run — so on the bench prototype, the only hardware there is, `EST` reads as "my watch's estimate" while meaning "a different watch's projection", on the one number this product exists to be trusted about. The fix is withholding, forced by arithmetic rather than preference: the settings row has 21 cells and spends 20 on `> GNSS PERF EST 110H`, `EST`→`PROJ` fits at exactly 21 but still reads as *this* watch's projection, and naming the target hardware needs 22. Every qualifier that fits misleads and the one that wouldn't does not fit. Both rows now render `GnssMode::cadence_label` — `1 FIX/60S`, at most 9 cells, widest row exactly 21 — which is a fact about the device in front of the wearer and carries the same battery/fidelity ordering. `battery_est_h` survives for bench logging and tier-2 planning, with its doc naming both reasons it is not this build's runtime.

## 418. A cadence-aged heading says so — closing § 412's owed half

**Date:** 2026-08-01

§ 412 scaled the heading freshness budget to the GNSS cadence so a Back-to-start arrow stops blanking for 83 % of Expedition mode, and explicitly recorded the honesty half as owed: an arrow may now legitimately be up to ~60 s old, and presenting a minute-old bearing as current is the § 389 defect in a different field. The HDG row on both the back-to-start and waypoint pages now carries `~` once the heading is older than the base window — exactly the slack § 412 granted, so Performance mode can never mark. **The drawn arrow cannot carry the mark**, which is why the row is where the age is disclosed for both: § 411 established that a marked value demotes out of the numeral face, and an arrow is a glyph, not a string. Widest marked case `HDG  NNE~` is 9 cells against `TRACKBACK_TEXT_COLS` = 10.

## 419. Flash writes yield every 256 bytes; a page erase is irreducible and the `ble` build is not exempt

**Date:** 2026-08-01

The non-`ble` `flash_erase`/`flash_write` wrapped synchronous `NorFlash` calls in `async fn` bodies with no `.await`, so a mid-run checkpoint monopolised the single-threaded executor. The proposed fix — a hand-rolled RAM-resident NVMC poll — rests on a false premise, and the datasheet says so: the nRF52840 **halts the CPU** while the NVMC writes or erases, which is a *bus stall, not a fault*. That is why embassy's driver needs no RAM-resident thunk and has none, and it is equally why yielding cannot help during an erase — every other task also lives in flash, so handing control to the scheduler stalls on its first instruction fetch. So a 4 KiB page erase is **atomic and irreducible at ~85 ms**, while a write's halt ends with each word and is therefore divisible. Writes now go in 256-byte bursts with `yield_now()` between them (~42 ms → ~2.6 ms max contiguous, matching the `ble` path's existing bounce-chunk size), and `factory_erase` erases one page per call (~425 ms → ~85 ms). The recording path is deliberately unchanged: `SLOT_LEN` == `PAGE_SIZE` == 4096, so a checkpoint erase is one page and keeps its single 85 ms stall. Embassy's bounds and alignment checks are hoisted up front so chunking cannot turn an up-front rejection into a partial write. **Two corrections to the audit that raised this:** the `ble` build is *not* exempt — `sd_flash_page_erase` halts the core for the same 85 ms, so "it awaits, therefore it is fine" is true of the executor and false of the CPU. And the residual NMEA loss cannot be fixed here at all: `gps.rs`'s single 32-byte DMA read fills in 33.3 ms at 9600 baud, well under the stall, so the fix is DMA depth — see § 421.

## 420. The settings pipe reads to the idle gap; NMEA cannot, and its fix is blocked in the simulator

**Date:** 2026-08-01

§ 407 recorded that a burst read on the settings UART was unsafe because `UarteRx::read` resolves only on a full buffer and returns no byte count, so the gap-cancelled read that ends every unprefixed `SET1` frame would silently truncate it. The durable fix is `read_until_idle`, which does report a count but exists only on the `split_with_idle` receiver, needing a spare TIMER and two PPI channels supplied where the UARTE is built. Those are now claimed in the **board crate** — `Board::split` takes `Peripherals` by value, so `main.rs` cannot grab them first, and `steal()` would put a peripheral claim outside the one crate whose documented job is peripheral assignment. TIMER1 and PPI 0/1 are free (`split` hands out no TIMER or PPI, embassy's time driver is on RTC1, `gpiote` consumes no PPI channel) and sit outside the S140's TIMER0 / PPI 17–31 reservations. The software gap timeout **stays**: `with_idle`'s window is fixed at two byte-times — 173.6 µs at the link's baud — against a 100 ms push boundary, so a hardware idle means "the sender paused", never "the frame ended"; what changed is that a cancel is no longer lossy, because the hardware has already surrendered every byte 174 µs after the last one. **The same technique is wrong for GPS**: NMEA has an inter-sentence gap after every sentence, so an idle-terminated read would disarm the receiver several times a second instead of once per 33.3 ms. `BufferedUarte` is the correct fix there — it pre-arms the next transfer and chains it over PPI, so a CPU halt loses nothing — and it is blocked on the simulator, not the silicon: it wraps its byte counter with `short_compare_clear`, and Renode's stock timer model never defines SHORTS, so after ~1024 bytes the counter guard returns 0 permanently and GPS dies a second into every sim run. § 421 removes that blocker; the driver change itself is deliberately not landed.

## 421. The simulator gains a timer model with SHORTS, so a DMA fix can be verified rather than hoped for

**Date:** 2026-08-01

`sim/NRF52840_Timer_Shorts.cs` replaces Renode's stock `NRF52840_Timer`, following the precedent `watch.resc` already sets for `rtc1`, `twi0` and `twi1` — local models existing precisely because the upstream ones omit a register we depend on. Upstream carries `Shortcuts = 0x200` in its `Register` enum but never calls `.Define()` on it, so the write is unhandled **and the read returns 0**, which also defeats embassy's `shorts().modify(...)` read-modify-write. The model defines it per the Nordic SVD (`COMPARE[i]_CLEAR` at bits 0–5, `COMPARE[i]_STOP` at 8–13) and applies the shortcuts on both the clocked and the `TASKS_COUNT` counter paths — embassy writes `MODE = LowPowerCounter`, which upstream's counter path already handled, so only the wrap was missing. The counter loop is restructured from *increment-and-test each channel* to *increment all → test all → apply shortcuts*, which is behaviour-identical at SHORTS = 0 and required otherwise: a mid-loop CLEAR would mask a match on a later channel or manufacture one on a channel whose CC is 0, which is exactly the state embassy leaves unused CCs in. **This is unvalidated locally** — Renode is not installed in this environment, so no *sim-verified* claim is made for it; CI's Renode jobs are the acceptance gate, and they run because a `sim/*.cs` diff is not docs-only. Two upstream gaps are left alone and documented in the model's header (`BITMODE` unimplemented; the counter path sets `EVENTS_COMPARE[n]` without raising the PPI event the clocked path does) so the model cannot quietly start lying later.

## 422. The idle timer survives a reboot by measuring the gap — or says it could not

**Date:** 2026-08-01

§ 375's timer was RAM-only, so a brown-out on a cold battery silently discarded an armed aid-station or nap countdown with no tell, unlike a recovered run which announces itself. It now persists as a 20-byte `TMR1` record on the config page. The interesting part is not the storage but what can honestly be reconstructed: a **stopped** reading needs no anchor at all, since it does not advance; a **running** leg is anchored on the *absolute wall clock* (§ 372's corral-bell anchor, leap-aware, refusing an implausible receiver year), never on uptime, so the reboot gap is a *measurement* — and absolute rather than a time-of-day, because a nap starting at 23:30 crosses midnight and a time-of-day alone cannot tell 10 minutes from 24 h 10 min. When the gap **cannot** be measured — no fix either side, or a clock that ran backwards — the instrument comes back **stopped and marked**, never resumed: it reports elapsed and never a remaining (the remaining is exactly what the unmeasured gap destroyed), shows `>` rather than `+` so the prefix qualifies the digits, still reports expiry when the elapsed *floor* already proves it lapsed, keeps its page seat even at a zero floor, and survives its own re-persist so a second reboot cannot launder an inherited floor into an exact reading. Only `reset()` clears the mark. Writes are gated on the **transition** (arm/stop/resume/clear), never the record's bytes, which move every second: ~66 page erases for a Moab-240-shaped race against a ~10,000-cycle rating, where per-tick would spend 5,400 in one 90-minute nap. The stamp is deliberately **not** freshness-gated, unlike every other consumer of a fix — a position goes stale because the runner moves, a wall clock does not, so an hour-old fix still yields an exact anchor, which is what lets a watch that browned out in a canyon measure its gap at all.

## 423. A code space is not a magnitude: an unknown byte refuses the frame instead of saturating onto a verdict

**Date:** 2026-08-01

`Snapshot`'s summary views carried enum verdicts as `u8` and clamped them — `feasible.min(2)`, `band.min(2)`, `direction.min(7)` — while `record.rs`'s documented byte scheme disagreed with the source enums' derived discriminant order. Nothing cast a verdict yet, so nothing was live; the first `verdict as u8` would have rendered `GoalFeasibilityVerdict::FarBehind` (3, clamped to 2) through the face's `_` arm as **"AHEAD"** — the worst verdict displaying as the best outcome, on a page a runner uses to decide whether to continue. The clamps were the deeper defect, and the same in all three: because these ladders run least-to-most, saturating always lands on the most consequential member — a corrupt readiness byte read as **HIGH** to a fatigued athlete, a corrupt turn byte as **U-TURN**, sending a runner back down the trail they just climbed. **The clamps were written as if the byte were a magnitude, and it was a name.** So the views now carry the enums themselves, with an exhaustive `*_code` encode and a total `*_from_byte` decode that returns `None` — refusing the whole frame — at the wire edge only; the clamps did not move, they became inexpressible, and inserting a variant is now a compile error rather than a shifted verdict. Genuine numeric clamps (`score.min(100)`, `percent.min(100)`) are deliberately untouched: 100 is a real, meaningful value, so saturating there bounds a magnitude and loses nothing. Two display facts fell out: `FarBehind` gains its own `FAR BEHIND` (10 of 21 cells), having been folded onto `BEHIND` while the field was a three-code byte; and the turn ladder loses `SHARP L`/`SHARP R`, two labels with **no variant behind them** — `direction_code` cannot emit 3 or 6 — kept alive by a `_ => "U-TURN"` catch-all, with neither ladder carrying a single label assertion until now. `TurnCueView::direction` alone stays a byte, deliberately: its wire ladder reserves those two rungs for a sharp class the model does not yet classify, and `direction_from_byte` refuses them by name, so the reservation is explicit rather than silently renderable.

## 424. The demo workout leaves `sim-autostart` for its own `sim-workout` feature — the storm scenario's quiet slot, part two

**Date:** 2026-08-01

§ 391 gave the `storm` and `workout` scenarios `--no-course` because `--no-alerts` cannot silence a data-driven arm; this closes the arm § 391 left in the boot. The sim's canned 5-step demo workout rode `sim-autostart`, so every auto-started session carried its step banners — and in the storm session (CI run 30709260463) the chain § 391 described replayed with the workout in the OffCourse role: Storm at 79 s, WorkoutEnding at 86 s displacing it, the displaced storm **re-queuing** (§ 376 — no later reminder exists) and re-taking the slot at 94 s, WorkoutStep at 96 s, Storm again at 104 s. The slot never held a Some → None transition inside the harness's 30 s window, so both "one front, one banner" and the TTL-clear wait were phase-alignment lotteries — the scenario passed or failed on where the front happened to land against the workout's rep boundaries. The fix is the same scenario isolation, one seam deeper: the workout arming moves to its own `sim-workout` Cargo feature, `bin/watch-sim.sh` keeps it on by default (`--no-workout` drops it), and the `storm` session boots without it — `--no-alerts --no-course --no-workout` now unarms every non-storm arm, making one front exactly one banner and the clear deterministic. `idle` takes `--no-workout` too, purely to keep its boot identical to when the workout rode the autostart feature it drops. The scenario now also asserts its own precondition — the `sim demo workout queued` boot line being present fails the run by name — so a re-coupling regresses loudly instead of resurrecting the lottery. The engine's re-queue semantics stay untouched, for § 391's reason: on hardware a front that arrives mid-workout *should* keep being announced, and the `alerts`, `pages` and `workout` scenarios still exercise the workout rail.

## 425. The dropout scenario's pause deadline models the whole-second flip, and the firmware's strict `>` stays

**Date:** 2026-08-01

The `dropout` scenario failed twice in one day (runs 30706635377 on main, 30712529705 on PR #658) with the recorder reading `recording` 10.3 s and 10.9 s into the void — past the harness's `void_start + FIX_STALE_BUDGET_S` deadline, and squarely inside what the firmware's own contract allows. `fix_stale` compares **whole-second** clocks strictly past the budget, so `> 10` first holds at an integer delta of 11 (up to one second past the budget), and the recorder stamps its anchor when it *consumes* the fix off the channel, which can cross a second boundary after the `gps: fix` line the harness anchors `void_start` on (up to one more). The scenario had already survived one round of this — its comment records moving the deadline from `void_start` to `void_start + budget` after a local-pass/CI-fail split — and the bare budget just re-created the lottery one second later. The deadline now carries a derived `FIX_STALE_FLIP_SLACK_S = 2`, with the derivation in the constant's comment rather than a measured-and-rounded fudge; the frozen-distance assertion still covers the void from its first snapshot, and a recorder still `recording` at 13 s still fails. **The firmware's comparison was deliberately not changed to `>=`**: the strict `>` on whole seconds is the shape every staleness gate in the recorder shares (`route_position_stale`, the heading and GAP holds), flipping to `>=` would let an unluckily-phased tick pause a run ~9 s of real time after a fix — earlier than the documented budget — and re-shaping firmware timing to satisfy a harness bound is the tail wagging the dog.

## 426. The sim window renders a device, not a diagram — 3x shell with a cached backdrop — and the page compositions become viewable without Renode

**Date:** 2026-08-01

Two presentation moves, no firmware byte touched. (1) `SharpMipDisplay.cs` stops drawing the § 360 window as a 230x144 strip — flat grey bezel bars, 27x18 outlined boxes, 5x7 labels — and renders a device: the panel at **3x** (each LCD pixel a 3x3 cell whose last row/column is nudged dark, the inter-pixel gap a real MIP shows) recessed behind glass inside a bezel ring inside a gradient-shaded case, with the five keys as rounded tabs riding the case edges, each carrying its § 350 function word over its BTN number — the function prominent, because the number alone made the window a wiring diagram. Edges are anti-aliased by signed-distance coverage; the static shell (case, ring, glass, resting keys) is composed **once into a cached backdrop**, so a repaint is an `Array.Copy`, the panel blit, and at most one pressed key — the same order of work as the flat version. The two contracts § 360 separated are untouched and were verified separately: **`DumpFrame` is byte-identical** (the panel-only PPM every assertion reads never included the shell), and the click map cannot drift from the pixels because `HitButton` and the key painter read the same geometry arrays. (2) Since the machine doing this work had no Renode, the model was compiled and rendered **on the host** — a scratch dotnet harness stubbing the four Renode types the class touches, replaying a real page over the model's own wire path (`OnGPIO`/`Transmit`), pressing BTN2 through the same `IAbsolutePositionPointerInput` route the analyzer window uses, and dumping the canvas to PNG. That harness also exposed the missing rung the § 360 sheet left open: layout review needed a booted sim. `render/src/preview.rs` now dumps each preview composition as a 1:1 PPM when `WATCH_PREVIEW_DIR` is set, and `bin/watch-preview.sh` wraps it into PNGs plus a contact sheet — cargo + ImageMagick, seconds, no renode/defmt-print/board. The honest split stands: the preview shows what the *compositions* render (a host claim), `watch-shots.sh` shows what the *firmware* drew (a sim claim), and the reshaped window itself was **host-rendered first, then sim-verified the same day**: renode 1.16.1 was installed on the workstation, `bin/watch-shots.sh` runtime-compiled the reworked model, walked the full 23-page cycle plus the idle faces (27 screens, cycle closed), and `DumpCanvas` returned the 724x548 device shell as designed.

## 427. The live watch window rides the telnet monitor, not Renode's UI

**Date:** 2026-08-01

`--gui` turned out to be unrunnable on the macOS workstation: the arm64 .NET Renode build cannot start its Avalonia UI from a terminal (renode/renode#886), prints `Couldn't start UI - falling back to console mode`, and the fallback is an interactive monitor on stdin — which the backgrounded launch in `watch-sim.sh` has closed, and the monitor reads a closed stdin as `quit`. So the machine booted, ran for a tenth of a second, and disposed itself, with the only symptom "Renode exited during startup". Two changes. (1) `watch-sim.sh` recognises the fallback line in the failure path and names the real cause plus the working route, instead of dumping thirty lines of SVD warnings. (2) The working route: `bin/watch-view.sh` + `sim/live_view.py`, a Tk window that attaches to the **running headless sim's** telnet monitor, polls `DumpCanvas` (~5 fps; the dump is a synchronous ~1.2 MB PPM the first frame of which can race the repaint, so a missed load skips a tick rather than dying), and resolves clicks through the display model's own new monitor-callable `HitButtonAt` — the model owns the key geometry, so the viewer copies none of it. Presses fire the watch.resc **virtual-time** button macros rather than raw `OnGPIO` drives, for the reason the macros exist: a press/release pair issued over a socket lands milliseconds apart in wall time, under the firmware's ~10 ms poll, and virtual time lags wall time enough under host load that the tap-vs-hold classifier would misread a wall-clock hold. Right-click / ctrl-click maps to the hold macros where one exists (BTN3/BTN4 grid, BTN5 waypoint). Detach semantics were verified live, not assumed: an abrupt socket close leaves the emulator running (the documented `echo cmd | ncat` kill is the half-close EOF path, not this), so closing the window is `watch-monitor.sh` Ctrl-C, and the sim survives it. The viewer needs a tkinter-capable python; the wrapper probes `python3` → `python3.13` → `python3.12` rather than assuming the Homebrew default has Tk. Verified end to end on the workstation: window opens on the live sim, renders the § 426 shell, macro presses land, sim alive after close.

## 428. The 8x16 text face is a designed bitmap font (Spleen), not a thresholded outline — and its generator loses the rasteriser entirely

**Date:** 2026-08-01

Every text row on the panel was rasterised from Source Code Pro at 8x16 and thresholded to 1-bit, and at that size the pipeline itself was the defect: strokes narrower than a device pixel vanish (the '+'=='-' collision, the invisible '|', the '!' that read as ':' — each already needed its own repair machinery and its own pinning test), and the survivors carried visibly uneven weights, which is most of what made the screens read as pixelated artifacts rather than designed pixels. The face is now **Spleen 8x16** (Frederic Cambus, BSD 2-Clause), a font drawn pixel-by-pixel *for* small monochrome panels: uniform two-ish-px strokes, every pixel intentional, and markedly heavier ink — which on a reflective panel read by headlamp is legibility, not styling. The cell is the same 8x16 monospace, so `TEXT_COLS`/`TEXT_ROWS`, every layout budget, and every row-pinning face test hold by construction; nothing outside the glyph table moved. `gen_font.py` becomes a **pure bit transcription of the vendored, digest-pinned BDF** (every Spleen glyph is a full-cell `BBX 8 16 0 -4`, asserted rather than assumed; BDF MSB-left rows bit-reversed into the wire convention): no ImageMagick, no supersampling repair pass, no baseline window — regeneration is reproducible by construction, a stronger form of § 342's pin, and the generator keeps the pairwise-distinctness gate as its one invariant check. The numeral hero faces deliberately stay rasterised from Source Code Pro Bold (§ 292/§ 339): at 32x48 and 16x32 the outline has whole pixels to land in, and the failure mode this ADR removes does not exist there. Two test pins were rewritten for the properties they were actually protecting: the exact-bitmap bar-glyph pin (an artifact of "the repair pass must not touch innocent glyphs" — there is no repair pass) became a shape pin ('-'/'='/'_' are pure bars of one shared weight), and the § 339 "medium hero inks more than doubled text" proxy — which broke the day the text font became bold enough to out-ink the numerals — now asserts the real claim: the medium face is a native rasterisation (no duplicated row pairs), with a control leg proving `draw_text_2x` still row-doubles. Host sweep green (28 suites); previews regenerated; the sim walk re-run for the composed screens.

## 429. Labels and chrome render in a 6x12 face — the one-grid discipline yields exactly two row kinds, and values never shrink

**Date:** 2026-08-01

Every row below the hero shared the single 8x16 face, so `PACE` carried the same visual weight as `6:20` — the last hierarchy lever software had on this panel, and the owner chose to spend it. The spend is deliberately narrow: a second Spleen face (6x12, same 2.2.0 tag, digest-pinned, transcribed by the same rasteriser-free generator) renders **exactly two kinds of row** small — the metric-label row under the hero band and the GPS status footer — via `face::chrome_rows`, which derives the label row from `body_top_row` rather than keeping a second page list that can drift (§ 339's page-list hazard). Labels shrink; **values never do** — pinned by a face-walk test asserting every page carrying the footer bit composes that row as the GPS line or blank, so data can never be silently demoted to the label face. The exclusions are structural, not stylistic: the Dashboard is the ruled field grid (every row is data), Nav's row 0 titles a map panel, the composed screens own every row; the idle Home hint row and ICE heading are chrome, the diagnostics face stays the raw bench view. The row grid itself is untouched — `draw_text_row_small` centres 12 px glyphs in the same 16 px band under the same composed-band compare-write, so an unchanged chrome row still flushes zero lines and no layout budget moved. One genuinely new rule: strings composed for the 8 px grid re-derive their anchors from their own shape at 6 px (a last ≥2-space gap splits left/right so `REC` stays at the edge; leading whitespace centres, which is the footer; single spaces never split), because grid-space padding stops 42 px short at the narrower advance. What this walks back of § 292/§ 350-era thinking is recorded honestly: the one-text-size grid was defended as glanceability-under-duress, and the counter that won is that hierarchy IS glanceability — the eye finds the value faster when the label stops competing with it. Whether 6x12 chrome reads by headlamp at hour 60 is a bench claim no simulator settles; if it fails on the wrist, the revert is one `RowPaint` arm.

## 430. The Climb page gains a crest thermometer — banked height over the climb's whole height, refusing without a total

**Date:** 2026-08-01

The Climb page's right shoulder sat blank beside four short rows — the sparsest fed surface in the cycle. It now carries a vertical gauge filled bottom-up by `ClimbView::crest_progress`: active gain over gain-plus-still-to-climb, both halves net height (the detector's and `crest_ahead`'s existing semantics), so a dip on the way distorts neither side. **Vertical because the number is a height** — the fill literally is how much of the hill is under the runner. The refusals carry the design, per the face's honesty rule: with no crest the total is unknowable and a fraction of a guess would render as progress, so the gauge draws only when both halves exist; a zero or non-finite total refuses too, and the courseless-climb layout (banked block as headline) is unchanged. Geometry follows the widget idiom (`draw_*_overlay`, erase-your-own-tail fill like `draw_progress_bar` rotated), the fraction is host-tested in `core/src/climb.rs`, and the composition is pinned by a preview. The ICE face was surveyed for the same treatment and deliberately left alone: its sparse form is the § 338 unfed state speaking the shared vocabulary at the shared position, and its fed card already fills the face — densifying the empty state would break the one consistency that makes NOT SYNCED legible everywhere.

## 431. The numeral faces are transcribed from Spleen too — cropped, synthetically bolded, zero unslashed — and no table on the panel is rasterised any more

**Date:** 2026-08-01

§ 428 said the numeral heroes could stay rasterised because at 32x48 "the outline has whole pixels to land in" — true for the stroke-loss failure class, and beside the point for the one the owner then saw on the clock: **a thresholded outline carries staircase edges on every curve at any size**, and next to the newly designed text face the ragged '0's were suddenly the worst pixels on the panel. Both numeral faces now transcribe from Spleen like everything else. The medium face is Spleen 16x32 taken whole (the cell matches, and it is a native design, not a doubling — the § 428 control test confirmed that empirically). The big face is **Spleen 32x64's glyph band cropped to 48 rows**: the numeral set has no descenders, its ink stands 40 rows tall, and the crop is anchored so the big face's bottom ink margin equals the medium's — which makes `draw_bignum_hero`'s shared baseline hold **by construction**, where the old generator got it from two rasterisations coincidentally centring to the same margin. Two documented transformations ride the transcription. (1) A **synthetic bold**: Spleen ships these sizes at regular weight (4 px / 2 px stems) and § 292 chose bold for a reflective panel, so the generator dilates rightward — two steps on the big face, one on the medium, optical sizing — which preserves designed edges (a clean edge dilates to a clean edge) where re-rasterising a bold outline would bring the staircase back; the counters are 12 px / 6 px natively and survive. (2) **The zero slot takes Spleen's `O` bitmap**: the slash on Spleen's `0` exists to tell it from the letter O, a distinction a 14-glyph numeral face cannot need, and at clock size it busied the largest glyph on the panel; `O` sits on the identical ink band (asserted by the crop maths). With this, `gen_bignum.py` loses ImageMagick like `gen_font.py` did — no table on the panel is rasterised, every face is one type family, and both generators are pure transcriptions reproducible by construction. All driver and render pins pass unchanged, including the baseline split, the widest-signed-hero geometry, and the not-a-row-doubling control.

## 432. Bond formation gates on a wearer-armed 90 s pairing window — the settings menu's PAIR PHONE row is the lost-phone path, not FACTORY ERASE

**Date:** 2026-08-01

The 2026-08-01 audit found bond formation ungated: `can_bond` returned `true` unconditionally, so any central in radio range of a worn, already-set-up watch could just-works-pair silently, read the whole run history, push settings / course / workout, and evict the owner's bond — broader than the risk § 285 recorded, which scoped the accepted MITM exposure to "the one-time pairing". The same-day hardening refused every second pairing outright (`can_bond` plus `request_mitm_protection` — the latter because a refused *bond* still completes a *pairing* to Mode 1 Level 2, exactly what every characteristic's `justworks` gate accepts, so only failing the pairing procedure itself keeps the data plane shut), but that left FACTORY ERASE (§ 378) as the only way to give a bonded watch a new phone — a wipe that destroys any run the phone never pulled. This entry adds the deliberate exception: `watch_core::pairing` (host-tested) defines `may_bond(bonded, window_open)` — always true before the first bond, since first-time setup has no owner to evict; afterwards true only inside a **90 s window** the wearer opens from the settings menu's **PAIR PHONE** row. The row is two-press guarded on FACTORY ERASE's exact idiom (same stop-guard confirm window — one learned dwell for every guarded action), its LEFT press closes an open window early, the window closes the moment a bond forms (an admitted bond spends it — a 90 s tail would invite a second replacement behind the phone that just paired), and the deadline lives in an atomic (`state::PAIRING_WINDOW_UNTIL_S`) because the SoftDevice's event-context callbacks can neither await nor hold a `Watch` receiver; a reboot zeroes it, so the gate fails closed. The row seats at index 4 — the 8-ring's one true far seat, the only zero-tax placement (§ 378's `min(k, n-k)` arithmetic one ring wider: every pre-existing row keeps its exact cursor cost, pinned by test) — and the eighth item puts the menu body on § 333's row-scrolling window, the layout's last slack having been spent by § 378. What remains accepted: an active in-range attacker still wins a just-works MITM during first-time setup or during an open window (no passkey UI at tier 1, § 285's original caveat) — the change turns a standing exposure into 90 wearer-chosen seconds. The advertising call stays `advertise_pairable` on every pass **deliberately**: in this crate "pairable" is not an on-air property, it only attaches the security handler whose `get_key` serves the stored LTK when the owner's phone reconnects — dropping it once bonded would close the data plane against the one peer it exists for. Gate logic host-tested; the radio leg is build-verified only (no SoftDevice in Renode, § 314's ladder) and real re-pair behaviour is a bench item.

## 433. Lambda OAC needs two grants and a client-side payload hash; env rotations repoint the CI-owned alias by script, not by removing ignore_changes

**Date:** 2026-08-01

Issue #590 found all eight web Lambdas had never served a request through CloudFront, three stacked defects deep, every one masked by the SPA 403/404→shell fallback. The fixes each encode a trade-off worth keeping explicit. (1) AWS's OAC-for-Lambda contract requires **two** resource-policy grants per function — `lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl` AND `lambda:InvokeFunction`; the module carried only the first, and the config reviewed as correct from every angle because operator sigv4 probes ride identity policies that carry both actions. The second grant now sits beside each first in `web-stack/main.tf`; a source guard is impractical in HCL, so the pairing is documented at the pattern-setter resource. (2) POSTs additionally need the **client** to send `x-amz-content-sha256`: CloudFront cannot hash a body it streams through and OAC-signed Function URLs reject unsigned payloads. The hash is computed at every fetch seam (web `payloadSha256Hex` via crypto.subtle, mobile via package:crypto) over the exact posted bytes, pinned by security-guard tests; GET surfaces are exempt. The alternative — dropping AWS_IAM auth on the Function URLs — was rejected: it would let anyone who learns the `.lambda-url.*` hostname bypass CloudFront and the WAF. (3) An env-only `terraform apply` publishes a new version but the `live` aliases are CI-owned (`ignore_changes = [function_version]`), so the rotation never reaches the Function URL's serving qualifier. Removing `ignore_changes` was rejected because Terraform's known version is stale the moment CI deploys — an apply would then *roll back* the alias to an old bundle, a worse failure than the one being fixed. Instead `bin/lambda-alias-sync.sh <env>` repoints every alias to its newest published version, and the rotation recipes in infra/README.md, docs/ops/deployment.md, and apps/web/deployment.md all end with it.

## 434. A live share's public flip ends with the run — keeping the run public is an explicit post-stop choice

**Date:** 2026-08-01

Issue #664 (the woman-runner persona hunt's top finding): the recorder's stop path called `makeRunPublic` unconditionally whenever a live broadcast was active, so a runner who shared a live link *for safety* — including every run under the Settings → Safety `auto_live_share` pref — had the finished run left permanently `is_public=true` with no consent step, bypassing the deliberate `_confirmMakePublic` dialog run-detail requires for the same flip (§33's consent posture), while the toggle copy described only the live window. The fix scopes the opt-in to what the runner actually opted into: `beginLiveBroadcast`'s `is_public=true` stub is the LIVE window only; on stop, `saveRun` writes the runner's default, `concluded_at` is stamped *before* any flip (so an open spectator's ~15 s poll can catch the conclusion card), and `_resolvePostLiveVisibility` resolves the remainder off a pure decision helper — a still-active broadcast prompts (`AlertDialog`; "Keep public" is the only path to `makeRunPublic`, decline/dismiss fails closed to `makeRunPrivate`), a share the runner already stopped mid-run reverts quietly (which also clears the stub when the cloud save failed — the offline leak of the same defect), and a `public` privacy default resolves to nothing because the save already honoured it. The whole step is auxiliary to the save (L4: a failed flip banners, never rethrows). Accepted consequence: a default-private runner who declines leaves the spectator link dead on reload (`public_runs` + the `live_run_pings` SELECT policy both key off `is_public`) — for a safety share that is the correct end state, and the issue #613 frozen-trace-on-reload behaviour survives exactly as long as the run stays public. Mobile-only by construction (recording is mobile-only, §235 — no web twin owed). An architecture guard pins `makeRunPublic` behind the dialog in `run_screen.dart` the same way the §33 guard pins run-detail's.

## 435. Mobile IconButtons never carry VisualDensity.compact — the #255 "compact + 48dp constraint" idiom was a measured placebo

**Date:** 2026-08-01

Issue #664's sweep of the remaining sub-48dp mobile tap targets started by verifying the idiom the four #255-fixed screens had established (`VisualDensity.compact` + `BoxConstraints(minWidth: 48, minHeight: 48)`), and it failed the measurement: Flutter's M3 IconButton maps `constraints:` into a minimum size that visual density adjusts *afterwards*, so compact's −8dp/axis lands on top of the explicit floor and the button hit-tests as 40x40 — taps at the 48dp perimeter miss (probed with a widget test tapping 23px off-centre; a min48 button without compact catches the same tap). The premise "the constraint governs the hit area, the density only tightens visuals" is simply false, so the sweep replaced the idiom rather than propagating it: IconButtons drop `visualDensity: VisualDensity.compact` entirely and keep the explicit min-48 constraints; visual tightness comes from the small glyph (`size:`/`iconSize:`), which is what the 40dp-visual/48dp-target M3 spec intends anyway. The alternative — keeping compact and inflating constraints to 56 so the adjustment nets out at 48 — was rejected as an encoding of a private Flutter offset that reads as a typo. `tap_target_guard_test.dart` grew from four anchored pins to a lib/-wide balanced-paren scan banning three patterns on IconButtons (compact density, sub-48 `minWidth`/`minHeight`/`tightFor`, and a sub-48 `SizedBox` cap around the button); labeled buttons keep compact deliberately — their padded target stays ≥40dp with a wide label surface, above WCAG 2.5.8's 24px floor, and the 48dp bar is the icon-button spec where the glyph is the whole target. Convention in conventions.md § Mobile tap targets.

## 436. The Apple Watch route push rides `WCSession.transferUserInfo`, is capped at 512 points, and is refused rather than truncated

**Date:** 2026-08-02

`RouteNavigator.swift` shipped in #663 as a fully unit-tested off-route engine with no route source and no surface, so none of it was reachable by a user (issue #664). Closing that needed a transport choice. `sendMessage` was rejected: it requires a reachable counterpart with the watch app running, and a runner picks a route on the phone precisely when the watch is idle on a charger — the common case is the failing case. `updateApplicationContext` survives a disconnect but is a single latest-wins dictionary that would clobber, and be clobbered by, the `preferred_unit` push the watch already anticipates. `transferUserInfo` queues durably across app launches and watch reboots, delivers in order, wakes the watch app in the background, and the watch's `didReceiveUserInfo` handler already existed. The payload is five flat plist values — id, name, total distance, and two parallel `[Double]` coordinate arrays rather than per-point dictionaries, which would cost more plist overhead than the doubles they carry. The point budget is 512, the same literal in Dart (`kMaxAppleWatchRoutePoints`), phone Swift (`WatchIngestBridge.maxRoutePoints`) and watch Swift (`ArmedRoute.maxPoints`), and every hop re-validates: an over-cap, mismatched-length, non-finite or out-of-range payload is dropped whole. Nothing truncates, because a polyline that stopped at position 512 would make the watch report the runner off route against geometry the route does not have and announce the finish early — worse than no route at all; a denser route is thinned by priority Douglas–Peucker (`simplifyToBudget`, both endpoints preserved) and a shorter-than-two-point one is refused with a reason the runner sees. The push reads the privacy-clipped `_displayWaypoints` per § 33. Guidance is an L4 auxiliary effect fed at the very end of `didUpdateLocations`, after distance, the NDJSON track write and pace are committed, so a route with no usable geometry cannot cost the run a GPS fix; `RouteGuidanceView` shows an explicit "Route position unknown" rather than a false on-route reading when the projection fails. 512 is deliberately looser than the custom watch's 256-point `CRS1` cap, which encodes a flash-capacity limit this device does not have. Deliberately narrower than Wear OS: no on-wrist picker, no mini-map, no `is_starred` read — the phone chooses the route. **The Swift half is uncompiled** — this repo's toolchain is Linux-only, so `xcodebuild build` + `xcodebuild test` on a Mac remains the outstanding gate, and `parity.md`'s Apple Watch cells stay qualified by its deferral banner.

## 437. The `runs.metadata` registry is enforced by a source-level guard on every writing platform, not just Dart

**Date:** 2026-08-02

`runs.metadata` is schemaless jsonb, so codegen cannot see drift and `docs/backend/metadata.md` is the only coordination point — but until now only the Dart test enforced it, and the Dart test's own header carried the TS/Kotlin/Swift twins as a TODO (issue #664). Each of Dart, TypeScript, Kotlin and Swift now carries a guard that scans its own sources and fails on a key with no table row, all four parsing the registry with the same `^\|\s*` + backticked-key regex so they cannot disagree about what "registered" means. Each guard extracts only what its language can express statically — dotted and subscript reads, depth-1 object-literal writes, and where one exists the language's key-constant indirection (`METADATA_KEYS.<x>` resolved back to the wire key) — and each carries an exemption set for a `metadata` identifier that genuinely is not `runs.metadata`. Depth is load-bearing: the per-lap field names nested inside `metadata.laps` belong to the `laps` shape, not the key registry, so only depth-1 entries count. The watchOS guard additionally exempts the run **columns** (`id`, `started_at`, `duration_s`, `distance_m`, `source`) that ride the `WCSession.transferFile(_:metadata:)` transport envelope beside the three real metadata keys the phone lifts out — the envelope is a transport shape that happens to be called `metadata`, not the jsonb bag. The pre-existing web guard, a Playwright spec, was **deleted** rather than kept alongside the new unit test: it paid for the whole e2e harness to run a static source scan, never saw object-literal writes or `METADATA_KEYS` indirection, did not strip comments (forcing a special case for the registry's own filename), and counted any backticked lowercase token anywhere in the doc — prose included — as "documented", which made it weaker than no guard in the cases that matter. The TS and Kotlin guards were each verified to fail as well as pass, by injecting bogus keys and confirming the nested/depth-2 decoys were correctly ignored; the Swift guard is uncompiled on this Linux toolchain and its extractor was instead port-verified against the real watch sources, so one macOS CI run is still owed before anyone calls it green.

## 438. The three watch verdict enums number their variants against the wire codes, not their declaration order

**Date:** 2026-08-02

`record.rs` encodes `RaceDayView.feasible`, `PlanAdaptiveView.trend` and `.confidence` through explicit `*_code` / `*_from_byte` pairs whose numbering deliberately differs from the source enums' declaration order — and issue #664 flagged the gap that left: nothing stopped a future `verdict as u8` from reaching the wire, and because the two orderings disagreed, such a cast rendered the *opposite* verdict. On `GoalFeasibilityVerdict` that is the difference between telling an ultra runner near a cut-off they are `AHEAD` and telling them `FAR BEHIND`; on `AdaptiveReason` it is the difference between "do more" and "ease off". There was no live caller, which is exactly why it was worth closing while it was still cheap. The fix pins the enums' discriminants to the wire codes (`Behind = 0, OnTrack = 1, Ahead = 2, FarBehind = 3`, and the matching low→high ladders for the two adaptive enums), leaving declaration order untouched so no `match` arm, doc reference or reading order moves — only the numbering. A cast and the codec now render the same verdict, and `verdict_discriminants_match_their_wire_codes` asserts that equality over every variant, so a future renumber on either side breaks a test rather than shipping an inverted readout. Rejected alternatives: reordering the variants to match (churns every site that reads them, for no added safety), and leaving it as a documented hazard (the doc comments already said "a cast would send the opposite" and that prose is precisely what a future `as u8` would not read).

## 439. A guard nothing runs enforces nothing — § 416's cross-language GATT check joins the `CI gate`

**Date:** 2026-08-02

§ 416 built `scripts/check_watch_ble_uuids.mjs` to make the firmware's GATT table and the phone's `reactive_ble_watch_transport.dart` agree by parsing both, replacing § 410's transcription snapshot. It was never wired to a workflow. For its whole first day the script existed, passed when run by hand, and was referenced from nothing but this log and its own test file — so the drift it was written to catch would have merged exactly as § 410's did, and the repo would have believed itself defended. It now runs as its own `watch-ble-uuids` job, in the `CI gate` aggregator's `needs:` list. A dedicated job rather than a step inside `parity-matrix`, which the script's own header had proposed: the failure signal has to name what broke, and a firmware-only PR that moves a UUID failing a check called "Parity matrix drift" is the wrong sentence — the check also needs Node where that job needs Flutter, so sharing bought nothing but a misleading name. Only the Android copy of the client is read; the iOS twin is byte-identical by `twin-parity` (§ 39), so reading both would guard the same bytes twice. The step runs the script **and** its `node --test` suite, the `parity-types` idiom for a source-parsing guard: a parser that silently stops matching passes vacuously, which is what the script's "zero rows is a loud error" rule and those tests together prevent. Verified in both directions — a drifted phone constant and a renumbered firmware characteristic each fail it, the latter being the direction a transcription snapshot can never catch.

## 440. The manifest-rebuild predicate is equality on a wrapping counter, and it belongs in `watch_core`

**Date:** 2026-08-02
