`ble_sync`'s module doc says every decision the BLE transport makes lives there, host-tested, precisely because the `ble` build needs the S140 SoftDevice and so gets no integration coverage at all (§ 210). § 402's "has the manifest moved" test was the last one still inline in the `app/` task body — the bond half of that same task having already been lifted to `watch_core::pairing` (§ 432). It moves to `ble_sync::manifest_needs_rebuild`. The predicate is `built_gen != Some(store_gen)`: equality, deliberately, never ordering. `bump_manifest_gen` is a `wrapping_add`, so a `store_gen > built` reading would go permanently quiet the first time the counter passed `u32::MAX`, leaving a connected phone reading a manifest of runs that no longer exist for the rest of the session. The counter says only *that* something moved, never how far, so ordering is not information it carries. Four host tests pin it — fresh connection, unmoved generation, any move in either direction, and the wrap boundary — and the ordering mutant fails two of them.

## 441. `svelte-check` joins CI, because it is the only gate that type-checks inside a `.svelte` file

**Date:** 2026-08-02

`/gym/[id]` had been reconstructing a `SetAdherence[]` from persisted `gym_step_results` without `stepIndex` since § 304 moved the planned↔actual match identity onto it (2026-07-25). That commit updated the type, both runners, both twin suites and the registry, and missed two web readers. Nothing caught it for a week: `tsx --test` never loads `.svelte` files, and `vite build` compiles Svelte without cross-module type checking, so the only gate that could see it was not running. It runs now, as a step in the existing `build-web` job. Warnings do not affect its exit code, so it goes green today against two pre-existing `state_referenced_locally` warnings without suppressing future ones from the log — `--threshold error` was rejected for exactly that reason. The fix underneath is a *replay*, not a recomputation: `reviewFromMetadata` reads the stored verdict rather than re-grading stored targets, because re-grading would let a later scoring change silently restate a finished session. `step_index` stays optional and falls back to `set_index` — not a guess, but the exact identity rows written between the P3 runner (2026-06-12) and § 304 were persisted under; jsonb history is immutable, so a reader copes rather than hides working UI. The same omission was also discarding two persisted delta columns and blind-casting the verdict; both are fixed in the same reconstruction.

## 442. Both lockfiles are audited, because CI installs the one that was not

**Date:** 2026-08-02

`audit.yml` ran `pnpm audit` only, while `package-lock.json` is what CI's `npm ci` jobs — including the web build compile gate and `cross-client-roundtrip` — actually install. The two lockfiles drift independently, and the gap was not theoretical: `pnpm-lock.yaml` was clean while `package-lock.json` carried two high-severity advisories (`brace-expansion` GHSA-mh99-v99m-4gvg, `postcss` GHSA-r28c-9q8g-f849) that no job reported, which is how issue #633 came to read as fixed when half of it was not. Dependabot does not close the gap either — it bumps *declared* dependencies, so a transitive six levels under `@sentry/sveltekit` behind a `^` range is only ever refreshed by `npm audit fix --package-lock-only`. The workflow now runs both and ORs the exit codes into the one output the issue-open/issue-close steps already key on, so the tracking issue keeps its label-based identity and closes itself when both are clean. All three advisories were build-time-only — `@sentry/vite-plugin` is not referenced by `vite.config.ts` at all, and neither package appears in the client bundle or the Lambdas — so the exposure was a build machine, not a user; that is a reason to report them accurately, not a reason to leave them unreported.

## 443. A review row's `{#each}` key is `step_index`, the only identity unique across blocks

**Date:** 2026-08-02

`GymWorkoutReview.svelte` keyed its planned-vs-actual rows on `(exercise_key, set_index, status)`. `set_index` restarts per block — the registry has said so in as many words since § 304, and the sibling `/gym/[id]` page already carried a comment about `each_key_duplicate` wedging a page for this same class — so the one routine shape § 304 was written about, an exercise programmed into two blocks, mints the same triple twice and Svelte throws, taking the whole review down. The key is now `step_index ?? set_index`, mirroring the reader's own pre-§ 304 fallback. It is built by `reviewRowKey` in the gym lib rather than spelled inline, because an expression inside an `{#each}` cannot be unit-tested and this one is load-bearing: a test now asserts four rows from a two-block routine yield four distinct keys, and fails if the old expression returns. The helper takes a `Pick<>` of the four fields it reads rather than the whole row, so the test fixtures state the identity under test instead of padding eleven irrelevant columns.

## 444. The Fuel page falls back to the runner's own drink/eat cadence when no roadbook is pushed, and `Metric::Fluid` (wire byte 40) joins the composed-screen catalogue

**Date:** 2026-08-02

The Fuel page was inert for every run without a pushed course — `fuel_snapshot` returned `None` on an empty roadbook, so the page dropped out of the cycle and `Metric::FuelCarbs` read `NOT SYNCED`. That was wrong on its face: `alerts` has been firing drink and eat reminders since the first tick of every run, off `DEFAULT_FLUID_PER_HOUR_ML` / `DEFAULT_CARBS_PER_HOUR_G`. The one page named FUEL could not state the plan the watch was already running.

`FuelView` now carries a `FuelBasis` whose payload is basis-specific — `NextAid { total }` or `Cadence { per_hour }` — rather than a pair of `Option`s a caller could read both of. Without a roadbook the basis is `Cadence`: the intake the reminders have already called for, integrated over **moving** time (the clock `alerts` schedules on — a runner who spent an hour at an aid station was not told to drink four more times), at the pushed `SET1` cadence or the same defaults `alerts` starts at. The rate derivation is extracted to `fuel_rates_per_hour()` so the two bases cannot drift. The page header names the basis, because the row below it is grams in one case and grams an hour in the other. `Page::Fuel` is consequently available on every run, not only a coursed one.

The carry-load gauge is **absent** on the cadence basis rather than empty: `gauge::fuel_fill` returns `Option<f32>` and the widget skips a `None`. A zero-fill bar under a live fuel page reads as "nothing to carry", the opposite of what a cadence run is telling the runner, and there is no race for the carry to be a share of.

`Metric::Fluid` takes wire byte 40, `wire_name` `"fluid"`, slot label `FLUID`. It is the fluid half of the pair `Metric::FuelCarbs` already leads with, separate because the Fuel page's hero is carbs while a desert runner's binding constraint is the other one — a composed screen is the only way to put millilitres in the 32x48 face. Fail-closed on an unknown byte like every other metric. The phone catalogue, the editor's label switch, and all seven mobile ARBs follow; **the web has no watch-metric surface at all**, so nothing is owed there — the issue's "six locales" meant the mobile ARBs.

## 445. The HR arbitration reaches the panel, not just the log — the zones row names the sensor

**Date:** 2026-08-02

`hr_source::select_hr` decided whether a chest strap or the wrist optical AFE was authoritative, and the arbiter task then threw the answer away: the winning *rate* went to `state::HR` and the winning *sensor* went to a `defmt` line. On the wrist a strap that never paired was indistinguishable from one that won — the same blind spot the zones page's `CEIL --` exists to close.

`hr_to_publish` now returns `HrPublication { sample, source }` — the source rides out with the rate on one publication, so no consumer can pair one with the other's. The synthesised blank carries `source: None`; nothing produced it, and naming a sensor there would credit a reading that does not exist. The arbiter publishes `state::HR_SOURCE` beside `state::HR`, `record` mirrors it onto `Snapshot::hr_source`, and the zones row spends its existing five-cell label on `STRAP` / `WRIST` / `HR` instead of repeating the metric the hero's own `BPM` unit already names (§ 361). No extra cells, no moved column.

The label resolves against the BPM the render was handed, not the snapshot alone: the two arrive on different clocks — the face ages its reading through `hr_duty::shown_bpm` every frame while the snapshot is stamped at the last fix — and a row naming a sensor over a `--` hero would credit a reading that is not on the screen.

Host-tested only, and the strap half can never be more: the GATT central that feeds it is behind the `ble` feature and Renode has no SoftDevice (§ 210 / § 365).

## 446. FACTORY ERASE retires the live bond, not just its flash record

**Date:** 2026-08-02

Found by the pre-deploy security review this round asked for, and confirmed by reading: § 378's factory erase wiped the `BND1` flash record but left the SoftDevice's keys sitting in RAM inside the security handler, and **nothing in this firmware ever resets the device**. `state::FACTORY_ERASE` is a `Channel` with exactly one receiver — `record` — so the BLE task never learned an erase had happened. A previously-bonded phone therefore kept full encrypted read/write access to a watch its owner had just wiped, until the battery died. That is precisely the lost / stolen / handed-on case the action exists for, and `privacy.md` states the opposite in as many words: the bond is "a live **credential**, not a stale record: a kept bond lets the previous owner's phone read the new owner's runs and live position".

The fix is a generation counter, `state::BOND_ERASE_GEN`, bumped by the erase and recorded on the `Bonder` whenever a peer is adopted. `watch_core::pairing::bond_is_live(bonded_at_gen, current_gen)` is the host-tested predicate; every read of the stored peer now goes through `Bonder::live_peer()`, so `get_key` stops serving the LTK, `save_sys_attrs` stops matching, and `can_bond` / `request_mitm_protection` see an unbonded watch. An atomic rather than a second channel receiver for the same reason § 432's pairing deadline is one: the security callbacks run in the SoftDevice's event context and can neither await nor hold a `Watch` receiver — so the retirement has to be *legible* to them rather than *delivered* to them, and it takes effect on the very next key request instead of waiting for a task to be scheduled.

A **generation**, never a boolean "erased" flag, because the watch must be able to pair again immediately: a re-pair stamps the current generation, so the next erase invalidates it in turn — a flag would have to be cleared on re-pair, and a missed clear would leave the next erase inert. This also makes the erase's own comment true at last: an erased watch really does pair freely, because `may_bond` now sees no bond and admits a new phone with no window, which is correct — a wiped watch *is* first-time setup.

Host-tested (the predicate and its three cases) and build-verified on the `ble` feature set. The radio behaviour itself remains a bench item: § 210 stands, there is no SoftDevice under Renode, so "the old phone is actually refused on reconnect" is a claim only hardware can settle.

## 447. Watch status frames reach spectators through `LiveBroadcaster`, and a dropout is shown as a gap rather than smoothed over

**Date:** 2026-08-02

The custom watch notifies one `link::status_frame` per second on the `frame` characteristic, but the frames terminated at the developer-only Sim Watch screen, so a watch-recorded run had no spectator surface at all. `WatchLiveForwarder` (`live_watch_forwarder.dart`, mobile-only — recording is mobile-only per § 235, so no web twin is owed) carries them into the **same** pipeline a phone run uses. Everything goes through `LiveBroadcaster.pushPing` and never a second path, so privacy-zone clipping (§ 33) is inherited rather than re-implemented — a negative control that swapped in a direct insert turned the in-zone test red.

The gap rules are refusals, not smoothing: a fix older than 10 s is dropped (mirroring the recorder's own GPS-lost threshold, so both live paths go quiet on one clock), a repeated `uptime_s` is dropped because the characteristic is read+notify and a reconnect re-delivers, and a backwards frame is dropped rather than rewinding the spectator's marker unless three arrive consecutively — a watch reboot. Reboot detection counts consecutive backwards frames instead of thresholding the jump size, because a "big jump = reboot" rule wedges permanently when the watch reboots at low uptime.

There is deliberately **no keep-alive ping and no back-fill on reconnect**: silence lets the spectator's own `freshnessFor` age the position and flip it stale at 90 s, and either mechanism would re-date an old position as fresh — the exact failure `live_freshness` exists to prevent. The web side needed no change for that reason and none was made. The v1 frame carries no distance/elapsed/HR and `uptime_s` is device uptime rather than run elapsed, so those stay null: an honest position-only feed until the frame schema grows a `run` object. The BLE subscription itself is not yet wired — the phone client does not claim that characteristic, and the UUID guard records it as deliberately unclaimed — so the forwarder is reachable today only from the dev link.

## 448. The `live`-alias sync list is derived from Terraform by a CI guard, not maintained by hand

**Date:** 2026-08-02

§ 433's remedy for issue #590 was `bin/lambda-alias-sync.sh`, whose coverage was a hardcoded bash array of eight function suffixes. The pre-deploy review that passed § 433 passed it with exactly this condition: the array was correct against all eight, and nothing tied it to Terraform's actual `aws_lambda_alias` set. A ninth Lambda would have merged with no alias repoint and no signal — the same drift class #590 was opened over, reintroduced one function at a time, and invisible in the same way, because a Lambda serving a stale env snapshot returns 200s from the version it is pinned to.

`scripts/check_lambda_alias_sync.mjs` parses **three** sources: the module's `aws_lambda_alias` resources resolved through to their function names, the script's `FUNCTIONS` array, and `release-web.yml`'s per-function `update-alias` steps resolved through the step outputs that define them. Three rather than two because the script's own header already claimed lockstep with the release workflow, and a Lambda that workflow does not deploy never gets code at all — enforcing half a stated lockstep leaves the other half exactly as latent as before. Terraform is the source of truth: it is where a Lambda comes into existence, and both consumers are checked against it.

Parsed, never transcribed. § 410's fix was a transcription snapshot and § 416 had to replace it for the reason that applies here too — a snapshot agrees with its source right up until the source moves. The HCL is read with a string- and comment-aware brace scan, aliases resolve to functions by reference rather than declaration order, and each source's own environment spelling (`${var.env}`, `${ENV_NAME}`, `${ENV}`) normalises to one sentinel so the comparison is on names and not on syntax. Beyond the set difference in both directions, a drifted name prefix and a renamed alias each fail too: a repoint of an alias nothing serves through is a silent no-op, not an error anyone would see.

It runs as the `lambda-alias-coverage` job in the `CI gate` aggregator's `needs:`, per § 439. Offline by construction — three file reads, no AWS credentials, no `terraform init`. The job runs the script **and** its `node --test` suite, the § 439 idiom, because a parser that silently stops matching passes vacuously; zero parsed resources from **any one** of the three sources is a hard error, tested both all-blind and one-blind, the latter being the dangerous case where the two surviving sources still agree with each other.

The same change fixes a defect found while verifying it: `CURRENT=$(aws lambda get-alias …)` is a bare command substitution, so under `set -euo pipefail` a function whose `live` alias does not exist yet killed the **entire** sweep — every function after it in the array silently unverified, with nothing in the output saying so — while the branch directly above already treated "not deployed yet" as a skip. The two branches disagreeing about what "not ready" means is what made the failure invisible. It now skips with a warning and a count, and the summary refuses to read as a clean sweep when anything was skipped.

## 449. The cut-off and sleep pages refuse to guess a course position, and project the future against the race clock

**Date:** 2026-08-02

Two defects in one projection, both found by the round-3 core audit.

`Recorder::cutoff_snapshot` and `sleep_snapshot` read an absent along-course position as `0.0` — the course *start*. Leg selection is by distance-along-course, so that picks cut-off **one**, and `CutoffEta::limit_passed` is computed before the staleness gate can withhold anything: a runner four hours in read `SLEEP MISSED` for a gate cleared before dawn, with the Cut-off page counting down to the wrong checkpoint. The audit's stated trigger needed one correction, and it matters: a *lost* fix does not cause this — `nav.rs` continues on a rejected fix, so the last position stands and ages correctly into `route_position_stale()`. `NavView::NoFix` is sent at boot with a course loaded and on a course push/replace, persisting until the first successful projection, so the reachable triggers are a course pushed or rerouted mid-race, or a run that starts coursed and never gets a projectable fix.

Both now take `self.route_along_m?`, the same refusal `route_position_permille` and `climb_snapshot` already make. A **stale** position still projects, deliberately: the last known position names the right checkpoint, and `cutoff_eta` withholds only the projected time. The two absences are different instructions to a runner, so `Snapshot::cutoffs_loaded` keeps them apart — no cut-offs pushed says `NOT SYNCED`, cut-offs with no position says `AWAITING FIX`. Returning `None` alone would have told a runner with a perfectly good synced course to sync it, and would have dropped both pages out of the BTN3 cycle until the first fix, renumbering every page behind them.

Second, the ETA was projected from whole-run **moving** pace into a parameter named `recent_pace_s_per_km`, whose canonical web caller feeds an elapsed-clock pace. Moving pace is race pace scaled by (1 − stopped fraction), so projecting a future the runner will also stop during understates the remaining leg by exactly that fraction — error in one direction only. Measured on the new test: 2405 m banked, 600 s moving, 1800 s elapsed, cut-off 4 km ahead. Moving pace projects arrival at 2796 s, margin +1904 s, graded `On`; race pace projects 4794 s, margin −94 s, graded `Behind`. A 33-minute swing on the single number a runner uses to decide whether to keep going. It now projects from `Recorder::race_pace`, which is also what `sleep_budget`'s conservative-pace rule already resolves to (elapsed ≥ moving always), so the two pages finally share one projection — what `page.rs` already asserts and what the audit found they contradicted.

What this does **not** give is a genuinely *recent* pace. The recorder holds no rolling window and one was not invented: a faithful port of web's five-sample window would be ~5 s of data here, noise for a 22 km projection. A runner who has come apart in the last hour still reads their whole-race average. Adding that window must move both pages together — it interacts with § 373's argued conservatism — and deserves its own entry.

## 450. A composed screen's slots take the hero band's width gate, not just its glyph gate

**Date:** 2026-08-02

`ui_frame::slot_band` asked only whether the numeral faces could *spell* a value, never whether the panel could *fit* it, while `hero_band` has checked both since § 345. `draw_bignum_hero` drops the glyphs past the right edge, so a slot showing a 100-hour elapsed rendered `100:00:` and an hour-scale cut-off margin `+999:5` — a wrong number drawn as confidently as a right one, which is the failure § 345 exists to prevent. Verified against the driver's own loop rather than by inspection.

Slot 0 was covered because it rides `hero_band`; slots 1+ were the hole, and a § 364 screen is runner-authored, so any metric can land in any slot and no per-slot value range can be assumed. An over-wide value now steps down to the medium face — half the width per glyph, and it shows every value the catalogue can spell, whole. Smaller and complete beats larger and truncated: the rule `tall_hero_fits` already stated, which only half its callers obeyed. The existing catalogue sweep is widened from "can spell" to "can spell **and** fit", so the gap cannot reopen one metric at a time.

## 451. A phone-pushed race configuration persists as its own `RCF1` record whose body is a `SET1` frame

**Date:** 2026-08-02

Everything a `SET1` push configures — pacer goal, HR-zone ceiling, QNH reference, fuel cadence, gear, race phases, alert cadences — lived in RAM alone, so a brown-out on a cold battery at hour 30 handed the rest of a race a watch with none of it and nothing on the wrist saying so. Three of the eighteen fields had already earned persistence one at a time (§ 351 hide-empty, § 358 ICE, § 374 auto-lap), which issue #664's bullet does not mention; this is the general answer for the remaining fourteen.

A **new record**, not a `CONFIG_VERSION` bump: § 372 spent `CFG1`'s last free flags bit, and `decode_config` validates the version exactly, so a bump makes every existing record read as "no saved config" — costing the runner the GNSS mode, profile, backyard arm and auto-lap rung they had set, in order to store a pacer goal. The same trade `WPT1` / `ICE1` / `SCR1` / `TMR1` each already made.

The record's **body is a `SET1` frame**, not a second set of typed fields. A parallel codec over the same values would have to be extended in lockstep with every future settings field or silently stop persisting it, and would need its own sentinel conventions for the doubly-optional disarms half these fields carry. Embedding means restore is byte-for-byte the push, `WatchSettings::decode`'s accept-v3-through-current rule already discharges the older-record compat obligation, and each field's plausibility guard stays the only one there is — a stored value a later widened guard would accept is re-evaluated at restore rather than inheriting a verdict baked into flash. `persistable()` destructures all eighteen fields with no rest pattern, so a new settings field is a compile error rather than one that quietly stops surviving a reboot.

**Whole-page rewrite stands; no ping-pong.** The write is one erase per frame whose stored subset actually changes, gated on the record's **bytes** — a pushed NaN QNH is never equal to itself, and a struct comparison would re-erase the page on every repeated push. A realistic race costs single-digit erases against the page's 10,000-cycle endurance, three orders of magnitude under the 1 Hz rate `persist_timer`'s doc already names as the red line. Ping-pong would buy 2×, which neither the realistic nor the adversarial rate turns on. Its real value — surviving a brown-out inside the 85 ms erase, which today loses all six records on the page at once — is a page-level defect needing a second 4 KiB carve-out, a generation counter, a live-page selector and a change to `plan_factory_erase`'s contiguous-span claim, and belongs in one change for the whole page rather than riding in behind one record. `RCF1`'s own torn-write story is complete regardless: CRC32-sealed, and a torn, erased, mis-magicked or mis-lengthed record reads as **absent**, which means the boot defaults — never a value the runner did not set.

Restore runs in the record task's init, strictly before the first drain of the settings queue, so a phone that pushes two seconds after boot is simply a later delta and wins field by field, exactly as a second push wins over a first. Excluded: `pages` (the persisted activity profile already re-derives the mask at boot — two writers of one setting), the three fields that already persist elsewhere, and the pushed course / workout / roadbook, which are multi-kilobyte chunked frames needing a page each rather than a settings record.

## 452. The custom-watch course push builds its schedule from a persisted per-route race plan, and asks when there is none

**Date:** 2026-08-02

The RBK1 push built its roadbook from a canned 390 s/km and passed no `startClockMin` at all. The lesser consequence: arrivals on the wrist were guaranteed to disagree with the crew sheet, whose goal and start-clock controls were screen-local state the push could not see — so `checkpoint_projection` on the phone and the watch's Roadbook page described different races. The greater: `_cutoffLimitS` can only resolve a `cutoff_clock` marker against a known gun time, so with a null start clock **every wall-clock barrier was dropped from the frame**. A race whose barriers are all "closes at 11:00" — the ordinary ultra case — pushed zero cut-off legs, leaving CutoffEta, SleepStation and the Roadbook page with nothing to project against. It was disclosed (`unresolvedCutoffCount` reaches a banner) but unfixable from that surface, which collected neither input.

Goal time, start clock and pacing model now live in one `RoadbookPlan` persisted per route in `SharedPreferences`, written by the crew sheet and read by the push. Device-local and per route, because a plan is one runner's attempt at one course, not a property of the shared route row. When no plan exists the push **asks**; a declined prompt sends the course alone rather than inventing a pace, because a schedule nobody chose is worse than no schedule — a cut-off margin is read as fact. The start clock stays optional (an elapsed-barrier race needs none) and skipping it costs exactly the clock-only cut-offs, which the existing banner already counts. Decode is fail-closed: an unparseable record reads as absent and re-asks. The pacing model is persisted alongside the other two for the same reason they are — "Even" on the sheet must not become "Effort" on the wrist.

The pinning test decodes the pushed bytes and asserts the crew sheet renders that same margin with its own independent formatter, so "phone and watch visibly agree" is tested directly rather than by proxy.

## 453. The barometric vert totals belong to the run, and a second run opens at zero

**Date:** 2026-08-02

`elevation::Reading`'s doc has always said "the run's cumulative ascent and descent". It was the power cycle's. `VertAccumulator::reset` had exactly one caller in the tree — its own unit test — and `app/src/tasks/baro.rs` builds the accumulator once at boot and never touches it again, so a second run's VERT row and the Elevation page's `D+`/`D-` opened holding run one's climb, directly under a sparkline (`Snapshot::elev_profile`, reset by `Recorder::start`) that correctly starts empty. Two numbers about the same run, on the same screen, disagreeing.

The reset is run-scoped rather than a fresh accumulator. `start_run` clears the totals and drops the deadband anchor — the anchor because it is what the next delta is measured from, so a sub-deadband climb left pending before the gun would bank into the new run's first sample — and **keeps** the complementary filter's bias. That bias estimates the atmosphere's offset from the barometer, not anything about the run; re-seeding it would step the published altitude and leave the seed window's samples of vert uncorrected at the moment a race starts. It is the rule `Recorder::start` already states for the sticky altitude and HR: a current reading is not run state. `reset` is replaced rather than kept beside it — it had no callers, and two ways to clear an accumulator whose difference is invisible at the call site is how the wrong one gets used.

The edge is taken off the run clock, not a state transition. The baro task sees the recorder only through `state::RECORD`, an `embassy_sync::Watch` that overwrites rather than queues, and polls it once a second between pressure samples — so an `Idle → Recording` edge can pass entirely between two polls and "entered Recording" is not a signal it can rely on. `Snapshot::elapsed_s` restarts at zero in `Recorder::start` and never goes backwards inside a run (`advance_now` clamps), so `elevation::run_restarted` fires on a clock that went back, however many states were skipped getting there — including the whole-recorder replacement a factory erase performs. A resume, an auto-pause and a signal void all keep the clock climbing and reset nothing. The first snapshot ever observed resets nothing either: the accumulator is already fresh at boot, and treating a mid-run subscribe as a restart would throw away a run's banked climb.

The sim cannot arm a second run — every scenario boots exactly one — so this is host-tested and build-verified only; the green `terrain` scenario shows the guard against a *spurious* reset, not the reset itself.

## 454. The roadbook page refuses a guessed position too, and fuelling falls back to the cadence rather than to an empty state

**Date:** 2026-08-02

§ 449 took `unwrap_or(0.0)` out of `cutoff_snapshot` and `sleep_snapshot` and left the same expression in `roadbook_snapshot` and `fuel_snapshot`, where it has the same cause and a quieter consequence. Both select by distance-along-course, so an absent position reads as the course start: a runner at km 180 gets the roadbook's first checkpoints with their plan-time safe/tight flags, and the Fuel page's carry-to-next-aid is the start line's. The reachable triggers are § 449's — a course pushed or rerouted mid-race, or a run that starts coursed and never gets a projectable fix.

`roadbook_snapshot` now takes `self.route_along_m?` and `Snapshot::roadbook_loaded` carries the presence bit exactly as `cutoffs_loaded` does: no roadbook pushed says `NOT SYNCED`, a roadbook with no position says `AWAITING FIX`, on the glance page and in a composed screen's slot alike. `available_pages` keys the page on that bit rather than on the projection, for § 449's reason — a page that left the cycle until the first fix would renumber every page behind it.

Fuel takes the refusal differently, and deliberately: it falls back to the **cadence basis** rather than to an empty state. There is no next aid to carry to without a position, but the drink/eat cadence needs none, is true whatever the sky is doing, and is the plan `alerts` is running on regardless — so an `AWAITING FIX` on the one page named FUEL would repeat exactly the defect § 444's cadence basis was added to fix. The header already names which basis the numbers are counted against, and the Roadbook page one tap away carries the `AWAITING FIX` that explains why.

`roadbook_glance` had no content test at all before this — the page that names three checkpoints, their projected arrivals and their cut-off flags was pinned only by the sweeps that walk every page for width and hero rules.

## 455. A composed screen declares the hero band it has always drawn into

**Date:** 2026-08-02

`face::body_top_row` returned 0 for `Screen1..4` — "a composed screen owns every row… Nav's rule, for Nav's reason". It is not Nav's case. Nav has no hero at all (`hero_metric` returns `None`) and genuinely writes row 0. A composed screen's lead slot is a three-row hero: § 364's `slot_placements` seats it in the 32x48 face at row 0 and labels it on row 3, and `no_layout_overruns_the_panel_or_eats_the_gps_row` has been reserving rows 0–2 for it since the day it was written.

Everything downstream reads the band off that table, so declaring 0 answered the wrong question twice. `ui_frame::hero_band` resolved slot 0 to `MedNumHero` while `slot_placements` asked for `BigNumHero`, so a Duo drew its lead value at **half** the size of the value beneath it — the inverse of the hierarchy the layout exists to state, and against the Duo's own documented claim of "both values in the 32x48 face". And `write_unfed` put an unfed screen's label on row 0, which `composed_screen` had already filled to `COLS` with the right-anchored state tag, so heapless refused the label whole and the page read `NOT SYNCED` with nothing naming what — on every even second, since the tag blinks. The existing test `an_uncomposed_screen_page_says_it_was_never_pushed` passed throughout because it only checked the reason row: a test that ran at the exact frame the label was dropped and asserted around it.

One line fixes both: the screen pages join the `TALL_HERO_BAND_ROWS` arm. The state tag moves with them, from row 0 to slot 0's label row — not cosmetics: `apply_hero_clearance` blanks any band row the hero's glyphs reach, and a ten-hour elapsed reaches 20 of the 21 cells, so leaving the tag on row 0 would have cost `REC` / `AUTO` / `PAU` on exactly the runs long enough to compose a screen for. That is the move every other tall page already made.

Host-tested, build-verified and sim-verified — all nine Renode scenarios pass, and `screens` shows the three seeded layouts still seating immediately after the Dashboard and rendering byte-distinct frames. No sim assertion reads a glyph, so the 32x48 *size* claim rests on the host rung plus the composed-screen previews `render/src/preview.rs` never had until now.

**A recent-pace window for the cut-off and sleep pages was considered and refused.** § 449 left the recency gap open deliberately; closing it was examined here and should not be built as specified. Web's `recentPaceSecPerKm` is not a shared parity helper at all — it is a `$derived.by` inside `/live/[id]` over a five-ping slice at a 5 s interval, a ~20 s window, returning null when the runner has not moved. So there is nothing to port, and a 30–60 minute ring with a stop policy and a void policy is a new estimator design, which § 24 says belongs on web first. Worse, it breaks § 373's central mechanic: the Sleep page exists to be read *while lying down for forty minutes*, and a recent-pace term would go `Unknown` exactly when it is being read, while the Cut-off page flipped to `BEHIND`. A twenty-minute canyon inside a thirty-minute window poisons the pace for thirty minutes *after* the fix returns, outliving the `route_position_stale` guard that exists for it. Even the apparently safe composition — "slower of `race_pace` and `recent_pace`", which would honour § 373's one-directional asymmetry — fails for the same reason it looks safe: a stop or a void makes the recent term slower than anything, so it is picked every time. RAM is not the obstacle (a 60-mark ring is 480 B); the semantics are. If it is wanted, web's window should first become a bounded *time* window that is explicit about a stopped runner, and the port should then use the inputs the phone does not have — `is_moving`, `signal_lost`, `route_position_stale` — to pause the window on a deliberate stop rather than read it as pace.

## 456. The watch's BLE status feed is its own connection, and a drop is a bounded reconnect rather than a lie

**Date:** 2026-08-02

§ 447 built `WatchLiveForwarder` but left the BLE subscription unwired: the firmware notifies one `link::status_frame` per second on the `frame` characteristic (read+notify) and the phone had no constant for it at all, with `check_watch_ble_uuids.mjs` recording the row as deliberately unclaimed — so the forwarder was reachable only from the dev TCP link.

**Its own connection object, not a method on `WatchBleTransport`.** Run sync scans, connects, pulls and disconnects per operation; status forwarding must hold the link open for a whole run, so a frame stream hung off the transport would tear the spectator feed down every time a sync finished. `ReactiveBleWatchFrameSource` therefore owns its own scan/connect/subscribe and duplicates ~30 lines of radio boilerplate rather than sharing a connection with the thing that exists to close it — and rather than refactoring a shipped, untested-by-design radio path that run sync depends on. The cost is named in the code, not hidden: two simultaneous `connectToDevice` streams against one watch is not something `flutter_reactive_ble` promises, and none of this can be run (§ 210 — no SoftDevice under Renode, no DK). Until a bench says otherwise the contract is that a caller driving both surfaces stops the status link around a sync.

**One decoder, not two.** `link.rs` makes the payload identical on both transports by design, so the BLE bytes go through the same `simWatchFrames` the sim's TCP link uses. That is what makes the line-oriented decode worth keeping over a packet-per-frame assumption: a notification normally carries exactly one newline-terminated frame, but a frame split across two, two frames in one, and a `FRAME_CAP`-truncated frame all resolve the same way.

**The reconnect is bounded, and it resets on evidence rather than on hope.** `WatchStatusLink` retries on the chest strap's existing ladder and gives up after a bounded number of consecutive failures, so a watch that is switched off costs the phone a bounded amount of radio. The attempt counter resets on a **decoded frame**, not on a successful open: a link that connects and drops before the watch has said anything is flapping, and resetting there would retry it at the bottom of the ladder forever. Giving up closes the frame stream, which is the one thing that reaches the forwarder as link-down; a transient gap deliberately does not, because a gap is what § 447's freshness rule already covers honestly.

**`stop()` closes the byte source before cancelling the subscription, and that order is load-bearing.** `simWatchFrames` is an `async*` generator suspended on `await for`, and cancelling a generator suspended at an await does not complete until that await does — so cancelling a still-live stream hangs forever. The first implementation had it the other way round and every test with a live source timed out; the test fake now closes its controller on `close()` so a fake can never hide the same bug again.

`frame` moved from `UNCLAIMED` into the guard's checked pairs, so all eight characteristics plus the service are now enforced against `ble.rs`. `UNCLAIMED` stays (empty) with `compareTables` taking both tables as parameters: a rule only exercised by the production table stops being exercised the moment that table stops containing an example of it, which is exactly what claiming `frame` did to it.

## 457. Health Connect imports carry the workout's GPS route, on Android only, when the separate route grant allows it

**Date:** 2026-08-02

The importer hard-coded `track: const []` behind a comment claiming Health Connect does not expose route geometry. That was true of older `health` releases and false of the pinned 13.3.1, which reads `ExerciseSessionRecord.exerciseRouteResult` and surfaces it as `WORKOUT_ROUTE`. (Issue #664 pointed at `run_screen.dart`'s `_LiveStats.empty` instead — the live-HUD sentinel, where an empty track is correct.)

Routes are joined onto workouts by `ExerciseSessionRecord` id, the uuid both point types carry. `WorkoutRouteHealthValue.workoutUuid` is a trap: the Kotlin map nests `workout_uuid` under `metadata` while Dart reads it top-level, so it is null on Android.

Reading a route written by another app needs `READ_EXERCISE_ROUTES` on top of the session read, and Health Connect withholds routes from background reads even when it is granted — so a route is treated as a bonus, never a precondition. `ConsentRequired` arrives as zero locations and the session is dropped from the track map, so its run imports summary-only exactly as before, and the import screen's "no map" note is now computed from the batch rather than asserted unconditionally, so it cannot contradict the maps a user can see.

Gated on `Platform.isAndroid`. The same `WORKOUT_ROUTE` type maps to `HKSeriesType.workoutRoute()` on HealthKit, so shared Dart would have silently widened what the iOS build collects and what its usage string and App Store Privacy Nutrition Labels must declare — a decision of its own, not a side effect of a twin file. iOS behaviour is byte-for-byte unchanged.

No new track storage was invented: `saveRunsBatch` already gzips a non-empty track to the `runs` bucket and writes `track_url`. Routed imports now also run `enrichMetadataWithEmbeddedBests`, matching the Strava importer.

**Pre-release gate:** declaring `READ_EXERCISE_ROUTES` requires updating the Play Console Health Connect data-access declaration, and Play Data Safety must reflect that imported location data is now collected on Android. **Deliberately not done:** the in-app route-permission request — the plugin never asks for `READ_EXERCISE_ROUTES` for read access, so the grant is user-driven from the Health Connect app today and imports degrade correctly until then. A native `PermissionController` bridge needs a new gradle dependency, `MainActivity` wiring, and an owner call on showing a second permission sheet.

## 458. iOS background sync submits a `BGProcessingTask`, not an app-refresh task

**Date:** 2026-08-02

`registerBackgroundSync()` ran on iOS but could never fire. The Dart side called `Workmanager().registerPeriodicTask`, which submits a `BGAppRefreshTaskRequest`; that request type is authorised by the `fetch` background mode, and `Info.plist` declared only `processing`. `BGTaskScheduler.submit` threw and workmanager swallowed the error, so the failure was invisible — "never runs" with nothing to see. `AppDelegate` compounded it by registering the periodic launch handler, which dispatches on the delivered task's type. Issue #664 framed this as missing plist declarations; they were present, and the code was the drift — an existing guard already asserted `fetch` must be *absent*, reasoning that the sync is a `BGProcessingTask`.

We fixed the code to match the plist rather than adding `fetch`. The sync batch-uploads gzipped GPS tracks: it needs network, runs past the ~30 s an app-refresh task gets, and is fully deferrable behind the foreground `SyncService`. That is the `BGProcessingTask` profile — it honours `requiresNetworkConnectivity` (which `BGAppRefreshTaskRequest` has no field for, so the existing constraint was being silently dropped) and needs no `UIBackgroundModes` entry beyond the `processing` already declared, preserving the app-store-privacy posture that the binary must not claim `fetch`.

iOS promises nothing about when the task runs, and it may never run. It is one-shot per submission, so it is re-armed on each launch; Android keeps its self-repeating hourly periodic job, selected by `Platform.isIOS` inside the unified twin file per § 39. The registration future is caught and logged so a failure stays invisible to the foreground app.

The identifier is a bare string in three files no compiler links, so two guard tests pin it: one parses the Dart constant, the plist array and the AppDelegate literal and asserts all three agree; the other pins the submitted request type against the declared background mode. Both only assert when run from `apps/mobile_ios` — `apps/mobile_android` has no `ios/` directory, so plist guards early-return there, which is itself worth knowing: a guard that early-returns is a guard that passes vacuously.

**Not verified:** the Swift is uncompiled and unrun. There is no Xcode toolchain here, and nothing in CI covers `apps/mobile_ios/ios` — the only `xcodebuild` job targets `apps/watch_ios`, and `security.yml` explicitly excludes this path from CodeQL. That `BGTaskScheduler` delivers the task, that the expiration handler fires, and that `setTaskCompleted` is reached are all unexercised; `BGProcessingTask` does not fire on the simulator at all.

## 459. The wrist honours `show_calories`, labels an unweighted estimate, and `gender` stays off the watch on purpose

**Date:** 2026-08-02

Issue #664 listed "real body-weight calories (70 kg hard-coded, no female calibration)" against Wear OS / watchOS / Garmin. Verification found the bullet largely wrong: Wear OS has synced `user_settings.prefs.body_weight_kg` since § 77 (parsed with a 20–400 kg sanity gate, threaded to `RunCalories.estimate`), and 70 kg is only the same documented fallback web and mobile use. watchOS and Garmin compute no calories at all, so nothing there could be hard-coded.

Tracing it surfaced a real defect the bullet missed. `show_calories` is a universal opt-out (default on) that exists so a weight-conscious runner can stop the app surfacing calorie figures — honoured on web `/runs/[id]` and mobile `run_detail_screen`, and ignored entirely by the wrist. An opted-out runner still got a kcal line after every watch-recorded run. The PostRun summary now reads the pref (only an explicit `false` hides, mirroring web's `!== false`) and omits the line when off. Separately, the wrist showed a bare `kcal` even when the estimate rode the 70 kg median the runner never entered; it now renders an `(est)` variant when `body_weight_kg` is unset, mirroring web's `caloriesLabel` / `caloriesEstLabel` split. New string in all six watch locales.

We deliberately did **not** ship `user_profiles.gender` to the watch to close the ~5 % female-calibration gap. Gender is Art 9 special-category data behind explicit `health_data_consent_at` and deny-by-default RLS; the wrist figure is display-only and never persisted, and run detail recomputes authoritatively with gender within seconds of sync. Broadcasting special-category data to an additional device class to adjust an ephemeral glanceable number fails data minimisation (GDPR Art 5(1)(c)). Making the number honest and respecting the opt-out is strictly better for the runner than making it 5 % different. Recorded in `RunCalories.kt` so it is not "fixed" later. Don't re-litigate by adding `gender` to the prefs bag for the calorie estimate; if some future feature independently justifies gender on the wrist, it needs its own consent gate.

Known limitation, shared with every universal pref on the wrist: `show_calories` lands via `applyUniversalPrefsAsync` on session restore, so a cold start with no connectivity falls back to the default (on) until the first successful fetch — the same lifecycle as `hr_zones`, `preferred_unit` and `body_weight_kg`, which a persisted prefs cache would fix together.

Worth a future revisit: § 77 cites Ten Haaf & Weijs (2014) for the 0.95 female constant, but that paper predicts *resting* energy expenditure, not the cost of locomotion. The better support is the running-economy literature (J Appl Physiol 2020, PMID 32702267: ~6 % lower gross oxygen cost in speed-matched women, allometrically scaled). The constant is unchanged; only the citation is weak.

## 460. The watch's live relay is a screen a runner opens, not a background service

**Date:** 2026-08-02

§ 447 built `WatchLiveForwarder` and § 456 built `WatchStatusLink`, and nothing constructed either: the rail was fully tested and completely unreachable, so a watch-recorded run still had no spectator. `WatchLiveScreen` is the production caller, reached from **Settings → Integrations**, beside the chest-strap and treadmill tiles. That is the app's only surface that already means "a BLE peripheral this phone talks to", and it is where a runner already goes before a run; `DevicesScreen` lists account sign-in rows rather than peripherals, and the Sim Watch screen is gated on a loopback backend so it cannot be a user's answer. The run screen was rejected because a watch-recorded run is precisely the case where the phone is *not* recording.

**Screen-scoped, deliberately.** The relay lives exactly as long as the route is mounted; leaving stops the link and concludes the broadcast. Outliving its surface would need a foreground service of its own, and a runner would have no way to tell whether their position was still going out — the failure mode `live_freshness` exists to prevent, moved from the spectator to the runner. Starting is an explicit tap, never automatic: a position leaving the device is a consent action, matching the run screen's "Share live link".

**The five states are derived, not invented.** `Not connected / Connecting / Live / Gap / Gave up` come from `WatchStatusLink.state` and `WatchLiveForwarder.linkFreshness()` and nowhere else, and the freshness line reuses the spectator page's own `freshnessFor` labels, so a runner checking their phone reads the staleness their followers read (§ 447). A gap tears nothing down; only the exhausted ladder does, and that is what reads as `Gave up`, which offers a retry joining the **same** run rather than minting a second link. The repaint is driven by a 1 Hz ticker because freshness ages with the wall clock — with no ticker a link that went quiet would keep reading `Live` until a frame that is never coming arrived.

**§ 456's stop-around-sync is code, not a comment.** "Sync runs from watch" pauses the status link, runs the sync on its own transport, then arms a **fresh** link — a spent one is never restarted — while the forwarder keeps its run id. Two simultaneous `connectToDevice` streams against one watch stays unverified *and* unrelied-upon: the design never holds both at once.

`SettingsIntegrationsScreen` gained a `settingsSync` parameter for one reason: `LiveBroadcaster` needs a real `privacyZonesProvider` or the Go-hub transport has no privacy-zone enforcement at all (§ 33). A relay wired without it would publish the runner's home.

**Testing note.** Cancelling a subscription to the `simWatchFrames` `async*` stream never completes under the widget tester's fake-async clock, which is why `watch_status_link_test.dart` (a plain `test()`, real zone) never saw it. Every teardown path in the widget tests runs inside `tester.runAsync`, and `pumpAndSettle` is banned by the 1 Hz ticker.

## 461. Health Connect's route grant is asked for by name, and needed `FlutterFragmentActivity` to be askable at all

**Date:** 2026-08-02

§ 457 left the in-app route-permission request undone and named the fix: a `PermissionController` bridge. Building it surfaced why nobody had noticed the grant was missing — **no Health Connect permission could be granted at all.** `MainActivity` extended `FlutterActivity`, which extends `android.app.Activity`; the `health` plugin's `onAttachedToActivity` does an unguarded `(activity as ComponentActivity).registerForActivityResult(...)`. Because a fresh engine attaches to the activity *before* `configureFlutterEngine`, that cast throws from inside `GeneratedPluginRegistrant.registerWith`, whose generated template catches and logs every plugin registration. So the app did not crash: the plugin's launcher stayed null, `requestAuthorization` returned `false`, and the import screen reported "permission denied" without a sheet ever appearing. Import and the HealthKit-style write-back were both dead. The plugin's README has required `FlutterFragmentActivity` since v4; nothing in this repo said so. `MainActivity` is now a `FlutterFragmentActivity`, which is also the only way `registerForActivityResult` exists for our own bridge.

`HealthRoutePermissionBridge` requests `PERMISSION_READ_EXERCISE_ROUTES` and nothing else — not `READ_EXERCISE` (already held wherever the bridge is reachable), and explicitly not background access, which would buy nothing because Health Connect withholds routes from background reads regardless. It binds the androidx constant rather than a copied literal, so the string it sends cannot drift from the one the manifest and `res/xml/health_permissions.xml` declare; a Dart guard pins all four together, since a permission that isn't declared is refused with no dialog and no error a runner can act on.

**The second sheet is offered, never sprung.** Tapping "import" behaves exactly as before. The plugin renders `ExerciseRouteResult.ConsentRequired` as a `WORKOUT_ROUTE` point with zero locations and emits nothing for `NoData`, so an empty route point is proof that a map exists and was refused — the only state in which asking would buy the runner anything. Only then does the card grow a count and a distinct "Allow map import" button. Refusal is an ordinary outcome: the offer clears and every import stays summary-only.

A grant **backfills** rather than asking for a re-import. `isCrossSourceDuplicate` lists `healthconnect` in `kAggregatorSources` and compares same-source pairs, so re-importing skips every workout already stored and the tracks would never land — the grant would have been a dead end. Only trackless Health Connect runs whose session released a track are rewritten, re-running `enrichMetadataWithEmbeddedBests` so a backfilled run is indistinguishable from a first-time routed import. Runs that already carry geometry are never overwritten: Health Connect is not authoritative over a track the runner already has.

**Pre-release gates,** unchanged from § 457 and now load-bearing: the Play Console Health Connect data-access declaration must cover `READ_EXERCISE_ROUTES`, and Play Data Safety must reflect that imported location data is collected on Android.

**Not verified:** nothing ran on a device. The Kotlin was type-checked with `kotlinc` against the real `flutter_embedding` and `connect-client` artifacts and the compiled constants read back out of the bytecode, but no APK was built locally — `flutter build apk` fails at *baseline* here on a third-party plugin's own build file under a three-month-old local SDK — so CI's APK job is the first real Gradle compile. The `FlutterFragmentActivity` switch is a startup-path change that wants a device smoke test of launch, deep links and the share-target intents.

## 462. The watch's config page ping-pongs across two, sealed last, selected by successor generation

**Date:** 2026-08-02

§ 451 declined ping-pong for the `RCF1` record and named the reason the *page* still owed it: `rewrite_config_page` erased the single 4 KiB config page before rewriting it, so a brown-out inside the 85 ms `tERASEPAGE` took **every record at once** — the GNSS mode, the BLE bond, the marked waypoints, the ICE card, the composed screens, the armed timer and the race config. Seven, not the six § 451 counted; that text was already off by one when it was written. On a watch whose premise is multi-day ultras on a cold battery, that is the failure worth engineering against, and it is a page-level defect rather than one record's.

**Two pages, not a journal.** Both linker scripts carve 8 KiB instead of 4; the run region's base and every slot offset are byte-identical, and the S140 occupies the *bottom* of flash, so the extra page comes out of the app's own span (503 KiB free on the BLE build, 704 KiB on the default — measured, not assumed). This is the run store's own `SlotDir` idiom rather than a second mechanism: the settings deserve the protection the track already has, and a log-structured store would need compaction, a free-space policy and a recovery scan for a page rewritten a few times a race.

**The seal is written last, and it is what makes a page live.** Each record already carries its own CRC, so a torn *record* reads as absent; what a page of independent records cannot say about itself is "all of them landed". A 16-byte `PGN1` seal at the page's last word says exactly that and nothing more — it deliberately does **not** re-cover the record bytes, which would need the whole 4 KiB image in RAM at write time and would duplicate seven CRCs to catch nothing they miss. A failed record write returns early and leaves the seal unwritten, for the same reason a brown-out does.

**The selector asks for the successor, not the greater.** § 451 compared record *bytes* for equality precisely because ordering a wrapping counter goes wrong at the roll, and that reasoning survives here: a rewrite always stamps `live + 1` onto the other page, so two sealed pages differ by exactly one, and "which is the other's immediate successor" is an equality test on a wrapping difference. `u32::MAX → 0` is decided correctly with no epoch, no RFC-1982 half-space convention, and no window a long-lived device could age out of. A `>` would read the roll backwards and hand the rest of a race the settings from before it — the property suite finds exactly that, reporting `u32::MAX` as its minimal failing seed.

**A pair where neither succeeds the other resolves to page 0, not to defaults.** That state is unreachable from this writer. Answering "no live config" would nonetheless be *unrecoverable*: the next write would go to page 0 at generation 0 and leave the same undecidable pair, forever, with the runner's settings silently never persisting again. Page 0's records are CRC-valid bytes this firmware really did write, and one write from there restores the invariant. Fail-closed is right for a corrupt record; it is wrong for a store that would otherwise never heal.

**`plan_factory_erase` grew to cover both pages**, and its host test now walks every record offset on *every* page: the superseded page holds a full previous copy of everything, the bond's long-term key included, until the next rewrite lands on it. A wipe taking only the live page would leave the last-but-one of the runner's medical card and the LTK readable by a probe.

Sim-verified only for the **alternation**: the `idle` scenario reads the driver's own seal line back across the GNSS ladder and asserts each rewrite lands on the other page at the next generation, and mutating the planner to keep the live page fails it, naming the erase. That the mechanism *works* is not sim-verifiable at all — Renode's flash is plain memory behind an NVMC model that swallows `ERASEPAGE`, so a torn erase cannot be staged. **That is a bench item.** § 451's endurance argument is unchanged and now doubled: each page takes half the erases.

## 463. The along-course axis inherits the course's topology, and the forward bias may never outrank the geometry

**Date:** 2026-08-03

The nav task's forward-progress anchor (`prev_along`, the bias `Course::project_from` layers over the ported `snapToPolyline` geometry) was reset on exactly one event: a course push. Every *other* way a runner can arrive back at the start of a loaded course — which for a backyard ultra is every hour, for days — left the anchor reading the full course length while the runner stood metres past the corral. `Course::project_from` charged each candidate segment on the raw along-gap from that anchor, so the true segment cost `ALONG_BACK_BIAS_PER_M × L` while the finish segment cost only the runner's distance from the line. Measured on a 6.706 km square loop: the finish segment stayed cheapest until **3.1 km into every lap**, publishing `along_m` a lap ahead the whole way and `off_m` as the distance from the corral — 1,676 m at the first corner. `! OFF CRS` latched on a runner who never left the course, and `set_route_position` fed that along-distance to cut-off ETA, the roadbook, the fuel plan and the sleep-station budget, all four computing from the far end of the course. No test walked a second traversal, so none of it was visible.

**The reset hook is the wrong fix, and this is the interesting part.** "Who resets the anchor, and on what event" has no good answer: the nav task does not know about laps, a backyard runner may press nothing at the corral, a lap is not a lap of the *course* on a multi-lap track session, and a run that is stopped and restarted at the start line never touches the nav task at all. Every candidate event is a proxy for the thing that actually happened, which is that the runner passed the point where the course's along-axis wraps. So the projector is told the topology instead: a course whose ends meet within `LOOP_CLOSURE_M` (the off-course threshold — inside it, a runner standing at the finish also projects on-course at the start, so the two ends are one place as far as anything downstream can tell) has a *circular* along-axis, and the gap is measured the short way round it. Nothing needs telling that a new lap started, because on a circle nothing did.

**The charge is also bounded, which is the half that holds when loop detection does not.** The bias exists to break a tie between candidates the geometry cannot separate; charged on the raw gap it grew without bound, so a stale anchor could outrank kilometres of perpendicular offset. It now saturates strictly below `MAX_ALONG_BIAS_M` — the 20 m re-arm radius — which buys an invariant rather than a smaller number: no candidate more than that far off the nearest one can ever win, so **a runner within the re-arm radius of the line cannot be reported past the off-course threshold by the bias at all**. The function is strictly increasing, so it orders two candidates exactly as the raw product did; what is bounded is the bias's authority over the geometry, not its direction. That covers the loop whose GPX ends 60 m apart and misses the closure test, and it covers the case the loop wrap cannot: a canyon dropout that puts 3 km of honest progress between two fixes used to buy 150 m of equivalent offset, enough to hold the projection on a leg the runner left half an hour ago. Two rows of the pinned max-capacity projection table moved as a result, and both were the bias buying a segment *further from the runner* — one of them reporting a fix 33.4 m from the course as 51.4 m off, an excursion the bias invented.

**A circle leaves exactly one pair indistinguishable, and only continuity separates them.** At the shared start/finish vertex, `along = 0` and `along = total_m` are the same place, carry the same offset and sit the same wrapped gap from any anchor. Neither segment order settles it: the earlier representative is the honest read when a run *starts* on the line, the later one when a lap *finishes* on it, and a fixed tie-break gets one of the two wrong (both were tried; each broke a real case). `ALONG_CONTINUITY_PER_M` charges the *unwrapped* gap at 1e-6 m per metre, which resolves the pair toward continuity with the last reading and is far too small for the geometry to notice — a whole 100 km lap of unwrapped gap buys 10 cm of offset.

**The antimeridian, in the same branch, is the same shape of defect one layer down.** Every local planar frame in the position pipeline begins by subtracting two longitudes and calling the result metres east, which is wrong by a whole turn across 180°. A course straddling the line read 532 m off itself at the crossing and 3,087 m off a kilometre past it; a runner across the line from a course that stays east of it read 38,310 km off, a permanent `! OFF CRS`; and the Nav map was gone entirely, its bounding box spanning 359.92° so the panel fit's scale collapsed to a dot. The trigonometric formulae were never affected — `sin` and `cos` are periodic, so the haversine lengths, great-circle bearings and turn-cue headings were all correct, which is why the course's total length was right while its geometry was not. `watch_core::geo` owns the normalisation and every planar frame in the position pipeline takes its deltas through it (the course projection's per-segment frame and snapped point, the course bounding box and the panel fit's pixel transform, the trackback breadcrumb's origin frame, the recorder's per-segment hop — where a 4 m stride across the line read as 40,000 km, failed the implausible-jump cap and re-anchored mid-stride). It is identity, bit for bit, for any pair inside a hemisphere.

**The parity ports keep the bug on purpose.** `watch_core::route_geometry` is a one-way port of web canonical code, tested case-for-case against the web suite, and the originals carry the identical defect: `apps/web/src/lib/routes/route_geometry.ts` lines 93–95 and `route_snap.ts` line 83, plus their Dart twins `route_geometry.dart` 94–96 and `route_snap.dart` 100. Fixing the watch's copy would break the port without fixing the product, so it is left alone and the web↔mobile pair — which is an enforced lockstep, and a two-platform change — is reported for triage rather than widened into here. `course.rs` is different: it is the live nav path, its `project_from` bias was already declared watch-local and outside the `snapToPolyline` port, and the loop wrap is a concept web has no equivalent of — so it diverges deliberately, in the manner § 305 established for a port that must.

**Verification: host-tested + build-verified.** Eighteen tests, including the two the issue named as missing — a second traversal of a loop walked end to end through `project_fix`, and a course straddling 180°. Every one that pins a behaviour change was confirmed to fail against the arithmetic it replaces before the fix landed — four against the unbounded linear bias, one against a zeroed continuity weight, seven against the unnormalised longitude delta. The whole workspace builds and the `clippy -D warnings` gate passes for `thumbv7em-none-eabihf`. Nothing here is sim-verified: the Renode fixtures carry no multi-hour clock and no course near the antimeridian, and the canned sim course is a three-point rectangle edge that never closes, so a second traversal is not stageable there without a new fixture. Bench verification of the loop case needs a runner doing two laps of a pushed course, which is a tier-1 checklist item, not a claim this branch may make.

## 464. A refused phone push answers on both sides — one banner vocabulary on the wrist, one status characteristic to the phone

**Date:** 2026-08-03

All five phone→watch pushes are latest-value, so a refusal leaves the PREVIOUS value armed — and only `course` said so. `workout`, `roadbook`, `screens` and a settings queue with no room reached a `warn!` down a debug cable no runner carries, so a phone re-pushing a corrected roadbook mid-race that failed CRC left the runner racing the OLD cut-offs while the phone said "sent" (issue #664). The fix is one path, not four copies of § 400's: every outcome — accepted and refused alike — funnels through `state::note_push`, shared by the radio task's five characteristics *and* the sim transport's UART settings path, and stamps a `ble_sync::PushOutcome { seq, kind, accepted }`. `Alert::CourseRejected` generalises to `Alert::PushRejected(PushKind)`, keeping § 400's precedence (between cutoff and storm) and its re-queue, and rendering `! SET / CRS / WKT / SCR / RBK FAIL` — the frame's own three-letter tag, all five exactly filling the ten-cell band. The sequence moves on acceptance too and the wrist adopts that silently: § 400's rule stands that a confirmation banner teaches runners to wait for one that failure also never showed.

**The phone half needed a new characteristic, because the write response cannot carry the verdict.** `writeCharacteristicWithResponse` is answered by the SoftDevice out of the attribute table before `gatt_server::run`'s handler decides whether to keep the value, and `nrf-softdevice` gives the application no way to fail a write at the ATT layer — so the phone's "sent" was always a transport fact and never an application one. Extending the 1 Hz `link::status_frame` JSON was rejected on measurement: its `heapless::String<256>` already carries a ~215-char worst case and a push object is ~40 more, so the frame would truncate into invalid JSON — and it rides a *separate* connection the caller stops before a push anyway. So `push_status` takes the next free suffix (`..e9`, never renumbering a row above — § 410), **read** rather than notify: a read is one request/response inside the connection the phone already opened to push, with no subscribe-before-write ordering to get wrong on a path that can never be simulated (§ 210). The phone samples the sequence before its writes and polls it after; a moved sequence for that kind is the answer, and a refusal throws `WatchPushRejected` into the failure path every call site already had. **Silence is deliberately *unconfirmed*, not *failed***: an unmoved sequence, an undecodable value, or a read that throws all leave the push completing as before, because this path has never run on hardware and must not be able to turn a working push into a reported failure. A null pre-push read abandons confirmation outright rather than guessing, since a stale refusal read as this push's verdict would send a runner to re-push what is already loaded.

**The wrist stays silent for a push refused while idle, and that is the right split.** The alert slot is a run surface (§ 375 records the same for a lapsed countdown), so a rejection at the start line raises no banner — but the runner pushing from the start line is holding the phone, which now names the refusal, while the wrist banner covers the case the phone cannot: a mid-race re-push with the phone back in a drop bag. A third standing row on the idle face would duplicate the phone's answer at the cost of a row § 399 already spends.

Build-verified and host-tested (the funnel, the vocabulary, the codec both directions, and the phone's poll); **never sim-verified and never bench-verified** — Renode models no SoftDevice, so the only part of this that runs today is the sim's UART settings refusal.

## 465. A banner hands the page back before the next one takes the slot, and the sim waits on that promise in the firmware's own seconds

**Date:** 2026-08-03

Four times now a Renode scenario has gone red on `main` waiting for `record: alert cleared` — the record task's `Some -> None` transition, which is the only evidence the harness has that the panel is showing a page rather than a banner. Each time the fix was to unarm one rail for one scenario: `b2901442a` booted `alerts` course-free, `cad5fd1e9` gave `storm` and `workout` a quiet slot, `b7acc95ab` took the demo workout off `storm` as well. Each closed one symptom and left the next scenario to be caught the same way; `terrain` and `pages` had never been through the cycle at all and so still booted with all three rails armed. Issue #664 is `terrain` and `alerts` failing on runs that touch no firmware.

**The engine never promised the thing the harness was waiting for.** `AlertEngine::on_update` expires the active banner after `ALERT_TTL_S` at the top of the call and then, at the tail of the *same* call, promotes whatever is queued — and §214's re-queue rule deliberately keeps a displaced fuel reminder, storm, cutoff, off-course, lost-run, course-rejection or thinned-track notice queued rather than dropping it. So with anything owed at every expiry the slot went straight from one banner to the next, `on_update` never returned `None`, and the transition the harness waited on could not occur. Measured on `main`, a `terrain` run holds the slot **17–30 s of firmware time** with three or four banners chained and no clear between them; the harness allowed 30 s. That is not a margin, it is a coin toss decided by how fast Renode's virtual clock happens to be running.

**Which is the second half of the disagreement: the harness measured a firmware schedule in wall seconds.** `ALERT_CLEAR_TIMEOUT` was `time.monotonic()`-based, and Renode's virtual clock runs at a ratio to wall time that swings with host load — the same reason `WORKOUT_SKIP_MAX_GAP_S` and `dropout`'s void are already measured on the decoded stream's own stamps. On a 16-core workstation `terrain` passed 20 of 20; pinned to a single core, which is the closest thing here to a loaded `ubuntu-latest` runner, it failed 2 of 2 with issue #664's exact message. The wall deadline was reporting a busy runner as a broken alert engine.

**The firmware side is the honest root cause, so that is where the gap went.** A queued alert now waits `ALERT_QUIET_S` (3 s) after the previous banner's TTL expires — anchored on when the TTL ran out, not on when the record task's tick noticed, so a coarser cadence cannot stretch the silence. This is a product fix before it is a test fix: on a 168x96 1-bit panel the banner is a solid inverse-video band over the two hero rows, which are the distance and the pace, and a runner holding three owed reminders had them covered continuously for as long as the arms kept arriving. A banner is designed as a transient; this is what makes it one. The gap holds the **queue** only — an arm that calls `take_slot` (zone excursion, corral whistle, workout edge, waypoint answer) still displaces whatever is up the instant its event happens, because those are worth nothing shown three seconds late.

The cost is named rather than hidden: a distance or time **milestone** that comes due inside the gap is now dropped, as it already was when the slot was busy. The slot is deliberately empty rather than occupied, but the rule is the same one — a milestone is meaningful only where it is reached, the totals are on the page, and losing "5 KM" occasionally is a better trade than never seeing the pace again. Three host tests pin the new contract: the bare page through the whole gap, an event alert still pre-empting inside it, and — the one the sim rests on — a 1 Hz feed with something owed at every expiry still reporting an empty slot within `ALERT_TTL_S + ALERT_QUIET_S`.

**The harness now reads that promise instead of guessing at it.** `wait_for_no_alert` reads `ALERT_TTL_S` and `ALERT_QUIET_S` out of `core/src/alerts.rs` rather than copying them, and judges the wait in firmware seconds taken off the decoded stream, so a slow runner costs wall time and nothing else while a real regression still fails — naming the constants it was measured against. `dump_quiet` is the single acquisition every page dump shares: wait for the slot, dump, then re-read the slot, because `record: alert` is the record task's line and the banner is painted by the screen task, so an alert raised while the DumpFrame is in flight lands on a frame the wait had already called clear. Five dump sites were doing the wait with no such check and would have passed on a dump of a banner.

**And the per-scenario patches are folded into one declaration.** `SCENARIO_ARMED_RAILS` says what each scenario needs armed; the launcher flags are derived, so every rail a scenario does not name is switched off for it. That inverts the default the three earlier patches kept losing to: a rail added to `SCENARIO_RAILS` is off everywhere until the scenario that asserts on it opts in, instead of being armed in eight scenarios that never mention it. `pages` and `terrain` keep the course as a **data** need — RouteElev's presence bit is the sim course's per-point elevation and the climb crest is read off the same profile — so they keep the two course-driven alert arms, which is exactly the case no launcher flag can arrange away and the engine's guarantee has to cover.

**Verified.** 129 host tests over `alerts.rs`, the new one checked to fail as well as pass: with the gap removed it reports the slot occupied for 591 s straight, which is the starvation stated as a number rather than as a risk. The one-core reproduction that failed 2 of 2 on `main` passes 24 of 24 after (`terrain` 10, `alerts` 7, `pages` 7), and all nine scenarios pass end to end unpinned. Not verified: nothing about this ran on silicon, and the sim models no power — that a runner reads the hero band in the three seconds it comes back is a bench observation, not a sim one.

## 466. Mobile learns whether Pro is sellable from the web build's capability manifest, and treats "don't know" as "don't sell"

**Date:** 2026-08-03

Web has refused to sell a hollow subscription for a while: `/settings/upgrade` computes `proSellable = coachEnabled() || routeGenEnabled()` and renders a "coming soon" teaser with donations as the primary CTA when neither perk is live, pinned by a `security_guards.test.ts` guard that names the un-gated case a consumer-protection / chargeback risk. Mobile shipped the other half of that deploy with the purchase tile gated on nothing but a double-submit flag. On a rock-bottom deploy — `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` unset so `/api/coach` 503s, the route engines deferred so `/api/routes/generate` 501s — web teased and the phone took the money for a subscription with no perk behind it. `paywall.md` had recorded mirroring the gate on Flutter as a followup; it was a live defect, not a nicety.

**The flags are web-deploy env, so the channel has to carry them rather than restate them.** `PUBLIC_COACH_ENABLED` and `PUBLIC_ROUTE_GEN_ENABLED` are read from `$env/dynamic/public` and baked into the web bundle at build. A Flutter binary sitting in the App Store has no server-rendered env and no remote-config service in this stack; the only build-time channel it has is `--dart-define`/dotenv, which is exactly the wrong shape — an APK built in April cannot learn that Coach went live in June, and worse, cannot learn that it went away. A build-time copy of a deploy-time flag is the defect with an extra step. Supabase was the other candidate and knows nothing about either perk: both live behind AWS Lambda env, so a `feature_flags` table would be a second source of truth an operator has to remember to flip.

So the web build publishes what it already knows. `/app-capabilities.json` is a prerendered endpoint — the `/sitemap.xml` idiom, a plain file in `build/`, served from S3 with no Lambda invocation — whose body is `{coach: coachEnabled(), route_gen: routeGenEnabled()}`, calling the **same** two gate functions the storefront card calls. There is no second flag to keep in sync: flipping the env and redeploying web moves both storefronts at once, and a guard pins the manifest to those imports so a hand-rolled copy can't drift in later. Neither value is a secret — both are `PUBLIC_` flags already in the bundle every visitor downloads. The mobile app reads it from `WEB_BASE_URL`, the origin it already calls for `/api/coach` and `/api/coach/route-describe`, so no new host, CloudFront behaviour, Lambda, or Terraform is involved. The release workflow gives the file the short HTML-style `cache-control` instead of the immutable-asset one, because a year-long cache would keep phones selling a perk the operator has switched off.

**Unknown and not-live are deliberately the same answer.** `fetchProPerks` never throws: an unreachable host, a timeout, a non-200, a non-JSON body, a missing field, and a truthy-but-not-boolean field all resolve to `ProPerks.none`, and the screen holds the teaser until the manifest lands rather than starting from sellable. That costs an offline user the ability to start a subscription, which is close to free in practice — a StoreKit / Play Billing purchase needs the network anyway — and buys the property that matters: a client which cannot establish that a perk is live never takes a payment. `_startProCheckout` carries the same test as the render branch, so a future caller cannot route around the hidden tile.

**Restore purchases and Manage subscription stay reachable in both states.** They are not sales; they are the paths an existing subscriber needs to re-link a purchase or cancel one, and Apple Guideline 3.1.1 and the Play subscription policy require them regardless of whether the storefront is currently selling. Hiding them along with the CTA would strand exactly the users a deploy that stopped selling is most likely to have.

Mobile is now precisely as fresh as web and no fresher — both read the same flag from the same deploy, so a key pulled without a redeploy misleads them identically. Closing that gap means moving the truth to the server that owns the key, which is a larger change than the storefront needed and is not owed by this one.

## 467. The wrist's finished track is a file path, and its spoken splits are the runner's own unit

**Date:** 2026-08-03
