From inside the firmware a dead feed and a runner standing still are the same observation — the recorder auto-pauses either way — so the `workout` scenario, whose steps end on distance and on time-while-moving, waited out its whole 300 s budget after four fixes and reported a broken workout runner. The feed now survives a failed write by reopening the pty and says so on stderr (which `ci_smoke.py` folds into `sim-output.log`), and `gnss_silence_s` lets a scenario tell the two apart: virtual seconds between the newest decoded line and the newest published fix, measured on the firmware's own clock for the same reason `dropout` measures its voids that way. `dropout` is the one scenario it must never be applied to — its voids *are* the subject.

The same scenario had a second version of the bug. Its auto-advance deadline was `WORKOUT_STEP_TIMEOUT * WORKOUT_AUTO_STEPS` = 720 s against a 300 s budget, so the outer budget always fired first and the careful per-transition diagnosis underneath was unreachable in CI. The deadline is now re-armed on each transition, which both fits the budget and is the more honest bound: what is being asserted is that *a* step settles, not that four do inside one window. **An inner deadline longer than the outer budget is not a deadline.**

**The mobile sync test.** `sync_service_test.dart` fired `debugOnConnectivity` and called `pumpEventQueue()` between two connectivity events. The cycle does real disk I/O, and `pumpEventQueue`'s fixed round trips are a proxy for it, not a wait on it — so under load the second event landed while `_syncing` was still true, hit the reentrancy guard, and the test read one batch push where it expected two. The same overrun wrote the synced-ids sidecar *after* `tearDown` deleted the temp directory, which is where the suite's long-standing "Failed to persist synced ids sidecar" noise came from: a fire-and-forget that outlives its test is the same defect wearing a different hat. `debugOnConnectivity` now returns the cycle's future. Production is untouched — `Stream.listen` discards the returned future, so the observer still returns at its first await point.

The rule the three share: **a readiness or completion check must name a signal that only the thing being waited on can produce.** An intermediary's error, an event-loop turn, and a clock are all cheaper to observe and all answer a different question.

## 577. The recap's best streak belongs to the recap period, and a streak that reaches the period counts at its full length

**Date:** 2026-08-10

[§ 569](#569-the-recap-reads-one-column-of-a-lifetime-and-every-column-of-a-year-because-only-the-streak-looks-outside-the-period) named this one and deferred it. `buildYearInRunningRecap` handed the whole run set to `computeRunStreaks`, which clamps at the anchor day and nowhere else, so `bestStreakDays` was the runner's **all-time** best wearing the period's label. A 40-day streak from 2024 was the headline number on a card titled "My 2026 in running", earned the `streak-30` trophy on that card's grid, and shipped in the public share image — on a year the runner might have run three times. § 569 was right that this is a product decision about what the number claims rather than a fetch optimisation, and that the Dart twin has to move with it. This is that decision, with the twin.

**The rule is neither "all of history" nor "the year alone".** `computeRunStreaks` takes an optional `bestSince`, and a streak counts toward `best` only if it reaches that local day or later — but a qualifying streak counts at its **full** length, days before the bound included. So the 28 Dec → 3 Jan streak is still seven days on the January card, which is what § 569's three boundary tests pin, and it is why the split fetch that entry introduced is still necessary rather than now redundant: the out-of-period `started_at` values are exactly what give a boundary-spanning streak its length. A streak that ended before the period contributes nothing, and a period with no runs reports 0 rather than the 1 a non-empty day set used to floor it at.

**The bound is a test inside the existing walk, not a second pass over spans.** `run` is the length of the streak ending at the day being visited, so admitting the maximum only on days at or after the bound does both halves at once: it admits a streak the moment it reaches the period, and it records that streak's full length, because `run` keeps growing to the streak's end and the end is the largest key. `current` needs no bound — it is anchored at the period's last day and can only be non-zero by reaching it. The dashboard omits `bestSince` entirely and keeps the all-time best it deliberately went to SQL for in [§ 471](#471-the-best-streak-sub-label-reads-a-local-day-sql-aggregate-that-takes-the-source-filter-and-a-failed-fetch-suppresses-the-claim).

## 578. Along-route projection ranks its candidates in one frame, because a per-segment frame makes the numbers incomparable

**Date:** 2026-08-10

`distanceAlongRoute` projected the runner's live fix onto each segment in a local planar frame anchored at that segment's own start — correct, and the same construction `route_snap` uses — but then ranked the candidates by the perpendicular measured *inside* each of those frames. Those numbers are not comparable: each is scaled by the cosine of its own segment's start latitude. On an out-and-back the two limbs are the same ground twice over, and the return limb anchors further along, so it reports the smaller offset to a point that is exactly as far from both. On a 3.5 km out-and-back, moving the input 1 cm sideways moved the answer 3.5 km, onto the wrong limb — and the consumers are the spectator page's next-cut-off card, the mobile cut-off ETA, and the turn-by-turn cue announcer, all of which read that number as "where on the course is the runner".

The fix is the one `route_snap` already made: convert the projected foot back to lat/lng and rank on the great-circle distance to it, so every candidate is measured on the sphere. The per-segment frame still does the projection, where it is anchored and accurate; only the comparison moves. Coincident limbs then tie bit for bit and the first-match-wins walk resolves them stably, which is the property the pinning test asserts — a fix on the line and a fix 1 cm off it must not name places 3.5 km apart. Ranking two limbs of an out-and-back is genuinely ambiguous; producing a *different* ambiguous answer for every centimetre of GPS jitter is not.

## 580. `event_pricing` gets one non-partial unique index, because a partial index is not an upsert target

**Date:** 2026-08-11

`event_pricing` shipped with two partial unique indexes — one `where instance_start is null` (at most one series price per event), one `where instance_start is not null` (at most one override per occurrence) — because a plain unique constraint treats NULLs as distinct and would have allowed unlimited series rows. The invariant was right. The index shape made it unwritable: Postgres will only infer a **partial** index as an `ON CONFLICT` arbiter when the statement itself carries a `WHERE` clause matching the index predicate, and PostgREST never emits one. So `setEventPricing` raised 42P10 on every call, on both branches, and had done since `20261229_001`. A price could never be attached to an event; `events-checkout` requires an `event_pricing` row; the whole paid-registration rail was unreachable behind a UI that looked finished.

**`NULLS NOT DISTINCT` states the same invariant in an inferable shape.** One non-partial `unique (event_id, instance_start)` where the NULLs collide gives exactly the two guarantees the pair of partial indexes gave, and being non-partial it is a legal arbiter, so the caller stops branching and always names the composite target. The alternative considered was a stored generated `instance_key` (`coalesce(instance_start, '-infinity')`) under a plain unique — it also works, and was verified to work, but it rewrites the table, adds a column every client's generated row types would carry, and leaks a sentinel into a value clients read. The index property is the smaller change and the truer statement of the rule.

**What let this live for months is the more useful finding.** `paid_events_test.sql` inserted into `event_pricing` three times and never once through `ON CONFLICT`; no e2e called `setEventPricing`. The tests exercised the table, not the statement the app actually sends — and a plain `INSERT` succeeds against the broken index shape, so every one of them passed. A conflict target is part of the query, not part of the schema: **a test that writes a row a different way than production does has not tested the write.** `event_pricing_upsert_test.sql` now runs the exact PostgREST-shaped statement, as the organiser so the RLS write policy is in the path, through the insert and update branch of each shape.

**Amendment (2026-08-18).** This ADR's suite proved the arbiter was *inferable* — both upsert branches resolve instead of raising 42P10 — but every assertion in it ran as the organiser through `ON CONFLICT`, which left two properties the same objects owe unpinned. First, that the unique still *constrains* a plain `INSERT`: the service role, the seed, and `rls_events_test` all write `event_pricing` without a conflict target, and nothing stopped one of them planting a second series row. `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` is what makes the two NULL `instance_start` rows collide; under a plain unique they are distinct and the insert lands. Second, that a non-organiser cannot price an event they do not run — every prior assertion only showed the policy letting the *right* caller through, so a fully widened write policy failed nothing. Both are now pinned, and both were verified by mutation. The generalisation of this ADR's "a test that writes a row a different way than production does has not tested the write" is its mirror: **a suite that only ever exercises the authorised caller has tested the happy path, not the policy.**

## 581. An event instance is a point in time, so comparing two of them as strings is a bug the type system cannot see

**Date:** 2026-08-11

A recurring event's occurrence is identified by its start timestamp, and that timestamp reaches a client in two renderings of the **same instant**: PostgREST serialises `timestamptz` through Postgres' own JSON cast (`2026-06-01T18:00:00+00:00`), while anything derived from a `Date` is `toISOString()` (`2026-06-01T18:00:00.000Z`). Both are `string`, both are ISO-8601, and `===` between them is always false. Five comparisons across three files had it: the per-instance pricing lookups in `events-checkout`, `events-cancel`, and `fetchEventPricing`, plus the cancelled-occurrence lookup and the instance-pinned club-post filter on the event-detail page — where `activeInstance` genuinely carries both renderings depending on whether it came from `expandInstances` (a `Date`) or `event.next_instance_start` (the DB).

On the money path the failure is silent and one-directional: a per-instance override never matches, so checkout charges the series price and cancel reads the series refund policy — and an event priced *only* per-instance 404s `event_not_priced` and falls back to `no_refund`, denying a refund the host granted. It was latent only because `EventEditor` never wrote a per-instance row, which is a UI accident, not a guarantee.

**Server-side filters were never affected** (`.eq('instance_start', …)` hands the string to Postgres, which parses both forms to the same value), which is exactly why this class hides: the same value compares correctly in SQL and incorrectly in JS, so the bug is invisible in every query and lives only in the client-side reduce afterwards. The fix is a shared `sameInstant` — one in `apps/web/src/lib/social/event_instance.ts`, its twin in `apps/backend/supabase/functions/_shared/event_instance.ts` — that parses before comparing and treats an absent or unparseable side as *unknown* rather than as a match, so a bad parse falls through to the series default instead of charging an override's price off it.

## 582. A wedged sim guest is named by the harness, and only the wall clock can notice one

**Date:** 2026-08-11

The `storm` scenario went red on a PR that touches no firmware ([#752](https://github.com/Absence0760/project-running/pull/752); web share lookups, `api_client.dart`, docs). The reported failure was `expected the tracker's first measured tendency … no decoded log line matched /baro: storm (\w+) delta=…/`, which reads as a storm-classifier regression. The classifier was innocent. The firmware had stopped executing at t≈19 s — the log ends mid-run, Renode's own log goes silent for the remaining 287 s, and the `dev-blink` LED task stops toggling with everything else, so it is the whole executor that stopped, not one task. The harness then spent its full 300 s budget waiting and blamed whichever assertion happened to be holding the wait. Tracked as [#754](https://github.com/Absence0760/project-running/issues/754); the corrupting write is still unidentified.

**Liveness has to be measured on the wall clock, which is the opposite of every other silence measure in the harness.** `GNSS_SILENCE_S` — and `dropout`'s void reasoning — deliberately measure in the firmware's own virtual seconds, because the gaps they reason about are gaps the *firmware* saw and the two clocks drift apart under host load. That choice is right for them and useless here: a guest that stops executing stops stamping lines, so its virtual clock freezes with it and no virtual-time measurement can ever observe the stall. Only real time distinguishes *stopped* from *quiet*.

**The threshold is measured, not chosen.** Across all nine scenarios the widest gap between consecutive decoded lines is **1.01 s** — the baro task samples at 1 Hz and stamps a line every tick under `DEFMT_LOG=debug`, and that holds through the longest and quietest runs in the set (`idle`, 138 s; `dropout`, 120 s, whose GPS voids are its whole subject and still never quiet the stream). `defmt-print` writes through Rust's line-buffered stdout, so a line reaches the harness as soon as it is decoded rather than a block later. `GUEST_WEDGED_S = 90` is therefore ~90x the widest legitimate gap; a false positive needs a minute and a half of genuine silence.

**Two checks, because one of them cannot fire in time.** The 90 s check runs *during* a wait so an egregious silence stops burning budget. But a wait whose own timeout is shorter than 90 s would expire first and misattribute again — so the deadline path asks the same question at a lower bar (`LINE_CADENCE_S = 5`, ~5x the measured worst gap) and reports a wedge instead. The deadline path is consulted only on a run that is failing regardless, so it cannot turn a pass into a failure; the live-stream message now says so explicitly ("the firmware was running and the claim genuinely failed"), because the value of naming a wedge is only realised if the other branch is equally unambiguous.

**Two supporting changes, and one honest limitation.** The sim jobs now stage the firmware ELF into the artifact directory (staged rather than added as a second upload path, which would move the artifact root to the common ancestor and reshuffle every scenario subdirectory) — #754's symbols had to be resolved against a locally rebuilt binary and *hoped* to match. And `HardFault` now reports its stacked frame before halting, where cortex-m-rt's default is a silent infinite loop; it halts rather than resets because a reset boots a clean watch and erases the evidence. **It would not have caught #754**: Renode returns 0 for reads outside any modelled peripheral and keeps executing, so the corruption seen there never raises a fault. That handler is for the bench, and for telling a fault from a deadlock when there is one.

## 583. The panic that cannot name itself is made to, and the first attempt destroyed its own evidence

**Date:** 2026-08-11

[#713](https://github.com/Absence0760/project-running/issues/713) panics with `RefCell already mutably borrowed` inside `embassy_sync::watch`'s generic code. All 37 `Watch`es in `state.rs` monomorphise through that one line, so the message names a source location and nothing else — not which `Watch`, and not whether the borrow flag held a legitimate count or something that was never a count. Those two readings are the whole question: the first is a logic bug, the second is the corruption [#754](https://github.com/Absence0760/project-running/issues/754) shows. Twelve local reproduction attempts came back clean against a CI rate near 1 in 30, so waiting to catch it live is a poor bet. The firmware is made to explain itself on the next natural occurrence instead — the same wager as [§ 582](#582), one layer down.

**`panic_probe` is replaced rather than wrapped**, because a `#[panic_handler]` is singular and there is no hook to add to. The first two statements reproduce its behaviour exactly: the message still contains "panicked" (the substring `sim/ci_smoke.py` scans every scenario's log for) and the halt is still a halt. What is added is a dump of every `Watch`'s first and last two words, and interrupts are masked first so the snapshot is coherent.

**The first attempt dumped every byte of every `Watch` and lost the thing that mattered.** defmt-rtt's ring overwrites oldest-first when the host has not drained it, and a panic emits everything at once with no opportunity to drain in between. 37 full structs overran it: of 38 lines, **5 survived**, and the casualty was the `panicked` line itself — which would have turned a panic into a scenario failing on some unrelated assertion, the exact misattribution § 582 was written to stop. The fix is two-sided and both halves are load-bearing: the dump is **three words per `Watch`** rather than whole structs, and the message is emitted **last**, because under an overwriting ring what is printed last is what survives. Measured, not reasoned: the bad version printed 5 lines and no `panicked`, the current one prints 37 and one.

**Which three words is a hedge, and it is worth being honest that it is one.** `RefCell`'s borrow flag is `Cell<isize>` (align 4) beside a `WatchState` carrying a `u64` (align 8), so the compiler may place the value first and the flag after it; the first word covers flag-at-front, the last two cover flag-at-back with or without trailing padding. Every `Watch` read `0x00000000` in the first word of a quiescent dump, which is **consistent with** the flag living at offset 0 but does not prove it — an attempt to pin it by panicking from inside a live borrow was abandoned after the scaffolding proved unreliable under repeated emulation. So the dump's job is to hand a reader three concrete words per `Watch` and let them reason, not to decode the flag itself.

**A `Watch` absent from the macro's list is invisible in the dump**, since `no_std` cannot iterate statics and each is named by hand. `sim/test_watch_dump.py` fails if `state.rs` declares one the list omits (or lists one that no longer exists), runs under the same `unittest discover` § 582 added to `build-firmware`, and was verified to fail as well as pass by dropping a name and watching it go red.

## 584. A paid order names one instance, and a client cannot write the two columns that decide money and attendance

**Date:** 2026-08-11

`enforce_paid_order_for_priced_event` (20261229_001) validated the cited order on `id`, `buyer_user_id`, `event_id` and `status = 'paid'` — but never on `instance_start`, even though `event_orders.instance_start` is `NOT NULL` and `events-checkout` creates exactly one order per occurrence. So an order bought for one Wednesday satisfied the gate for every other Wednesday in a recurring series.

**The grant half was a half-finished lockdown, and that is the more interesting failure.** 20270102_001 set out to make `attendance` and `order_id` service-role-only, and its own comment says so. It rewrote the **UPDATE** grant per-column and left the table-level **INSERT** grant alone — and a table grant implies every column. The invariant `event_attendance_test.sql` pins against a direct UPDATE was therefore reachable through INSERT, and re-reachable after an organiser correction via DELETE + re-INSERT, since both are own-row verbs. Verified on the local stack under the buyer's own JWT: one $22 order seating two instances, the second carrying a self-written `attendance = 'attended'`.

**The fix is three narrow changes, and the third is deliberately redundant.** Bind the order to its instance; split the INSERT grant the way UPDATE was split; add a partial unique index on `event_attendees(order_id)`. With the instance predicate and the `(event_id, user_id, instance_start)` primary key the index is already implied — it exists so a future path that forgets the predicate cannot silently re-open the hole. Stating an invariant at the schema level is cheaper than re-deriving it.

**Refunds needed the same "which occurrence" thinking.** `handleOrderRefunded` read only `charge.payment_intent` and treated every `charge.refunded` as terminal, but Stripe emits that event for a partial refund too. A $5 goodwill refund on a $50 workshop flipped the order to `refunded`, deleted the seat, and let `promote_event_waitlist` hand it to someone else. `event_orders_status_check` has carried `partially_refunded` since the table was created and nothing ever wrote it — the intent to distinguish the two was already on record, only the code was missing. Unknown amounts fall back to `full`, which is the historical behaviour and the safe direction for the buyer.

## 585. A read that exists to hide something is not allowed to answer questions about it

**Date:** 2026-08-11

20260915_001 revoked `EXECUTE` on `clip_track_for_user` from `anon`, reasoning that the RPC "lets a determined attacker iteratively probe the clipping output to reconstruct approximate privacy-zone geometry". It kept the grant for `authenticated`, for "in-DB callers with a user JWT".

**That distinction does not hold.** Signup is free and unthrottled, so `authenticated` is not a trust boundary against someone who wants a stranger's home address. The function trims *leading* in-zone points, so a three-point probe returns two when the probe is inside a zone and three when it is outside: a clean one-bit oracle. Roughly forty calls binary-search a zone centre to metre precision, and the radius follows. It is a PostgREST RPC, so none of the Edge Function rate limiting applies.

**The revoke was safe only because the last client caller had already died.** Web's `clipTrackForUser` was the one direct `.rpc()` site, and the unclipped-blob pattern it belonged to was removed by 20260619_001 — it survived purely because `security_guards.test.ts` pinned its fail-closed body, which kept it looking load-bearing. A guard test on dead code is worse than no test: it argues for keeping the code. Both are deleted; every remaining consumer is SECURITY DEFINER or service-role and never needed the caller to hold the grant.

**Two smaller instances of the same shape landed with it.** `heatmap_points_in_bbox` gated on `is_public` alone while its sibling `discoverable_routes_in_bbox` and the `public_routes` view both also require `shadow_hidden = false`, so a moderator-hidden route kept drawing heat for anon viewers. And `recompute_challenge_completion` checked `challenge_badges` for an existing award, then inserted the badge `on conflict do nothing` and the notification unconditionally — the check and the insert are not one atomic step, so two racing callers both reached the tail and the badge deduped while the notification did not. The badge insert is now the serialization point: `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` leaves `FOUND` false, so exactly one caller proceeds.

## 586. A rejected GPS fix must not move the anchor it was rejected against

**Date:** 2026-08-11

Both native watch apps computed the per-fix haversine delta, credited it only inside a 2–100 m band, and then advanced the anchor **unconditionally**. A sub-2 m hop was therefore discarded rather than deferred, and that ground could never be recovered.

**The floor exists to reject noise, and advancing the anchor is what turns it into a filter that rejects signal.** GPS streams at 1 Hz, so a runner power-hiking a climb at 1.4 m/s produces about 1.4 m per fix — every one under the floor. A two-hour hike accrued 0.00 km. Holding the anchor is precisely what lets two such fixes sum to 2.8 m and count, which is the whole point of a distance threshold: it is a threshold on the *baseline*, not on the sample rate. With noisier fixes the error does not vanish, it changes sign — biased down while walking, up while standing still.

The canonical Flutter recorder had it right all along (`_lastTrackedPosition` is assigned inside the accepted branch), and so does the firmware, whose comment reads "keep the anchor so the next good fix measures from the last trusted position". Two ports drifted from a rule both references state explicitly. Both now carry the Flutter recorder's re-anchor escape as well, so a >100 m hop after dropped fixes cannot freeze the anchor the other way (#330).

**watchOS had a second window with the same shape.** `updatePace` walks the in-memory track backwards until 200 m accumulate and divides by the timestamp span, and `resume()` cleared only the distance anchor. After a twenty-minute aid-station stop the window crossed the pause: ~200 m over ~1300 s displayed 1:48:35 /km and fired a false "too slow" alert, self-correcting only after 200 m of post-resume running — on every stop, for the whole race. This is issue #371's defect, which was fixed for distance, given its own test file, and never applied to pace. When a fix is described as "clear the stale anchor on resume", it is worth asking which anchors exist.

## 587. A fix that introduces a new state must be followed to every predicate that reads the old one

**Date:** 2026-08-11

An adversarial review of §584–§586's own commits found that three of them were wrong or incomplete, and the pattern is worth naming because it is not carelessness in the small — each individual change was correct in isolation.

**`partially_refunded` is the clearest case.** One change taught the Stripe webhook to tell a partial refund from a full one, writing a status the CHECK constraint had always allowed and nothing had ever produced. A second change, *in the same PR*, gave `enforce_paid_order_for_priced_event` its `instance_start` predicate — and left that predicate's `o.status = 'paid'`, which had been correct for as long as the status was unreachable. The composition made a registration the first change deliberately KEEPS into one the second rejects: the instructor could no longer mark that attendee present, and `promote_event_waitlist` raised inside an AFTER-DELETE trigger, rolling back the seat release that provoked it. The rule is that introducing a value into a domain obliges you to find every predicate over that domain, not just the ones you edited.

**The other two are the same shape at smaller scale.** `markManySynced` was hardened to compare object identity, which is exact for the drain paths it was written against and can never match on the import paths, because `save()` stores a stamped copy rather than the caller's instance — so imported runs stayed unsynced forever. And the watch re-anchor escape was added to stop a >100 m hop freezing the anchor, but was written as `else if` on *any* rejected delta, so it also fired on the sub-2 m hops whose deferral is the entire point of the accompanying fix.

**Three tests asserted things that were true regardless of the fix.** `off_m` is assigned from `haversine_metres(fix, foot)` and its guard asserted it equalled that same call — `|0| < 1e-3`, unfailable, and the only guard on the metric. Both antimeridian tests were built from unwrapped longitudes and a zero-area spur, so one failed pre-fix only on a floating-point cancellation margin and the other passed pre-fix outright. **A test written alongside a fix should be run against the code without it.** That is now the habit: every regression test in the follow-up was verified by reverting its fix and watching it fail.

**And one claim was simply false.** §586's commit asserted web's `run_stats` haversine clamped and Dart's did not. The opposite was true — both used the unclamped `atan2` — so "fixing" Dart left the pair divergent with the NaN moved onto web. The lesson is narrow and practical: when a parity-pair claim names which side is wrong, read that side, not a sibling module with a similar function. `route_geometry.ts` does clamp, which is almost certainly what was read.

## 588. A typed comma is a decimal point, and a filter that drops it multiplies the number

**Date:** 2026-08-11

The mobile distance field carried `FilteringTextInputFormatter.allow(RegExp(r'[0-9.]'))`, which is not a validation rule so much as a silent edit: it deletes any character outside the class as the user types. On a German, Spanish, French or Portuguese keyboard the decimal key is a **comma**, so "5,2" became "52" before `double.tryParse` ever saw it and a 5.2 km run was stored as 52 km. Nothing rejected it, nothing warned, and the run detail screen then rendered the corrupted figure back as fact. Fields with no such filter failed the other way — `double.tryParse` returned null and the value vanished, which is what happened to every manually-typed food macro and to the WS100 weigh-in weight. Five of the seven shipped locales are comma-decimal, so this was the default experience for most of the non-English catalogue.

The fix is one reader, `parseTypedDecimal`, plus the input filter that lets a comma reach it, applied at every site that parses a `TextEditingController`. Several call sites had already grown an ad-hoc `.replaceAll(',', '.')`, which is the right instinct and the wrong scope: it fixes the sites someone happened to notice, and it corrupts "1,234.5" into an unparseable "1.234.5". The shared reader resolves grouping the way a person reads it — of two separators present the rightmost is the decimal point, and a separator that repeats can only be grouping. Where a single separator is genuinely ambiguous ("1,234" is 1234 in en-US and 1.234 in de-DE) it reads as the decimal point, because the damage is asymmetric: reading a mistyped weight as 1.234 kg is a value the user can see is wrong, while reading it as 1234 kg is the thousandfold error this ADR exists to prevent.

**No web twin is owed.** Web's numeric fields are `<input type="number">`, where the browser parses per the user's own locale and hands `.value` back in canonical dot form — a `parseFloat` there is already locale-correct, and this helper would be a second, worse parser. The obligation is instead a pair of source guards: one fails the suite on `double.tryParse` applied to `.text`, the other on an input filter that admits `.` but not `,`. Machine-formatted numbers (CSV, Strava exports, API JSON) deliberately stay on `double.tryParse` — there a comma is a delimiter, not a decimal point.

## 589. A date stepped by a fixed 24 hours is not a date, and the fifth occurrence bought a guard

**Date:** 2026-08-12

`DateTime.add(Duration(days: n))` on a local `DateTime` adds absolute time. A local calendar day is 23 or 25 hours across a DST transition, so a midnight cursor stepped this way lands at 23:00 the *previous* day on a fall-back — the calendar day repeats, the last day of a window is never produced, and every offset past the transition is shifted by one. Web's `Date.setDate()` normalises through the calendar and has no equivalent defect, so each occurrence is also a twin divergence.

The plan-detail week strip is the one that prompted this. Its seven cells were `startDate.add(Duration(days: weekIndex * 7))` plus `add(Duration(days: i))`, which in the week of a fall-back emits the sixth date twice and never emits the seventh — the long run, on a Sunday-ending plan week, simply is not in the ribbon. A plan whose start is a transition or more behind the current week loses the hour up front instead, shifting all seven cells onto the wrong days. Both were reproduced under `TZ=America/New_York` and pinned as widget tests.

**The sweep found ten more, and that is the part worth recording.** `recap._mondayOf` bucketed that week's runs onto the previous Sunday, splitting the "top week" the recap reports across two buckets — and it is half of a declared parity pair whose web side had always used `setDate`. The dashboard heatmap derived a grid start ~5 months back, so it crossed a transition every time and every column of the year's contribution grid — and the week a tap resolved to — sat one day off the calendar. The nutrition day window computed an exclusive end that landed at 23:00 of the same day, hiding the last hour's entries. The period-summary pager stepped its anchor by 168 hours, drifting an hour per transition until it crossed midnight and skipped a week. And `activity_timeline_list` compared a midnight `day` for equality against a "yesterday" that was no longer midnight, so the **Yesterday** heading silently stopped appearing for a week. The project had already fixed this same shape in `goals.weekStartLocal`, `streaks._previousLocalDay`, `recurrence._addDaysCalendar` and `plan_week` (issue #338), each time with a comment explaining it, each time only where someone happened to look.

Four fixes in four places is a pattern; the fifth buys a guard. `calendar_day_arithmetic_guard_test.dart` fails the suite on any `.add`/`.subtract(Duration(days:))` under `lib/`, and the interesting part is what it does *not* report. A `DateTime.now()` or `.toUtc()` receiver is an instant with no local midnight to drift off, so those are exempt structurally. Everything else — a rolling 90-day fitness cutoff, a Health Connect query bound, a ten-year recurrence horizon — opts out with an inline `// elapsed-time:` marker naming the reason. The marker is deliberately local rather than a file-level allowlist: `nutrition_meal_detail_screen` and `period_summary_screen` each carry both shapes in the same file, and an allowlist keyed on the path would have gone on covering the next offender added to them.

**The guard is the timezone-independent half.** The widget tests only reproduce the drift in a zone that has the transition, and CI runs in UTC, where they hold trivially — so a behavioural test alone would have been a permanent no-op on the machine that matters. The source guard catches the shape wherever it runs; the widget tests document what the shape costs. `run_intensity` stays on absolute arithmetic on purpose, because its web twin computes `nowMs - windowDays * 86_400_000` and a calendar step there would create the divergence this ADR is about removing.

## 590. A recovery prompt must prove the run still needs rescuing, and an absent track is not an empty one

**Date:** 2026-08-12

The Wear app checkpoints an in-flight run every 15 seconds so a killed process can be recovered. `checkRecovery` offered that checkpoint whenever one was on disk, which quietly assumes the only reason a checkpoint survives is that the run was lost. It is not, and the consequence is destructive rather than merely redundant: `saveRun` sends `Prefer: resolution=merge-duplicates` and the track goes to `{uid}/{run_id}.json.gz`, so recovering a run the app already captured does not create a second run — it overwrites the first.

Two paths reached it. A run banked into `LocalRunStore` by the normal stop path but not yet drained keeps its checkpoint if the process dies before the service's `NonCancellable` clear lands; accepting the prompt then replaced the queue entry's final distance, duration and laps with a snapshot up to an interval older. Worse, once the run *had* drained, `pushRun` deletes the track file as its last act — and `sealTrackFile` stubbed a missing file into `[]`. So the recovery uploaded an empty array over the finished run's Storage object and upserted the stale summary onto its row, and the runner's only evidence was a distance that had shrunk.

The checkpoint is now graded before it is offered. Already in the queue, or track file gone, means the run is captured somewhere strictly better than this snapshot, so the checkpoint is dropped without a prompt. A checkpoint belonging to a *live* recording is neither offered nor cleared — clearing it would disarm the safety net of a run still in progress, which is the opposite failure. The grade is taken again when the runner accepts, because `bootstrapAuth` drains the queue on the same cold start: a run that was merely queued when the prompt appeared can be uploaded, and its track deleted, while the prompt waits for a tap.

**The narrow rule underneath is that absence is not a value.** `[]` is a factual claim that the run had no points, and publishing it destroys whatever is already in Storage under that id. Sealing now returns null for a missing file and the caller declines to recover. This is safe to read as "already uploaded" rather than "indoor run with no GPS" because `TrackWriter.open` creates the file at run start and indoor mode seals a real `[]` stub through `close()` — a legitimate in-flight run always has a file. Where the two are genuinely indistinguishable (an OS cache purge, which reclaims `cacheDir` under storage pressure and is its own open finding) the fail-closed choice loses a summary rather than a track.

**The ordering that made the checkpoint droppable is fixed alongside it.** The service cleared the checkpoint inside its own teardown, concurrently with the ViewModel's queue write and immediately before `stopForeground` dropped the process out of foreground-service state — the exact moment the OS is most willing to kill it. A kill landing between the two erased the queue entry and the snapshot that would have rebuilt it, and the run was gone with nothing left to report it. The clear now belongs to the writer: `handleFinishedRun` clears only after `store.save` returns, so the safety net outlives the run it protects. The reason it can move is the grading above — the worst case flips from losing a run to a checkpoint outliving a banked one, which is graded `Discard` and dropped without a prompt. That the service no longer needs a `NonCancellable` coroutine to make its own clear durable is a consequence, not the point.

This also softens, without closing, the finding that a `Finished` stage can go unobserved when the activity is gone: the run is still not banked, but the checkpoint that would have been cleared underneath it now survives to offer it back.

## 591. A food diary that only knows today cannot be corrected, and the day it shows must own every window

**Date:** 2026-08-13

`/nutrition` derived every window it needed from `new Date()`: the day's food, the runs and gym sessions behind the exercise add-on, the seven trend buckets, the water counter's storage key, and the `href` on each meal header. Nothing else in the stack was today-locked — `/nutrition/[date]/[slot]` had always been parameterised by date, and `createFoodEntry` / `logMealTemplate` / `logRecipe` had always accepted a `started_at`. The consequence is the one failure every food diary has to survive: a day you forgot to log can never be corrected, and the per-slot detail route, though date-shaped, was only ever linked with today's date, so no other day was reachable at all.

The day is now a `?date=` query parameter, and the URL owns it. That is what makes a corrected day linkable, makes the browser's back button step days, and keeps `load()` and every write path reading the same value the header shows. `resolveDiaryDate` is deliberately fail-closed on both halves: a malformed value resolves to today rather than to an empty day the user cannot explain, and **a future date is clamped rather than honoured**. Refusing the future is not tidiness — a `started_at` ahead of now sits outside every "today" window the app has (the rings, the dashboard nutrition card, the Coach's 7-day rollup), so an entry filed there would be a row the product can never show back to the person who wrote it.

**The write timestamp is a contract, not a formality.** On today it is simply now, so meal ordering keeps its real clock time. On an earlier day it is the same wall-clock time on that date — inside the day in every case, and monotonic across a session so several back-filled items keep the order they were entered. It is resolved at **save** time rather than when the composer opens: a composer opened at 23:59 and submitted at 00:01 would otherwise stamp the entry onto the previous day while the page had already rolled over to the next, filing it exactly where its own host can no longer show it.

Two smaller things were fixed on the way in because generalising them would have spread them. The day windows step through the calendar (`new Date(y, m, d + n)`), never by a fixed 24 hours — [§ 589](#589-a-date-stepped-by-a-fixed-24-hours-is-not-a-date-and-the-fifth-occurrence-bought-a-guard) records what that costs, and the mobile nutrition day window is one of the ten it caught. And membership of a window is now decided by comparing **instants**: the page had been comparing `started_at` to the bound as strings, but Postgres renders the timestamp as `…T04:00:00+00:00` while the bound is built as `…T04:00:00.000Z`, and `'+'` sorts below `'.'`, so a row landing exactly on a local-midnight window boundary was silently dropped.

The water counter's localStorage key keeps its shipped **unpadded** `2026-8-3` shape rather than adopting the zero-padded date the rest of the module uses. Padding it would have been tidier and would have orphaned the count of everyone who had already drunk something on the day this shipped. The ugliness is bought deliberately and documented at the one function that produces it.

One limitation is accepted rather than hidden: `fetchGymWorkouts` has no date window (its run sibling does), so the page pulls the newest 50 sessions and filters. A diary day older than the caller's 50 most recent lifts contributes no gym calories to that day's add-on. That is an under-read identical in effect to "the lift isn't logged yet" rather than a wrong kind of number, and closing it means widening a shared data-layer function; it is tracked in `followups.md`.

## 592. A plan wizard that never looks at what the runner already runs, and the two directions of "wrong volume" are not one question

**Date:** 2026-08-13

`generatePlan` sizes every week from the goal race, the training days and the fitness anchor. It has never read a single one of the runner's actual runs. So a runner averaging 20 km a week could generate a marathon plan whose week 1 asks for 38.0 km — 1.9x their current load, on day one — and the wizard showed that number in its outline with nothing beside it to compare against. The opening step is where a plan injures someone, and the app already owned a tested policy for exactly this shape of question.

**The bands come from `coach_load`, not from new numbers.** A plan week *is* an acute (7-day) load and the runner's trailing 28-day average *is* the chronic base, so `plan_ramp.ts` runs the ratio through `injuryRiskBand` — the same helper the coach roster classifies athletes with. § 162 put that policy in one place deliberately, on the reasoning that a band edge which drifted between two surfaces would mislabel the same athlete's risk twice; inventing a second threshold set for the wizard would have been the drift that ADR exists to prevent.

**What is shared is the policy and its constants, not the population underneath them.** `plan_ramp` narrows the pool it measures three ways, each deliberate and each wizard-specific. It counts **running only** — cycling is excluded, matching `goals.ts` and `fitness.ts`, because a bike ride is not running volume and letting one inflate the chronic base would make an oversized opening week read as safe, the single direction this check must never fail in. It **counts a DNF'd run**, and that is the same rule rather than an exception to it. The rule is *count the running distance the legs actually covered, and never count distance they did not run* — a bike ride is out because none of it was run, a race abandoned at 30 km is in because all 30 km of it was. Nothing rewrites `distance_m` when the flag is set: every writer of `is_dnf` is a post-hoc toggle on an already-recorded run (the web run-detail edit form and its mobile mirror; no importer mints one, and the race-results importer carries a test asserting it does not), so the stored distance is what the runner covered before stopping. The roster's rationale — "not a training stimulus the athlete **completed**" — is about crediting a finished effort, the same instinct that keeps a DNF out of the PR table, and it does not transfer to a question about tissue loading. Excluding them would understate the base of exactly the runners most likely to carry one, and warn a high-volume ultra runner off a plan their history comfortably supports — a warning that fires when it should not being the failure this entry has already named. And it says **nothing at all** below three of four active windows. The roster RPC does none of the three: `20270314_001` records that it applies no `activity_type` filter *on purpose*, so a coach's chip agrees with the athlete's own dashboard load, and it excludes `is_dnf` runs instead; nor does it require a minimum history, so it will band an athlete off a single run in the window where this note stays silent. So a runner who also cycles, who DNF'd, or whose month is sparse can read a verdict here that their coach's chip would not compute over the same 28 days. The band edges are guaranteed identical; the population behind them is not, and claiming otherwise would be a promise the code does not keep. Both narrowings belong at this call site rather than in `coach_load` — the roster's job is to describe an athlete's actual load, this one's is to decide whether a plan is safe to start.

**The two directions are graded off different weeks, and this was wrong first.** *Too much* is a question about the first step, so `elevated` / `high` grade the opening week. *Too little* is a question about the whole plan, so `under` grades the **peak** week. The first cut graded both off the opening week, which is backwards: every well-formed plan opens far below its own peak — the generator's week 0 is 0.6x — so a runner already training at the plan's peak volume was told the plan was too light for them. A 55 km/week runner building that same marathon plan has an opening ratio of 0.69 and a peak ratio of 1.07, and now correctly hears nothing at all.

**Silence is a feature in two places.** Below three of the four trailing windows carrying a run, the check refuses to speak: ACWR needs ~28 days of *consistent* history to mean anything, and without the gate a runner with one 3 km jog in a month divides a C25K opening week by a 0.75 km base and is told their beginner plan is a high injury risk — the exact runner the walk-run plan exists to protect. And `matched` renders nothing, because a note that fires on every plan is one a runner learns to skip; the check earns its place only when it has something to report. The `under` variant is additionally withheld from a beginner walk-run plan, which is *meant* to be gentle; the safety warnings still show there.

**This is not the § 144 P2 gate.** That gate covers health-derived load — HR / TRIMP through TSB / ATL / CTL — feeding a training *prescription*. This reads plain non-cycling distance totals, the same distance-proxy load § 162 already surfaces to coaches, changes no prescription, persists nothing and logs nothing. Treadmill runs count here even though they are barred from anchoring fitness, because a belt kilometre is real load even when it is an unreliable pace. Web-only and deliberately not a parity pair: mobile's wizard has the same blind spot, but a twin nothing renders is dead code, so the mirror is a tracked follow-up rather than a second copy to keep in lockstep.
## 593. A curated catalogue nobody can browse is a catalogue of things you have already found

**Date:** 2026-08-13

§ 233 shipped the free-standing `global_segments` catalogue with two surfaces: the run-detail "Famous segments" chips and a `/segments/[id]` detail page. Both are reachable only by having ALREADY run the segment — the chip appears because the backfill matched your track, and the detail page is where the chip points. So the curated layer built for a fresh market with zero routes could only be discovered by a runner who had, by coincidence, run one of its geometries. Two comments in the tree name a browse page that was never built: the migration documents `region` / `country_code` as the coarse filter columns "on the browse page", and `fetchGlobalSegmentsWithError`'s doc comment carries a browse-page error contract for a caller that did not exist. The fetcher had zero UI consumers.

**Filtering is client-side, and that is a property of the fetch, not a shortcut.** The catalogue is bounded by `GLOBAL_SEGMENT_SCORING_LIMIT` (500 rows) and already pulled whole on the run-detail scoring path, so the browse page pays a round-trip it was going to pay anyway and then filters in memory. A server-side `ilike` search over 500 rows would need a new index and a new RPC to be slower per keystroke. The bound is the real constraint: when the catalogue outgrows 500 rows the FETCH is what has to change first, and the filter follows it — so putting the search on the server today would be building the second half of a migration whose first half has not started.

**Two properties of the shaping are worth stating because getting them wrong is invisible.** The text fold (NFD decompose, drop combining marks, lowercase) is applied to both sides of every comparison and is character-wise, so it can only ever widen a match — an ASCII keyboard reaches "Champs-Élysées" and the accented spelling still finds it. And every numeric order puts an absent or unparseable value LAST, including the descending ones: a segment with no recorded elevation must never be presented at the top of a most-climb sort. Both are pinned in `catalogue_browse.test.ts`, along with the coercion of the stringly `numeric` columns PostgREST hands back — sorted as text, `"857"` is longer than `"2135"`.

**The page is deliberately not in the global nav yet.** The only navigational slot that fits is `RunSurfaceTabs`, a shared four-tab strip rendered by every run surface; widening it is a change to `/runs`, `/routes`, `/plans` and `/races`, not to segments. Discovery today is the two pages that already name the catalogue: the run-detail block gains a "Browse all" link, and `/segments/[id]`'s back-link — which pointed at `/dashboard`, a Back arrow to a page the reader had never been on — now names and returns to the catalogue. The nav slot and the sitemap/SEO question (the catalogue is public, world-readable, crawlable content) are tracked in `followups.md`.

**Web-only on purpose.** Mobile carries the `computeGlobalSegmentEffort` twin but no catalogue UI of any kind, so a Dart twin of the browse shaping would be a dead file with no consumer; per § 24 the mirror lands when the mobile surface does. The round also closed a unit bug the browse page would have copied: `/segments/[id]` hard-coded a metres suffix on elevation, so a runner on miles read a climb in metres beside a distance in miles.
## 594. A rank and the leaderboard it links to are counted from one population, and an athlete is not their own competitor

**Date:** 2026-08-13

Issue #393 reduced `segment_leaderboard_tiered` to one row per athlete — their best visible effort — before ranking, and `20270513_001` did the same for the catalogue board. Neither touched `segment_effort_ranks` / `global_segment_effort_ranks`, the RPCs behind the run-detail chips, which kept computing `1 + count(strictly faster effort rows)`. So the same athlete could be handed two ranks for one segment: with A holding 60 s and 65 s and B holding 70 s, the board seats B second while B's own run page says third — and the chip is a link straight to the board that contradicts it. The gap widens with every repetition, so on a climb a neighbour runs weekly the chip drifts arbitrarily far from the board.

**The reduction needs no CTE.** An athlete's best time is below `t` exactly when they hold *some* effort below `t`, so `count(distinct f.user_id)` over the strictly-faster rows equals `count(*)` over the `distinct on (user_id)` bests the boards materialise. That identity is what keeps the fix free: the correlated subquery still range-scans `segment_efforts (segment_id, time_seconds)`, and no covering index has to grow to carry `user_id`. That mattered — `segment_efforts` is on the high-volume list in `migration_locks.md`, `create index` there blocks writes for the build, and `concurrently` cannot run inside Supabase's wrapped apply transaction, so an index would have been the expensive half of a cheap fix.

**Excluding the effort's own athlete is the load-bearing choice, and it is not what a literal port of the board's `distinct on` would do.** Three readings were available. Dedupe including self counts A's 60 s as a competitor standing above A's 65 s and reports #2 for it — reintroducing on the chip the exact "one athlete, two ranks" artifact #393 removed from the board, and printing a number (#2) that on the board belongs to B. Ranking the athlete rather than the effort — every effort of A's reports A's board row — always agrees with the board but smears the crown across runs where A was minutes off, since the pill goes gold at rank 1. The shipped reading ranks the effort's *time* against the other athletes' bests: the effort the board actually shows (each athlete's best) gets precisely its board rank, the rank stays monotone in the time displayed beside it, and the crown stays on the run that earned it. The honest boundary is that a *slower* repeat effort can still print a number that is not its athlete's board row — A holding 60 s and 65 s against a C at 62 s reads #2 on the 65 s run — but that number is now a true statement about that time rather than an artifact of how often somebody else ran the segment.

**The block filter is a deliberate narrowing, not a ride-along.** The boards are SECURITY DEFINER and filter `is_blocked_either_way`; the rank RPCs are SECURITY INVOKER and leaned on RLS alone, which carries route visibility (the segments EXISTS resolving through `private.is_route_visible_to`) and run visibility (`private.is_run_visible_to`) but knows nothing about the block graph — so a blocked athlete's time kept pushing the caller down a ranking they were absent from. Adding it can only remove rivals from a count, never admit a row RLS excluded, so it fails closed, and it closes a small inference channel where a blocked user's times stayed observable through a rank number. It is applied to the comparison set only: the run's own efforts stay unfiltered because `fetchEffortsForRun` renders a missing rank row as `rank ?? 1`, so filtering the outer set would print a crown on a blocked athlete's run. An anon caller has a null `auth.uid()`, `is_blocked_either_way(null, x)` is false, and nothing is dropped — correct, anon holds no blocks. The boards' `p_gender` / `p_age_band` / `p_club_id` tiers stay unmirrored on purpose: the chip states a standing on the default all-comers board, which is the board a reader lands on.

**Two adjacent gaps were found and deliberately left.** Both boards inline their own visibility predicates instead of calling the canonical helpers, and both predate the §206 shadow-hidden backstop: `segment_leaderboard_tiered`'s route branch is a bare `r.is_public = true` where `private.is_route_visible_to` also demands `shadow_hidden = false`, and both boards join `user_profiles` under DEFINER, bypassing the "authenticated read profiles except shadow-hidden" policy. They point the other way from this ADR — the *boards* are too permissive, not the ranks — and they change no rank anywhere, because on a shadow-hidden route the invoker path returns no efforts at all and no chip renders. Re-emitting a SECURITY DEFINER moderation body deserves its own triage and its own tests rather than riding inside a rank-semantics migration, so they are tracked in `followups.md` instead.

## 595. A `return` that is not awaited is outside the `try`, and an unpinned SDK is what found it

**Date:** 2026-08-13

Dart 3.13 added the `unawaited_return_in_try_block` warning and it fired twice on `social_service.dart`, code no PR had touched. The first hit is not a style nit. `searchClubs` wraps the `search_clubs` RPC *and* the `_enrichClubs` follow-up reads in one `try` whose `catch` deliberately degrades to the plain ILIKE `browseClubs` — the comment there says why: a search that misses must not surface a red error toast. Returning `_enrichClubs(rows)` without `await` returns the future to the caller *before* it completes, so the enrichment reads ran outside the `try` that was written to protect them. The RPC-failure branch worked; an enrichment failure escaped to the caller and the fallback never ran at all. The `catch` was half dead and nothing said so.

**This is the layered-resilience contract, one layer up from the recording stack.** A fallback that cannot fire is worse than no fallback: the code reads as if the degradation is handled, so no reviewer looks again. The general rule the entry adds to § Layered resilience is that a `try` covers what it *awaits*, not what it *starts* — returning a future bare hands the error to whoever is upstream of your `catch`. `await` costs nothing here; both methods were already `async` and already had a synchronous continuation.

**The second hit is latent, and saying so matters more than fixing it quietly.** `fetchClubSlugForEvent` returns `fetchClubSlugById(clubId)` inside a `try` whose contract is "never rethrows — a deep link is an auxiliary effect". Today the inner method catches everything itself and returns null, so the outer `catch` is never reached and no behaviour changes when the `await` goes in. The fix is still right — the contract now holds on its own rather than resting on a second method keeping its internal catch — but no test can distinguish the two versions, because there is no input that makes the inner call reject. The test that landed pins the *contract* instead, so narrowing that inner catch later fails in CI rather than in a push-notification tap handler. Claiming a regression test where only contract coverage is achievable is the thing worth not doing.

**The fixture is a loopback PostgREST stand-in, not the live stack.** `services_integration_test.dart` already drives `SocialService.withClient` against a real local Supabase, but the bug turns on failing the enrichment reads *independently of* the RPC that precedes them — a distinction a real server cannot be asked for. A `dart:io` `HttpServer` that routes on path and on the `vnd.pgrst.object+json` Accept header is enough to fail exactly one read, and it adds no dependency.

**The SDK was the only unpinned thing in the file that found it.** Every `subosito/flutter-action` in `ci.yml` is SHA-pinned, but took only `channel: stable`, so the toolchain floated: Flutter 3.47.0 published at 18:52 UTC on 2026-08-12, 51 minutes after main's last green run finished, and the next PR inherited it. `dart analyze` exits 2 on any warning and 0 on any number of infos — the suite carries ~3000 of the latter — so a PR touching only web code went red on two mobile warnings in code it did not touch, and the failure pointed at the PR rather than at the SDK bump. `FLUTTER_VERSION` at the workflow level pins all six jobs from one value. The trade-off is deliberate and is a trade: floating means new lints, deprecations and engine changes arrive free but land on whichever unrelated PR is open when upstream publishes; pinning means they arrive on a bump commit that can be read, tested and reverted on its own, at the cost of someone having to raise the number. That bump belongs with the repo's other manual pins — the same sweep should pin `release-android.yml` and `release-ios.yml`, which still float and are the worse exposure, since a release binary built against an unknown SDK is not reproducible. Dependabot does not watch this version, so it is a human cadence, not an automated one.

**Amendment, 2026-08-13 — the pin covers releases too, and three declarations are enforced rather than trusted.** The first cut pinned only `ci.yml` and named the release workflows as a follow-up. That was the wrong half to leave floating: CI is what validates the code a release ships, so a tagged build on a different SDK than CI tested is an untested binary, and unlike CI a release has no green/red signal to tell you the toolchain moved — the first evidence would be a shipped artifact. Both now declare `FLUTTER_VERSION` and pass it to their `flutter-action`.

**A single source of truth is not reachable in workflow syntax, and the two ways to fake it are worse than the duplication.** A workflow-level `env` is per-file. `flutter-version-file` wants an exact version in a `pubspec.yaml` or FVM config, and the pubspecs carry a range (`flutter: '>=3.19.0'`), so pointing at one would pin nothing. A local composite action *would* collapse all three to one literal — and the repo already uses that pattern in `.github/actions/start-supabase`, created for this exact "byte-identical copies were drifting" reason — but Dependabot's `github-actions` ecosystem scans `.github/workflows` plus a **root** `action.yml` only. Moving the pinned `subosito/flutter-action@<sha>` into `.github/actions/` would have quietly ended SHA updates for all eight call sites, trading a live security pin for a deduped version literal. So the duplication stays and `scripts/check_toolchain_pins.mjs` makes it safe: it resolves every `flutter-action` step's version across every workflow and fails when they disagree, when one reverts to a bare `channel: stable`, or when *nothing matches at all* — a guard that inspects nothing enforces nothing, which is a failure mode the sibling guards' own comments record. It runs in `workflow-lint`, already inside the `CI gate` aggregator.

**The pub half of this failure class was already closed, by the same lesson learned earlier.** `flutter_lints: ^6.0.0` looks like a second floating upstream, but the caret is a resolution *constraint*, not the pin: the root `pubspec.lock` is committed — `.gitignore` says why, citing a third-party publish that turned main red on 2026-08-05 — all seven Flutter packages are members of that one pub workspace, and the lockfile holds `flutter_lints` at `6.0.0`. `melos bootstrap` runs `pub get`, which honours a lockfile; a `flutter pub get` in a fresh worktree left `pubspec.lock` unmodified, confirming it. What the check *did* surface is that `dart pub global activate melos` is unpinned at six sites while the lockfile pins melos to `7.8.2` — the one tool in the build path still floating. That is tracked in `followups.md` rather than fixed here, because it drives every Flutter job and both release builds and could not be verified without installing melos globally on the workstation.

**Second amendment, 2026-08-13 — melos is pinned too, and its version is derived rather than duplicated.** `dart pub global activate melos` passed no version at six sites, so CI and both release builds installed whatever melos was newest when the job started. Deferring it was wrong for the reason given for deferring it: melos drives every Flutter job and both releases, and blast radius is the argument for pinning, not against. Unlike the Flutter SDK, melos has an in-repo source of truth — `pubspec.lock` resolves it as a direct dev dependency of the workspace root — so the guard **reads the version from the lockfile** and checks each activation against it, rather than checking the six sites against each other. Six sites can agree with one another and all be wrong; and because `pub global activate` ignores the workspace entirely, CI could otherwise run a different melos than `dart run melos` resolves locally with nothing to say so. That asymmetry is deliberate and is written into the guard: Flutter has no in-repo file that resolves the SDK, so there the workflows *are* authoritative and need only agree with each other. The precedent for deriving is `check_watch_ble_uuids.mjs`, whose header states the same principle — the firmware owns its own table, so every UUID is read from a file rather than transcribed.

**One guard, not two.** The melos check has the same shape as the Flutter one — N sites, a drift failure, and a vacuous-pass hazard — so it went into the same script (renamed `check_flutter_version_pin.mjs` → `check_toolchain_pins.mjs`) rather than into a near-identical sibling, sharing the file walk, the reporting and the empty-set guard. What the two checks do *not* share is the source of truth, and that is the one thing worth reading the file for.

**What is now pinned, and what still is not.** Pinned to an exact version: the Flutter SDK (three workflows), melos (six sites), the Supabase CLI, actionlint, every pub dependency via the committed root `pubspec.lock`, and every *live* GitHub Action by SHA — the one tag-only reference, `apple-actions/upload-testflight-build@v1`, sits inside release-ios.yml's commented-out TestFlight block and must be SHA-pinned when that block is uncommented. Still floating, in descending order of exposure: `cargo install defmt-print --locked --version '^1.1'` in the two firmware-sim jobs, where `--locked` pins the crate's own dependency tree but the caret still admits any 1.x; and the `node-version: 24` inputs, which track a major line. Both are decode/lint surfaces whose breakage is loud and local rather than a silent change to what gets built or shipped, which is why neither was pulled into this round — but `defmt-print` is the same shape as the two pins above it and is the next one worth closing.

**Third amendment, 2026-08-13 — defmt-print, and the pin that would not have worked.** The last float in the build path was `cargo install defmt-print --locked --version '^1.1'` in the two firmware-sim jobs: `--locked` pins the crate's dependency tree, not the crate, so the caret still admitted any 1.x. Pinning the version alone would have changed nothing, and that is the part worth recording. The install is `command -v defmt-print || cargo install ...` behind an `actions/cache` keyed `defmt-print-1.1-<os>` — a key with no patch component, which therefore never changed. A bumped version would have hit that key, restored the old binary, and `command -v` would have skipped the install entirely. CI run 31623789083 shows it happening: cache hit, `command -v` wins, `cargo install` never executes. So the version CI was actually decoding with **was not expressible from the configuration at all** — it was whatever a cache entry of unknown date happened to hold. The exact version now lives in the key, so a bump misses it and forces a real install; the guard checks that coupling, because a pin the cache can veto is not a pin.

**1.1.0, determined rather than chosen.** crates.io lists only `1.0.0` and `1.1.0` in the 1.x line (1.1.0 published 2026-05-12); the `^1.1` constraint landed 2026-07-26 in `b9076bd1a` and excludes 1.0.0; so the cached binary can only be 1.1.0. Here "what CI demonstrably passes on" and "newest available" happen to coincide, which is why no trade-off had to be made — but they were established separately, from the registry and from the job log, not assumed to be the same. The major line is deliberately kept equal to the firmware's own `defmt` dependency (`1.1`, resolved to 1.1.0 in `apps/custom_watch/Cargo.lock`): the decoder has to understand the wire format the firmware emits.

**Its source of truth is self-consistency, and that is a finding, not a shortcut.** The obvious guess is that `apps/custom_watch/Cargo.lock` resolves defmt-print the way `pubspec.lock` resolves melos. It does not, and cannot: defmt-print is a host-side CLI that decodes an RTT stream, not a dependency of the firmware crate, so it is absent from that lockfile entirely. That puts it with Flutter rather than with melos — no in-repo file resolves it, so agreement across the sites plus the cache-key coupling is the honest ceiling. The guard now carries all three shapes and says which is which, so a future reader does not "fix" the inconsistency by inventing a derivation that has nothing to derive from.

**The sweep is closed.** Every toolchain the build installs is now pinned to an exact version and guarded: the Flutter SDK, melos, defmt-print, the Supabase CLI, actionlint, every pub dependency via the committed root `pubspec.lock`, and every live GitHub Action by SHA. What remains is deliberate and recorded in `followups.md`: the `node-version: 24` inputs track a major line, and `apple-actions/upload-testflight-build@v1` is tag-pinned inside release-ios.yml's commented-out TestFlight block — dead code, which is why it was left rather than SHA-pinned.

## 596. A pasted visibility predicate is a moderation control with an expiry date, and a hidden athlete is redacted from a leaderboard rather than dropped

**Date:** 2026-08-13

The §206 shadow-hidden sweeps tightened the oracles and the policies — `private.is_route_visible_to` and the `user_profiles` SELECT policy in `20270329_001`, the clubs + events policies in `20270328_001`. Every consumer that *called* one of those inherited the fix. Five SECURITY DEFINER bodies had pasted the predicate instead, and a definer has no RLS underneath it to catch what its own copy misses, so each kept serving moderation-hidden content: `segment_leaderboard_tiered` handed any caller holding a segment id the entire board of a hidden route — verified live, one board row against zero readable efforts under RLS — while it, `global_segment_leaderboard` and `challenge_leaderboard` all rendered a hidden athlete's name and avatar, and `is_event_visible` (with its own copy inside `claim_event_result`) kept a hidden club's events visible along with the `event_pricing`, `event_checkpoints` and `checkpoint_crossings` rows whose policies lean on it.

**The fix is delegation, because re-inlining is the defect.** A corrected copy is a copy, and the next tightening will miss it exactly as this one did. Routes now go through `private.is_route_visible_to` and clubs through `is_public_club_by_id`, the same oracles the policies and the `public_routes` view use. In `segment_leaderboard_tiered` the check also leaves the per-row CTE: every effort on a segment hangs off one route, so route visibility is a per-call question, and hoisting it removed the `routes` join entirely — cheaper and harder to misplace. The profile half stays an inline `(shadow_hidden = false or id = caller)`, which is a deliberate asymmetry: it is one column on an already-joined row, and `search_user_profiles`, `public_profile_by_id` and `discoverable_runners_near` all already express it that way, so minting an oracle here would leave three surfaces inconsistent with the new one — trading a known drift for a fresh one.

**Redact the identity; do not drop the row.** For a hidden athlete on a ranked board the obvious move is to filter them out, and it is wrong twice. It restates every slower athlete's position — a ranking computed over efforts the viewer is entitled to see, now misreported because of a moderation decision about someone else. And it would silently reopen [§ 594](#594-a-rank-and-the-leaderboard-it-links-to-are-counted-from-one-population-and-an-athlete-is-not-their-own-competitor): `segment_effort_ranks` is SECURITY INVOKER over `segment_efforts`, which carries no profile gate, so the run-detail chip would go on counting an athlete the board had dropped, and the two surfaces would disagree again one commit after being reconciled. Moderation hides a person, not other people's places. So the row and its rank stand and only `display_name` + `avatar_url` go null — which both web surfaces already render through a fallback label, so no client change was owed. The caller's own row is exempt, mirroring the soft-hide carve-out in the policy itself. A bare `user_id` uuid remains, but every surface that resolves one to a name is already gated.

**The sweep is the durable part.** Rather than fix the two known instances, every SECURITY DEFINER body in `public` + `private` was checked against the three tables that carry `shadow_hidden` (`routes`, `clubs`, `user_profiles`) — reading live `prosrc`, not migration archaeology, since a body is only as current as the last create-or-replace. That turned two reported leaks into five, and it also produced the negative results worth recording so they are not re-litigated: `nearby_routes` and `routes_within_box` read through the `public_routes` view, which carries the gate; `search_public_events` is SECURITY INVOKER, so the tightened policies already bind it; the challenges surfaces matched only because `challenges.is_public` shares a column name with a table that has no `shadow_hidden` at all. `coach_roster_summary` was left alone on purpose: it joins profiles for the caller's own consented athletes, and hiding one there would delete an athlete from their coach's triage view — a narrowing that breaks a legitimate viewer, which is the failure mode opposite to the one this ADR is about. `join_club_by_token` is also untouched: it never consults `is_public`, and whether a moderation-hidden club should still accept an explicit invite is a product question about freezing hidden entities, not a leak.

**Every change moves in the closing direction only, and the tests say so in both directions.** Nineteen assertions across three suites; seven fail against the pre-fix bodies (the hidden route's board, the hidden name + avatar on all three boards, the visible event, its readable checkpoints, the accepted claim) and the other twelve pass before and after — the hidden route's *owner* keeps their board, an active club member keeps a club route's board, an ordinary public board is unchanged row-for-row, the hidden athlete still sees their own name, the hidden club's owner and members still see its events. `is_public_club_by_id` coalesces a missing club to false, so even a dangling reference fails closed.

## 597. A page that only asks the clock when you navigate never sees midnight, and a day window belongs in the database

**Date:** 2026-08-13

[§ 591](#591-a-food-diary-that-only-knows-today-cannot-be-corrected-and-the-day-it-shows-must-own-every-window) made `/nutrition` date-navigable and left two things behind, both recorded as follow-ups rather than shipped half-done. Both are closed here, and neither turned out to be the size it first looked.

**The rollover is a label bug, and it is sized to that.** `todayIso` / `yesterdayIso` were recomputed only inside the `$effect` that reads the URL, which fires on a navigation or an auth change and never on the clock, so a tab left open past local midnight kept calling the previous day "Today" and kept the Next-day step disabled. It is worth stating what this was *not*: no write path was affected, because `entryTimestampFor(viewDate, new Date())` resolves at **save** time — the contract § 591 argued for on the composer-open-at-23:59 case buys this too. Escalating a stale header into a data-integrity fix would have been the wrong repair for the wrong bug.

**`visibilitychange` alone does not reach the tab the report describes.** The follow-up proposed a visibility check and explicitly refused a polling timer, and the refusal is right: a per-minute interval spends 1440 wakeups a day on every open tab to catch an edge that happens once. But a visibility listener never fires on a tab that *stays visible* across midnight — a kitchen screen, a second monitor, the diary left open beside something else — which is precisely "a tab left open past local midnight". So both triggers ship, and the cost argument survives intact because a **single `setTimeout` armed for the next local midnight is also one wakeup a day**, not a poll. It is the cheapest possible schedule for the event: exactly one, at the instant the thing becomes wrong. The two are complements rather than belt-and-braces — the timer covers the visible tab, and the visibility check covers the case the timer cannot be trusted for, a backgrounded tab whose timer the browser throttled or whose machine slept through the transition and fires it late.

`msUntilNextLocalMidnight` steps `new Date(y, m, d + 1)` like everything else in `diary_day.ts`, so it lands on midnight on a 23- or 25-hour day. A fixed 86 400 000 would not: a timer that re-arms itself at midnight fires at 23:00 on a fall-back day and at 01:00 on a spring-forward one, so the header is wrong for an hour in one direction or claims tomorrow an hour early in the other. That is [§ 589](#589-a-date-stepped-by-a-fixed-24-hours-is-not-a-date-and-the-fifth-occurrence-bought-a-guard)'s shape again — caught before it shipped this time, and on the web side, where the Dart source guard that ADR bought does not reach. The rollover **re-resolves the day from the URL** rather than stepping `viewDate`: a bare `/nutrition` means "today" and must follow the clock onto the new day, while an explicit past `?date=` stays exactly where it is and only changes its label. Leaving a bare URL parked on yesterday would have been worse than the bug — `isViewingToday` would go false while the URL still said today, so the Today button would render and navigate to the URL already showing.

**The gym window had to move into the database, not be re-tested more carefully in the browser.** `fetchGymWorkouts` took a row cap and nothing else, so the page pulled the newest 50 sessions and filtered them client-side; a diary day older than the caller's 50 most recent lifts read as a day with no lifts in it. It now takes the same `startedAtFrom` / `startedAtBefore` bounds `fetchRuns` has, applied as PostgREST `.gte()` / `.lt()`. The `limit` moved into an options bag in the same change — not tidying: the windowed call site has no row cap to state, and an optional positional second argument would have left `fetchGymWorkouts(undefined, {…})` as the only way to say so. Converting three untouched call sites to `{ limit: n }` also makes a missed one a compile error rather than a silently wrong read.

**The client-side membership test was then removed rather than kept as a backstop, and auditing who else ran one found two more.** With the bounds in PostgREST the comparison is a real timestamptz comparison; a second copy of the predicate in the browser could only ever mask a dropped bound, and § 596 is one entry old on why a corrected copy is still a copy. But the audit of every `fetchGymWorkouts` caller turned up the § 591 string compare — `iso >= startIso && iso < endIso`, where Postgres' `…+00:00` sorts below a `…Z` bound — still live on `/nutrition/targets` and on `/dashboard`. The two get different repairs because their constraints differ, and that difference is the point: `/nutrition/targets` fetches solely for today, so both its reads window server-side and it keeps no client predicate at all (which retires its fixed-24-hour day bound as well); `/dashboard` **cannot** window, because `runs` and `gymWorkouts` are the shared batch a dozen cards consume, so it keeps a client filter and routes it through `isWithinWindow`. That is also what keeps that helper honest — it exists for the case where filtering in the browser is forced, not as a duplicate of a filter the server already applied.
