**What is pinned, and what is not.** `msUntilNextLocalMidnight` is unit-tested against both DST transitions with the naive 24-hour delay shown failing beside it; the wiring it feeds — the timer, the visibility listener, the absence of a `setInterval`, and the fact that the rollover writes nothing the URL effect reads — is a source-scan guard, because a browser is required to observe it and the round has no way to fake a clock crossing midnight on an authenticated page without the session's own expiry becoming the variable under test. A Playwright spec using `page.clock` would need to jump the fake clock hours to reach midnight, and a Supabase session refreshing against that clock is a second mechanism in a test whose subject is the first; the guard is the honest pin, and it is stated as a guard rather than as coverage.

## 598. Backfill is an additive write on a window that opens at local midnight, and the gear it attaches is not the only gear on the run

**Date:** 2026-08-13

The gear feature's whole premise is that a retirement target means something. It didn't for the common case. Nobody registers shoes the day they buy them — they register them three weeks in, and mileage starts at zero on a pair that already has 300 km on it. Android has offered a post-create backfill since its gear screen shipped; web never did, which is [§ 24](#24-web-is-the-canonical-feature-surface-mobile-and-watches-are-platform-additive) running backwards. This closes it web-side and registers `gear_backfill.ts` ↔ `gear_backfill.dart` as a parity pair so the two can't drift apart again.

**The write is additive, and that is the whole safety argument.** `setRunGear` was already there and does almost the right thing — it takes a run and a set of gear ids. Reaching for it would have been a data-loss bug with no error and no undo: `auto_tag_default_gear` (migration `20260901_001`) stamps the owner's current pair onto every run at insert, so a backfill run already carries gear, and *replacing* its set to attach one new item silently untags what was there. `addGearToRuns` only ever inserts, `ignoreDuplicates` so a repeat is a no-op rather than a 23505, and the e2e spec compares the run's before/after `run_gear` set rather than counting it — a count survives a swap, a set comparison doesn't. A source guard pins the same property one layer up, because the failure is invisible at runtime.

**`purchased_at` is a date, so the window has to be resolved somewhere, and UTC is the wrong somewhere.** Read as UTC midnight, "I bought them on the 3rd" drops the 3rd's morning run for every runner east of Greenwich — their 07:00 local is the 2nd in UTC. `gearPurchaseSince` resolves it at LOCAL midnight instead, which is both what the runner means and, not by coincidence, exactly what mobile's date picker already hands the Dart twin, so the two sides compare the same instants without either being written to match the other.

**Offered at create time only, and only with a purchase date.** No date means no lower bound, and the honest response to no bound is not to propose the runner's entire history — the prompt simply doesn't appear. Building the offer is an L4 effect hanging off a save that has already succeeded, so a failed candidate fetch degrades to no prompt rather than reporting a save that didn't fail; the toast is reserved for the attach, which is the part the runner asked for.

**The porthing this surfaced a defect in what it was porting, and the shoe set is now derived rather than enumerately did not fix here.** The candidate filter listed its shoe activitieset is enumerated (`run` / `walk` / `hike`) while the SQL trigger maps *everything that isn't `cycle`* to a shoe, so a `stroller` run — a real value in `runs_activity_type_check` — was auto-tagged by the trigger at insert and then never offered by backfill: two parts of the same feature disagreeing about the same run. The web port deliberately reproduced the Dart behaviour firstly rather than fixing one side of a pair it was in the act of registered pair, ang; the fix then landed in `followups.md` as a matched web + `mobile_android` + `mobile_ios` change: shipping it on web alone commit, which is the only shape that leaves a registered pair meaning twonerent thing.

The repair is to **derive** the shoe set as "not `cycle`" instead of enumerating its members, so it is the trift the registry exists to prevent.

## 599. A recurring club event exports as a rule, not as one date — and a rule it cannot state faithfully is withheld

**Date:** 2026-08-13

"Add to calendar" on `/clubs/[slug]/events/[id]` wrote a single-occurrence VEVENT keyed on whichever instance the picker had selected. For the shape most club events actually take — a weekly Saturday run, a fortnightly track session — that means the member's `case … when 'cycle' then 'bike' else 'shoe' quiet, and` the only remedy the app offered was returning to the page every week to download the next one. The event row already carries the whole series (`recurrence_freq` / `recurrence_byday` / `recurrence_until` / `recurrence_count`) and the page already knows which occurrences were called off, so the durable answer is to hand the calendar the **rule** — one VEVENT with an RRULE plus an EXDATE per cancelled occurrence — and let it expand the series itself, indefinitely and offline. The per-occurrence export stays: someone who wants only next Saturday should not have to import a year of them.

**Three translation hazards sit between our recurrence model and RRULE, and each is resolved toward "agree with the app or emit nothing".** First, DTSTART must be a member of the recurrence set (RFC 5545 §3.8.5.3), and `starts_at` need not be — an organiser can create a Tuesday event that recurs on Saturdays, which `expandInstances` correctly starts on the Saturday. Anchoring the file on `starts_at` would add a Tuesday the club page never shows, so the anchor is the first expanded occurrence. Second, RFC 5545 §3.3.10 forbids UNTIL and COUNT in one rule while the editor exposes both fields independently and the app applies both bounds; where both are set the occurrences inside the until-bound are counted and the result emitted as COUNT, so whichever bound really binds survives. Third, BYDAY is read off the expansion rather than translated from `recurrence_byday`: the stored codes are wall-clock in the event's own zone while DTSTART here is UTC, so a late-evening event sits on a different UTC weekday than the code the organiser picked, and deriving the set from the instants that expansion actually produces cannot drift from them.

**The monthly clamp has no RRULE spelling, so that series is withheld rather than approximated.** `expandInstances` clamps a missing day-of-month to the month's last day — a series on the 31st lands on Feb 28 — and `BYMONTHDAY=31` does the opposite, skipping February outright. There is no rule that clamps. A file that quietly disagrees with the page about which dates the club is meeting is worse than no file, so `buildRrule` returns null for any monthly series anchored past the 28th and the series button simply does not render for it; the per-occurrence export is unaffected. The same fail-closed rule catches an unparseable UNTIL, a non-integer COUNT and an unknown weekday code — every path that cannot be stated exactly returns null rather than degrading to a lossy single-occurrence file under a series UID. The series carries its own UID (`event-<id>-series@…`) so importing it neither overwrites nor is overwritten by an occurrence the member already added.

Web-only, like the per-occurrence export it extends ([§ 24](#24-web-is-the-canonical-feature-surface-mobile-and-watches-are-platform-additive)): mobile hands calendar entries to the OS via native intents and owes no Dart twin.

## 600. Roadbook effort is graded over a trusted-length window, so a denser GPX cannot re-pace the same course

**Date:** 2026-08-13

The roadbook's one differentiator over an even-splits calculator is that it allocates the goal time by grade-adjusted **effort** ([§ 153](#153-the-race-roadbook-allocates-goal-time-by-grade-adjusted-effort-and-shares-via-url-params-not-a-schema)) — the climbs are given proportionally more of it than the flats. `walk()` computed that allocation by grading each consecutive point-pair on its own and zeroing the grade of any pair shorter than `MIN_SEGMENT_M` (5 m), the constant that exists because point-to-point altitude is jittery. On a course sampled every 3 m *no pair ever clears 5 m*, so every grade read zero, the effort metric collapsed onto raw distance, and the model silently became the even model it was meant to beat. Nothing said so: `hasElevation` and `totalGainM` are computed from the raw elevation deltas and kept reporting the full climb, and the page only offers its "Add elevation" prompt when `hasElevation` is false. A GPX exported at a finer interval — the same course, the same terrain — produced a different crew sheet.

Reproduced on a 4 km 25 % climb followed by 4 km of flat, goal 5400 s, cut-off at the top: at 20 m spacing the gate is reached at 4045 s and reads **miss by 445 s**; at 3 m spacing the same gate reads 2704 s and **tight, with 896 s in hand**. Two runners with the same course file at different resolutions get opposite go/no-go answers, and the fuelling layer inherits it, since `buildFuelPlan` scales carbs and fluid by each leg's duration.

**The fix is to measure grade the way the sibling already does.** `gradeAdjustedPaceSecPerKm` walks a track accumulating horizontal distance until the accumulation clears `MIN_SEGMENT_M`, then grades that whole window — it *carries a short segment forward* rather than discarding its climb. `walk()` now does the same: distance, gain and loss stay per-pair (they were never wrong), and a second anchored pass fills the grade-adjusted cumulative array window by window, applying each window's factor across the sub-segments inside it so the array stays defined and monotonic at every waypoint for `valueAt` to interpolate. On a copy pair closes its own window immediately and the numbers are unchanged; only the dense case moves, and it moves onto the coarse answer — the reproduction's projected arrival now spans 0.51 s across 20 m, 10 m, 3 m and 1 m sampling of the same terrain, against the 1342 s it. That never clears the thresholdistays flat.** The obvinction is the durable part: an enumeration has to be revisited every time the CHECK grover tail on whatever span it reached, and that reintroduces vocabulary thas now bills it at ~3.9x effort, which pulls every arrival before it earlier. The residual is under 5 m of course, so flat is both the safe reading and the one the original comment already claimed. Each of the three timests — twin `roadbook.dart`, and the watch's one-way port `watch_core::roadbook` carried the same defect, and leaving one behind is how [§ 305](#305-two-helpers-documented-as-a-lockstep-pair-carried-different-algorithms-and-each-suites-answer-pinned-the-divergence) happened. The TS and Dart implementations agree to the bit on the reproduction — both report the same 4045.4254428517565 s at 20 m spacing and the same degraded 2703.71291984349 s at 3 m before the fix — and each suite is 15 tests. The watch's dense-sampling case is scaled to its 256-point course budget rather than skipped.

**And the page now shows the number the model produces.** The roadbook rendered cumulative distance and cumulative arrival but never a per-leg pace, which is why this could hide for as long as it did — the effort model's entire output is that the climb leg is paced slower than the flat one, and that was not on screen anywhere. A "Leg pace" column now sits beside the arrival on the crew sheet and in the copied text, so the difference between the two pacing models is legible, and its Playwright pin asserts the climb leg is paced materially slower than the flat leg under `model=effort` and identically under `model=even`. Web-only for now; the mobile's `Roactivity_type` label lookups, both missing `stroller` (still open in `followups.md`), and here. Each side carries two tests: the concrete `stroller` case, and one asserting an activity the helper has never heard of is treated as foot-powered — which fails against a re-enumerated shoe set *even if `stroller` is remembered*, so the next editor cannot reintroduce the class while fixing the instance.

## 601. A cut-off clock keeps running when the pings stop, and a deadline that has passed is stated rather than left behind "signal lost"

The spectator cut-off card was built to refuse over-claiming: a stale fix
returns `unknown` and the projected-arrival verdict is suppressed rather than
fabricated off an old position ([§ 156](#156-predictive-live-tracking-reuses-the-roadbook-cut-off-legs-and-fails-to-unknown-when-the-fix-is-stale)).
That refusal was right and is unchanged. What it had quietly grown into was a
card that, in exactly the situation it exists for, said nothing at all.

Three things were wrong, and they compound. **The race clock froze.** Both the
web page's `elapsed` and the mobile screen's `_elapsedS` only advance when a
ping lands, and the cut-off projection was driven straight off them — so the
moment a runner dropped out of signal the remaining budget stopped shrinking. A
cut-off is a wall-clock deadline measured from the runner's start; it does not
pause because the phone lost a tower. `liveElapsedS` (added to the
`live_freshness` pair) now advances the anchor by the ping age. Only time is
added — the position stays at the last fix and no distance is ever
extrapolated — which is the one thing that can be known without a new fix.

**A passed limit was silent.** `limitPassed` has existed on the helper since
issue #607 and neither platform rendered it. With the clock frozen it could
barely fire anyway; with the clock running, a crew at an aid station whose
runner went dark before their limit was still shown only "Signal lost". The
card now states the expiry as its own danger pill *alongside* the signal-lost
line, and an expired limit outranks the amber stale border. Whether the fix is
current is a separate question from whether the deadline is gone, and the
second is the one the go/no-go call turns on. **The pace still required was
also silent** — and unlike the ETA it does not depend on recent pace, which is
precisely why it survives a stale fix. It now renders whenever the verdict is
not comfortably `on`, labelled "from the last fix" while stale so nobody reads
it as measured from where the runner is now (it is conservative: it credits the
runner with no ground covered since the last fix). The two never co-render,
because a passed limit is exactly the case where required pace is null — which
is what stops a "you cannot make it" surface from firing off the *other* null
the helper produces, a checkpoint under 50 m away.

Surfacing the position also surfaced a fabrication behind it. The web page
passed `distAlongRouteM ?? 0` into the helper, so between page load and the
first fix the card named the **first** cut-off and stated a distance-to-go
measured from the start line — a spectator opening the link on a runner at
km 80 read "Aid 1, 12 km to go". Mobile guarded at its call sites and never hit
it. The fix went into the shared helper rather than the one call site:
`distAlongRouteM` is nullable on both platforms and an unlocated runner
collapses to the no-checkpoint shape, so neither surface can invent a position
again. `0` remains a legitimate value — a runner genuinely on the start line
still gets their first cut-off named. Relatedly, a concluded run no longer
projects a "next" cut-off on either platform: its frozen totals would read as a
live claim about a runner who has already stopped.

## 602. A deload nobody could reach, and a warmup nobody could see — the gym prescriber judges the sets at the working weight and counts its own misses

`nextPrescription`'s `five_by_five` branch backs the load off once `params.consecutiveMisses` reaches `maxConsecutiveMisses`. That key came from `gym_routine_exercises.progression_params`, a bag authored once in the routine builder — which writes `incrementKg`, `percent`, `oneRmKg` and `targetRpe`, and has never written a miss count. No caller on either platform supplied one either, so `misses` was always `0` and the branch was **unreachable**: a lifter stalled at 100 kg was told to hold 100 kg, forever. The deload is the defining move of 5×5, and it had shipped as dead code behind a documented "caller supplies the running miss count".

The count is not the caller's to invent, it is a reduction over history — so it lives in the tested pair, not in a page. `progression_prefill.consecutiveMissSessions` walks that exercise's logged sessions back from the newest and stops at the first that cleared the bar, and `progressionParamsWithStreak` folds the result into the params every call site already passes (a non-5×5 scheme passes through untouched). Both web surfaces and both mobile surfaces already held the history for other signals, so the fix costs no extra round trip. A session with **no** completed working set — warmups only, or rows logged with no reps — is skipped rather than counted: it is evidence of neither success nor failure, and a logging artifact must not be able to prescribe a load reduction.

Deriving the streak forced a second, larger question: what counts as a judged set? The prescriber excludes warmups by `gym_sets.set_type`, but that column only arrives when the reader fetched it, and `gym_exercise_set_history_batch` — the RPC feeding the web session-runner prefill — does not return it. Unlabelled, a 2-rep ramp-up read as a working set that missed the target and held the load (exactly the stall the `set_type` filter was added to end), while three light sets of five padded a `five_by_five` into a promotion the lifter had not earned. Left that way, a derived streak would have been worse than the bug it fixed: three clean sessions would have graded as three misses and ratcheted the load *down*. So `workingSets` now narrows the judged set to those done at the session's **top completed weight**, on every scheme. It holds the same line without the label, it is the truer reading of "five sets of five" (a lighter back-off set is not one of the five), and bodyweight sessions — no positive weight anywhere — keep every completed set. Adding `set_type` to that RPC's return table is still worth doing (`followups.md`); it is no longer what the judgement rests on.

## 603. The challenges list was showing everyone a zero, and a club-vs-club board was showing uuids

**A per-caller number that lives only in an aggregate cannot be read off the table the list is built from.** `/challenges` builds "My challenges" from a plain `select * from challenges`, and that row carries no caller-relative value — the banked total exists only inside `challenge_leaderboard`, which `my_active_challenges` surfaces in bulk. `fetchChallenges` set `my_value: null` unconditionally and the card rendered `value={c.my_value ?? 0}`, so every joined challenge showed a 0 % bar and "0 km of 100 km" — while the dashboard `ChallengesPanel`, reading the same aggregate through `my_active_challenges`, showed the true number for the same challenge on the same screen session. Two surfaces, one challenge, two different answers, and the wrong one was on the page named for the feature. The list now folds the aggregate in with one extra round-trip on the `mine` path, and picks up `completed_at` for free from the `challenge_participants` read it was already issuing (the column was simply not selected).

**The `?? 0` is the part worth naming, because it is a claim, not a default.** `my_active_challenges` deliberately spans only challenges live now or ended within seven days, so a challenge that ended a month ago has no value to fold in — and coercing that absence to zero tells a runner who *finished* a 100 km challenge that they ran none of it. `myProgressView` grades a row into `known` / `not_started` / `unknown` instead: a value from the server always wins (so a client clock behind the server's cannot downgrade a real number to a presumed zero), an unopened window is a *true* zero because the aggregate's window is `started_at >= starts_at`, and everything else renders "Progress unavailable — open for your result" rather than a bar. A non-finite value or an unparseable `starts_at` falls to `unknown` too — fail closed to claiming nothing. The enrichment call is auxiliary and wrapped: a failure leaves `my_value` null, which lands in the same honest state rather than in a fake zero.

**On the club-vs-club board the same shape of mistake was leaking an internal identifier.** The detail page built `clubNames` from `fetchMyClubs()` — the viewer's *own* clubs — and `ChallengeLeaderboard` fell back to `row.team_club_id`, so on a board whose entire premise is rival clubs, every club the viewer was not a member of rendered as a bare uuid. The page now resolves the board's own team ids in one `fetchClubNames` read (RLS already scopes it to public clubs plus the viewer's own), and the component's fallback is a localized label: `teamLabel` separates `no_club` — a real bucket, since `challenge_participants.team_club_id` is nullable with `on delete set null`, so a deleted club leaves its people unaffiliated and the aggregate still sums them — from `unresolved`, a club RLS would not hand over. Neither renders the id. Web-only at the time: the mobile challenges list showed no progress bar and no leaderboard team column, so there was nothing to mirror yet.

**Amendment (2026-08-19, § 694).** The mobile list has grown the progress signal, so `social/challenge_list.ts` ↔ `apps/mobile_android/lib/challenge_list.dart` is now a registered pair in both registries (18 web / 17 Dart tests). Mobile's own club-vs-club column was carrying exactly the leak described above — `_clubNames[id] ?? id`, i.e. a raw uuid for any club RLS would not hand over — and now goes through the ported `teamLabel`.

**Addendum — the same round's third finding, closed on all four rails.** Hunting the two surfaces above turned up a third disagreement with the aggregate, in `rankParticipants` itself. `challenge_leaderboard` ends both branches `order by rank, <key> nulls last` — the team branch on `pt.team_club_id`, the per-user branch on `pu.user_id` — and has done so in all four definitions since `20270210_001`. The helper collapsed a missing key to `''`, which sorts *first*, so an unaffiliated team would have been listed **above** the named clubs it tied with rather than below them. The null bucket is reachable three separate ways: `challenge_participants.team_club_id` is nullable, the join RLS policy explicitly permits `team_club_id is null`, and the FK is `on delete set null`, so deleting a club converts its members into exactly that bucket while the aggregate keeps summing them. Fixed in lockstep across `challenge_progress.ts`, `challenge_progress.dart`, the byte-identical iOS twin, and the watch's one-way port `watch_core::challenge_progress`, each gaining two tests: the nulls-last ordering, and a guard that a keyless entry still outranks a *lower* value — because the obvious over-correction is to sort nulls last unconditionally rather than only inside a rank group, and that would be a worse bug than the one being fixed. Worth stating plainly: `rankParticipants` has **no production caller on any rail** — every board is rendered in the order the server already returned — so this changed no pixel. It is a correctness fix to a documented contract, made now because the divergence was found now, and because a helper whose entire stated purpose is "mirror the aggregate exactly" is worth nothing the moment that claim stops being true.

## 604. The TS↔Dart parity-pair registry is written down twice, so a guard makes the two copies agree — and it runs on docs-only PRs, because that is how the drift arrives

**The list of parity pairs lives in two files, and only one of them does any work.** `CLAUDE.md`'s "TS↔Dart parity helpers must stay in lockstep" bullet is the human-facing registry — what a session reads to decide whether the helper it just edited has a twin. `.claude/agents/shared-library-syncer.md`'s "The pairs (canonical list)" table is what the `shared-library-syncer` agent works from, and that agent is the only automated detector of divergence the convention has. The two had drifted nineteen pairs apart: fifteen registered in the prose with no row in the table (`route_markers`, `roadbook`, `fuel_plan`, `route_geometry`, `route_snap`, `run_heatmap`, `recap`, `finisher_certificate`, `challenge_progress`, `onboarding`, `meal_template`, `recipe`, `race_predictor`, `safety_nudge`, `undo_queue`) and four the other way (`coach_load`, `nearby`, `off_route_alert`, `profile_query`). Each direction fails differently and both fail silently. A pair missing from the table is one the agent will not check — its own instructions tell it to stop rather than invent a parity claim about a pair it cannot find there — while `CLAUDE.md` reads as though it is covered. A pair missing from `CLAUDE.md` reads as a single-platform helper, so the edit never reaches the agent at all. `roadbook` was in the first state on the day a change altered it on web, in Dart and in the watch port at once. This is the § 305 failure one level up: there, two helpers' doc comments claimed lockstep while the code carried different algorithms and each suite pinned the opposite answer.

**`scripts/check_parity_pair_registry.mjs` reads both files rather than transcribing either**, the same shape as `check_watch_ble_uuids.mjs` and `check_toolchain_pins.mjs`. It checks membership in both directions, that a path `CLAUDE.md` annotates is the path the row names, and that every file either registry points at exists — a rename that leaves a registry aimed at nothing is the same defect one step later, and it was already live: `profile_query.ts`'s own header named a Dart twin at `apps/mobile_android/lib/profile_query.dart`, which does not exist, because that pair's Dart side sits in the shared `core_models` package. The anti-vacuity work is deliberate and is most of the test suite: every anchor the parsers depend on is asserted present, each parser fails if it matched nothing, and two empty registries are an error rather than agreement. Bidirectionality carries that weight too — a parser that quietly stops understanding one entry drops it from one set and is immediately reported as missing from it, so the guard cannot degrade into a pass.

**It runs unconditionally, which is a change to the job that hosts it.** `parity-matrix` was gated on `needs.changes.outputs.code == 'true'`, and the `changes` filter classifies `docs/`, `.claude/` and every `*.md` as a docs-only diff. Every file that job's guards read is markdown — `docs/product/parity.md` for the matrix check, `CLAUDE.md` and the syncer agent for this one — so the gate skipped the job on precisely the edits it exists to police, and the CI gate counts a skip as a pass. That is the same "green having tested nothing" shape the `changes` job's own comment warns about when it argues for an exclusion list over an inclusion list. The gate is gone; a docs PR now pays a Flutter setup it did not before, which is the right trade against a registry that can be invalidated by a single markdown edit nothing verifies.

## 605. A warmup at the working weight is invisible without its label, so both set-history RPCs return `set_type`

**Decided (2026-08-13, migration `20270525_001`).** § 602 narrowed the gym prescriber's judgement to the sets done at the session's top completed weight, which drops a ramp-up whether or not anyone typed it as one. That held the line and it is the truer reading of "five sets of five" — but it was doing a job the label was supposed to do, because the label was not arriving. `gym_exercise_set_history_batch` (and its singular sibling) never returned `gym_sets.set_type`, so every set the web progression read from history reached `completedSets` unlabelled and was treated as working. What the narrowing cannot reach is the residual case: a warmup logged **at** the working weight is not lighter, so nothing but `set_type` separates it. Mobile reads its local store, which carries the column, and excluded that set; web did not. One prescriber, two platforms, two different loads on the bar.

**The fix is the column, not a cleverer heuristic.** Both RPCs now select `set_type` and carry it in their return table. Reading the code first widened the scope by one and a half: the singular `gym_exercise_set_history` had the identical gap, and `fetchGymSetHistoryWithError` was already *selecting* the column from PostgREST and silently dropping it in its row mapping. All three `GymSetWithDate` producers in `core/data.ts` now map it, and the field is **required** on that interface rather than optional — an optional field is an invitation for a fourth producer to omit it and re-open exactly this defect. It is nullable at that boundary only: the column is `NOT NULL DEFAULT 'working'`, so nothing from the database can be null, and `gym_progression` remains the single place that resolves an absent value to `'working'`.

**Adding a column to a `returns table` is a drop-and-recreate, and a `DROP FUNCTION` takes the privileges with it.** `create or replace` refuses a changed return type (42P13), so both functions were dropped and recreated with their bodies re-emitted verbatim — the normalisation expression and the explicit `auth.uid()` filter unchanged — and the `revoke execute … from public` / `grant execute … to authenticated` pair re-issued. That last clause is the part worth writing down: an unre-issued grant leaves a `SECURITY INVOKER` RPC callable by nobody, which reads at the client as a permission error on a page that worked yesterday. `20261231_001` set this pattern when it landed `duration_s`; this migration follows it. No table is locked — the DDL touches `pg_proc` only, and the migration's own transaction makes the swap atomic for concurrent callers.

**A behavioural test could not have caught this, which is why the guard is a source guard.** `nextPrescription` and `lastSessionSets` always honoured `set_type`; they were simply never handed it, so every unit test that passed a labelled set in by hand passed both before and after. The regression lived in the seam between the RPC and the row mapping. `gym/set_history_set_type.test.ts` therefore pins both halves: the semantic claim (an explicitly-typed warmup at the working weight is excluded, and the same session without the label holds the load — so the label is demonstrably what decides), and a source guard over the three producers, which is the half that fails against the pre-fix file. The pgTAP suites pin the other end: each row carries its logged `set_type`, and a set logged without one reads back as `'working'` rather than null.

## 606. A race on the calendar can seed the plan that peaks on it, and the link carries the race's facts rather than the derived dates

**Decided (2026-08-14).** The race calendar and the plan generator were two shipped features that never spoke. A runner could find their goal race, follow the entry link, and — months later — import the result, but nothing carried them from *"my half is on the 15th"* to a plan built around that date. The arithmetic in between is the part people get wrong by hand, and it is not one calculation but three: `generatePlan` hard-anchors day 0 of the start week to the Sunday long run (`plan_start.ts`), so a start date that isn't a Sunday silently shifts every day-role; the generated plan's last week is the `race` week, so race day has to land inside `[start + (weeks-1)*7, start + weeks*7 - 1]` whatever weekday it falls on; and the count of weeks between now and then is a span of calendar days, not of milliseconds. `racePlanPreset` does all three, and the wizard grew the four props (`initialName` / `initialStartDate` / `initialWeeks`, beside the existing `initialGoalEvent`) to receive them.

**Weeks are capped at the goal's own default rather than filling the gap.** A marathon eight months out does not want a 32-week build; it wants the standard 16-week one starting in four months. So the preset takes `min(weeks available, defaultPlanWeeks(goal))` and pushes the start date later, which is also why the start date is derived backwards from race week rather than forwards from today.

**It refuses rather than proposes when it cannot do the job.** A race already run, or one closer than `RACE_PLAN_MIN_WEEKS` (4 — the wizard's own `min` on the week field), returns a reason instead of a squeezed plan, and the CTA is simply absent on those cards. The same refusal is honoured a second time in the wizard, because a link can go stale in an open tab or arrive hand-edited; there it renders a note saying why the dates are the usual defaults, which is the one thing a silent fallback could not do.

**A distance matching no standard rung claims no goal event.** The four rungs are matched within 2 % (listings round — "21.1 km"), and anything else — a 50k, a 10-miler — leaves `goalEvent` null and preselects nothing. The temptation is to snap to the nearest rung, and it is wrong in the direction that matters: the wizard has no custom-distance input, so a 50k presented as a marathon would not be an imprecise label, it would be a plan for a different race. Presetting only the dates is half an answer, and it is the half we can stand behind.

**The URL carries the race's facts, not the derived dates.** `/plans/new?raceDate=&raceDistance=&raceName=` is re-derived against today by the wizard rather than replaying a `start`/`weeks` pair computed when the card rendered. One home for the arithmetic, and a bookmarked link cannot resurrect a start date that is now in the past.

**Web-only, deliberately.** Mobile has both a races screen and a plan wizard, so this is a genuine mirror candidate — but neither carries the bridge yet, and a Dart twin written today would be dead code that the parity guard would then police forever. Tracked as a mirror in `followups.md` instead, per the § 24 web-canonical rule.

## 607. A date-only string is a calendar day, not an instant — the shared formatters now parse it as one

**Decided (2026-08-14).** `new Date('2026-11-15')` is UTC midnight, per ECMA-262's special case for the date-only form. `formatDate` / `formatDateShort` pushed that straight into `toLocaleDateString`, which renders in local time — so every `date` column the app formats read **one day early everywhere west of Greenwich**, and correctly everywhere east of it. A race listed on the 15th showed as the 14th across the Americas; so did a plan's start and end dates, a coached athlete's scheduled workout, and a personal-record date. The formatters now build the Date from the calendar components when the input matches `yyyy-mm-dd`. (This entry originally also claimed the Learn guide date; that surface reaches the formatter as a serialised timestamp and needed its own fix — see § 608.)

**A full timestamp keeps its timezone conversion, and that is half the contract.** An instant genuinely belongs to different calendar days in different places — a run recorded at 23:30 UTC *is* the next day in Tokyo — so anything that isn't date-only falls through to the normal parse untouched. Both directions are pinned, because the obvious "simplification" of this fix is to treat every input as a calendar date, which would silently misdate every run in Asia.

**The codebase had already worked this out five times, locally.** `plan_start.ts`, `fmtIsoDate` on the workout page, `fmtRaceDate` on two others, and `planMidnight` on the dashboard each hand-roll a component-based local parse; another eight call sites append `'T00:00:00'` to force one. The convention was right and widespread — the *shared* helper was the one place that got it wrong, so every call site that trusted the helper instead of hand-rolling around it inherited the bug. That is the argument for fixing the formatter rather than adding a ninth workaround: the four nutrition call sites that appended the suffix are now redundant and were removed, and no new call site has to know about any of this.

**It was invisible in CI by construction.** `tests-e2e/playwright.config.ts` pins `timezoneId: 'UTC'`, where the bug cannot reproduce — a zero or positive offset hides it completely. The unit tests set `process.env.TZ` per case across the full offset range including both extremes, and `tests-e2e/cross-cutting/date-only-timezone.spec.ts` overrides the browser timezone to a negative offset and back. Both were confirmed to fail against the pre-fix code; a guard that passes either way would have been worth nothing here.

## 608. The Learn guide date reached the formatter as a timestamp, so § 607 did not fix it — the frontmatter parser was the second source

**Decided (2026-08-14, amending § 607).** § 607 listed a Learn guide's updated date among the surfaces it fixed. It did not fix it, and the review that caught this is the reason the claim isn't still sitting in the ADR unchallenged. `GuideFrontmatter.updated` is typed `string`, and every reader believed it — but mdsvex parses frontmatter with js-yaml's **default** schema, which resolves a bare `YYYY-MM-DD` scalar through the YAML 1.1 `!!timestamp` tag into a `Date` at UTC midnight. mdsvex then JSON-serialises the metadata export, so what actually reaches the app is the string `2026-06-15T00:00:00.000Z`. That is a full ISO timestamp, so § 607's date-only branch never saw it, the instant branch handled it correctly-as-specified, and the guide still rendered a day early west of Greenwich.

**Worth recording precisely because the diagnosis was half-right twice.** The review reported the value as a live `Date` object reaching the formatter, having probed mdsvex's `preprocess.markup()` and read the pre-serialisation frontmatter; the built app sees the serialised string instead. Same root cause, same symptom, different runtime shape — and a fix written against the reported shape alone would have passed its own unit test and left the page broken, which is what the first attempt here did until the browser test contradicted it. **The e2e was what settled it.** A unit test can only assert against the shape you believe in.

**Normalised at the index boundary, not by quoting the frontmatter.** Quoting `updated: "2026-06-15"` in each guide would work and would be forgotten by the next author; `frontmatterDate` in `guides_index.ts` runs once in `buildIndex` and the type no longer claims a bare date string it never holds. It accepts both shapes — the `Date` a raw-frontmatter reader sees, the serialised string the compiled module does — and the string branch strips **only** a suffix that is precisely UTC midnight, because a value carrying a real time of day is a genuine instant and flattening it would be § 607's error running in the other direction.

**The lesson generalises past dates.** A type annotation on a value that crosses a build-tool boundary is a claim about that tool's behaviour, not a fact the compiler checked — `metadata` is whatever mdsvex chose to emit. Where a parser, serialiser, or codegen step sits between a declaration and its runtime value, the annotation is documentation until something asserts it.

## 609. The runner sees their own injury-risk band, and it is graded on distance because the coach roster's stress proxy is linear

**Decided (2026-08-14).** ACWR and its injury-risk bands have been in the codebase since the coach roster, and until now only a *coach* could see one. `/coaching` classifies other people's athletes through `coach_load.ts`, and `plan_ramp.ts` grades a hypothetical future plan with the same edges — but the runner opening their own dashboard, who in the overwhelming majority of cases has no coach at all, was never told that their last seven days run 60 % above their own month's average. The most actionable safety signal in the app had no reader.

**It is not the readiness ring, and the distinction is the reason it earns a second card.** `readiness.ts` scores *today* — form, sleep, resting HR — and answers "should I run hard this morning". ACWR scores the last month's ramp and answers "have I built too fast to keep getting away with it". A runner can be fully recovered today and still sitting in the spike zone that surfaces as an injury three weeks out; a card that conflated the two would let the good news hide the bad.

**Graded on distance, not on the roster's stress proxy — because they are the same number.** `coach_roster_summary` sums a `km × 10` proxy and divides the 7-day sum by the 28-day average. That proxy is *linear* in distance, so the quotient is identical whether you divide stress or metres, and reproducing the constant client-side would only create a second place for it to drift. `acwr` remains the one implementation doing the division, and a unit test pins the equality explicitly — so if anyone makes the roster's stress non-linear (an elevation or HR term, say), that test fails and names the divergence instead of letting the runner's band quietly disagree with their coach's.

**It counts DNF distance, which the coach roster does not.** That divergence is deliberate and follows § 592: nothing rewrites `distance_m` when the flag is set, so a DNF's distance is work the body actually absorbed, and dropping a 100 km did-not-finish from the acute window would *under-report* a spike. Under-reporting is the failure that hurts for a safety signal; the roster's question ("which athletes need my attention") tolerates the other trade-off.

**It refuses to grade a thin history, for the reason `plan_ramp` already wrote down.** Below `MIN_ACTIVE_WEEKS` of the chronic window the ratio is arithmetic on noise — one 3 km jog in a month divides into any week at all and produces a terrifying number. The card self-hides rather than showing a zeroed ratio, because a zero here reads as a reassuring "safe". Inventing a spike is how a safety signal teaches people to ignore it.

**`shouldSurfaceSelfLoad` is a type predicate, not a boolean.** The band union carries an `insufficient` member the card has no copy for, and `svelte-check` caught the missing keys on the first draft precisely because the predicate narrows. Making an unlabelled band a compile error is worth more than the four i18n keys a dead `insufficient` label would have cost.

## 610. A stacked PR ran no CI at all, so the `pull_request` triggers lost their base-branch filter

**Decided (2026-08-14).** Eight workflows — including `ci.yml`, which owns the required **CI gate** — filtered their `pull_request` trigger to `branches: [main]`. A *stacked* PR, one based on another feature branch rather than on `main`, matched none of them and therefore ran nothing: no gate, no `gitleaks` secret scan, no CodeQL, no bundle budget, no env-isolation check. Stacking is the normal way to split a large change into reviewable pieces, and this repo's own convention of one-piece-one-commit makes it likely.

**The failure mode is why this is worth an entry rather than a one-line fix.** The PR did not go red — it went *green*, showing two passing checks (`lint title` and the labeller, the only two workflows that had no base filter) and reporting `MERGEABLE`. Nothing on the PR page distinguishes "50 checks passed" from "the 2 checks that exist passed". Branch protection requires the gate only on pushes to `main`, so a stacked PR could merge into its parent branch entirely unscanned, and the parent could then carry that content to `main` under a single gate run that never saw it in isolation. An invisible absence of enforcement is worse than a visible failure.

**Seven lose the filter; `dependabot-auto-merge.yml` keeps its, and that distinction is the point.** That workflow is a `pull_request_target` job holding `contents: write` whose whole purpose is to *merge* code. Its base filter is a safety scope — the set of bases it has been reasoned about — not an accident of copy-paste. Dependabot only ever targets `main`, so widening it would gain nothing and would permit a bot PR to auto-merge into a branch nobody reviewed. It is now commented to say so, because the obvious next sweep is "make them all consistent". Every `push:` trigger is untouched: a push run's job is to re-validate `main` after a merge, and a feature branch is already covered by its PR.

**A guard, not just a fix.** `security_guards.test.ts` parses the `on:` block of every workflow and fails on any `branches:` key under `pull_request` / `pull_request_target` outside the exempt set, naming the file and the remedy. It was verified to fail against the pre-fix config before being trusted — a guard for an invisible defect earns nothing if it passes either way.

**One related gotcha is documented but deliberately not fixed.** Retargeting an existing PR's base does not start a run: `pull_request` fires on `opened` / `synchronize` / `reopened`, and a base change is `edited`. Adding `edited` would rebuild ~19 jobs on every description typo, against the same hosted-runner budget `ci.yml`'s concurrency block already rations. Pushing a commit or reopening the PR forces a run, and with the filter gone a stacked PR is gated from the moment it opens, so retargeting should rarely be needed at all.

## 611. Refusing Android's "While using the app" grant recorded nothing at all, so the recorder now records under it and discloses the limit

`RunRecorder.prepare` threw `LocationPermissionWhileInUseError` on Android whenever the location grant was `whileInUse`, and `_startGpsRetryLoop` gated on the same predicate so the loop would not re-open the stream either (§ the #671 fix made both agree). The reasoning in § the May 2026 commit was sound as far as it went: under a foreground-only grant Android can stop delivering fixes once another app takes focus, and that freeze is invisible until you look at the finished run.

**The cure was worse than the disease, and it landed on the default path.** Android's first-run runtime dialog cannot grant more than "While using the app" — `ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION` is a separate trip to Settings that the OS deliberately makes awkward. So every runner who accepted the dialog and pressed GO got: no position stream, no fixes, `LiveRunMap` parked on its "Waiting for GPS" spinner for the entire run (that branch renders whenever there is no fix and no planned route — the reported symptom, "the map doesn't load"), distance frozen at 0, and the run saved with `indoor` + `indoor_estimated` + a pedometer distance. Trading a *possible* background freeze for a *certain* total recording failure is the wrong trade, and it hit the majority case rather than an edge one.

**A foreground-only grant is a limitation, not an error.** `prepare` now opens the stream for it and sets `backgroundLocationLimited`; `_permissionAllowsStream` refuses only `denied` / `deniedForever`, and prepare routes its own gate through that same predicate so § #671's no-drift property survives (the retry loop still cannot open a stream prepare just refused). `run_screen` reads the flag at `_begin` and on the crash-resume path and shows the existing `runGpsAllowAllTheTime` banner with its Settings shortcut, so the runner is told exactly what they were told before — the difference is that the run is now recording while they read it. The pre-run `_maybeNudgeBackgroundLocation` dialog is unchanged and still the primary escalation path.

**iOS is untouched**: "While Using the App" plus `UIBackgroundModes:location` is a supported background-recording configuration there, so `backgroundLocationLimited` is always false on iOS and the flag is derived per-platform in one place.

## 612. The comeback runner gets an honest signal, because the ratio that refuses to grade them is the wrong instrument, not the wrong threshold

§ 609 gave the runner their own ACWR band and, correctly, made it refuse to grade below `MIN_ACTIVE_WEEKS` of the chronic window: dividing a comeback week by a near-empty month manufactures a terrifying ratio out of thin air, and a safety signal that cries wolf gets ignored. But that refusal is silent exactly where the runner is most exposed. Someone back from three months off, logging a 30 km first week, has `activeWeeks = 1` and sees no card at all — in the case that most warrants one.

**The threshold is right; the instrument is wrong.** ACWR asks "how does this week compare with the month you just trained", and a comeback runner has no such month. `training/comeback.ts` asks the question their history can actually answer: how does this week compare with the weeks they were running *before* the break. Their own pre-break average is real data; the near-zero month is not. Lowering § 609's gate would have been the cheap fix and the wrong one — it would have kept a ratio whose denominator is noise.

**The two cards are mutually exclusive by construction, not by the caller choosing.** `comebackLoad` early-returns whenever `activeWeeks >= MIN_ACTIVE_WEEKS` — the same gate `selfLoad` uses, read the other way round — so no history can surface both. The dashboard mounts them side by side and never arbitrates. A unit test sweeps histories asserting the two predicates are never both true, and a Playwright case asserts `load-ramp` has count 0 on a comeback dashboard, so the invariant is pinned at both layers rather than asserted in a comment.

**A break is `kLayoffResetDays`, reused rather than redeclared.** 28 days is already the point at which `training_load.ts` writes the runner's fitness EWMAs to zero. A break big enough to erase their modelled fitness is the same break this card is about, and two constants for one idea is how they drift apart.

**A base older than a year grades nothing, and that is the fail-closed direction.** A year-stale weekly average describes a body that no longer exists. Grading a return against it produces a *reassuring* number for a runner who is effectively starting over, and over-reporting safety is the failure that hurts — the mirror of § 609's reasoning about under-reporting a spike. Likewise a week with no running is not graded at all: an "easing in" verdict off zero kilometres is praise for not running.

**`RETURN_WEEK_SHARE` is one flat line at 0.5, deliberately not a curve.** The widely-taught return-to-running shape is to resume at around half of what you were doing and rebuild. Decaying the threshold by layoff length would invent precision the underlying evidence does not carry, and a runner can reason about "half" in a way they cannot reason about a decay constant.

**`volumeSample` was extracted for a correctness reason, not a tidiness one.** Both sides of this comparison reduce the same runs over different windows. Two copies of "does this row count as running volume" would let the two halves come from different run sets, which is the one way a comparison between them can lie silently. It is also why the future-timestamp clamp `recentRunVolume` documents had to be repeated here: an unclamped stamp from a device whose clock runs ahead opens a phantom gap to the run before it and reads as a break the runner never took. Two tests pin that a skewed stamp grades identically to an honest one. Web-only, matching the `self_load` / `plan_ramp` precedent — no Dart twin owed until mobile grows a load surface.

## 613. Gear rotations hand the `is_default` star over explicitly — the rotation stays a grouping, but it is no longer inert

A rotation (§ 183) was deliberately built as a named many-to-many grouping that changes *nothing* about auto-tagging, on the reasoning that it must not be conflated with the single `is_default` current pair. That separation is right, but shipping it with no bridge at all made the feature actively harmful: the `runs`-insert trigger kept stamping whichever pair last held the star, so a runner rotating three pairs banked every kilometre onto one of them and all three pairs' wear classification, progress bars and replacement targets were wrong. A rotation that cannot influence what you are recorded as wearing is a filter, not a rotation.

**Decided:** `/settings/gear` names the pair with the most life left on each rotation row and offers a one-click handoff of the star to it. The rotation still never moves the star by itself — the runner does, which keeps § 183's separation intact while closing the gap. The pick (`gear/rotation_pick.ts`, pure) ranks on each pair's share of **its own** replacement target so a 500 km road shoe and a 1000 km trail shoe compare fairly; sorts pairs the classifier already calls `worn` **last** regardless of share, because recommending a shoe flagged for replacement is worse than recommending nothing; **drops** retired pairs rather than ranking them last (a retired pair is not a pair you could be asked to wear); measures an untracked pair against the rotation's **median** target, not the mean, so one outlier target cannot swing it, degrading to raw distance when no member is tracked at all; and breaks ties on id so a row never reorders between renders. The affordance gates on the count the pick actually **ranked**, not on membership count — a rotation holding one live and one retired pair has no choice to offer.

**Scope:** web-only, per § 24. `rotation_pick.ts` is deliberately **not** registered as a TS↔Dart parity pair — there is no Dart twin, so registering it in one registry would fail `check_parity_pair_registry.mjs` and registering it in both would claim a lockstep that does not exist. Not built: any automatic rotation of the star (a run you did not record in the picked pair would then be silently mis-tagged — the whole failure this fixes, inverted), and any recency/rest signal, which `gear_with_distance` cannot answer without a `last_used_at` the view does not carry.

## 614. Roadbook checkpoints are graded against their own target times, with a proportional on-schedule band

Course markers have carried a target time since issue #608 and the roadbook has been able to seed them ("Save as marker targets"), but `buildRoadbook` never read one back — so changing the goal time or the pacing model re-projected the sheet with no signal of how far it had drifted from the plan the crew agreed. The target was write-only from the roadbook's side.

`buildRoadbook` now emits a `target` verdict on every leg whose marker carries one, symmetric with the cutoff verdict: the resolved `targetElapsedS`, a `marginS` signed the same way as the cutoff's (positive is time in hand), and an `ahead` / `on` / `behind` status. Both resolve through one shared `limitFromParts`, so a clock-only target takes the identical first-occurrence-after-the-start rule as `cutoff_clock` and the two cannot disagree about what "06:00" means on one row.

The on-schedule band is deliberately **proportional** — `max(60 s, 1 % of the target)` — not flat like `CUTOFF_TIGHT_S`: two minutes down at a 30-minute checkpoint is a real problem and two minutes down at hour twenty of a 200-miler is noise, so a fixed band would grade every ultra checkpoint off-plan and every 10K one on it. Both suites pin that by running the same five-minute slip at an hour goal and a 24-hour goal and requiring `behind` / `on`. Web renders a Target column that appears only once a checkpoint carries a target (no empty column on an unplanned route) and states the verdict in words rather than by colour alone. The web resolver takes its parts structurally rather than borrowing `CutoffParts`, because `parseCutoff` and `parseTarget` return two separate interfaces that are identical only by coincidence; the Dart twin passes the clock and elapsed as plain parameters for the same reason.

## 615. A challenge leaderboard states the viewer's standing, not just the board

`/challenges/[id]` rendered every entrant's rank and value but nothing relating the viewer to their neighbours — and on a board of any size the viewer's own row is off screen, so "#7 of 24" was the whole answer. `social/leaderboard_standing.ts#standingFor` re-shapes the rows already fetched into rank, board size, tie count, and the metric gap to the nearest entry strictly above and strictly below; it adds no query and shows nothing the board below does not.

Two properties are load-bearing. Rank is **derived** as one plus the count of strictly better values rather than read off the row — that is `rank() over (order by value desc)` by definition, so the card cannot contradict the rank the SQL sent and the list renders, and the helper works on any unranked board. Neighbours tie-break on `entryKey` ascending, mirroring `challenge_leaderboard`'s `order by rank, <key> nulls last`, so two refreshes name the same entrant. A tied leader reports the tie rather than "Leading": sole leadership is a claim the data does not support.

On a club-vs-club board the entrant is the club the viewer **joined under**, carried on `ChallengeWithMeta.my_team_club_id` off their own `challenge_participants` row. Resolving it instead from whichever of the viewer's clubs appears on the board is wrong whenever a runner belongs to two competing clubs, and told the trailing team it was leading — caught during the audit and pinned by a spec that fails against the old derivation. The RLS policy that makes participants readable with their challenge already exposes that column and `team_club_id` is already on every leaderboard row, so no new surface is opened. Web-only, like `challenge_list.ts`: the mobile challenge detail renders the raw board with no standing card, so a Dart twin would be a helper with no caller and a parity obligation policed forever for nothing.

**Amendment (2026-08-18).** The original entry closed with "web-only, like `challenge_list.ts`: a Dart twin would be a helper with no caller and a parity obligation policed forever for nothing." The mobile challenge detail has now grown the card, so that clause no longer holds and `social/leaderboard_standing.ts` <-> `apps/mobile_android/lib/leaderboard_standing.dart` is a registered pair in both registries, 16 mirror tests each. Two things came with the port rather than out of it. Mobile's `ChallengeView` carried no analogue of `my_team_club_id`, so a club-vs-club standing had nothing correct to key on — the one derivation this ADR explicitly rules out (whichever of the viewer's clubs appears on the board) was the only one available; `fetchChallengeById` now reads `team_club_id` off the viewer's own participant row, the same column the web fetch already selects, so no new surface is opened. And the *suppression* rule turned out to be as load-bearing as the card: web gates on `standing && rows.length > 1`, and a port that renders whenever a standing exists says "#1 of 1" to the first person who joins — worse than saying nothing. Both platforms now pin that as a test rather than leaving it to the reader of the Svelte template. The Dart `StandingEntry` is a declared abstract interface where TS's is satisfied structurally, and `ChallengeLeaderboardEntry` implements it; that is an idiomatic shape difference of the same kind as `password_change`'s union-versus-class, not a divergence. (`challenge_list.ts` was still web-only on that date; it stopped being so on 2026-08-19, § 694.)

## 616. Extended nutrients roll up to a day only with their coverage attached; a claim that partial coverage cannot support is withheld, not estimated

The five nullable `food_log` nutrients (`fiber_g` / `sugar_g` / `sodium_mg` / `saturated_fat_g` / `cholesterol_mg`, issue #492) now roll up to a self-hiding Nutrients section on `/nutrition` via the web-only `nutrition/extended_nutrients.ts`. The obvious implementation — sum them the way `sumMacros` sums calories, with null counting as 0 — is fail-open for exactly this data: both food sources carry these fields unevenly, so a day of eight items of which two report sodium produces a total that reads as the day's intake and sits comfortably under a ceiling the day may in fact have blown past.

Every total therefore carries how many entries reported it, and the module offers only the claims that survive partial coverage. `exceeded` (a ceiling nutrient past target) and `reached` (a floor nutrient at or past target) are **monotone** — the reported entries alone already clear the line and the unreported ones can only add — so they are stated regardless of coverage. `remaining` ("600 mg left") is a claim about the day's *whole* intake, and the unreported entries could have consumed all of it, so it is withheld (null) whenever coverage is partial and the row is rendered "at least X" instead. A nutrient no entry reported is omitted rather than shown as zero.

Targets are public reference intakes and two of the five deliberately have none: **sugar** is ungraded because the stored field is *total* sugars while every published ceiling (WHO's 10 % of energy) is about *free/added* sugars, so grading it would flag a bowl of fruit as an overshoot; **cholesterol** is ungraded because the 300 mg/day cap left the Dietary Guidelines in 2015 and no numeric limit replaced it — inventing a threshold is worse than showing none. **Fibre** is a floor at 14 g/1000 kcal scaled off the *base* calorie goal rather than the exercise-inflated one, because the reference is an adequacy figure for ordinary intake while the extra carbohydrate a long-run day earns is deliberately low-residue; scaling it by workout calories would prescribe 50 g+ of fibre on precisely the day a runner wants least of it. **Sodium** is a ceiling of 2300 mg that *rises* with logged exercise on the same "base + exercise" model as the calorie goal (§ 134) and the water goal — the population ceiling is the wrong ceiling for someone who just sweated out two litres — at 6 mg/min, derived from `hydration.ts`'s own 480 ml/hr sweat-replacement assumption at a conservative ~700 mg of sodium per litre, and capped at that module's `MAX_EXERCISE_MINUTES` for the same reason: past four hours this is a race fuel plan (`fuel_plan.ts`), not a daily baseline. Sodium is also the one target that resolves with **no body metrics at all**, exactly as `hydrationTargetMl` always answers.

`exceeded`/`reached` grade against the rounded total the row displays, not the raw sum, so a sub-half-unit overage cannot flag a warning whose overage chip would read "0 mg over" — the same reasoning `nutrition_budget.ts` records for its own rounded `over`. The module is web-only and adds no obligation to the `nutrition_targets` / `nutrition_budget` / `hydration` parity pairs, which are untouched; it imports `MAX_EXERCISE_MINUTES` from the `hydration` pair one-directionally so the two caps cannot drift.

## 617. A gym routine's history counts a "save as is" session as performed but grades it as neither hit nor miss

Every guided gym session stamps `gym_workouts.metadata.routine_id`, but until now nothing read that link back per routine, so a lifter could see one session's adherence and never the routine's. `/gym/routines/[id]` now carries an owner-only history panel over `gym/routine_history.ts` — sessions performed, days since it was last done, a completed-of-graded ratio, and the five most recent sessions as links.

The judgement it encodes is which rows count as what. A row carrying `routine_id` with **no** `gym_adherence` verdict is not a failure: `stripSessionDraft` produces exactly that shape when the runner leaves mid-session and chooses "Save as is", deliberately keeping the link while claiming no adherence because the session never ran to completion. Counting it as a miss would punish the honest exit and make the completion rate a worse signal than the one the P1 validation gate wants; counting it as a completion would be a lie. It counts toward sessions performed and sits outside the rate denominator. An in-flight draft (still carrying `gym_session_draft`) is excluded outright — a page refresh must not inflate a routine's usage.

The panel self-hides at zero sessions per the routine surface's self-hide contract but does **not** self-hide on a failed read, because "couldn't load" and "you have never run this" are different claims; it owns its own fetch so that failure cannot blank the prescription the page exists to show. `routine_history.ts` is deliberately **web-only and not a parity pair** — mobile's routine detail screen reads `LocalRoutineStore` and has no consumer for the shaping, and a twin with no caller is dead code the parity guard would then police forever.

## 618. A bulk-import failure carries a reason, and the importers throw rather than return a reason-less disposition

Both web bulk importers previously caught the thrown error, incremented `failed`, and dropped the error, so a multi-year migration reported a bare count with no way to tell a transient network drop (re-run and it lands) from a corrupt archive member (it never will). `apps/web/src/lib/integrations/import_failures.ts` now classifies each caught value into one of seven reasons and records the activity name, its start, and a log-safe `code: message` detail — never PostgREST `.details` / `.hint`, which echo row fragments including coordinates (the `supabase_error.ts` contract), pinned by a test asserting a lat/lng planted in `.details` never reaches the detail string.

Classification checks the network / auth / rate-limit / size *message* signals first, then treats any remaining non-empty SQLSTATE or PGRST code as `rejected`, mirroring `settings_write.ts`'s `classifyWriteFailure`: a code at all means the server answered and refused, so a `22P02` "invalid input syntax" is a rejection, not an unreadable file. The log is capped at 200 entries with the overflow counted rather than dropped, so a pathological archive cannot turn the failure record into the OOM it is reporting.

As a consequence, `garmin-zip.ts`'s `importFitFile` / `importRouteFile` no longer return a `'failed'` disposition — they throw, because a disposition cannot carry a reason and the loop's single catch is the only place one can be recorded. Both helpers are module-private, so nothing outside expected the old return. The per-member try/catch inside the `.fit`-zip wrapper additionally fixes a pre-existing gap where a non-parse throw (a failed `saveRun`) escaped the inner loop and abandoned later `.fit` members — the fall-through is now stricter, not looser. **No retry button is offered, deliberately**: re-running an import *is* the retry, because both importers dedupe against what already landed; what the runner lacked was the information to decide whether re-running is worth it. Web-only — the mobile importers keep a bare counter and owe no Dart twin until one grows a report surface.

## 619. Run-detail pacing is analysed by distance, not by time, and its grade-adjusted second opinion is gated on the same margin as the key-stat GAP cell

The splits table on `/runs/[id]` listed twelve rows and interpreted none of them: it never said whether the second half was faster, and its pace column was raw, so a split that climbs 80 m read as a blow-up (that grade costs ~51 % more by Minetti) even when the effort never wavered. `apps/web/src/lib/runs/pace_analysis.ts` adds both reads.

The halves are cut at the run's own **distance** midpoint rather than its time midpoint — "negative split" is a claim about the second half of the *course*, and a time cut lands short of halfway on exactly the runs that faded, which are the ones the verdict is for. The verdict band is **relative** (2 % of the runner's own first-half pace), so it does not need a distance floor to stay honest at short distances the way an absolute second-count would; deliberately no minimum-distance guard, because the splits table this card annotates already prices a sub-kilometre run and a floor only on the summary would make the two disagree.

Both grade-adjusted reads — the second-opinion sentence and the per-split column — are suppressed unless they move the number by at least 2 s/km, reusing the threshold `showGradeAdjustedPace` already applies to the key stat: on flat ground GAP *is* raw pace, and a column restating it is noise, not information. The slicing primitive shares each interpolated cut point by reference between adjacent slices so no metre and no second falls between them, and interpolates longitude through `lonDeltaDeg` / `wrapLonDeg` (§ 463) — a plain subtraction would place a cut point on a track crossing 180° a whole turn away and hand both halves a nonsense distance. Per-split grade-adjusted paces take their boundaries from the running sum of the already-rendered `split.distance_m` rather than re-deriving tick boundaries, so the column cannot drift by a point from the table beside it. Web-only and deliberately not a registered parity pair: mobile's `run_detail_screen.dart` has no per-half or per-split consumer, and a Dart twin with no caller is dead code `check_parity_pair_registry.mjs` would then police forever (§ 604).

## 620. A called-off occurrence is subtracted by every surface that names one, and `next_instance_start` is nullable rather than falling back to a stale date

`event_exceptions` (per-instance cancellation, migration `20261019_001`) was read by exactly one surface: the event-detail instance picker. The club Events tab, the club feed's next-event card and the dashboard's next-RSVP card each kept advertising an occurrence the organiser had already called off — while the server-side reminder job (`enqueue_event_reminders`, `20261130_001`) had skipped them from the day it was written. This was the client half never catching up to what the server already knew.

`social/event_occurrence.ts` closes that asymmetry client-side. `nextLiveInstance` layers the subtraction over the pure `expandInstances` (which deliberately knows nothing about exceptions), searching `cancelledIso.length + 1` candidates — provably enough, since at most that many can be cancelled — and degrading to exactly `nextInstanceAfter` when nothing is cancelled. Cancellation identity compares via `sameInstant`, so PostgREST's `+00:00` and a client `.000Z` are not read as different instants.

`EventWithMeta.next_instance_start` became **nullable** in the same change: the old fallback to `starts_at` when a series had no next occurrence is exactly the shape of the bug — a stale date a caller reads as "the next one". The counting key keeps that fallback, deliberately and separately, so a past event still reports who attended it. A second consequence of the same half-modelling was fixed alongside: because the picker hides cancelled occurrences and the page landed on the next one, the reinstate control was reachable **only** for the very next occurrence, so cancelling anything further out was irreversible. Organisers now get an explicit "Cancelled occurrences" list of everything still ahead, each row with its own Reinstate. `/social` Discover needs no subtraction: `search_public_events` returns the *series* and the card shows a cadence label, never a particular occurrence's date.

## 621. The spectator page states when a runner has stopped moving, and refuses to state it across a gap in the telemetry

`live_freshness` (§ 601, § 607) made the surface honest about the runner we *cannot* see. It said nothing about the one we can: a phone still pinging every few seconds from the same spot rendered as a fresh green LIVE dot, and the only derived stat that would have exposed it — recent pace — computes a zero distance delta, returned null, and vanished. So "not moving" and "no data yet" looked identical, and the more alarming of the two was the one that disappeared.

`apps/web/src/lib/safety/live_motion.ts` grades a window of recent pings into `moving` / `stopped` / `unknown`, and `/live/[id]` states the result neutrally, with a duration — a runner stopped six minutes is at an aid station, one stopped ninety is a question for their crew, and the surface draws neither conclusion. It fails closed in three directions, all the same principle reached by different doors. A **stale** fix is `unknown`, because an old position is exactly when "they have not moved" is unknowable. A **gap** over `MOTION_MAX_GAP_MS` discards everything before it, because a claim about a runner staying put is a claim about every moment in between, and an outage is precisely where they could have left and come back — without this, a runner who dropped out in a canyon and re-acquired near the same spot an hour later would have been reported as "not moving for at least 60 min", an hour nobody observed. A window under `MOTION_MIN_WINDOW_MS` (180 s) is `unknown`, because every runner alive stands still for twenty seconds at a road crossing.

The gap bound is stated as a **proportion, not a guarantee**. It was first written at 120 s under a comment claiming no accepted gap could be most of a minimum-length claim; 120 s of 180 s is two thirds, so the comment asserted something the arithmetic did not support. It is now 30 s — at most a sixth of the shortest claim the helper will make — and a unit test pins that ratio so a future widening must argue with it. No gap length is perfectly safe: at a slow jog a runner clears the 25 m stopped radius and returns in about twenty seconds, and the doc says so rather than overclaiming. A stop that reaches the start of the vouched window reports as a floor ("at least N min") rather than a figure the data cannot support, and a rewound odometer is read as absolute ground covered so it cannot manufacture a stopped verdict.

In the same change the Recent-pace tile stopped wearing a present-tense label on a fix the cut-off card had already refused to project from: under staleness it reads "When last seen", keeping a real fact about the last sighting without dressing it as current. **No new data reaches an anonymous viewer** — the readout is derived entirely from the `distance_m` and `at` fields the page already renders. Web-only and deliberately not a parity pair: mobile's `live_spectator_screen.dart` renders the same pings but has no motion readout, so a Dart twin would be a helper with no caller.

## 622. The GPS link runs at the receiver's factory 38400, because a configured baud silently lapses in a drawer

`main.rs` had configured UARTE0 at 9600 since the GNSS bring-up, and no decision ever set that number — it was an assumption inherited from the u-blox M8 generation. The MAX-M10S is M10, whose documented UART1 default is **38400**; SparkFun's hookup guide for the exact breakout on [`parts.md`](../custom_watch/parts.md) says the same. A receiver out of the bag would therefore have delivered nothing a 9600 parser could resync on, and the failure presents as "no fix" — indistinguishable at the bench from a bad antenna, a wiring error, or a driver bug, which is the worst possible first hour with new hardware.

The fix is to meet the part where it is rather than to configure it. Configuring it was the tempting option, and `ublox_nmea::ubx` already has the framing and Fletcher checksum a `UBX-CFG-VALSET` would need, so the work was small. It was declined because of where the setting *lives*: the breakout's MS621FE backup cell holds battery-backed RAM for about two weeks without power, so a u-center or firmware-set baud is a value with an expiry date. A prototype that sat out a holiday would come back mute, and the person debugging it would have no reason to suspect a setting they configured once and never thought about again. A firmware that assumes only the factory default has no such state to lose, and cold-boots correctly on a receiver nobody has ever touched.

**Two derived figures move with it, and the second is a live trap.** A 32-byte burst read now fills in 8.3 ms rather than 33.3, and the ~85 ms NVMC page-erase stall (§ 419) can cost up to 326 bytes of NMEA rather than ~82 — though only in the worst case: the receiver emits one epoch of sentences per second whatever the line rate, so a faster link packs that burst into a smaller slice of the second and a stall is proportionally less likely to land on live bytes. Expected loss is roughly baud-independent. What genuinely breaks is the **sizing of the fix § 421 is holding open**: `BufferedUarte`'s guaranteed headroom is `half_len`, so the 512-byte ring that note specified buys 66.7 ms at 38400 and no longer covers even one erase, having covered three at 9600. The ring must be 2048 bytes to restore the intended margin. That is recorded here rather than left in the earlier note, because a sizing that was correct when written and is now wrong by 4x is exactly the kind of stale premise a later implementer inherits without re-deriving.

Nothing about the change is sim-observable — Renode delivers the fixture over a PTY and its UARTE model does not rate-limit against the baud register — so this is **build-verified**, and the first evidence either baud has ever had will be the step-3 bench item.

Pinning: `apps/custom_watch/app/src/main.rs`, `apps/custom_watch/app/src/tasks/gps.rs`, [`docs/custom_watch/parts.md`](../custom_watch/parts.md), [`docs/custom_watch/quality_standards.md`](../custom_watch/quality_standards.md) step 3. Supersedes the 9600-derived figures in § 419 and § 421 without amending them.

## 623. Tier-1 optical HR is a commodity MAX30101, not the production MAX86177 — and the part-agnostic half of the driver has to move out of the part crate

The parts list had named the **MAX86177** since the beginning, and the 2026-08-17 pre-order audit ([`tier1_log.md`](../custom_watch/tier1_log.md)) found three reasons that could not stand: its `MAX86177EVSYS#` is a two-board evaluation *system* rather than a breakout, it is discontinued at Digi-Key with no lead time, and — the one that decides it — **its register map is NDA-gated**, which [`vendor_research.md`](../custom_watch/vendor_research.md) established in July 2026 and nothing acted on. Buying the kit would not have produced a correct driver, because `drivers/max86177`'s register map is modelled on the MAX86171 family idiom rather than read off this part's datasheet.

The resolving observation is that the MAX86177 is a **production** pick from [`bom.md`](../custom_watch/bom.md) that was imported into tier 1 without ever being argued for at tier 1. [§ 82](decisions.md) asks for a run that records HR and explicitly accepts "raw photodiode reads + naive peak-detect", putting the licensed Maxim algorithm after tier 1 entirely. It does not ask for the launch AFE. So choosing the tier-1 part on tier-1 grounds is inside § 82's scope, not a retreat from it — and § 90's production pick is untouched.

**MAX30101 specifically, not the MAX30102 the option was first written as.** They are not interchangeable here: the MAX30102 carries red and IR only, which is a fingertip-SpO2 part, while the MAX30101 adds a **green** LED — the wavelength every wrist-worn optical HR sensor uses, because green is absorbed strongly by haemoglobin and penetrates shallowly enough to read the capillary bed through a moving wrist. A device whose whole point is the wrist would have been ordered with the wrong LED. The MAX30105 is an acceptable near-identical sibling.

Three things follow, and the second is the one that will cost time if it is not said out loud.

**The register map is public, so board vendor stops mattering.** This is the structural upside of leaving the NDA part behind: the map is in the MAX30101 datasheet (status `0x00`–`0x03`, FIFO `0x04`–`0x07`, config `0x08`–`0x0A`, LED pulse amplitudes `0x0C`–`0x10`, multi-LED slots `0x11`–`0x12`, die temperature `0x1F`–`0x21`, I²C `0x57`), identical whoever assembles the board. SparkFun `SEN-16474` and Pimoroni `PIM438` are both thin at the big distributors as of 2026-08-17, and it does not matter — a generic module answers the same registers.
