Compare the position the MAX86177 left us in, where one discontinued kit was the only way to obtain a part whose documentation was also gated.

**The part-agnostic logic is not separable today, and the audit overstated how cleanly it ports.** The claim made when this option was drafted — that everything above the raw sample survives unchanged — is true of the *logic* and false of the *packaging*. `peak_detect` (374 lines: the band-limited peak detector, `Contact`, `Reading`) and the LED AGC (`AgcConfig`, `agc_next_pa_ambient`) are modules of the **`max86177` crate**, and `app/src/tasks/hr.rs` imports them from there alongside the genuinely part-specific `Max86177`, `FifoWord`, `I2C_ADDR`, `LED_PA_DEFAULT` and `MEAS1_TAG`, calling a concrete type rather than a trait. So the port is not "write a second driver": it is **move the part-agnostic half out first** — into `watch_core` or a shared `ppg` crate — then write a thin `max30101` register driver under it, and let `hr.rs` name an abstraction rather than a part. Doing it in that order keeps one peak detector; doing it in the other order forks it, and a forked detector is two things to tune against one wrist.

**Three concrete deltas the port must not gloss.** The MAX30101's ADC is **18-bit**, so the saturation ceiling `PPG_DATA_MASK`/`0x0007_FFFF` and every "pinned at the 19-bit full scale" claim moves down a bit. The ambient (LED-off) channel that makes bright-sun subtraction work is reached through the **multi-LED slot registers** rather than the MAX86177's MEAS1/MEAS2 pair with FIFO tagging, so the mechanism changes even though the design does not. And the **register-retention-across-shutdown assumption** the duty-cycle path depends on is a *new* open question against a *new* part — it does not carry over from the assumption already logged for the MAX86177, and [`quality_standards.md`](../custom_watch/quality_standards.md) step 5 now asks it of whatever part is delivered.

`drivers/max86177` is deliberately **kept, not deleted**. It is host-tested, sim-verified against a Renode model, and it is the head start on the production part for the day an ADI NDA lands; what it is not is a driver anyone should believe until silicon answers it, which its own doc comment now says.

Pinning: [`docs/custom_watch/parts.md`](../custom_watch/parts.md) (the ordered part + what is owed), [`docs/custom_watch/quality_standards.md`](../custom_watch/quality_standards.md) steps 0 and 5, [`docs/custom_watch/roadmap.md`](../custom_watch/roadmap.md) step 5, [`docs/custom_watch/bom.md`](../custom_watch/bom.md) (production pick unchanged), `apps/custom_watch/drivers/max86177/src/lib.rs`. Supersedes nothing; § 90's production BOM row stands.

## 624. Both Go services declare a patch-level `go` floor and both are Trivy-scanned, because one shared builder digest puts the same stdlib CVEs in two images

Trivy raised eight HIGH alerts (179-186) against the `job_worker` container: the image's Go binary linked stdlib `v1.26.5`, which carries denial-of-service and content-injection bugs across `crypto/tls`, `net/url`, `net/http`, `encoding/asn1`, `encoding/xml`, `html/template`, and `golang.org/x/net/dns/dnsmessage`. The alerts are not about our code — they are about the toolchain that compiled it, which comes from the `golang:1.26-alpine` builder pinned by digest in the Dockerfile. Re-pinning that digest to the current `golang:1.26-alpine` (Go 1.26.6) clears all eight; a control scan on the old digest reproduces exactly the eight alerted CVEs, and the same scan on the rebuilt image reports zero.

Two things about the fix are non-obvious enough to write down. **The `go` directive is a patch-level floor** — `go 1.26.6`, not a bare `go 1.26`. Seven of the eight CVEs are fixed in both 1.25.13 and 1.26.6, but **CVE-2026-46600 has no fix in the 1.25 line at all**, so the previous `go 1.25.11` floor named a version series that can never be patched against it. That floor is not decorative: `setup-go` in `ci.yml` and `security.yml` resolves its toolchain from `go-version-file: <module>/go.mod`, so CI was compiling and vetting on exactly 1.25.11, and anyone building the worker outside Docker got the same vulnerable stdlib the container scan would never see. A future "tidy" of that line back to a bare minor silently reopens the hole, which is why the reason sits in a comment beside it.

**And `graph_cycle` is now scanned too.** It is a separate Go module in a separate image, but its Dockerfile deliberately shares one builder digest with `job_worker` ("Kept identical … so both Go services share one base"), so it shipped the identical unpatched stdlib — with nothing to say so, because Trivy only ever scanned `job_worker`. Scanning one of two images built from one base is the coverage gap that let a known-CVE binary sit in production invisibly, not a saving. The new job is a copy of the existing one under its own SARIF category (two uploads sharing a category make the alert set flip-flop between whichever scan ran last, the same failure the merged-CodeQL header records); like its sibling it runs `exit-code: '0'` and reports through the Security tab rather than blocking the PR. Both images scan clean at the new digest, so the added job starts quiet.

Pinning: `apps/job_worker/Dockerfile`, `apps/graph_cycle/Dockerfile` (builder digest), `apps/job_worker/go.mod`, `apps/graph_cycle/go.mod` (the floor + its reason), `.github/workflows/security.yml` (the `trivy-graph-cycle-image` job + the corrected header — `job_worker` is no longer "the only Dockerfile in the repo").
## 625. The tier-1 HR part is identified by capability, not by its part id — because the MAX3010x family shares one

`drivers/max30101` opened with a `PART_ID` read and refused anything that did not answer `0x15`, and both the driver's doc comment and [`parts.md`](../custom_watch/parts.md) said in as many words that this refused a MAX30102 before a register was written. It does not. **The MAX30101, MAX30102 and MAX30105 all report `0x15`** — the register identifies the family, not the die — so the check rules out an unrelated device that happens to answer on `0x57` and achieves precisely nothing against the one part worth refusing. This was written into the driver, its tests, the parts list, the step-0 bench checklist and the tier-1 log, and it was never true.

What made it worth finding: the commodity market for these modules is dominated by the MAX30102, the boards are visually near-identical, and § 623 chose this part partly *because* it is a commodity. So the procurement advice ("buy a listing that names the MAX30101") was resting on a silicon-level backstop that did not exist.

**What a mis-shipped MAX30102 would actually have done is worth stating precisely, because it is not what the old comment claimed.** It would not have produced a confident wrong pulse. Slot 1 selects LED3, which that part does not have, so the LED-on and LED-off slots both read ambient, the corrected DC collapses to ~0, and `PeakDetector::contact` refuses it against `contact_dc_min` — the reading stays invalid. The damage is diagnostic, not numerical: HR that never validates, an auto-gain loop walked to maximum and stuck there, and a `Contact::OffWrist` that is indistinguishable from a strap problem — which is exactly the failure [`quality_standards.md`](../custom_watch/quality_standards.md) step 5 warns will eat a bench day. The one path to a genuinely wrong number is narrower and unquantifiable: slot values 3-7 are undefined on a MAX30102, so an undocumented mapping onto a red or IR emitter would give a real but wrong-wavelength pulse. Undefined behaviour is not a thing to reason about at the bench, which is its own argument for refusing the part at init.

**The replacement is a capability check.** `init` writes `LED3_PA` and reads it back; a part with no third LED channel cannot hold it, and the refusal happens before the mode write so nothing streams. This is a strictly better test than the id even setting the family problem aside — it asks the question that matters (is there a green emitter?) rather than a proxy for it, and it catches an emitter that is present but unreachable: a broken LED3 line, a cold joint on a hand-wired breadboard, a driver stage that never came up.

**And it is backstopped, because it is not airtight.** Reserved-register behaviour on the MAX30102 is unspecified; the likely read is `0x00`, but silicon whose register file simply echoes writes would pass. So `watch_core::ppg::EmitterCheck` rides the existing auto-gain tick and names the one scene a working optical stack cannot produce: drive pinned at `max_pa`, `raw_dc` showing the diode is plainly receiving light, and a corrected DC still at the dark floor. Since the corrected DC *is* the LED's own contribution — ambient cancels out of it by construction — that combination says the drive is going nowhere.

Three deliberate constraints on that backstop, all in the direction of not accusing the hardware:

- **A dark diode is never evidence.** `raw_dc` below the worn floor means nothing is in front of the sensor, where a genuine emitter also returns almost nothing.
- **It reports, it does not gate.** The contact floor already withholds a BPM from that scene; all this adds is the reason, as one `error!` line on the transition. A sensor face-up under bright light can reach the qualifying scene with a perfectly good emitter, so a verdict that withheld data would be a false negative with teeth, while a verdict that only explains one is a hypothesis the operator can check in ten seconds.
- **Both verdicts latch.** A corrected DC that has once cleared the worn floor proves an emitter exists, and no later scene may revise that into missing silicon; equally, `NoResponse` is a conclusion about the part, and the part does not change mid-run.

The stronger test — modulate the drive and require the corrected DC to follow — is the one to reach for if the dwell proves noisy at the bench. It is not built now because it needs the loop to move the drive on demand, which the auto-gain loop only does when the DC is out of band, and the simple version answers the shipping question.

Pinning: `apps/custom_watch/drivers/max30101/src/lib.rs` (`Error::NoGreenChannel`), `apps/custom_watch/core/src/ppg.rs` (`EmitterCheck`, `EMITTER_DWELL_TICKS`), `apps/custom_watch/app/src/tasks/hr.rs`, `drivers/max30101/tests/driver_logic.rs`, `core/tests/ppg_agc.rs`, [`parts.md`](../custom_watch/parts.md), [`quality_standards.md`](../custom_watch/quality_standards.md) steps 0 and 5. Does not disturb § 623's choice of part or § 90's production row; it corrects a claim § 623 was landed alongside.

## 626. The firmware reports its supply mode at boot and refuses to program it — a 1.8 V rail is the untethered build's default, and a reset loop is worse than a bad rail

An interoperability pass over [`parts.md`](../custom_watch/parts.md) — checking the ordered breakouts against each other rather than each against its driver — turned up a configuration in which the tier-1 rig cannot work, and it is precisely the configuration § 82's outdoor run requires.

The nRF52840 has two supply paths. Fed on **VDD** it runs in normal mode and its GPIO high level is whatever rail it was given; on the DK off USB that is the board's 3.0 V and everything is fine. Fed on **VDDH** it runs in high-voltage mode, where VDD — and therefore every GPIO's logic high — is produced by an internal regulator whose output is set by `UICR.REGOUT0`, **defaulting to 1.8 V on an erased UICR**. SW9's Li-Po position is that path: [`parts.md`](../custom_watch/parts.md) has said since it was written that the Li-Po position "feeds the SoC's high-voltage regulator", without anyone noticing what that implies for the rail.

**And the DK spreads it to the whole board.** The first reading of this looked like a mixed-rail hazard — a 1.8 V SoC against 3 V breakouts, with their outputs over-volting its inputs. Nordic's hardware user guide says otherwise, and the truth is simpler and worse: "to make sure the rest of the DK has the same voltage level, the VDD of the DK is sourced by a regulator following the `VDD_nRF` voltage when the high voltage regulator is used" (§ 4.3.2). The board rail *follows the SoC down*. So the header supply every breakout is powered from is also 1.8 V, against a Sharp breakout wanting 3-5 V, a BMP581 breakout wanting 3-5 V, a MAX-M10S wanting 2.7 V minimum and a MAX30101 board built for 3.3 V. Nothing comes up. Nothing is damaged either — one rail moving together is a clean brownout, not a hazard — but the untethered build, the only one § 82's outdoor run can use, does not run at all. Note this catches the **USB** switch position too; only the default `VDD` position uses the onboard 3 V buck.

**Reporting it in firmware, and not fixing it in firmware, is the decision.** One `REGOUT0` write would settle it, and it is refused here for a specific reason: a UICR write takes effect only after a reset, so the write-then-reset sequence becomes a **boot loop** wherever the write does not stick — a simulator that models UICR loosely, or a part whose UICR page has already been written and would need an erase first. A boot that reports a wrong supply is recoverable by anyone reading the log. A boot that resets forever, on a bench where the log is the only instrument, is not. `app/src/supply.rs` therefore reads `POWER.MAINREGSTATUS` and `UICR.REGOUT0` and emits exactly one line: `info!` in normal mode, `error!` naming the fix when high-voltage mode meets an unset `REGOUT0`, and a middle `warn!` for a set-but-low rail. The fix is a one-time host-side step in the step-0 checklist.

Two consequences worth recording. Reaching those registers needed embassy-nrf's `unstable-pac` feature, taken deliberately for one read-only call site: typed PAC enums beat volatile reads at literal addresses for a check whose whole job is to be obviously correct. And **3.0 V is the target, not 3.3 V** — a nearly-flat 1S cell cannot hold 3.3 V through the regulator's dropout, and 3.0 V matches what the board supplies over USB, so behaviour does not change with the power source.

One process note, because it is the reusable part. This was found by an interoperability pass that asked a question no previous pass had: not "does each part match its driver" — every row had been checked that way, twice — but "does the set work as one rig". Secondary sources contradicted each other for an hour and settled nothing; Nordic's own hardware user guide answered it in one sentence. The lesson for the next parts question is to go to the primary document earlier, and the same pass paid for itself twice more the same way, reading a boost converter's feedback divider off SparkFun's schematic and the GNSS receiver's real current draw off u-blox's datasheet.

Pinning: `apps/custom_watch/app/src/supply.rs`, `apps/custom_watch/app/Cargo.toml` (`unstable-pac`), [`parts.md`](../custom_watch/parts.md) note 0 + the interoperability table, [`quality_standards.md`](../custom_watch/quality_standards.md) step 0.

## 627. `playwright install --with-deps` is split into its two subcommands — the apt half needs a budget of its own, because a dead Ubuntu mirror hangs it past the job cap

The `CI gate` on `main` went red twice in five hours on 2026-08-17/18 — runs 32069680540 (shard 13) and 32090988359 (shards 9, 10 and 14) — with **every other job green** and no failing assertion anywhere. The shards were not failing. They were killed by `timeout-minutes: 25` while still inside `Install Playwright Chromium`, a step whose healthy duration is 14-17 seconds.

The cause is upstream and boring: `azure.archive.ubuntu.com` answered `Ign:` instead of serving. What made it a 25-minute outage rather than a blip is ours. `playwright install --with-deps chromium` runs `apt-get update` *from inside* the browser install, so the apt half has no timeout, no retry and no budget of its own — apt fell through to `archive.ubuntu.com` for the `InRelease` files, then sat in silence on the `Packages` indices for 23 minutes. Nothing in the log distinguished the hang from ordinary progress until the cap hit, and the cap kills the job bare, so the run's only evidence was a `cancelled` conclusion.

**Splitting the command is the fix, because the two halves have nothing in common.** The browser download is cache-backed, hits Playwright's CDN, and must succeed. The apt half touches an unrelated set of mirrors, and — this is the part that decides the policy below — installs *nothing*: on the GitHub-hosted image every package it names is already `already the newest version`. It is a verification step wearing an install step's clothes. Split, `playwright install chromium` stays as it was, and `playwright install-deps chromium` gets `timeout -k 10 120` x 3 attempts: ~7x headroom over a healthy run, ~6 minutes worst case against a 25-minute cap that the slowest observed shard leaves ~13 minutes of. An `apt.conf.d` drop-in caps each index fetch at 15s so the ordinary case exits non-zero on its own long before the outer timeout; the outer timeout still bounds the pathological case that ~20 index files x a retried per-fetch cap can reach. Between attempts the apt/dpkg tree is reaped — `timeout` kills the node process but not the `sudo apt-get` beneath it, and a survivor would fail attempt 2 on `Could not get lock`, hiding the real cause behind our own leftovers.

**It fails loudly rather than `continue-on-error`, and that is a deliberate trade against the evidence above.** Since the step installs nothing on today's image, skipping it on apt failure would almost always pass, and it is tempting. It is refused because the step's only remaining value *is* the verification: the day the runner image drops a library, a swallowed failure turns one named red step into every spec in the shard failing with `browser closed unexpectedly`. Six bounded minutes and an `::error::` naming the mirrors is diagnosable in seconds and re-runnable; a silent skip trades a rare honest red for a rare incomprehensible one. If the noise ever outweighs that, the knob to turn is the attempt count, not the exit code.

**A composite action, and only `run:` steps in it.** The install was three byte-identical copies (e2e-web's 14 shards, e2e-web-livehub, e2e-web-sso), which is exactly the drift `start-supabase` was extracted to stop, so the logic moved to `.github/actions/install-playwright`. The `actions/cache` step beside it deliberately did **not** move: [§ 595](#595-a-return-that-is-not-awaited-is-outside-the-try-and-an-unpinned-sdk-is-what-found-it) established that Dependabot's `github-actions` ecosystem scans `.github/workflows` plus a *root* `action.yml` only, so a SHA-pinned action relocated under `.github/actions` quietly stops receiving updates — it declined that trade for `flutter-action`, and `start-supabase` carries no `uses:` for the same reason. The cache block stays triplicated at the call sites; it is seven lines of declarative config with no logic to drift, and the pin stays where Dependabot can see it.

Pinning: `.github/actions/install-playwright/action.yml`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (the three `e2e-web*` jobs), [`testing.md`](../testing/testing.md).

---

**Amendment (2026-08-18): the apt half is now conditional on a real Chromium launch failing.** Splitting the command bounded the mirror outage but did not stop it failing test shards — five did across two pushes on 2026-08-18 (round 4: shards 1, 7, 13; round 5: shards 6, 7), each three timed-out attempts then a hard fail, no test ever run, clean on every re-run. The step only ever *verified* (every library it installs is already the newest version on the hosted image), and it verified by talking to a third party, so a third-party outage was failing shards that would have passed. It verifies directly now — by launching Chromium, which is the exact thing the shards go on to do and strictly stronger than reading `ldd`, which cannot see what Chromium dlopens — and reaches for apt only when that launch fails. The verdict afterwards is another launch rather than apt's exit code, because install-deps can succeed with the launch still broken and can fail on a mirror having already installed what was missing. The check is not allowed to pass vacuously: any launch failure for any reason sends the job to apt, and a launch that still fails there fails the step with the browser's own error naming the library. No retries were added — three already run, and the failure mode was an outage, not slowness.

## 628. A recurrence candidate is judged not-before its series start at SECOND resolution, because that is the only resolution the stamp has

`expandInstances` walks calendar days and stamps each matching day with `starts_at`'s hour/minute/second and a **zero** millisecond — dropped by construction on both platforms, because the instance start is an RSVP capacity key every viewer must compute identically and a sub-second component carries no meaning for a wall-clock event. The guard that kept an instance from preceding its own series (`stamped < start`) nevertheless compared against the raw, millisecond-bearing `starts_at`, so a `…T02:49:18.132Z` series rejected its own first occurrence: the candidate `…:18.000` legitimately sorts before it. That occurrence then vanished from the picker, the listings, and every RSVP key derived from them — silently, because every later occurrence was fine. Production `starts_at` values come from a `datetime-local` input (whole minutes), so this bit API-written and fixture-written rows rather than user-created ones.

The fix compares at the stamp's own resolution (the start truncated down to the second) rather than widening the comparison with an epsilon: a sub-second difference on the very first stamped candidate is an artifact of the stamp, not a real ordering, and any tolerance large enough to absorb it would start absorbing real ones too. Dart uses `ms - ms % 1000`, which is floor-based for a positive divisor so a pre-epoch start truncates downward as well.

Pinning: `apps/web/src/lib/social/recurrence.ts`, `apps/mobile_android/lib/recurrence.dart` (+ the `mobile_ios` twin), one mirror test each.

## 629. `social/event_occurrence` becomes a parity pair, and its exception read is batched per list, not per event

[§ 620](#620-a-called-off-occurrence-is-subtracted-by-every-surface-that-names-one-and-nextinstancestart-is-nullable-rather-than-falling-back-to-a-stale-date) closed the cancelled-occurrence leak on web; mobile still had it, because although `fetchCancelledInstances` existed, only the event-detail screen consumed it — `SocialService._enrichEvents` and `fetchNextRsvpedEvent` resolved an event's next instance with a bare `nextInstanceAfter`, so the club Events tab and the Run-tab upcoming card advertised occurrences the organiser had called off.

The Dart port carries `isOccurrenceCancelled` + `nextLiveInstance` only. Web's `upcomingCancelledOccurrences` backs an organiser reinstate picker mobile does not have, and porting it would have been dead code the parity guard then polices forever. The exception read is **batched** — one chunked `in`-filtered query per list, bounded to `instance_start >= now`, fail-closed to "none cancelled" — because the per-event shape would have been an N+1 against a list with no server-side cap. `EventView.nextInstanceStart` stayed non-nullable and gained a sibling `hasLiveOccurrence` flag rather than becoming `DateTime?`: web models "no live occurrence left" as a null `next_instance_start` but still needs a count key, which its count map supplies by falling back to `starts_at`; the flag is that same two-valued answer without rippling null-handling through four mobile screens that only want the display instant.

Pinning: `apps/mobile_android/lib/event_occurrence.dart` (+ twin + mirror suite), `social_service.dart`, both parity registries.

## 630. The "Allow all the time" disclosure fires on the evidenced background gap, not at run start

[§ 611](#611-refusing-androids-while-using-the-app-grant-recorded-nothing-at-all-so-the-recorder-now-records-under-it-and-discloses-the-limit) made a foreground-only Android location grant a recording state rather than an error, but kept telling the runner about it at `_begin` and on crash-resume — a warning at the one moment nothing has gone wrong, which reads as "recording is broken" (#784). The disclosure now hangs off `run_screen`'s `WidgetsBindingObserver`: leaving the foreground during an active, not-manually-paused recording stamps `_leftForegroundAt`, and on `resumed` the pure `shouldDiscloseBackgroundLocationLimit` grades it.

It demands evidence rather than asserting a behaviour we cannot observe: away for at least 15 s (one fix interval plus margin) **and** no fix accepted while away, read off `_lastSnapshotAt`, which is a fix's own acceptance time and not the 1 s snapshot tick. A run that has never had a fix (indoor / treadmill) and a run that kept receiving fixes under geolocator's location-typed foreground service both stay silent — Android does not always cut delivery, and telling that runner their tracking paused would be false. Once per run, so an app switch every kilometre does not nag. The copy (`runBackgroundLocationPaused`, all seven locales) states what the code actually does — the monotonic stopwatch kept timing, the in-progress file means nothing already recorded was lost, the ground covered off screen was not counted — instead of the old "runs stop recording", which was never true (#785). The whole path is L4: its own try/catch, so a disclosure failure cannot touch recording state. The pre-run `_maybeNudgeBackgroundLocation` dialog is unchanged and remains the primary, before-the-fact escalation.

Pinning: `apps/mobile_android/lib/screens/run_screen.dart` (+ twin), `test/run_screen_background_location_test.dart`, the rewritten guard in `architecture_guards_test.dart`.

## 631. e2e `globalSetup` proves the dev server is rooted in THIS checkout, and a transitive advisory is closed by refreshing the lockfile

Two harness decisions from the same sweep.

**The dev server.** `playwright.config.ts` sets `reuseExistingServer: !CI`, so a `vite dev` left on `:7777` by another worktree is adopted silently and serves *its* bundle: a spec for a brand-new surface fails with no console error while every pre-existing spec passes, and when that foreign server dies mid-suite the result is a wave of `ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED` indistinguishable from real breaks. Several rounds lost cycles to it. `globalSetup` now probes the server with Vite's `/@fs/` route, which serves an absolute path only when it falls inside the server's own `server.fs.allow` root: `200` means this tree, `403` means the file exists but belongs to another one and fails the run naming that reason. Anything else — `404`, a non-Vite server, a network error — only warns. The guard must never turn an unfamiliar local setup into a failing suite, so only the positively-proven mismatch is fatal, and it is skipped entirely on CI, which always boots its own server.

**The lockfile.** Issue #746 reported `dompurify` (GHSA-55q2-fjhq-7xh7) and `nanoid` (GHSA-2v37-7h3g-55p8) in `package-lock.json`. Both are transitive — `dompurify` under `isomorphic-dompurify` (`^3.4.12`), `nanoid` under `postcss` (`^3.3.16`) — and in both cases the patched version already satisfied the parent's declared range, so the lockfile was merely pinned to an older resolution and a refresh reached them. No `overrides` entry was added. That is the opposite case from the `cookie` / `devalue` / `undici` / `brace-expansion` overrides already in `package.json`, where the patched line sits *outside* the parent's range and only a forced override reaches it. Prefer the refresh: an override is a standing obligation someone must later notice and remove. `pnpm-lock.yaml` had already resolved both correctly on its own, which is why `pnpm audit` stayed green while `npm audit` failed, and it needs no entry either. Note that `npm audit fix` rewrites the whole lockfile with the local npm's metadata conventions — run on a newer npm than CI's it also stripped `libc` fields from optional platform packages and re-hoisted `@types/node`; that churn was reverted so the security fix reads as a security fix.

Pinning: `apps/web/tests-e2e/fixtures/dev_server_guard.ts`, `tests-e2e/fixtures/auth.ts`, `package-lock.json`, [`testing.md`](../testing/testing.md).

## 632. `events-checkout`'s Stripe idempotency key is scoped to the pending order, and every clock-shaped field of the body is derived from that order's `created_at`

Stripe's idempotency contract is joint, not one-sided: a key replayed with a request body that has changed is answered `idempotency_error` — it is not replayed — and the key is retained for roughly 24 hours. `events-checkout` keyed on `(buyer, event, instance)`, a scope spanning every hold that pair will ever open, while the body carried a freshly-minted `order_id` and an `expires_at` computed as `Date.now() + 30 min`. The body therefore moved on every attempt under a key that never did, so a genuine double-click 502'd and kept 502'ing for a day. The header comment claiming "a double-click reuses the same session" described the opposite of what shipped.

The correct scope is the widest unit over which the *whole request* is constant, and that unit is the pending order — the hold — not the buyer/event/instance triple. The key is now `events-checkout:<order_id>`, `expires_at` comes from the order's persisted `created_at`, and the insert writes `created_at` explicitly so the anchor used is the anchor stored.

Three consequences follow from the same reasoning rather than being separate patches. `reserved_until` is no longer extended when a hold is reused: the hold is 15 minutes from the first click and the session 30, both anchored on one instant, so extending the hold would let it outlive the session backing it and would let anyone hold a seat indefinitely by re-clicking. A lapsed hold is *superseded*, not merely abandoned — its Checkout Session stays payable for another ~15 minutes after the seat was released, and two open sessions for one registration is a double charge, so it is expired at Stripe first and the resulting `checkout.session.expired` CASes that order `pending -> canceled` through the webhook, which remains the sole status writer. And the capacity precheck is skipped on the reuse path, because the caller's own pending reservation is already inside the going + pending count and re-checking it answered `event_full` to a double-click on any class the caller had themselves filled.

The property this turns on is not visible in any single helper, so `events-checkout/lib.test.ts` asserts it on the composition: two attempts eight minutes apart against one live hold must produce an identical key *and* an identical serialised body. The same round added source-level wiring guards to both money paths in the `delete-account/wiring.test.ts` idiom. That was prompted by a stale follow-up: the "partial refund processed as a full refund" entry had already been fixed by PR #758 (`refundScopeOfCharge` + the `partially_refunded` transition), but every assertion lived in `lib.test.ts`, which cannot see whether `index.ts` asks the lib anything — deleting the `scope` argument or hoisting the seat delete above the partial short-circuit would have restored the bug with a green suite. Neither money path can run end to end without operator Stripe keys, which is exactly why the wiring needs pinning by source.

## 633. Trigger-maintained counts recompute from the authoritative query, never from a plus-or-minus-one delta

`clubs.member_count` and `routes.run_count` were the last two derived caches still maintained by delta arithmetic, and both were wrong. The club trigger had two non-exclusive `if` blocks on UPDATE (status changed, `club_id` changed) while its own watch list is `OF status, club_id`, so a statement changing both ran both and moved the count by two. The route trigger decided whether a decrement was owed by re-evaluating `is_route_visible_to` on the OLD row at trigger time — which reads the route's *current* visibility, not the visibility in force when the increment happened — so a run detaching from a route that had since gone private never gave the count back.

The second is the load-bearing half: it is not a missing branch, it is unfixable in the delta form. "Was this row counted?" is a fact about the past that is not derivable from the row's own OLD image, and no number of extra `if`s recovers it. `20270526_001` therefore has both triggers call a refresher that runs the cache's documented authoritative query from scratch for each affected parent — rule 2 of `derived_state.md` § Adding a new derived cache, and the shape `challenges.participant_count` and `gym_workouts.set_count` already use. Recompute-from-source is self-healing; a delta accumulates. The accepted route-visibility drift is unchanged in scope but now *heals* on the next `route_id` touch instead of compounding, and both refreshers no-op when the cache already agrees, so the trigger path stops writing a row version per unchanged parent.

The reconcile is keyset-batched for routes (chunks of 500) per `migration_locks.md`, and a single scoped statement for clubs, which that playbook classifies as small and bounded. The clubs pass touched zero rows and was expected to: no shipped writer changes `club_members.club_id`, so that drift is only reachable by direct SQL today. It is included so the invariant is true *as of* the migration rather than only going forward.

Also corrected: `derived_state.md` claimed `clubs_member_count_test.sql` "guards every branch" while that suite never changed `club_id`, and `routes.run_count` was the one cache in that file with no "Pinned by" line at all. A coverage claim nobody checked is how the double-count survived. Both are now true, with `routes_run_count_test.sql` as the route cache's first pgtap — and each combined-UPDATE case runs on its own fresh club or route, because a double increment and a double decrement on the same parent cancel out and let the broken trigger pass.

## 634. The recorder's headline run distance is one continuous total handed between sources, not two rival accumulators

Treadmill mode can only be engaged mid-run, so every activation lands on an already-accumulating run. Anchoring the belt at its own cumulative total therefore discarded the GPS kilometres already run (measured: 60 m became 0.0, and a later belt reading of 100 m reported 100, not 160) and made the next lap split a negative delta that `lapsToCanonicalJson` clamped into a silent 0 m lap. The symmetric rule is now: switching INTO belt mode carries the accumulated total onto the belt accumulator, via the same re-anchor the pause and console-reset paths already used, and `clearTreadmillMode` hands it back to the GPS accumulator. Exactly one accumulator is authoritative at a time and the headline never steps at a switch, in either direction. This deliberately supersedes the earlier two-independent-accumulators behaviour that `run_recorder_test.dart` pinned from the other side; that test was re-pinned in the same change. `stop()` still tags a mixed run `indoor: true` / `distance_source: 'treadmill'`, which stays conservative for the VDOT ceiling.

## 635. `resumeSession` rebuilds the monotonic route floor by replaying the seeded track, within a fixed projection budget

`_minMatchedSegmentIdx` exists because route matching must not walk backwards: on a loop or an out-and-back the perpendicular-closest segment is often one already passed. `prepare()` resets it to 1, so a resumed run started with a matcher that had no memory of the ground covered — distance-remaining read 1298.5 m where a fresh run read 699.2 m, and never self-corrected, because the floor is by design never lowered. The floor is not persisted with the partial, and deriving it from the last waypoint alone cannot work: an out-and-back's return leg is geometrically ambiguous with its outbound leg, and only history separates them. So the recorder reconstructs it from what it already has — the seeded track holds exactly the fixes the live run advanced the floor on. The replay probes an evenly spaced subset of that track inside a fixed 200k-projection budget, with the last point always probed, because the floor advances by the ORDER points are matched in rather than by sampling density, and an unbounded replay of a multi-day track against a dense route is the whole run's route maths in one burst on the UI isolate.

## 636. `RunRecorder.dispose()` is terminal, not a return to idle

The self-healing GPS retry loop awaits an async service and permission precheck. A callback parked on that await when the recorder was disposed resumed afterwards and re-opened the position stream — a subscription nothing was left to cancel, holding the GPS radio and the foreground service for the life of the process while every fix raised on the closed snapshot sink. `dispose()` now latches a `_disposed` flag that `_openPositionStream` refuses outright, clears `_prepared` / `_recording`, and makes `prepare()` on a disposed recorder throw a `StateError` rather than hand back a recorder that silently records nothing. Every run already constructs a fresh `RunRecorder`, so nothing legitimate depended on reuse.

## 637. The Art 20 export pages every read, and `manifest.json` counts the database rather than the archive

PostgREST clamps every response to `db-max-rows` (1000 on Supabase) and reports the truncation only in `Content-Range` — an explicit `limit=5000` comes back with 1000 rows just the same, which is why the export's stated 5000-run cap was never actually in force. Both export paths issued one unbounded GET per table and then wrote the returned length into `manifest.json` as the count, so a runner past their thousandth run, photo, food-log row or gym set received a silently short archive whose manifest asserted it was whole. The manifest lying is the worse half: it defeats the one completeness check a data subject can actually run.

Both paths now walk 1000-row pages until the server returns a short one, ordered by each table's primary key — offset paging under a non-total order repeats one row and skips another, and a skipped row is one the subject never receives. `counts.<section>` is the authoritative count from `Prefer: count=exact` (first page only, so one COUNT per section rather than per page), not the fetched length, so counting the rows in a file and comparing them against the manifest is now a real test. `complete` and `incomplete` make any shortfall explicit: a section that fails part-way keeps the rows it read and is named, never silently dropped and never counted as whole. A section whose fetch failed still appears in `counts` at its true total even when zero rows shipped, deliberately — an absent key must not read as "the subject has none of these".

The two remaining caps — 5000 runs, and 50,000 rows per section — are kept rather than removed because both builders assemble the entire zip in memory before uploading it, so an unbounded walk of `live_run_pings` (one row per ~10 s of every run) on a deep history is an OOM, not a slow export: removing the truncation without a ceiling would have turned a completeness bug into a crash. They are now stated in the manifest instead of hidden. Removing them means a chunked / resumable Storage upload on both builders, which is tracked as a follow-up.

Nothing new leaves the system: no new tables, columns, joins, or relaxed redaction — the token exclusions and the reporter anonymisation are untouched, and delivery is the same service-role upload to the caller's own prefix behind a 10-minute signed URL. What changed is volume, which is the point, plus the meaning of `counts.<section>` (rows in the database, not rows in the file) for any downstream consumer that treated it as an array length.

## 638. A not-yet-synced run payload is not a cache; it lives where only the app can delete it

Both watch apps kept an unsynced run's GPS track in the OS-purgeable cache directory (Wear `context.cacheDir`, watchOS `.cachesDirectory`). Until the run uploads, that file is the only copy of the trace in existence, and the platform reclaims those directories under storage pressure without asking and without telling the app — so a purge destroyed recorded runs while the queue went on promising to sync them. Wear moved to `filesDir/tracks` (Auto-Backup is already off via `allowBackup="false"`, so no new exposure), watchOS to `Application Support/run_checkpoint` marked `isExcludedFromBackup` — matching Wear's posture, because a GPS trace is personal location data with no business in an iCloud device backup on its way to being uploaded once.

Moving the directory is a third of the fix. An upgrade over an install with runs already queued must carry the files across: Wear rewrites the queue entry inside the same DataStore transaction that moves the file, so the pair can never disagree; watchOS migrates from `WorkoutManager.init` before anything reads a payload, refusing a directory onto itself and dropping the legacy directory only once it is genuinely empty — `removeItem` on a populated one would delete the very payloads a failed move left behind. And the durable home must be swept, because unlike a cache it reclaims nothing on its own — carefully, since a sweep that guesses wrong destroys exactly the run this change exists to protect. Wear's keep-set is the queue plus the pending crash checkpoint plus the live recording, behind a 1 h age gate, and it does not run at all while recording; watchOS sweeps only exports and keys on `WCSession.outstandingFileTransfers`, so a file a transfer is still reading is never pulled out from under it. The watchOS export had to move as well as the NDJSON: WCSession reads it off disk for as long as the transfer is outstanding — days with the phone switched off — and by then `reset()` has deleted the NDJSON it was built from.

## 639. The queue entry goes first, the track file second; and a payload that is genuinely gone still syncs

Wear's `pushRun` deleted the track file after a successful POST but before the queue entry was removed. A process death in that window left an entry pointing at a payload that no longer existed — and because the row upserts with `resolution=merge-duplicates`, re-posting it with a null `track_url` would have erased a track already in Storage. Reversing the order makes "file missing" mean "never uploaded", which is what licenses the honest behaviour on the other side: a queued run whose payload the platform purged is posted **without** a track (`track_url: null`, the same shape an indoor recording already takes) rather than left in the queue promising a sync that can never succeed. The runner keeps the run and loses only its map. The worst residue is a stranded file, which the sweep collects. watchOS reaches the same conclusion by a different route — it still transfers, but tells the runner the trace was unavailable rather than handing the phone an empty array indistinguishable from an indoor run.

## 640. One drain, one refresh: the watch's sync path is guarded at three different levels, because it has three different races

Wear's cold start fires two `drainQueue` calls (the cached-session restore and the phone-bridge restore) and neither is held off by backoff at zero failures. Both took the same queue snapshot, so the loser re-uploaded a multi-MB ultra track over LTE or tripped over the winner's file deletion. A `Mutex` fixes that one, with `awaitAuth()` deliberately **outside** the lock — a 3 s wait for a session that may never arrive must not make a runner's manual Sync chip queue behind an automatic drain — and the backoff check and the queue snapshot deliberately **inside**, so the second caller re-reads a queue that is by then drained.

`LocalRunStore.save` / `remove` / `clear` needed a second, independent guard at the storage level: they read through `queue.first()` outside `dataStore.edit` and wrote back a whole list built from that stale snapshot, so a concurrent save could undo the drain's removal and resurrect an uploaded run after its file was deleted. All three now reduce against the transaction's own `Preferences` snapshot via pure `queueAfterSave` / `queueAfterRemove`.

The token refresh needed a third shape again, and this is the one worth remembering: `refreshIfExpired` sits outside `drainQueue` entirely, so the mutex does not cover it — and serialising would not have helped anyway, because GoTrue *rotates* the refresh token and the second caller would simply POST later with one the first had already spent. Mutual exclusion is the wrong primitive when the resource is consumed rather than merely contended. `SingleFlight` coalesces instead: the first caller runs, and everyone who arrives while it is in flight awaits the same result.

## 641. A turn cue's angle is measured across the corner, never across a segment the thinning invented

`generateTurnCues` thinned densely-sampled polylines by keeping one vertex per `mergeWithinM` of arc and advancing the kept vertex to the newest point in the window. That deleted the one vertex the generator exists to find. A 90-degree corner at 100 m sampled every 10 m survived as a point 10 m past the corner carrying the cumulative distance of a point 10 m before it, so the bearings were taken across a segment drawn *through* the corner — a diagonal carrying exactly half its angle. One corner announced twice, both under-classified, the first 20 m early, "turns remaining" 2 on a one-corner course; a 40-degree bend split into two sub-threshold halves and produced nothing at all. Confirmed independently in all three implementations.

**Deleting the offending line is not the fix, and this is measured rather than argued.** With only that line removed, the 10 m / 100 m case passes by alignment luck (100 m is a whole number of merge windows) while a corner rounded over several vertices, and the same corner sampled at 4 m, still split into two cues. The defect is that the thinning chose survivors **by distance alone**: a distance thinner has no notion of which vertex carries the turn, so a corner is dropped whenever it lands within `mergeWithinM` of the previously kept vertex, and dropping it still leaves a segment spanning it.

The contract now: legs below `MIN_LEG_M` (5 cm, no usable bearing) are the only thing dropped. Each interior vertex's bend is taken from the segment ending at it and the segment starting at it — every bearing TOUCHES its pivot, none spans it. A turn is the net direction change accumulated within `mergeWithinM` metres of the first bend over `TURN_EPSILON_DEG`, classified on the sum and reported at the vertex where that turning passes its halfway point; a window that does not clear `minTurnAngleDeg` slides by one rather than being consumed. The two knobs then read as one sentence — at least `minTurnAngleDeg` of direction change within `mergeWithinM` metres is a turn, anything slacker is a curve and is not announced — which is also why a long gentle arc stays silent and a sub-window out-and-back spike cancels to net zero instead of firing two u-turns. The deliberate trade: a corner spread over more than `mergeWithinM` reports as consecutive cues, a bounded under-report rather than a false positive.

The pair was registered in **neither** parity registry, so `check_parity_pair_registry.mjs` saw no disagreement and the syncer had no row to work from — which is precisely how one bug came to live in three implementations at once. Registering it in both was part of this change, per § 604.

## 642. A dead `HKWorkoutSession` degrades loudly, and its partial average is withheld rather than stamped

watchOS's `didFailWithError` was empty and nothing nilled the session, so a failed workout session left the last heart rate frozen on the run screen as a plausible live number and handed `WorkoutManager.stop()` an average covering only the minutes before the sensor died — written to the run row as `avg_bpm` as if it had covered the whole run. Both halves are dishonest in the same direction: a wrong number that looks right. The fix drops the reading and the average, raises a `heartRateUnavailable` flag the run and summary screens render in the same idiom as the existing "GPS track unavailable — synced without it" notice, and refuses any late sample that would put a number back on a screen that has already said it has none.

Two details are load-bearing. The failure flag is a plain stored property set **synchronously**, not only the `@Published` mirror: HealthKit delivers the callback on an arbitrary queue while `stop()` reads the summary on main, so a guard that takes effect only inside the `DispatchQueue.main.async` hop can land after the run has already been stamped — the race would restore the exact bug. And `didChangeTo` is deliberately left empty: `.ended` is not a failure, since `stopWorkout()` ends the session itself, and treating it as one would wipe the average moments before `stop()` reads it, converting the fix into a regression for every healthy run.

The failure path touches nothing but HealthKit state. Per the layered-resilience contract HR is an L4 auxiliary: the GPS stream, the distance accumulator, the on-disk track and the timers all keep running across the failure, and the run still finishes and syncs. Losing the heart rate must never cost the run.

The same round pinned the pace-window seal from `028bb5e41`, which had been authored without a Swift toolchain and therefore never compiled, run, or tested — the follow-up stayed open because nothing proved it worked, not because the code was missing. A runner holding 300 s/km through a 12-minute aid stop read 4594 s/km on the first post-resume window before that fix.

## 643. A truncated data export says so on the client, and states counts rather than a cause

The Art 20 export endpoint reports `{count, total, complete}` and the `backup` archive's `manifest.json` additionally names every short section (§ 637). Until this change both clients said only "your export is ready", so a runner past the 5000-run ceiling had to open `manifest.json` to learn their archive was short — on the one surface whose entire job is getting their data out.

Both clients now gate on `complete` and disclose the shortfall persistently (web: a notice under the export buttons on `/settings/account`; mobile: a warning row under the Full backup tile), not only in a toast that expires. Three constraints hold on both platforms. **State the counts, never the cause** — a shortfall has two causes, the per-export run ceiling and a page that failed to read, and the response distinguishes neither, so copy naming the cap would be wrong half the time. **Only an explicit `complete: false` claims a shortfall** — a response without the field, from an older deployment of either transport, is not evidence of truncation, and warning on every export would be its own dishonesty; `total` is floored at `count` so a malformed pair can never render "12 of 3". And **a locally-built archive makes no completeness claim either way**, because mobile's local writer has no server verdict to read.

Falling back from a truncated server archive to the local writer was considered and rejected: `fetchRunRowsRaw` is unranged and PostgREST clamps it to 1000 rows, so the "fix" would hand the runner a shorter archive with no disclosure at all. That cap is now tracked as its own follow-up.

## 644. Altitude plausibility is a claim about the number, not about the sensor — and every refusing gate on the watch needs a way out of refusing forever

Three round-2 firmware bugs turned out to share one shape: a guard that was correct about the case it was written for and silent about the case beside it.

The altitude window was named for the receiver (`GPS_ALT_MIN_M`), applied to the receiver, and documented as protecting the vert filter from a spurious receiver altitude. But the barometer is PREFERRED over the receiver at every site that takes an altitude — the vert accumulator, the live GAP grade, the elevation profile, the climb segmenter, the stored track point, the manual QNH re-zero — so the one source nothing gated was the one everything trusted first. A stuck-high I2C burst at the BMP581's 1/64 Pa LSB reduces to -8789.741 m, banks 10,413 m of false descent, and survives every later profile thinning for the rest of the run. The window is now `ALT_MIN_M..ALT_MAX_M` and `plausible_alt` is source-blind, applied where the barometric altitude is PRODUCED (one call in the baro task, which also drops the storm sample, because the bad datum is the pressure) and again at each core entry point, so a future consumer that never knew the gate existed cannot skip it. The storm reduction gained the same treatment from the other end: `sea_level_pa` only refuses an arithmetically impossible inversion, so a stuck-high station pressure banked a QNH three times any weather system on earth and the recovery read as a catastrophic pressure fall. It must now land inside the same ~870-1080 hPa window a pushed QNH passes. Representability was also mistaken for plausibility in the flash track's point stamping: the decimetre field spans ±3276.7 m, which happily stores an altitude 3 km below the sea floor.

The nav `FixGate` and the backyard bell are the same error in the time domain. The gate's ceiling grows with `dt`, which self-heals a relocation only while the runner is slower than the ceiling; above `MAX_SPEED_MPS` the displacement outgrows it and the gate refuses everything, forever — a course pushed at home and 40 km driven produced 0 acceptances in 129 fixes and no off-course latch at the gun, under a map marker still moving from the raw fix. The phone recorder has always had the escape (`_gpsReanchorAfterSeconds`); the gate now carries it, gated on BOTH a time span and a rejection count, because the time alone would adopt the very first outlier in a throttled mode where one fix already spans a minute. The backyard bell trusted a backward clock step as evidence of an hour boundary, when the local time it reads is an extrapolation that retreats a second whenever a fix re-disciplines it — so it must demand a drop of half a window, which the 1 Hz fold cadence guarantees a real bell always produces. Its bank-consume window, finally, was justified by one sentence ("a loop cannot be run this fast") and sized by another ("a walk-in takes about five minutes"); when a guard's justification and its value disagree, the gap between them is the bug, and the value now follows the justification.

All three fixes are **host-tested and nothing more**. The barometer's trigger is a bus fault, which the Renode BMP581 model cannot produce — it serves the value a scenario scripts, which is to say it models the driver's own belief. The gate's trigger is a receiver that has actually been driven somewhere. The bell's is multi-hour wall time no NMEA fixture carries. Bench items for the first two are on the tier-1 checklist in `quality_standards.md`, and the three new chosen constants are registered there as derived, not measured. The acceptance half of the barometer bench item matters more than the refusal half: a gate that refuses real data is worse than the bug it fixed, and its failure mode is a missing ALT row rather than a wrong one.

## 645. A 5xx means WE failed; an engine that answered "not here" is a 4xx — the alarm contract depends on it

Four production paths answered 5xx for outcomes that were not failures of ours, and on three of them a CloudWatch metric filter turns that status into a page. `osrm-proxy` collapsed OSRM's own 4xx (`NoSegment` — a pin outside the loaded extract) into 502, and its Lambda logs `engine_unreachable` on every 502: one user dropping one pin in the sea raised "the OSRM engine is unreachable, all users degraded". `generate-route` gave FOUR distinct outcomes 502 — graph-cycle reporting loop-poor, the graph-cycle sidecar throwing, every seed raising `no_route`, and a candidate set the selector declined — so a Pro user in a cul-de-sac neighbourhood paged someone and a genuine GraphHopper outage was indistinguishable from that noise. The followups had named three; the fourth surfaced because a sidecar outage and a cul-de-sac shared one branch. `lambda/share-entity` 503'd on a malformed percent-escape, telling crawlers to retry a link that can never resolve.

The rule is now: **a 5xx is reserved for a failure on our side of the wire.** An upstream that answered and said "not these coordinates / no loop at this start" is 422; input we cannot parse is a not-found. Concretely the OSRM proxy answers `422 no_route_for_coordinates` on any upstream 4xx, generate answers `422 no usable route` on loop-poor / `no_route` / no-usable-candidate, and share-entity answers the branded `noindex` 404 on a malformed key. Distinguishing them needed real state, not a status rename: generate now tracks whether the graph-cycle call THREW, because with no round_trip fallback configured a sidecar outage and a loop-poor start had previously been one branch. Clients are unaffected — `RouteBuilder.svelte` treats every non-200 except 403 as "fall back to the in-browser heuristic", and `routing.ts` treats every non-ok as a failed segment.

The inverse failure is the same bug read backwards. `share_session_lookup` and `share_workout_lookup` never inspected Supabase's `error` at all — on the parent or the child queries — and `alarms.tf` registered no metric filter for either, so a Supabase outage on those paths was invisible: a branded 404 is a HANDLED response, the Lambda `Errors` metric never moves, and nobody is paged. Both halves are now enforced rather than remembered — `share_upstream_alarm_guard.test.ts` derives the surface set from the lookup files themselves and fails when a lookup stops inspecting `error` or logs a tag `share_log_groups` has no filter for. A doc note would have been forgotten the same way the first one was; the guard is the durable half.

## 646. A read whose contract is "every row" pages with a tiebreaker, no ceiling, and no swallowed errors

PostgREST answers an unbounded SELECT with the first `db.max-rows` (1000) rows, a 200, and nothing that says it truncated — so "every row" cannot be expressed as a bare `.select()`. Six mobile reads were written that way; the worst fed `backup.dart`, so a 1,400-run account archived 1,000 runs and restored 1,000, with no error on either side of the round trip.

`readAllPages(fetchPage)` (`packages/api_client/lib/src/paged_read.dart`) requests explicit inclusive ranges until a short page proves exhaustion. Three choices are deliberate and differ from the web twins (`collectRunIdentities` / `collectStravaDedupeSet`), which predate this. **No `safetyMax`:** web's twins stop at 50,000 rows, but a ceiling is the same silent truncation one order of magnitude further out, and the loop needs no guard — `from` advances monotonically and a range past the end is always short (`.range()` compiles to `?offset&limit`, not a `Range` header, so an out-of-range page is a 200 with `[]`, never a 416). **Errors propagate:** web's twins break on error and return what they have; a caller archiving a history would rather fail loudly than write a file that is partial but reads as complete, which is the bug this exists to remove. **Every paged read imposes a total order:** a range over an ambiguous ordering lets the row on a page boundary come back twice or not at all, so each read carries a unique tiebreaker (`id`, or `user_id` for `event_attendees`, whose PK has no id column).

This also settles the "local backup writer is capped at 1000 runs" note carried into this round: there was no separate cap: it was this truncation. The local path is now genuinely complete, so it still makes no completeness claim, and the server path's explicit `{count,total,complete}` disclosure (§ the 2026-08-18 export-shortfall change) remains the only one — the two paths agree rather than needing a second contract.

Two sibling bugs travelled with it. `_hydratePeopleSuggestions` tallied public runs off the `runs` base table, whose non-owner SELECT policy migration `20260701_001` dropped — that migration states the outcome verbatim ("returns zero rows") — so every People suggestion read "0 public runs" and `comparePeopleRank`'s PRIMARY sort key had been a constant ever since; it now reads the SECURITY DEFINER `public_run_counts` RPC that `20270118_001` added for exactly this and that web already used. And six writes stamped local wall-clock into a `timestamptz` via `DateTime.now().toIso8601String()` — the bug `saveRun`'s own comment has documented the whole time — including two in `training_service.dart` that had diverged from the identical `completed_at` write `api_client` already had right. The guard for that one scans the app plus every package and allowlists by exact source line the four occurrences that are genuinely not instants (a `date` column with local-calendar semantics, the on-device NDJSON checkpoint stamp, the crash-recovery key cleared before upload, an export filename), so a new wall-clock write even inside an allowlisted file still fails.

## 647. The spectator stopped-runner readout is a registered parity pair, and its mobile buffer is stamped from the ping clock

§ 621 shipped `live_motion` web-only and argued a Dart twin would be a helper with no caller. That was true for exactly as long as mobile had no motion readout, and it is the mobile spectator — the person refreshing a link at 3 a.m. because their runner has gone quiet — for whom "still pinging, not moving" matters most. The port is faithful test-for-test (18/18) and carries all three fail-closed branches, which are the point of the helper rather than trimmings on it: a stale fix claims nothing, a telemetry gap discards everything before it, and too short a window claims nothing.

One thing the mobile side had to decide that web did not. The screen hydrates a backlog of pings on load and then streams new ones, and the naive buffer stamp is the device clock at ingest — which would land an hour of replayed history as a burst of "now", collapsing the observed window below the minimum and silently turning every freshly-opened link into `unknown`. The buffer is therefore stamped from each ping's own `at` column, UTC-normalised, exactly as the freshness clock already is. The Dart `atMs` is an `int` where web's is a `number`, so the non-finite guard covers only the odometer on that side — an idiomatic shape difference like `password_change`'s union-vs-class, recorded in both registries so it cannot later read as a divergence.

## 648. The `pace_analysis` Dart twin takes the split LENGTHS, not the splits

Web's `gradeAdjustedSplitPaces(track, splits)` reads `distance_m` off each `Split` to build the cut boundaries. Mobile's split producer is a different function with a different row type: `computeSplitDurations` returns `RunSplit(tick, duration)` and carries no distance, because — unlike web's `computeRealSplits` — it only emits at exact tick boundaries and never emits a final partial split, so every mobile split is exactly one tick long by construction. Rather than widen `RunSplit` (which would ripple through the splits list, the bar-scaling reduction, and the run-detail widget tests for a value the caller already knows), the Dart twin takes `List<double> splitDistancesM` and the caller passes `List.filled(n, tickLength)`. The algorithm, the boundary derivation, and every edge case are identical; this is an idiomatic shape difference of the same class as § 647's, and is recorded in both parity registries so it cannot later read as a divergence. The corollary is that the two mirror suites report different split counts for the same synthetic track (3 vs 4) — that difference belongs to the split producers, not to `pace_analysis`, and both suites pin it deliberately.

## 649. Mobile gear rotations can move the `is_default` star, which mobile had no writer for at all

§ 613's scope paragraph said the mobile mirror was not built. It is now: `rotation_pick.ts` ↔ `apps/mobile_android/lib/gear_rotation_pick.dart` is a registered parity pair (18 mirror tests each) and the "Next up / Make current" affordance renders on `GearRotationsScreen`. The load-bearing discovery is what the port needed underneath it: mobile had **no** `is_default` writer whatsoever, which is why the star could not follow a rotation on the phone and a runner rotating three pairs banked every kilometre on the pair that last held it. `ApiClient.setDefaultGear` mirrors web's, clearing siblings first so the partial-unique index cannot trip.

The one shape difference is where the gear kind comes from: web runs the pick within the tab it is showing, mobile once per distinct kind the rotation holds, because the rotations screen has no kind tab and the star is `(owner, kind)`-scoped either way. Two port-fidelity details are pinned by the mirror suite because a reasonable Dart idiom would break them: a `null` total maps to `0.0` exactly as `Number(null)` does, and the retired filter treats an empty string as *not* retired to match the JS `!m.retiredAt` truthiness test — a `retiredAt != null` check would drop a member web keeps. Everything § 613 declined to build stays unbuilt on both platforms: no automatic rotation of the star, no recency or rest signal.

## 650. The mobile import failure report fixes each swallow at its catch, and discloses a deferred cloud push

§ 618 shipped `import_failures.ts` web-only and said mobile owed no Dart twin until it grew a report surface. It has one now, and building it turned up more than the port. The counter was the least of it: Health Connect dropped an unmappable workout into a `debugPrint` with **no counter at all**, so those activities simply never appeared; `csv_run_importer.dart`'s metadata branch used `catch (_)` and discarded the error object outright; and the shared save loop named a failed run by its UUID, which tells a runner nothing. Every one is fixed where the error is caught, because a reclassification downstream of a discarded error can only invent a reason.

Two decisions are worth recording. First, `fetchRoutes` swallowing its read left **exactly** the shape a source with no routes leaves — empty tracks, empty withheld set — so the import's "these runs have no map" note was asserting something it could not know. `HealthConnectRoutes` now carries the error, and a failed read reports as a failure rather than as an absence. Second, mobile saves locally and then batch-pushes, where web imports one activity at a time; a push that throws is therefore not N per-item failures but one deferred upload of runs that are safely on disk and that `SyncService` will retry. It gets a status note, not N entries — over-reporting it as data loss would be its own dishonesty. That note is the one string in the surface with no web counterpart.

The Dart port is faithful test-for-test (22/22) including the precedence that is the whole point of the classifier — an "invalid token" is auth rather than an unreadable file, and any remaining SQLSTATE means the server answered and refused. Two idiomatic differences are recorded in both registries so neither later reads as divergence: web's structural `.message` / `.code` / `.status` reads become a `Map` branch plus a duck-typed getter read, and a Dart `Exception` exposes no `.message` getter at all, so its `toString()` is the only message there is. CSV rows are named `Row N` — for a summary CSV the row is the identity, and a row need not carry a title.

## 651. § 617 amended — `routine_history` is a parity pair, read from the server, and neither platform claims all-time

§ 617 called `routine_history.ts` "deliberately web-only and not a parity pair" on the ground that mobile's routine detail reads `LocalRoutineStore` and had no consumer for the shaping, and that a twin with no caller is dead code the parity guard would police forever. That condition has been **met rather than reversed**: the mobile caller now exists, so the pair is registered in both registries — the ADR's own precondition, not an exception to it.

Two things about the port are load-bearing. The mobile panel reads the server through `ApiClient.fetchGymRoutineSessions`, **not** the `LocalGymStore` § 617 imagined it would: that store holds only the most recent page of workouts, so a routine last run months ago would read as never run, and a "you have never done this" claim made from a cache that simply does not reach back far enough is worse than showing no panel at all. And the Dart sort carries an input-index tiebreak the TypeScript does not need, because `Array.sort` has been stable since ES2019 and Dart's `List.sort` is not; two sessions sharing a `started_at` would otherwise order differently on the two platforms, from the same server rows.

Both callers still window at 500 rows, and that symmetry is deliberate. Mobile could have been made complete on its own by routing through `readAllPages` (§ 646, which landed in the same branch), but a complete phone count standing beside a capped web one is precisely the cross-platform drift the parity pair exists to prevent — and neither surface words its count as all-time, so neither lies. Closing the gap is a SQL-aggregate change on web first per § 24, then mirrored; never a mobile-only paged read.

## 652. A guard that only fires on the merged tree is the argument for running the suite after a merge, not only inside each agent's worktree

Two agents worked disjoint file scopes in isolated worktrees this round and both ran the suites their own changes touched. One of them introduced a boundary colour into a `TextStyle` (`colorScheme.outline` on the ungraded verdict badge), which `outline_text_token_guard_test.dart` catches — and it caught it, in that agent's own run, and that agent fixed its own instance. The other agent's panel carried the same violation in a different file, and its targeted run did not include the guard, so it landed green.

The violation therefore existed only on the merged tree, and only a full-suite run after the merge could see it. This is not an argument against worktree isolation, which is what let the two run at all; it is the reason a merge is not complete when it is conflict-free. The tree-wide source-scan guards in this repo — the icon-variant guard, the outline-token guard, the wall-clock-write guard, the parity-pair registry check — are exactly the class whose input is the whole repository rather than a diff, so they can only be trusted after everything has landed. Run the full suite on the merged result, every time, before the push.

## 653. Every `.inFilter` id list in `api_client` is either a chunk or an allowlisted bound, and a source guard enforces which

PostgREST serialises `.inFilter(col, ids)` into the request URL, so a list past the gateway's request-line budget returns an **empty result rather than an error** — the read looks like "this runner follows nobody", not like a failure. `kInFilterChunk` has stated that ceiling since the web feed fix, but only `fetchFollowingBadgeAwards` honoured it: the people-search hydrate handed over up to 120 candidate ids, the run and lift feeds handed over the viewer's entire followee set, and `fetchFollowing` was already being called with `limit: 200` by the feed toolbar. Seventeen sites now go through `readChunked`, and the cursor-paginated feeds merge their per-chunk pages with `topByRecency` — the Dart analogue of web's `feed_merge.ts`.

The rule is enforced rather than documented. `in_filter_bound_test.dart` collects every `.inFilter` line not handed a `chunk` and requires it to appear in an allowlist **with its occurrence count**, so a second unbounded read cannot hide behind an identically-written bounded one; a companion test parses the four methods whose `limit` defaults that allowlist leans on and fails if any is raised above the chunk. Chunking beat lowering the search candidate cap because the cap would have fixed one of the hydrate's two callers and left the unbounded one — `fetchSuggestedPeople`, whose id list is the co-member set of every club the viewer belongs to — untouched. One cost is recorded rather than hidden: `deleteNotifications` is now N statements instead of one, so a partial dismiss is possible where a >100 list previously deleted nothing. Partial beats a silent no-op, but it is not transactional.

**Amended 2026-08-18 — the failure mode above is wrong as written, and the correction is measured.** The first paragraph states that an over-long `in` filter "returns an **empty result rather than an error**". That did not reproduce. Driven against the local stack (Kong in front of PostgREST, `GET /rest/v1/user_profiles?id=in.(<n uuids>)&select=id`, anon key), the request is refused with **`414 URI too long`**, and the boundary is the gateway's **8 KiB request-line buffer** rather than any id count: 207 uuids (an 8128-byte request line) answered `200`, 209 uuids (8206 bytes) answered `414`. Below the buffer every size from 50 to 207 answered `200` with a correct — here empty, because the ids were synthetic — result set. So the ceiling is ~208 uuids for this shape, and it moves with whatever else is in the query string.

What survives the correction is the rule, not the mechanism: `kInFilterChunk = 100` sits far under the 8 KiB line on any plausible query shape, and the source guard is worth exactly what it was worth before. What does **not** survive is the diagnosis. An empty 200 is a *silent* failure that reads as "this runner follows nobody"; a 414 is a *loud* one that reaches the caller's error path. Those want different handling, and code that assumes the silent one is reasoning about a symptom this deployment does not produce.

Which of the two a deployment produces is a property of the **gateway**, not of `api_client` — an 8 KiB buffer is nginx's and Kong's default, but a different proxy, a raised buffer, or a PostgREST reached directly will draw the line somewhere else or answer differently at it. **Verified locally only.** Nothing here has been measured against the production gateway, and the original empty-200 observation is not disproved for whatever stack it was made on — it is simply not what this one does. Treat "an over-long `in` filter fails, and the shape of the failure is deployment-specific" as the durable claim, which is how [§ 667](#667-a-bulk-dismiss-is-one-transaction--delete_notificationsuuid-is-security-invoker-and-refuses-past-its-cap-rather-than-truncating) and `api_database.md` already word it, and why `delete_notifications(uuid[])` moves the id list into a POST body where no such bound exists. Confirming the prod gateway's behaviour is still owed; until then no surface should branch on which error it will get.

`chunk.dart` (the constant's own doc, where the claim originated on the Dart side) and `api_client.dart`'s badge-feed comment are corrected in the same change. The web call-site comments in `core/data.ts` and `social/feed_merge.ts` still restate the empty-result mechanism as fact, are wrong for the same reason, and are tracked in `followups.md` rather than swept here.

## 654. `runRowFromRun` is the only place a Run becomes a `runs` row, and the promoted-column set is a registry a test derives

`BackupService.rawRunRowForBackup` carried its own copy of the promoted-column lift so a device-only archive row would match what `saveRun` writes. The copy had already drifted: migration `20270302_001` promoted elevation and made the wire writers populate both `elevation_gain_m` and `metadata.elevation_m`; the archive copy never learned it, so a **restored local-only run banked no vert** on the challenge board. The shaper now lives in `core_models`, all four writers call it, and the private duplicates are deleted rather than left beside it.

The load-bearing half is the anti-drift guard, and it deliberately does not restate a column list: the strip iterates `kRunPromotedMetadataColumns` (lifted **and** dropped from the bag) and `kRunMirroredMetadataColumns` (`elevation_m`, kept in the bag per `20270302_001`), and the test parses `RunRow`'s generated column constants and `MetadataKeys`' values and asserts their name-identical intersection **is** the promoted map's key set. Promoting a metadata key into a same-named column therefore fails a test until someone decides promoted-vs-mirrored and teaches the shaper the lift, instead of shipping a column no writer fills.

A cross-client guard had to follow the code rather than be relaxed. `data.test.ts` pinned a Critical data-loss finding — that `route_id` round-trips on read and on both write paths — by grepping `api_client.dart` for the literal `routeId: run.routeId`. The refactor moved the write half into the shaper, so the guard failed on a tree where behaviour was entirely correct. The fix was to point the write assertion at `run_row_shape.dart` **and** add an assertion that each writer builds its row through `runRowFromRun`, keeping end-to-end coverage; both halves were verified to fail by deleting the field and by making a writer bypass the shaper. Weakening or deleting the assertion would have retired a guard over a real data-loss bug because a refactor moved its subject.

## 655. A shared vocabulary is not shared until every rendering platform is on it

`runs.activity_type` was localized on mobile and web, each behind a guard that derives the value set from the `runs_activity_type_check` migration. Wear OS was not, and kept a fourth copy covering four of five values with a `replaceFirstChar { it.uppercase() }` fallback. `stroller` was reachable there **without ever being cycled to**, because `default_activity_type` primes the pre-run chip straight off the phone's settings bag with no allowlist — so the one value the wrist could not name was the one the phone could hand it.

Two lessons are now encoded. First, a "route every call site through one helper" sweep must enumerate *rendering surfaces*, not language ecosystems: a Kotlin or Swift surface cannot import the Dart helper, so it owes its own guard rather than an exemption. Second, an unrecognised value is rendered **verbatim** on all three platforms rather than title-cased — a capitalized token is indistinguishable from a real translation, which is precisely why this leak survived the rounds that fixed the surfaces where it would have been noticed. The wrist guard also asserts there is exactly one resolver, so a second per-screen vocabulary cannot re-grow beside it. What was deliberately *not* done: the wrist's four existing words still differ from the phone's, and one of those differences (`hike` -> "Trail run") is a product rename rather than a translation fix, so it is an owner call rather than a mechanical re-align.

## 656. `plan_ramp` becomes a parity pair, and the shared volume reduction stays where web put it

The plan wizard's opening-week ramp check shipped web-only, and the mobile wizard carried the same blind spot: it previewed six weeks of volumes with nothing to compare them against, so a runner could generate a plan opening at triple their recent load with nothing saying so.

The non-obvious part is *what* was ported. `recentRunVolume` / `volumeSample` and the `CHRONIC_WINDOW_WEEKS` / `MIN_ACTIVE_WEEKS` constants are not private to the ramp check on web — `self_load.ts` and `comeback.ts` both import them from `plan_ramp.ts`, because two copies of the "this row is running volume" filter would let a runner's pre-break base and their current week come from different run sets.
