Porting the ramp check faithfully therefore lands that shared reduction in `plan_ramp.dart` at the identical module boundary, and a later `self_load.dart` / `comeback.dart` imports it rather than growing a second definition. `acuteM` is carried on the Dart `RecentVolume` even though the wizard never reads it, for the same reason: it is the acute half of the same single traversal. The standing constraint that a phone must never show both a ratio card and a comeback card is a *dashboard* concern and is untouched — there is no mobile dashboard load card, and the wizard is a different consumer.

## 657. The mobile nutrition diary's viewed day is a local `YYYY-MM-DD`, and the writes follow it

Mirroring web's `?date=` day stepper onto `nutrition_screen.dart` needed a day identity, and the two obvious candidates were both wrong. A `DateTime` instant is not a day — the screen keys a preferences bucket, a trend map and a route parameter off it, and each wants an identity, not a moment. UTC is worse: a 23:30 entry belongs to the day the runner was living, not to tomorrow in Greenwich. So the screen holds what web holds, a **local** zero-padded `YYYY-MM-DD`, only ever assigned from the `diary_day` helpers, which step exclusively through `DateTime(y, m, d + n)`. That is what makes a 23- or 25-hour DST day safe: a millisecond step repeats or skips a day and puts an exclusive window end at 23:00 of the same day, which is the bug § 589 records being fixed in this very screen. Instants appear only at the two boundaries, so nothing here emits the naive local string the wall-clock guard polices.

The stepper is worth having only because the writes follow it: a surface that lets a runner *review* yesterday but silently logs to *today* is worse than no stepper. All three write paths the screen owns stamp `entryTimestampFor(viewedDay, now)` at **save** time rather than at open time — so a composer left open across midnight still files into the day its host shows — and each is pinned by a widget test that reads the stored `started_at` back. One behavioural quirk is reproduced on purpose: web's `parseIsoDate` rejects a two-digit year as a side effect of `new Date(26, …)` meaning 1926, where Dart's `DateTime(26, …)` accepts year 26, so the Dart side carries an explicit guard or the mirrored suites would answer differently on the same input.

## 658. `gym_routine_history` is a server-side aggregate returning complete tallies plus an honestly-bounded page — a count is not something a windowed client read can answer

The routine-history panel (§ 617, mirrored to mobile in § 651) showed a session count derived from whatever rows the client happened to read. Both platforms windowed that read at 500 `gym_workouts` rows carrying `metadata.routine_id`, because an unbounded PostgREST select truncates silently at `db.max-rows` and still answers 200 — so the choice was between a cap the code states and a cap it does not. Neither panel worded its figure as all-time, so neither lied outright, but a lifter running one routine weekly for a decade was shown a wrong number, and shipping the same window on both platforms made the drift invisible rather than absent. Migration `20270528_001` moves the reduction into SQL, the shape `gym_exercise_records` and `run_streaks_for_user` (§ 471) already took: `gym_routine_history(p_routine_id, p_recent_limit)` returns exactly one row of complete tallies — `session_count`, `last_performed_at`, `graded_count`, `completed_count`. SECURITY INVOKER with a load-bearing explicit `auth.uid()` filter, because the `gym_workouts` select policy also admits other users' `is_public` rows.

It returns a bounded **page** of recent sessions alongside the aggregate rather than the aggregate alone, because the panel renders a list as well as a roll-up. Two round trips would let the rows and the count above them come from different snapshots, and a resume landing between them could show four sessions under a count of five. One call applies one `WHERE` to both, `p_recent_limit` is clamped to `[0, 50]` so a caller cannot re-open the unbounded read the RPC exists to close, and the page is named for what it is on both clients (`recentSessions`, never `sessions`) so no surface can present it as everything.

The two § 617 exclusions are the contract and the SQL reproduces them exactly: a row still carrying a `gym_session_draft` object is an in-flight session, dropped from tallies AND page so a resume cannot inflate the routine's usage; a "save as is" row keeps `routine_id` while claiming no verdict, so it counts as a session but sits outside `graded_count` rather than reading as a miss. What did NOT move to the server is days-since-last: it is floored against the *reader's* clock and clamped so a row stamped ahead of it reads as today, which is a display rule, not a stored fact. The `routine_history` parity pair therefore keeps a real job — `summariseRoutineHistory` is replaced by `routineHistoryFromAggregate`, which classifies and orders the page, floors the elapsed days, and derives the completed-of-graded ratio (16 mirror tests each). It still filters drafts out of the page even though the server already did, so the listed rows can never contradict the count under any future caller. `lastPerformedAt` is taken from the aggregate and never from the page's first row — a bounded page can be empty while the routine has been run hundreds of times, and reading the date off the list would lose it.

## 659. A partially-failed import push is disclosed with its count, in the import's existing vocabulary, not as failure-report entries

`ApiClient.saveRunsBatch` signals a partial failure by *returning* the ids whose track upload failed and were therefore skipped from the row upsert; it throws only when every upload fails. `ImportScreen`'s two push sites — the shared `_saveImportedRuns` loop and `_backfillHealthConnectTracks` — set the deferral only from their `catch`, so a half-landed batch reported a clean import while those runs sat on the device and not on the server. Both now count the returned set as well as the throw, changed together so the two cannot drift, and `importStatusCloudPushDeferred` became an ICU plural: a runner who imported 400 runs and had 3 fail is told it was 3, because "some are pending" makes 3-of-400 indistinguishable from 400-of-400 and only the second is worth acting on. It stays that one key rather than gaining a sibling — the string's claim (on this device, the upload did not go through, `SyncService` retries) is true verbatim for a partial failure, which is why § 650 already reused it for the route backfill.

It is deliberately **not** routed into `ImportFailureReport`: an entry there names an activity that did not import and exists so the runner can decide whether re-running is worth it, whereas these runs did import and retry on their own — and the batch returns only ids, so an entry would carry a synthesised reason and an empty detail in a report whose whole purpose is saying why. Testing it for real needed a seam, since `requestHealthRoutePermission` and `fetchRoutes` both refuse off Android: the four Health Connect platform calls became nullable `…Fn` constructor seams defaulting to the real statics (the pattern `run_heatmap_screen` / `route_builder_screen` / `settings_about_screen` already use — no test-mode flag, no production branch), and `ApiClient` needed nothing new because subclass-and-override is the seam `sync_service_test` has always used. One fake now covers both the route-backfill path and the batch-push disclosure, which retired `import_route_backfill_deferred_test.dart`'s three source assertions for six behavioural tests driving the real widget.

## 660. An `OfflineSyncStore` refuses to write before `init()`, and refuses before touching memory

`NutritionScreen` constructed its meal-template and recipe stores and called `loadAll()` on each. `loadAll` tolerates a null `dir` and returns, so the stores read as alive while `persist()` died on a bare `dir!` — and because `_persistRow` installed the row into `rowsById` *first*, the saved meal appeared in the list, the screen reported a failure over the top of it, and nothing reached disk or the server. The shipped widget test printed `Null check operator used on a null value` and passed, because it asserted on the in-memory row.

Three changes, in ascending order of durability: the screen now calls `init()`; every write path goes through `requireInitialised`, which raises a `StateError` naming the store *before* any in-memory mutation, so a write that cannot be durable leaves no trace claiming it was; and a source-level guard in `architecture_guards_test.dart` fails any future screen that constructs one of these stores without `init()`ing it. `nutrition_screen` was the only offender — every other owning screen already called `init()`. The general rule the incident illustrates: a test that asserts on optimistic in-memory state proves only that the optimism happened. Where a write's whole purpose is durability, the assertion belongs on the persisted result — which is why the pinning test polls the file on disk rather than the list. Left deliberately: `rewriteAll()` still returns silently on a null `dir`, which drops a server-to-local cache fill rather than a user write.

## 661. A CI-only wedge must be diagnosable from its own failure message, so the sim harness reports a measured signature rather than a fixed issue reference

The `ci_smoke.py` wedge detector named issue #754 on every wedge it fired on. #754 has since been closed and describes a *different* wedge — scenario `storm`, ~1-in-30, dying at t=19.0 s mid-run — so when a second, unrelated wedge appeared on `pages` (three consecutive CI runs on PR #787; 0/4 reproductions on arm64 macOS at CI's own `--budget 300`), the message told its reader to go and read a resolved bug. A failure that cites a closed issue trains people to dismiss it, which is worse than citing none. The message now carries what it actually measured: the last **stamped** firmware clock (the CI wedge ends on an unstamped continuation line of embassy-nrf's multi-line UICR warning, so quoting only the last line drops the `0.000000` that says it died at boot), the last decoded line, and a probe of the machine itself.

The probe closes the gap that made this undiagnosable: silence cannot say whether the *firmware* stopped or the *Renode executor* did, and no artifact distinguished them — it samples the CPU `PC`, the retired-instruction count and the elapsed virtual time twice 1.5 s apart, resolves the PC through the loaded ELF's symbols so no local rebuild is needed to read it, and names which of the two stopped. The `renode.log` tail is filtered of host-side UART noise for the same reason: on a boot-time wedge all twenty of its last lines are the host feeder writing NMEA at a UARTE the guest never enabled, which buried the `gpio1 … LATCH` write that located this wedge inside `embassy_nrf::init`. The forensics are deliberately **not** a fix: #788 records the finding that the only blocking construct in that window is embassy-nrf's `RtcDriver::init` spin `while r.counter().read().0 != 0 {}`, whose single missed read costs a full 512 s counter wrap, and the harness must not be quietened with a longer budget, a retry, or a skipped scenario while that stands.

## 662. The `gym_session_draft` marker is a draft only when it is a JSON *object*, on all three rails

`hasSessionDraft` tested `typeof snap === 'object'`, which is true for an array — so web read a row as in-flight that Dart's `is Map` and the `gym_routine_history` RPC's `jsonb_typeof(...) = 'object'` both read as a session performed. The predicate is now one `isJsonObject` helper covering the marker and the bag around it, which is exactly the SQL and Dart test rather than an `Array.isArray` patch over the old one. `stripSessionDraft` mattered on its own: given an array bag it previously spread it into an index-keyed object (`['a']` -> `{0:'a'}`), and `saveDraftAsIs` writes that result back to the row.

A fourth, looser copy lived in `fetchGymSessionDraft`: PostgREST cannot ask `jsonb_typeof`, so its `.not('metadata->gym_session_draft', 'is', null)` filter also matched JSON null and arrays — a jsonb `null` under a key is not SQL NULL — and the row it returned was adopted as the draft, with `replaceGymSets` then running over a workout the resume card and the routine-history exclusion both count as performed. That filter is now a cheap prefilter and the helper decides.

The "unreachable in production" framing this was filed under is half right, and the half that is wrong is worth stating. Every *app* writer does emit an object (web `draftMetadata`, mobile `_draftMetadata()`), and no Edge Function, Go worker, or SQL statement writes the bag at all. But nothing *enforces* it: `metadata` is unconstrained jsonb, `backup.dart`'s restore passes a user-supplied ZIP archive's row through `OfflineSyncStore.restoreFromBackup` to `createGymWorkout` verbatim, and a row owner can PATCH their own `metadata` through PostgREST directly. It only ever affects that user's own data, but it rests on writer discipline rather than a constraint — which is why the contract is pinned as an assertion on each rail (the web helper suite, both routine_history mirror suites, the pgTAP suite) so the next divergence fails a test rather than sitting in a doc comment.

## 663. `rewriteAll` refuses too, and the refusal belongs at the top of `replaceFromServer` rather than at the bottom of the call chain

§ 660 left `rewriteAll()` returning silently on a null `dir` on the grounds that it drops a server-to-local cache fill rather than a user write. That is true of the data but not of the state: the eight `replaceFromServer` overrides clear and rebuild `rowsById` from the fetch *before* calling down, so a silent return left the screen showing rows that nothing on disk agreed with — a store more inconsistent than the one that refused. Gating `rewriteAll` alone would have raised at the same too-late point, so `requireInitialised('replaceFromServer')` is now the literal first statement of all eight overrides as well, and `rewriteAll` carries its own gate for any future direct caller. The predicted ripple through ~19 test files did not exist: every one of those suites already `init()`s with an `overrideDirectory`, so nothing was changed to accommodate the throw — which is the outcome the follow-up should have been able to check for before pricing the work.

Auditing the callers found one that could genuinely reach it uninitialised, and it is the same mistake in a different disguise. `gym_screen._initRoutines` catches a failed `init()`, logs it, and then sets `_routineStoreReady = true` — readiness derived from *the absence of a throw* rather than from the store having a directory — so the Routines destination was offered over a store where, since § 660, every write refuses. It reads `_routineStore.dir` now. The general shape worth naming: a boolean called "ready" that is assigned unconditionally after a try/catch is not a readiness check, it is a completion check, and the two differ exactly when it matters. The architecture guard gained the complementary rule — § 660's guard polices construction sites, which are screen fields, and could never have seen a method that mutates before it validates.

## 664. A sidecar write that fails after a successful push is not a deferred upload, and gets no disclosure

§ 659 made both `ImportScreen` push sites count `saveRunsBatch`'s returned `failed` set as well as its throw, but `markManySynced` still ran inside the same `try` — so a failed sidecar write fell to the catch and reported the WHOLE batch as sitting on the device when every upload had succeeded. Splitting the catch forced the question of what the second branch should say, and the honest answer is nothing. `markManySynced` only runs after `saveRunsBatch` returned, so those runs are already on the server and the `failed` set has already been excluded; `LocalRunStore` mutates `_syncedIds` in memory before awaiting the disk write, so a persist failure costs only this device's record of the fact. The next cold start re-reads them as unsynced, `SyncService` pushes again, and `saveRunsBatch` upserts on `id` / `external_id` onto the rows already there — no duplicate, no loss, one wasted track upload. `importStatusCloudPushDeferred` asserts the upload did not go through, which is false here, so reusing it would be the wrong half of § 659's rule; minting a sibling key would be inventing a message to fill a branch. It gets its own catch and a `debugPrint`, which is what the layered-resilience contract asks of an auxiliary effect whose failure the runner cannot act on.

The same round seamed `FilePicker` — the one platform call § 659 left, and the reason the Strava / CSV / backup-ZIP paths had no cover for their own parsing. Driving them turned up a silent cross-platform data loss the seam existed to find: Strava leaves `Filename` empty for a manually-entered or indoor activity, and the mobile importer `continue`d past those rows before any counter, so a migrating runner's whole treadmill history vanished from an import that reported cleanly. Web's importer puts the same guard inside `importOne` and keeps the row trackless off the CSV's own numbers, so this was a parity gap rather than a product choice and needed no web-first pass. An empty path now skips only the archive lookup; a `Filename` that names a file the archive does not hold, or a format neither parser reads, still throws into the `ImportFailureReport` — the export promised something it did not deliver, which is a different fact from never promising one. The existing test asserting the drop was named `row with empty filename is silently skipped`, encoding the bug in its own title; it was replaced rather than relaxed. A suspected file-handle leak on `BackupService.restore`'s manifest-rejection path was measured (40 rejected restores, open-fd count unchanged) and left alone rather than fixed on suspicion.

## 665. A jsonb-expression index cannot serve a query RLS enforces — the fix is a column, not an index

The round-7 follow-up asked for `gym_workouts (user_id, metadata->>'routine_id')` to back the `gym_routine_history` aggregate (§ 658). Measured against the RPC's own predicate as `authenticated`, it is strictly worse than no index. The RPC is `security invoker`, so the query runs under RLS, and the planner may not evaluate a non-leakproof qual below an RLS security qual; `jsonb_object_field_text` is not `LEAKPROOF`, so the expression stays a heap `Filter` and only `user_id` ever reaches `Index Cond`. Over 60,000 synthetic rows (one account holding 2,008 sessions, 153 on the target routine) the existing `gym_workouts_user` index reads 1,278 heap blocks / 1,296 buffers in 1.7 ms; the partial expression index reads 1,277 heap blocks / 1,300 buffers in 2.5 ms — identical heap work plus an index to walk and to maintain on every write. `jsonb_contains` is not leakproof either, so the GIN + `@>` path is ignored outright. The mechanism was isolated by running the same query with the same index as the table owner, where RLS is not enforced and the expression does reach `Index Cond`; only the role differs.

The only shape the planner will use is a promoted plain `uuid` column (154 heap blocks / 158 buffers / 0.37 ms, `Index Cond` on both columns, `uuid_eq` being leakproof), which makes this a column-vs-bag question under the activity-table checklist rather than an index one. Nothing is promoted yet: 1.7 ms on a page-open path does not earn a `runs`-style promotion (`20261207_001`) plus its batched backfill, and the trigger to revisit is a typical account reaching five figures of `gym_workouts`. Two options were considered and rejected — marking the jsonb accessors `LEAKPROOF` (superuser-only, unavailable on Supabase, and a schema-wide security decision to buy one plan) and flipping the RPC to `SECURITY DEFINER` (every sibling gym aggregate is `security invoker` with a load-bearing explicit `auth.uid()` filter, worth more than the milliseconds). The general rule is recorded in `conventions.md` § Activity-table column checklist: a bag key you filter on cannot be rescued later with an expression index, so weigh that when deciding column-vs-bag in the first place.

## 666. The sim's RTC counts from when the guest starts it, because Renode's clock source would otherwise back-charge it for the quantum it slept through

The `pages` sim scenario went red on every CI run and wedged before the firmware's first log line. § 661's probe named `pc=0x1a000` with instructions still retiring, and the job's staged ELF disassembles there to `ldr`/`cmp`/`bne` against `0x40011504` — RTC1's COUNTER, i.e. embassy-nrf 0.10's `RtcDriver::init` spin `tasks_clear; tasks_start; while counter != 0 {}`. Two things § 661 and #788 asserted were wrong, both in the direction of blaming the environment rather than the artifact: it *does* reproduce on arm64 macOS when you boot the ELF CI itself uploaded, and it is deterministic per **binary**, not per host — so it was never a race and no `PerformanceInMips`, `SetGlobalQuantum` or `CyclesPerInstruction` knob could have found it.

The mechanism, measured: Renode grants the CPU a quantum and folds the executed slice into `BaseClockSource` only when the CPU reports, and `Update` then charges that accumulated `elapsed` to every *enabled* entry — so a timer enabled part-way through the slice absorbs the part that ran before the guest started it. `TASKS_START` landed at virtual time `0.001000000 s` and the COUNTER read one instruction later at `0.001065330 s`: 65.33 us, two 32768 Hz ticks. The spin does not recover from that on the next read — it waits for the 24-bit counter to wrap, `2^24 / 32768` = 512 s, past every budget in the job — and whether the slice falls under one 30.5 us tick is just how many instructions a given build spends before RTC init.

The fix belongs in the model, not the firmware: `sim/NRF52840_RTC_Overflow.cs` now syncs the CPU's executed-but-unreported time into the clock source before START / STOP / CLEAR / TRIGOVRFLW touch the timers (`machine.SystemBus.TryGetCurrentCPU` + `cpu.SyncTime()`, the idiom Renode's own `MAX32650_RTC` uses at the revision this model was forked from), so the counter starts at the instant the guest starts it. **The firmware was not changed** — that spin is upstream and correct against silicon; a firmware workaround would have been dodging a model bug. The guard is `sim/test_rtc_model.py` rather than the scenario, because dropping the sync fails only for the builds that land the wrong side of a tick, which is precisely how this survived a week of green local runs while failing every CI run. No budget was widened, no retry added, no scenario skipped — the standing § 582 / § 661 rule against all three is unchanged, and the probe that made this diagnosable in an afternoon is the reason it holds.

## 667. A bulk dismiss is one transaction — `delete_notifications(uuid[])` is SECURITY INVOKER, and refuses past its cap rather than truncating

§ 653 chunked every `.inFilter` id list in `api_client` and recorded one cost rather than hiding it: `deleteNotifications` became N statements, so chunk 3 of 5 can fail and leave the inbox half-dismissed with the undo offer already spent and the rows already gone from the list. Partial beat the alternative, but the alternative was never the only other option — the reason the list had to be split at all is that PostgREST serialises an `in` filter into the request URL, and that is a constraint of the transport, not of the operation. Migration `20270529_001` moves the operation off that transport: `delete_notifications(p_ids uuid[])` takes the array in the RPC's POST body, so there is nothing left to chunk and one call is one statement in one transaction — every id goes, or none does. The pgTAP suite proves that rather than asserting it, by failing one member of a batch from a row trigger and checking that the ids a chunked client would already have committed are still there; the same fixture run against a swallow-and-continue loop returns a success count and deletes a prefix, which is what makes the assertion worth having.

It is **SECURITY INVOKER with no owner predicate of its own**, deliberately unlike `run_streaks_for_user` (§ 471) and `gym_routine_history` (§ 658), whose explicit `auth.uid()` filters are load-bearing because their select policies also admit other users' public rows. The `notifications` DELETE policy is already exactly `auth.uid() = user_id` and there is no second leg to close, so re-deriving that predicate inside the body would be a second copy of it with nothing left to catch a drift between the two. A caller naming a stranger's id therefore deletes nothing and learns so from the returned count. `anon` is revoked alongside `public`: Supabase's default privileges hand every new public function to `anon`, and a mutation should not be reachable without a session even where RLS would match zero rows for one — the pgTAP grant assertion is what surfaced that, since the revoke-from-`public` alone left the default `anon` grant standing.

The cap is the part worth arguing. An unbounded array is not free — it is row locks held for the length of one statement — but a silent truncation would re-open, in a new place, precisely the class of bug the RPC exists to close, and quietly dismissing a prefix of what the runner asked for is worse than the original failure because the surface would report success. Past 1000 ids the call raises `22023` and deletes nothing; both inboxes page at 100 rows, so the ceiling sits an order of magnitude above any dismiss a surface can assemble, and the refusal reaches the caller through the same `onCommitError` path a network failure already uses.

One inherited claim did not survive being checked. § 653 states that an over-long `in` filter "returns an empty result rather than an error"; measured against the local stack the DELETE is refused with a **414** past roughly 200 ids (~15 KB of URL), and answers 204 below it. Both failures lose the whole dismiss and both are removed by moving off the URL, but which one a deployment gets is a property of the gateway in front of PostgREST rather than of the code — so the comments and docs around this change say exactly that, rather than restating either mechanism as the fact. § 653 itself is left as written; the history only moves forward.

## 668. The mobile local backup archive declares its own completeness, in the server writer's vocabulary

`ApiClient.fetchRunRowsRaw` issued an unranged PostgREST select, so the server clamped it to `db-max-rows` (1000) and answered 200 with no flag: a 3,000-run account took a backup, was told it succeeded, and got 1,000 runs — discovered at restore. The read is paged through `readAllPages` and deliberately carries **no ceiling**; unlike the Go exporter, which caps at 5,000 because it builds the whole zip in one buffer, the mobile writer streams to disk and pulls blobs in bounded batches, so peak heap is flat in run count (~15 MB at 5,000 runs, the same order as the run index the app already holds resident) and a cap would buy nothing while reinstating the silent truncation. It would also leave the deepest histories with no complete path at all, since mobile skips the server export once past that ceiling and the local writer is what covers the long tail.

With the row reads exhaustive, the only remaining way a local archive can come up short is a per-blob download the writer swallows to keep the rest alive — the right trade, but the silence was not. `writeBackupZipStreaming` now returns a `LocalArchiveSummary` and stamps `complete` + `incomplete` into `manifest.json`, reusing the `BuildBackupZip` vocabulary rather than inventing a second one, and Settings → Account renders both a banner and a persistent notice. Restore reads the pair back into `RestoreResult.archiveIncomplete`, where **only an explicit `complete: false` claims a shortfall** — a web-built or older archive says nothing about itself, and warning on all of those would be its own dishonesty.

The same pass closed a data-loss path the audit surfaced: the online restore assigned `track_url = null` whenever the archive carried no track entry, so restoring a track-short archive into the account it was taken from orphaned the Storage object and cost the run its trace. A missing blob now leaves the column *out* of the upsert, which PostgREST does not touch, so an existing row keeps its own valid path while a fresh insert still lands null. That also preserves the § 116 rule the old code was written for — the archived `hr_series_url` holds the previous owner/run path and would fail `runs_hr_series_url_path_shape`, so it must never survive as-is; omitting the key drops it just as assigning null did.

## 669. Draining a widget-test tap waits on the screen's own busy state, never on a fixed span of wall clock

`import_cloud_push_deferred_test.dart` drove its taps through real `LocalRunStore` disk I/O — which no fake clock can advance past — and drained each one with a fixed `Future.delayed(300 ms)`. That is a bet on how fast the host is, and CI run 32197031350 lost it: the assertion read a screen still mid-import (0 widgets matching the finished status), and the test's `tearDown` then deleted the store's temp directory out from under the writes still in flight, producing a trailing `PathNotFoundException` trio that reads like a temp-dir race but is only the wreckage of the real failure. The CI timestamps say so directly — the three store errors land 1.6 to 60 ms *after* the test ended — and instrumenting the atomic-write counter identified the failing pair as `synced_ids` then `index` from the single `save()` of the backfill tap, i.e. the 300 ms expired mid-save. Every test in the file sat on the same edge; CI merely lost it on that one.

The drain now polls the screen's own `CircularProgressIndicator` — rendered for exactly as long as an async entry point is in flight and cleared on every exit path including the catches — so it costs nothing when the work is already done and cannot expire early when it isn't; the 30 s bound only turns a hung screen into a named failure. Widening the sleep was rejected outright: it moves the edge instead of removing it, and the fixed version now passes with a 250 ms delay injected into every atomic write (~40x the local baseline) while the original fails under 45 ms with the identical signature. In the same change, the file-level `late Directory _runsDir` plus one shared `tearDown` was replaced with an `addTearDown` registered inside `_initStore` at directory creation — the shared global only ever removed the LAST directory a test made and named the wrong one for a test that made none. § 664's split of the `markManySynced` catch was cleared as a cause: the sidecar write succeeds on this path and the backfill's failure branch reports honestly.

## 670. The runner's own load ramp reaches the phone by porting three helpers at once, not one

**Decided (2026-08-18.)** `self_load.ts` and `comeback.ts` had no Dart twin, and `followups.md` was explicit that porting either alone was the wrong move: they share `plan_ramp`'s `recentRunVolume` / `volumeSample` reduction, and the `MIN_ACTIVE_WEEKS` gate is read one way by the ratio card and the other way by the comeback card, which is the *only* thing keeping the two from claiming the same week. `plan_ramp.dart` had already landed at the identical module boundary (§ 655), so the port is the remaining two — both importing the reduction from `plan_ramp.dart` rather than re-declaring it. A private copy would have been the easy version and would have re-opened exactly the failure the web module's own comment names: a runner's pre-break base and their current week reduced from different run sets, which is the one way a comparison between the two can silently lie.

**The mutual exclusion is pinned as behaviour, not asserted as intent.** Both Dart suites run the same set of histories the web suite does through `shouldSurfaceSelfLoad` and `shouldSurfaceComeback` and assert the conjunction is never true, and the widget test does it again at the render layer against the two cards. The dashboard therefore mounts both unconditionally and never chooses; each self-hides, exactly as web's `/dashboard` does.

**One conversion of the runner's runs feeds both cards.** `_runVolumeInputs` maps `Run` → `RunForVolume` once in `dashboard_screen.dart` and both cards take the reduced list, rather than each card mapping for itself. That keeps the mobile-only model adaptation out of the twinned helpers — `plan_ramp.dart` must not learn about `core_models` — while still leaving one place where the two windows are derived from.

**Two idiomatic shape differences, neither a divergence.** Web's `shouldSurfaceSelfLoad` / `shouldSurfaceComeback` are type predicates, so an unlabelled band or verdict is a compile error there; Dart cannot narrow a field's enum through a boolean, so both return plain bools and the guarantee is carried by the cards' exhaustive `switch` plus a test that pins which values may surface. The switch arms for the ungradeable values are unreachable past each card's guard and exist only for exhaustiveness — noted in the source, because an arm that can never run otherwise reads as dead code someone will later "simplify" into a default.

## 671. "Train for this race" carries the listing's facts across the phone's navigation too, not the derived dates

**Decided (2026-08-18.)** § 606 built the web bridge and recorded the URL contract: `/plans/new?raceDate=&raceDistance=&raceName=` hands over the *race*, and the wizard re-derives the plan shape against today rather than replaying a `start`/`weeks` pair computed when the card rendered. The mobile mirror has no URL — the races screen pushes `PlanNewScreen` directly — so the shape could have been "compute the preset on the card and pass a `RacePlanPreset`". It carries `raceDateIso` / `raceName` / `raceDistanceM` instead, and derives inside the screen, for the same reason the URL does: one home for the arithmetic. It also keeps the refusal reachable rather than theoretical — a list rendered before midnight and tapped after it, or a screen constructed by any future caller, lands on the same `past` / `too_soon` / `invalid` note the web wizard renders instead of silently falling back to the usual defaults.

**The race name is withheld on a refusal, along with the dates.** Web clamps the name to the field's own 80-character budget and only seeds it when the preset succeeded; the mobile screen does both, and the second half is the load-bearing one — a wizard still titled "Autumn Half" while its dates quietly reverted to the defaults is the failure the note exists to prevent, stated twice.

**The card hides the action rather than offering one that refuses.** `_RaceCard` runs the same `racePlanPreset` call the screen will and shows nothing when it is not `ok`, mirroring `RaceCalendarCard`'s `planHref`. The races-screen tests therefore build their fixtures from `DateTime.now()` offsets rather than from a pinned calendar date: a fixture hard-coded to a future year stops exercising the gate on the day it falls into the past, and would have gone on passing while testing nothing.
## 675. The web backup archive declares its own completeness too, and a restore omits a storage path rather than nulling it

§ 668 gave the mobile writer a `complete` / `incomplete` pair in the Go writer's vocabulary and left web as the last of the three writers whose archive could be short and say nothing. `buildBackupZip` skips a track whose download rejects so one dead blob cannot sink the file — the right trade, and the row still ships in `runs.json` — but the only record of the skip was a `console.warn`, which nobody reads before trusting a backup. It now returns a `BackupArchive` (blob + `incomplete` + wanted/written counts) and stamps `complete` + `incomplete` into `manifest.json`; `/settings/account` renders the shortfall on the download and carries an archive's own `complete: false` through restore into a notice. Only an explicit `false` claims a shortfall, matching `cloudExportShortfall` and the mobile reader: a web- or mobile-built archive from before the field says nothing about itself, and warning on all of those would be its own dishonesty.

Writing that pair is what exposed the bigger half. § 668's root cause was an unranged PostgREST select clamped to `db-max-rows`, and **`createBackup` had exactly the same two reads** — `runs` and `routes`, both unranged — so a 3,000-run account took a backup, was told it succeeded, and got 1,000 runs. A manifest declaring `complete: true` over a clamped read would have been a worse lie than the silence it replaced, so both reads page through a new `readAllRows` with no ceiling: the local archive is what the deepest histories rely on, and a cap only reinstates the truncation an order of magnitude higher. `readAllRows` never throws — a read that dies half-way still holds runs worth archiving — and `createBackup` draws the line where the outcome differs: a `runs` read that returned **nothing** is a failed backup and raises, while a partial one ships flagged. The routes read used to discard its `error` entirely (`const { data: routes } =`), which is the same silence one table over; it now reports `routes` as a section.

The disclosure is a **notice, not a warning inside `warnings`**. Web's restore result renders `warnings` as a bare count, and the mobile equivalent pushes an English sentence into that list; doing the same here would have inflated a count with an untranslatable string. The verdict is therefore two fields (`archiveIncomplete` + `archiveIncompleteSections`) that the page localizes — an idiomatic difference from the Dart side, not a divergence in what either platform claims.

The same pass closed the data-loss path § 668 found on mobile, which web had verbatim: the restore assigned `track_url = null` whenever the archive carried no blob for a run, so restoring a track-short archive *into the account it was taken from* orphaned the Storage object and cost the run its trace. The column is now **omitted** — PostgREST leaves an absent column untouched on the update leg, so an existing row keeps its own valid path while a fresh insert still lands null. Letting the archived value through instead would have been worse than either: it names the run and owner the archive was taken from. `hr_series_url` is always in that case on web (no web archive carries hr blobs), so it is dropped unconditionally rather than re-homed into a path that would fail `runs_hr_series_url_path_shape` (§ 116).

## 676. A Strava row that names a member the archive does not hold fails; the refusal is worded so the report can name a reason

§ 664 made the mobile importer refuse a `Filename` that names a file the ZIP does not contain, or one in a format neither parser reads, and recorded that web already did the same. It did not: web's `importOne` guarded the whole track block on `if (entry && parser)` and fell through to a summary-only run, and additionally swallowed a parse throw into a `catch (_)`. So the leniency was not a product choice for a different platform, it was a gap — an export that promised a track it did not deliver imported clean and said nothing, which is exactly what the `ImportFailureReport` exists to prevent. The decision moved into a pure `resolveStravaTrackMember(filename, archiveHas)` so it is testable without `saveRun` (and therefore without supabase-js), sibling to the `classifyStravaMember` / `classifyStravaRow` helpers already beside it. An empty `Filename` still imports trackless — a manual or indoor activity promised nothing — and a member that parses to *zero* waypoints still falls back to the CSV's own numbers, because "unreadable" and "has no points" are different facts.

The one case left lenient is a **failed gunzip**, deliberately: `gunzipBlob` returns null for a corrupt member and for a browser with no `DecompressionStream` alike and cannot tell them apart, so failing every gzipped row of a five-year export over the reader's own engine would trade one silence for a worse one. That asymmetry with mobile (where `GZipDecoder` throws) is recorded here rather than papered over.

The wording is load-bearing. `classifyImportFailure` buckets on the message, and *neither* platform's original strings — "Track file not found in zip", "Unknown track format" — matched any pattern in the shared classifier, so both refusals would have reached the report as **"Unknown error"**: the least useful thing to tell a migrating runner, because the one question a report answers is whether re-running the import can land the missing runs. It cannot; the member is not in the file. Rather than teach a generic classifier two importer-specific phrases, both platforms now throw `Malformed export: track file not found in zip: <path>` and `Unsupported file format: <path>`, which the existing `malformed` / `unsupported file format` patterns bucket as `unparseable` — and the mobile test that asserted `ImportFailureReason.unknown` was pinning the bad answer, so it was corrected rather than kept.

## 677. The segment catalogue joins the run-surface tab strip, and only its index is crawlable

`/segments` shipped (§ 593) reachable from a run-detail effort chip and from `/segments/[id]`'s own back-link — a surface with no door in any global nav slot. The slot it takes is a fifth tab on the shared `RunSurfaceTabs` strip (Runs · Routes · Segments · Plans · Races) rather than an eighth sidebar row: the sidebar is ordered by frequency of use and a curated catalogue nobody opens daily does not belong above Social, while the strip is exactly where Routes, Plans and the race calendar were already relocated to. The strip's own comment had anticipated five tabs and it already scrolls itself rather than wrapping, so nothing had to change to fit it.

In the sitemap, the **index is listed and the per-segment pages are not.** A `/segments/[id]` page is a leaderboard of named runners; enumerating every one of them builds the people-directory that keeps profiles out of the manifest (`entityEntries`' standing rule), and the pages are CSR besides, so a crawler would be handed the empty shell for its trouble. Making them genuinely indexable is a `share-entity` branch — lookup + meta builder + route + Lambda dispatcher + CloudFront behavior + the alarm registration step 3 of *Adding a new indexable surface* requires — not a sitemap append, and the followup now says that instead of implying the append was the work.

The `<loc>` also had to be worth following. `global_segments` carries an explicit `grant select … to anon` (migration `20270512_001`) and the page takes no auth gate — its own comment says so — but the layout's guard bounced anon anyway, so the catalogue was about to be advertised to crawlers as a login form. `/segments` is now in `anonExtraExact`. `/segments/[id]` deliberately is not: the catalogue is curated content, the leaderboard names people.
## 680. A deliberately submaximal set is not evidence about the working load — `backoff` and `dropset` join `warmup` outside the progression judgement

`gym_progression` excluded only `warmup` from the sets a prescription is graded over, and the open question was whether `backoff` and `dropset` belonged there too. They do, and for the reason the warmup exclusion already states rather than a new one: every "did they hit the target?" test in `nextPrescription` is an `every` over the judged sets, and a set the lifter *chose* to run light can only ever answer no. The consequence is not a cosmetic mis-grade — it holds the load forever for anyone who programs a back-off, and under `five_by_five` it feeds `consecutiveMissSessions`, so three such sessions bank a deload nobody earned.

The exclusion is mostly redundant and that is the point of stating where it is not. `workingSets` narrows to the session's TOP completed weight, and a back-off or drop set is lighter by definition, so a weighted session already dropped them label or no label. A **bodyweight** session has no positive weight to narrow on and keeps every completed set — so three clean sets of eight pull-ups followed by an assisted set of four typed `dropset` failed the rep target and stalled the exercise permanently. That is the same shape as the unlabelled-warmup bug, in the one branch the narrowing cannot reach. The label is reachable in production: `GymEditor.svelte` offers all six `set_type` values on a logged set.

`amrap` and `failure` were considered and deliberately left judged. Both are performed AT the working weight, so their rep count is real evidence about it — a 5×5 whose last set went to failure at three reps is a genuine miss, not a set to look away from. `gym_adherence` is deliberately NOT changed to match: it grades planned-vs-actual against the target the routine author wrote for *that* set, and a planned back-off set's target already IS the back-off target, so skipping it would discard a real comparison. The two modules ask different questions ("was the plan followed?" vs "should the working load go up?") and the answers differ for exactly that reason; `warmup` is skipped in both only because skipping a warmup should never mark a session incomplete either.

## 681. The gym resume card asks the same question about the draft marker as the other three rails

§ 662 made the marker a draft only when it is a JSON object on web, in the `gym_routine_history` RPC and in `routine_history.dart` — and left `gym_screen.dart`'s resume-card scan testing `meta[gymSessionDraft] == null`, a fourth predicate, on the platform that had not drifted. An array, a string or a jsonb `null` under the key therefore offered "Workout in progress · Resume" for a row the routine's own history panel counts as a session performed, and the resume then landed in `_restoreFromDraft`'s `snap is! Map` fallback and started fresh — a resume that resumes nothing, on a workout that was never in flight.

The three Dart copies are now one `hasGymSessionDraft`, in `lib/gym_session_draft.dart`. It is deliberately not a twin of web's `gym_session_draft.ts`: mobile writes and replays the snapshot inside the session screen, so only the predicate is shared and the module claims nothing more. The follow-up filed this as "harmless today" because the restore path re-checks, which was true of the data and false of the offer — and rested on the same writer discipline § 662 declined to trust, `metadata` being unconstrained jsonb that `backup.dart`'s restore and a direct PostgREST PATCH can both fill.
## 685. An ADR whose stated mechanism turns out to be wrong is amended in place with the measurement, not left standing beside a correction three hundred entries later

§ 667 measured, in passing, that § 653's "an over-long `in` filter returns an empty result rather than an error" is not what the local stack does, and then wrote "§ 653 itself is left as written; the history only moves forward." Half of that is the right instinct and half of it is not. Not rewriting a history entry's *reasoning* is the convention, and it holds. But an ADR is read by someone who navigated to it, and § 653 asserted the wrong mechanism in its opening sentence with nothing on the page saying so — so the reader who arrived there and never arrived at § 667 got the wrong fact, which is exactly the drift the log exists to prevent. The distinction that resolves it: **the original text is never edited; an amendment is appended under it, dated, and says which sentence it corrects.** History moves forward and the reader is not left holding a claim the project knows is false.

The correction itself is a measurement rather than a re-reading. Driven against the local stack (Kong fronting PostgREST) with synthetic uuids, the boundary is the gateway's **8 KiB request-line buffer**, not an id count: 207 uuids (an 8128-byte request line) answered `200`, 209 (8206 bytes) answered `414 URI too long`, and every size from 50 to 207 answered `200`. That retires two figures at once — § 653's empty-200, and § 667's own "~15 KB of URL", which was roughly double the real bound. Stating the bound in bytes rather than in ids is the durable form, because the ceiling moves with whatever else is in the query string; an id count is only ever true for one query shape.

What does **not** change is `kInFilterChunk = 100` or the source guard around it, and that is worth saying explicitly, because "the recorded reason was wrong" invites retiring the rule with it. A hundred uuids is ~3.9 KB, far under either bound, and both failure modes lose the whole read. What *does* change is how a caller may reason about the failure: an empty 200 is silent and reaches the success path, a 414 is loud and reaches the error path, and nothing may branch on which one it will get — the gateway is the deployment's choice, not ours. **Verified locally only**; the prod gateway is unmeasured, and confirming it is still owed. The Dart-side comments that originated the claim (`chunk.dart`, `api_client.dart`) are corrected with the amendment; the web restatements in `core/data.ts` and `feed_merge.ts` are tracked rather than swept, because a comment-only sweep of a file three other sessions are editing is a merge conflict bought for nothing.

## 686. Challenges gets its parity rows as a group, and the row that mattered was the one nobody had built

Challenges shipped create, join, leave, goal progress, the on-pace hint, two board modes and a completion badge across web and both mobile twins without ever acquiring a single row in `parity.md` — while a *sub*-feature of it, the "Your standing" card, had one. A matrix that carries the refinement and not the feature is worse than one missing both: the gap is invisible precisely because the area looks covered. So all seven rows land together rather than one per round, which is also the only way the cells can be graded consistently.

Two cells are non-obvious. **Create is `✗` on both mobile twins** even though `SocialService.createChallenge` exists and is fully implemented — it has no caller anywhere in `lib/`, `challenges_screen.dart` hosts no create affordance, and the Social hub deliberately hoists no FAB for that sub-tab. A matrix grades the *surface a user can reach*, not the method that would serve it, or every unwired service call becomes a phantom `✓`. It is marked web-canonical per § 24 rather than with the 🔸 drift marker, which the legend reserves for web being behind — here web is the canonical one and the mobile form is additive. **iOS is `✓`, not the doc's default `✗`**, following the adjacent standing-card row: the three challenge files are byte-identical to Android (diff-verified) and the surrounding challenge row already made that call, so splitting the family across two conventions would read as a real platform difference where there is none.

The completion badge is called out in the Notes as the challenge's own server-stamped `completed_at` and explicitly *not* an entry in the `badges` catalogue, because the two surfaces share a word and nothing else — a reader who assumes finishing a challenge mints a trophy will go looking for a bug that is a product gap.

## 687. The route-carrying `onStartRun` callback chain is deleted, because the screen it depended on stopped popping a route

`FitnessHubScreen` took a `void Function(cm.Route)? onStartRun` and threaded it into `RoutesScreen`, which threaded it into `ExploreRoutesScreen`; both leaf screens pushed `RouteDetailScreen` as `Navigator.push<cm.Route?>` and called the callback with whatever came back. It read as live wiring — a field, a constructor argument, a pass-through and two call sites on each hop, all reachable, all analysed clean.

It could not fire. § 298 moved route-detail's Start-run FAB onto the global `pendingStartRunWithRoute` notifier precisely so it would work from *any* pusher (a deep push, the shared-file import landing) rather than only from one that handled a returned value. From that point `RouteDetailScreen` never popped a `cm.Route`: its remaining pops are dialog and bottom-sheet results and one bare `Navigator.pop(context)` on delete. So `picked` was always null, the guarded call was unreachable, and the typed `Navigator.push<cm.Route?>` was a type annotation describing a value that no longer existed. This is the failure mode a callback chain has and a notifier does not — removing the *producer* leaves the consumers compiling.

No shim and no deprecation marker: the whole chain is gone, `home_screen` stops passing the argument, and the two pushes become `Navigator.push<void>`. `_startRunWithRoute` stays — it is still the drain for the notifier, and its comment, which claimed it was "only called from the Routes tab's start-with-this-route flow", is corrected to name the handoff it actually serves. Guarding the deletion is a behavioural test on the surviving path rather than a source-level assertion that the field is absent: `route_detail_screen_test.dart` taps the FAB and asserts the notifier carries the route, plus that a route under two waypoints offers no FAB at all. A source guard would pin the shape of the fix; this pins the thing the deleted code was pretending to do. The dashboard's separate zero-argument `VoidCallback? onStartRun` is untouched — same name, different job (an empty-state CTA), genuinely wired.

## 688. `release-graphhopper.yml` verifies the engine answered, not merely that Fly accepted the deploy

GraphHopper was the one Fly service with no release workflow — `worker`, `osrm` and `graph-cycle` all had one, and `releasing.md` recorded the gap as "deployed by a hand-rolled `flyctl deploy`". The missing file is modelled on its three siblings rather than on the sketch `apps/job_worker/deployment.md` had been carrying since the app was planned: that sketch fires `on: push: tags:` and floats `actions/checkout@v4` + `setup-flyctl@v1`, both of which the house convention has since moved off — releases trigger on a *published* Release (so a tag alone cannot deploy prod) and every action is SHA-pinned because these jobs consume `FLY_API_TOKEN`. A stale sketch inside a doc is a worse trap than no sketch, so the doc now says "shipped, read the workflow" and names why the sketch differs, rather than being quietly deleted.

The one deliberate departure from the siblings is a `/health` probe after `flyctl status`. OSRM and graph-cycle stop at status, which is defensible for them; GraphHopper imports its graph from the volume on boot and its own `fly.toml` sets a **10-minute** health-check grace period for exactly that reason. Inside that window a machine can read healthy to `flyctl` while the engine is not yet serving `/route`, so a status-only verify greens a tag over an engine that answers nothing — and the caller is a Lambda that would surface it as a 502 on route generation, far from the release. The probe polls for the same 10 minutes and fails the job otherwise. It targets `/health` and not `/route` on purpose: the Caddy front guards `/route` on the `X-Engine-Key` shared secret, which is a **Fly app secret** read by the Lambda from sops, and pulling it into a GitHub Actions context to make a nicer smoke test would put a production bypass credential somewhere it has never needed to be. The workflow therefore verifies liveness, not authorised function, and says so in its own header.

## 689. A checklist box is ticked against what the migration did, not against what the box asked for — and "index `routes.name` for search" was cited to the migration that deleted the index it named

`backend_scaling.md` carried `[x] Add full-text search index on routes.name for route library search — 20270316_001_search_trgm_indexes.sql`. Every part of that is checkable and the check fails: `20270316_001` adds a **trigram** GIN index (`routes_name_trgm`, `gin_trgm_ops`) and, twenty lines later, `drop index if exists routes_name_search` — the real `to_tsvector('english', name)` GIN index `20260407_001` had added. So the box claiming full-text search on `routes.name` pointed at the change that removed full-text search on `routes.name`.

The underlying work is nevertheless done, which is why the box stays ticked rather than being re-opened. `search_public_routes` matches with `ILIKE '%term%'`; a `to_tsvector` index cannot serve that predicate, so the FTS index had never been used by anything and was pure write cost plus a false "already indexed" signal — dropping it was correct, and the trigram index is what actually backs the surface the line exists for. The fix is therefore to the *wording*: the line now names trigram, names the drop, and says why, in the same "done, but not the way this line asked" form lines 441 and 484 already use for Vault-not-pgcrypto and `start_point`-not-`geom`. A checklist that records the intent rather than the landing is how a future reader concludes the wrong thing is indexed and re-adds the index that was deliberately removed.

Two neighbours were corrected in the same pass for the same reason. The live-hub line and the file's status banner both said the WebSocket hub "awaits a Fly deploy + DNS flip" — the worker deployed 2026-07-21 and `live.threkir.com` is a live CNAME in `infra/dns/main.tf`; the only thing outstanding is the client env cutover, so the `[~]` is right and the stated blocker was not. And the one genuinely open box, "ensure materialized views are performant for dashboard queries", now says why it cannot be closed: `mv_weekly_mileage` is the repo's only materialized view and has no read path at all, so there is nothing to grade until someone decides between a `SECURITY DEFINER` reader and dropping it. An open box whose blocker is unstated reads as neglect; stated, it reads as a decision waiting.

**Amended 2026-08-19.** The decision that box was waiting on has been made: the matview is dropped, not wrapped (§ 690). Nothing in the paragraph above was wrong — `mv_weekly_mileage` did have no read path, and stating the blocker was the right call — but the box is no longer open, so a reader arriving here should not go looking for a pending choice. `backend_scaling.md` now carries the closed form.

## 690. `mv_weekly_mileage` is dropped rather than given a reader, because the surfaces it was said to serve could never have read it

Issue #789 I.3 offered two ways to close a matview that had a pg_cron refresh and no consumer: wire a `SECURITY DEFINER` reader, or drop it. The evidence points one way, and the decisive part is not the missing reader — it is that the view's aggregate is the wrong shape for every surface anyone imagined reading it.

The missing reader is easy and was already half-recorded: `20260517_001` said "zero callers" outright while revoking public SELECT, and 386 migrations later `git grep mv_weekly_mileage` still finds it in exactly two kinds of place — the four migrations that create, revoke and schedule it, and prose. No client, RPC, Edge Function or Go worker selects from it. `apps/web/src/lib/database.types.ts` mentions it, but that file is generated, so it records that the object exists, not that anything reads it.

`api_database.md` asserted that "the `weekly_mileage` RPC and the dashboard's 'This Week' card" read it. Both halves are false and were false from the start. `weekly_mileage(weeks_back)` aggregates `runs` directly under `user_id = auth.uid()` — in `20260406_001` and again in its `20260710_001` `search_path` re-emission — and it has no caller of its own on any platform. The dashboard's weekly chart goes through `fetchWeeklyMileage`, which selects a bounded 14-week `(started_at, distance_m)` window off `runs_user_started_at` and buckets it in TypeScript via `bucketWeeklyMileage`; `ThisWeekStrip` is handed runs already in memory. Neither path has ever touched the view.

Then the shape argument, which is why a wrapper would have been the wrong build rather than merely an unnecessary one. `date_trunc('week', ...)` is ISO Monday-start and cannot express the Sunday-start `week_start_day` preference both dashboards honour. `started_at` is `timestamptz`, so the bucket boundary falls at the *session* timezone's midnight — UTC under PostgREST — while `bucketWeeklyMileage` cuts at the runner's local midnight; a Sunday-evening run west of Greenwich lands in a different week in the view than on the page. And the aggregate is unfiltered over all history, where every surface windows and filters. A pre-aggregation that is actually correct has to be keyed per user timezone and per week-start preference: that is a different object, not a wrapper over this one. Building a reader would have meant either shipping a reader whose numbers disagree with the page, or shipping the honest reader and *still* not using it — the dead-code trap in a new costume.

The cost side is settled and small in absolute terms, which is worth stating so the decision does not read as a cost panic. 96 refreshes a day, each a full-table `GROUP BY` over every user's runs, serving zero reads, for the whole of its life — the cost-controls audit had already flagged the cadence and `20260706_001` cut it 5 min → 15 min, which reduced a number that should have been zero. Meanwhile the thing the view was meant to accelerate was measured at 10× target volume in `roadmap_shipped.md`: `fetchWeeklyMileage` at 0.99 ms against a 2074-run user. There is no hot aggregate here to accelerate, and per-user weekly mileage is bounded by one runner's training, not by the table.

So: the matview, its `mv_weekly_mileage_pk` index and the `refresh-mv-weekly-mileage` cron entry all go in `20270530_001`. Deliberately without `CASCADE` — nothing depends on it today (verified against `pg_depend`) and a fail-loud drop is the correct behaviour if that ever stops being true. `weekly_mileage()` stays: it is unused but it is the *correct* sanctioned shape for this read — `auth.uid()`-scoped, `search_path`-pinned — and deleting the right answer alongside the wrong one would leave the next caller with neither.

The guard, `mv_weekly_mileage_dropped_test.sql`, pins the drop as **complete** rather than partial, because a half-drop is the expensive outcome in both directions: an orphaned cron entry errors on every tick against a missing relation, and an orphaned relation resumes costing the moment anyone reschedules. It asserts against `pg_class` with no relkind filter, so re-adding the name as a plain view or table fails too, and it matches the cron entry on its *command* as well as its name, since a refresh rescheduled under a different jobname costs exactly the same. The relation assertion also covers the grants: a privilege row cannot outlive its object.

The generalisable rule, and the reason this is an ADR rather than a cleanup commit: **an aggregate provisioned ahead of a reader is not free optimism, it is a standing bill plus a false signal.** The bill ran 422 migrations. The false signal was worse — a doc claimed two surfaces read it, an audit command listed it as a thing to grade for performance, a feature spec offered it as an available aggregate, and a `backend_scaling.md` box could not be closed because of it. None of that would have existed if the view had been created the day a query actually needed one, keyed to what that query asked for.

## 691. The watch's battery gauge selects its SAADC input from the supply mode, because on the tier-1 wiring the VDD channel measures an internal regulator and never the cell

**Decided (2026-08-19, issue #789 § I.3.)** § 294 gave the watch a battery gauge and pointed the `battery` task at `saadc::VddInput` unconditionally, recording as a bench follow-up that the driver's default gain 1/6 (3600 mV full scale) rails below a fresh 4.2 V charge; § 316 then made a railed conversion read *absent* rather than a confident ~8 %, and described the residue as "the gauge blanks across 4.2→3.6 V and reads honestly below that". **That description was wrong about the configuration the DoD run actually uses.** The nRF52840 has two supply paths. Fed on VDD it runs in normal-voltage mode and the rail the SoC runs on *is* the cell, which is what `VddInput` reads. Fed on VDDH it runs in high-voltage mode, and VDD becomes the output of an internal regulator whose level is `UICR.REGOUT0` — so `VddInput` measures the regulator, returns the same ~3.0 V at every state of charge, gets refused by the plausibility band, and the gauge is absent at *all* charge levels, not merely near the top. High-voltage mode is not a corner case here: `app/src/supply.rs` exists precisely because it is what the nRF52840 DK's SW9 Li-Po position selects, and `docs/custom_watch/parts.md` note 0 is explicit that the Li-Po position is the configuration § 82's untethered outdoor run needs. So the gauge shipped unable to read the cell on the only wiring that has one.

**The input and its scale are now chosen from the supply mode, not fixed.** `supply::report` already reads `POWER.MAINREGSTATUS` at boot — it exists to warn that high-voltage mode drives the breakouts at 1.8 V on an erased UICR — and it now returns the `watch_core::battery_sense::SupplySense` that read implies. Normal mode keeps `VddInput` at gain 1/6 (`FULL_SCALE_VDD_MV` = 3600); high-voltage mode takes `VddhDiv5Input` at **gain 1/2**, which is 1200 mV at the converter and therefore `FULL_SCALE_VDDHDIV5_MV` = 6000 mV of VDDH once the divider's ×5 is applied. Gain 1/2 rather than the driver's default 1/6 (18000 mV full scale) for one reason that is not resolution: **6000 mV strictly exceeds five times VDDH's 5.8 V absolute maximum, so this input cannot saturate anywhere the SoC is permitted to run.** Bounding the scale by what the rail can legally be is exactly the reasoning whose absence produced the original bug, and doing it deliberately is what stops the same class of defect recurring one rail up. Four times the resolution against a cell-sized rail (a 4.2 V cell at 70 % of the converter instead of 23 %, so every LSB-fixed error is a quarter as large against the reading) is a real benefit and the secondary one.

**Selecting is the durable answer; hard-swapping the channel would have been a regression.** An unconditional move to `VddhDiv5Input` would have made the DK in its default USB/VDD position read whatever VDDH happens to be there — plausibly a number the band accepts — replacing today's honest *absent* with a confident wrong one. That is the opposite of the § 316 posture, which chose to admit a gap rather than publish an unearned figure, so both wirings must stay honest and the mode is the only thing that knows which is which. The scale travels with the channel as a single `SupplySense` handed to the task alongside its `Saadc`, so a channel and a scale that disagree are not constructible; `mv_from_raw` and `percent_from_raw` both take it.

**The curve and the plausibility band needed no change, and saying so is part of the finding.** `battery::PLAUSIBLE_MAX_MV` is 4350 and the curve's top anchor is 4200 mV → 100 %, both already correct for a charger-fresh cell — the only thing that had ever prevented a full cell reading 100 % was a full scale that saturated before reaching them. What does change is that the band's **upper** bound becomes reachable for the first time and now earns its keep: SW9's USB position also runs the high-voltage regulator, so VDDH sits at ~5 V there and the ceiling is what refuses to read a USB rail as a cell. `railed` is kept on both senses even though the VDDH sense cannot reach it inside spec — the voltage behind a saturated code is not knowable from the code, on any input.

**Verification, at the § 314 rungs and no higher.** Host-tested: +7 tests over the existing suite (a charger-fresh 4.2 V cell reads 100 % on the VDDH sense; the DK's ~3.0 V regulated rail stays absent on *either* sense; VDDH's 5.5 V operating and 5.8 V absolute maxima both fail to rail; the codes immediately either side of both plausibility bounds; monotonicity over every single code from the 3.3 V empty cutoff to full charge; and `sees_a_full_cell` false for the VDD sense, which is the bug stated as an assertion). Build-verified on the default, `ble` and sim feature sets with all three clippy gates and `cargo fmt --check` green. The Renode `smoke` scenario passes, and its POWER model happens to report high-voltage mode, so the sim does execute the new branch and the battery task still parks cleanly on it — **but Renode models no SAADC at all, so nothing about the reading is sim-verified and none of this is bench-verified.** The on-silicon figure, and whether the default 10 µs acquisition time is long enough for the internal divider's source impedance, are bench items recorded in `quality_standards.md` (issue #597). § 294 and § 316 are amended in place to point here rather than left stating the old behaviour as current, per § 685.

## 692. Mobile's "add to calendar" hands the OS an event, not a file — and the series crosses the channel as an RRULE

**Date:** 2026-08-19

Web's per-occurrence and whole-series `.ics` exports ([§ 599](#599-a-recurring-club-event-exports-as-a-rule-not-as-one-date--and-a-rule-it-cannot-state-faithfully-is-withheld)) exist because a browser has nothing to hand an event to; it can only offer a download. A phone has an OS calendar with its own insert surface, so the mirror is the platform hand-off — `ACTION_INSERT` on `CalendarContract.Events` on Android, `EKEventEditViewController` on iOS — and the `.ics` text builder owes no Dart twin per [§ 24](#24-web-is-the-canonical-feature-surface-mobile-and-watches-are-platform-additive). Both hand-offs open the calendar app's *own* new-event editor pre-filled from the event, so the runner confirms the save: Android needs no calendar permission at all, and iOS asks only for write-only access (`NSCalendarsWriteOnlyAccessUsageDescription`, falling back to `requestAccess` below iOS 17). The app never writes to a calendar behind anyone's back and never reads one.

**The series travels as an RFC 5545 RRULE value, because both platforms already speak that grammar.** Android stores the string verbatim in `Events.RRULE`; iOS parses the small emitted subset (`FREQ` / `INTERVAL` / `COUNT` / `UNTIL` / `BYDAY` / `BYMONTHDAY`) into an `EKRecurrenceRule`. The alternative — sending structured fields and building the rule twice natively — puts two representations on one channel and two places for the shaping to be wrong. `buildRrule` in `calendar_intent.dart` therefore mirrors web's decision for decision, including the fail-closed ones: DTSTART is the first *expanded* occurrence rather than `starts_at`, `until` + `count` resolve to whichever binds first, BYDAY is read off the expansion in UTC rather than translated from the stored wall-clock codes, and a monthly series anchored past the 28th is withheld outright (the app clamps a missing day-of-month, `BYMONTHDAY` skips the short month, and no rule clamps). Web's guards for an unparseable UNTIL and a non-integer COUNT have no analogue — a Dart `DateTime` and `int` cannot arrive in those states. The Swift parser is held to the same bar: anything outside the emitted subset yields no rule rather than a different one.

**Neither hand-off carries exception dates, so the surface says so instead of implying otherwise.** Web subtracts each cancelled occurrence with an `EXDATE`; `ACTION_INSERT`'s documented extras have no such slot and `EKRecurrenceRule` has no exception concept, so a repeating entry added from the phone will keep showing occurrences the organiser called off. Withholding the series button for a year because one Saturday was cancelled would cost the feature its main use, and passing an `EXDATE` most calendar editors ignore would be the silent-disagreement failure § 599 refused. So `calendarSeriesFor` returns the called-off occurrences within the next year — reusing `event_occurrence.dart`'s `isOccurrenceCancelled`, the same helper the picker hides them with — and the screen names the count under the button. The per-occurrence hand-off is unaffected and is withheld entirely for a past or called-off instance.

One shared bug surfaced while wiring this and is fixed on the Dart side: `expandInstances` stamps every occurrence at whole-second resolution, so searching *from* `starts_at` — which only this caller does, every other one searches from `now` — sorts the series' own first occurrence as strictly before the window and anchored the rule one period late, undercounting an `until` + `count` pair by one. The anchor search now floors to the whole second.

## 693. The phone's segment catalogue ports the four shaping helpers and nothing else, because the chips it unblocks were already pointing at a screen that did not exist

**Decided (2026-08-19, issue #789 § A.)** Web shipped `/segments` on 2026-08-13 (§ 593) over a web-only `segments/catalogue_browse.ts`. Mobile already carried the `computeGlobalSegmentEffort` half of the catalogue in `segments.dart` — it matched runs against curated geometry and rendered per-run effort chips on run detail — but had no catalogue surface of any kind. So the chips computed a real effort, drew a real rank, and then led nowhere: the one platform that could match a route-less run against a famous segment was the one that could not show you the segment.

Both halves of the followups entry's shape land together, and the ordering is the point. `catalogue_browse.dart` is written *with* its consumer, not ahead of it. A Dart twin with no caller is dead code that the parity guard then polices in perpetuity — the same trap § 671 and § 670 avoided by refusing to port on web's schedule — so the pair and the two screens are one change.

Two asymmetries in the port are deliberate and are the interesting part of the pair. **Region folds on both sides of the comparison; surface does not.** A region is free-text curator input, so the filter vocabulary dedupes on the folded form and the row match compares folded too — a dropdown that collapses "Zürich, CH" and "zurich, ch" into one option must not then hide half the rows that option claims to contain. `surface` is a CHECK-constrained token, so it is compared verbatim: folding a database identifier would invent an equivalence the schema does not have, and the schema is the thing that decides what a surface is. **And an absent distance or elevation sorts last under every numeric order, including the descending ones.** Under "most climb" the natural reading of a null is "no climb", which sorts it against zero; but the value is unknown, not zero, and an unknown climb presented as the biggest climb on the list is the one output nobody can recover from. Last under both directions is the honest position.

The accent fold itself is the one place where the two implementations cannot be spelled the same way. Web decomposes to NFD and strips combining marks; Dart's core library carries no normalisation at all, so the Dart side spells out an explicit precomposed-Latin table plus the combining-mark ranges, exactly as `gym_prs` spells out its whitespace class. The letters NFD does not decompose in the first place — `ø`, `đ`, `ł`, `ß`, `æ` — are therefore absent from the table on purpose rather than by omission: including them would make the phone fold a pair of characters the web deliberately keeps distinct, which is a divergence dressed as thoroughness. That is why the suites are 28 web / 27 Dart rather than matched: the extra web case pins an NFD behaviour that has no Dart analogue to pin.

The detail screen renders the curated polyline through `TrackPreview` and says why in the one comment it carries: catalogue geometry is public curated data, not an athlete's GPS track, so there is nothing here for `clipTrackForUser` to protect. That is worth a comment precisely because every *other* polyline on this platform does need the clip, and a reviewer's correct instinct on seeing an unclipped track render is that a privacy boundary has been missed.

## 694. The phone's challenge list carries a progress signal only because the value it would otherwise invent is a zero nobody measured

**Decided (2026-08-19, issue #789 § "Challenges: two things this round deliberately did not ship")** `challenges_screen.dart` listed joined challenges as plain rows — no bar, no value, no rank — which the followups entry correctly read as *carrying no false-zero bug and therefore owing no urgent mirror*. It also meant the one number a participant actually wants was two taps away on every row, so the list is now the surface the web one is: value against goal, bar, rank, earned badge.

The reason `challenge_list.ts` was web-only was not that the shaping is web-shaped; it is that the shaping's whole content is a refusal, and a surface with nothing to draw has nothing to refuse. **The per-caller value does not exist on the `challenges` row.** It lives only in the `challenge_leaderboard` aggregate, surfaced in bulk by `my_active_challenges`, whose window is `now() >= starts_at and now() < ends_at + 7 days`. A joined challenge outside that window therefore arrives with `my_value` null — and null is not zero. `myProgressView` splits the two cases the null covers: a window that has not opened yet is a *known* zero (the aggregate counts runs from `starts_at`, so nothing can have counted), and everything else is *unknown*, which both platforms state as "Progress unavailable — open for your result" rather than drawing an empty bar beside the goal. A bar at 0 % is a measurement claim; on a challenge the page never fetched a value for, it is a false one.

Two fail-closed details carry over verbatim and are the reason the helper is worth twinning rather than re-deriving. A served value always outranks the clock comparison, so a client clock running behind the server's cannot downgrade a real number to a presumed zero; and a non-finite value falls through to *unknown* rather than to zero. The web twin's unparseable-`starts_at` guard has no Dart analogue — a typed `DateTime` cannot arrive in that state — which is why the suites are 18 web / 17 Dart rather than matched.

**Dart has no object spread, so `mergeMyProgress` returns each row paired with the values it should carry** and `ChallengeView.withProgress` applies them, where web returns rebuilt rows; the `MyProgressRow` bound TS satisfies structurally is a declared abstract interface here, as `leaderboard_standing`'s `StandingEntry` already is. Both are idiomatic shape differences, not divergences, and both are recorded in the two parity registries the pair is now registered in.

Porting the module also closed two things the *detail* screen was getting wrong, because a list row that says "open for your result" is a promise the next screen has to keep. Its bar read `c.myValue ?? 0`, and `fetchChallengeById` never fills `myValue` — so every participant saw a confident zero. It now reads the caller's own row off the board it already holds, exactly as web's `myRow?.value ?? challenge.my_value ?? 0` does. And `teamLabel`'s existence is the fix for the other: the club-vs-club board printed `_clubNames[id] ?? id`, so a club RLS did not let the viewer read rendered as a raw uuid. The two id-less kinds are distinct claims and are localised separately — an unaffiliated group (`team_club_id` is nullable and its FK is `on delete set null`, so a deleted club leaves its people as a group the aggregate still sums) is not a club the viewer cannot see.

The mobile bar is the shared `widgets/challenge_progress_bar.dart`, extracted from the detail screen's inline copy rather than duplicated into the list — web shares one `ChallengeProgressBar.svelte` between the same two surfaces, and two callers is a real abstraction rather than a speculative one.
