## 695. The phone's targets peer is a derivation view, not a second editor — the two non-sensitive levers travel, the four Art 9 fields stay behind their one consent gate

**Decided (2026-08-19, issue #789 § followups)** Web closed issue #666 M1's structural half on 2026-08-05 (§ 527) with `/nutrition/targets`. Mobile carried the whole engine — `nutrition_targets.dart` is a registered parity pair and already exported every constant plus `mifflinStJeorBmr` — and still had no way to reach the number. `nutrition_screen.dart` linked `SettingsBodyMetricsScreen` from its **untargeted** state only (§ 490), so the affordance vanished at exactly the moment the number became real: a runner with metrics on file saw four rings measured against a figure nothing on the phone would name, let alone derive.

The mirror adds no arithmetic, and that is the constraint that shaped it. Every term the derivation prints is read back out of the engine — `mifflinStJeorBmr` for the resting rate, `activityLevels` for the factor, `goalKcalDelta` for the delta, `minCalorieTarget` for the floor note, `proteinGPerKg` / `fatKcalFraction` for the macro hints — and a guard test fails the build if any of `1.8` / `0.3` / `1200` / `-500` reappears as a literal on the screen, mirroring the four the web guard bans. A copied constant here would drift from the TS twin silently, because the twin's own mirror suite compares the two *libraries*, not their consumers.

**The Art 9 boundary is the reason this is a peer and not a second editor.** Height, weight, date of birth and sex are special-category data behind an explicit-consent toggle; a second place to type them is a second consent surface, and the withdrawal path (`withdrawHealthDataConsent` erasing the height and the whole weight series) then has two front doors to keep honest. So the screen *displays* all four read-only and links to the one editor. The guard enumerates the five consent-path api methods plus `TextField` itself and fails on any of them, because "read-only" is a property of the widget tree, not of an intention.

The two levers that *do* travel — activity level and weight goal — are ordinary universal-bag prefs, and they write through `SettingsSyncService.updateUniversal` on exactly the keys the body-metrics editor writes. Their label switches were **promoted** out of that screen to `activityLevelLabel` / `weightGoalLabel` rather than copied: two surfaces showing one stored value must not be able to name it differently, and a duplicated `switch` is the cheapest way to end up doing so.

The entry point is deliberately **ungated**. A data gate would hide the derivation from the runner whose targets do not resolve yet, which is the same §63-amendment entry-point rule web applied to its header link — and the widget tests pin the entry in both states rather than only the interesting one. Its cost was one measured surprise: the extra row grew the rings card enough to push a single-entry day's delete affordance ten pixels past the bottom of the 800x600 test viewport, which failed five existing `nutrition_screen_test` cases. Those were fixed by scrolling to the affordance, not by shrinking the card — a test that only passes while the card stays a fixed height was pinning the viewport, not the behaviour.

One divergence from web is real and is a consequence of platform, not of taste: the web page's exercise add-on is read for **today** because the route is its own URL with no parent state, and the mobile screen does the same rather than inheriting the host's viewed diary day. The host can be showing last Tuesday; the peer always answers "today", which is what its own copy claims, so the two never contradict each other on screen.

Both screens need the same reduction of the `activities` view into a day's exercise inputs, and that reduction now lives in `lib/exercise_day.dart` — not in either screen. It was written inside `screens/nutrition_screen.dart`, so the peer's first cut imported it from there and the two screens formed an import cycle. The cycle is legal Dart and would have worked; it was still the wrong shape, because it is the *symptom* rather than the problem. The problem is that a pure day-bucketing reduction was living in a widget file, which made one screen a library for another — and the moment a second consumer appeared, the only way to reuse it was to point a screen at a screen. Moving it to the lib layer gives both screens one dependency and neither a dependency on the other, and its six tests moved with it out of the screen's widget-test file, where they had never needed a screen mounted. It is **mobile-only glue and not a parity pair**: web resolves the same day by pushing the window into PostgREST as `fetchRuns` / `fetchGymWorkouts` bounds, so there is no TS twin to drift from. The general rule this settles is recorded in [conventions.md § Mobile pure helpers](conventions.md).

The one measured cost of the ungated entry deserves recording, because the first read of it was wrong. The extra row grew the rings card by exactly 48 dp, which pushed a single-entry day's delete affordance past the bottom of the **800x600 default test viewport** and failed five `nutrition_screen_test` cases. That viewport is wider and shorter than any real phone, so the honest fix was to scroll to the affordance the way a user does — and it was verified as honest rather than assumed: probing 320x568 / 360x640 / 390x844 at 1x and 2x text scale, on this branch and on the parent commit, the delete stays reachable after a scroll in all twelve runs, and every horizontal overflow reported (48 px and 5.8 px at 1x on a 320 dp phone, from the rings row's `spaceAround` and the water card's title row) is present **identically on the parent commit** and is untouched by this change.
## 696. The phone's segment chip was the third population — and the follow-up that would have caught it had been shipped, not ticked

**Date:** 2026-08-19

[§ 594](#594-a-rank-and-the-leaderboard-it-links-to-are-counted-from-one-population-and-an-athlete-is-not-their-own-competitor) reconciled `segment_effort_ranks` with `segment_leaderboard_tiered` on 2026-08-13 — same population, same block filter, two pgtap suites, `api_database.md` rewritten to match. The follow-up that raised it was written in the same PR and never ticked, so six days later it read as open work needing a migration. It did not: re-deriving the alignment predicate by predicate found the server side already correct in all three respects. The board's `private.is_run_visible_to` is not an extra filter the RPC lacks — it is literally the `segment_efforts` SELECT policy (`20260812_001`), so SECURITY INVOKER supplies it; route visibility arrives the same way through the segments EXISTS, which delegates to `private.is_route_visible_to`; and the block graph, the one predicate RLS cannot carry, was added by `20270523_001`. The catalogue twin holds too — `global_segment_efforts`' policy is `segment active AND run visible`, matching the catalogue board's own two gates.

**What the audit did find was a third population, on the phone.** `ApiClient.fetchEffortsForRunWithSegments` never moved to the RPC when web did. It counted, per effort, the `segment_efforts` rows with a strictly faster time on the same segment — the exact pre-§ 594 reduction, now living one layer out where no migration could reach it. So the defect § 594 closed was still shipping to mobile users: a rival's repeat effort inflated the chip without limit, the caller's own faster efforts counted against their slower ones, and a blocked athlete kept pushing the caller down a ranking they were absent from. Two things made it invisible. The mobile *board* had been on `segment_leaderboard_tiered` all along, so the phone contradicted itself across two adjacent surfaces rather than contradicting the web. And the file's own catalogue twin, `fetchGlobalEffortsForRun`, was written against the RPC from the start — the correct pattern sat forty lines away from the incorrect one. The fix is to call the RPC, which also retires an N+1 that had survived the perf-hunt that removed web's.

The lesson is about the ledger, not the ranking. **A shipped fix with an unticked follow-up costs more than an unfixed one**, because the next reader believes the entry over the schema and starts by writing the migration that already exists. The tick is not bookkeeping — it is the only thing that says "this was looked at". And a rank contract now lives in five places (two RPCs, two clients, `api_database.md`); the two client comments were both still stating the row-count contract, which is how a reader talks themselves out of checking the code. Both are corrected here, and mobile's is pinned by a source guard rather than a wire test, following `public_run_counts_source_test.dart`: the old query is well-formed and succeeds, it simply answers a different question, so only the source can fail.

One residual difference between the chip and the board is deliberate and stays: the boards inner-join `user_profiles` and so drop an athlete with no profile row, where the chip counts them. No path reaches that state — the Art 8 consent gate makes a profile row a precondition of writing a run — and closing it by dropping the rival would restate every slower athlete's rank, which [§ 596](#596-a-pasted-visibility-predicate-is-a-moderation-control-with-an-expiry-date-and-a-hidden-athlete-is-redacted-from-a-leaderboard-rather-than-dropped) already refused for shadow-hidden athletes on the same reasoning. The demographic tiers, `p_limit`, and the anon caller (whom the board refuses outright) are likewise unmirrored by design.
## 697. A CI wait loop states a deadline it can keep, and a harness guard compares served content rather than the server's root

**Decided (2026-08-19, issue #789 § G.)** Two CI-reliability follow-ups, one shape: a check that reported something other than what it actually did.

**The sidecar wait's budget is wall-clock, not an attempt count.** The `Start local Supabase stack` probe loop ran `for i in $(seq 1 45)` with `sleep 2` and failed with "never became ready within 90s". That arithmetic charges the sleeps and nothing else, so an attempt that spends curl's whole `--max-time` costs the budget nothing. The two 2026-08-14 failures took ~9 minutes to report a 90 s timeout, and 45 x (10 s `--max-time` + 2 s sleep) = 540 s is exactly that: **the loop was telling the truth about the wait and the message was understating it 6x** — the entry's "one of them is lying" resolves against the error string. The same arithmetic re-dates the incident's own reading of `000`: an attempt that returns instantly on a refused connection cannot take 12 s, so kong was accepting the connection and hanging for the full `--max-time`, which is why the wall clock ran six times the stated budget while the log looked like 45 quick retries. Every attempt is now charged against a real deadline and the last attempt's `--max-time` is clamped to what is left of it, so the failure costs what it says it costs. The budget is deliberately **not** widened: a probe whose upstream answers quickly (kong's 503 while the runtime boots) still gets the same ~45 tries it always did, and a probe where every attempt burns the full `--max-time` is a stack that is not coming up at all — the only thing a longer wait buys there is a more expensive failure.

**The 90 s was then measured rather than inherited, because turning an attempt count into a deadline tightens the effective ceiling ~6x and that is exactly where a new flake would come from.** Across 277 jobs carrying this step in 14 workflow runs (2026-08-13 to 2026-08-19, every stack-using job type: the 14 e2e shards, the SSO/OAuth and Go live-hub lanes, pgtap, edge-functions, api_client integration, cross-client round-trip, schema drift), the 275 green ones took a **median of 1.21 s and a maximum of 12.15 s**; 274 of the 275 finished under 2 s, and exactly one needed a retry at all — a single attempt, e2e shard 10/14 in run 32150279557. The worst healthy boot on record therefore spends 13 % of the deadline, and the hypothesis the measurement was taken to test — a healthy-but-slow boot spending 3-5 s an attempt over many attempts — does not occur: an attempt that fails here fails by exhausting the whole 10 s `--max-time`, which the incident log shows to the millisecond (attempts 2-45 of run 31834502152 are 12.013 s apart, i.e. 10 s of curl plus the 2 s sleep). 90 s still affords eight such attempts against the one ever observed, and ~45 against a probe whose upstream answers fast, so the tightening is only ever spent by the failure mode it exists to bound. The same sampling turned up a **third occurrence** of the incident the follow-up recorded as twice: run 31834502152 (2026-08-14, e2e shard 12/14) spent **530.04 s over 45 attempts** and reported "within 90s" — the arithmetic above, measured rather than reconstructed. Its first attempt got kong's instant `502`, and every attempt after it timed out, which is the evidence for reading `000` as a hung upstream rather than a refused connection.

Two smaller lies came out with it. `code=$(curl … || echo 000)` appended a second `000` to the one curl writes itself, which is the whole of `(last status 000000)` in the incident log. And the loop's forensics only ever saw kong's side of the conversation, so neither 2026-08-14 failure left anything in the run log that could say *why* the container never served; giving up now dumps the stack's container list, every container's state and exit code, and the failing sidecar's plus kong's `docker logs` tail. The loop moved out of `action.yml` into `wait_for_sidecars.sh` for one reason: shell inside a composite action runs in no job's test suite, and the accounting is exactly the kind of thing that drifts back. `wait_for_sidecars.test.mjs` drives it with stub `curl`/`docker` on `PATH` under the `workflow-lint` job, and each accounting assertion was verified to fail against the old arithmetic.

**The Playwright dev-server guard compares content, because a root check cannot see a stale bundle.** § 631's `/@fs/` probe proves the reused server's `server.fs.allow` admits our path: a `403` is a server rooted in another checkout. But `403` is only reachable when the allow list excludes us — a server rooted in an ancestor, or one with a widened allow list, answers `200` for our file while still serving its own copy of every module the app imports, and that is the case several agents sharing one machine actually hit. The guard now asks Vite for the file's bytes through `?raw` twice: once by absolute path (ours, byte for byte) and once at the same path relative to the server's own root (whatever tree it is serving), and either one disagreeing with disk fails the run naming the file. The probe set is this tree's own uncommitted `apps/web/src` sources — the files whose staleness would break a spec — falling back to a fixed module on a clean tree. Everything inconclusive still only warns: a 404 on both routes, a non-Vite server, an unreachable port. The guard must never turn an unfamiliar local setup into a failing suite, and the failure it *does* raise has to name the cause, because the symptom it replaces (a new-surface spec failing with no console error while every pre-existing spec passes) reads as a real break.

Its unit tests live under `apps/web/tests-e2e/fixtures/`, which every Playwright config ignores, so the web unit suite's glob grew to cover that directory. The harness is code too, and the guard's inconclusive-vs-fatal boundary is the part worth pinning.
**Amendment (2026-08-19, same day):** the forensics earned their keep before the PR that added them had merged. `Edge Function tests (Deno)` hit this exact failure on PR #793 and the dump named the cause on the first occurrence: the edge runtime was serving normally and it was the per-function *worker* that died, `failed to create the graph: Failed loading https://registry.npmjs.org/@types%2fnode … Network is unreachable (os error 101)`. The blocking fetch is for **types**, pulled transitively through the `X-TypeScript-Types` header the esm.sh supabase-js import advertises, so a worker cannot boot without a network round-trip it needs none of to execute. That is why every probe hung to `--max-time` and reported `000`, and `os error 101` being a routing failure rather than a refusal is what makes it intermittent. Three prior investigations had inferred a cause from the wait loop's own output and got it wrong — including this entry's parent, which read `000` as connection-refused. The remaining work (removing the boot-time npm dependency) is tracked as its own follow-up rather than folded in here: the diagnosis is what the forensics were for, and the dependency change is a separate piece with its own type-safety trade-off.

## 698. The GPS link moves to `BufferedUarte` with a 2048-byte ring, and the second simulator gap — a UARTE whose events never reached the PPI matrix — is closed to prove it

**Decided (2026-08-19, issue #789 § I.2)** `gps.rs` re-armed a single 32-byte EasyDMA read, which fills in 8.3 ms at the link's 38400 baud ([§ 622](#622-the-gps-link-runs-at-the-receivers-factory-38400-because-a-configured-baud-silently-lapses-in-a-drawer)) and then leaves the receiver disarmed until a task runs again. An NVMC page erase halts the CPU for ~85 ms and that halt is irreducible ([§ 419](#419-flash-writes-yield-every-256-bytes-a-page-erase-is-irreducible-and-the-ble-build-is-not-exempt)), so a mid-run checkpoint could cost up to 326 bytes of NMEA — an L4 flash write degrading L1 distance, which the layering contract forbids. `BufferedUarte` pre-arms the next transfer and chains it over PPI (ENDRX -> STARTRX), so the receiver stays armed *in hardware* across a CPU stall and the halt costs nothing.

**The ring is 2048 bytes because that is what the arithmetic says, not 512.** The driver runs half-buffer transfers with one in flight and one pre-armed, so the *guaranteed* headroom is `half_len` — the in-flight one may be about to end. At 38400 8N1 the line delivers 3840 B/s, so a 512-byte ring buys 256 B = 66.7 ms and does **not** cover one erase, while 2048 buys 1024 B = 267 ms, a little over three erases. The 512 figure the earlier notes carried was derived at 9600, where the same ring covered three erases; § 622 flagged the staleness and this is the change that spends it. Cost is 2 KiB of `.bss`, plus a 32-byte transmit ring — the only thing that ever leaves on this port is a 24-byte `pmreq_backup` frame or the single wake byte.

**Peripheral budget, claimed in the board crate rather than stolen at the call site.** `Board::split` takes `Peripherals` by value, so `main.rs` cannot grab them first and a `steal()` would put a peripheral claim outside the one crate whose documented job is peripheral assignment. `GpsPort` now carries TIMER2 + PPI channels 2/3 + PPI group 0; UARTE1's idle-line receiver keeps TIMER1 + PPI 0/1 ([§ 420](#420-the-settings-pipe-reads-to-the-idle-gap-nmea-cannot-and-its-fix-is-blocked-in-the-simulator)). Everything claimed sits outside the S140 SoftDevice's reservations — TIMER0, PPI channels 17-31, PPI groups 4-5 — and Embassy's time driver is on RTC1, so it spends no TIMER. TIMER3/TIMER4, PPI channels 4-16 and PPI groups 1-3 remain free. The board crate's header now states the whole budget in one place, because the next DMA-assisted peripheral will need to read it.

**§ 421's timer model was necessary and not sufficient, and the missing half was findable only by running it.** With the SHORTS-bearing timer in place the swap still delivered not one byte, and the guest then died at ~16 s of uptime. The cause is in the log rather than in the firmware:

```
[ERROR] ppi: Failed to register PPI from 0x40002108 for channel 2
[ERROR] ppi: Failed to register PPI from 0x40002110 for channel 3
```

`NRF52840_PPI` resolves an event endpoint by asking the system bus which peripheral owns the address written to EVENTP[n] and casting it to `INRFEventProvider`. Renode 1.16.1's `NRF52840_UART` (`renode-infrastructure @ add012af`) does not implement that interface, so **every** PPI channel sourced from a UARTE event is refused at configuration time. Both of `BufferedUarte`'s UARTE-sourced chains are exactly that: EVENTS_RXDRDY -> TIMER TASKS_COUNT, whose count *is* the ring's write index, and EVENTS_ENDRX -> TASKS_STARTRX, the hardware pre-arm the whole change exists for. With the counter frozen at 0 the reader sees an eternally empty ring. The same error is present in a run of unmodified `main`, for UARTE1 channel 0 — so § 420's hardware idle chain has never once fired under the simulator, and the software gap timeout it kept "as well" was in fact carrying it alone. `gps.rs`'s claim that "the sim's PPI, UARTE and TIMER models all implement the pieces it needs" was wrong when written.

`sim/NRF52840_UARTE_Events.cs` closes it, following the precedent § 421 set and with the same restraint: the delta is **upstream's own**. Renode master added `INRFEventProvider`, an `EventTriggered` event, and thirteen `EventTriggered?.Invoke(...)` calls beside the `SetInterrupt(...)` calls already there; nothing else in the file differs from v1.16.1. Retiring the model is a one-line `watch.resc` change the day the packaged Renode carries the interface itself.

**One second delta is a fix rather than a port, because the investigation tripped over a corruption bug.** v1.16.1 raises ENDRX when the RX byte count reaches RXD.MAXCNT but never disarms the receiver, so once the guest clears EVENTS_ENDRX the counter passes MAXCNT, the equality test never matches again, and `currentRxPointer` walks forward **without limit** — writing guest memory past the buffer the driver handed over for as long as bytes keep arriving. That is what killed the first attempt, and the way it presented is worth recording: `panicked at embassy-sync-0.8.0/src/watch.rs:172: RefCell already borrowed`, a corrupted borrow flag several kilobytes from any UART buffer, which is **the signature of issue #713** — the 1-in-30 mystery panic that twelve local reproduction attempts never caught. This does not establish that #713 *is* this bug: the plain `Uarte` path reads into a 32-byte stack buffer and the same walk-off would smash the stack, which fits, but nothing here measures that. It is a mechanism candidate with a reproduction, not a diagnosis. The model now clears `rxStarted` where ENDRX is raised — set before the event, so a PPI chain re-arms on top of it — which routes those bytes into the model's own existing receiver-disarmed path (dropped, with a warning) instead of out of bounds. Silicon does the same: the receiver stops at MAXCNT and loses bytes until STARTRX.

**What each rung actually proved, per [`quality_standards.md`](../custom_watch/quality_standards.md).** *Host-tested*: nothing new — the change is peripheral plumbing, and the parse / merge / cadence / power modules it feeds were already covered (the workspace suite passes unchanged). *Build-verified*: all three feature sets build and are clippy-clean on `thumbv7em-none-eabihf` — default, `--no-default-features --features ble`, and the sim set. *Sim-verified*: all nine Renode scenarios pass with the swap in, including the three that are actually about this code path — `smoke` (a fix parsed off the fixture, a run recorded, a blob committed), `dropout` (a 44 s fix void re-anchored rather than frozen), and `workout` (five step transitions over a ~150 s run, the longest continuous GPS drain any scenario asks for). One `workout` attempt failed before the bounded-DMA delta with the fix stream going silent at t = 7.0 s and no firmware panic and no UART warning in `renode.log`, i.e. nothing arriving at the emulated pin; it passed on re-run and passed again after the delta, so it is recorded as an unexplained flake rather than attributed. *Bench-verified*: **nothing**, and the item this change exists for stays open. Renode has no NVMC model at all, so the simulator cannot produce the 85 ms erase the ring is sized against — it proves the ring delivers NMEA, never that it survives a stall. `quality_standards.md`'s step-7 residual-stall item keeps its pass criterion unchanged: capture UARTE0 RX across a checkpoint boundary and count lost sentences. What changes is the prediction it is measured against — the expectation is now zero lost bytes rather than up to 326 — and the clause saying the fix is blocked on the simulator, which is no longer true.

## 699. A worker that must reach the npm registry to boot is a CI dependency nobody declared — and the obvious fix costs 10x the bundle, so it is applied only where a job's setup depends on it

**Decided (2026-08-19, issue #789 § G, PR #793.)** § 697 added forensics to the sidecar wait because three investigations had inferred a cause from the wait loop's own output. They fired on the next run and named it: the edge runtime was serving, and the per-function **worker** was dying with `failed to create the graph: Failed loading https://registry.npmjs.org/@types%2fnode for package "@types/node" … Network is unreachable`. esm.sh's default (denonext) build of supabase-js imports `node:buffer` / `node:process`, and the runtime resolves the **types** of a bare `node:` specifier from npm before a worker may boot. So every function carried an undeclared boot-time dependency on registry.npmjs.org, and when that fetch failed the probe hung to its timeout and the job died in setup with no test run. `os error 101` is a routing failure rather than a refusal, which is why it presented as intermittent.

**The fix was chosen against a reproduction, not a hypothesis, and the first hypothesis was wrong.** `edge-runtime start --main-service` under `--add-host registry.npmjs.org:127.0.0.1` reproduces the CI error byte for byte outside CI, and that harness graded every candidate: `?no-dts` still fails (it is the specifier, not the declarations — the entry that guessed "pin the imports so no npm type reference enters the graph" had the mechanism backwards); the latest released edge-runtime images, v1.73.15 and v1.74.3, still fail, so a CLI bump buys nothing; an import map redirecting `npm:@types/node` to a local stub is not consulted, because the dependency is injected rather than written. Only `?target=deno` boots offline, and **a type-only import is enough to re-arm the failure** — leaving `_shared/rate_limit.ts`'s `import type { SupabaseClient }` at the default keeps clip-public-track un-bootable by itself, which is worth knowing because an `import type` is erased at emit and reads as free.

**It is applied to two files rather than twenty-one, and the reason is a measured cost.** `?target=deno` has no `node:` specifiers because it swaps them for esm.sh's `deno.land/std@0.177.1` node polyfill tree, which takes one function's eszip from **228 KB to 2.4 MB** (`edge-runtime bundle`, same entrypoint, both targets). Paying that on all seventeen non-stripe functions would slow every cold worker boot in every e2e shard to convert a test-time failure that names itself into a marginally earlier one, and it would trade a dependency on npmjs for 150 requests to deno.land, which is in maintenance mode. So the change covers exactly the load-bearing path — `clip-public-track`, whose 405 every stack-using job's setup polls, plus the shared type import that re-arms it — and the four stripe functions are left as they are, because stripe's own SDK imports `node:http` and **no esm.sh parameter can reach that**. The residue is therefore stated rather than closed: an npm outage can still fail a test that calls one of those functions, but it can no longer kill a job before a test runs. Closing it needs a pre-seeded runtime module cache, which is a different piece of work.

The guard is `_shared/offline_worker_boot_guard.test.ts`, and it pins the property rather than the string: both probe-path imports must carry `?target=deno`, with the reason in the failure message, because the next person to tidy a query parameter off an import URL will not otherwise know they have re-armed a setup flake that three rounds failed to diagnose.
## 700. The two invariants a template sync can break while every check stays green are guarded in tests, because passing CI is not evidence that a re-add is safe

**Decided (2026-08-19, prompted by PR #794.)** A `templates`-repo sync proposed 21 files into this repo, additive by path and therefore blind to what it collided with by *name*. Three of them were regressions, and the two classes are worth guarding rather than re-catching by review, because both fail in the one direction review is worst at: green.

**A second emitter of the required check.** The sync re-added `ci-gate-docs.yml`, which [§ 577](https://github.com/Absence0760/project-running/pull/577) had deleted. The required status check on `main` is a job *named* `CI gate`, and GitHub does not require every check sharing that name to pass: on #457 the PR read `mergeStateStatus = UNSTABLE` — mergeable — with `CI gate = success` published by a workflow that passes trivially in ~2 s, while 40 real checks were still queued. Since this repo asks for a docs update with nearly every change, most PRs pass through that window. The re-added file's own header still asserted the assumption #457 disproved ("both emit a CI gate check and GitHub requires all of them green"), and its stated premise was stale twice over: `ci.yml` no longer carries a docs `paths-ignore`, having been made the sole emitter with its heavy jobs skipping instead. Worth noting how well-camouflaged the re-add was — the file had been rewritten to satisfy the existing base-branch workflow guard, so it would have gone green on exactly the suite that exists to catch workflow mistakes.

**Two files, one agent name.** The same sync added `.claude/agents/repo-security-auditor.md` and `.claude/agents/compliance-auditor.md` while this repo already carried both under `.claude/agents/auditors/`. A subagent resolves by its frontmatter `name:`, so those are two definitions of one agent with no rule saying which answers, and the incoming pair described a *different application* — a `<CMS>` webhook HMAC, `backend/src/routes/cms-webhook.ts`, an `orders-store` PII table on DynamoDB, "static site, no SSR" — none of which exists here, while dropping the `Write` tool the `/audit/*` commands need to persist findings to `reviews/`. A confidently wrong auditor is worse than a missing one: it reports against paths the repo does not have, and the reader has no reason to doubt it.

Both guards are mutation-checked against the actual files from #794 rather than against a hand-written imitation, and each failure message names the offending paths and the incident behind the rule. The upstream half — teaching the sync script that a file a project deleted on purpose should not be re-proposed — belongs to the `templates` repo; these guards are what does not depend on that repo behaving, which matters because `ci-gate-docs.yml` has now been synced in, removed, and synced in again.

**Amended same day — the upstream half landed, and it was bigger than the sync script.** `templates` now reads a `.github/template-sync-ignore` from each target repo, so a decline travels with the code it protects rather than living in a hardcoded list in that repo (the list `sync-projects.sh` used to carry had emptied itself, which is why every project drifted for months before #794 arrived at all). This repo's file records the three rejected classes and why. But the deeper fault was not the script: `base` was *shipping* `ci-gate-docs.yml` and `docs/USING.md` was *prescribing* the two-emitter pattern as the estate design, so the sync was faithfully propagating a documented mistake. Base no longer ships it, and USING.md now prescribes the shape this repo converged on — no `paths-ignore`, a `changes` job the heavy jobs gate on, skipped-counts-as-passing carrying the docs-only case. Two sibling repos in the estate still carry the pair and therefore the #457 window; migrating them means editing their own `ci.yml`, so it is tracked there rather than here.


## 701. The mobile runners-nearby surface is built whole behind its own fail-closed dotenv gate, and the gate is forwarded as a dart-define so the deploy flip is actually possible

**Decided (2026-08-21, issue #789 I.3.)** § 270 shipped opt-in coarse-location discovery complete on the backend and on web, behind the default-off `PUBLIC_ENABLE_NEARBY_RUNNERS`, and explicitly deferred the mobile client UI. That deferral is what a compliance gate is not allowed to buy: the sign-off reviewers need shipped code on `main` to evaluate, and "mobile UI unbuilt" plus "flag flip needs counsel" reads as one blocker when it is two. So the phone half is built now — the nearby list on `people_screen.dart` (coarse bucket label per row, follow toggle, its own empty / loading / retry states, suppressed while a search is active exactly as `SocialPeople.svelte` is), the `discoverable_nearby` switch in the Settings privacy group, and `nearby_area_screen.dart` for the coarse area — and every one of them is inert until the flag is on.

**The gate is a per-surface `dotenv` parse, matching the two mobile gates that came before it** (`OFF_ROUTE_ESCALATION_ENABLED`, `ADAPTIVE_FITNESS_GATE`) rather than the shared `core/env_flag.ts` web routes every `PUBLIC_*` flag through. `nearby_flag.dart` accepts the same affirmatives web's `isTruthyFlagValue` accepts (`1` / `true` / `yes` / `on`, trimmed, case-insensitive) and reads OFF for everything else including a throw from an uninitialised dotenv. It is deliberately a **new file rather than a function added to `nearby.dart`**: `nearby` is a registered parity pair whose web twin carries no flag, so putting the parse there would have registered a divergence the syncer must then report forever. The cost is a fourth inline copy of one four-value predicate on mobile, filed in `followups.md` — consolidating it means moving the parse out of two *other* registered pairs whose web twins also hold private copies, which is a matched cross-platform change, not a mobile extraction.

**The load-bearing detail is that `main.dart` now forwards the define.** Mobile builds env from a fixed `String.fromEnvironment` list merged into `dotenv`, and release builds never read `.env.development` (the §13 secret-leak guard). A flag absent from that list is therefore readable in debug and **unreachable in production** — which is how the two pre-existing gates shipped, so neither could ever have been turned on in a release build. `ENABLE_NEARBY_RUNNERS` is in the list, and `nearby_flag_test.dart` asserts both halves of the forwarding by parsing `main.dart`, because a gate that cannot be opened is not a gate, it is a deletion with extra steps.

**Two deliberate departures from the web surface.** The area setter is a **place-search picker**, not web's geocode-the-top-hit: the runner is publishing this, and confirming which "Richmond" they meant is the difference between an area they chose and one guessed for them — and mobile's `searchPlaces` already distinguishes a provider that is down from a place that does not exist, a distinction the picker renders and a single-hit geocode cannot. And "Forget my area" is confirmed through `confirmDestructive` before it clears, where web clears on one click; the row also disappears entirely when no area is set, so there is never a destructive affordance for data that is not there. What is *not* different: distances are only ever the shared bucket bounds from the `nearby` pair, formatted in the reader's own unit, and no surface renders metres or a map pin at a person's position.

The flag flip — web and mobile together — stays the owner + CISO/counsel pre-deploy item it was, tracked in `followups.md` as a deploy step rather than as blocked-on-legal code.
## 702. The watchOS in-run mini-map draws itself in `Canvas` with no basemap at all — a map that cannot load its tiles is worse on a wrist than a map that never promised them

`parity.md` held "live position marker on planned route" at `Partial` for one reason: Wear OS shipped `ui/RouteMiniMap.kt` and watchOS consumed `RouteNavigator` as text only. The gap is now closed by `WatchApp/RunMiniMapView.swift` over the pure `WatchApp/MiniMap.swift`, and two choices in it are worth recording because both went the other way from the obvious one.

**MapKit was considered and refused.** `Map` is available on watchOS 10 and would have given a real basemap for a few lines of SwiftUI. But the watch app's whole reason to exist is the standalone workout — GPS on the wrist with the phone in a drop bag or absent entirely — and MapKit's tiles come over the network, through the paired phone, with no cache this app controls and no offline mode to fall back to. On the run this feature is for (a multi-hour effort out of signal) MapKit renders a grey grid with a dot on it, which is not an absent map but a *broken* one: the runner cannot tell "no tiles" from "no fix" from "app is wedged". A vector basemap also runs a continuous render loop and a tile pipeline for a view that shows a polyline. So the map is drawn directly — `Canvas`, two `Path` strokes and three circles, recomputed only when the recorder publishes a new fix (~1 Hz, the cadence the elapsed-time label already redraws at, so it adds no wakeups). The Wear sibling reached the same shape from the opposite direction: it draws its polyline in Compose `Canvas` and layers raster tiles *underneath only when a MapTiler key is present*, so the tile-less rendering is the behaviour both watches share, not a watchOS shortcut.

**The frame is a local planar metre frame, not Web Mercator.** Wear projects through `MercatorTiles` because its polyline has to line up with 256-px raster tiles at integer zooms. With no tiles there is nothing to line up with, and Mercator's integer-zoom quantisation actively costs a fit (the polyline accepts slack at the bounds to stay tile-aligned). A continuous metres-per-point scale fits the track exactly, and it is the frame `RouteGeometry`, the firmware's breadcrumb and every other local projection in this codebase already use. East-west deltas go through a folded `longitudeDeltaDegrees` (`geo::lon_delta_deg`'s lesson, § 463/§ 468) and longitudes are unwrapped onto the first point's side of the line before the bounds are taken, so a track straddling the antimeridian frames as a few hundred metres rather than as most of the world.

**The map keeps its own trail, because the recorder's cannot be drawn.** `WorkoutManager.track` is a 600-fix rolling window (§ 467) — by design it no longer holds the start of a long run — and materialising the full track is exactly the ~360k-point array that window exists to prevent. So `MiniMapTrail` is a second, far cheaper representation: a fix is admitted once it is 20 m from the last kept one, capacity is 96 points, and on overflow the trail *halves and the spacing doubles*, so the whole run stays represented at coarsening resolution at flat memory for as long as the run lasts. The halving is the firmware's `route_simplify::simplify_to_budget` ported to Swift rather than index parity, for the reason `trackback` records: parity thinning is blind to shape and can delete the apex of a switchback, replacing it with a straight chord across the terrain the switchbacks exist to avoid — on exactly the surface a lost runner is looking at. Both endpoints always survive, so the start of the run is anchored.

**Every honesty case fails to "I don't know" rather than to a plausible default.** `MiniMapContent.make` returns nil when there is no route, no track and no fix, and the view says "Waiting for GPS"; a fix that is non-finite or out of range is treated as no fix at all, not as (0, 0), which would be a confident claim about the Gulf of Guinea drawn in the middle of the map. A near-degenerate span is floored at a 200 m ground width so a stationary runner's jitter is not stretched across the screen and read as movement. And the map lives on a *second page* of a paged `RunningView`: the elapsed clock, the stats and the Pause/Stop buttons keep the page and the positions they have always had, because an auxiliary L3 surface does not get to move a core control. The map reads published state and calls nothing back, so there is no path from anything it does into the L0 clock or the L1 distance.

Verification rung reached (`docs/custom_watch/quality_standards.md`): **build-verified + host-tested** — `xcodebuild test` green on the watchOS 26.4 simulator under Xcode 26.4, 203 tests. **Not device-verified**: nothing here has been looked at on a wrist, so the on-panel legibility check stays an open item in `followups.md`.
## 703. The Art 20 export streams into a chunked Storage upload, so its two caps are gone and the only bound left is the request clock

**Decided (2026-08-21, closing the `followups.md` "the export builds the whole archive in memory" item.)** `export-data` assembled the entire archive as one in-memory `Blob` and handed it to `storage.upload()`. Everything that looked like policy in that function was really a consequence of that one allocation: `MAX_RUNS = 5000`, and `EXPORT_ROW_CEILING = 50_000` per section. Both were honest in the manifest (`complete: false` + `incomplete`), which is the right thing to do about a bound you have — but neither is a data-minimisation decision. A cap that exists to keep an allocation alive is a data subject not receiving their data, and the arithmetic was worse than the cap suggested: 5,000 runs of gzipped track is on the order of a gigabyte, so the deepest histories were not being truncated at 5,000 runs, they were failing.

**The archive now streams.** `resumable_upload.ts` speaks tus 1.0 to Supabase Storage's `/storage/v1/upload/resumable`, buffering to the 6 MiB chunk the server requires and flushing. `zip.js`'s `ZipWriter` writes into that sink instead of a `BlobWriter` — legal only because zip.js emits a data descriptor per entry by default, so nothing ever has to seek back and patch a local header — and each section is a `ReadableStream` produced page by page (`stream_section.ts`), serialised into the archive and dropped. Peak memory is one chunk plus the `EXPORT_FETCH_CONCURRENCY` blob window, flat in the size of the history. Roughly 200 bytes per run is retained — the track / HR / photo keys the later object sweeps need — instead of the rows.

**Two details of the tus flow are load-bearing.** A deflate stream's length is not knowable when the upload opens, so creation uses `creation-defer-length` and the *final* PATCH declares the total; an archive that fits in one chunk skips the deferral entirely, because by then the length is known, which keeps the overwhelmingly common case on the plainest path the server offers. And because tus materialises the object only once the declared length arrives, the failure mode is exactly the one we want: any creation, chunk, offset-mismatch or build error aborts the session and answers 500 with **no object at all**. A truncated archive can never be signed and handed over as a complete one — which is a stronger guarantee than the old single-shot upload gave, where a short-but-successful build uploaded a short-but-real file.

**What survives is a real platform limit, and it is now explicit rather than proxied.** The function is killed at 150 s wall clock, and for `gpx` / `backup` the per-object Storage fetch dominates; no amount of streaming changes that. So the builders run against an `ExportBudget` (120 s of the 150, leaving the final chunk, the signed URL and the response un-cut). Every paged walk checks it between pages and every blob sweep checks it per object; a section it cuts short is named in `manifest.json`'s `incomplete` and folded into the response's `complete`, and a section *opened* past the deadline is shed outright rather than half-read — spending a dying request's last seconds on a `count=exact` query whose rows will never be written buys nothing. A per-object download failure stays tolerated by contract, as before: the line is between a systematic shortfall, which is reported, and one dead blob, which is not.

**The streaming rewrite surfaced a third cap, tighter than either documented one, and it needed its own bucket.** Both rails wrote the artifact to the `runs` Storage bucket, whose `file_size_limit` is 25 MB (`20260620_001` — the right cap for what else is in there, a single gzipped track). A gzipped track is ~0.2–1 MB and the `backup` format archives every one verbatim, so the real ceiling on a full-history export was on the order of *tens* of runs, not five thousand. storage-api enforces `file_size_limit` for `service_role` too, so it was not bypassable from the server, and it surfaced as a failed upload — the subject got an error, not a short archive. Removing `MAX_RUNS` without moving the artifact would have been meaningless. `file_size_limit` is per bucket, not per prefix, so migration `20270602_001` gives exports their own: 5 GiB, `text/csv` + `application/zip`, and **no `storage.objects` policies at all** — `20260816_001` had deliberately carved `exports/` out of the owner-folder SELECT on `runs` so an export is reachable through its 10-minute signed URL and nothing else, and `service_role` (the only reader and writer) is RLS-exempt, so zero policies is both the tightest expression and the one that preserves that earlier decision. Two things had to move with it or they would have become gaps rather than stayed invariants: `delete-account` now drains `exports` in the same fail-closed mandatory loop (an Art 17 erasure gap here would leave a complete copy of the subject's history behind, the worst possible one), and `cleanup_stale_export_blobs` now sweeps both the new bucket and the legacy prefix (an Art 20 artifact outliving its 10-minute URL forever is exactly what that cron exists to prevent). One bound is still not expressible in SQL and is a pre-deploy operator step: Supabase enforces a *project*-level upload limit (50 MB by default), and the effective ceiling is the lower of the two — so until it is raised, the project setting is the export's honest bound.

**This is the Edge Function only, and that is the honest scope.** `export-data` is the deprecated rollback path; production traffic goes to the Go worker's `POST /v1/export`, which still buffers into a `bytes.Buffer` and therefore still carries `MaxRunsPerExport = 5000` and `exportRowCeiling`. The two constants are consequently **no longer in lockstep**, and the comments and `data-subject-rights.md` now say so per rail rather than pretending to one number. The Go rail is the better long-term home for an uncapped export precisely because it has no request clock — its own streaming pass (an `io.Pipe` into the same tus chunker, and ultimately an async `jobs` kind so no client connection is held open at all) is tracked as the remaining follow-up. Doing the EF first was not arbitrary: it is the rail whose memory ceiling is tightest, and the only one whose streaming boundary conditions can be tested offline, which is what `resumable_upload.test.ts` (16 cases, including a real zip round-tripped through a 64-byte chunk boundary) and `stream_section.test.ts` (16, including 120,000 rows through what used to be a 50,000-row ceiling) do.
**Two things only a real Storage stack could say, both found by CI and both fixed here.** The sink followed the create response's `Location` header verbatim. Storage sits behind a gateway that reports its *own* origin there — `http://kong:54321/...` on the local stack — which is not routable from the function container, so every export died with ECONNREFUSED on the first PATCH after a 201 create, and the function answered 500 with the archive already built. The unit suite could not have caught it: its fake answered `Location` on the origin it was called on, which is the one case that works. The path is the server's to assign and the origin is ours to keep, and the two Playwright data-rights journeys are what actually failed. Second, folding a failed section into `complete` made two *pre-existing* projection bugs visible for the first time, on **both** rails: `user_profiles` was asked for `bio` and `location` (which exist nowhere) plus `hr_zones`, `activity_default` and `privacy_default` (which live in the `user_settings.prefs` bag both rails export separately), so `profile.json` shipped as null; and `reports_against_me.json` asked for `resolved_at` where the column is `reviewed_at`. A PostgREST projection is a string, so a stale name is not a type error but a 400 that fails the whole read — and the export tolerates a failed section by design, so the subject silently received less than Art 15/20 requires and only a log line said so. An earlier audit had fixed exactly this failure mode on exactly this projection (a `birth_year` typo) and guarded that one *name*; five more were sitting beside it. So the guard is no longer a list of names: `backup_spec.test.ts` reads the generated row types — the schema's own account of what exists — and checks every backup projection and filter against them, which fails on any future stale column rather than on the ones we happened to think of.

## 704. A device-state toggle states the device's state, not merely the last figure it sent — the treadmill subtitle switches on `BleTreadmillStatus`

The run screen's treadmill-mode toggle shipped (2026-06-19) computing its subtitle from the belt speed: show the reconnecting hint while reconnecting, else show the speed if one is known, else show nothing. Three of `BleTreadmillStatus`'s five values therefore rendered identically to a fourth, healthy one. With the toggle **on** and the belt `disconnected`, `connectFailed`, or `connecting`, the card read "Treadmill mode" with the switch engaged and no subtitle at all — which is exactly what "connected, first sample pending" looks like. The drop banner is transient (6 s ceiling, `top_banner.dart`), so a runner who glanced away and back saw an engaged treadmill toggle while the headline distance was really coming from the GPS/pedometer path. The `connecting` arm was worse than blank: it fell through on a bare `break` with no `setState`, so the previous belt speed stayed painted as though the belt were still sending it.

The subtitle now switches on the status, and `connected` is the **only** arm that can format a speed. That ordering is the point: the status listener already nulls the speed on the three non-feeding transitions, but making the formatting structurally unreachable outside `connected` means a future edit that drops one of those null-outs still cannot present a stale belt figure as current. Two ARB keys carry the new states in all seven locales (`runTreadmillConnecting`, `runTreadmillNoBeltData`); `disconnected` and `connectFailed` share one line because the fact the runner needs is the same in both — the belt is not feeding and distance is coming from GPS — and the difference between "lost it" and "never reached it" is what the banner and the one-tap reconnect already say.

This is the same claim discipline `live_freshness` and `live_motion` apply to a spectator's view of a runner: a surface may not present an auxiliary source's last known value as its current value, and "no data" must not render as "data, fine". It is also the L4 contract read from the UI side — the layering rules say a belt failure must not break L1 distance, and it does not, but a failure the runner cannot see is still a failure that changes what the numbers mean.

The audit that found this was triggered by a **stale follow-up**: `followups.md` still listed the run-screen wiring as unbuilt two months after it landed, while `parity.md`, `roadmap.md` and `integrations.md` had all been flipped at landing. The pre-existing tests are why the gap survived: all three replicated the screen's wiring in unit tests ("mirror the screen's guard", a fake stream plus a hand-written listener) rather than driving the screen, so they would have stayed green through any screen-side regression — including this one — and one of them seeded its paired-belt precondition before the harness reset the mock store, so the pairing was wiped and the case asserted nothing. The twelve replacements drive the real `_toggleTreadmillMode` and the real status listener through `BleTreadmill`'s `@visibleForTesting` emit seams, which is what the seams were added for. Reverting either half of the fix fails them.

Hardware-in-the-loop verification against a real FTMS belt remains owed and is recorded as a device gate, not as unwritten code: nothing ships disabled, the belt is opt-in and off by default, and the decode is already pinned by 20 unit tests against known-good byte sequences.

## 705. The firmware's Rust channel is pinned to an exact version, because `-D warnings` on a floating toolchain makes every new lint a broken build on code nobody touched

`apps/custom_watch/rust-toolchain.toml` said `channel = "stable"`, and the firmware job runs clippy with `-D warnings` across three feature sets. Those two facts are fine separately and a time bomb together: clippy 1.98 added `chunks_exact_to_as_chunks`, and the next CI run failed on two call sites — a 16-bit UUID scan in `hr_source.rs` and the MAX30101 FIFO decode — that had been untouched for weeks. The PR that hit it was changing docs and an export function.

This is the same failure `FLUTTER_VERSION` is pinned against (§ 595): a zero-warning bar plus a floating toolchain means the toolchain vendor decides when the build breaks, and it breaks on whoever pushes next rather than on whoever chose to upgrade. So the channel is an exact `1.98.0`. Bumping it is now a deliberate commit that carries its own fallout, which is the only way a zero-warning bar stays honest.

The lint itself was worth taking: both sites read better as `as_chunks`, and the FIFO decode now hands `decode_sample` the `[u8; 3]` it already takes instead of re-indexing three bytes out of a slice. Worth recording *how* the second site was found, because it generalises — the CI log named exactly one, since clippy stops at the first crate that errors, so fixing what the log said would have failed the next run identically. Installing the pinned toolchain and reproducing locally is what surfaced the other one; a CI failure enumerates the first error, not the class.

## 706. `deno.lock`'s `workspace` section is regenerated by deno and guarded in CI — the half nothing resolves against is the half that kept drifting

**Decided 2026-08-19, landed 2026-08-24.** The committed `deno.lock` has two halves with very different standing. `remote` + `redirects` are 339 integrity pins plus 54 redirects across `deno.land` and `esm.sh`, written by the Supabase CLI inside its Docker container during `supabase db reset` / `functions serve`, and they are what the Edge Function tests resolve against. `workspace` is a transcription of every dependency spec in the npm workspace's `package.json` files; nothing resolves against it, and it exists only because the lockfile happens to sit at the root of an npm workspace, so deno records what it saw.

**Both halves move; only one of them ever needed a human.** The load-bearing half moves whenever an Edge Function's dependency graph changes — nine commits since the lock was committed, most recently `fc671f7a5` — and every one of those was the CLI writing it as a side effect of the backend change that caused it. The incidental half moves on every *web* dependency bump, which the CLI has no reason to run for, so it was hand-synced six separate times by six sessions who each had to work out what the file was first: `91889cfed`, `afa789f6f`, `b25c5f027`, `1a4c31456`, `f7fc65d4a`, `ff612631d`. Each of those six touched the `workspace` section and nothing else.

**Drift is not only "the lock is behind".** The re-sync that landed with this entry moved ten specs, nine of them ordinary bumps the lockfile side was never carried for — and one going the other way: the lock claimed `@types/node@^26.2.0` where `apps/web/package.json` had rolled back to `^26.1.2`. A hand-sync habit catches the direction people expect and misses the one they do not.

**Deno writes the section; the script only decides when.** It canonicalizes npm ranges on the way in, and only for `0.x`, where caret and tilde semantics coincide: `^0.45.8` reads back as `~0.45.8` and `^0.120.0` as `0.120`. That was established rather than assumed — a generator that copied `package.json` verbatim reproduced the `workspace` section of every in-sync commit *except* precisely those `0.x` ranges. So a hand-written transcription of `package.json` produces a file deno immediately rewrites, which is why `scripts/sync_deno_lock.mjs` shells out to deno instead of assembling JSON. Regeneration stages the `package.json` files and the lock in a temp directory and runs `deno check --no-remote --node-modules-dir=none` there: no network, no `node_modules`, no Docker, nothing to resolve but the workspace config — and, because several sessions share this checkout, nothing running against the real tree.

**It fails closed on the load-bearing half.** A regeneration that comes back with a changed `remote`/`redirects` refuses to write and says so, rather than quietly relocating a supply-chain pin: moving those is the Supabase CLI's business, and a lockfile sync that can also rewrite an integrity hash is a different and much more dangerous tool than the one this is meant to be.

**The guard lives in `parity-types`, not `edge-functions`.** It is a generated-artifact-matches-its-source check of the same kind as the `gen:types:check` that closes the same job, it costs about a second, and the two migration guards ahead of it already record why a cheap source-only check must not sit behind the Supabase stack start — a stack that fails first takes the signal with it. `edge-functions` owns deno otherwise, so the trade is one extra `setup-deno` step in a job that had none. Per § 711 the step carries its own `::error::`, since that job's name cannot say which of its six checks broke. Its two commands run in the reverse order of the migration guards beside it, and deliberately: those run their own suite first because a broken guard's verdict is worthless, but here the suite's last case *is* the drift check, so running it first would report "the tool is broken" over an ordinary stale lockfile. Checking drift first keeps both messages true — the second can only fire once the first has ruled drift out.

**The accepted cost is that a minor/patch npm Dependabot PR no longer auto-merges itself.** `dependabot-auto-merge.yml` queues those on the required checks, so a bump that touches `package.json` now waits for someone to run `pnpm sync:deno-lock` and push the result. That is deliberate and consistent with how twin parity already behaves here — the mobile `pub` entry has always needed a manual iOS mirror before merging — and a silent drift that a session rediscovers every few months is the worse of the two. One fragility is worth naming: the check compares against whatever deno version runs it, so if a future deno changes its range canonicalization the guard reports drift once, until the lock is re-synced with the newer deno.

**Alternatives rejected:** gitignoring the lock (it would discard the integrity pins and the `DENO_DIR` cache key with them), and deriving the section in JavaScript (wrong on every `0.x` range, as above). Having CI sync and push onto the Dependabot branch so auto-merge survives was rejected outright in § 711, not deferred: a `GITHUB_TOKEN`-authored push starts no workflow run, so `--auto` would wait forever for a `CI gate` context that can never appear, and the durable credential that would fix that also publishes GitHub Releases — which all three release workflows trigger on. § 711 also names the better direction if this is ever picked up again: ask whether deno records a `workspace` section at all when the lock does not sit at the workspace root, because a lockfile with no generated half needs neither this guard nor a bot.

## 707. Dead scaffolding is deleted rather than kept consistent, an unverified iOS row is `Partial` rather than `✗`, and an override count that shrinks is not the template's trigger

Three follow-ups left standing by § 663's round, resolving the same way: make one place say the true thing rather than keep several places disagreeing.

**`LocalSessionStore` is deleted.** It was never wired — not by the commit that introduced it, which added the store and the mobile follow-along runner together and gave `session_detail_screen.dart` no import to it, and not since; `sessions_screen.dart` has always read `fetchSessionPlans` straight from the server. Its only reference under `lib/` was the sign-out wipe registry. Four documents nevertheless said the runner was "backed by" it, inheriting the claim from that commit's own message. The general shape is worth naming: a commit message and a spec both asserting a screen is backed by a store are not evidence that the screen imports one, and the check is a single grep nobody ran for two months.

Whether to wire it up instead turns on the spec, and the spec answers no. `session_planner.md` does require offline building and an offline runner, but P2 and P3 have both shipped without it and P4's remainder (pose catalog, multi-week courses, wrist follow-along, AI sequencing) needs none of it — so the offline slice is design of record with nothing pulling on it, not imminent work. Wiring it would have been building that feature, which is a product decision on its own merits, and the store as written would not have survived the exercise anyway: `createLocal` mints a row with no `club_id`, a column the P3 club-template slice added after it. Carrying it was not free either — it was one of the eight `replaceFromServer` overrides § 663 had to gate, a row in the crash-atomic-write guard's hardcoded store list, a slot in the wipe registry, and a suite whose only subject was itself. Git holds the whole thing at `19e377e6`, which is what makes deletion the cheap direction and re-adding it against the schema of the day the offline slice is actually built the better one. `ApiClient.createSessionPlan` / `deleteSessionPlan` stay: a typed client's surface is its API rather than app code, roughly ten of its methods already have no mobile caller, and both are exercised by the package's own integration test.

**The `replaceResident(build)` template stays unbuilt, and the deletion is the reason.** The follow-up named its own trigger — reach for the template if a ninth store lands. Deleting one takes the count to seven, so the condition moved further away, not closer, and rewriting seven cache-fill paths that differ in signature and in how each reads `rowsById` while building would be spending the blast radius § 663 declined to spend, for less duplication than it declined to remove. The architecture guard's floor moves 8 → 7 in lockstep so it still enforces the invariant on every remaining override; the guard is what makes the duplication safe, and it is the part that must never be deleted.

**The iOS "Sync and backup" column is `Partial`, not `✗`, and the matrix was contradicting itself before the follow-up got to it.** The entry allowed that the column might be right and the twin might carry an untested path. It could not be right: `parity.md` marked "Backup ZIP restore (lossless)" iOS `✓` under Import while marking the whole Sync-and-backup block `✗`, for the same `BackupService` methods in the same byte-identical file, with the `✓` row's own note naming the Settings tile the `✗` rows implicitly denied. The code shows no iOS obstruction anywhere on the path: no `Platform` gate on the Full backup or Restore tile, on their handlers, on the containing section (its only condition is `runStore != null`), on the screen, or on the screen that pushes it; no method channel; `archive` is pure Dart and `file_picker` / `share_plus` / `path_provider` each declare iOS; `Info.plist` already carries the photo-library keys `file_picker` transitively forces, and a document picker and a share sheet need no entitlement. Even the background-sync row is wired both ways, `registerProcessingTask` against a declared `BGTaskSchedulerPermittedIdentifiers`. So `✗` ("not started") is false and `✓` ("shipped and working end-to-end") has never been observed; the rows take `Partial` with the notes idiom the matrix already uses for a wired-but-unverified iOS row, and the device run stays recorded once, on the single iOS-verification item, where the matrix says per-row tracking does not belong.

What that exercise also found and is deliberately **not** fixed here: `parity.md` is inconsistent about its own iOS convention — the top banner licenses `✓` to mean "wired but unverified on Mac hardware", while the column key and the intentional-asymmetries list both say cells stay `✗` / `Partial` until verified, and the column reads 134 `✓` / 39 `Partial` / 147 `✗` today. Picking one reading is a whole-column edit against a rule that has to be settled first, not a side effect of resolving two rows about one class. And one genuine iOS defect surfaced on the way: all nine `Share.shareXFiles` call sites omit `sharePositionOrigin` while the target is `TARGETED_DEVICE_FAMILY = "1,2"`, which share_plus documents as a crash or an unresponsive UI on iPad. It is filed rather than fixed here because it is a cross-cutting mobile fix, and it is exactly the class of thing the device run exists to catch — a matrix cell that says "wired" is not a cell that says "works".

## 708. The Go export rail streams too, so both its caps are gone — and what bounds it now is the artifact's Storage ceiling and the connection the caller is holding open, not a row count

**Decided (2026-08-24, closing the `followups.md` "the Go worker's `/v1/export` still buffers" item left by § 703.)** `POST /v1/export` is the rail production actually calls, and it assembled the whole archive in one `bytes.Buffer` before uploading it. Both of its bounds were consequences of that single allocation — `MaxRunsPerExport = 5000` and `exportRowCeiling = 50_000` per section — and both are now deleted rather than raised. Every section is read page by page and serialised into a chunked tus Storage upload as it arrives, the same sink and the same wire contract § 703 built on the Edge Function rail.

**The measurement is the argument.** Against 500 runs carrying 512 KiB tracks — 250 MiB of blob bytes archived verbatim, and a tenth of the deleted 5000-run cap — the buffered builder peaked at **521.6 MiB of heap** and the streaming one at **4.6 MiB** (plus the sink's fixed 6 MiB chunk, so ~11 MiB in production). The Fly machine has 256 MB. So the cap was never protecting a truncation: at a tenth of its own limit the old builder was already past the machine, which is the Go-side confirmation of what § 703 found on the function rail — the deepest histories were failing, not being shortened. On the row side, a 120,000-row history (the figure the EF's own streaming suite uses against the same deleted 50,000-row ceiling) peaks at 17.9 MiB and holds ~128 bytes per run, because what is retained per run is a run id plus two booleans for the track and HR sweeps, not the row. The Storage keys are derived rather than kept: the path-shape assertion has already proved they are exactly `{uid}/{id}.json.gz` and `{uid}/{id}.hr.json.gz`, so keeping the strings would be storing what the id already determines.

**No `io.Pipe`, and the follow-up's wording should not have implied one.** `archive/zip` writes into an `io.Writer` and always emits a data descriptor per entry, so it never seeks backwards and the chunker can simply *be* the writer. A pipe would add a goroutine, a `CloseWithError` protocol, and a second place for an error to be lost, and would buy nothing: `io.Pipe` is unbuffered, so it gives no producer/consumer overlap either. The zip writer calls `Write` on the sink, the sink fills a 6 MiB slice and PATCHes it. That is the whole mechanism.

**Fail-closed had to grow a new shape, because a new failure became possible.** On the buffered rail a mid-build failure happened before any byte reached Storage. Now chunks are already at the server when a section read dies, so every failure path — a page that would not read, a zip write, a rejected chunk, an offset the server disagrees with — aborts the tus session before the signing path, and tus materialises nothing until the declared length arrives. The observable outcome is identical to before (500, no artifact) and strictly better than the old single-shot upload, which would happily have stored a short-but-real archive and handed back a signed URL to it. One distinction is load-bearing and is a type rather than a convention: a failure raised by the *consumer* of a page walk is wrapped as an `emitError` and returned unwrapped to the handler, where a failure raised by the *read* of a per-table section stays tolerated and is recorded in `manifest.json`'s `incomplete`. Without it a dead upload would have been written into the archive's own manifest as "this table came up short", blaming the database for a write that never happened — and the walk would have carried on writing into an archive that no longer existed.

**The artifact had to move buckets or none of this would have meant anything.** This rail was still writing to `runs`, whose `file_size_limit` is 25 MB — on a full-history backup a far tighter ceiling than either row cap, enforced for `service_role` too, and § 703 had already moved the function rail off it. Both rails now write to `exports` (migration `20270602_001`, 5 GiB, no `storage.objects` policies) and mint the signed URL on the same bucket. The orphan sweep still skips the legacy `runs/{uid}/exports/` prefix, so an export still never archives a previous export.

**What actually bounds this rail now, stated plainly, because "uncapped" would be a lie.** There is no request clock — the worker is a long-lived Go process, not a 150 s function — so there is no `ExportBudget` equivalent to add and none was added. What remains is two real limits and neither is a row count. First, the **Storage object-size ceiling**: the bucket admits 5 GiB but Supabase's project-level upload limit (50 MB by default) is the lower of the two, so raising it stays the pre-deploy operator step § 703 recorded; past it the upload fails and the subject gets a 500 with no artifact, which is an error rather than a short archive. Second, the **client connection**, which the caller holds open for the entire build. That is the honest remaining bound and the reason the async `jobs` kind is the next piece rather than part of this one: moving the export to a queue changes the client contract from "hold the connection, get a URL" to "poll a job", which is web and mobile work — a new job kind, a status surface, a delivery mechanism for the finished URL — and none of it is server-side streaming. Doing it inside this change would have coupled a memory fix that ships today to a UI change that does not. A third bound worth naming because it is invisible in the code: each individual HTTP request is capped by the shared client's 30 s timeout, which for a 6 MiB chunk is a floor of ~1.6 Mbit/s — comfortable between Fly `ord` and Supabase `us-east-1`, but it is a per-request bound, not a per-export one.

**One client-visible change, and it makes the response agree with the archive.** The response's `complete` used to fold in the runs walk alone, so a `backup` export whose `food_log` section came up short answered `complete: true` while its own `manifest.json` said otherwise. It now folds in every section, matching the Edge Function. Both clients already gate their truncation notice on an explicit `complete: false` (§ 643) and neither needed a change; what they gain is a disclosure that was previously suppressed.

**Guards, because every one of these invariants would regress silently.** `wiring_test.go` greps the source the way the EF's does: no `bytes.Buffer` in the builders, no cap constant back in either package, no collecting pager, the abort ordered before the signing path, the full personal-data entry set still wired, `manifest.json` still the last entry written, the path-shape assertions still gating the downloader, and the artifact still landing in `exports`. Beside them sit the behavioural ones: a real zip round-tripped through a 64-byte chunk boundary and reopened, a 120,000-row history streamed whole with the biggest page the builder ever sees pinned at one PostgREST page, a mid-stream chunk failure leaving no artifact and no recorded upload, an offset mismatch aborting rather than splicing, and — the one a buffered implementation would fail and every content assertion would pass — bytes having reached the sink before the walk that produces them has ended.

## 709. One fail-closed flag parser per platform, and a gate is only a gate if a release build can read it

**Decided (2026-08-24, issue #789 R10.)** Eight modules across the two clients each spelled out the same four-value predicate — `1` / `true` / `yes` / `on`, trimmed and case-insensitive, everything else off. Web had a canonical `core/env_flag.ts#isTruthyFlagValue` that three of its own gates did not use (`off_route_alert.ts`, `cycle_plan_flag.ts`, `weigh_in_flag.ts`); mobile had no canonical one at all and four copies (`nearby_flag.dart`, `off_route_alert.dart`, `plan_adaptive_replan.dart`, and `checkpoint_checkin_screen.dart`'s `_weighInGate`). § 701 filed the mobile half as a followup and named the reason it could not be fixed there and then: two of the copies sit inside *registered parity pairs* whose web twins held their own copies, so extracting on one platform would have registered a divergence in two pairs at once.

**The accepted set is now one contract, not a convention.** `apps/mobile_android/lib/env_flag.dart#isTruthyFlagValue` is the Dart twin of the web function, registered as a parity pair in both registries (§ 604), and every gate on both platforms delegates to it. The two flags whose parser lives inside another pair keep their named function — `offRouteEscalationEnabled`, `adaptiveFitnessGateEnabled` — and delegate, on both sides symmetrically, which is the same re-export shape `auth_gates` uses for the password floor: the feature keeps owning its flag, the parse has one home, and neither pair's export surface or test count moves. Each suite carries a source guard that no other module may spell the set out, because the copies were not added maliciously — each was written by copying the gate next to it, which is precisely what a guard catches and a doc comment does not (§ 305 is the same lesson one level up).

**The narrowest copy was a live defect.** `_weighInGate` accepted `1` and `true` only. An operator who set `WEIGH_IN_GATE=yes` — an affirmative every other gate on both platforms honours — got a checkpoint screen that silently never collected the Art 9 weigh-in fields, with no error and nothing in the UI to say the flag had been read and rejected. A widget test now pins that `yes` opens the weigh-in sheet and that an unrecognised value does not; it fails against the old parse.

**The second half is worse, and § 701 called it while fixing only its own flag.** Mobile builds its env from a fixed `String.fromEnvironment` list merged into `dotenv`, and release builds never load `.env.development` (the § 13 secret-leak guard, § 137 for the file convention). A key absent from that list is readable in debug and **unreachable in production**. `OFF_ROUTE_ESCALATION_ENABLED`, `ADAPTIVE_FITNESS_GATE` and `WEIGH_IN_GATE` were all absent: all three are documented as "flipping the flag on for a prod build IS the sign-off-gated action" (§ 144, § 150), and none of the three could have been flipped by any deploy configuration. The audit found two more keys in the same state — `USDA_FDC_API_KEY`, so the second food-search source was dead in every shipped build, and `TILE_URL_TEMPLATE`, the § 68 override that is also the wire for a self-hosted-tiles migration. All five are bridged now.

**A per-flag assertion would have kept missing this, so the guard is a scan.** `nearby_flag_test.dart` already pinned that *its* flag was forwarded, and that test passed the whole time the other three were not. `env_flag_test.dart` instead collects every `dotenv.env[...]` read under `lib/` — resolving a file-local const key, and an accessor's literal call sites — and fails when any of them is missing from the bridge. It refuses to pass over a read it cannot resolve, because a scan that quietly skips what it does not understand is the failure mode it exists to prevent.

**Whether a release *workflow* passes a define stays a separate, deploy-time decision.** The bridge makes the flip possible; the sign-off is what makes it happen. `release-android.yml` still passes none of the four gated flags, and `apps/mobile_android/deployment.md` now lists them with what each unlocks rather than describing them as dev-only, which is what they had accidentally become.

**One deliberate exception, left alone.** Web's `PUBLIC_BYPASS_PAYWALL` is compared against the literal string `'true'` in `settings/features.ts` and pinned there by `security_guards.test.ts`. That is not a copy of this predicate — it is a deliberately narrower one on the only flag that *removes* a restriction rather than adding a capability, and widening it to accept `yes` would be a strict loss. It is not a `*_flag.ts` module, so the routing guard does not claim it.

## 710. An embedded mobile surface opens a Settings sub-screen by NAMING it, not by acquiring its dependencies

Every settings screen takes some slice of `Preferences` + `SettingsSyncService` + `ApiClient` + the two BLE handles, and the surfaces that most want to link into Settings are exactly the ones holding none of that. The People tab's runners-nearby list is the case that forced it: the opt-in switch and the area setter both live on `SettingsPreferencesScreen`, and `PeopleScreen` is embedded in `SocialScreen`, which was handed a social service, a training service and a route store. So the empty state recited the path in prose — "Settings → Preferences → Privacy" — where web's empty card has always carried an ordinary link to `/settings/preferences`.

Threading `Preferences` and `SettingsSyncService` down through `SocialScreen` would have worked once. It is the wrong shape for a second reason each time: it makes an intermediate host carry dependencies it has no other use for, and the next surface that wants a Settings link is a different intermediate host with a different set to thread. `IntensityCard` is the proof it generalises — it shows the same age-estimated-max-HR caveat run-detail shows, with the same copy, and could not carry run-detail's "Set max HR" button because it holds only a `SettingsSyncService` while the screen also wants a `Preferences` and an `ApiClient`. The same advice was actionable on one surface and inert on the other, for no reason a reader could see.

So `settings_destination.dart` names the destinations (`SettingsDestination`) and parks an intent (`openSettings`) that `HomeScreen` drains — the shell being the one place in the tree that already holds every dependency the settings screens take. This is not a new mechanism: it is the handoff shape `pendingPushTarget`, `pendingStartRunWithRoute` and `pendingStartWorkout` already use in `main.dart`, for the same reason each of them gives (§ 490's note that every entry path routes through the same shell). It lives in its own file rather than in `main.dart` so a leaf surface can depend on the seam without importing the app's entrypoint, mirroring `shared_file_import.dart`'s `incomingRouteImport`.

Three details are contract, not incident.
