The shell drains on its first frame as well as on the notifier, so an intent parked before any `Navigator` existed is honoured rather than dropped — and, just as importantly, a slot left full would silently swallow the next identical request, since a `ValueNotifier` is quiet on an unchanged value. The push lands on top of the current tab rather than switching to You first: a runner sent to Preferences from the nearby list wants one Back to return to the list they were reading, not to be relocated into Settings. And only the *pushable* sub-screens are destinations — the Settings landing is embedded in the You tab rather than pushed, so "open Settings" is a tab switch with different back-stack semantics and no caller has asked for it.

Two candidate conversions were deliberately refused. `run_detail_screen.dart`'s existing "Set max HR" button already holds the dependencies for its own reads, and its direct `Navigator.push` works whether or not a shell is above it — routing it through the seam would trade a working button for one that depends on the shell being mounted. The nutrition screens' `_openBodyMetrics` **awaits the pushed route and refreshes on return**; a parked intent is fire-and-forget and cannot report a pop, so converting them would quietly drop a refresh. A fire-and-forget seam is the right instrument only where the caller has nothing to do afterwards.

## 711. A CI diagnosis may only speak for the step that produced it, a commented-out action pin is not dead code, and the Dependabot lockfile sync is refused rather than automated

Three CI follow-ups closed in one round. The first two share a root cause — a confident sentence asserted from a place that could not know whether it was true — and the third is a refusal to buy a small weekly convenience with a standing repository-write credential.

**A step's `failure()` condition cannot name the step that failed, so a diagnosis printed from one speaks for every step above it.** `parity-types` ended in a bare `- if: failure()` step printing "apps/web/src/lib/database.types.ts is out of sync with the Supabase schema" and "Run 'npm run gen:types' locally and commit the result." The job runs five unrelated checks before the one that message describes, so a web source-guard failure five steps up printed it, and the first look went to the migration and the generated types — neither of which was involved. Same class as the stack-start wait loop's "within 90s" (§ 697): a message confident about something it did not observe is worse than no message, because it redirects the search rather than merely failing to help it.

Each check now carries its own `::error::` and its own remediation, in the `if ! cmd; then echo "::error::…"; exit 1; fi` form `twin-parity` and `schema-codegen-drift` were already using, and the trailing step is deleted. Two smaller corrections came with it. The two migration guards now run **their own unit suites first**: a guard whose tests fail has no verdict worth reporting, so "the version-key guard is broken" is strictly more useful than whatever that broken guard concluded about the migration set. And the job is renamed `Schema / type drift + web unit tests`, because "Schema / type drift" was a false description of a job that also runs the entire web TypeScript unit suite — half of the misdirection was in the job name, before any step ran.

**Splitting the job was the alternative, and it was rejected on runner budget rather than on principle.** Splitting is the only change that makes the job *name* answer "which check broke", and it would also decouple two things that are serially coupled today: a unit-test failure currently stops the drift check from running at all, so a PR with both problems costs two round trips. Against that, a second job means a second `checkout` + `setup-node` + `npm ci` and a 26th entry in the `CI gate` aggregator's `needs:` list, on every PR, out of the same hosted-runner budget the concurrency block above already rations at ~19 jobs and 85–90 minutes a run. An `::error::` annotation renders on the checks summary without opening a log, which is most of the benefit at none of the cost, so per-step diagnosis won. Revisit if the serial coupling ever costs more than a runner slot.

**The guard is over the shape of the bug, not over the one instance of it.** `scripts/check_ci_diagnostics.mjs`, in `workflow-lint`, fails the build when any `failure()`-conditioned step in any workflow prints an `::error::` without its condition naming a step outcome, and when a named `run:` step is added to a registered bundled job with no diagnosis of its own. The first half is deliberately about *claims* and not about running on failure: the eight remaining `if: failure()` steps stage sim logs and upload Playwright reports, which assert nothing about which step failed and are untouched. Run against the pre-fix file it reports the defect five ways — the trailing step plus the four checks that had nothing of their own to say.

**A commented-out action reference is not dead code. It is what someone uncomments on the day they are trying to ship, which is the worst possible day to discover the pin.** `apple-actions/upload-testflight-build@v1` was the repo's only tag-pinned action, inside release-ios.yml's commented TestFlight block, and the pin sweep that moved every live reference to a SHA recorded it as "dead code, which is why it was left rather than SHA-pinned". Being unread is what let it drift, not what made it safe.

**It is pinned to v5.3.0, not to v1.** `@v1` resolves to a 2020 commit whose `action.yml` declares `runs.using: node12`, a runtime GitHub has removed — so SHA-pinning that tag verbatim would have frozen a reference that cannot execute at all, which is a different landmine in the same hole. v5 takes the same five inputs the commented step passes (`app-type` still defaults to `ios`) and adds only optional ones. Two details from resolving it are now in the convention because they generalise: the floating `v5` tag is itself stale against the newest v5 release (2026-05-14 versus v5.3.0's 2026-08-10, upstream simply did not move it), and `v5.3.0` is an *annotated* tag whose own object hash is not a commit — pinning what `git/ref/tags/v5.3.0` returns without dereferencing produces a ref that resolves to nothing.

**Nothing enforced the SHA rule, which is why one reference outlived the sweep that applied it.** conventions.md has stated it for a long time, but a one-time audit is not a guard. `check_toolchain_pins.mjs` grows a fourth check — the same file, because the ADR that closed the pin sweep already grouped actions with the toolchains — over every `uses:` in `.github/workflows` **and** in `.github/actions/*/action.yml`, and it reads **commented lines**. Skipping comments would have re-created exactly the blind spot the check exists to close. The composite-action half matters for the same reason the § 595 Flutter pin is declared three times: Dependabot's github-actions ecosystem scans `.github/workflows` plus a *root* `action.yml` and nothing else, so a reference inside a composite action gets neither a pin guard nor an update PR. The check also requires the trailing `# vN` comment that makes a 40-hex pin reviewable, which caught four bare `actions/checkout` lines. 150 references pass; the pre-fix file fails on exactly one.

**The third item is refused rather than built, and the refusal is recorded here because the reasoning outlives the specific proposal.** The proposal, whose enabling work lands separately and is not on this base: `deno.lock`'s `workspace` section is generated from the npm workspace's `package.json` files, a guard in `parity-types` is to start failing the build when it drifts, and Dependabot cannot regenerate it — so every weekly minor/patch npm PR would go red and stop auto-merging until a human regenerates the section and pushes. The proposed close is CI doing that sync itself and committing onto the Dependabot branch. The blocker was framed as "`dependabot-auto-merge.yml` runs with a read-only token today". That is true and is not the binding constraint; four separate things are wrong with the automation, and none of them depends on how the regeneration is implemented.

- **Granting write does not make it work.** A push authenticated with `GITHUB_TOKEN` does not start a new workflow run — GitHub's documented loop prevention, and the only reason a bot commit cannot re-trigger itself. So the sync commit would move the PR's head SHA to a commit that *no* CI run ever reports on, and `gh pr merge --auto` would wait forever for a required `CI gate` context that can never appear. The automation is not merely unauthorised with the safe token; it is inoperative with it.
- **The standard safe `pull_request_target` recipe does not apply here.** That recipe is "check out the base ref only, never the head". It works when the elevated job's work is independent of the PR's contents. Here the PR's changed `package.json` **is** the input — regenerating from the base reproduces what is already committed, a no-op — so any working design reads head content in a job holding write credentials. That reading can be made defensible: staging the `package.json` files into a temp directory and resolving them with no network, no `node_modules` and no install step executes nothing the PR authored. But a regenerator written for a trusted checkout will not have been written to that standard, and the one drafted for this task is not — it joins each workspace member path declared in the PR's own root `package.json` onto the checkout root having filtered only for `*` globs, so a member path containing `..` reads outside the tree. Small in isolation, and the point is not that one bug: it is that a trusted-input tool has to be re-audited as an untrusted-input tool before a credential is pointed at it, which is work the proposal did not account for.
- **Making it work means a long-lived `contents: write` credential, and in this repo that reaches production.** A PAT or GitHub App token is the only way a push re-triggers CI. `contents: write` is also what publishes a GitHub Release, and all three release workflows — `release-web.yml`, `release-backend.yml`, `release-ios.yml` — trigger on `release: [published]`, not on tag push, so that one permission deploys the web stack and applies Supabase migrations against production. Branch protection blocks a direct push to `main` even for admins; it does not block publishing a release. The existing auto-merge job holds `contents: write` today, but on an ephemeral `GITHUB_TOKEN` and over a job that never reads PR content; storing a durable token and pointing it at bot-branch content is a different object.
- **The one `GITHUB_TOKEN`-only path degrades the property the CI gate exists to have.** Workflows started by `workflow_dispatch` are the documented exception to loop prevention, so the sync job could give `ci.yml` a dispatch trigger and fire it at the branch. That makes the required `CI gate` context satisfiable by something other than a real `pull_request` run — the same shape as the two-emitter hazard § 577 removed, where a check with the right name and the wrong provenance reported green while the real jobs were queued. It also runs 25 jobs down `github.event_name` branches that neither the `changes` filter nor the concurrency group was written for.

Against all of that, the thing bought is one regeneration command plus a commit and a push, on the weekly npm dependency PR, for a chore that already collapses to a single command. Landing an unsafe workflow to save it would be a strictly worse outcome than the manual step, and so would landing a safe-looking one that hangs. **If this is picked up again, remove the class rather than automate it**: that `workspace` section exists only because the lockfile sits at the root of an npm workspace and nothing resolves against it, so the question worth answering first is whether deno records the section at all when the lock does not sit there — a lockfile with no generated half cannot drift, needs no guard, and needs no bot.

## 712. The spectator's "Elapsed" was two quantities under one label — the race clock is stated from `started_at`, and the runner's own timer keeps its own tile

The open follow-up framed this as a single-stat problem: the `/live/[id]`
stat strip renders the last ping's `elapsed_s`, which freezes the moment
the pings do, so a crew doing cut-off arithmetic during an 18-hour dead
zone on a 240-mile race reads a number 18 hours short. Advancing the
displayed figure by wall clock was rejected because `elapsed` excludes
paused time and advancing it would overstate a runner who paused. Both
answers are wrong for the same reason: **one tile was being asked for two
different quantities.**

- The **race clock** is wall-clock time since the runner started. A
  cut-off is a deadline measured from the start — that is [§ 601](#601-a-cut-off-clock-keeps-running-when-the-pings-stop-and-a-deadline-that-has-passed-is-stated-rather-than-left-behind-signal-lost)'s own
  reasoning for `liveElapsedS` — and it does not pause because a phone
  lost a tower.
- The **runner's timer** is `elapsed_s`: the recorder's stopwatch as of
  the last fix.

The race clock needs no estimate, because **the start instant is already
available to an anonymous spectator**. `beginLiveBroadcast` pre-creates the
`runs` row with `is_public = true` and the recorder's real `started_at`,
and `public_runs` projects `started_at` with `grant select … to anon`
(migration `20270430_001` is the current definition; the column has been in
the view since `20260626_001`). Both surfaces were already reading it —
web into `visibleRun.started_at`, mobile into `run.startedAt` — and neither
was subtracting it from now: it fed a `cutoff_clock` marker's time of day on
both, plus the `isFinishedStale` / `runIsFinished` end inference. So the race
clock is `now - started_at`: a subtraction of two values the page already
holds, not a reconstruction. `raceClockS` joins the `live_freshness` parity
pair and states it; `liveElapsedS` stays as the fallback for a caller that
cannot resolve the start, and both suites now pin that it can only ever be
a **lower bound** on the same clock.

**The trade the follow-up was gated on no longer exists, and that is worth
recording separately.** The entry says `elapsed` "excludes auto-paused
time". There has been no auto-pause layer since moving time became a
track-derived post-run metric (`run_stats.dart` / `run_stats.ts`
`movingTimeSeconds`); `run_screen.dart` says so outright and
`RunRecorder.pause()` has exactly one caller, `_toggleManualPause`. So
`elapsed_s` is not moving time — it is wall time less any stretch the
runner *explicitly* paused. Naming it "Moving" would have been a fresh lie
in place of the old one, which is why the tile is labelled **Timer**.

What each figure now claims, on both platforms:

- **Race time** — `raceClockS(startedAtMs, atMs)`. Ticks on the page's
  own second clock. `atMs` is `now` while live and the **conclusion
  instant** once terminal, so a finished run's clock stops where the run
  did rather than counting on forever. A run that concluded before the
  `concluded_at` marker existed has no end to measure to: the tile is
  **withheld**, not measured to now. A start stamped in the viewer's
  future clamps to 0, the same clamp `freshnessFor` makes on an age.
- **Timer** — the ping's `elapsed_s`, unchanged. Once the fix is stale it
  is muted and relabelled *"Timer, last fix"*, exactly as the recent-pace
  tile already relabels to "When last seen". Qualifying rather than
  withholding is the right call here and the distinction is consistent:
  the page withholds *projections* off a stale fix (the cut-off verdict,
  the motion claim) because they require extrapolation, and qualifies
  *measurements* taken at the fix, because the measurement is real and
  only its currency is in doubt.

Clock skew argues for the race clock rather than against it. A
`cutoff_clock` limit is resolved as `cutoffClockMin - startClockMin` off
that same `started_at`, so a recorder whose clock ran an hour fast shifts
the limit and the race clock by the same hour and the remaining budget is
exact. Driving the same comparison off the runner's stopwatch shifts only
one side of it. Cut-off maths therefore runs on the race clock wherever the
start instant resolves.

The `raceElapsedS` derivation the page already had is unchanged in spirit
and now correct in fact; what changed is that it is also *shown*, and shown
next to the figure it is not. The stat tiles gained `data-testid`s so the
existing Playwright assertions stop depending on tile order, and mobile's
`_Metric` label scales instead of ellipsizing, because five cells fit on a
narrow phone only if the labels do — and the label is the whole mechanism
by which a spectator tells the two clocks apart.

**The watch rail does not share this bug and needs no port.**
`watch_core::record`'s `elapsed_s()` is `now_s - start_s` and its
`moving_s` is a separate accumulator; `cutoff_snapshot` already feeds the
cut-off the race clock, and its doc comment already reasons about why race
pace rather than moving pace is the honest projector. Porting `raceClockS`
there would be inventing a subtraction the device does not need — it has a
monotonic clock from the start rather than two epoch stamps to difference.
`live_freshness.rs` carries only `freshness_for`; it never ported
`liveElapsedS` either.

## 713. The wrist takes the phone's activity words, because the chip that was supposed to justify shorter ones truncates either way

The Wear OS pre-run Activity chip carried its own words for four of the five `runs.activity_type` values: German `run` "Lauf" against the phone's "Laufen", Spanish `run` "Correr" against "Carrera", Spanish `walk` "Caminar" against "Caminata", and Japanese `run` / `walk` / `cycle` "ラン" / "ウォーク" / "サイクル" against "ランニング" / "ウォーキング" / "サイクリング". Three of those six are the *same* within-locale disagreements § 547 resolved on web and mobile — the wrist simply was not in that sweep and kept the losing side of each. Portuguese was already aligned in full, English differs only on the `hike` rename below, and French only there too.

The standing defence was that the chip needs shorter words, so the question was settled by measuring the chip rather than by preferring a vocabulary. `CompactChip` applies `ChipDefaults.CompactChipContentPadding`, which is 12 dp on each side, so `widthIn(max = 56.dp)` leaves the label **32 dp**; `caption3` is 10 sp Roboto Medium with 0.1 sp tracking and `DuskTypography` does not override it. Against Roboto-Medium metrics at that size the wrist **already ships** `Radfahren` at 47 dp, `Poussette` at 46, `Caminhada` at 52, `ベビーカー` at 50 and `Kinderwagen` at 60. The short words do not fit either — `Caminar` is 38 dp, `Course` 32, `ウォーク` and `サイクル` 40 each. So the abbreviation never bought the fit it existed for; it bought a fourth vocabulary. The chip is `maxLines = 1` with `TextOverflow.Ellipsis` and its `contentDescription` carries the whole word, so truncation is a display degradation with an accessible full readout — which is the right way for a cramped surface to handle a long word, and is what makes forking the words unnecessary. The phone's words win, and the rule generalises in `conventions.md`: a narrow surface truncates, it does not get its own dialect.

`hike` is deliberately **not** touched. Web and mobile display it as "Trail run" / "Traillauf" / "Trail" / "トレイルラン" since § 547, on recorded user evidence that "Hike" was why trail runners did not see themselves in the picker; the wrist still says "Hike" / "Wandern" / "Senderismo" / "Rando" / "ハイク". That is a product rename, not a translation fix, so it stays an owner call and `docs/product/followups.md` now carries it as a decision-ready question rather than a vague box. Worth recording two facts that question needed: the rename is **display-only** on every platform — the stored token is still `hike`, in the `runs_activity_type_check` CHECK, in `challenges.activity_type`, in the watch→phone payload, in `UNIVERSAL_ACTIVITY_TYPES`, in the calorie coefficient table and in the Strava / Garmin importers' ingest mapping — and French "Rando" belongs to this half, not to the translation half the original box filed it under: it is the pre-rename French word for hiking, so changing it *is* making the rename call for French.

The guard lives with the vocabulary it protects. `ActivityTypeVocabularyTest` already parsed the CHECK out of the migration to assert the wrist carries a label for every value; it now also asserts each label **equals the ARB's and the web catalogue's**, locale for locale, so a fifth vocabulary cannot grow back the way the fourth did. `hike` is exempt, and the exemption is asserted **non-stale** — the day the wrist takes the rename, the guard fails until the entry is removed, so the exemption cannot outlive the question. The test also pins the one phone locale the wrist does not mirror (`app_pt.arb`, European Portuguese, which web is short too), so a seventh phone catalogue cannot appear without the wrist being told.

## 714. Every mobile share goes through one helper that cannot be called without a popover anchor — the app ships to iPad, where an unanchored share sheet does not open at all

Sharing on the Flutter apps reached `share_plus` from 21 places: nine `Share.shareXFiles` (CSV export, account backup, GPX/KML route export, the run / route / period / finisher-certificate card PNGs, the import-failure report), ten `Share.share` for a link or a block of text, and two already-modernised `SharePlus.instance.share` calls in the recap screen. **Not one of them passed `sharePositionOrigin`**, and `apps/mobile_ios/ios/Runner.xcodeproj` sets `TARGETED_DEVICE_FAMILY = "1,2"` in all three build configurations — the app is an iPad app.

That combination is a broken feature, not a stylistic gap. iPadOS presents `UIActivityViewController` as a popover, and a popover needs a source rect. The pinned plugin (`share_plus` 12.0.2 / `share_plus_platform_interface` 6.1.0, resolved in the workspace `pubspec.lock`) makes the consequence explicit rather than crashing: `FPPSharePlusPlugin.m` builds `originRect` as `CGRectZero` when the four `origin*` keys are absent, and then refuses — `if (isIpad && hasPopoverPresentationController && (!isCoordinateSpaceOfSourceView || CGRectIsEmpty(origin)))` returns a `FlutterError` whose message is literally `sharePositionOrigin: argument must be set`. In Dart that surfaces as a `PlatformException` and **no sheet ever appears**. Worth stating precisely, because the failure shape has moved: older plugin versions had no `isIpad` guard and let UIKit raise, so the received wisdom is "it crashes". On 12.0.2 it does not crash — it throws into whatever `catch` the call site happens to have, which on most of these sites means a one-line banner and a share that simply never happens. Every rail routes through the same `atSource:` check, so the ten text shares were as broken as the nine file shares; the count that mattered was 21, not 9.

The fix is one module, `lib/share_sheet.dart`, and the point of it is the **signature**, not the code. `shareFilesFrom(BuildContext, {required List<XFile> files, …})` and `shareTextFrom(BuildContext, {required String text, …})` take the context they derive the anchor from as a required positional parameter; there is deliberately no overload accepting a bare `Rect` and none accepting nothing. A caller therefore cannot express a share without an anchor, which is the property nine independently-patched call sites would not have had — the original bug was not that anyone chose to omit an optional parameter, it was that omitting it is invisible on the two platforms every developer tests on. The module is also the only file under `lib/` permitted to import `package:share_plus/share_plus.dart` (it re-exports `XFile`), so a future call site cannot even name `Share`. Four source guards in `architecture_guards_test.dart` hold all of that, and each was verified to fail against a deliberately broken tree before being committed.

Anchor derivation degrades instead of throwing, because a share is an L4 auxiliary effect and a screen must not go down because a `RenderBox` could not be resolved: the invoking widget's global bounds **intersected with the view** (the plugin also requires the anchor to lie inside the host view, which a part-scrolled or mid-animation box need not), else a small rect at the view's centre, else a one-pixel rect at its origin. It never yields an empty rect, since an empty rect *is* the failure. The centre fallback is a real anchor, not a fabricated one — a popover pointing at the middle of the screen is what UIKit does for a source-less presentation — and no call site needed it: all 21 already held a `BuildContext`, including the three that share after an async gap from inside a modal sheet and the route-detail link share that fires after a confirm dialog has popped, where the correct anchor was always the screen underneath rather than the dead dialog.

Migrating off the deprecated API came free in the same pass and was worth taking now rather than touching 21 sites twice: on 12.0.2 the whole `Share` class carries `@Deprecated('Use SharePlus instead')` and `shareXFiles` carries `@Deprecated('Use SharePlus.instance.share() instead')`, while `SharePlus.instance.share(ShareParams(...))` is present — the deprecated statics are thin forwarders to it. Nothing in the dependency graph moved; the pin is untouched.

**What this does not claim.** None of it has run on an iPad. There is no Mac and no iPad here, so the crash was not reproduced and the fix was not observed working — what was verified is the plugin's own source, the Xcode target's device family, the lockfile pin, 6 host tests over the derivation (including a zero-size box, an unmounted context, a box hanging past the view and a box entirely off it), the four guards, and byte-identical mirroring to the iOS twin per § 39. Device verification is recorded in `followups.md` as a device gate. One residual is upstream and cannot be closed from Dart: the plugin compares the anchor against `controller.view.frame` rather than `bounds`, so under iPad Split View or Stage Manager — where the Flutter view's frame is not anchored at the origin — a correct view-local rect can still fail the containment test. That is strictly better than today, where every iPad share fails unconditionally, but it is not nothing.

## 715. A widget test waits on a condition with a deadline that fails, never on a duration that hopes

`run_screen_recording_flow_test.dart`'s `holdFinish` fired the Finish button's `onHoldComplete` inside `tester.runAsync` and then slept a fixed 200 ms. That sleep was doing synchronisation work: `_stop()` awaits `recorder.stop()`, whose position-stream cancel only resolves on the real event loop, then a real disk write, and only after both does the screen leave its recording state. On a loaded runner the chain does not finish inside 200 ms, so the assertions ran against a screen that was still recording. It failed on two consecutive Dependabot PRs (#803, whose entire diff is one `.terraform.lock.hcl`, and #807, four workflow SHA pins) while the same job passed on `main` at the same base SHA, and it passed 30/30 six times over on a developer machine. A duration cannot be tuned out of this: raising it buys a longer fuse, and every value is simultaneously too long for a healthy run and too short for a loaded one.

The rule is that a test waits on the thing it is actually waiting for. `pumpUntil` (in `test/pump_until.dart`, mirrored to the iOS twin like every other test file) turns the real event loop in short slices, pumping a frame between them, until a caller-supplied predicate holds. Its `timeout` is a **failure bound, not a synchronisation mechanism**: on expiry it calls `fail()` naming what never happened, so a genuine regression is loud instead of being slept through and then reported as some unrelated assertion. This is the same discipline the project already applies to production code — do not inflate a timeout or a retry to hide a bug — carried into the test harness, and it is why the deadline is deliberately generous (10 s) rather than tight: a tight deadline is a sleep wearing a different hat.

For the stop path the completion signal turned out to be exact rather than a proxy. `HoldToStopButton.onHoldComplete` is declared `VoidCallback` but is wired straight to the async `_stop`, so invoking it through `dynamic` hands back that future. Everything `_stop` does is ordered behind it, and the ordering is what the callers depend on: `runStore.save(run)` completes **before** the `setState` that swaps the recording view for the finished summary (that ordering is itself load-bearing — § 7d's save-then-clear invariant, pinned by `architecture_guards_test.dart`), and the cloud push, the live-broadcast conclusion and the post-live visibility resolution all run after it. So one wait covers both classes of assertion in the four call sites — three on `runStore.captured`, one on the recording view being gone. The two sibling files that had copy-pasted the same 200 ms helper (`run_screen_conclude_retry_test.dart`, `run_screen_live_visibility_test.dart`) assert on those later legs and were exposed to a strictly wider race; they now share the helper. The visibility tests are the one case where `_stop` deliberately does *not* finish — it parks on the keep-public dialog until the runner answers — so they wait for the dialog, then for the stop path itself once the choice is made, which is why `holdFinish` takes an optional predicate and returns a stop-completed one.

The fix was demonstrated rather than assumed, since a loaded CI runner cannot be reproduced here. Making the stop path's save take 400 ms — the shape of a slow runner, and no more artificial than the real disk write the treadmill group already performs — failed all four `holdFinish` callers pre-fix, reproducing the CI message verbatim (`Expected: no matching candidates / Actual: Found 1 widget with text "Treadmill mode"`), and passed all four post-fix under the identical drag; the same before/after held for the two sibling files.

The sweep behind this found the pattern had already been re-derived by hand five times (`gym_screen_test`, `gym_session_screen_test`, `nutrition_screen_test`, `gym_compose_sheet_test`, `checkpoint_checkin_screen_test`), two of them carrying comments naming the CI runs where a fixed sleep had flaked — and three copies, plus two bounded loops in `runs_screen_runlist_test` and `run_detail_screen_test`, simply fell out of the loop when their deadline expired, waiting a hung screen out and then reporting whatever assertion came next. All of them now delegate to the one helper, so there is a single deadline policy. What was deliberately **not** converted is the residue of roughly fifty fixed real-clock delays elsewhere in the mobile suite that drain a fire-and-forget write or a one-shot load before teardown: each needs its own observable condition, several have none without adding a test seam to production code, and none has flake evidence behind it. They are a conversion to make as each file is next touched, not a suite-wide rewrite to do blind. A delay that *models elapsed time* is not in that residue at all and must stay a delay — the 11 s GPS blackout in the recording-flow file, the live broadcaster's ping throttle, the routes bridge's debounce window, and the hanging fetchers that exist to prove a `.timeout()` fires are each the test's subject, not its plumbing.

## 716. A sim panel dump waits on a line the composer emits AFTER the flush, and a launcher that fails exits non-zero — two harness races, neither of them the firmware

Two Renode jobs went red in the same afternoon on PRs that touch no firmware at all — a Terraform lockfile bump and an npm dependency bump — and both passed on re-run. They were separate defects with one shape: a harness deciding an outcome by *when it happened to look* rather than by anything the guest promised.

**The `alerts` scenario was sampling a repaint.** It waited for `record: alert <Kind>`, dumped the panel, and read the first sample as a verdict — retrying four times if the frame came back bannerless. That line is the RECORD task's, and `record.rs` emits it **before** `alert_sender.send(alert)`, so at the moment it is written the composer has not been told an alert exists, let alone drawn one; on this fixture the flush lands about 11 ms of firmware time later. Whether a DumpFrame issued on the strength of that line arrives either side of the repaint is therefore decided by how much of Renode's virtual clock passes during the host's decode-and-dump round trip — a property of the runner, not of the firmware. Measured here: **three of eight identical local runs missed on the first attempt**, which puts four independent misses at a couple of per cent locally and evidently much higher on a contended two-core hosted runner, where all four missed and the scenario reported "+340 ink" against the 500 an inverse-video band has to add. Four attempts is not a fix for that; it is the same lottery with four tickets. Every perturbation tried — raising the RTT drain from 50 Hz to 1 kHz, inserting a monitor round trip ahead of the dump, pinning the whole sim to one core — flipped the first attempt from miss to hit, which is the clearest statement of the problem available: nothing about the firmware moved.

The fix is the one § 361 already made for pages, applied to the banner. The screen task now states **its own** condition after `display.flush` returns — `ui: banner <Kind>` / `ui: banner none`, change-gated like `ui: page`, and emitted at the first render so a scenario arming no alerts still has a state to wait on. It reports the banner the frame will SHOW rather than the alert the engine holds, because the armed-stop prompt and the page grid both take the hero band back and a line that ignored them would vouch for a frame carrying no banner. `ci_smoke.py` waits for that line, takes a tail cursor at the point it read it, dumps, and re-reads from that cursor: a repaint that collided with the DumpFrame is **detected** rather than sampled around, and the remaining attempt counts are failure bounds. The quiet baseline's lowest-of-three sampling is gone — it existed only to guess which sample was not lagging. Eight consecutive post-fix runs landed the banner on the first attempt with no retry. `screenshots.py`'s three-second settle before re-shooting a bannered frame is the same defect (three seconds against an eight-second TTL) and becomes the same wait; its stale-frame settle stays fixed, because a repeat of the previous screen is not a state the composer announces.

**`bin/watch-sim.sh` failed silently, in two different ways at once.** Its EXIT trap ended `exit 0` unconditionally, so every `fatal` in the script reported SUCCESS to its caller — which is why `ci_smoke.py` could only detect a failed launch by an effect that never appeared, and said so as "exited early with **status 0**". And the trap ran under the script's own `set -e`, where the first best-effort step to return non-zero abandoned the rest of the teardown: `pkill -P $$` returns 1 whenever nothing is left to sweep, which skipped both the `wait` and the removal of the latest-run pointer and left the next session free to follow a symlink into a dead run directory. Both are fixed at the trap: the status that is ending the script is preserved, teardown runs under `set +e`, and SIGINT is the one deliberate exception (Ctrl-C is how an interactive stream ends, not how it fails, and `pnpm watch:sim` would print a lifecycle error on every normal stop).

**The ports are claimed now, not checked.** The phone-link socket binds a fixed 7788 and `watch.resc` reaches it several seconds into the include, after Renode compiles seven C# peripheral models — so `ss` could only report who held the port a moment ago, and two sims launched inside that window both cleared the check. The loser's include aborts at the socket and the only symptom is a pty that never appears; reproduced here by launching two sims together and getting the CI message verbatim, with the port already free again by the time its advice says to go looking. Each port now takes an advisory `flock` on a per-port lock file, held on a descriptor Renode inherits, so it stays claimed for as long as anything in the session can still hold the socket and a second sim waits for the real release. The monitor port had no check at all — a bare draw from a 20k-wide range — and gets the same claim with a re-draw on collision. `ss` stays, after the claim, for the holder no lock can coordinate with. macOS has no `flock(1)`; there the fallback says so rather than leaving the weaker guarantee looking like the strong one.

**The boot deadline was a synchronisation mechanism wearing a deadline's clothes.** Thirty seconds, flat, with no way to tell a Renode still compiling from one that had died — against a boot that takes ~4.4 s on this workstation of which ~3 s is the C# compile, and several times that on a cold, contended runner. It is now 180 s, which is a *failure bound*: expiry means something is actually wrong. What the boot GOT TO is no longer guessed at either — `watch.resc` writes `watch.resc stage: <name>` after each of its risky steps, so a failed boot names the last stage reached and the step after it is the one that died. The old message ended by speculating about a stale sim on the phone port; the new one reports, for the same provocation, that the include "got as far as 'platform built, ELF loaded' and stopped there", which is the phone socket without having to guess.

**The rule the harness follows from here:** a panel dump, or any assertion about what the device SHOWS, synchronises on a line the firmware emits *after* the thing being measured has happened, and is re-checked against that same line once the artifact is on disk. A deadline may bound the wait and must fail loudly naming what never arrived; it may never be the thing that decides. And a launcher reports its own failure as an exit status, because a downstream absence is a symptom, not a diagnosis.

**What this does not claim.** The full CI failure — all four attempts missing — was not reproduced locally; what was reproduced is the per-attempt coin flip it is made of, at 3 in 8. The phone-port TOCTOU was reproduced exactly, both by racing two sims and by taking the port from outside after the claim. The swallowed exit status was reproduced with the real script (a SIGTERM'd sim reported 0 before, 143 after). Nothing here has run on the hosted runner: the argument that a cold two-core runner sits further along the same timing axis is reasoning, not measurement.

## 717. The Art 20 export is a queued job, the signed URL is minted when the subject asks rather than when the worker finishes, and the synchronous endpoint survives only because deleting it would demote mobile's export

**Decided (2026-08-24, closing the last code box in the `followups.md` export thread — the one § 703 and § 708 each left standing.)** Both rails already stream into a chunked Storage upload, so neither carries a row cap any more. What § 708 named as the honest remaining bound was the **connection**: the caller POSTed `/v1/export` and waited while the worker walked every section and pushed every 6 MiB chunk, so their timeout, a closed tab, or a backgrounded mobile app could end an export that would otherwise have completed. That is now a `data_export` job. `POST /v1/export/jobs` enqueues and answers with a job id; the worker builds with nothing attached; `GET /v1/export/jobs/latest` reports the outcome.

**Two rows per export, because the repo already had a shape for this.** `run_matched_tracks` established it: the generic `jobs` row is the queue entry the worker claims, and a sibling state table holds the outcome the owner reads. So `data_export_jobs` (migration `20270603_001`) carries status, the artifact's Storage key, the two run counts, the completeness verdict and a failure code, and `enqueue_data_export` inserts both rows **in one statement**. Two round-trips from the HTTP handler could have left a state row nothing would ever build, and a subject then polls a `queued` row for ever.

**The signed URL is not stored, and that is the whole answer to a queue's worst interaction with a 10-minute TTL.** A URL minted when the build finished starts its clock at a moment the subject had no part in choosing — they closed the tab, the worker finished four minutes later, and by the time they came back the link they were told about was already dead. So the row holds the object **path**, which is inert on its own (the `exports` bucket has no `storage.objects` policies at all, § 703), and the status endpoint signs at read time. The TTL now starts when the subject asks. The web page goes further and re-reads at half the URL's own lifetime while a ready export is on screen, so the download link cannot expire under someone who is looking at it.

**Status is an endpoint, not an RLS read, and the reason is that a path is not a download.** The obvious alternative was an owner-SELECT policy on `data_export_jobs` and a client-side read. It does not work: only the service role can sign an object in a bucket with no policies, so the client would learn a Storage key it cannot use and *still* need this endpoint for the URL — two ways to learn the same status, one of which can act on it. Adding a client read path would also have been the first crack in § 703's deliberate zero-policy design. `data_export_jobs` therefore ships RLS-on-with-no-policies **and** no `authenticated` grant at all, which puts it beside `app_quota` and `deletion_audit_log` on `role_grant_matrix_test.sql`'s service-role-only list — denying at the grant level as well as through RLS, so a policy added by mistake later still opens nothing. And the endpoint answers for the subject's **latest** export rather than by id, because a page that reloads mid-build has to find its way back with nothing stored locally; the one-in-flight unique index is what makes "latest" unambiguous.

**The synchronous endpoint stays, and not for small exports.** A size split was considered and refused: the server cannot know an archive's size before building it, so the split would have to be guessed from a row count, and it would make one endpoint's response shape depend on the caller's data. The real reason `/v1/export` survives is narrower and expires: the mobile client has not moved to the queued rail, and `BackupService.tryServerBackup` swallows any non-200 and falls back to its **local** writer by design. Deleting the synchronous rail would therefore not have broken mobile — it would have silently demoted every mobile Art 20 export to the on-device archive, which carries runs, routes, profile, prefs, gym and food but **not** the personal-data table set the server export bundles. Shipping a data-rights regression to close a data-rights follow-up is not a trade worth making. So `/v1/export` is marked deprecated in source and docs, both rails go through one `BuildArtifact` so they cannot drift in what they include, and the mobile migration plus this endpoint's deletion is re-filed as its own follow-up — the same rail-by-rail closure § 703 → § 708 used.

**Four failure modes, and each one is a decision rather than a default.**

*A job that dies mid-build.* Unchanged from § 708 and now load-bearing in a new place: tus materialises nothing until the declared length arrives, so a failed build leaves no object, and the state row only becomes `ready` after `Finish` returned **and** the path was recorded. There is no state in which the subject is offered an archive that is short.

*A retry that double-charges Storage.* An at-least-once queue will re-deliver a job whose build already succeeded, and rebuilding would push a second whole archive and orphan the first. The handler returns immediately when the row is already `ready` with a path. The one window it cannot close is a crash between `Finish` and the row write — that costs exactly one orphaned archive, which the 7-day sweep collects, and the alternative (swallowing the write error) would leave the subject watching a `running` row whose export is sitting in Storage. `max_attempts` is **2**, not the table default of 5, for the same reason: an export retry is not cheap the way a push retry is.

*A row that says `running` for ever.* The handler marks the row failed only when no further attempt is coming, so a retry in progress still reads as "being tried again" rather than as a failure. That leaves the crash case, where nothing ever writes again — so the status reader derives it: a `queued` or `running` row nothing has touched for longer than `ExportJobStaleAfter` reads as `stalled`. That number is **derived, not picked** — 2 attempts × the 15-minute per-attempt clock is the longest a live job can legitimately be working, and the remainder covers queue wait — and the derivation is pinned by a test rather than left in a comment, because two constants in two packages will drift. An unparseable timestamp fails the *other* way and claims the row is still healthy: telling a subject their live export died sends them to start another one, and being slow to give up is recoverable.

*An artifact that outlives nothing, or a row that outlives its artifact.* `cleanup_stale_export_blobs` deleted objects at 7 days and knew nothing about rows, so a `ready` row would have kept offering a download that 404s. It now composes `expire_stale_export_jobs`, which flips those rows to `expired` against the same window. Split into its own function because `storage.objects` refuses a direct DELETE on a current local stack ("Use the Storage API instead"), which puts the blob sweep itself out of pgtap's reach — the half that can be asserted now is.

**`data_export` needs a wider clock than every other kind.** The worker's generic `HandleTimeout` is 5 minutes, which is right for a push or an email and wrong for an archive whose cost is dominated by per-object Storage fetches; capping the queued rail there would have made it *worse* than the synchronous endpoint it replaces, which had no clock at all. So the timeout is per-kind (15 minutes for this one) rather than raised for everything.

**What the subject sees, which is the point of the whole change.** Clicking export now returns at once with "building — you can close this page". A reload mid-build resumes from the status endpoint with nothing persisted client-side. A finished export renders a real download link rather than a popup, because the completion arrives on a timer and a `window.open` outside a user gesture is blocked — which also makes the reload case and the completion case the same code path. And the client fails closed in both directions on a status it does not recognise: it stops polling rather than spinning until the tab closes, and it never presents a `ready` job with no URL as a download.

**What is not verified.** No Playwright spec covers the queued rail, and adding one would have been dishonest rather than expensive: `PUBLIC_EXPORT_HUB_URL` is unset in the e2e dev server, so every existing export spec exercises the Edge Function rail, and setting it would flip all twelve onto a transport they do not mock. The livehub config's second-dev-server pattern is the shape that would work, and it needs a Go worker booted with a service key and a real Storage stack — a CI job, not a spec. The rail is pinned by 19 web unit tests, 13 endpoint tests and 11 handler tests instead, and the honest statement is that the queued path has not been driven end to end against a live stack.

## 718. Date of birth is two records, not one field: the age record is child-safety and ungated, the prefs-bag mirror is Art 9 and follows consent

**Decided (2026-08-24, issue #789 follow-up "Consent-flow consistency for health-data fields").** The filed premise was that `/onboarding` was the outlier — that it "still writes the bare `date_of_birth` column unconditionally … `/settings/account` and `/settings/preferences` are aligned". It is wrong in both halves. Onboarding was the only surface applying a coherent rule; the two settings pages were neither aligned with it nor with each other, and they wrote to **different stores**:

- `/onboarding` (`+page.svelte`, and the phone's `completeOnboarding`) wrote `user_profiles.date_of_birth` whenever the runner supplied one and gated only the `user_settings.prefs` mirror.
- `/settings/preferences` wrote the **column** and never the mirror, and refused the save outright when a DOB was present without consent (`hasDemographic && !healthDataConsent`) — so a minor who declined the Art 9 checkbox could not record a birth date at all and kept a NULL age record.
- `/settings/account` wrote the **mirror** and never the column, and aborted the whole save on `dateOfBirth && !healthDataConsent` while the same condition `disabled` the input — a deadlock: a runner whose stored DOB outlived their consent could not save their display name and could not clear the DOB either.
- The phone's Preferences row wrote the mirror **ungated**, which is the fail-open the other three were trying to avoid, and never wrote the column at all — while `nutrition_targets_screen.dart`'s docstring and § 695 both claimed DOB was editable only behind the body-metrics consent gate, where there is no DOB field.

**The rule, because the field carries two purposes on two lawful bases.** `user_profiles.date_of_birth` is the **age record**: its consumer is the under-18 exclusion inside `search_user_profiles` (`20261017_001` / `20261104_001`) and `discoverable_runners_near`, a child-protection purpose that does not rest on the runner's consent and must not be defeated by declining it. `user_settings.prefs.date_of_birth` is the **Art 9 health-use mirror**: its consumers are `coach/context.ts` (which re-gates on `health_data_consent_at` at read time) and the HR-max derivation. So the column is written by every entry point whenever a date is supplied and carries no consent term; the mirror is written only under consent and is cleared on withdrawal, on every surface. Gender keeps its consent term unchanged — it has no child-safety purpose.

**Ordering is load-bearing.** `withdraw_health_data_consent()` (`20270418_001`) nulls `date_of_birth` along with `gender` and `height_cm`, so every save path now writes the age record **after** the withdrawal RPC rather than before. That is an interim: the durable fix is the RPC dropping `date_of_birth` from its null list, which is a function-only migration this change deliberately did not land (see below).

**What this does not claim, and the two server-side items it leaves open.**

1. **The withdrawal RPC still erases the age record.** Clients put it back in the same handler; a client that crashes between the two calls leaves a declared minor discoverable until their next save. `withdraw_health_data_consent()` should stop nulling `user_profiles.date_of_birth` — a bare-body `create or replace`, no type regen — and `withdraw_health_data_consent_test.sql`'s "nulled the consent stamp + height + gender + DOB" assertion splits into "nulled the Art 9 columns" plus "kept the age record". Not landed here: the round that found it could not start the local Supabase stack, and a pgtap edit nobody has run is worse than a filed one.
2. **The age-banded leaderboards read the column with no consent term.** `segment_leaderboard_tiered` / `global_segment_leaderboard_tiered` band on `extract(year from age(up.date_of_birth))` and check nothing. That was already true before this change — onboarding has written the column ungated since the persona round-5 fix — but this ADR makes it explicit rather than incidental: an age tier is an Art 9 *use* of the date and belongs behind `health_data_consent_at`, exactly as the coach context gates its own read. Until that migration lands, gender-tiered boards are consent-correct (gender is only ever populated under consent) and age-tiered boards are not. **CLOSED 2026-08-25 by migration `20270606_001` — see [§ 727](#727), which also records the two things this item got wrong: the catalogue RPC is `global_segment_leaderboard`, and both bodies named above had been superseded by `20270524_001`.**

3. **Four client surfaces derive age from the column with no consent term, and this change widens who reaches them.** `dashboard/+page.svelte` (`viewerDobIso` → `ageGradeForRun`, and `ageFromDob` → `computeNutritionTargets`), `nutrition/+page.svelte`, `nutrition/targets/+page.svelte` and `PlanEditor.svelte` all read `date_of_birth` off `get_my_profile()` and use it directly; their mobile counterparts (`dashboard_screen.dart`, `nutrition_targets_screen.dart`, `training_service.dart`) do the same. This was already true — onboarding has written the column ungated since the persona round-5 fix — but before this change `/settings/preferences` refused a DOB without consent and `/settings/account` never wrote the column at all, so the ungated population was onboarding-only. It is now every runner who supplies a date. Mitigating, not excusing: every one of those computations ALSO needs `gender`, `height_cm` or the `body_metrics` weight series, all of which stay consent-gated and null without consent, so a non-consenting runner gets no nutrition target and no gendered age-grade — the open-category age-grade on `/dashboard` is the one claim age alone can still produce. The durable fix is the same shape as `coach/context.ts`: each site takes `health_data_consent_at` from the row it already reads and emits null age without it. Deliberately not landed here, because a web-only fix would recreate exactly the web↔mobile divergence this ADR exists to remove, and the mobile half needs fixture changes across several Flutter suites the round could not run.

All three are pre-deploy compliance items in the § 150 sense — code to write, not a legal question to wait on. The decision above is stated so that neither branch of it is implied by which code path happens to run.

## 719. The safety net's SMS leg and its "not back by X" deadline reach the phone; the number is repaired before it is graded, and a stored number nobody consented to says so

§ 240 shipped the SMS escalation channel and the per-run expected-return override backend-first with a web reference surface, and recorded the mobile half as deferred. It stayed deferred long enough to become the wrong shape of gap: recording is mobile-only, so the one client that can actually be mid-run — the client the "not back by X" deadline exists for — was the client without the control. A runner could arm their own return-time alert only by opening their own live-spectator page in a browser, on the phone that was recording the run.

**The deadline hangs off the live-share sheet, and nowhere else.** `set_run_expected_return` writes `runs.metadata.expected_return_at` on an *owned, in-progress* run row, and the only thing that creates that row on mobile is `beginLiveBroadcast`. There is therefore no pre-run or no-broadcast surface to put the control on that would not be a button which silently fails: the escalation is scoped to live-broadcast runs by design (§ 235), and the RPC's own guards say the same thing. Hanging it off the sheet the live indicator already opens puts it exactly where a run has the row the write needs.

**The picker is a ladder of offsets, and every rung states the deadline it lands on.** Web uses a `datetime-local` input, which is the right primitive for a spectator page and the wrong one for a phone held at arm's length by someone who has been running for four hours. What a runner thinks is "I should be done in about two hours"; converting that to a wall-clock instant is arithmetic the app can do. The rung still names the resulting time, because the *deadline* is what is being armed and a runner should be able to sanity-check it — and a deadline that falls past midnight carries its date, since a bare "2:00 AM" reads as this morning, on the one control where reading it wrong means contacts are woken sixteen hours early or not at all.

**The server is the truth about the alarm, so the screen reads it rather than remembering it.** This is the whole point of the feature stated as an implementation constraint. Once armed, the deadline lives in the run row and is read by the cron scan, so killing the app, flattening the battery or destroying the handset leave the alert standing — which is precisely the "never came home" case. It follows that in-memory state is not evidence: a run recovered after a crash has no memory of what it armed, and a picker that defaulted to "nothing set" would quietly invite the runner to believe that. The current value is fetched before the picker renders. A fetch that *fails* refuses outright instead of opening the ladder — an alarm we cannot read is an alarm we cannot write, and offering the choice would end in a control that reports a deadline the server never took. An RPC returning `false` (not my run, no longer in progress) is surfaced as a failure for the same reason; a safety control that claims an alert nobody armed is worse than no control.

**The honest cost is disclosed in the dialog rather than discovered in the field.** The deadline clears when the run saves, because `saveRun` upserts the whole metadata bag and takes `in_progress` and `expected_return_at` with it. That holds only for an *online* finish. A run that finishes out of signal is queued locally, the server row stays in-progress, and the scan escalates a runner already sitting at home — the same false-positive posture the overdue net has always had (§ 207: the email says signal loss is a possible cause), sharpened by an absolute deadline. The dialog says both things: the deadline outlives the phone, and a run finished with no signal can still alert until it syncs. Neither is a bug to fix client-side; a phone with no network cannot tell the server anything, and the alternative — not arming an absolute deadline at all — is the gap this closes.

**The phone number is repaired before it is graded, and the repair is a shared parity pair.** `safety_contacts.contact_phone` carries a CHECK of bare E.164. Nobody types a number that way. Web graded the raw string against the constraint, so `+44 7700 900123` pasted off a contact card was reported as invalid, which reads to the owner as "this number is wrong" when it is merely punctuated. `normaliseE164` (`safety/e164.ts` ↔ `e164.dart`, 16 mirror tests each) strips the separator families, reads the ITU access prefix `00` as `+`, and refuses anything it still cannot bring to E.164 — a national-format number carries no country, and inventing one would arm the escalation at a stranger. The one repair that is not cosmetic is the parenthesised trunk zero: `+44 (0) 7700 900123` stripped of brackets alone yields `+4407700900123`, a **different number that still passes the CHECK**, so the alert would deliver to nobody while every surface reported success. `(0)` is deleted whole, before any other bracket is touched, and both suites pin it. Extracting this into a pair rather than transliterating the regex is what stops the two platforms accepting different input; web now takes the punctuated paste it used to reject.

**A stored number the contact never consented to is stated, not left as silence.** SMS sends only where the owner stored a number AND the contact set `sms_opt_in_at` — two separate consents, one held by each party. Web renders a badge for the armed case and nothing otherwise, which collapses "no number on file" and "a number on file that reaches nobody" into the same blank. The second is the one that matters: the owner typed that number, believes it is the SMS channel, and is told nothing to the contrary. The mobile contact row renders three states, so a number awaiting an opt-in says so. This is a deliberate mobile-additive divergence from the canonical web surface (§ 24 permits additive; it does not permit a *less* honest client) and web mirroring it is filed as a follow-up rather than smuggled into this change. The inbound-request opt-in is offered only where `has_phone` is true, and confirming without ticking it consents to email only — silence is not consent to be texted, and both are pinned.

**What is still not built.** Neither platform can change an SMS consent *after* confirming. `set_safety_sms_opt_in` exists and works, but no surface on either client lists the relationships a user is the contact *of*, so nothing can call it; the Dart binding was removed rather than left as an unused method, and the gap is in followups. iOS carries the byte-identical Dart and stays `✗` in the matrix per the column key — code-equivalent is not runtime-equivalent, and none of this has run on Mac hardware.

## 720. The safety-contact list scopes itself to `owner_id`; RLS is a security boundary, not a query specification

`fetchMySafetyContacts` selected from `safety_contacts` with no `owner_id` filter on both clients, and both doc comments said "RLS scopes to `owner_id = me`". It never did after `20261218_001`, which shipped four permissive policies rather than two: `safety_contacts owner read` / `owner delete` (`owner_id = auth.uid()`) **and** `safety_contacts linked contact read` / `linked contact delete` (`contact_user_id = auth.uid()`), all four still present after `20270416_001`'s initplan wrap. Permissive policies OR. So the list read returned the union — the contacts the caller added, plus every relationship in which someone else added *them* and they confirmed — and both surfaces rendered that union as "your safety contacts", the second half of it under the caller's own email address.

**The Remove button on those rows was destructive, not refused and not inert.** `removeSafetyContact` deleted by `id` alone; the linked-contact DELETE policy permitted it; so pressing Remove on a row you merely appeared on deleted the *other* person's emergency contact, and told you your own list had been tidied. That is the worst of the three outcomes the surface could have had, and it is the one nobody would guess: an over-permissive read usually degrades into clutter, but here the read handed a working destructive control to the wrong party. Withdrawing from a relationship you are the contact of already has a named path that says what it does — `declineSafetyRequest` over the SECURITY DEFINER `decline_safety_contact`.

**The fix is client-side scoping, not a narrower policy.** The tempting move is to drop the contact-side SELECT policy, since every contact-facing path today goes through a definer RPC and nothing else needs it. That would be wrong twice over: the rows are legitimately the contact's own data (they are a party to the relationship, and the columns are ones they may read), and the pending follow-up — a "you are a safety contact for…" section, the only place `set_safety_sms_opt_in` can ever be called from — needs exactly those rows. The union was not the policies being wrong; it was two queries declining to say what they wanted. Both now filter `owner_id` on the read **and** the delete, and both refuse outright when signed out rather than issuing an unscoped query with a hole where the filter goes.

**The general rule this records.** RLS answers what a caller *may* read. A query has to state what it *wants*. Treating the first as the second is safe exactly as long as the two coincide, and a later migration widening a policy for an unrelated reason silently changes the meaning of every query that leaned on it — with no diff on the query, no type error, and no failing test. Any client read whose correctness depends on the row set being narrower than the policy allows must carry the predicate itself.

**Why it is pinned three ways.** The clients get source guards (`data.test.ts` covers both files; `packages/api_client/test/safety_contacts_scope_test.dart` covers the Dart side inside the Flutter job), because the property is static and a single-account local stack has no second party to produce the union — a wire test would pass against the bug. `safety_contacts_test.sql` gets the behavioural half: the union exists, the scoped read is empty for a contact, the unscoped delete destroys the owner's row, and the scoped one leaves it alone. The first and third assertions are the ones that describe the defect, and they are written to keep failing usefully — if a later migration narrows the contact-side policies, that section is what says so.

## 721. Withdrawing health-data consent stops erasing the age record: Art 7(3) ends the health processing, and child protection is a different lawful basis running underneath it

**Decided (2026-08-24, issue #789 — § 718 open item 1).** § 718 established that `user_profiles.date_of_birth` is the **age record** (child-safety, no consent term) and `user_settings.prefs.date_of_birth` is the **Art 9 health-use mirror** (written under consent, cleared on withdrawal). `withdraw_health_data_consent()` (`20270418_001`) contradicted the first half: it nulled the column alongside `gender` and `height_cm`. Migration `20270605_001` drops it from the null list — a bare-body `create or replace`, same signature, both generators re-run with no diff.

**Why retaining a birth date after a withdrawal is lawful, not merely convenient.** The column has two consumers doing two different things on two different bases. The Art 9 use — HR-max derivation, the coach context, age-banded boards — rests on Art 9(2)(a) explicit consent and reads the prefs mirror, which the withdrawal clears everywhere. The other consumer is the under-18 exclusion inside `search_user_profiles` (`20261017_001` / `20261104_001`), `discoverable_runners_near` (`20270424000005`) and the auto-hide report path (`20270218_001`): keeping a declared minor out of adult-facing name search and proximity discovery. That is a child-protection safeguard the service owes regardless of what the runner consents to, and its lawful basis is not the consent being withdrawn. Art 7(3) withdrawal ends the processing the consent authorised; it does not reach processing that never depended on it. Erasing the record there produced the perverse result the floor exists to prevent — a minor became name-searchable and locatable **because** they exercised a data-subject right.

**Withdrawal is not erasure, and the split is visible in the code.** Art 17 is the separate right, and its path is `delete-account`, which drops the `auth.users` row; `user_profiles_id_fkey` is `on delete cascade` (`20260728_001`), so the column goes with it. The age record therefore survives a withdrawal and does not survive a deletion, which is exactly what the two rights describe. Nothing in this change touches that path or weakens it.

**Nothing downstream reads the surviving column as evidence of consent.** Swept before landing: `withdraw_health_data_consent()` was the only writer in the migration set that nulls it, and every reader either does child-protection work (the four floors above) or performs an Art 9 use. No site infers `health_data_consent_at` from the column being populated — `coach/context.ts` re-gates on the stamp at read time and reads the mirror, not the column. The two Art 9 *reads* that carry no consent term are already filed and unchanged by this: the age-banded segment boards (§ 718 open item 2) and the four client age-derivation surfaces (open item 3). Both pre-date § 718 and neither is widened here, because as of § 718 the clients already re-asserted the column immediately after the RPC — this change makes the same outcome reliable rather than crash-dependent.

**The clients stop compensating, which was the point.** § 718 had both web settings pages order their `user_profiles` write *after* the RPC purely to put the column back, and had mobile's body-metrics screen load the profile's DOB solely to re-write it. A client that died between the two calls left the minor discoverable until their next save. All of it is removed; what stays is the rule, not the workaround — the ungated column write on the surfaces that *edit* a DOB, and the consent-gated mirror clear on withdrawal. The web guard that pinned the ordering is inverted to pin its absence (the withdrawal arm must not grow a `date_of_birth` write of its own), and the server contract is pinned where it belongs: `withdraw_health_data_consent_test.sql` splits its old "nulled the consent stamp + height + gender + DOB" assertion into "nulled the consent stamp + height + gender" plus "kept the age record the under-18 floor reads", 10 tests to 11.

**What is deliberately untouched.** `height_cm`, `gender` and the `body_metrics` weight series still go in the same transaction — they are Art 9 through and through, have no child-safety consumer, and a partial withdrawal is the failure `20270418_001` existed to close.

## 722. An age used for a health inference goes through one gate, not seven remembered checks — and the follow-up that filed it had the count, the sites and the mitigation wrong

**Decided (2026-08-24, § 718 open item 3.)** § 718 split `date_of_birth` into two records: the `user_profiles` column is the **age record**, written by every entry point with no consent term because the under-18 floor in `search_user_profiles` / `discoverable_runners_near` is a child-protection purpose that must not be defeated by declining consent; the `user_settings.prefs` key is the **Art 9 health-use mirror**, written only under consent and cleared on withdrawal. It then filed the obvious consequence against itself: the readers of the column had never learned the distinction. Reading the ungated record and feeding it to a health inference spends the child-safety record on the gated purpose.

**The filed list was wrong three ways, and the sweep is the point of this entry.** Seven sites were named. Nine reads exist across the two platforms, and they sort into three classes:

- **Already fail-closed, for a second reason** — the PR age grade on web `dashboard/+page.svelte` and mobile `dashboard_screen.dart` (`ageGradeForRun` returns null without a binary `sex`, and `withdraw_health_data_consent()` nulls `gender`), and the calorie target on web `nutrition/+page.svelte` and mobile `nutrition_screen.dart` (`computeNutritionTargets` returns null without `height_cm` and the `body_metrics` weight, which the same RPC nulls and erases). These are gated now anyway: relying on a *neighbouring* field's gate is not a rule, it is a coincidence that survives until someone makes one of those inputs optional.
- **Genuine, and the reason the item was not merely tidy** — web `PlanEditor.svelte` ↔ mobile `training_service.fetchViewerAge`, where age **alone** reshapes the generated plan (`MASTERS_AGE` 50 → wider hard-day spacing and a 3-week build/recover cycle), and the nutrition-targets metrics card on both platforms, which printed the runner's age outright on a health surface.
- **Never on the column at all** — web `runs/[id]`, mobile `run_detail_screen.dart` and `intensity_card.dart` read the settings-bag mirror for the Tanaka HR-max fallback. The mirror already follows consent in both directions, so a second gate there would be noise.

**The filed mitigation was false in both halves.** It read: "every one of those computations also needs gender, height or the weight series … so the open-category age-grade on `/dashboard` is the only claim age alone still produces." There is no open category — `ageGradeForRun` refuses without `male`/`female`, and both suites pin it. And the claim age alone actually produced was not an age grade at all: it was a differently-shaped 16-week training plan. A mitigation that names the wrong surface is worse than none, because it argues for deferring the one thing that was really broken.

**One accessor, not seven checks — and that is not a preemptive abstraction.** The house rule is that three similar lines beat a premature helper. This is the other case: the duplication already existed, at nine sites on two platforms, and it had already drifted — which is what the follow-up was. `healthUseDob` (`core/health_consent.ts` ↔ `health_consent.dart`) takes the `get_my_profile()` row a surface already reads — the RPC returns the whole row, so the consent stamp arrives with the date and costs no round trip — and answers with the date only under consent. The decisive argument is not brevity but detectability: a remembered check cannot be tested, while a registered parity pair is unit-tested on both platforms, watched by `shared-library-syncer`, and backed by a source guard that fails the build if a health-use surface reads `date_of_birth` off the row again. § 718's whole argument is that two stores with two rules must not be read as one field; leaving the rule in nine comments would have been that same mistake one layer up.

**It grades rather than merely gates, because a surface has to be able to explain itself.** `healthUseDobState` separates `absent` (no date on record) from `consent_withheld` (a date on record the runner asked us not to use this way). Both nutrition-targets metrics cards previously printed "Not set" beside Age in the second case, which is a lie about a date the runner did set and sends them to a settings screen where they will find it already filled in. They now say so outright. Fail-closed everywhere else: an unreadable row, a missing or empty stamp, and a value too short to be a date each withhold.

**Two things the sweep found that the follow-up did not.** `training_service`'s `fetchViewerAge` *and* `fetchViewerGender` read `user_profiles` with a direct `.select('date_of_birth')` / `.select('gender')`. Neither column is in the authenticated column grant (`20260707_001`, restated by `20270408_001`), so PostgREST refuses both with 42501 and the L4 catch turns that into `null` — meaning neither the masters calibration nor the gender pace calibration has ever fired on the phone, silently, since each was written. `ApiClient.fetchAiDisclosure` carries a comment describing this exact defect on a different pair of columns. Both now share one `get_my_profile()` read, which is in any case the only way the consent stamp is reachable; the gender read needs no consent term of its own, since gender is only ever written under consent. Fixing it was not optional scope: leaving the neighbouring line on a pattern the same method had just proved dead is the kind of knowingly-broken code the root-cause rule exists to forbid.

**What this does not close.** § 718's remaining server-side item stands: the age-banded segment leaderboards still band on `extract(year from age(up.date_of_birth))` with no consent term. That is a function-only migration, and this round was not the one holding the local Supabase stack. Nothing here is verified against a live database — the rule is pinned by unit tests, two source guards and the widget suites, and no Playwright spec covers a consent-withheld nutrition-targets page. (Its sibling — `withdraw_health_data_consent()` nulling the age record — was closed in this same round by [§ 721](../architecture/decisions.md), migration `20270605_001`, which also removed the client-side compensation.)

## 723. Working § 715's residue down: a store's row list is populated BEFORE its write, so the predicate is the store's own notification — and every conversion is graded by whether its condition was ever false

**Decided (2026-08-24, closing round 11's "~50 fixed real-clock delays" box.)** § 715's residue was 58 real-clock delays sitting next to `tester.runAsync` in the mobile widget suite. 44 of them are gone; 14 remain and each now has a stated reason. The work was a classification exercise, and the two things worth recording are the *method* that graded it and the one conversion that made a test measurably worse before the method caught it.

**A conversion is only real if its predicate was ever false.** § 715 says a `pumpUntil` whose condition already holds when it is first evaluated has converted nothing, and that is not something you can tell by reading. So `pumpUntil` was temporarily instrumented to print the number of loop iterations it actually spent, every converted file was run under it, and the count was read per call site. It separated three groups that look identical in a diff: waits that genuinely spin (the food composer's three manual-add cases spend ~50 ms, which is exactly the sleep they replaced — the margin was zero), waits that never spin because the work is microtask-only and the preceding `pump()` already drains it (the five sim-watch push cases, whose fake transport writes resolve without touching the real loop; those tests pass with no wait at all, and the `pumpUntil` there is a guard, not a wait), and predicates that are simply wrong. The run-detail success case is the third kind: `pumpForEdit` leaves its run **already synced**, so `unsyncedRuns.isEmpty` was true before the save as well as after it, and the test passed for the wrong reason until the count exposed it — the condition is the push having happened *and* the re-mark.

**The row list is not the write.** The first attempt at the gym session's six Finish cases waited on `store.workouts.isNotEmpty`, which is the obvious reading of "the save landed" and is wrong: `OfflineSyncStore.persist` puts the row into `rowsById` **before** `writeJsonAtomic`, and ends with `notifyListeners()` only once the row file and the index are both down. Waiting on the row count therefore returns while the write is in flight, and the `addTearDown` that deletes the temp dir then races it — the converted file printed a `PathNotFoundException` per case that the 50 ms sleep had been hiding. The fixed sleep was, in that narrow sense, doing the job better. So the signal is the notification, or a UI state ordered *after* `persist()` returns: the gym session waits on its saved banner, the gym detail toggle on the chip the notification repaints, and the food / routine / gear fixtures expose a `persisted` probe built from `addListener`, which is a public `ChangeNotifier` API and not a seam added to production code. Demonstrated rather than assumed, the way § 715 demonstrated its own fix: a 400 ms drag on `createLocal` fails seven cases in `gym_session_screen_test.dart` against the fixed sleep and none against the conversion.

**Two hard limits on what `pumpUntil` can wait for**, both discovered by a wait that timed out rather than by reading the helper. It never advances the fake clock, on purpose — so **no route transition, animation, or dialog dismissal can ever be a predicate**. `run_detail_screen_test.dart`'s save helper had a 200-iteration loop watching for its `AlertDialog` to disappear; it never did, so the loop ran to exhaustion on every call and the 500 ms drain behind it was the actual wait. And `pumpUntil` calls `tester.runAsync`, which cannot nest, so a test whose whole body already runs inside `runAsync` (`dashboard_streak_card_test.dart`) cannot use it without being restructured first.
