**What is left, and why.** Fourteen sites, in three groups. **Models elapsed time** — the 11 s GPS blackout § 715 already named. **No condition that is ever false**: five absence assertions (a cancelled barcode scan whose only state change is `_scanning` true-then-false; a pick carrying no readable path, which returns before the screen sets any state; an empty bib; the idle treadmill toggle), plus two drains of a *mocked, in-memory* preference store that the assertions read straight back, where any predicate holds the moment `setString` is called. **No observable outcome at all**: three teardown drains that run after the last assertion, and three shared helpers whose callers want different things and whose most common case is a read resolving to `null` (the roadbook / route-detail race-plan adoption, 21 call sites, where 13 of 14 tests have no stored plan for the read to change anything about). None of these should get a test seam added to production code to make it convertible; that trades a real invariant for a cosmetic one.

**Every deadline in a converted file names its own condition.** The two local `_pumpUntil` wrappers that supplied one generic string for eleven call sites between them now require a `describe`. A deadline that expires has to say which condition never held — that was the point of the helper, and a wrapper that answers "the nutrition screen to reach the expected state" for eight different waits has given it away.

## 724. Mobile's Art 20 export is queued too, its silent fall-back to the on-device archive is gone, and with it the synchronous endpoint

**Decided (2026-08-24, closing the two follow-ups § 717 left standing.)** § 717 moved web onto `POST /v1/export/jobs` and deliberately kept the synchronous `POST /v1/export` alive, for a reason it stated plainly: `BackupService.tryServerBackup` swallowed any non-200 and fell through to the **local** writer, so deleting the endpoint would not have broken mobile — it would have silently demoted every mobile Art 20 export to the on-device archive, which lacks the personal-data table set. That reason is spent. Mobile is on the queue, and the endpoint is deleted.

**The killed-app case is the ordinary case, and the resume path is the server, not a file.** A phone that enqueues an export and then goes to the lock screen is what usually happens; the app being killed before the archive lands is not an edge case worth a special mode. So nothing about the job is persisted on the device. `GET /v1/export/jobs/latest` answers for the subject's most recent export and the one-in-flight unique index makes that unambiguous, so the Account screen simply reads it on mount and renders what it finds. A job id written to disk would have been a second source of truth that a reinstall loses while the server still holds the archive — and it would have needed a migration of its own the first time its shape changed.

**What mobile deliberately does NOT do is promise a notification.** The obvious next step is an "your export is ready" push, and the precondition for it now holds — `followups.md` had ruled the equivalent email out *because* the endpoint was synchronous and any such message would arrive stale. It is still not built here, and the honest statement on the surface is the weaker one it can keep: the build survives the app, and the download is waiting on this screen. A background poller was refused rather than deferred — iOS background refresh is opportunistic, so a client that promised to notice would be making a promise the OS does not let it keep, and the battery cost would be paid by every runner to shave a screen visit off a request most people make once.

**The signed URL is minted at the tap, not held on the card.** Web re-reads at half the URL's lifetime because its card can sit on screen with a live `href` in it. Mobile has no link to keep alive: the card carries a Download action, and that action re-reads the status endpoint and downloads what it is handed. That is strictly better than the timer — the ten minutes start when the runner acts — and it means the screen needs no polling at all once a job is ready.

**The silent fall-back is deleted, and the two archives are now two tiles.** `tryServerBackup` is the thing that made the endpoint safe to delete *and* the thing that hid failure from the data subject: a refused Art 20 request reached them as a smaller file nobody told them was smaller. It is gone. `BackupService` builds one thing — the on-device archive — and the queued rail is orchestrated by the surface. "Account export" and "Full backup" are separate tiles because they are separate archives: the first is the server-built Art 20 copy, the second carries runs, routes, profile, prefs, gym and food but not the account-record set, and says so in a persistent notice once it has produced one. Every server refusal is surfaced, and the one the runner can act on — a 429 — names its own retry window. The undrained-run case became a disclosure instead of a switch: the server cannot see a run that has not synced, so the account-export tile says how many are missing rather than quietly building the local archive instead.

**Deleting the endpoint moved its tests rather than shrinking them.** Its handler had accumulated two unrelated kinds of coverage: the auth, quota and configuration gates, and the archive's behaviour. The gates moved to `jobs_test.go` against `/v1/export/jobs` — and pinning them there surfaced four the queued rail had never had (the 503 with no verifier, an expired token, a token with no `exp`, and the fail-closed quota RPC), so the rail that survived is better covered than before, not worse. The build-behaviour tests now call `BuildArtifact` directly, which is what they were always about; the mapping from its errors to the machine codes a client renders lives in `main.go`'s adapter and is the queued rail's. `wiring_test.go` gained a guard that the synchronous rail cannot come back.

**The e2e half is a lane, not a spec, and § 717 was right about why.** `PUBLIC_EXPORT_HUB_URL` is unset in the e2e dev server, so all twelve existing export specs exercise the Edge Function rail; setting it would have flipped them onto a transport they do not mock. So the queued rail gets the live-hub lane's shape — `playwright.exporthub.config.ts` with its own dev server and the real Go worker, one unsharded CI job (`e2e-web-exporthub`), one spec the sharded suite ignores. The worker boots with **auth on**, which the live-hub lane deliberately disables: an export is the caller's own data and a permissive verifier would be testing a different endpoint. `start-exporthub.sh` therefore has to resolve a JWT signing secret, and it **verifies** the one it resolved by re-deriving the local stack's own anon-key signature from it before booting — a wrong secret would otherwise surface as a 401 in the middle of a spec, which reads as a broken app rather than as a misconfigured harness. The spec also asserts `POST /v1/export` answers 404 against the running binary: a deleted route is worth checking where it was mounted, not only where it was called. And the journey is one test signed in as the PRO seed user rather than three tests signed in as the free one, because every enqueue spends a `check_rate_limit_tiered` token — free allows two an hour and the lane retries once, so a free-user split would have sat exactly on the ceiling and answered a 429 that reads as a broken rail.

**One new parity pair, registered in both registries.** `cloud_export_helpers` (web) ↔ `export_job.dart` (mobile) carries the job half — the status vocabulary and the fail-closed normalisation. Both clients read the same two endpoints, so an unrecognised status has to be terminal on both (a client that keeps polling a status it cannot interpret polls until the tab closes or the battery dies) and a `ready` job with no URL has to be a failure on both rather than a dead download button. The names differ because the registry keys a pair on its web basename; "cloud export" is not mobile's vocabulary and the Dart file is named for the job.

## 725. The queued export rail could not have worked from a browser, and its download link 404'd — both found by running the e2e lane § 724 shipped without running

**Decided (2026-08-25.)** [§ 724](#724) added an export-hub Playwright lane, a boot script and a CI job, and could not run any of them (port contention, and another agent held the local Supabase stack). Running them on the integration branch found two defects in the rail § 717 and § 724 had already landed, neither reachable by the unit, endpoint and handler tests that covered it.

**The preflight was refused.** The web client posts to the worker from the site's origin and never from the worker's — that is true of every deployment, since the worker is a separate Fly app. A cross-origin POST carrying `authorization` and `content-type` is preceded by an `OPTIONS` probe, and the mux answered it `405 Method Not Allowed` with no `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers at all, so the browser dropped the request before it was sent. The worker logged nothing, the page showed no job, and every layer looked healthy: the handler tests drive the endpoint directly, where no preflight exists. The allowlist is exact-origin rather than a wildcard because the endpoint is authenticated and a browser rejects `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on a credentialed request outright; it reuses `LIVEHUB_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` because it is the same site talking to the same service, and a second variable would be one more thing to set and exactly one more to forget. `Vary: Origin` is not optional — without it a cache can serve one origin's allow header to another. The preflight is answered *before* the JWT-configuration gate: an `OPTIONS` probe carries no credentials, so refusing it 503 would hide a working endpoint behind a browser-level failure.

**The signed URL pointed at nothing.** Supabase Storage answers a sign request with a path relative to the STORAGE API — `/object/sign/<bucket>/<path>?token=…`, with no `/storage/v1` on it — and the client fronted it with the project base URL alone, producing `…:54321/object/sign/…`, a 404 on every download. Confirmed against the local stack rather than inferred: the job row read `ready`, the object was really in the `exports` bucket, and only the URL was wrong. Both shapes are now accepted, because which one a deployment returns is the storage service's business.

**What generalises.** Both defects sit in the seam between two things that were each tested properly. A handler test cannot see a preflight because it is not a browser; a unit test cannot see a 404 because it does not fetch the URL it built. The lane § 724 wrote is what found them, so the rule is not "write more unit tests" — it is that a lane written and never executed is not evidence, and the round that writes it owes the run.
## 726. A consent you can only ever grant is not a consent: the contact-of section is the second, deliberate half of the read § 720 scoped

`set_safety_sms_opt_in` shipped with migration `20270410_001`, was granted to `authenticated`, and worked. It had no caller on either platform for four months, because the only thing it can act on is a row where `contact_user_id = auth.uid()` and neither client ever asked for one: both listed `safety_contacts` scoped to `owner_id`, which is the *other* half of the table. So SMS consent could be granted exactly once — inside `confirm_safety_contact`, at the moment of confirming — and after that the only way out was to leave the relationship. GDPR Art 7(3) says withdrawal shall be as easy as giving; here giving was a checkbox and withdrawing was destroying the safety net it belonged to. The fix needed no migration and no policy change: `safety_contacts linked contact read` (`20261218_001`) has permitted `contact_user_id = auth.uid()` since the table shipped, and § 720 predicted this section by name as the reason not to drop that policy when it looked unused.

**The rows this section renders are exactly the ones § 720 removed from the list**, which is why the two changes are one idea seen from both sides. Before § 720 the owner list's missing `owner_id` filter meant the permissive policies OR'd and the contact-of rows appeared *inside* the owner's own list — under the caller's own email address, with a Remove button that deleted the other person's emergency contact. Scoping the list did not delete those rows; it stopped a query claiming them as something they were not. `fetchSafetyContactOf` now asks for them under their own name, with `.eq('contact_user_id', uid)` said out loud for precisely the reason the owner read says `owner_id` out loud: both halves are legitimately readable, so RLS cannot be what distinguishes them.

**The action on such a row is `decline_safety_contact`, and getting that wrong would have been invisible.** `removeSafetyContact` is owner-scoped on both clients since § 720, so pressing a withdraw button wired to it issues `DELETE … WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $me`, matches zero rows, raises no error, and returns success — the client toasts "removed", re-reads, and the relationship is still there. PostgREST does not distinguish a delete that matched nothing from one that matched something, so no layer between the button and the database would have complained. The Playwright leg therefore asserts both directions: that `rpc/decline_safety_contact` fired once, and that **no** `DELETE` reached `/rest/v1/safety_contacts`.

**The owner's phone number is reported as a fact, never as digits.** The contact may read the column — it is their own number, stored by someone else — but the surface has no use for it beyond deciding whether the toggle would mean anything, there is no owner UPDATE policy so a contact could not correct a wrong number from here, and `my_pending_safety_requests` already established `has_phone` as the shape for exactly this question. A relationship carrying no number renders a sentence saying so rather than a toggle: `set_safety_sms_opt_in` returns **true** for that call (a row was updated) while the `CASE` clears the stamp, so a client trusting the return value would report a consent the database just refused — which the pgtap now pins alongside the re-arm direction that had no coverage at all (only the withdraw did, in `safety_sms_escalation_test.sql`).

**One web-specific hazard is worth recording.** Svelte 5 guards `checked` behind a compare against the last value it wrote, so when a refused write reloads the row to the same boolean the DOM is left holding the user's click. On a consent control that is the one failure mode that matters — the box reads "on" while the server has it off — so the handler re-asserts `input.checked` from the reloaded row rather than trusting the render pass. Flutter has no such gap: `SwitchListTile` takes its value from the rebuilt row every frame, which is why the mobile half needs no equivalent and its test pins the refusal by asserting the switch stayed put.

## 727. An age band is an Art 9 use of the child-safety age record, so it goes behind the consent stamp — and the item that filed it named the wrong function and the wrong bodies

**Decided (2026-08-25, [§ 718](#718) open item 2 — the last of its three.)** § 718 split `user_profiles.date_of_birth` into two records under one column name: the **age record**, written by every entry point with no consent term because the under-18 floors in `search_user_profiles` / `discoverable_runners_near` and the auto-hide report path are child protection resting on a lawful basis the runner's consent does not supply — which is why [§ 721](#721) stopped `withdraw_health_data_consent()` erasing it — and the `user_settings.prefs` **Art 9 health-use mirror**, written under consent and cleared on withdrawal. [§ 722](#722) then taught the column's *client* readers the distinction, through the `health_consent.ts` ↔ `health_consent.dart` parity pair. The two segment boards were the readers no client gate reaches, because the derivation happens in SQL. Migration `20270606_001` is the same rule where it actually runs.

**Two sites per function, not one, and the second is about the caller's own age.** `segment_leaderboard_tiered` and `global_segment_leaderboard` each derive an age twice: once in the band-membership filter inside `best_per_athlete`, and once in the outer select's `age` echo for the caller's own row. Gating only the filter would have left the second, which is the smaller leak but the same processing. Withholding the caller's own age *from the caller* is not protecting them from themselves — the derivation **is** the Art 9 processing, and the consent is what authorises performing it at all; `healthUseDob` returns null for `consent_withheld` on the runner's own row for exactly this reason, so the server now answers as the client does.

**Falling out of the tier is the right failure, and it is not a new shape.** An unconsented runner is absent from every age band rather than placed in a wrong one, which is precisely what the adjacent `up.date_of_birth is not null` branch has always produced for a runner with no date — the suite pins the two as indistinguishable, across the target band and both neighbours, so this cannot be read as a band-edge artefact. They are deliberately **untouched on the unfiltered all-comers board**: dropping them there would spend a privacy gate on a competitive ranking that never needed their age, and would shift every slower athlete's displayed rank, the same wrong kind of narrowing § 596 refused when it redacted a shadow-hidden athlete's name instead of dropping their row. **Gender gains no term and needed none** — `gender` is only ever populated under consent, so the gender tier was already correct; a test pins that it did not move, because a fix that widened the gate to every demographic column would be a silent behaviour change wearing a privacy label.

**The filed item named a function that does not exist and two bodies that were no longer live.** It called the catalogue RPC `global_segment_leaderboard_tiered`; there is no such function. More consequentially it pointed at `20270424000003` and `20270513_001` as the bodies to amend. Both had been re-emitted by `20270524_001`, the §206 shadow-hidden definer backstop — so a bare-body `create or replace` built on the text the item named would have silently reverted the profile carve-out and, on the route board, the delegated `private.is_route_visible_to` per-call check, reopening a moderation leak while closing a consent one. This is the failure mode those migrations' own headers warn about, arriving through a follow-up note rather than through carelessness at the keyboard: **a bare-body rule is only as good as the reader's check of which body is live**, and a follow-up written months earlier is not that check. The new bodies are `20270524_001`'s, diffed line-by-line against them to confirm the consent predicate is the only edit.

**Verified against a live database, which the two sibling ADRs could not be.** § 722 recorded that "nothing here is verified against a live database" and § 718 deferred its own pgtap edit for the same reason — neither round held the local Supabase stack. This one did: `supabase db reset` applied the migration, and the full pgtap suite ran. The new `segment_leaderboard_age_band_consent_test.sql` (10 tests, both boards, two runners identical but for the stamp plus a no-date control) passes. Two suite failures remain and are neither caused nor fixed here — `coach_roster_summary` test 10 and `donations_status_lock`'s `fundraiser_totals` both fail with `permission denied for function`, the known workstation-CLI 2.109.1 vs CI-pinned 2.84.2 divergence in `service_role` default EXECUTE privileges; both are green in CI and neither file references anything this change touches.

**No type regeneration, asserted and then actually checked.** Signatures, return types, volatility and search_path are unchanged, so nothing reaches the row types. Rather than reason about it, both generators were re-run — `npm run gen:types` and `dart run scripts/gen_dart_models.dart` — and produced a zero diff across `database.types.ts`, `db_rows.dart` and the Wear OS `DbRows.kt`. The claim in the migration header is a measurement, not an expectation.

**The fixture change was load-bearing and is the reason to look for others.** `segment_leaderboard_tiered_test.sql` seeded seven profiles with dates of birth and no Art 9 stamp, so four of its age-band assertions would have gone dark the moment the gate landed — the suite would have caught the change, but only as a failure to explain rather than as coverage. Those fixtures now carry `health_data_consent_at` and are documented as consenting runners. Worth noting for the next consent gate: `tests.confirm_consent()` stamps the Art 8 `age_confirmed_at` / `terms_accepted_at` columns and deliberately does **not** supply the Art 9 stamp — two gates, two lawful bases, one helper that only serves the first.

## 728. A Playwright seed's calendar day belongs to the browser's zone, not the runner's — and the guard that enforces it is a source scan, because nothing else can see the seam

`playwright.config.ts` pins every browser context to `timezoneId: 'UTC'`, so a page that buckets rows into "today" resolves that day in UTC. Seven nutrition specs resolved that day in the **Node process's** zone instead — four building seeds with `new Date(y, m, d, h, 0)` or a local midnight, and three through the shared `waterStorageKey()` fixture, which composed the water tracker's per-day localStorage key from local getters and so addressed a key the page never reads. The two agree only while the local and UTC calendar dates agree, which in EDT is sixteen hours a day: for the other eight the seeded `food_log` row lands on the adjacent day, the page renders nothing, and a visibility assertion fails on a ten-second timeout that says nothing about why. Hosted CI runners are UTC, so the seam does not exist there — the suite was green on every PR and red on the workstation, which is the shape that trains people to re-run rather than to read.

Two things made it survive. The offset is not only a date offset: a seed at 19:00 in a zone eleven hours behind UTC crosses the *next* UTC midnight even when the two calendar dates match, so "is my local date the same as UTC's" is not the test for whether a spec is affected. And each spec that had already been bitten fixed itself in place — two `noonUtcToday()` helpers and a `noonUtcDaysAgo()`, written by three separate rounds, each correct, none shared, none of them stopping the next spec from re-deriving the bug. `tests-e2e/fixtures/dates.ts` is now the one place a day-relative timestamp comes from (`browserDate` / `browserDateOf` / `browserDayStart` / `browserDayAt` / `noonOnBrowserDay` / `waterStorageKey`), and its `waterStorageKey` composes the page's own `waterDayKey` rather than a second copy of the deliberately-unpadded shape.

The guard is a **source scan**, in `fixtures/dates.test.ts`, run by the web unit suite rather than by Playwright. It has to be: the defect is invisible to any run whose two zones happen to agree that hour, so no assertion inside a spec can catch it and no green suite is evidence of its absence. The scan bans the local-zone date getters and setters outright over the whole `tests-e2e` tree, with a reasoned allowlist — a converted file must be deleted from it and an allowlisted file that stops matching fails the test, so the list cannot rot into stale exemptions. It also asserts the config still pins UTC, because `dates.ts` builds in UTC and a moved pin would make every helper silently wrong at once. The allowlist's four `not yet converted` entries are the same bug on the dashboard, gear and dashboard-journey surfaces, filed rather than fixed here; the rest are sites the scan cannot distinguish — a read inside `page.evaluate` already runs in the browser, a `y/m/d` constructed and formatted in one zone is zone-neutral, and a calendar *year* only diverges across New Year.

Verified by running the pre-fix specs under the divergence rather than by reasoning about it: at 15:40 UTC, `TZ=Pacific/Kiritimati` (local date one day ahead of UTC) failed six of the thirty-two nutrition tests and `TZ=Pacific/Midway` (same calendar date, wall clock eleven hours behind) failed the evening-seeded grouping test; the converted specs pass thirty-two of thirty-two under both, and under no override. One of the six, `meal-detail`, was not on the filed list — the report that named the affected specs had enumerated them by hand.

## 729. The data-export-ready notification: the staleness objection is answered by read-time URL minting, not waived — so the message links to the page and carries no URL at all

**Decided (2026-08-25, closing the `followups.md` entry that had stood as NOT planned longer than any other in the email thread.)** Its stated reason was specific and, at the time, correct: "the export endpoint is **synchronous** and returns a 10-minute signed URL inline; an async email would arrive stale. Revisit only if export moves to an async/job model." Both halves of the precondition have since expired. The export IS an async job model ([§ 717](#717)), and the queued rail is the only rail on either client ([§ 724](#724)).

**The staleness objection is answered by the design that closed it, not hand-waved past.** § 717 refused to store the signed URL and stored the object **path** instead, precisely because a URL minted when the build finished starts its clock at a moment the subject had no part in choosing. Web's status endpoint signs at read time; mobile signs at the tap. That property is what makes a notification honest here: the message carries a link to **`/settings/account`** and nothing else — no URL, no token, no expiry of its own. The archive behind it lives 7 days (`cleanup_stale_export_blobs`), and the ten-minute window opens when the subject arrives. **The moment this notification carries a signed URL, the original objection is back**, so the deep-link tables on both sides say so at the arm rather than in a comment somewhere else: `pathForKind`, `notificationLinkFor`, and `pushTargetFromUrl` each point at the page.

**It is one `notifications` row, not a fourth job kind.** Every transport already exists as a sibling consumer of that table — `notification_email`, `web_push`, `native_push` — so a new kind gets email, browser push and locked-phone push for the price of a CHECK widen and a catalogue entry. Nothing about the export is special enough to earn its own rail, and a rail of its own would need its own preference, its own suppression check and its own idempotency stamp, all of which already exist here.

**Idempotency is one statement, and it lives in SQL.** The queue is at-least-once and `data_export` carries `max_attempts = 2`, so a redelivery after a successful build is the ordinary case, not the edge. `notify_data_export_ready()` (migration `20270607_001`) takes the row `for update`, refuses unless it is `ready` with an `object_path` and not already stamped, then inserts the inbox row and writes `notified_at` in the same statement. The stamp is a column on `data_export_jobs` rather than a derived "does a notification row exist" check, because the subject may delete a notification from their own inbox — and a deleted row must not read as *never notified* and re-announce a fortnight-old export the next time anything touches the job.

**The handler asks on the already-built path too, and that is the point of putting the stamp in the RPC.** § 717's early return — "row is `ready` with a path, skip the rebuild" — used to end the handler. It now announces first. The window that covers is a crash between the `Finish` write and the announcement: the archive exists, the row says ready, and the only thing missing is that nobody told the subject. Announcing only on the fresh-build path would inherit that gap; announcing on both **repairs** it, and is safe only because the stamp is server-side. The handler keeps no flag of its own.

**A failed announcement never fails the export**, and the reason is stronger than the general layered-resilience rule. The archive is in Storage, the row says ready, and the status endpoint the message merely points at is already reporting it — so returning an error would spend the second attempt rebuilding a whole archive to fix a missing email, *and that attempt would find the row ready and skip*, so it could not even repair what it cost. The failure is logged and the job finishes.

**The preference is a per-kind MUTE, opt-out, and its direction is the opposite of the engagement streams' on purpose.** `email_weekly_digest` / `email_lifecycle_drip` are opt-IN because they are marketing, where the absence of a choice is the absence of consent. This is transactional in the strongest sense available — the subject requested the export minutes earlier — so an opt-in default would mean the feature does nothing at all for everyone who has never opened `/settings/preferences`, which is the gap the follow-up was filed to close. The channel-level `email_notifications` was rejected as the only control for the opposite reason: muting it to stop one notice also stops direct messages and event-day reminders, which is not a proportionate instrument for "no mail about my own data-rights requests".

What IS preserved is that the key can only ever **subtract**. `kindMuted` is consulted inside `shouldEmail` / `shouldPush` alongside the channel mode, never instead of it, so `email_notifications = 'off'` still silences the kind and no per-kind key can promote a kind past a channel mute — pinned in both directions. Only the literal `'off'` mutes: an absent key is a runner who never chose, and a non-string or unrecognised value is a corrupt bag, neither of which is a decision to stop being told about their own archive. And the **inbox row is never withheld** — the mute has exactly the scope `email_notifications` / `push_notifications` have, which is the outbound channels.

**Both gates now take the whole prefs bag rather than a pre-resolved mode.** `shouldEmail(kind, mode)` became `shouldEmail(kind, prefs)`, and the same for `shouldPush`. Every call site derived the mode from that same bag one line earlier, so nothing is lost — and a caller that had to remember to consult a second key separately would eventually be a channel that forgot to, with a miss that is invisible because the mail still sends.

**`notifications` is a guarded table and the widen takes the two-step.** It is the first `notifications` kind widen to do so; all twelve before it (`20260903_001` through `20270218_001`) dropped and recreated the CHECK in one statement, which scans every notification ever written under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for a widen that cannot invalidate a single existing row. `GRANDFATHER_CUTOFF` moves to `20270607` as the max-version bookkeeping its own test enforces, not as an exemption.

**Mobile gets the inbox row and the tap, not a preference surface.** The kind's arm in `profile_screen.dart`'s `_verbFor` is not optional — `profile_screen_test.dart` reads the `NotificationKind` union and fails a kind with no arm, exactly as the worker's copy and link guards do — and a tap parks `SettingsDestination.account` for the shell to drain (§ 710), because the inbox screen holds none of that screen's dependencies. `pushTargetFromUrl` gained a `settings/account` arm for the same reason: a native push landing on the notification list would leave the runner one screen short of the thing it is about, and mobile push is where this matters most, since § 724 refused a background poller on the grounds that iOS background refresh is opportunistic. The **mute toggle is web-only** per § 24: mobile's Preferences screen enumerates channels and engagement streams, not notification kinds, and inventing a per-kind section there to host one row would be a mobile-first surface.

**What is not verified.** No Playwright spec drives the notification end to end. The rail it rides is the one every other kind rides, and the new parts are pinned by 14 pgtap assertions, 6 worker handler tests and the existing copy / deep-link / kind-coverage guards on both platforms — but the honest statement is that nobody has watched an export finish and an email land in Mailpit from a browser.

## 730. A security override is guarded as a declaration AND as an outcome — and § 711's closing question is answered: relocating `deno.lock` does not remove its `workspace` section

**Decided 2026-08-25.** Two lockfile guards, one of them new and one of them now justified by a measurement rather than by an open question.

**The `pnpm.overrides` block went missing and nothing but a wall of red said so.** Dependabot PR #812 (`@types/node` 26.1.2 → 26.2.0) regenerated `pnpm-lock.yaml` and dropped its top-level `overrides:` block entirely. Every job running `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` then aborted with `ERR_PNPM_LOCKFILE_CONFIG_MISMATCH  Cannot proceed with the frozen installation. The current "overrides" configuration doesn't match the value found in the lockfile` — 17 checks went red, all 14 Playwright shards and the live-hub and SSO lanes among them, every one of them failing at dependency install before a single test ran, under an error that names pnpm and says nothing about what changed. It cost a full red CI cycle to work out.

**That loud failure is not what the guard is for.** It announced itself and then fixed itself. The failure worth building against is the quiet one: those four entries — `cookie` ^1.0.2 (GHSA-pxg6-pf52-xh8x), `devalue` ^5.8.1 (GHSA-77vg-94rm-hx3p), `undici` ^7.28.0 (the five SOCKS5/cookie/websocket/cache CVEs fixed in 7.28.0), `brace-expansion` ^5.0.8 (GHSA-mh99-v99m-4gvg) — are supply-chain pins, each nudging a transitive dependency off a version with a live advisory its own parent has not bumped past. Any path where the declaration and a lockfile diverge *without* a frozen install reading them (a plain `pnpm install`, a hand-edit, the other resolver) leaves the pins declared and not applied, and the vulnerable versions come back with nothing to say so. A pin that can go missing unnoticed is not a pin.

**So `scripts/check_pnpm_overrides.mjs` checks the outcome, not only the intent.** Four assertions, in the order a reader wants them: `pnpm.overrides` is present and non-empty; `pnpm-lock.yaml` carries an `overrides:` block matching it key for key (what #812 deleted); the npm-style top-level `overrides` block matches too once flattened; and every version each pin names, **in both lockfile package trees**, satisfies the pin — with at least one such version present, so a pin whose package has left the tree fails rather than passing over nothing. The fourth is the one no frozen install can perform: a lockfile that *declares* an override and resolved around it looks healthy to `--frozen-lockfile`, which compares the declaration and stops.

**Both lockfiles, because both are installed from.** The repo carries `package-lock.json` and `pnpm-lock.yaml`, and the split is real: `parity-types`, `build-web` and `cross-client-roundtrip` install with `npm ci`, while `e2e-web` (14 shards), `e2e-web-livehub`, `e2e-web-exporthub` and `e2e-web-sso` install with `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`. Two resolvers reading two declarations of one security decision must agree, or half of CI installs a patched tree and half does not — hence the npm-vs-pnpm declaration comparison. The npm side is checked by **outcome only**, and that is measured rather than assumed: npm 12.0.1 writing a lockfileVersion-3 lock records no `overrides` key in its root `packages[""]` entry even when the override demonstrably redirected a resolution (built as a scratch project with a `file:` override that genuinely moved a dependency; the tree moved, the block was absent). npm's lock records what the pins *did*, so that is what the guard reads there.

**The flat spelling is canonical.** pnpm writes a scoped override as `'@sveltejs/kit>cookie': ^1.0.2`; npm writes the same thing as a nested object under the parent's name. This repo declares both, because both resolvers install here. The script normalises npm's nested form **into** pnpm's flat form rather than the reverse, because the flat form is the only one pnpm ever writes into `pnpm-lock.yaml` — so it is the spelling the frozen-install comparison actually runs against, and everything downstream (target resolution, the tree scan) then deals with one shape. The one npm spelling that has no pnpm equivalent, the `"."` key pinning a parent's own version, is reported rather than silently dropped.

**Check-only, deliberately — the contrast with `sync_deno_lock.mjs` is the argument.** That script auto-writes because the section it owns is inert (nothing resolves against it) and deno canonicalizes the ranges so a hand-edit does not stick ([§ 706](#706)). This one is the opposite on both counts. The `overrides:` block is load-bearing, and the only thing that can legitimately rewrite it is a real resolution pass (`pnpm install --lockfile-only`), which re-resolves the whole graph and can move versions the guard never looked at — the same class of write `sync_deno_lock` already refuses for `remote`/`redirects`. Regenerating a lockfile is a human's decision to review, so the guard reports and names the command instead of running it.

**Verified against the real regression, not only against fixtures.** #812's state was reconstructed in a scratch copy — the committed tree with the `overrides:` block deleted and nothing else touched — and `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` against it reproduces `ERR_PNPM_LOCKFILE_CONFIG_MISMATCH` verbatim, which is what makes the reconstruction faithful rather than merely plausible. The guard exits 1 on it naming the missing block, exits 1 on a second reconstruction where the block is intact but `cookie` was resolved to 0.6.0 (the quiet case: two errors, one per pin that reaches `cookie`), and exits 0 on the committed tree — 6 overrides, honoured by all 788 resolved package entries across the two lockfiles. It runs in `parity-types` beside the deno check, drift first then its own suite, for the reason § 706 records: this suite's last cases read the committed tree, so running them first would report a broken tool over an ordinary stale lockfile.

**§ 711's closing question is answered, and the answer is no.** That entry asked whether `deno.lock` records a `workspace` section at all when the lock does not sit at the root of an npm workspace — because a lockfile with no generated half needs no guard, no weekly `pnpm sync:deno-lock` chore and no Dependabot problem. The experiment it named was run: a copy of the lock staged at `apps/backend/deno.lock` with the workspace root still above it, checked with the same `deno check --no-remote --node-modules-dir=none` the sync script uses. It exits 0 and the lock comes back with all four sections — `redirects`, `remote`, `version`, `workspace` — the `workspace` half carrying the same 32 specs, the same `members: ["apps/web"]` and the root `overrides` block, identical to the baseline with the lock in place. Adding a sibling `apps/backend/deno.json` naming `{"lock": "./deno.lock"}` changes nothing except a warning that `"lock" field can only be specified in the workspace root deno.json file`. (deno 2.9.3.)

**The mechanism, established rather than inferred.** A third variant removed the root `package.json` — the one declaring `workspaces` — from above the nested lock and left everything else identical: deno then writes `["redirects", "remote", "version"]` and no `workspace` section at all. So the section is a function of *whether an npm workspace exists anywhere above the lock*, not of whether the lock sits at its root. Relocating the lock within the repo cannot remove it; only taking the lock out of the npm workspace entirely would, and that is not on the table — the lock's load-bearing half is the Edge Functions' integrity pins, which the Supabase CLI writes at the repo root. **`sync:deno-lock` therefore stays**, and this result is what justifies keeping it rather than an unexamined assumption that it must.

**What this deliberately does not do.** It does not add `pnpm` to the `parity-types` job — the guard is stdlib-only `node` over two committed files and needs no resolver, which is also why it can run before any install in a bare checkout. It does not attempt to keep the two `package.json` declaration blocks in sync automatically; they are four lines each, and a guard that fails on disagreement is a better instrument than a generator that picks a winner. And it does not widen into a general advisory checker: the pins' rationale lives in `package.json`'s `_overrides_rationale`, and deciding when one may be dropped is a reading of upstream's lockfile, not a thing CI can compute.

## 731. A freeze assertion anchored on the last fix's timestamp races that fix's own credit — and the mis-anchor was quietly weakening the assertion below it

**Decided 2026-08-25.** The custom_watch `dropout` sim scenario went red on CI while passing locally on the same commit, on a branch that changes no firmware, no Rust and no harness code. The recorder was correct in both runs — it settled on the same 110.4 m inside the void — so the defect was in how the scenario read it.

**The race.** `void_start` is the decoded stamp of the last `gps: fix` line, but the recorder publishes that fix's *credited distance* after the fix line rather than with it: the fix is logged when it is decoded, the snapshot once it has been folded into the running total. `frozen` was taken from the first snapshot strictly past `void_start`, so it raced the credit. Locally the credited snapshot landed in the same millisecond as the fix and the anchor was right; on CI (run 32870450327) a `paused` snapshot carrying the pre-fix distance arrived 1 ms after the fix, became the anchor at 104.4 m, and the credit that followed it read as 6 m of movement "inside a void with no fixes in it". The displacement was measured by the last real fix and belongs to it, not to the void.

**The fix is the shape already in this file.** The pause assertion twelve lines below had been bitten by the same class of lottery and carries `FIX_STALE_FLIP_SLACK_S` for it, with a comment recording that it "passed locally and failed on a CI runner from that alone" — the frozen-distance check simply never got the same treatment, and the constant's own comment still claimed it "covers the void from its first snapshot", which had stopped being true. The freeze is now asserted from a `DROPOUT_FIX_CREDIT_SETTLE_S` window past `void_start`, and nothing inside that window may read *above* the settled anchor, so a lump of the void's own displacement credited early still fails rather than becoming the anchor.

**What makes this more than a flake, and the reason it is written down.** `frozen` is also the baseline the re-anchor check measures `DROPOUT_RESUME_M` from. With the anchor sampled one fix low, the void's own settled value already cleared the 3 m threshold before the reacquire happened at all — so on any run that lost this race, the assertion guarding run_recorder #330 would have passed for a firmware that never re-anchored. A racy anchor did not just produce a false red; it produced a false green one assertion later. The tell that this was harness and not firmware was that both runs agreed on the settled distance to the millimetre, which is worth reaching for first the next time a sim scenario disagrees with itself across hosts.

**Verified by replay, not by re-running until green.** The recorded CI log that failed and the local log that passed were both replayed through the old and new logic: the CI timeline now anchors at 110.4 m and passes with 47 of its 50 in-void snapshots still asserted frozen, the local run is unchanged, and injected creeping-credit, far-edge-lump and early-lump regressions each still fail. A retry would have hidden all of it.

---

## 732. A spec's backend cross-check stacks two claims, and collapsing them turned 28 assertions into false greens

**Decided 2026-08-25.** `const { data } = await admin.from(...)` discards the error. An absent result becomes `null`, and the `?? 0` / `?? []` at the assertion renders that absence as a legitimate value. A spec's service-role cross-check is really two claims — that the read reached the database, and that what came back is what the feature wrote — and that one line collapses them into one.

**The loud failure is not the one that mattered.** 69 sites across 42 specs did this. **41 misdirect**: the gear-lifecycle rollup reported `Expected: 6000, Received: 0` and read exactly like a broken derived cache when the read had in fact been refused, which is how it cost a debugging session pointed at the trigger. **28 were false greens** — a failed read *satisfies* a zero-or-empty expectation, so the assertion silently stops testing anything. Those 28 include the club member-write RLS negatives, the DM permission boundaries and the safety-contact withdrawal: precisely the assertions whose whole job is to prove that something is *refused*, and precisely the ones a broken read makes vacuous. A negative assertion that cannot tell "denied" from "never asked" is not a security test.

**`fixtures/db-read.ts` keeps the two claims apart.** `readRow` / `readRows` / `readMaybeRow` / `readCount` either produce rows or throw naming themselves, the SQLSTATE and the driver message, so the `expect` that follows is only ever about the feature. Two distinctions are deliberate: zero rows stays a real answer rather than an error, and `.single()`'s PGRST116 is reported as an absent row rather than as a broken read — the two point at different bugs and flattening them would rebuild the original defect one layer up.

**Same rule the product code already follows.** `fetchMySafetyContacts` reports its error instead of degrading to `[]` because on a safety surface "you have no emergency contacts" is the one wrong answer a runner might act on ([§ 720](#720)). This is that rule applied to the harness, where the cost is not a wrong answer to a runner but a green suite that has stopped asking.

## 734. Sending a route to one person offers the DM-*eligible* set, not the follower list — and widens nothing the copy-link share didn't

**Decided (2026-08-25.)** [route_direct_share.md](../features/route_direct_share.md)'s v1 ships on web: a "Send to a follower" button beside Share on `/routes/[id]` opens `SendRouteDialog.svelte`, which sends the public `/share/route/[id]` URL as a plain `direct_messages` body through the existing `sendDm`. No migration, no column, no new RLS — v2's typed attachment (a route card rendered in the thread) is still owed and deliberately unbuilt.

**The picker is built from both follow directions, because that is what the INSERT policy admits.** `direct_messages`' send gate (migration `20261026_001`) requires an edge in *either* direction plus no block either way. A picker fed by `fetchFollowers` alone would therefore hide every person the sender follows one-way — a send RLS would have accepted, offered nowhere — while a picker fed by an open people search would offer sends the server is going to refuse with a 42501. `social/dm_recipients.ts` merges the two fetches into one deduped, name-ordered list tagged `mutual` / `follows_you` / `you_follow`, and the e2e pins the asymmetric case end to end: the seed's Morgan follows nobody, so her appearing at all is the union being real rather than incidental. The **block** half of the same gate is deliberately *not* mirrored client-side — `user_blocks` is owner-read only, so a client cannot see a block placed *on* it, and rendering a "can't be messaged" marker would require leaking exactly the fact the block exists to hide. Those sends fail server-side and surface through `sendDm`'s existing 42501 branch.

**Privacy: the send rides the copy-link share's step rather than inventing a second one.** A route polyline can start at someone's front door, so the question is what a recipient can newly see. The DM carries a *link*, and what it resolves to is decided at read time by the route's own visibility — `/share/route/[id]` reads the `public_routes` view and pulls the track through `clip_route_for_viewer`, so a non-owner still gets the owner's privacy zones clipped server-side. The one exposure-widening act is the public flip, and both affordances reach it through the *same* `runShare()` and the *same* `share-confirm-dialog` §298's amendment added, with a `shareIntent` flag recording which asked; cancelling leaves the route private **and** leaves the picker closed. A non-owner can only send an already-public route (the button is gated `is_public || isOwner`, and `setRoutePublic` is owner-scoped by RLS anyway). The dialog says outright that the recipient receives the *public* link and can forward it, because targeting a delivery is not an access-control narrowing and copy that implied otherwise would be the real privacy failure. A per-recipient grant on a route that stays private is a different feature needing its own table and RLS — not a DM body.

**No second anti-spam mechanism was added, and the rail's gap is recorded rather than papered over.** v1 opens no new insert path, so it inherits the follow-graph + block policy and nothing else. While wiring it: the `direct_messages` rail has **no rate limit at all** — the follow gate is its entire abuse story, and `check_rate_limit` is used by the route generator and the OSRM proxy but never by DMs. Adding a route-send-only throttle would have left `/messages` itself unlimited and put two mechanisms on one rail, so the durable fix (a trigger over the existing `check_rate_limit`, covering every sender) is filed in `followups.md` instead. What this change *does* carry is a single-send-in-flight guard, so a double click cannot post twice.

**Fail-closed on both reads and writes, because the two silences look identical otherwise.** A failed follower fetch renders an error + Retry, never the empty-picker copy — "you have nobody to send to" and "we could not find out who you can send to" are different sentences and only one is worth acting on, and the honest one is the one that vanishes under a `catch { return [] }`. A refused or thrown send renders the reason and never the sent confirmation.

**Mobile stays gated, re-verified rather than assumed.** §24 puts web first, and the mobile leg was already gated on a mobile `/messages` twin existing. It still does not: nothing under `apps/mobile_android/lib/` or `packages/` references `direct_messages` or a `sendDm` equivalent, and `parity.md`'s "Direct messages (1:1)" row is `✗` on both device columns. So `parity.md` records this row `✗` on Android and iOS with the reason spelled out — a route-detail send button on a phone with no inbox to deliver into would be drift, not parity. Mobile's targeted send remains the shipped Share link → OS share sheet.

## 735. Two plan-week bugs from the same root: a duration is not a calendar span, and a generator offset is not a weekday

**Decided 2026-08-25.** A training bug hunt over the parity pairs turned up two defects that both come from treating a derived quantity as if it were the thing it is derived from.

**`/plans` named a plan week short for the whole of DST.** `/plans/[id]` buckets today through `currentPlanWeekIndex`, which works in whole UTC epoch-days for the reason issue #338 records. The list page rolled its own: two local midnights subtracted and floored over `7 * 86_400_000`. A local-midnight span crossing a spring-forward is 167 h, so the floor lands a week short on every week-rollover day and stays wrong for the rest of DST. Measured in `Europe/London` for a plan starting 2026-03-23: on 2026-03-30 the span is 601200000 ms (6.958 d), the list card read Week 1 while the detail page read Week 2. Two surfaces, two numbers, same plan. The list now routes through the shared helper and a source guard forbids the elapsed-millisecond division on both plan surfaces — the fix is the guard as much as the call, because this is the second time this arithmetic has been written by hand.

**The mobile plan wizard accepted a non-Sunday start.** `generatePlan` hard-anchors day 0 of the start week to the Sunday long run: `longDow` / `restDow` / `qaDow` / `qbDow` are OFFSETS from the start date, not weekdays. Web enforces it (the editor snaps forward on change and refuses to persist a misaligned plan); the phone seeded a Sunday default and then let `showDatePicker` return any day unchanged, on all four create paths. Picking Wednesday produced a plan whose long run is Wednesday, rest day Thursday and quality days Friday and Sunday — contradicting the generator's own comments and the plan the same inputs build on web. Fixed as a registered parity pair consumed as the picker's `selectableDayPredicate`, so a non-Sunday is *unpickable* in both the calendar and keyboard-entry modes rather than snapped after the fact.

**And a test that documented the bug it was meant to catch.** The Dart suite asserted `currentVdot([parkrun])` is null while `_sourceQualifies` maps parkrun to true and a sibling test asserted every source qualifies. It passed on the wall clock, not the source filter — the fixture defaulted to 2026-01-01 and the call was unpinned, so the rolling 90-day recency guard answered first. Pinning `now` to 2026-04-05 returns 69.6, not null. The test would have re-introduced the removed behaviour for anyone who pinned the clock to de-flake it, which is the failure mode worth naming: **an assertion that passes for a reason other than the one it claims is worse than no assertion**, because it actively defends the old bug.

## 736. A live region only announces what changes while it is already mounted

**Decided 2026-08-25.** `ToastContainer` mounted the live region and the toast text in the same `{#if}`, so the region and its first message entered the accessibility tree as a single mutation — and a live region announces changes made *inside* it, not its own arrival. One toast at a time is the ordinary case across ~400 `showToast` call sites, so in the common path nothing was announced at all (WCAG 4.1.3). Both regions are now permanently mounted with only their text changing, the idiom `CoachChat`'s announcer already used. They carry a bare `aria-live` rather than `role="status"` / `role="alert"` deliberately: a permanent alert role on every page would make the bare `getByRole('alert')` in two existing specs ambiguous, so the technique is chosen to fit the app rather than copied from the spec sheet.

**The remedy mattered as much as the diagnosis, and the first one was wrong.** The fix originally used a visually-hidden mirror carrying the message with the visible stack marked `aria-hidden`. That announces correctly and puts the same sentence in the DOM twice — and `aria-hidden` hides an element from the accessibility tree, not from a text query, so every `getByText('<toast text>')` in the e2e suite became a strict-mode violation resolving to two elements. It passed on its own branch and on every other branch, and only broke where both met: three specs failed on the integrated branch that pass on either half alone. The stacks themselves are now permanent and only their children change, so the announcer and the visible toast are ONE element and the message renders once. The guard pins the absence of a mirror, not just the presence of a region, because "announced correctly" and "announced once" are different properties and only the first is obvious from reading the component.

**The login page's only route home was focusable, nameless and roleless.** `.brand-pane` is `display:none` below 56rem and `.logo-mobile` is its exact mirror above it, so on every desktop viewport the brand pane's `<a href="/">` is the ONLY link home — and `aria-hidden="true"` on the aside left keyboard focus landing on a void (axe `aria-hidden-focus`; WCAG 4.1.2 and 2.4.3), on the app's busiest page. Exposing the aside duplicates nothing because only one of the two logo links is ever rendered; the brand kicker, which IS rendered twice above 56rem, keeps its `aria-hidden`. The password-reset fields were named by placeholder alone — a name that vanishes on the first keystroke — while the sign-in form one route away already paired each field with a visually-hidden label.

## 737. Bounding a flood and admitting a burst are two different windows — and a throttle in a trigger counts differently from the same call in an RPC

**Decided 2026-08-25.** The `direct_messages` rail shipped with no throttle of any kind. Its whole anti-spam story was the INSERT policy's follow-graph + block gate (`20261026_001`), so anyone already inside a sender's follow graph could be messaged without bound, from `/messages` or from the route-send dialog [§ 734](#734-sending-a-route-to-one-person-offers-the-dm-eligible-set-not-the-follower-list--and-widens-nothing-the-copy-link-share-didnt) added. `check_rate_limit` had existed since `20260604_001` and backed the route generator (60/h) and the OSRM proxy (1200/h), but nothing on this path. Migration `20270608_001` closes it with a `before insert` trigger on the table.

**The throttle is on the rail, not on an affordance, because the rail has exactly one write path.** `direct_messages` is written by a PostgREST INSERT and by nothing else — no RPC, no Edge Function, no Go worker touches it, which the sweep confirmed rather than assumed. A per-row trigger is therefore total: `/messages`, the route-send dialog, and every affordance not yet written are covered by one mechanism, and the pgtap pins that even a multi-row `insert … select` is refused per row rather than smuggled through. § 734 declined a send-only throttle on exactly this reasoning and the reasoning still holds; the trigger reuses `enforce_create_rate_limit` (`20260907_001`) rather than a second helper, so the DM buckets get the same service-role / null-auth / forged-sender skips the clubs and routes buckets already have.

**One fixed window cannot both admit a burst and bound a flood, so there are two.** `check_rate_limit` buckets by `floor(epoch / window) * window`, which means an "N per hour" limit admits all N in a single instant at the top of the hour. Set N high enough that a spirited two-person exchange never trips it and a script delivers the entire allowance in about two seconds; set N low enough to stop that and a real conversation trips it in minutes — and a limit a normal conversation trips is worse than no limit at all. So the rate and the volume are bounded separately: **`send_direct_message_burst` at 30 per 60 s** and **`send_direct_message` at 250 per 3600 s**. 30/min is one message every two seconds sustained for a full minute from a single sender, deliberately placed above any plausible human rate because a false positive on a genuine conversation is the failure this is sized to avoid; 250/h averages one message every 14 s for an hour, heavier than any real thread and sitting between the route generator's 60/h and the OSRM proxy's 1200/h. Together they cap a flood at 250 messages spread over at least ~8 minutes rather than 250 in two seconds — long enough for the recipient to block. Neither bucket is decoration: the hour bucket is the tighter of the two in aggregate (30/min would otherwise permit 1800/h), and the burst bucket is the only thing that stops the hour's allowance arriving all at once.

**The hour bucket is checked first, and the reason is not the one it looks like.** `20260604_001`'s own header says a denied call still counts, because it increments before it compares. That is true of the standalone RPC the Edge Functions call, in its own transaction — and false here. Inside a `before insert` trigger the raise aborts the statement, and the increment rolls back with it: measured, a refused send left the burst bucket on 30 rather than 31 and never created the hour bucket's row at all. On this rail the counter therefore counts **successful sends**, which is the semantics a cap should have — a flooder cannot be punished into a longer lockout by hammering, and equally cannot slow themselves down by their own refusals. Bounding the refused attempts is the per-IP WAF's job, not this counter's. What the order *does* decide is which refusal the sender is told about when both windows are spent, and the honest answer there is the binding one: checking the burst first would say "try again in 40 seconds" to someone who has forty minutes to wait.

**The refusal reuses the existing parser rather than inventing a second path.** `sendDm` re-threw the `PostgrestError` verbatim for anything that was not a 42501, and both surfaces render `e.message` in a `role="alert"` line — so the sender would have read `rate limit exceeded for send_direct_message_burst, retry in 41s`. It now routes the P0001 through `rateLimitErrorMessage`, the existing TS↔Dart pair, *after* the 42501 branch (a follow-graph refusal and a "too fast" refusal are different answers and only one is worth waiting out), with a source guard pinning that order. The bucket names are snake_case because the pair's regex is `(\w+)` — the followups entry proposed `'direct-messages'`, which that regex cannot match, so a hyphenated bucket would have fallen straight back to the raw exception the wiring exists to prevent. Both new buckets land on the pair's generic `'doing that'` verb: adding a DM-specific verb means editing the Dart side too, and mobile has no DM surface at all, so a dead branch there is not worth a lockstep edit. The e2e pins that the composer never shows the raw string and that the typed draft survives the refusal.

**Locking, stated rather than assumed.** `CREATE TRIGGER` takes `SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE` — measured on the local PG 17.6 stack, not recalled. It conflicts with `ROW EXCLUSIVE`, so concurrent writes to `direct_messages` wait; it does not conflict with `ACCESS SHARE` or `ROW SHARE`, and a queued request only blocks later *conflicting* requests, so the thread list, `dm_threads()` and the unread badge all proceed even while it waits. The work is catalogue-only — no scan, no rewrite, no validation pass — so the hold is O(1) whatever the table holds. `migration_locks.md`'s lock-reference table had no row for `CREATE TRIGGER`; it does now.
## 738. The § 728 allowlist's "deliberate" half was not deliberate: four of its five reasoned exemptions were the same defect wearing a different sentence

**Decided 2026-08-25**, finishing the [§ 728](#728) sweep. The filed follow-up named four unconverted specs and said the rest of `LOCAL_ZONE_ALLOWED` "are deliberate and need no work". Both halves of that were wrong, and in opposite directions.

**The enumeration was already stale and was never right.** Round 14 (#816) converted `dashboard/week-strip`, `dashboard/consistency` and `dashboard/dashboard-readiness-gym-journey` without touching the follow-up or the guard's own "the four marked not yet converted" doc comment, so the entry still listed three specs that no longer matched it. And the original list of "four" was five: `settings/gear-backfill.spec.ts` carried a `not yet converted` reason from the first commit and appears in neither the follow-up's enumeration nor its count. § 728's prose gets it right — it names "the dashboard, gear and dashboard-journey surfaces" — while its own numeral says four. Two entries were actually outstanding at this branch's base.

**The `datetime-local` exemption does not survive, and the reason it was written is the reason it fails.** It was carried as a different shape — a wall clock typed *into* the DOM rather than a row seeded through the admin client. But `RunEditor` submits `new Date(startedAt).toISOString()`, and a `datetime-local` control holds no zone, so the browser resolves that naive string in its own — pinned to UTC. Filling it from the runner's clock submits an instant off by the runner's whole offset, and the dashboard goal card buckets instants into a Monday-to-Monday **UTC** week. Swept hour by hour across one UTC week, the submitted run lands outside the week the browser computes for **4 of 168 UTC hours in America/New_York, 11 in Pacific/Midway, 14 in Pacific/Kiritimati, 10 in Australia/Sydney and 0 in UTC** — Monday 00:00 onward for zones behind, Sunday's tail for zones ahead — and both the 40 % and 100 % goal assertions fail there. Same defect, different door.

**The three coaching specs were exempted for a property they did not have.** Their reason — "shifts an instant by whole days and reads the UTC date back, so the result already tracks the browser day" — describes `d.setDate(d.getDate() + n)`, which preserves the **local** wall clock. A local day is 23 or 25 hours twice a year, so across a transition the instant moves 23 or 25 hours and the UTC date read back is a day off. Swept 400 days × 24 UTC hours × the offsets these specs actually pass: **0 mismatches in UTC, Pacific/Midway and Pacific/Kiritimati** (no DST) and **168 in each of America/New_York, Europe/London, Australia/Sydney, America/Santiago and Asia/Beirut** — two per transition per day of offset, so `browserDate(-1)` and `browserDate(1)` can name the same day and a workout seeded as past renders as upcoming. Three private copies of one helper is also exactly the pattern § 728 was written to delete, so they route through `browserDate` rather than being repaired in place.

**`routes/segments.spec.ts` was the worst of them and its reason was wrong on its face.** "Derives a birth YEAR for an age-grade fixture, not a day" described `new Date(new Date().getFullYear() - 32, 0, 1).toISOString().slice(0, 10)`, which builds **local** Jan 1 and reads it back in **UTC**. Measured at `2026-08-25T14:30Z` it yields `1993-12-31` in Australia/Sydney and Asia/Beirut against `1994-01-01` in UTC: a whole year off for every zone east of Greenwich, **every day of the year**, not only across New Year. Nothing failed only because the cohort band is five years wide and 32 sits at its centre. The birth date is now composed as a string, so no `Date` is built in one zone and read in another.

**`settings/gear-backfill.spec.ts` was wrong about the fixture it built, not about the result.** `gearPurchaseSince` resolves `purchased_at` at LOCAL midnight — local being the browser's. The spec typed the *runner's* yesterday, so over 24 UTC hours the window it opened differs from the browser's yesterday for **4 hours in America/New_York and 11 in Pacific/Midway** (a day too wide) and **14 in Pacific/Kiritimati** (a day too narrow, registering a pair "bought yesterday" as bought today). The planted run is stamped `now`, and `now` is inside the window under every offset up to ±14, which is why no assertion ever caught it.

**One exemption survives and it is the only one that ever should have.** `plans/calendar.spec.ts` reads the day inside `page.evaluate` — which runs in the browser, and *must*, because that read is the assertion's whole point — and formats two fixed `y/m/d` values by constructing and rendering them in one zone. That is zone-neutral by construction, and it was checked rather than assumed: both formatters over all 366 days of 2026 hash identically across UTC, America/New_York, Pacific/Midway, Pacific/Kiritimati, Australia/Sydney, America/Santiago, Asia/Beirut and the half-hour-DST Australia/Lord_Howe. `fixtures/plan-today.ts` joins it as the second entry only because the widened scan below now reaches its `toLocaleString`, which names `timeZone: 'UTC'` explicitly.

**Four holes in the scan are closed, each proved by planting the shape and watching the suite go red.** The scan is the only instrument that can see this defect — no green run is evidence of its absence — so a shape it misses is a shape that returns. (1) Only `playwright.config.ts` was asserted to pin UTC; there are **four** lane configs (sharded, livehub, exporthub, sso), each with its own `use` block, and `dates.ts` is silently wrong for a whole lane if any pin moves — all four are read and the count is asserted, so a rename cannot make the loop vacuous. (2) `getTimezoneOffset` was unbanned, and subtracting it from an instant is the standard spelling of a local wall clock (`RunEditor.nowLocalIso` uses it), reaching the bug with no banned getter in sight. (3) A date-time literal with no zone designator handed to `new Date` / `Date.parse` is parsed in the runner's zone by specification — a date-ONLY literal is UTC, so the time part is required and `'2026-08-25T12:00:00Z'` is left alone; both directions are pinned. (4) Only `.ts` was read, so a `.mjs` under `tests-e2e` was invisible. `toLocaleDateString` was banned while `toLocaleString`, `toLocaleTimeString`, `toDateString` and `toTimeString` were not, which is half a family; all are banned now.

**Verification, and what it could not show.** Every converted spec was run under the ambient runner zone and under two zones on opposite sides of UTC — `Pacific/Midway` (UTC−11) and `Pacific/Kiritimati` (UTC+14) — green in all three: dashboard-journey 1/1, gear-backfill 2/2, the three coaching specs 12/12, and the recap + segments batch 37/37. **The pre-fix specs also pass under both probe zones today**, and saying so matters more than the greens do: today is a Wednesday in UTC, the goal week has fifty hours of slack either side, and no offset on earth can push the stamp out of it. That is the seam § 728 describes, not an argument that the defect is theoretical — it is why the per-zone hour counts above were measured by sweeping the clock rather than by running the suite, and why the guard is a source scan in the first place.

**Not fixed, and named rather than left to be rediscovered.** Thirty-odd sites across `tests-e2e` hard-code `http://localhost:7777` — including four `grantPermissions({ origin: 'http://localhost:7777' })` calls in the recap specs — while `playwright.config.ts` offers `PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL` as a supported override. Running this batch on a second port to get past another worktree's dev server therefore produced three clipboard failures that vanished on 7777, which is a false red for anyone who needs a second port (concurrent agents on one box do). Out of scope here and too broad to sweep alongside a date fix, but it is a real trap.
## 739. `parity.md`'s iOS column is derived from Android, not observed — so it carries no `✓`, and one guard reads the rule out of the document rather than restating it

**Decided 2026-08-25.** The matrix defined what an iOS cell means in three places and the three disagreed. The banner licensed a wired-but-unverified row to read as `Partial` / `✓`; the column key said cells stay `✗` until verified on a Mac build, simulator or device; the intentional-asymmetries list said `✗` / `Partial` *by design* until simulator-verified. Under the first reading a wired row is `✓`, under the other two it is `✗` or `Partial`, and the column read 133 `✓` / 47 `Partial` / 140 `✗` — so both readings were in live use and no reader could tell an unbuilt iOS row from an unverified one by its symbol. That is what let the Sync-and-backup block sit `✗` while the same `BackupService` sat `✓` two sections up (§ 707), and § 707 explicitly declined to settle it because picking a reading is a whole-column edit against a rule that has to be agreed first.

**The rule adopted is the honest one, and the data argues for it rather than merely permitting it.** `apps/mobile_ios/lib/` and `test/` are byte-identical to `mobile_android` (§ 39, re-verified by `diff -rq` at the time of the sweep), so for a pure-Dart feature an iOS cell contains no information the Android cell does not already carry — except when something on the iOS side obstructs the shared Dart. The cell is therefore a **derivation**, not an observation: Android `✓` → iOS `Partial`, `Partial` → `Partial`, `✗` → `✗`, `N/A` → `N/A`, with a departure allowed only where the row names the obstruction. The column keeps no `✓` at all, which sounds severe until you notice it is simply true — nothing in this matrix has been run on a Mac — and that it is what makes the column *readable*: every cell that is not `Partial` is now a claim about the code rather than about the absent device, so `✗` means unbuilt and `N/A` means impossible and neither is confusable with unverified. The alternative rule (keep `✓` for wired, per the banner) was rejected because it makes the Legend's `✓` mean one thing in four columns and another in the fifth, which is the disease rather than the cure. 44 rows had already reached for `Partial` with exactly this meaning, so the rule mostly ratifies the idiom the document was groping towards.

**The recorded counts were right on their date and are worth restating anyway.** The follow-up's 133 / 47 / 140, recounted 2026-08-24, reproduces exactly on the 2026-08-24 commit; by this round's base it was 133 `✓` / 47 `Partial` / 142 `✗` / 15 `N/A` over 337 rows, two `✗` having arrived since. What the entry omitted is the 15 `N/A` and the row total, and counting the column is less trivial than it looks: two tables head their first column `Key` rather than `Feature`, and several Notes carry a GFM-escaped `\|`, so a naive third-field count and a naive header match disagree by 22 rows. After the sweep: 313 `Partial`, 11 `✗`, 13 `N/A`, no `✓`. 268 cells moved — 133 `✓` → `Partial`, 131 `✗` → `Partial`, two `N/A` → `Partial` (wakelock during a run and the higher Pro coach cap are neither Android-only nor inapplicable — `wakelock_plus` ships iOS and the cap is server-enforced), one `N/A` → `✗` (the admin moderation queue is unbuilt on both twins, and the doc's own convention for a web-only back-office row is `✗`, which Android already carried), and one `✗` → `N/A` (Play In-App Updates has no iOS counterpart).

**Five rows depart, and each names what obstructs iOS.** The two watch-push rows, in mirror image: Wear OS dropped iPhone pairing at Wear OS 3, and the Apple Watch push is iOS-only inside the twin, dispatched on `defaultTargetPlatform`, so Android is `N/A` and there is no Android cell for the derivation to read. Health Connect is an Android platform service. Play In-App Updates likewise. And the live lock-screen notification is the one genuine unbuilt-on-iOS row the sweep found by § 707's method: `run_app/run_notification` is answered by `RunNotificationBridge.kt` and by nothing on the iOS side, which `run_notification_bridge.dart` already documented as inert there. Everything else survived the check — the pubspecs are identical apart from the package name, the only Android-only plugin is `in_app_update`, `Info.plist` already carries the location / health / bluetooth / motion / photo / camera / calendar strings plus the background modes and the auth URL scheme, and all three build configurations point at the entitlements file. Two notes that asserted otherwise were simply false: "iOS chest-strap pairing not wired" (`ble_heart_rate.dart` has no `Platform` gate, `flutter_reactive_ble` ships iOS, and `NSBluetoothAlwaysUsageDescription` is present) and "iOS roadmap item unticked" on GPX import.

**The ~30 per-row "pending Mac-runtime verification" clauses are deleted, not retained.** A rule restated once per row is a rule with thirty copies to keep in sync, which is the mechanism that produced three disagreeing prose statements in the first place; the same reasoning retires the 25 `**Android/iOS ✓**` Notes prefixes, which asserted a symbol the column no longer carries. `check_parity_matrix.dart` therefore exempts the iOS cell from its Partial-needs-Notes rule — the explanation is the column's, not the row's — and drops its iOS-ahead-of-Android rule outright, since the derivation forbids a bare iOS `✓` and a rule that can never fire is a rule nobody maintains.

**The guard reads the rule out of the document instead of restating it.** `scripts/check_parity_ios_column.mjs` parses the derivation table inside the `<!-- parity-ios-rule -->` block and enforces the column against *that*, so the mapping has literally one home and a second guard cannot drift from it; it also fails on a second block, on any prose line outside the block that pairs the iOS column with a cell symbol, and on a Legend symbol the derivation does not cover. All three deleted statements were re-added one at a time and watched to fail, along with the § 707 shape. **The exemption that was tried and removed is the interesting part**: allowing a line that *links* to the block let the reinstated column key pass, because the real sentence both linked to the block and contradicted it — a link buys nothing, so the two legitimate prose lines were reworded to name no symbol instead. A `✓` is likewise unreachable through the Notes marker: when the device run lands, the derivation table is the one line that changes and the column is swept again in one pass, which is exactly the discipline this round exists to install.

**It runs in `parity-matrix`, not `parity-types`.** `parity-types` is gated on `needs.changes.outputs.code`, the `changes` filter classifies `docs/` and `*.md` as a docs-only diff, and the CI gate counts a skip as a pass — so a guard for a markdown file placed there would be skipped on precisely the pull requests it polices. `parity-matrix` is ungated for that documented reason and already parses this file. The step still carries its own `::error::`, on the same principle § 711 records: a job that bundles unrelated checks cannot say through its name which one broke.
## 740. A catalogue only ships if a reader can reach it, so the reachable set is derived and guarded rather than listed

**Decided 2026-08-25.** [followups.md](../product/followups.md) carried "`app_pt.arb` is not reachable at runtime", measured 2026-08-05. Re-measured on `b103c9388` the filed entry is **half stale and right about the class**. The half it named was fixed the next day: [§ 547](decisions.md) put `Locale('pt')` into `supportedLocales`, so a `pt-PT` / `pt-AO` / bare-`pt` device does now land on the European catalogue. The half nobody looked at was still broken. `_editLanguage` in `settings_preferences_screen.dart` listed its options as `['', 'en', 'de', 'fr', 'es', 'ja', 'pt-BR']`, seven hand-written literals beside a seven-entry `supportedLocales`, so **European Portuguese was selectable only by a reader whose device already asked for it.** A Portuguese speaker on an English phone, or anyone who had ever touched the picker, could not get to 3,758 translated strings that ship in every build. The entry's other figures have moved too — the catalogues are 3,758 keys now, not 3,477, all seven complete with zero missing and zero orphan keys, and `pt` differs from `pt_BR` on 349 of them, not 226.

**Settled by making it reachable, not by deleting it.** The two honest ends were ship it or drop it, and completeness decides between them: a catalogue that resolves to a half-empty dictionary is worse than one that falls back cleanly, and this one is not half-empty. It is also already half-shipped — reverting §547 to delete the file would take a locale away from the devices that reach it today.

**The durable half is deriving rather than listing.** The picker now builds from `supportedLocales` on mobile, which is what web already did (`{#each SUPPORTED_LOCALES}`). A hand-written second list is the whole defect: it agreed with the first one on the day it was written and there was nothing to notice when it stopped.
