**How a `pt-PT` device resolves, precisely, because it is not obvious.** `main.dart` passes a `localeListResolutionCallback` that delegates to `negotiateLocale`, and `LocalizationsResolver._resolveLocales` consults that callback on **both** paths — the device list and an explicit `MaterialApp.locale` — falling through to Flutter's own `basicLocaleListResolution` only when the callback returns null, which ours never does. So Flutter's default algorithm does not run for this app at all, and the resolution is entirely `_exact` then `_baseToLocale`: `pt-PT` misses `_exact` and takes `_baseToLocale['pt']` → `Locale('pt')`. Worth recording what that spares us. Under the default algorithm the answer would be the same but for a different reason — `basicLocaleListResolution` builds its language-only index as `languageLocales[locale.languageCode] ??= locale`, first-wins over `supportedLocales` in order — so the European catalogue would beat the Brazilian one purely because its line comes first, and swapping two lines in a list would silently re-point every European device at Brazil. With the callback in place that ordering is not load-bearing, which is why the guard checks `_exact` and `_baseToLocale` rather than list position.

**The guard is the point, not the fix.** Nothing in either tree connected "a catalogue file exists" to "a reader can select it", which is why this defect survived a round that was explicitly about it. Mobile's guard (`architecture_guards_test.dart § locale reach`, mirrored to the iOS twin) reads `lib/l10n/` as the source of truth and holds five declaration sites to it — `supportedLocales`, the generated delegate's own list, `localeLabels`, `_exact`, and `l10n_parity_test.dart`'s hand-written locale list — plus the two platform manifests, each a reachability gate in its own right: `CFBundleLocalizations` in the iOS `Info.plist` (a locale absent from it is one the App Store will not offer the app in, however complete its ARB) and `android:localeConfig` on Android, which populates Settings → Apps → Threkir → Language. The phone had no `locales_config.xml` at all while the *watch* has carried one since its own i18n landed, so that OS-level path simply did not exist; it does now, with all seven. The byte-identical test reads both through `../mobile_ios/…` and `../mobile_android/…`, paths that resolve from either twin's directory. Apple names a locale by region, so `pt` is `pt-PT` there — the one spelling difference, carried as an override with its own companion test; Android spells them the way we do. It also asserts the picker contains no locale-tag literal at all. Web's twin (`locale_reach.test.ts`) does the same for `lib/i18n/locales/`, `EXACT`, the `<select>`, and the localized Learn guides, closing the direction TypeScript cannot: `CATALOGUE_LOADERS` is a `Record<Locale, …>` so a *list* entry without a file is a compile error, but a *file* without a list entry is silent.

**Base-language fallback is the one rule a catalogue may legitimately fail**, because `_baseToLocale` can name one variant per language, so a language shipping two catalogues necessarily leaves one off it. That carries a reason-per-entry allowlist with a companion test asserting each entry is *still* exempt, the [§ 728](decisions.md) `dates.test.ts` shape. Mobile's single entry is `pt-BR`; web's is empty, which is the positive claim that every web catalogue is its own language's base target rather than an absence of checking. Both directions fire: pointing the `pt` base at Brazil makes the European catalogue unreached *and* makes the `pt-BR` exemption stale, and the suite says both.

**Three gaps left open, all of them missing translations rather than unreachable ones**, filed rather than fixed because writing a locale is not mechanical: web ships no European-Portuguese catalogue (a `pt-PT` reader gets Brazilian there, so the phone and the browser disagree), Wear OS ships the same five plus English and no `pt`, and the auth-email rail collapses every `pt*` tag onto `pt-BR` by design. None of those is a file going nowhere; each is a reader served their second-best language, which is the correct behaviour until someone writes the first-best one.
## 741. The pgtap refusals mostly hold — 3 of 104 were vacuous, and the third was visible only on a clean database

**Decided 2026-08-25.** [§ 732](#732) found that 28 of the e2e suite's backend cross-checks were false greens, because a read that never happened *satisfies* a zero-or-empty expectation. The same question was put to the pgtap suite, one layer down, where it is sharper: under RLS a refused SELECT does not error at all, it returns no rows — so `is_empty(...)` / `is(<count>, 0, ...)` is simultaneously what a refusal looks like, what a fixture that never inserted looks like, what a `WHERE` clause matching nothing looks like, and what a typo'd uuid looks like. **The answer is that the suite is rigorous: 2 of 104 refusal assertions were vacuous, and 1 of 298 negatives pinned no error.** A measured near-zero is the result, and it is worth recording as loudly as a pile of findings would have been.

**Reading the assertions could not have produced that number; running them did.** Two independent mutation operators were injected immediately before each assertion under test and agreed on 206 of 207 candidates: `alter table ... disable row level security` across all 90 public tables, and — the one the guard keeps — dropping the session to the table owner for the span of that one statement. Every public table is owned by `postgres`, which holds `BYPASSRLS`, and none sets `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`, so `reset role` is a complete bypass that takes no lock and costs nothing. Whole-file mutation is *not* good enough and produced three false positives on its own: disabling RLS at the top of `rls_route_markers_test` lets test 18's owner DELETE actually land, so test 20's marker is legitimately gone by the time it is read. Only a mutation scoped to the single statement leaves the fixture history intact.

**The two real ones are `rls_route_conditions_test`'s private-route reads.** Tests 10 and 13 asserted that a non-owner and then anon read no `route_conditions` rows on the private route — and no fixture ever filed a report on that route; every insert targeted the public one. Both passed against an empty result set, and would have passed with the SELECT policy dropped, with RLS off, or with the table truncated. The file's own header names "a private route's reports leaking to anon / non-members" as the blast radius it exists to cover. **The policy itself is fine**: filing a real report on the private route as its owner and re-asking as the non-owner and as anon returns zero rows both times, so this was a vacuous test rather than a hole. The fix is a subject to refuse — the owner now files that report and reads it back — and both assertions now die under the mutation.

**The other named suspicions did not survive contact.** `throws_ok` is well disciplined: of 292 calls, 271 pin a SQLSTATE and 20 pin an exact message; the single unpinned one was `activities_view_windowed`'s view-write refusal, whose comment guessed the code would be 42501 or 0A000 and pinned neither — it is in fact **55000**, because a UNION view is not auto-updatable and the rewriter refuses before the privilege check is ever reached. It now pins 55000, and the missing INSERT grant, which no write attempt can observe, is asserted directly against the catalogue. On the role axis, all 2155 assertions were instrumented with `current_user` and `auth.uid()`: no refusal assertion runs as `authenticated` with a null uid, and the 47 that run as `postgres` are catalogue and grant-matrix checks or deliberate full-visibility read-backs after a refused write, which is the correct construction rather than a leaked role. The 23 "X can DELETE Y, proven by an empty read" positive controls were mutated too — drop the table's DELETE policy, or replace a `FOR ALL` policy with a SELECT-only clone so the read survives — and every one of the 17 the operator could reach went red.

**The third was found by the guard's own first CI run, and the local baseline is why it took one.** The audit measured 2 of 104 on this workstation; CI reported a third immediately — `rls_fitness_snapshots_test`'s "anon cannot read fitness_snapshots". It is the most clear-cut of the three and the reason it hid is worth more than the fix: **test 5 of that file deletes the only snapshot the fixture inserted**, so test 6 reads an empty table and passes whether or not the policy exists. It survived mutation on CI because there the table is genuinely empty — `seed.sql` files one `fitness_snapshots` row as a source-gate self-test and deletes it again at line 2597 — while the shared workstation database held **41 committed rows** accumulated by Playwright and api_client integration runs, which pgtap does not roll back because they were never in its transaction. With RLS removed those 41 rows satisfied the mutation, the assertion went red, and the operator scored it killed. **So the contamination did not merely hide the defect, it inverted the verdict**: ambient debris is indistinguishable from a policy doing its job, and a mutation operator is only as honest as the database it runs against. Reproduced deterministically by emptying the table inside a rolled-back transaction — 0 rows visible to anon before the fix, 1 after. The fix is the same as the other two: file the subject before the read. The durable answer is that the guard runs in CI against a database built the way production is, not against whatever the last fortnight of local testing left behind.

**The guard is the mutation run, not a regex, because the defect is not visible in the source.** `apps/backend/scripts/check_pgtap_refusal_assertions.mjs` re-runs every refusal-worded zero-or-empty assertion over a base table under the owner bypass and fails on any that still passes: 104 assertions across 256 files in about eight seconds, one `psql` per file (the assertions are read-only, so bypassing one changes nothing the next one sees). `EXPECTED_SURVIVORS` carries the four whose empty result is a real answer — three trigger claims and `safety_contacts`' data-shape claim — each with its reason, and a stale entry fails as loudly as a new offender, so the list cannot outlive what it excuses. The static half fails any `throws_ok` pinning neither a code nor a message. **What it does not cover is recorded rather than implied**: the population is selected by the description's own vocabulary, because a claim is what makes an empty result a security assertion, and 103 zero-or-empty assertions that read only through a definer view or RPC are outside it — dropping RLS does not change a view's `WHERE`, so that class needs a different operator and is filed in `followups.md`.

## 742. iOS capability declarations are derived from the code that needs them — because the twelve tests that read them had never once run

**Decided 2026-08-26.** Two capabilities the shipped Dart depends on were undeclared in `apps/mobile_ios`, and both were filed by the [§ 739](#739) iOS-column sweep. Both are real. The finding worth recording is not either gap — it is that a `group('iOS Info.plist')` in `architecture_guards_test.dart` existed to catch exactly this class and **had never executed a single one of its iOS assertions**, nor had the `group('iOS PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy')` beside it.

**The `audio` background mode.** `audio_cues.dart` calls `setIosAudioCategory(playback, [mixWithOthers, duckOthers], voicePrompt)` — the navigation-cue configuration, and deliberate — while `Info.plist` declared only `location` and `processing`. iOS licenses background audio *output* on the `audio` mode specifically; `location` keeps the process alive for GPS and says nothing about the session. So a runner who pockets the phone mid-run, which is the case spoken cues exist for, hears nothing, and the recording is unaffected, which is what makes it silent rather than obvious. `apps/mobile_ios/deployment.md` has said "Background Modes → Location updates + **Audio (for TTS)**" for a long time: the requirement was written down and the declaration file never followed, which is the whole argument for a machine rather than a note.

**The `aps-environment` entitlement.** `firebase_messaging` is a live dependency and `push_messaging_bridge.dart` asks it for a device token on every sign-in, but `Runner.entitlements` carried only `healthkit` and `applesignin`. Without the entitlement `registerForRemoteNotifications` never yields an APNs token, so `getToken()` returns null forever and the device registers nothing — again silently, because the bridge is L4 and swallows. The pubspec comment and `native_push.md` both called it an "operator-supplied deploy-time artifact" alongside `GoogleService-Info.plist`; it is not. It is a checked-in capability declaration, and the § 150 rule is that a compliance or credential gate never justifies leaving code — or a declaration — unwritten.

**It is written as `$(APS_ENVIRONMENT)`, not as a literal.** One entitlements file serves all three of the Runner target's build configurations (`CODE_SIGN_ENTITLEMENTS` points every one at it), and the sandbox and production APNs hosts reject each other's tokens — the worker already carries `APNS_SANDBOX` for its half of that pairing. Pinning `development` and trusting the distribution export to rewrite it is precisely the shape that ships a TestFlight build whose every push answers `BadDeviceToken`: silent, and indistinguishable from nobody having enabled notifications. So `APS_ENVIRONMENT` is defined per configuration in the pbxproj — `development` on Debug and Profile, `production` on Release, which is what `flutter build ipa --release` archives — and the guard fails if a configuration leaves it undefined. An undefined setting expands to the literal `$(APS_ENVIRONMENT)`, which no provisioning profile carries, so that failure is loud at signing rather than in production. **The release pipeline owes one thing:** `release-ios.yml` builds `--no-codesign` today, so nothing is embedded; when the commented-out signing block is enabled, the distribution profile must carry the Push Notifications capability, and the exported IPA's `aps-environment` must be verified as `production` (`codesign -d --entitlements`) rather than assumed. A dev-signed *release* build now mismatches by construction and will refuse to install; override it with `xcodebuild … APS_ENVIRONMENT=development` rather than editing the file.

**The dead guard is the real finding.** Fifteen tests across the two groups read `File('ios/Runner/…')` behind `if (!file.existsSync()) return;` — the twin-share idiom, since `apps/mobile_android` has no `ios/` directory. But CI's `test-packages` job runs `melos exec --scope="run_recorder" --scope="mobile_android" --scope="api_client" --scope="gpx_parser" --scope="ui_kit" --scope="core_models" -- flutter test`, and **`mobile_ios` is not in that list**, so the only working directory where those files exist is never a working directory. Every iOS assertion skipped on every run they ever had. This is [§ 741](#741)'s shape one layer up: a verdict decided by the environment rather than by the code, reading green for a reason that says nothing. It also explains how both gaps survived a matrix sweep — there was a guard family that looked like it covered them. The repo already had a working idiom for the same job: `apple_watch_route_bridge_test.dart` reads `../mobile_ios/ios/Runner/WatchIngestBridge.swift` unconditionally and does run. Note also that `test_inventory.md` asserted every test file "runs on the iOS target too"; that is true of `melos run test` locally and false of CI.

**So the coverage moved out of the Dart twin entirely.** `scripts/check_ios_native_declarations.mjs` runs in its own always-on `ios-native-declarations` job against the one tree where the files exist. It **derives** each requirement from the source that obliges it rather than restating the plist — `IosTextToSpeechAudioCategory.playback` obliges `audio`, `allowBackgroundLocationUpdates: true` obliges `location`, `package:health/` obliges the HealthKit entitlement and both HealthKit purpose strings, `package:pedometer/` obliges `NSMotionUsageDescription` and `NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypeFitness`, and so on across 43 declarations. That is the [§ 739](#739) / [§ 740](#740) rule again: a guard that restates `['location', 'processing', 'audio']` is a second copy of the plist and drifts the same way the first one did, whereas deleting the TTS call deletes its requirement with it. The reverse direction is checked for background modes and is an **error**, because App Review rejects a capability the binary does not exercise — which subsumes the old hand-written "does not claim unused `fetch`" test and generalises it. Both manifests are parsed rather than substring-matched, since a category named in a comment satisfies `contains`. The blindness checks are the ones [§ 416](#416)'s BLE guard uses: an unparseable plist, an empty Dart source set, or a derivation pattern that matches nothing all fail rather than passing vacuously.

**What this does not claim.** Nothing here has been built, signed, or run — there is no Mac in the loop, and a background-audio behaviour is not host-testable at all. The guard proves the *declaration* matches the code that needs it; whether iOS then keeps speaking with the screen locked is still owed to the one device run `followups.md` tracks. The parity matrix needed no cell change: the TTS-cues and push rows are `Partial` on iOS by derivation either way, and neither departs from the rule, so per § 739 neither states a per-row claim. **The watchOS sibling was checked and is clean** — `apps/watch_ios` has no `AVSpeechSynthesizer` and no push registration, so its `WKBackgroundModes` of `location` + `workout-processing` and its HealthKit-only entitlements match its code exactly.

## 743. Two-thirds of the hard-coded e2e origins were live defects and the rest were a different one, so the guard bans the ports the configs declare rather than keeping a list of exceptions

`playwright.config.ts` has advertised `PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL` for as long as the suite has existed, and 34 sites across 20 files under `apps/web/tests-e2e` named `http://localhost:7777` anyway. The filed count was exactly right; the filed *reason* — "any run on a second port fails" — was right about 20 of them and wrong about 14, and the two groups want different fixes.

**The 20 that were live.** Fourteen were `request.get` / `request.post` calls with an absolute URL, which is simply redundant: Playwright's `request` fixture resolves a relative path against the resolved `use.baseURL`, so `'/sitemap.xml'` is what those eight sitemap assertions, four `/api/coach` wire probes and two OG-image fetches always meant. One was a bare Node `fetch` in `tier-cache-resilience.spec.ts`, which has no `baseURL` notion at all and now takes the lane's origin as an argument. **The five sharpest were `context.grantPermissions(['clipboard-read', 'clipboard-write'], { origin })`**, which takes an exact origin and does not resolve anything: on any other port the grant lands on an origin the page never visits, `navigator.clipboard.writeText` rejects, and `handleShare` takes its catch branch — so `recap/toast-feedback.spec.ts`, whose whole claim is that the success path shows a toast rather than an `alert()`, would fail for a reason unrelated to the code it tests. A permission grant is the one shape here whose breakage does not look like a missing page.

**The 14 that were not.** Four were `?? 'http://localhost:7777'` after a value the config always sets — dead code, not defects. Two were `redirect_uri` payloads posted to the `strava-import` Edge Function, whose asserted branches (`invalid_code`, `invalid_scope`) return before the gate that reads the field, so the literal was inert; they now derive the origin because the field *means* the app's own callback, not because it was broken. Two belong to the config, which is where a default may live. The remaining five re-read `process.env.PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL` and restated the default beside it: right in the sharded lane, wrong in the three lanes (livehub `:7778`, exporthub `:7779`, sso `:7780`) that set no override and run on ports of their own. That is the failure mode a "just use the env var" fix would have preserved.

**The override itself did not work end to end.** `webServer.command` was `pnpm run dev`, and that npm script *is* `vite dev --port 7777`, so setting `PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL` moved every test onto another port while the config booted the server on the old one. Converting the 32 spec sites without fixing that would have been half a fix. The command is now `pnpm exec vite dev --port ${DEV_PORT}` with an explicit `cwd` — the shape the three single-spec lanes already use, `pnpm exec` not moving cwd the way `pnpm run` does — and the port, the readiness probe and `use.baseURL` all come off one resolved value. A base URL with no port throws at config load rather than handing vite an empty `--port`.

**The sweep also found two lanes sharing a port.** `playwright.sso.config.ts` and `playwright.exporthub.config.ts` both pinned `:7779`. CI runs them as separate jobs, so they never collided there, and that is precisely why it survived: locally `reuseExistingServer` means whichever lane starts second adopts the first lane's dev server, and a lane's entire reason to exist is an env var that server does not carry — an export-hub run inheriting the sso server has no `PUBLIC_EXPORT_HUB_URL` and silently takes the Edge Function fallback the lane was built to bypass. SSO moved to `:7780`; GoTrue's `additional_redirect_urls` in `config.toml` moved with it, so a local run needs the stack restarted once.

**The guard carries no allowlist, and that is a design choice rather than luck.** `fixtures/base-url.test.ts` follows `fixtures/dates.test.ts`'s shape — scan the tree, strip comments, report file and line — but § 738 is the reason it is scoped differently: that guard's allowlist rotted until four of five "deliberate" exemptions turned out to be the defect wearing a reason. Here the banned pattern is a loopback origin **on a port some lane config itself declares**, read out of the configs at scan time. The loopback literals that survive — Supabase `:54321`, Mailpit `:54324`, `dev_server_guard.test.ts`'s deliberately unbound `:1` — are not exempted from the rule; they are outside it, so there is no list to keep honest. A second check bans any reader of `process.env.PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL` outside the module that defines the resolution, and a third asserts the four lanes bind four distinct ports, which is what would have caught the `:7779` collision. Against `main` the guard fails 4 of its 6 tests and names all 32 sites; block comments are blanked rather than deleted so the line numbers it prints are the file's own.

One nearby literal was fixed on the way past and one was left. `routes/heatmap.spec.ts` hard-coded `http://localhost:54321` *and* the demo anon key inside a `page.evaluate`, where every other spec takes both from `loadSupabaseEnv()` — the same class one port over, and the fixture already honours `SUPABASE_STATUS_WORKDIR`. `ci.yml`'s `STRAVA_ALLOWED_REDIRECTS=http://localhost:7777/settings/integrations` stays as found: no spec exercises the allowlist-accept path, so nothing reads it today, and it becomes load-bearing only when someone pins that path.
## 744. The rate-limit refusal is localized by cutting the parity pair at the parse — and both direct-message buckets had been telling every sender "you're doing that too quickly"

`rateLimitErrorMessage` was a TS↔Dart pair that took a postgres P0001 and returned a finished English sentence: a bucket→verb-phrase map, a seconds→"a few seconds"/"N seconds"/"N minutes" humaniser, and the frame that joined them. Every throttled caller on both platforms therefore read English, and no locale could ever get anything else — the prose was inside the one module the lockstep forbids either platform from diverging on. It is now **parse-only**: both halves return `{bucket, seconds}` and hold no sentence at all. The wording moved into the six web catalogues and the seven ARBs, and is assembled by per-platform render glue — `apps/web/src/lib/i18n/rate_limit_message.ts` resolving through `m`, `apps/mobile_android/lib/rate_limit_message.dart` resolving through `AppLocalizations` — which is deliberately outside the enforced lockstep, the same way `badges` keeps its label keys out of it.

**Two of the three things the filed entry said were wrong, and the third was a decision rather than an oversight.** It was filed as a `direct_messages` copy problem; it is not a DM problem, it is the whole helper — ten buckets, six surfaces, both platforms. It attributed the generic `'doing that'` fallback for the two DM buckets to the Dart side; **web fell through to the same generic sentence**, so a throttled sender on either platform was told "You're doing that too quickly" about a message they had just tried to send. And that fallback was not forgotten: § 737 priced a DM-specific verb as *a lockstep edit to a platform with no DM surface* and declined it on purpose. That price was real while the prose lived in the pair. It is zero now — the mapping is render glue, so naming an activity on one platform costs nothing on the other — which is the argument for the split independent of the translation.

**Ten buckets reach the parser; an eleventh exists and never can.** `enforce_create_rate_limit` is called with `create_club`, `create_route`, `create_report`, `clone_plan_template`, `clone_public_plan`, `clone_session_template`, `clone_gym_routine_template`, `publish_gym_routine_as_template`, `send_direct_message` and `send_direct_message_burst` — nine sentences, because the two plan-adopt paths are the same act from two libraries and the two send windows are our fixed-window accounting rather than anything a sender should be told apart. `create_challenge` (migration `20270308_001`) is a twelfth call to `check_rate_limit` but goes through its own trigger, which raises the bare string `challenge_create_rate_limited` with no bucket and no retry figure. The parser cannot match it, nothing else handles it either, and a throttled challenge creator reads the raw postgres exception on both platforms. Recorded in `followups.md` rather than fixed here: the durable answer is to route that trigger through `enforce_create_rate_limit` like every other bucket, which is a migration plus both type regenerations, and the local Supabase stack was another agent's exclusive use this round.

**The wait is the only slot, because it is the only fragment that survives translation.** The tempting shape is one sentence with an `{activity}` slot and eleven activity phrases, which would have cost twelve keys instead of twelve. It does not work: German puts the finite verb second and the object last (`Du erstellst zu schnell Vereine`), so "creating clubs" is not a fragment that can be dropped into a German frame. So the bucket picks a **whole** translated sentence and `{wait}` — an object noun phrase, `42 Sekunden` / `42 secondes` / `42秒` — is slotted in. The plural lives in the wait key as an ICU block, so `ja` declares only `other` and `fr`/`pt-BR` get their own categories, and the 90-second seconds-to-minutes cutoff (ceil, so we never invite a retry still inside the window) stays a rendering decision on both platforms rather than something the parser bakes in. `seconds` is **null**, not `0`, when the trigger reports a non-positive figure: zero is not a wait, and "please wait 0 seconds" invites the retry that fails again.

**Every named caller was checked for whether it can actually reach a localizer, because that is what decides where the sentence is assembled.** Mobile's three are all at the render layer already — `club_form_sheet` and `report_sheet` had `AppLocalizations` in scope in the very catch block that was returning hardcoded English, and `route_builder_screen`'s `formatSaveRouteError` takes an optional `BuildContext` and had the rate-limit branch **above** the context check, so it discarded a localizer it was holding. That branch now uses the caller's context when there is one (there always is, at the single production call site) and `lookupAppLocalizations(const Locale('en'))` when there is not, which is only the unit tests — looking English up in the catalogue rather than re-spelling it, since a hardcoded copy of a translated string is precisely what this change removes. Web's nine call sites are all in `core/data.ts`, which had no localizer at all; it now imports `m` and passes it in. That the lookup happens at the throw rather than in each of the ~30 components that render `e.message` is deliberate and safe here: the web app is adapter-static with client-side locale negotiation (the reason `i18n/locale.ts` negotiates from `navigator.language` rather than an `Accept-Language` header), so there is exactly one active locale and no per-request one to get wrong, and `training/workout_labels.ts` and `settings/features.ts` are existing non-component modules that resolve copy through `m` the same way. `packages/api_client` only mentions the helper in a doc comment and renders nothing.

**English does not move by a character.** Three Playwright specs match on `/creating clubs too quickly/i`, `/creating routes too quickly/i` and `/too quickly/i`, and the catalogue entries are the pre-split strings verbatim; both new render suites pin them against the old wording rather than against themselves. The guard against the copy creeping back is a source check on both parsers — `rate_limit_errors.ts` and `rate_limit_errors.dart` must contain none of "too quickly", "please wait", "try again", "a few seconds" or "doing that" outside their doc comments — because a helper that regrows its own English is a helper a non-English reader gets English from, and neither the catalogue parity suite nor the ARB parity suite can see it. The render suites additionally assert, per locale, that every bucket renders a non-empty sentence with no unsubstituted slot, that a one-second and a one-hour refusal do not render identically (a locale that dropped `{wait}` would), and that the nine distinct activities stay nine distinct sentences (a locale that pasted one translation over several keys would collapse them).
## 745. A relation's own `WHERE` is a second access-control mechanism, and Postgres cannot tell you which relations have one

**Decided 2026-08-26.** [§ 741](#741) mutation-checked the pgtap suite's refusal assertions by dropping the session to the BYPASSRLS table owner, and filed what that operator cannot reach: a `security definer` view and a SECURITY DEFINER RPC already run as their owner and filter in their own SQL, so removing row-level security leaves their results identical and every refusal assertion reading only through one survives for a reason that says nothing. A second operator was built for that class — a **permissive replacement per relation**, `create or replace`d inside a savepoint that restores the real definition before the next assertion runs. **The answer is the same as § 741's and worth saying as loudly: nothing was vacuous. 50 of the 51 assertions the new operator measures die under it, and the single survivor is a real zero** — an age band cannot contain a runner who has no age, and the positive control asserting that runner *is* on the unfiltered board sits two assertions above it. No RLS hole, no leak, no migration.

**The finding is that the premise drew the line in the wrong place.** The split is not definer-versus-invoker, which is what `pg_proc.prosecdef` and a view's `security_invoker` record; it is whether the relation carries an access predicate of its own, and the catalogue does not know. **Eight of the twenty-four relations that needed a permissive replacement are `SECURITY INVOKER`** — `gym_exercise_names`, `gym_exercise_records`, the two set-history RPCs, `gym_workout_summaries`, `run_streaks_for_user`, `search_clubs`, `search_public_events` — each refusing with a `= auth.uid()` or an `is_public = true` written into the body, where RLS was never the mechanism. They were found by measurement, not by reading: all eight survived the owner bypass on a database where their fixtures demonstrably exist. `search_public_events` is the clearest demonstration, because both halves can be observed in one statement: with RLS fully bypassed the base-table read of the members-only event returns the row while the RPC still returns nothing.

**The line each replacement is drawn on, and why a false kill is the dangerous direction.** A replacement keeps every predicate that says *which* rows the assertion asked about — the arguments, the join keys, the subject's own id — and drops every predicate that says *whether the caller may see them*: ownership, consent, opt-in, blocks, shadow-hiding, the under-18 floor, `is_*_visible_to`, a privacy-zone clip. Dropping too little leaves the mutation inert, which makes a good assertion look vacuous: loud, and safe. Dropping a *subject selector* reveals rows the assertion never asked about, which makes a vacuous assertion look good: silent, and the exact false green the guard exists to find. So each entry carries a **witness** — a subject the real relation provably hides, which the replacement must provably reveal, checked before the mutation run in its own CI step. An inert operator is invisible inside a green mutation run, which is § 741's inversion pointed the other way. Two witnesses had to be rebuilt during construction: a whole-world geography envelope `&&`-intersects nothing, so both geometry witnesses measure inside one real route's own envelope, and the heatmap's gives every route owner a globe-sized privacy zone so it proves the *clip* is dropped rather than the `is_public` term beside it. The instrument is also checked end to end on two assertions written to have known verdicts — one with a real hidden subject that must go red, one with no subject at all that must stay green — because "the guard ran and was green" was exactly the evidence § 741's third defect defeated.

**The population's selector was the other open question, and it was answered by running the operators over everything.** The guard picks its population from the assertion's own prose, because a claim is what turns an empty result into a security assertion — a trigger that correctly did not fire produces the identical SQL. Both operators were therefore run over **all 294** zero-or-empty assertions in the suite, not just the ones worded as refusals. The regex selected 126 and killed 121: **96 % precision**. Of the 168 it did not select, **28 died too**, and those 28 split in two. Seven unambiguous words (`never sees`, `unfindable`, `enumerate`, `exposes no`, `reads nothing`, `gets nothing`, `absent from`) close 11 of them for **zero** new excuse entries. The largest remaining word is `excluded` / `excludes`: **21 assertions, roughly half access control** (a declared minor, a search opt-out, a block, a members-only event) **and half ordinary filters** (`byday=MO excludes it`, `free filter excludes the priced class`). One word, two claims. **So the recorded trade stands, but the alternative is smaller than it was estimated at**: not a 207-entry allowlist but a 117-entry one, because 117 of the 157 assertions outside the vocabulary legitimately survive — cascade deletes, triggers that did not fire, positive DELETE controls. The durable answer is neither regex nor allowlist: an opt-in **`-- refusal: <why>`** comment above the assertion, where the author says once, at the claim, which of the two claims they meant. 31 assertions carry one; all 31 die under mutation, so the marker bought coverage without buying a single excuse. The colon is load-bearing — one existing comment wraps onto a line beginning `-- refusal,` and is not a marker — and the marker is opt-**in** only: nothing can take an assertion *out* of the population, which still requires a reviewed `EXPECTED_SURVIVORS` entry.

**Two things are deliberately still outside, and one is a real limit.** `distance is returned as coarse bucket 0` and `a long-broken streak reports current = 0` expect a zero *value* rather than an empty result, and a widening mutation moves a value — a "kill" there would mean the mutation changed an answer, not that access control was hiding a row, so the guard's verdict is only evidence when the zero was an emptiness. The real limit is the **owner-scoped** shape: where the caller's own identity is the assertion's only subject selector ("a stranger sees NONE of the lifter's sets"), the permissive replacement also reveals whatever `seed.sql` left in that table, so the kill proves a subject exists in the transaction rather than that the test filed one. Seven assertions are in that shape. It is § 741's exposure at one remove, deterministic here because the seed is committed rather than accumulated Playwright debris, and it is filed in `followups.md` with the reason the obvious `xmin` scoping is unsound: for `public_run_gear` the rows revealed (`run_gear`, `gear`) are not the rows the fixture wrote (`runs`).

**Guard population 104 → 168 assertions**, of which 51 are now measured by the second operator and 117 by the first. The `baseTables` filter that scoped the old population was doing damage beyond the definer class — it also excluded two `activities`-view reads the *first* operator could have measured all along. `psql` now runs under `spawnSync` so a mutant whose transaction aborts quotes the SQLSTATE back instead of reporting an unexplained missing assertion.
## 746. An absent segment rank is not first place — and the RPC the degrade trusted has been unexecutable by anon for months

**Decided 2026-08-26.** Both clients spent a missing segment-effort rank as `?? 1`. That is a crown: the single most flattering claim the run-detail chips can make, produced by having no answer at all — the exact inversion of the fail-closed default the codebase holds everywhere else, where `live_freshness` claims nothing on a stale fix, `live_motion` claims nothing across a gap, `health_consent` withholds rather than guesses, and `leaderboard_standing` returns null rather than a fabricated rank. **Rank is now nullable end to end on both platforms and an unanswered standing renders a neutral placeholder.** The [followups](../product/followups.md) note that raised this listed three call sites; there are **four** — `apps/web/src/lib/core/data.ts` carries the degrade twice, in `fetchEffortsForRunWithError` and in `fetchGlobalEffortsForRun`, and only the first was named.

**Rank is not a property of the effort row, which is why the absence has to be representable.** It arrives separately, from `segment_effort_ranks` / `global_segment_effort_ranks`, so an effort the RPC did not answer for has a genuinely unknown standing and there is no honest value to substitute. `20270523_001`'s header leaned on the other direction — the block filter is applied to the comparison set only, "because the web client falls back to `rank ?? 1` on a missing row and would print a crown" — which is a server working around a client defect, and made the degrade a silent dependency on the call never failing rather than a fallback.

**The two clients fail differently, and that is why the mobile half looked harmless.** `supabase.rpc` on web **resolves** with `{ data: null, error }` rather than throwing, so a failed call left the map empty and `?? 1` crowned *every chip on the page at once*, while `fetchEffortsForRunWithError` still reported success — the panel's error state could not fire. postgrest-dart **throws** on a non-2xx, so on mobile a failure propagated out to the widget's own guards and the degrade was only ever reachable on a call that succeeded while omitting an effort. It was therefore an untested default sitting one refactor away from web's behaviour, which is a worse position than a bug that fires.

**Verifying the "the RPC always returns a row" claim is what found the real defect.** It does not. `20270523_001` added the block filter as `not public.is_blocked_either_way(auth.uid(), rival.user_id)` to both bodies; both are **SECURITY INVOKER**, so that call is ACL-checked against the *calling* role, and `20261108_001` had already revoked anon's EXECUTE on `is_blocked_either_way` as anti-oracle defence-in-depth. `anon` does hold EXECUTE on `segment_effort_ranks` itself, so a logged-out caller is admitted into the body and then denied inside it. The migration's own header reasons the anon case through and concludes it works — "an anon caller has `auth.uid() = null`, `is_blocked_either_way(null, x)` is false, and nothing is filtered — correct, anon holds no blocks." **That is true of the predicate and false of the privilege**, and `20270402000001` had written the distinction down for this same function one layer up: a function reference is ACL-checked at evaluation time for the querying role regardless of short-circuiting, which is why the club policies could not name it directly even behind an `auth.uid() is null` guard.

**The failure is data-dependent, and the shape is the finding.** The predicate is only evaluated once the rival subquery yields a row, so an anonymous reader gets a clean answer for an effort with *no* strictly-faster rival — a genuine `#1` — and an error as soon as any effort on the run has one. Paired with `?? 1`, the RPC therefore succeeded exactly when the crown was real and failed exactly when it was not: **every logged-out reader of a public run saw `#1` on every chip the runner had not actually won.** This is reasoned from the grants, the bodies and Postgres' evaluation-time ACL rule rather than measured against a live database, which the round could not reach; the pgtap assertions land the claim in CI. `global_segment_effort_ranks` carried a second, independent hole: `20270411_001` granted it to `authenticated` only while `20270512_001` granted `anon` SELECT on *both* catalogue tables, so anon read the effort rows and could not ask for the ranks over them even with the body fixed.

**Both are fixed by delegating, not by re-inlining or by re-granting the oracle.** `20270609_001` re-emits both bodies to call `private.viewer_blocks(rival.user_id)` — the SECURITY DEFINER wrapper `20270402000001` created for precisely this shape, granted to anon, keyed on `auth.uid()` as the viewer and outside PostgREST's exposed schemas so no anon RPC oracle appears — and grants anon EXECUTE on the catalogue twin. `viewer_blocks(t)` *is* `is_blocked_either_way(auth.uid(), t)`, so nothing about the counted population changes for an authenticated caller, `20261108_001`'s revoke stands untouched, and the grant admits nothing new because a SECURITY INVOKER body reads under the caller's own RLS. Re-inlining a corrected copy is the drift class [§ 596](#596) exists about.

**The guards sit where the defect lived, which was never inside a function.** The degrade was at four call sites and two renders, so no behavioural test could reach it: web's `segments/effort_rank.ts` now owns both the wire read and the pill mapping (13 tests, four of them source guards over `data.ts` and `RunSegmentEfforts.svelte`), and `packages/api_client`'s `effort_rank.dart` owns the Dart read half (6 tests). The api_client source guard that previously asserted the twin **keep** web's `?? 1` — "web `fetchEffortsForRun` uses `?? 1`; the twin must not drift" — now asserts the opposite; the two were in lockstep and wrong together, which is what a parity guard costs when it pins a shape rather than a claim. The four mobile widget tests were each verified failing with the degrade reinstated. On the SQL side `global_segment_grants_test.sql` gains six assertions, one of which fails on **any** SECURITY INVOKER rank body naming `is_blocked_either_way` directly, whatever its own EXECUTE grant says — the class of defect, not the instance.

**Deliberately not made a parity pair.** The render halves cannot mirror: web's returns a CSS class string and mobile's a `(Color, Color)` record off `ThemeData`, and the wire half lives in `api_client`, which is not a Flutter package and cannot resolve a theme. Registering a pair whose two sides share one of four exports would weaken the registry rather than strengthen it; the two source guards are what hold the contract instead. The crown *label* helper in the `segments` pair (`crownLabel`) turns out to be unrelated — it names which demographic tier a rank-1 holder owns and never sees a rank, so it needed no null handling.


## 747. The eleventh rate-limit bucket now reaches the parser — but the refusal a throttled challenge creator actually saw was swallowed, not leaked

`challenges` has carried a create throttle since `20270308_001`: a `before insert` trigger calling `check_rate_limit` itself and raising the bare string `challenge_create_rate_limited`. Migration `20270610_001` replaces that body with one line — `perform enforce_create_rate_limit('create_challenge', new.creator_id, 30, 3600)` — so the eleventh bucket produces the same `rate limit exceeded for <bucket>, retry in Ns` message the other ten do, and inherits the parser, the localized sentence ([§ 744](#744-the-rate-limit-refusal-is-localized-by-cutting-the-parity-pair-at-the-parse--and-both-direct-message-buckets-had-been-telling-every-sender-youre-doing-that-too-quickly)) and the helper's skips for free. Replacing the *function* rather than the trigger is enough — the trigger keeps pointing at the same name — so nothing takes a lock on `challenges` at all; `migration_locks.md`'s lock reference had no row for `CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION` and does now.

**Two of the filing's three claims were wrong, and the wrong one was the user-facing half.** § 744 recorded, and `followups.md` repeated, that "a throttled challenge creator reads the raw postgres exception on both platforms." Measured, neither platform did. **Mobile cannot produce the bucket at all**: `SocialService.createChallenge` exists in both twins and has zero callers anywhere under `apps/mobile_*/lib` — there is no challenge-create surface on the phone, so the mobile half describes a code path that cannot run. That was not even an unrecorded fact: `parity.md`'s "Create a challenge" row already reads ✗ / ✗ / ✓ and says the service method "has **no caller anywhere**". A cross-platform claim was filed about a platform whose own parity row said the surface does not exist. **Web never showed the string either**: `ChallengeEditor.svelte`'s catch discards the error and toasts `m('challenges.createFailed')` — "Couldn't create the challenge." So the real defect was the *opposite* shape from the one filed. Not a leaked postgres exception but a swallowed one: a refusal naming neither the cause nor the wait, indistinguishable from a validation failure or a dropped connection, on the one class of failure whose entire remedy is knowing how long to wait. A leak is ugly; this was worse, because a reader who sees `rate limit exceeded for create_challenge, retry in 900s` at least learns to come back.

**Which also makes "a migration plus both type regenerations, not a client change" wrong in both directions.** The migration alone changes nothing a reader sees, because the editor drops `e.message` on the floor; the client change is the half that reaches a person. `createChallenge` in `data.ts` now routes the error through `rateLimitErrorMessage(m, …)` and rethrows the friendly string like the nine wrappers beside it, and the editor renders `err instanceof Error ? err.message : m('challenges.createFailed')` — the `ClubEditor` idiom, which is safe precisely because a `PostgrestError` off a destructured `{ data, error }` is a **plain object**, not an `Error`, so only a message `data.ts` deliberately wrapped can reach the toast. And there was nothing to regenerate: a trigger function returns `trigger` and never appears in `database.types.ts` (only `enforce_create_rate_limit`, `check_rate_limit` and `check_rate_limit_tiered` do), and the Dart generator reads only `create table` / `alter table`. Both generators were re-run and both produced a zero diff — verified, not assumed.

**Three behaviours change with the helper besides the message, all deliberate.** The bucket is keyed on `new.creator_id` rather than `auth.uid()`: identical on any insert the `WITH CHECK` policy admits, and different on the forged one, where the helper returns without raising so the policy answers 42501 instead of the trigger raising P0001 out of the *forger's* spent bucket and mis-classifying an attack as impatience — the reason `20260907_001` carries that skip, now pinned for this bucket too. `service_role` is skipped explicitly, where before an Edge Function writing under a user's JWT was throttled by that user's own queue. And the `exception when others then return new` fail-open wrapper is gone: `20270308_001` justified it as "mirroring the helper's own fail-open philosophy", and the helper has never had one — behind its guards the only two errors `check_rate_limit` raises (a foreign `p_user_id`, a non-positive max/window) are unreachable here, so the wrapper was buying a subtransaction per insert to catch nothing.

**The guard is on the producer, at the class level, because pinning this one bucket would not have caught this one bucket.** `security_guards.test.ts` walks every migration, keeps the *last* definition of each `returns trigger` function (later migration wins, the same shape `activity_type_vocabulary.test.ts` uses), and asserts that any body mentioning `rate_limit` calls `enforce_create_rate_limit` and never `check_rate_limit` directly. Against pre-fix `main` it fails on exactly one function and names it; a future throttle that rolls its own counter fails the same way on the day it lands. The consumer side gets the cheaper pin: `createChallenge` joins `saveRoute` / `createClub` / `submitReport` in the existing wrapper guard. pgtap coverage is `challenge_create_rate_limit_test.sql` (8 assertions, modelled on `direct_message_rate_limit_test.sql`), and the stale `throws_ok(..., 'challenge_create_rate_limited')` in `challenge_browse_test.sql` — which would have gone on passing forever against a message no client could read — is now the anchored format assertion every other bucket's suite uses.


## 748. The wrist named its locales in five places and disagreed with none of them, because nothing read the resource set

**Decided 2026-08-26.** [followups.md](../product/followups.md) recorded that `locales_config.xml` and `L10nResourceParityTest`'s `localeDirs` "both enumerate the six by hand with nothing holding either to the `values-*` directories on disk", and asked for the Kotlin equivalent of [§ 740](#740-a-catalogue-only-ships-if-a-reader-can-reach-it-so-the-reachable-set-is-derived-and-guarded-rather-than-listed). It named two sites. Counting them found **five**, the same way § 740 found seven where the phone's filing named two — and the two the entry missed are the two a `values-*` directory is checked by.

**The five, measured on `aa30c53b0`.** `res/xml/locales_config.xml` lists six `<locale>` entries. `AndroidManifest.xml` carries the `android:localeConfig="@xml/locales_config"` reference, without which that file is inert and the OS per-app language picker never lists the app at all — a reachability gate in its own right, exactly as § 740 read the iOS `CFBundleLocalizations`. `L10nResourceParityTest.localeDirs` lists five translated directories. `ActivityTypeVocabularyTest.localeCatalogues` lists six directories again, each paired with the phone ARB and web catalogue it answers for, and `unmirroredPhoneCatalogues` records the one phone locale the wrist skips. A sixth site is absent rather than wrong: no Gradle file declares `resConfigs` or `androidResources.localeFilters`, so nothing strips a string set out of the APK after every check above has passed it — the filing's claim of no filter is confirmed by measurement, not restated. The other filed figure needs one correction: each directory carries **99 `<string>` plus 3 `<plurals>`, so 102 named resources**, identical across all six.

**The defect was reproduced before it was fixed.** A seventh `values-pt/strings.xml` — a copy of the Brazilian set with one key deleted — was dropped into the tree on unmodified `main` and `./gradlew testDebugUnitTest` reported **BUILD SUCCESSFUL, 627 tests, 0 failures**, with `L10nResourceParityTest` and `ActivityTypeVocabularyTest` each 5-for-5 green. A string set that ships in every build, that no reader can select because the OS picker never hears of it, and that is missing a key that would throw `Resources.NotFoundException` on any device set to it, was invisible to the entire suite. That is the same shape as `app_pt.arb` shipping dark twice, one platform over.

**The fix derives the set and holds every site to it.** `WearLocales` reads `src/main/res`, keeps each `values-*` directory that carries a `strings.xml`, and classifies the qualifier — the BCP-47 `b+pt+BR` form, the legacy `pt-rBR` form, and a bare language. The legacy form is validated against `Locale.getISOLanguages()` so a two-or-three-letter non-locale qualifier is not read as a language; `values-round` and `values-notround` are idiomatic on a Wear module and have the shape of language subtags. A directory whose qualifier is not recognised is **reported, never skipped** — silently dropping one would reintroduce the gap the object exists to close — and `WearLocalesTest` pins the grammar in both directions rather than leaving it to a probe.

**One site stays declared, deliberately.** Which phone and web catalogue a wrist locale *answers for* is a judgement — web spells Brazilian `pt-BR.ts` and there is no settled answer for what a European file would be called — so `localeCatalogues` keeps its explicit pairing and its **key set** is asserted equal to the directories on disk. That is § 740's `plistTagOverride` shape: a derived set plus a declared table with a companion assertion, not a second list to remember. The `unmirroredPhoneCatalogues` message now names both directions, because derivation makes the reverse live for the first time — the wrist catching up on `app_pt.arb` now fails the test that used to only notice the phone getting ahead.

**The guard was reported green by the build system on the change it exists to catch.** With everything above written and a `values-round/strings.xml` probe in place, `testDebugUnitTest` came back UP-TO-DATE and passed. `src/main/res` is an input to no test task: a locale directory adds no new resource *name*, so nothing on the unit-test classpath changes and Gradle correctly concludes it has nothing to do. Every source-level guard in this module that reads a file the compiler never compiles has the same hole; the ones over `src/main/kotlin` and the manifest are covered only by accident, because those are compile inputs. `src/main/res` and the three build scripts are now declared inputs of the test task, and only then did the probe fail. A CI run has never been affected — a fresh checkout has nothing to be up to date about — which is precisely why it could sit here unnoticed.

**Verified by observation, not by construction.** With the input declared and no test source touched, re-planting the seventh string set fails three tests at once, one per site: `locales_config` does not advertise it, `L10nResourceParityTest` finds the missing key, and `localeCatalogues` does not pair it. Removing it returns 635 tests, 0 failures, and `assembleDebug testDebugUnitTest` — the exact CI command — is green.

**Still owed, and unchanged by any of this: the wrist ships no European-Portuguese string set.** 102 resources of translation work, filed beside web's missing `pt-BR`-vs-`pt` catalogue. A `pt-PT` watch falls back to the Brazilian set through Android's own same-language region matching, which is the right degradation; the guard's only claim is that whatever the wrist ships is declared everywhere it needs to be.


## 749. Nothing typechecked the Playwright tree — and the fix is a second `tsc` root, because TypeScript does not merge `include` across `extends`

**Decided 2026-08-26.** The [followups](../product/followups.md) entry held exactly as filed on the mechanism and undercounted the fallout. `.svelte-kit/tsconfig.json` is generated by SvelteKit and its `include` names `src/`, `test/` and `tests/` — never `tests-e2e/` — so `npm run check` (svelte-check, in `build-web`) has never read a spec, and Playwright transpiles specs with esbuild, which strips types without checking them. **The one lane that already touched the tree is not a typecheck either**: `parity-types` runs `tsx --test 'tests-e2e/fixtures/**/*.test.ts'`, and `tsx` also strips rather than checks. So the premise survives the obvious rebuttal — the tree was outside *every* type check the repo runs, not merely outside svelte-check's.

**Six was measured before round 16 landed; the real figure is ten.** The filed six are all present and all real (two `BrowserContext` narrowings, two `string | null` arguments, an options object misused, a `.catch` on a `PromiseLike`). Four more were not in the entry: a stale `@ts-expect-error` in `tests-e2e/fixtures/auth.ts`, and three in `tests-e2e/scripts/start-mock-oidc.mjs`, which the entry's hand-run of `tsc` cannot have covered because it is `.mjs`. The `.mjs` is included here deliberately — `checkJs` is already on for the whole web app, its sibling `scripts/env_isolation.mjs` is already checked transitively through `vite.config.ts`, and a guard that covers "the `.ts` part of the Playwright tree" is a guard whose claim needs a footnote.

**Two of the ten were more than cosmetic.** `extended-nutrients.spec.ts` passed an assertion message as `toHaveCount`'s second argument; that parameter is an options bag and Playwright reads only `timeout` and `signal` off it, so the sentence explaining *why* a "N g left" chip must be absent has never once been printed on a failure — the author wrote a diagnosis the harness silently discarded, which is the failure mode `check_ci_diagnostics.mjs` exists to prevent one layer up. And `account-deletion.spec.ts` carried `plantedRunId` as `string | null` purely to serve a trailing `plantedRunId = null` whose comment said the `afterAll` reads it; the `afterAll` calls `deleteSagaUsers` and nothing else, so the assignment was dead and the nullability it forced was what broke two call sites. The other eight are type-level only: the two coaching specs assign a `BrowserContext` into an outer `let` from inside a `test.step` closure, which the checker cannot see, so at the `finally` the value is still its `null` initialiser and `if (ctx)` narrows it to `never` — fixed by creating both contexts up front and closing them unconditionally, which also deletes two `!` the same blindness had required.

**A separate config root, not a wider `include` on `tsconfig.json`.** The entry proposed "a `tests-e2e` entry in the check config", and that is the shape to avoid: TypeScript does not merge `include` across `extends` (`apps/web/tsconfig.json` says so in its own comment), so widening the app's own means pasting SvelteKit's generated list into a committed file and re-pasting it every time SvelteKit changes what it generates. A copy like that does not fail — it goes stale and silently stops covering whatever was added, which is the same class of quiet coverage loss as [§ 739](#739)'s skip-counts-as-a-pass. `apps/web/tsconfig.tests-e2e.json` instead extends the app config (inheriting `strict`, the `$lib` paths, `verbatimModuleSyntax`) and replaces `include` with the e2e tree alone. It is additive: SvelteKit keeps owning the app's include, and neither config can shrink the other.

**It runs in `parity-types`, ahead of the Supabase stack, and that job's `code` gate is not [§ 739](#739)'s trap here.** The gate is `needs.changes.outputs.code == 'true'`, which is false only for a diff confined to `docs/`, `.claude/` and `*.md`. Every diff that can introduce a type error into `tests-e2e/` — a spec, a fixture, or a `$lib` module a fixture imports — is by construction outside that set, so the check cannot be skipped on a diff it polices. (This is the opposite of `parity-matrix`, which had to be left ungated precisely because everything it reads *is* markdown.) It sits before `supabase start` alongside the other source-only guards, so a broken stack cannot silently skip it — the failure mode that hid two days of drift in run 26822355308 — and it carries its own `::error::` because `parity-types` is the one job `check_ci_diagnostics.mjs` requires per-step diagnoses from.

**The guard is guarded.** `tests-e2e/fixtures/tsconfig-coverage.test.ts` (in the web unit suite, so it runs in the same job) fails if any file under `tests-e2e/` carries a compilable extension that no `include` pattern matches, if the config stops extending the strict app config, or if `ci.yml` stops running the script. Both halves were observed failing before they were made to pass: the typecheck reports 10 errors on the pre-fix tree and 0 after, an injected `const x: number = 'y'` in a fixture takes it red again, and dropping `.mjs` from the include list takes the coverage test red naming `scripts/start-mock-oidc.mjs`.


## 750. The Strava redirect allowlist had no test at either end, and the CI value that looked like the gap was in a different job

**Decided 2026-08-26.** `STRAVA_ALLOWED_REDIRECTS` is the only thing between an OAuth `code` captured off some other path under our own domain and a live Strava grant: Strava's `/oauth/authorize` pins the callback to the registered Authorization Callback Domain, but that check is **path-prefix loose**, so a code that landed on an unrelated route of ours would token-exchange without it. Nothing exercised the comparison, in any suite. **Both branches — a redirect in the list accepted, one outside it refused — are now pinned in `apps/backend/supabase/functions/_shared/redirect_allowlist.test.ts`, and the workflow no longer names a port.**

**The filed premise was right about the count and wrong about the mechanism, in the direction that mattered.** Three spec bodies carry a `redirect_uri`, as filed. But "each of which the Edge Function answers before it compares against the allowlist" is true of only two: `invalid_code` and `invalid_scope` are answered in the top-level shape validation, upstream of `handleConnect` entirely. The third **does** reach the allowlist block — it short-circuits *inside* it, on `allowed.length === 0`, one line above `allowed.includes(redirectUri)`. That distinction is the whole finding, because it means the guard passes on an **empty** allowlist rather than on a rejected foreign origin, and its "deliberately foreign origin" is doing no work at all: any string reaches the same 503. Measured, not reasoned — the spec was re-run with that URI replaced by the lane's own callback, the one value the workflow used to pin, and it still returned 503.

**The CI literal was never in that spec's path.** `STRAVA_ALLOWED_REDIRECTS` is written into the `edge-functions` job's `.env.local` and consumed by a separately-booted `supabase functions serve`; `strava-import-guards.spec.ts` runs in the sharded `e2e-web` job against the CLI's auto-started edge runtime, which is given no such variable. So the value is unread for a stronger reason than "the asserted branch returns first" — **no `strava-import` test posts to the host that holds it**, and the two jobs disagree about whether the function is configured at all. Setting it in `e2e-web` would flip the existing 503 test rather than add coverage: that lane can pin exactly one of the three branches, and it already pins the most valuable one.

**Verified unexercised across all four suites**, not assumed: `strava-import/index.test.ts` is pure-helper and imports only `_shared/strava.ts`, never `index.ts`; `_shared/handler_envelope.test.ts` names `strava-import` once, in a comment about the platform gateway; no pgtap test and no web unit test reaches the function.

**The accept path cannot be tested at the wire, which is why it is tested pure.** Accepting means falling through to `POST https://www.strava.com/oauth/token`. A positive integration test would therefore make CI depend on a third party's availability and post junk OAuth codes at it, and the only observable difference from a rejection would be a 502 from a failed exchange. The decision itself is pure, so the parse and the comparison moved into `_shared/redirect_allowlist.ts` and the branches are pinned there — with four **source guards** covering what a pure test cannot: that `strava-import` still calls the gate, still calls it **before** the exchange (after it, the grant already exists and the check protects nothing), still fails closed on an unset allowlist, and that no function re-spells the parse inline.

**The comparison stays whole-string rather than adopting the sibling's origin match.** `events-connect-onboard/lib.ts`'s `validateReturnUrl` — written explicitly "the way strava-import pins STRAVA_ALLOWED_REDIRECTS", and the one of the two with tests — compares by **origin**, which is right for a Stripe `return_url` that legitimately carries a path and a query. Applying it here would re-open exactly the path-prefix window this allowlist exists to close, and would collapse `threkir://strava-callback` against every other opaque-scheme URI besides. The two semantics are deliberate and now documented at both ends; `api_database.md` meanwhile claimed an empty allowlist **disabled** the check "(single-tenant / dev)", the precise fail-open the code has always refused — corrected.

**One parse, four functions.** All four call sites that gate a redirect on an operator-declared allowlist (`strava-import`, plus `donations-checkout` / `events-checkout` / `events-connect-onboard` on `STRIPE_EVENTS_ALLOWED_REDIRECTS`) had copied the same split / trim / filter inline. Most divergences in that copy fail closed, which is why four copies survived; the one that does not is dropping `.filter(Boolean)`, after which `'a,,b'` admits the empty string and a caller claiming `redirect_uri: ''` walks through a gate the operator believes is armed. A guard now fails a fifth copy — the § 738 shape, a rule derived from the source rather than a list of the functions currently known to be fine.

**And the port derives from the lane instead of being restated.** § 743 made the specs resolve their origin through `tests-e2e/fixtures/base-url.ts`; the workflow was still hand-writing `http://localhost:7777/settings/integrations` — a second copy of a port, in a job that runs no web server. It now reads the line out of `.env.development`, the committed local-dev value, and two further guards pin **that** file (and `.env.example`) to the port `base-url.ts` declares and the callback path `apps/web/src/lib/integrations/strava.ts` actually sends. Moving the lane moves all of it with no second edit.

**Every guard was verified by breaking what it guards.** Six mutations, each observed killing the tests that claim to catch it and only those: widening the comparison to `startsWith` (2 dead), dropping `.filter(Boolean)` from the parse (2), removing the gate's call site (3), re-inlining the parse in `events-checkout` (1), moving the gate below the token exchange (1), and moving `DEFAULT_E2E_PORT` (2). Against pre-fix `main`'s sources the four source guards fail as written; the thirteen behavioural tests have no pre-fix seam to run against at all, which is the coverage that did not exist.


## 751. A mutation that widens a relation must be scoped to the rows the test filed, and the alias it is scoped on is not the one carrying the access control

**Decided 2026-08-26.** [§ 745](#745) built a second pgtap mutation operator — a permissive replacement per relation, dropping the predicate that says *whether the caller may see* a row — and filed the limit it could see: where the caller's own identity is the assertion's only subject selector, the replacement also reveals whatever `seed.sql` left in that table, so the kill proves a subject exists in the transaction rather than that the test built one. **The filing was right about the defect and wrong about its boundary in both directions.** It is not confined to identity-only selectors: `gym_exercise_set_history('Bench Press')` carries a subject selector — an exercise name — and the RPC normalises it, while the seed commits **six `Bench press` sets**, so that assertion was killed by committed data whether or not its fixture existed. And it named "seven assertions" while listing seven *relations*; the assertions over those seven number **eleven**, five of them `coach_roster_summary`'s alone.

**The fix is a per-entry `subject` alias, and the alias is the point.** Every permissive replacement now reveals only rows whose `xmin` is the current transaction's, so a kill means the test *wrote* the subject. The filing recorded that `xmin` "is not sound as written" and gave the counterexample, which turns out to be an argument for scoping the right relation rather than against scoping at all: for `public_run_gear` the predicate dropped is a visibility check on `runs` while the rows returned are `run_gear` joined to `gear`, so scoping the access-controlled table restricts nothing the caller ever sees. **The rule is therefore "scope the relation the replacement's rows come from", not "scope the relation the dropped predicate guarded"** — `run_gear rg`, `coach_athletes ca` (the roster link, not the athlete profile it names), `gym_sets s` (the sets the view returns, not the parent workout carrying the `is_public`). An UPDATE writes a new row version, so a test that establishes its subject by mutating a seed row is transaction-local too; what stays outside is a row the test only ever SELECTed, which is exactly the exposure. Rows written inside a subtransaction read as foreign, and that direction is the safe one — the mutation goes inert, the assertion survives, and the guard names it. `pg_xact_status` would cover those and is unusable: it is superuser-only, and the SECURITY INVOKER replacements run as `authenticated`.

**Six of the twenty-four witnesses were `select 1;`, which is the same defect wearing the instrument's clothes.** § 745 required every replacement to carry a witness — a subject the real relation provably hides, which the replacement must provably reveal — precisely so an inert operator could not hide inside a green run. The six owner-scoped gym and streak RPCs satisfied it by pointing at the seed: they set up nothing and probed whatever was already committed, so they proved the replacement reveals *the database*, which is the very thing the scoping exists to stop. They now file their own workout, set and run. This is why the round's own instrument had to be re-validated before its result was trusted rather than after.

**The result of the scoping is that nothing moved, and that is the finding.** All **51** definer-measured assertions still die, so every one of them had already filed its own subject; no pgtap fixture changed, and the population is unchanged at **168** (117 owner bypass, 51 additionally replaced), with the same 5 expected survivors. The tightening can only reveal fewer rows, so an assertion can move from killed to surviving and never the reverse — the guard cannot have got weaker. That it *would* have caught something is shown rather than asserted, by deleting a fixture inside a rolled-back transaction and re-running both operators over the same file: with the fixture present both kill; with it deleted the **old** operator still kills — a refusal scored healthy by a row nobody filed — and the new one lets it survive, so the guard reports it. Demonstrated on four tables (`gym_sets` twice, `coach_athletes`, `runs`); on `user_settings` both operators leave it standing, because the seed commits no discoverable runner for either to reveal.

**A third end-to-end control makes that permanent.** § 745's control pair — a known-good refusal that must be killed and a known-bad one that must survive — cannot tell a scoped replacement from an unscoped one, since both differ only in whether a subject exists *in the transaction*. The **known-debris** case is a private route `seed.sql` already committed: the real view hides it, the unscoped replacement revealed it, and the scoped one must leave the assertion standing. Removing `mine('r')` from `public_routes` fails it by name, and a static unit test fails first for the same removal on any of the twenty-four.

**The second half of § 745's filing was two relations, not four.** `get_event_meet_point` and `public_run_counts` *are* registered and their refusal assertions die; what those two contribute is one non-refusal shape claim each (a coord-less event, an empty input array), which is a different fact. The definer relations genuinely read by a zero-or-empty assertion with no replacement are **`fetch_pending_reports`** and **`challenge_leaderboard`**, one assertion apiece. Both stay unregistered, with the reason recorded and checked rather than rediscovered: the first's zero is the RPC's own `status = 'pending'` filter, so a replacement may only drop the admin gate and the assertion would survive — an `EXPECTED_SURVIVORS` entry bought with a second copy of the queue query; the second expects a zero *value* rather than an emptiness, the class § 745 already put outside. `UNREGISTERED_DEFINER_RELATIONS` is re-derived from the suite in the validation phase and fails in both directions, so a third such relation is a decision someone makes rather than a chore the guard hands them at merge.

**What is not closed is the same exposure on operator 1**, and it is filed with a measured bound rather than a guess. The owner bypass is a role change with no query to add a predicate to, and dropping RLS reveals the whole table exactly as a dropped `WHERE` does — § 741's third defect *was* this, answered by 41 committed `fitness_snapshots` rows. **63 of its 117 assertions read at least one table `seed.sql` leaves rows in**; the other 54 read only tables that are empty on a seed-only database and cannot be answered by debris at all. Most of the 63 carry a uuid the test inserted, so the real number is smaller than the bound.

## 752. Three trees under `apps/web` were outside every typecheck, not one — including eight production Lambda handlers and the service worker

**Decided 2026-08-26.** The [#789 filing](../product/followups.md) named `apps/web/scripts/*.mjs` and got the mechanism exactly right: `.svelte-kit/tsconfig.json`'s `include` is `src/`, `test/`, `tests/` and `vite.config.*`, TypeScript does not merge `include` across `extends`, and `scripts/env_isolation.mjs` is in the app program only because `vite.config.ts` imports it — `tsc -p tsconfig.json --listFilesOnly` names that one file under `scripts/` and no other. What the filing understated is how much else lives in the same blind spot. Every compilable file under `apps/web` outside `src/`, `tests-e2e/` and `vite.config.ts` was in no `tsc` program at all: **eight of nine files under `scripts/`, sixteen under `lambda/` — eight `build.mjs` wrappers and the eight production AWS handlers behind `/api/coach`, `/share/{event,profile,club,race}`, the OG images, `generate-route` and `osrm-proxy` — plus `svelte.config.js` and `static/sw.js`.** Only `lambda/share-entity/src/index.ts` was covered, and only because something under `src/` imports it. The scripts were the filed defect; the Lambda handlers are the one that mattered.

**Two new roots, and the second is not optional.** `apps/web/tsconfig.node.json` covers `scripts/`, `lambda/` and `svelte.config.js`; `apps/web/tsconfig.service-worker.json` covers `static/`. They cannot be one file: a service worker's globals come from the `WebWorker` lib, which cannot share a program with `DOM` — both declare `Event`, `EventTarget` and their kin. Both are separate roots rather than a wider `include` on `tsconfig.json` for the reason [§ 749](#749) recorded and that config states in its own comment. Both declare `"types": ["node"]` / `[]` explicitly, because the automatic type-root scan does not fire under this config chain and `moduleResolution: bundler` skips `node:`-prefixed specifiers outright: without it every `process` and every `import ... from 'node:fs'` reads as an unresolved name. § 749's own root is given the same declaration in this change — it had node globals only because `jszip` happens to carry a `/// <reference types="node" />`, which is a dependency bump away from disappearing.

**47 errors in the Node root — and the largest cause was one missing annotation.** (The service worker's 23 were all one thing: a plain-JS service worker under `DOM` cannot see `ServiceWorkerGlobalScope`, `waitUntil` or `clients` at all, so they are the environment being wrong rather than the code.) `fail(msg)` in all four `cross_client_roundtrip_*.mjs` scripts ends in `process.exit(1)`, but TypeScript infers `void` for a *function declaration* whose endpoint is unreachable (only expressions get `never`), so no guard below it narrowed anything: `if (!url || !anonKey) fail(...)` left `url` as `string | undefined` at every use. `@returns {never}` on those four closed 24 of the 47 at once — which is the shape of most of the rest too, symptoms of a handful of causes rather than 47 independent defects.

**Four were more than type-level.** `svelte.config.js` passed `prerender: { default: true }` to `adapter-static`, which has never had that option — `AdapterOptions` is `pages/assets/fallback/precompress/strict` — so it is dead config left over from the SvelteKit 1 template, silently ignored on every build since. The same file built `paths.base` from `process.env.BASE_PATH || ''` without checking the shape SvelteKit requires (empty, or a leading `/` and no trailing one); a value breaking that rule is not rejected, it is concatenated into every URL the app emits, so the whole site 404s with nothing naming the cause — it now normalises the trailing slash and throws on a missing leading one. `cross_client_roundtrip_read.mjs` and `_sync_read.mjs` decoded the gzipped track through `new Response(buf).body.pipeThrough(ds)`, where `.body` is nullable, when the `Blob` they already hold streams directly. And `cross_client_roundtrip_live_read.mjs` fed `public_runs.started_at` — nullable in the view — to `new Date(...)` unchecked, which would have compared the epoch against the fixture instead of failing.

**The `.mjs` blind spot is shared with the repo's own guards, and that half is closed too.** `apps/web/scripts/check_production_env.mjs` — the guard that refuses a production build against placeholder endpoints — carried a full inline copy of [§ 709](#709)'s four affirmative literals. Not a divergence today, but § 709's source guard could not have caught one: it walked `src/` and `lambda/` for `.ts` and `.svelte`, and this copy was a `.mjs` under `scripts/`, outside both. The script now imports the canonical `isTruthyFlagValue` (Node 24 strips types off the `.ts` import, so the plain-`node` release and CI invocations are unchanged) and the guard's walk covers `scripts/` and `.mjs`, verified by putting the copy back and watching it name the file.
