**The coverage guard derives its requirement rather than listing it.** `apps/web/scripts/tsconfig_coverage.test.mjs` reads *every* `tsconfig*.json` at the top of `apps/web`, resolves each one's effective `include`/`exclude` by following `extends` until one declares them — which is how the generated `.svelte-kit/tsconfig.json` is read rather than transcribed — and asserts that every compilable file git reports under `apps/web` is matched by at least one. Nothing in it names a tree, so a root added later counts the moment it exists, a tree added later is uncovered the moment it appears, and SvelteKit changing what it generates changes what the guard expects. Its second half asserts every root is named by an npm script that `ci.yml` runs. All three failure modes were observed: an added `apps/web/tools/thing.ts` is named, `scripts/**/*.mjs` removed from the include names all ten files under it, and rewiring the CI step to the wrong script fails by name. The typechecks run as one `parity-types` step alongside § 749's, each of the three invocations carrying its own `::error::` per that job's contract.

**What is not closed is the same hole outside `apps/web`, filed with a measured count.** Thirty-three of the repo's fifty-two tracked `.mjs` files live under the root `scripts/`, `apps/backend/scripts/`, `.github/actions/` and `infra/`, in a repo with no root `tsconfig.json` at all; a `tsc` pass over them reports **369 errors**, worst in `check_ios_native_declarations.mjs` (46), `check_pnpm_overrides.mjs` (36) and `check_toolchain_pins.mjs` (35). That is its own slice — those files are CI guards under three different package roots — and the guard added here is deliberately scoped to `apps/web`, whose coverage it can state completely.

## 753. The pgtap owner bypass did have a query to add a predicate to — a row-level security policy is one — and the residue it was filed for was zero assertions wide

**Decided 2026-08-26.** [§ 751](#751) closed the seed-debris exposure on the second mutation operator and filed the same exposure on the first with a measured bound: the owner bypass is "a role change with no query to add a predicate to", **63 of its 117 assertions read at least one table `seed.sql` leaves rows in**, and the other 54 "cannot be answered by debris at all". **Both counts are exactly right on a seed-only database** — re-measured after a `supabase db reset`, 63 and 54, with `runs` at 9 assertions over 251 rows as the worst, and every one of the other 54's tables genuinely empty. **Everything the filing concluded from them is wrong, in both directions.**

**The 63/54 split is a census of TABLES, and the assertions are what carry selectors.** Run each of the 117 candidates' own SQL against a seed-only database with row-level security off — which is precisely what the old operator's kill was worth — and **not one of them returns a row.** The residue being closed was zero assertions wide today, not 63 and not "smaller than the bound". Only one of the 117 has a selector that depends on session state (`safety_contacts_test.sql:193`), over a table the seed leaves empty, so the probe measures what it claims to. The 54 is wrong the other way: **three of them read `activities`**, which is not a table at all but a `security_invoker` view unioning `runs` (251 seed rows), `gym_workouts` and `food_log`, so it is absent from the table census while being answerable by debris in a way the entry says is impossible. A count of the tables an assertion mentions predicts neither.

**The framing is the part that mattered, and "no query to add a predicate to" is false.** Row-level security is not only a role check; it is a set of policy expressions, and **a policy is a query to add a predicate to.** So operator 1 is no longer `set role` to the BYPASSRLS owner. Every RLS-enabled table in `public` — 90 of them, all with RLS on, none FORCEd, no restrictive policies anywhere — gains one extra permissive `SELECT` policy revealing only the rows this transaction wrote, and the assertion then runs **as the role the test gave it** rather than as the owner. That is § 751's shape one layer down: the same scope, on the mechanism instead of on the relation. Neither mechanism the entry proposed was needed — no savepoint-and-delete (whose FK cascades it rightly feared) and no double run. The policies are created once per file, immediately after its `begin;`, and gated on a GUC so they are inert outside a mutated span; all 90 cost **14.8 ms**, against ~90 DDL statements per assertion if the span carried them.

**The second operator keeps the owner bypass, and that is a decision rather than an omission.** All **51** of its assertions read the replaced relation and nothing else, so the replacement's own transaction-local scope is the whole of their subject selection and no base table they asked about is reached. Restoring the caller's role there also breaks: `events` carries **column-level** SELECT grants rather than a table-level one, and `xmin` is a system column, so a `SECURITY INVOKER` replacement scoped on `xmin` and run as `anon` fails with `permission denied for table events` — a fact about how Supabase grants that no amount of predicate-writing removes.

**Underneath it was a defect in § 751's own predicate, and it is the more useful finding.** `xmin = pg_current_xact_id()::xid` matches only a TOP-LEVEL write, and pgtap's `lives_ok` / `throws_ok` run their payload in a subtransaction — which is the idiomatic way a pgtap test states that a write succeeded. § 751 recorded this as "the safe direction" because the mutation goes inert and the guard reports a survivor; at operator 1's scale it is **11 false survivors across 9 files** on the first scoped run, three of them `public_recaps_rls_test`'s, all resting on one `lives_ok(... update ...)`. § 751 also recorded why the exact test was out of reach — `pg_xact_status` is superuser-only and these predicates run as `authenticated` — and a `SECURITY DEFINER` wrapper owned by `postgres` is the answer to that. Given a row the caller can already SEE, an xmin still IN PROGRESS can only be this transaction's own, because every other in-progress transaction's rows are invisible under MVCC; so "visible and in progress" is exactly "written here", subtransactions included. The epoch is put back as `pg_current_xact_id()` less its own low 32 bits, and the `w >= c` guard keeps that honest — an xid older than ours may be from a previous epoch or have had its clog truncated, and is never one of ours, so it is answered without asking. Both operators share the one predicate, so neither can drift.

**With the predicate right, nothing moved — the same result § 751 got, and the same reason to state it.** The population is unchanged at **168** (117 base, 51 replaced), all **163** non-excused assertions still die, the same 5 expected survivors, and no pgtap fixture changed: every one of the 117 had already filed its own subject. The pgtap suite is untouched and still 258 files / 2188 tests green. The guard costs 10 s → 34 s, which is the per-row policy call on the mutated statements.

**Both halves are pinned by the end-to-end control rather than by this entry.** It grows a second trio over a base table read as a stranger — known-good, known-bad, known-debris — beside the definer trio, and its known-good is filed through `lives_ok` on purpose so the scope can never narrow back to top-level writes. Reverting operator 1 to the role change fails the **base known-debris** case by name and nothing else, which is the demonstration that the old operator scored a refusal healthy off a row nobody filed while the new one reports it; reverting the predicate to § 751's fails **both** known-good cases. A static unit test fails first for a span that changes role or a policy that drops the scope.

## 754. The one filing in this round that was true as written — and the port that would have honoured it faithfully was the one that shipped a broken goal field

`SocialService.createChallenge` really was dead code in both twins: 58 public methods on `SocialService`, and it is the only one with **zero** references anywhere under `apps/mobile_*/lib`, `apps/mobile_*/test` or `packages/`. The three other candidates a mechanical sweep turns up — `myActiveChallenges`, `recomputeChallengeCompletion`, `fetchCancelledInstancesForEvents` — are each called from inside `social_service.dart` itself. `parity.md`'s ✗ / ✗ cells were accurate, and so was its claim that closing the box means building the form rather than doing backend work.

**Deleting it was the wrong half of the choice, and the codebase says so in three places.** § 24 makes mobile *additive*, not forbidden. The FAB seam `SocialScreen` uses for Clubs is written as a general contract — "each embedded sub-tab exposes its own FAB widget via a `buildXFab` method on its public State" — so Challenges carried no FAB because no create surface existed, not because one had been refused; `parity.md`'s "deliberately hoists no FAB" was reading a selective hoist as a decision against the tab. And the round-17 work that put `rateLimitCreateChallenge` into six web catalogues and **seven ARBs** ([§ 747](#747-the-eleventh-rate-limit-bucket-now-reaches-the-parser--but-the-refusal-a-throttled-challenge-creator-actually-saw-was-swallowed-not-leaked)) shipped a mobile sentence that no mobile code path could reach. Deleting the method would have stranded that string too — one dead artifact removed by leaving a second one.

**The goal field is where a faithful port would have been wrong.** `challenges.goal_value` is metres for `distance`, metres for `vert`, seconds for `duration` and a bare count for the other two, and `ChallengeEditor.svelte` asks for that number through a field labelled only "Goal (optional)". A person typing `100` into it means 100 km and creates a **100 metre** goal that every entrant clears on their first run — silently, because the value is valid, the insert succeeds, and the progress bar fills. The mobile field therefore carries the reader's own unit as a suffix and converts at the boundary (`challengeGoalSuffix` / `challengeGoalToStored`), which is not an invention but the idiom `goal_editor_sheet.dart` already uses for its distance / time / pace targets; `UnitFormat.elevationToMetres` was added beside the existing `elevationLabel` gap so entry and display share one feet-per-metre constant, the same entry/exit split `paceSecPerUnit` / `paceSecPerKm` keeps. Switching the metric clears a typed goal, because a 100 that meant kilometres must not become 100 hours. **Web is left as it is and filed**: it is a different surface's defect, and fixing it needs the six catalogues this round has four other agents in.

**Two refusals are handled where they can name themselves.** `challenges_window_ck` raises a 23514 that names neither bound, so the end-after-start rule is checked before the insert and flagged on the row the author has to move; the widget test drives the real Material picker a year out rather than asserting the predicate, so the check is pinned where it runs. And the create throttle's P0001 goes through `rateLimitErrorMessage` **before** `friendlyError` — `classifyAuthError` matches `rate limit` in the message and would answer `authErrorRateLimited`, a generic "too many attempts" naming neither the bucket nor the wait, which is the swallow § 747 had just removed from web arriving by a different route.

**The layer beneath: `privacyZonesTitle` was declared twice in all seven ARB catalogues, and `l10n_parity_test.dart` cannot see a duplicate at all.** `jsonDecode` keeps the last of a repeated key, so key-set parity, empty-value and placeholder-faithfulness assertions all run against a map that has already discarded one copy; gen-l10n takes the getter's *position* from the first occurrence and its value and description from the last, so the two halves can disagree and only one ships. Here both copies carried the same string under two different descriptions — the Settings tile and the AppBar title of the screen it opens — which is the only reason nothing broke. The guard scans the raw catalogue for repeated top-level keys and pins that its scan sees exactly the key set `jsonDecode` does, so a reformat fails the test rather than making it pass vacuously; against a re-inserted duplicate it fails naming `privacyZonesTitle`. Regenerating after the de-duplication produced a one-line diff — the merged doc comment — which is the proof that no shipped string moved. The web catalogues were checked for the same class and carry no duplicate.

## 755. Both Portuguese boxes were true, both counts were right, and the phone's own European catalogue turned out to be a tenth finished

**Decided 2026-08-27.** [followups.md](../product/followups.md) carried two open boxes and a third in section S: web ships no European-Portuguese catalogue, the wrist ships no European-Portuguese string set, and — separately filed — "the Wear OS pt-PT string set, 102 resources". The two entries disagreed about the wrist's size, 99 against 102. Both filings were **accurate**, which is the first round of this issue where the premise survived measurement intact; what did not survive was the assumption underneath them, that `app_pt.arb` is a finished European catalogue the other two platforms are merely behind on.

**The counts, measured.** The wrist carries **99 `<string>` plus 3 `<plurals>` = 102 named resources**, identical across all six shipped directories — so section E's "99 strings" and section S's "102 resources" are the same file counted two ways, and [§ 748](#748-the-wrist-named-its-locales-in-five-places-and-disagreed-with-none-of-them-because-nothing-read-the-resource-set)'s correction stands. Web's catalogue is **5,049 keys**, not the ~2,682 [parity.md](../product/parity.md) claimed. Mobile ships `app_pt.arb` *and* `app_pt_BR.arb`, both 3,772 keys, where the filing named only the first.

**The premise that failed: `app_pt.arb` differs from its Brazilian sibling on 359 of 3,772 keys — 9.5%.** The other 3,413 are byte-identical Brazilian copies, and conspicuously so: the entire auth block is Brazilian (`authPasswordLabel` "Senha", `authErrorOffline` "Você parece estar offline. Verifique sua conexão"), as are `historyTimelineEmpty` "Nada registrado", `gymOfflineCached` "treinos salvos", and `settingsAccountRestoreTileSubtitle` "backup .zip salvo". Two of its curated strings are half-converted — `safetyAutoLiveShareSubtitle` still reads "compartilhamento ao vivo … em andamento" inside a sentence that was otherwise rewritten, and `ttsPaceAlertFast` keeps "Acelere" where the neighbouring `ttsPaceAlertSpeedUpByKm` was moved to "Acelera". So the thing web was "behind" is a catalogue a tenth of the way there. Building web by lifting from it would have imported those Brazilian leftovers as European.

**What the 359 are good for is not text but evidence.** Diffing the pair token by token yields a substitution corpus this project's own curators produced: `esteira`→`passadeira`, `controle`→`controlo`, `salvar`→`guardar`, `registrada`→`registada`, `excluir`→`eliminar`, `compartilhar`→`partilhar`, `tela`→`ecrã`, `arquivo`→`ficheiro`, `contato`→`contacto`, `recursos`→`funcionalidades`, `rápido demais`→`demasiado depressa`, `de novo`→`novamente`, `ao vivo`→`em direto`, `quilômetro`→`quilómetro`, and the gerund periphrasis `Você está criando`→`Está a criar`. The web catalogue was derived from `pt-BR.ts` through that measured corpus rather than invented: **133 strings lifted where the ARB already had a curated European counterpart, 1,165 rule-transformed, 5 pinned to the activity vocabulary the wrist cross-checks, 3,746 unchanged because the two variants genuinely share them.** The result differs from Brazilian on **1,288 of 5,049 keys, 25.5%** — against the phone's 9.5%, which makes the browser the most European surface we ship and the phone the box that is now behind.

**Register was a decision, not a default.** `app_pt.arb` mixes `tu` and third person inside one language: `challengesStandingTitle` says "A tua posição" while the whole `rateLimit.*` block says "aguarde … tente novamente". One catalogue cannot address one reader two ways, so both new surfaces use **subject-pronoun elision with third-person verbs** — the register European Portuguese software uses, and the one 3,746 untouched strings were already in, so it is also the smaller change. Orthography is the post-1990 Acordo throughout (`ativar`, `adotar`, `objetivo`), keeping the spellings it preserves rather than flattens (`contacto`, `facto`, `receção`, `bebé`, `quilómetro`).

**The derivation had four systematic bugs, each found by reading its output rather than by a test.** Case was mirrored upward only, so a capitalised table entry leaked its capital mid-sentence ("Métodos que Pode usar"). `Pular` became `Ignorar`, which is *dismiss* — the accessibility skip link read "Ignorar para o conteúdo principal" where Portugal says "Saltar". Singular `configuração` was renamed to `definição`, though only the Settings *screen* is "Definições". And sentence-initial recasing ran after every interior full stop, capitalising the "o" inside "(ex.: o app do Wear OS)" while leaving a pronoun elided from the front of an interior sentence lower case. All four were classes, not instances; the last is now guarded on three letters before the stop, never `etc.`, and never `parkrun`, which is lower case wherever it falls.

**Making pt-PT real would have cost a Lisbon reader the Learn guides.** Eight guides exist in English plus five translations, and `getGuide` fell back to English alone. Before this change a pt-PT browser negotiated onto `pt-BR` and read the Brazilian prose; giving it a locale of its own would have dropped it to English — a regression introduced by an improvement. `getGuide` now resolves exact locale, then any guide in the same **language**, then English, and `isEnglishFallback` asks the same question, because "this guide is in English" above Brazilian prose is a lie. It generalises past Portuguese, and it makes the missing pt-PT prose cost nothing.

**The bare `pt` tag was the one genuine judgement, and the guard had already made it.** CLDR gives `pt` Brazilian default content, which argues for pointing the base there; the phone points it at European. `locale_reach.test.ts` settled it — the exemption list it shipped empty in [§ 740](#740-a-catalogue-only-ships-if-a-reader-can-reach-it-so-the-reachable-set-is-derived-and-guarded-rather-than-listed) was documented as the one "Mobile carries the pt-BR entry this list is shaped for", i.e. the design always expected Brazilian to be the variant reached by its exact tag. It costs a Brazilian reader nothing — Android, iOS and every browser report the region — and the bare tag is worth more to Portugal, which shares its orthography with `pt-AO`, `pt-MZ` and `pt-CV`, none of which we carry. `BASE_TO_LOCALE.pt` is therefore `pt-PT`, matching the phone, and `BASE_FALLBACK_EXEMPT` has its first entry with that reasoning attached.

**The machinery that failed is the same shape § 740 and § 748 each found, one layer along.** Round 17 killed the hand-written locale list in the language picker and guarded that one site. **Six other suites kept theirs** — `stage_labels`, `dashboard_fitness_source_guard`, `read_failure_guards` (twice), `segments_panel_guards` (twice) and `share_publish_consent_guard` each looped over a spelled-out `['en','de','es','fr','ja','pt-BR']` and opened the catalogue by name. Every one is an "every catalogue carries this key" claim, every one is *named* "all six catalogues", and every one would have gone on passing while checking nothing whatever about European Portuguese. They derive now, and a source scan over every `.ts`/`.svelte` file fails on any flat array literal naming three or more shipped tags, with must-flag/must-spare fixtures and a named allowlist holding the one deliberate subset (`number.test.ts`'s comma-decimal loop, which pt-PT joins). Verified by observation: re-planting the `stage_labels` list fails the scan and names the file.

**Verification.** Web: 4,278 unit tests, 0 failures, `npm run check` clean. The two Portuguese catalogues are proved apart end to end rather than on disk — a Chromium context at `pt-PT` gets `lang="pt-PT"` *and* "Saltar para o conteúdo principal" where Brazilian says "Pular", and a bare `pt` context lands on European; 7 passed in the negotiation block, 4 in the picker. Wrist: `assembleDebug testDebugUnitTest --rerun-tasks` green at 638 tests, 0 failures, with `--rerun-tasks` because § 748 found `src/main/res` reports UP-TO-DATE otherwise. The two declaration sites were re-verified the way § 748 verified them — with the string set on disk and both sites reverted, exactly two tests fail, one per site, and `unmirroredPhoneCatalogues` is now empty because the wrist mirrors every phone locale for the first time.

**What this does not claim.** Both catalogues are **model-authored and not natively reviewed**, and the existing native-review box has been widened to name pt-PT rather than left listing only the older five. Three surfaces still collapse every `pt*` tag to Brazilian — the auth-email Edge Function, the Go job worker's email/SMS/push catalogues, and the watchOS string catalogue — so a pt-PT reader now gets European Portuguese in the browser and on the wrist, and Brazilian in their inbox. That is newly sharper than before this change, and it is filed rather than fixed. `app_pt.arb`'s remaining 90% is filed too.

## 756. A third checkbox state was in use with its only documented meaning being nearly the opposite one, and the survey built to find open work could not see it

**Decided 2026-08-26.** Issue #789 § I.4 filed "12 `- [~]` partial boxes (built but not live) exist across the docs and are invisible to a `- [ ]` grep. At least one — runners-nearby — is tracked nowhere else." **Both numbers in that sentence are wrong, and the second is wrong in the direction that mattered.** There are **14**, not 12, and runners-nearby is tracked at `followups.md` § *Deploy gate: turn the runners-nearby flag on* — under a heading literally named *Surfaced by the #789 mobile runners-nearby build*, filed by an earlier round of this same issue. The item genuinely tracked nowhere else was the **live-hub Redis** bullet, which nothing in the filing named. The whole marker population is three: `[ ]` × 463, `[x]` × 675, `[~]` × 14. No `[?]`, no `[WIP]`, no fourth convention — the strikethrough bullets that look like a fourth state are all struck-then-shipped annotations, not checkboxes.

**The premise underneath the filing was sound, and worse than filed.** `- [~]` was not undocumented; it was documented to mean something else. `reviews/README.md` defines it as **deferred — won't fix now**, and `conventions.md` § *Audit & review findings* repeats that. The docs tree had been using the same glyph for **built but not yet live**, which is close to the opposite: one says nobody is working on it, the other says the code is merged and an operator step is owed. `docs/custom_watch/roadmap.md` read it a third way again — its own § 101 rule keeps every box in that section `[ ]` until **bench-verified**, and the single `[~]` there sat three lines below an ICE-card entry in the identical build state carrying `[ ]`. Three readings of one glyph, in one repo, none of them wrong given what was written down.

**Reconciled against the code, most of the 14 were stale docs rather than partial work — but not in the direction "tick them all".** Six (weekly digest, lifecycle drip, native push ×3 including two self-declared duplicates, engagement email) are **code-complete and deploy-gated**: every migration, handler, sender and client the bullets name exists and is dispatched, and `handler_native_push.go` leaves an uncredentialed row pending *without stamping it* so a later deploy delivers the backlog. Under the repo's own "compliance sign-offs gate prod, not code" rule those stay `[~]` — a feature no user can reach has not shipped — and what they were missing was a link to the open half, not a tick. The custom-watch box became `[ ]`, matching its file's stated rule. The four in `followups_archive.md` were verified complete and **left exactly as they are**: that file is a verbatim 2026-06-14 snapshot, and the four `[~]` are what the live file carried that day, confirmed by reading `followups.md` at the prune commit's parent. Rewriting a snapshot to satisfy a rule written afterwards makes it something other than a snapshot.

**The fix is that a partial box now names where its unfinished half is tracked**, generalising the rule `reviews/README.md` § 2 already states for a deferred finding. `conventions.md` gains a `<!-- doc-checkbox-states -->` block holding the vocabulary once, and `scripts/check_doc_checkboxes.mjs` **reads that block rather than restating it** (§ 738/§ 739): a fourth state must be documented before it can appear, the guard holds `reviews/README.md` to the same *set* of markers so the two homes cannot drift apart, and every `[~]` must link `followups.md` or `roadmap.md` — the files a survey actually greps. A dated snapshot declares `<!-- doc-checkbox-frozen -->` **in itself** and is exempt from the link only, so the guard carries no list of exceptions.

**The reconciliation found the tracking entries were themselves the stale artifact.** `followups.md`'s two native-push entries both said "no `firebase_messaging` wiring exists" and pointed at a `user_devices.push_token` column that has never existed; the bridge, the pubspec deps and `ApiClient.registerDeviceToken` all ship. Its SRV-1 entry filed localized auth email as "platform-limited, not a quick edit" while `functions/auth-email/` ships six locales with the hook enabled in `config.toml`, and the same file already tracked the real remainder — a prod deploy — correctly one section above. Pointing a `[~]` at a tracking entry that describes work as unwritten when it is merged is worse than not pointing at all, so those were corrected in the same change. Two genuinely untracked items were filed: the Redis one, and the engagement-email SMTP gate.

**The Redis bullet also hid unwritten code behind what read as provisioning.** It said "code only; no Redis is provisioned", citing `main.go:497` and `main.go:510` — both stale by ~59 lines. Reading the real lines shows `main.go:671` wires the Realtime→hub Bridge inside `if inProc, ok := hub.(*livehub.Hub); ok`, so setting `REDIS_URL` **silently drops the Bridge**, with no log line, and a hub spectator stops seeing runners still on the legacy transport — exactly the population that exists during the cutover Redis is wanted for. `bridge.go:37-40` says the cursor and hub-native state would have to move into Redis and are "not built". Provisioning alone would have made things worse than doing nothing.

**The guard runs in `parity-matrix`, not in the web unit suite, and that placement is the second defect.** `apps/web/src/lib/*.test.ts` runs in `parity-types`, which is gated on `needs.changes.outputs.code`; a `docs/**.md` diff sets that false, every code-gated job skips, and the CI gate counts a skip as a pass. A doc guard living there would never run on the PRs it polices — the failure `parity-matrix`'s own comment already records for `parity.md`, and the reason that job is deliberately ungated. Cost: one `node --test` step, seconds, on a job with no `npm ci`, so the guard is stdlib-only by construction.

## 757. The count outside `apps/web` was understated, "three package roots" was wrong twice over, and the one production artifact in the set was the one the filing did not count

**Decided 2026-08-27.** [§ 752](#752) closed the same class inside `apps/web` and filed the rest with a measurement: 33 tracked `.mjs` files under the root `scripts/`, `apps/backend/scripts/`, `.github/actions/` and `infra/`, **369 errors**, in a repo with no root `tsconfig.json` at all. Re-measured at this commit: **35 `.mjs` plus one `.js`, 386 errors.** The filing was right on its date and the arithmetic reconciles exactly — `check_doc_checkboxes.mjs` and its test (13 errors) landed in the *same commit* § 752 did, from another slice of the same round, and a same-commit edit to `check_pgtap_refusal_assertions.mjs` moved it from 35 to 38. 369 + 13 + 3 + 1 = 386. It was understated, and only because the tree moved under it.

**Two things in it were wrong on any date.** "Three package roots" is wrong in both directions: the filing's own sentence names *four* trees, and only *two* of them are package roots — the repo root and `apps/backend`; `.github/` and `infra/` carry no `package.json` at all, which is precisely why nothing had ever pointed a compiler at them. And the set is not `.mjs`: `infra/modules/web-stack/functions/www_redirect.js` is a **CloudFront Function**, JavaScript Terraform reads with `file()` and uploads verbatim, running at the edge on **every viewer request to the site** to 301 `www.` onto the apex. It was in no program either. That is § 752's own shape repeating — there the scripts were the filed defect and eight production Lambda handlers were the one that mattered; here the guards were the filed defect and the edge function is the artifact with users on the other end of it.

**Two roots over a shared base, and the second is not optional.** `tsconfig.scripts.json` covers the Node side; `tsconfig.cloudfront.json` covers the functions directory, for the reason § 752 gave the service worker: the runtime is neither Node nor a browser. `cloudfront-js-2.0` is ECMAScript 5.1 plus a subset of later features with no `Promise`, no timers and no `fetch`, so `lib` is `es5` and `types` is empty and the runtime's real surface is declared in `cloudfront.d.ts` beside the function — an `await` or a `setTimeout` that would throw at the edge now fails at the typecheck instead. (`target` is left inherited: TypeScript 6 deprecates `es5` there outright, and under `noEmit` it governs nothing `lib` does not.) `tsconfig.base.json` holds the strictness both share, deliberately the same settings `apps/web/tsconfig.json` layers onto SvelteKit's generated config, so a guard script is held to exactly the bar the app is.

**251 of the 386 were one diagnostic — and underneath them were ten guards that were not guarding.** The bulk is `TS7006`, an unannotated parameter, and most of the rest fell out as signatures were typed. What the pass was for is the residue, and it is worse than § 752's four:

- **`check_migration_online_safety.mjs` passed a blocking `ADD CONSTRAINT` on `runs`.** It tested the *whole* `ALTER TABLE` for `not valid`, but `NOT VALID` qualifies only the action it terminates — so an alter adding one constraint `NOT VALID` and a second one bare reported clean while the second takes a validating full scan under a blocking lock. That is the downtime [`migration_locks.md`](../backend/migration_locks.md) exists to prevent, and it is exactly the shape a half-applied two-step is written as. Actions are now split at paren depth 0 and graded individually; no committed migration changes verdict.
- **`check_lambda_alias_sync.mjs` let any one of its three sources fall silently out of the union.** The alias name is compared as a set across Terraform, the sync script and `release-web.yml`, and a source stating no name was *filtered out* rather than disagreeing — so the other two validated each other and the guard exited 0. All three cases were reproduced against the old module at zero errors, including a Terraform `aws_lambda_alias` whose `name` is not a literal, on the side the file itself calls the source of truth.
- **`check_toolchain_pins.mjs` could not see the cache key it exists to police.** It recognised a `defmt-print` key only by a pattern that already carried a version, so a key simplified to `defmt-print-${{ runner.os }}` parsed as no key at all. The install is `command -v defmt-print || cargo install --version`, so that key restores the old binary forever and the pin never runs — the incident the file's own header records.
- **`sync_deno_lock.mjs --check` could agree with itself forever.** Two *empty* workspace sections diff as in sync, so if deno stopped recording specs, one sync would write the sectionless lock and every run after would report "in sync (0 specs)" over a file nothing checks. **`check_doc_checkboxes.mjs`** had the same shape one layer up: an empty `git ls-files '*.md'` made its rules iterate nothing and print the tree clean, over 324 files and 1166 checkboxes. **`check_compliance_drift.mjs`** caught *any* `git diff` failure and returned no changed files, printing "skipping" and exiting 0 — so an unfetched base ref disabled every retention, export and deletion rule while reporting a pass. All three now refuse.
- **`check_ios_native_declarations.mjs` skipped its whole privacy-manifest block when the file was absent.** Every other input's absence is loud — `Info.plist` and `Runner.entitlements` hard-fail, a null `AppDelegate` and a null `pbxproj` each fall through to a named error — but deleting `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy` took the *unconditional* required-reason and collected-data checks with it and reported nothing at all. Separately, a key present with a shape other than an array of dicts reached `.filter()` and took the guard down with a `TypeError`, reporting a manifest problem as a crashed job; **`check_parity_ios_column.mjs`** died the same way on a markdown row opening fewer columns than its header, and two `.match(...).length` reads in the pgtap suite did too.
- Three more were narrower but real: `seed-run-tracks.mjs` called `.map` on an unchecked `res.json()` and could send `Bearer undefined` on every request rather than saying "start Supabase first"; `check_root_scripts.mjs` re-matched the whole command non-globally on its `run` branch, so the first target was checked against every package; and `check_pnpm_overrides.mjs` would have iterated a string `pnpm.overrides` character by character into fabricated pins.

**The coverage guard names no tree, and its one exemption is derived.** `scripts/tsconfig_coverage.test.mjs` reads every `tsconfig*.json` at the repo root, works out which are **roots** (a config nothing else extends) and which are shared bases, resolves each root's effective `include` by following `extends` until one declares it, and requires every compilable file git reports **outside `apps/web`** to match one. Two guards rather than one, deliberately: § 752's half must resolve SvelteKit's *generated* config and so cannot run before a `svelte-kit sync`, while this half has to run against a bare checkout — so neither can state the other's coverage, and this one asserts the other still exists, which is the seam that would otherwise open silently. The single exemption is the Supabase Edge Functions tree, located from where `config.toml` sits rather than written down, because it is a **Deno** program whose `npm:` / `jsr:` / `https:` specifiers tsc cannot resolve. All four failure modes were exercised: an added `tools/thing.ts` is named, the `apps/backend/scripts` include removed names all seven files under it, rewiring the CI step to another script fails by name, and deleting the `apps/web` guard fails by name.

**What the exemption is not is a claim that something else covers it.** `apps/backend/supabase/functions/` holds **85 tracked `.ts` files, 47 of them production handlers**, and nothing typechecks any of them: CI runs `deno test --no-check` twice and `deno cache --no-check`, and there is no `deno check` anywhere in the workflows. That is the same hole again in the one tier that answers requests from the public internet, and it is filed rather than fixed here because it is a different toolchain and a different failure surface — a `deno check` over that tree is its own slice, not a line in a `tsc` root.
**Amendment, 2026-08-27 (same day):** the root declaring `types: ["node"]` is not enough on its own — the *package* has to be declared at the root too. `@types/node` was a devDependency of `apps/web` alone, and npm installed it where the lockfile said: `apps/web/node_modules`. A root-level `tsc` on a clean `npm ci` therefore failed outright with `TS2688: Cannot find type definition file for 'node'` — no file in the program even read — while passing on a developer machine whose `node_modules` had drifted from the lockfile and carried a hoisted copy. **This is the same shape as the defect the ADR is about, one level up:** a thing that appeared covered because of an accident of layout rather than a declaration, and it failed only in the one environment that installs from the lockfile alone. Fixed by declaring `@types/node` at the root (all three lockfiles updated, `deno.lock`'s workspace section included) and guarded by a fifth assertion in `tsconfig_coverage.test.mjs`: every `types` entry a root names, following `extends` the way `include` is followed, must resolve to a package the ROOT `package.json` declares. That guard's first act was to catch a real type error in its own new code.

## 758. Both filings were true, the unit one exactly so — but the metric they named as the second window-bounded one is not, and the goal value that really completes for everybody was zero

**Decided 2026-08-27.** [followups.md](../product/followups.md) carried two boxes from the round-17 mobile challenge-form build ([§ 754](#754-the-one-filing-in-this-round-that-was-true-as-written--and-the-port-that-would-have-honoured-it-faithfully-was-the-one-that-shipped-a-broken-goal-field)): web's goal field asks for the stored number with no unit named, and nothing checks a goal is achievable inside its own window. The first is accurate to the letter. The second is accurate in its headline and wrong in both its example set and its sense of which shape actually hurts.

**Measured, the metric vocabulary is five and their units are three.** `challenges_metric_ck` admits `distance`, `duration`, `vert`, `activity_count`, `streak_days` (20270209_001 widened by 20270302_001). `challenge_leaderboard` and `recompute_challenge_completion` sum `distance_m`, `duration_s`, `coalesce(elevation_gain_m, 0)`, `count(r.id)` and `count(distinct (started_at at time zone 'UTC')::date)` respectively — so metres, seconds, metres, a count, a count of days. `ChallengeEditor.svelte` asked for all five through one `<input type="number">` labelled `challenges.goalOptional`, "Goal (optional)", with `min="0"` and no suffix. A person typing `100` meaning kilometres created a 100 **metre** goal: a valid value, a successful insert, a filled progress bar on the entrant's first run, and no error state anywhere to notice.

**`streak_days` is the only metric its own window bounds, and `duration` — the filing's second example — is not.** The distinct-date count over `[starts_at, ends_at)` cannot exceed the number of calendar dates a window of that length touches, which is a hard ceiling. The duration sum is over runs whose **start** falls inside the window; a run begun a minute before it closes contributes its whole `duration_s`, a 112-hour Moab finish included, and two overlapping imports contribute both. A `CHECK` refusing a duration goal longer than its window would therefore refuse a legitimate ultra challenge — the exact class of user this repo carries eight personas for. Both mirror suites and `challenge_goal_check_test.sql` pin that a 403,200-second goal in a one-day window is **accepted**, so a later tightening has to argue with a test rather than slip through as an obvious symmetry.

**The shape that actually completes for everyone was the one neither box named: a stored zero.** `recompute_challenge_completion` returns early only on a NULL goal, then compares `v_value >= v_goal` with no floor — so `0 >= 0` inserts a `challenge_badges` row, stamps `completed_at` and fires a `challenge_complete` notification for **every participant** on the next `sweep_challenge_completions()` (the sweep's own filter is `goal_value is not null`). Meanwhile `progressFraction` and `isComplete` both read `goal <= 0` as "no goal", so both clients render the board as pure-ranking and nothing on screen ever contradicts the badge. Web's field admitted it outright — `min="0"` — and mobile's `typed <= 0` guard was the only thing anywhere refusing it.

**The ceiling is `floor(window_seconds / 86400) + 1`, and it is deliberately the loose bound.** That is the count of dates a window of that length touches when it opens just after midnight; a window ending exactly at midnight UTC touches one fewer. Refusing a goal the aggregate could in principle award is worse than admitting one it cannot, so the slack is on the permissive side. `(x at time zone 'UTC')::date` is only STABLE and is illegal in a CHECK; `extract(epoch from (ends_at - starts_at))` is immutable and is what the constraint computes.

**The fix is a parity pair, not two copies of a suffix table.** The filing proposed giving web "a unit suffix derived from the metric and the reader's `preferred_unit`" — i.e. a second implementation of what `challenge_form_sheet.dart` had written inline the day before. Instead the mobile helper moved out into `challenge_goal` (web `social/challenge_goal.ts` ↔ mobile `challenge_goal.dart`, registered in both registries), so the conversion, the ceiling and the refusal vocabulary are single-sourced. It is a **three-rail** contract like `nearby`'s: the SQL computes the identical ceiling, and a client that disagreed would let a 23514 naming neither the goal nor the window reach the author — the swallow [§ 747](#747-the-eleventh-rate-limit-bucket-now-reaches-the-parser--but-the-refusal-a-throttled-challenge-creator-actually-saw-was-swallowed-not-leaked) had just removed from this same editor by a different route. `challengeGoalFromStored` is web-only glue for the edit path, which has no mobile surface per [§ 24](#24-web-is-the-canonical-feature-surface-mobile-and-watches-are-platform-additive).

**Both editors now say more than the unit.** The typed figure is echoed back through the leaderboard's own formatter — but only for the three metrics where a conversion happened, because for `activity_count` and `streak_days` the typed number *is* the stored one and a readback would only repeat it. The window's active-day ceiling is stated before the goal is typed rather than only on a refusal. Switching the metric clears the number, because a 100 that meant kilometres must not become 100 hours. And web gained the end-after-start check mobile already had: `challenges_window_ck` raises a 23514 naming neither bound, so until now web's only response was `showToast(err.message)` with the raw postgres string. An inverted window suppresses the ceiling error beside it — `maxStreakDaysInWindow` is zero there, so every streak goal also failed, and "At most 0 active days fit in this window" is noise next to the real complaint when moving the end fixes both.

**One thing the mobile form was quietly a day out on.** Its default window ran from `DateTime.now()` — seconds and milliseconds and all — to a minute-truncated `now + 30 days`, so the span was 30 days *less whatever was on the clock*, and `floor` therefore reported a ceiling of 30 active days for a window the author reads as 30 days long. Truncating the start to the minute the pickers actually offer makes the default window exactly 30 days. The web editor never had the bug (`toLocalInput` formats to `HH:mm`), which is why it took a shared ceiling to surface.

**Verification.** Web: 4,332 unit tests, 0 failures; `svelte-check` 0 errors (5 pre-existing `state_referenced_locally` warnings in `PlanEditor.svelte`); all 24 `tests-e2e/challenges/` Playwright specs green including three new ones — the unit follows the metric and switching it clears the number, an unwinnable streak goal is refused without navigating, and a zero goal is refused — plus an admin-client assertion that a typed `100` lands as `100000`. Backend: `db reset` + `supabase test db`, 259 files / 2,189 tests, the nine new `challenge_goal_check_test.sql` assertions green; the two failures in that run (`coach_roster_summary` test 10, `donations_status_lock`) are both `42501: permission denied for function` from the workstation's Supabase CLI 2.109.1 against CI's pinned 2.84.2, touch no challenge code, and predate this change. Both type generators re-run: a CHECK constrains no shape, so neither output moved. Mobile: 23 widget tests on `challenge_form_sheet_test.dart`, 14 on the new `challenge_goal_test.dart`, `l10n_parity` + `architecture_guards` green at 245, iOS twin byte-identical. Seven keys across all seven web catalogues, two across all seven ARBs.

## 759. The per-column grant on `public.events` is the fix, not the defect — and the one consequence that would have mattered does not happen

**Decided 2026-08-27.** [#789](https://github.com/Absence0760/project-running/issues/789) filed that `public.events` "grants SELECT per-column, not table-wide, so `has_table_privilege` is false while `select count(*)` succeeds — silently blocking any system-column read by `anon`/`authenticated`", and asked whether it is deliberate and whether other tables share it. **Both observations reproduce exactly. Both conclusions drawn from them are wrong, and the second one is wrong in the direction that would have leaked data.**

**The observations, measured.** `has_table_privilege('anon', 'public.events', 'SELECT')` is `false` while `set role anon; select count(*) from public.events` returns 12 — Postgres checks column privileges for the columns a query names, and a `count(*)` names none. A direct `select xmin` / `ctid` / `tableoid` as `anon` or `authenticated` raises `42501`, because a per-column grant enumerates user columns only. Neither is news: [§ 753](#753) already recorded the second in passing, as the reason its second mutation operator keeps the owner bypass.

**Four tables share the shape, and all four are lockdowns.** `user_profiles` withholds 16 columns (`20260707_001` + `20260810_001` — billing state, `parkrun_number`, `date_of_birth` / `gender` / `height_cm`, the consent stamps, `shadow_hidden`), `events` 3 (`meet_lat` / `meet_lng` per `20260723_001` + `20260806_001`, `host_user_id` the Stripe Connect payout recipient), `clubs` 1 (`invite_token`, `20260801_001`), `checkpoint_crossings` 5 (the Art 9 weigh-in fields plus `recorded_by`, `20270201_001`). Each has a named replacement read path — `get_my_profile()`, `get_event_meet_point()`, `get_club_invite_token()`, `fetch_checkpoint_crossings_for_organiser()` — and `20270408_001`'s header states the invariant outright: the restored matrix "never grants table-level SELECT on a column-locked table". **There is not one accidental case, so there is no migration in this change.** The filed fix — a table-wide `grant select` — would hand every signed-in caller an organiser's home coordinates, every public club's join token, every runner's date of birth and every racer's medical hold, and would fail `role_grant_matrix_test` and `rls_user_profiles_column_lockdown_test` on the way.

**The consequence that was supposed to matter does not occur.** The filing's stake was that round 18's mutation operator reads `xmin`, so a table blocking system-column reads is one it cannot reason about. Measured directly: a permissive `SELECT` policy whose `USING` references `xmin` — which is exactly [§ 753](#753)'s operator 1 — lets `anon` read `events` normally. **A policy expression is not column-privilege-checked; only the columns the caller's own query names are.** § 753's aside is true of a `SECURITY INVOKER` *replacement relation* selecting `xmin` as `anon`, which is operator 2's shape and precisely why operator 2 keeps its owner bypass. The guard's population is unchanged at 168 assertions / 5 expected survivors across 259 files, with the column-locked tables among them.

**The real defect is the drift the filing did not look for, and it has fired in prod.** A re-grant is cumulative, so a column added to a locked table is deny-by-default until an explicit `grant select (col)` lands — a fact both `20260707_001` and `20260818_001` state in their own headers as a known cost. `clubs.is_verified` (`20260909_001`) shipped without one and took down **every** non-service-role read of `clubs` with `42501 permission denied for table clubs`, because both clients enumerate the column; it was caught a day later by eleven `api_client` integration failures and repaired by `20260913_001`, which also had to rewrite `search_clubs` for the sibling reason. `20260817_001` had reverted the whole lockdown once already. The `select('*')` source scans (`architecture_guards_test.dart`, `select-star-discipline.spec.ts`) police the call-site half of that class; **nothing policed the grant half.**

**So the guard is a registry of what is withheld and why, pinned in the direction that detects drift.** `column_grant_lockdown_registry_test.sql` names all 25 withheld columns with a reason each and asserts the catalogue's withheld set equals it, per role, in both directions. Pinning the *granted* set instead would not move when a column arrives ungranted — which is exactly how the defect stayed silent. The same assertion catches a deliberate withholding granted away, a table-wide grant emptying the set, and a registry entry outliving its column; two more assert that no table outside the registry carries the per-column shape and that none of the four has regained table-level SELECT. Four probes, each rolled back, trip the intended assertion by name.

**Anon and authenticated are held identical, and that is its own assertion.** They have diverged before: `20260723_001` revoked the meet point from `anon` and `20260806_001` caught `authenticated` up eleven weeks later, so for eleven weeks any signed-in stranger could read coordinates `anon` could not. A divergence is a leak on the wider side, not a variant worth carrying silently.

**The write side is the same shape and is deliberately left for its own change.** Four more tables carry column-level INSERT/UPDATE grants for `authenticated` — `achievements` (UPDATE `is_public` only), `challenge_participants` (`team_club_id` only), `coach_messages` (`archived_at` + `reaction`, [§ 29](#29-security-patterns-from-the-data-isolation-audit)), `event_attendees` (`attendance` + `order_id` blocked on both verbs, `20270520_001`). Its drift is the mirror image — a new column is silently **unwritable**, `42501` on a PostgREST PATCH — and three of the four still hold a table-level INSERT beside a column-scoped UPDATE, which is the exact asymmetry [§ 584](#584) records for `event_attendees` before `20270520_001` closed it. Extending the registry to writes needs the same provenance pass per column that the SELECT side got here, so it is filed rather than bundled.

**Views carry none of this.** Four (`activities`, `gear_with_distance`, `public_gym_routines`, `public_profiles`) are revoked from `anon` wholesale rather than column by column, which is the clean shape and deliberate — `public_profiles`' revoke is `20261011_001`'s anti-enumeration fix. Functions and Storage policies have no column-privilege surface to share the class with.
## 760. The rename the box asked for is one the tool forbids, and the catalogue it was about turned out to be three tenths finished on a corpus that had never been mined for the auth block

**Decided 2026-08-27.** Two boxes from [§ 755](#755-both-portuguese-boxes-were-true-both-counts-were-right-and-the-phones-own-european-catalogue-turned-out-to-be-a-tenth-finished): `app_pt.arb`'s remaining ~90%, and its bare `pt` tag disagreeing with the `pt-PT` that web, the wrist and iOS's `Info.plist` all use. Both are closed. Neither closed the way it was filed.

**The counts were right and one round stale.** `app_pt.arb` differed from `app_pt_BR.arb` on **359 of 3,793 keys, 9.46%**, with **3,434** byte-identical Brazilian — not 359 of 3,772 with 3,413. Twenty-one keys landed between the filing and the fix, which is the whole of the discrepancy; § 755's arithmetic was sound. **822 strings changed** this round and the catalogue now differs on **1,164 of 3,793, 30.69%** — above web's own, so the phone has gone from the least European of the surfaces to the most.

**The corpus was re-derived rather than reused, and four of its rules were thrown away after reading their call sites.** Word-diffing both ALIGNED pairs the repo owns — `pt-BR.ts` ↔ `pt-PT.ts` (1,289 differing keys) and this ARB pair's own 359 — yields **717 distinct substitutions**. Corpus fidelity is not the goal: `meta`, `endereço`, `download` and `recursos` are ordinary European Portuguese in every place this catalogue uses them (`endereço de e-mail` is the *correct* form and `meta` appears 48 times), so those rules were dropped, and `mais rápido` was narrowed to its adverbial uses because "Ritmo mais rápido" is an adjective on a noun. Three rules the corpus could not contain were added, `senha` → `palavra-passe` first among them — **the corpus was mined from a source whose auth block had never been Europeanised, so it could not carry a rule for the word.** That is the same reason web shipped 33 keys still saying `senha`, fixed here in the same change.

**Gender agreement is the part a word-swap gets wrong.** `tela` → `ecrã`, `trilha` → `trilho` and `academia` → `ginásio` all flip grammatical gender, and the agreement reaches past the noun in both directions: `na sua tela ligada` carries two stacked determiners in front and a participle behind. Those three rules therefore carry a determiner *chain* and a closed adjective set, so the phrase reads `no seu ecrã ligado` rather than leaving the articles behind. § 755's four systematic defects are guarded by construction — case mirrors upward only, a full stop ends a sentence only after a real word that is not an abbreviation, a dash or colon never does, singular `configuração` is untouched, and `pular` is `saltar`.

**Half-converted strings: 17, not the 2 filed.** Both named ones were real. Beyond them, the entire voice-cue block spoke two registers: the curated cues address the runner as `tu` (`Acelera`, `Abranda`, `Mantém`, `Precisas`, `Dá`) while every cue the curation had not reached kept Brazilian's third-person imperative (`Acelere`, `Vire`, `Mantenha-se`, `Faça`) — eleven cues, not the one pair. A spoken coach cannot address one runner two ways mid-run, so the unreached cues joined the curated ones. And the curated set contradicted **itself** on the most-used word of the lot: nine keys called a shareable link a `ligação` where four called it a `link`, with thirty more derived keys on `link`. `link` wins, matching web (99 keys to 18) and the three server catalogues slice 5 landed, and `ligação` keeps the network-connection sense it holds in twenty-six other keys — so the two words now mean two things instead of one thing twice. `padrão` was deliberately **not** touched: it is a less-preferred synonym rather than a Brazilianism, the catalogue says it twenty times, and one of those twenty means *pattern*. Filed rather than guessed.

**The rename is not available, and finding that out is most of the second box's value.** `flutter gen-l10n` refuses outright when a country-coded catalogue exists without a bare base of the same language — "Arb file for a fallback, pt, does not exist, even though the following locale(s) exist: [pt_BR, pt_PT]" — and generates *nothing*, so `app_pt_PT.arb` cannot be the only Portuguese base. Reproduced before it was worked around. The alternatives are worse: a complete duplicate base, or moving Brazilian onto the bare tag, which would make the phone and web disagree about what `pt` means and undo § 755's own judgement. **So the filename is the tool's and the tag is ours.** `supportedLocales`, `localeLabels`, `_exact`, `_baseToLocale` and `locales_config.xml` all carry `pt-PT`; the generated delegate resolves `Locale('pt', 'PT')` through its `pt` base; and `arbTagOverride` holds the two spellings together with a companion assertion that each entry is still a real override, the shape [§ 740](#740-a-catalogue-only-ships-if-a-reader-can-reach-it-so-the-reachable-set-is-derived-and-guarded-rather-than-listed) already used for the plist. `plistTagOverride` is **gone**, because Apple names a locale by region and that is now what everything else does too.

**A defect one layer below the tag.** `ttsLanguageTag` mapped bare `pt` to `pt-BR`, so a European reader's *spoken* cues were Brazilian over European text — the same disagreement between a tag and its content, in the one place a reader hears rather than reads it.

**Registering the parity pair found a real divergence, which is the point of registering it.** `locale.ts` and `locale_support.dart` described each other as twins in their own doc comments and were in neither registry, so `shared-library-syncer` had never checked them; that is how they came to hold different Portuguese answers for eighteen days with nothing able to notice. Registered, they disagree on one thing that matters: **the order of `supportedLocales` is load-bearing on the phone and not on web.** Following the device locale leaves `MaterialApp.locale` null and Flutter resolves against the list itself, taking the first entry matching on language alone. Measured against Flutter's own `basicLocaleListResolution`: with `pt-PT` first a bare-`pt` device lands on European, and reversing the two sends it to Brazilian while `_baseToLocale` still says European. `locale_negotiation_test.dart` now pins the two paths against each other, and web's list is reordered to match so the twin reads as one thing.

**The durable half is a guard neither platform had.** Every existing locale guard — § 740's, § 748's, this repo's six hand-list sweeps — asks whether a catalogue is **reachable**. None asked whether it says what its tag claims, which is precisely why 3,434 Brazilian strings sat under a European tag for three weeks and why web shipped its auth block the same way. A catalogue tagged for one Portuguese variant may now not contain words only the other uses, on both platforms, from a deliberately narrow list: each entry is a word the other variant does not use *at all*, because a frequency rule needs a threshold and a threshold is a number nobody can defend. `excluir`, `arquivo` and `acessar` carry a second sense in Portugal, so the keys that use them that way are named rather than the words being dropped from the scan. Verified by observation in both directions: the guard flags **319** strings in the pre-derivation ARB and 0 in this one, and planting `Senha` back into `login.passwordPlaceholder` fails the web half by name.

**Three strings on web were casualties of § 755's own elision rule.** It dropped `você` wherever a word followed it, including where the pronoun was the verb's **object** rather than its subject — which deletes the person the sentence is about. `clubEvent.youTag` rendered as `()`, `messages.youPrefix` as `": "`, and `routeDetail.sendDm.intro` as "Escolha alguém que segue ou que segue". This round's elision requires a following word for the same reason and then names the five object sites explicitly, rather than trusting a rule to tell a subject from an object. `morada` was a second, quieter case of the same class: it is a **home** address, so six keys used it for an e-mail or an IP, four of them disagreeing with their own article ("envia seu morada IP").

**Vocabulary now agrees across all five Portuguese surfaces** — phone ARB, `pt-PT.ts`, the wrist's `values-b+pt+PT`, and the three server catalogues slice 5 landed: `palavra-passe` as the wrist already had it, and `link` over `ligação`. That slice owns the `pt*` → `pt-BR` collapse in the auth-email function, the delete-account function, the Go worker and watchOS; nothing here touches those files.

**Verification.** ARB 3,793 keys: 359 differing before (9.46%), 1,164 after (30.69%), 822 changed, 356 of the 359 curated preserved verbatim and the other three the named half-converted fixes. Placeholder sets and brace balance identical to Brazilian on all 3,793. Flutter: `architecture_guards_test.dart` 209 passed / 0 failed; the locale set (`architecture_guards` + `locale_negotiation` + `settings_language_locale` + `l10n_parity` + `audio_cues`) 320 passed / 0 failed; `flutter gen-l10n` regenerated and the iOS twin byte-identical on `lib/` and `test/`. Web: 4,317 unit tests passed / 0 failed, `npm run check` 0 errors over 2,425 files, `pt-PT.ts` now differing from Brazilian on **1,397 of 5,043 keys, 27.70%** (was 1,289 / 25.56%). `node scripts/check_parity_pair_registry.mjs`: 97 pairs registered identically, 391 paths on disk.

**What this does not claim.** The output is model-authored from a corpus, exactly as § 755's was, so the native-review box is widened to name the ARB rather than ticked. `padrão` → `predefinição` is filed, not done.

## 761. Three normalizers folded every `pt*` tag to Brazilian, four surfaces were filed and the count was right for the wrong reason, and the guard that could have caught it ran nowhere

**Decided 2026-08-27.** [§ 755](#755-both-portuguese-boxes-were-true-both-counts-were-right-and-the-phones-own-european-catalogue-turned-out-to-be-a-tenth-finished) shipped European Portuguese on web and on Wear OS and filed what it had just made sharp: a `pt-PT` reader now got European Portuguese in the browser and on the wrist, and Brazilian in their inbox. This closes that. All three server-side normalizers and the watchOS String Catalog now answer `pt-PT` in European Portuguese, and the tag rule is web's `locale.ts`, verbatim, in all four places.

**The filing said four sites. Measured, it is three collapse functions, five catalogue-shaped maps, and one surface that collapses nothing at all.** `apps/watch_ios` has no normalizer — bundle localisation is Apple's, decided by `CFBundleLocalizations`; the wrist folded to Brazilian because it shipped no pt-PT catalogue, not because any code read a tag. Conversely the two worker files filed as one site share **one** function: `sms_i18n.go` has no normalizer, it calls `normalizeEmailLocale`, which is also the chokepoint for `push_render.go` — so one line decided the language of **eight** job handlers (notification email, lifecycle email, lifecycle drip, weekly digest, safety email, safety SMS, web push, native push). And `delete-account` — filed as a fourth site with the same weight as the others — carries **zero** catalogue keys: it normalizes a tag into a job payload and the worker's `account_deleted` copy renders it. The translation work was three files, not four. § 755's own "three surfaces" was wrong in the other direction, omitting `delete-account` entirely. Neither enumeration is the shape of the code.

**Two of the four counts in the filing were off, and the second one matters.** watchOS is 56 entries with **five** explicit non-source locales plus an implicit `en` — 281 localizations, not the 336 that "56 keys × 6 locales" implies; the source string is the key in 55 of the 56 entries, and only the one plural entry declares `en` at all. And `knownRegions` holds **seven** rows, not six: `Base` is Xcode's development-region marker sitting among the locales, which is the difference between "add a row" and "know which rows are locales" — the derived guard below has to skip it by name.

**`check_xcstrings_parity.sh` not being in CI was the one filing that was exactly true, and running it found nothing hiding.** It passed on `3204ff84d`: `OK: 56 string(s) each translated for en, de, fr, es, ja, pt-BR`, exit 0. So the missing wiring was owed for the future rather than covering a live defect — worth stating, because "an unrun guard" and "an unrun guard that is red" are different findings and only the second is urgent.

**The § 748 / § 755 hand-listed-set shape exists here twice, not four times — and the site that most looked like it was already correct.** The Go `emailLocales` slice was the real one: **four** test loops range it (`TestEmailCatalogueParity`, `TestRenderNotificationEmail_NoKindRendersTheDefault`, `TestSmsCatalogueParity`, and the message `TestEmailCatalogue_CoversEveryNotificationKind` prints), so a seventh locale added to `emailCatalogue`, `emailSharedByLocale` and `smsCatalogue` and missed in that one slice would have been skipped by every guard in the package. `check_xcstrings_parity.sh`'s `LOCALES` was the second, and worse — it also read neither declaration site, so a locale translated but absent from `CFBundleLocalizations` loads as English at runtime with nothing thrown. But `AUTH_EMAIL_LOCALES` was **not** vacuous: its test opened by comparing the const against `Object.keys(authEmailCatalogue)` in both directions, so adding to either alone already failed. Its actual gap was next door — `authEmailShared` was only ever indexed inside the loop, never key-set-compared, so an entry there and nowhere else was invisible. Fixing what the pattern suggested rather than what the code did would have missed it.

**Both worker doc comments cite test files that do not exist.** `email_i18n.go` said "emailCatalogueParity_test.go pins that every locale carries every key" and `sms_i18n.go` said "smsCatalogueParity_test.go pins that every supported locale carries both variants". Neither file has ever existed; the tests are `TestEmailCatalogueParity` in `email_i18n_test.go` and `TestSmsCatalogueParity` in `handler_safety_sms_test.go`. The SMS comment was also stale on its own subject — the struct carries **four** variants since the off-route pair landed, not two.

**Where the four tables now agree, and the one place they deliberately do not.** `EXACT` / `BASE_TO_LOCALE` in `apps/web/src/lib/i18n/locale.ts` reads as `emailExact` / `emailBase` in `email_i18n.go`, `AUTH_EMAIL_EXACT` / `AUTH_EMAIL_BASE` in `auth-email/lib.ts`, and `RECEIPT_EXACT` / `RECEIPT_BASE` in `delete-account/lib.ts`. `pt-BR` resolves by its own tag — Android, iOS and every browser report the region — and the bare `pt` plus `pt-AO` / `pt-MZ` / `pt-CV` resolve to European, because they share Portugal's orthography and have nowhere else to land. The copies exist because these are four deployment units (a browser bundle, a Go binary, two Deno functions) with no module between them; four copies of a table is worse than one, which is why each carries a guard rather than a promise. The deliberate difference: all three **server** copies read `_` as a separator, because they read `user_settings.prefs.locale` — whatever a client wrote — where web negotiates a `navigator.language` that always uses hyphens. That was already true (`de_AT` → `de` was pinned) and is preserved.

**Three test files asserted the defect; the filing named one.** `TestNormalizeEmailLocale` pinned `"pt": "pt-BR"` and `"pt-PT": "pt-BR"`, auth-email's suite asserted `normalizeEmailLocale('pt-PT') === 'pt-BR'`, and delete-account's asserted `'pt': 'pt-BR'`. All three now pin the rule instead, and each also pins `pt-AO` / `pt-MZ` / `pt-CV`, which nothing anywhere had covered.

**Each surface gets a guard that fails on a half-declared locale, and each was proved to trip by removing a row.** Go: `emailLocales` is derived from `emailCatalogue`, and `TestEmailLocaleSetIsDerivedAndReachable` asserts the three catalogues carry one identical set **and** that every catalogue is reachable from a tag — the § 740 reachability question, which the server tier had never been asked. Deleting the pt-PT SMS block reports `smsCatalogue carries [de en es fr ja pt-BR], emailCatalogue carries [… pt-PT]`; deleting both Portuguese rows from the normalizer reports `catalogue "pt-PT" is unreachable`. auth-email derives `AUTH_EMAIL_LOCALES` from its catalogue and probes the normalizer both ways; `delete-account` renders nothing itself, so its guard is **cross-tier** — it parses the worker's `emailCatalogue` out of the Go source and fails when the receipt can name a locale the worker has no `account_deleted` copy for, which trips on an added `it` row. watchOS derives its set from the catalog and additionally holds `CFBundleLocalizations` and `knownRegions` to it; each of the three claims was tripped separately.

**The CI job is on Linux and gated on `code`, and the § 756 objection does not apply.** `check_xcstrings_parity.sh` is `python3` against a bare checkout — no Xcode, no `npm ci` — so it runs in its own `ubuntu-latest` job rather than in the macOS `test-watch-ios`, which builds the Swift suite and never reads the catalog. § 756 found `parity-types` gated on `changes.outputs.code`, which a docs-only diff sets false while the gate counts the skip as a pass, making it the wrong home for a guard over markdown. Here the inputs are `Localizable.xcstrings`, `Info.plist` and `project.pbxproj` — none of them `docs/`, `.claude/` or `*.md` — so every diff that can break this guard sets `code=true`. The step wraps its command in the `if ! cmd; then echo "::error::…"; exit 1; fi` form rather than a trailing `if: failure()`, which `check_ci_diagnostics.mjs` rule 1 forbids.

**Register and vocabulary follow the wrist's curated set where the two Portuguese sources disagree.** 293 new strings: 181 in the worker (28 catalogue keys × 4 scalars + 50 body paragraphs, 15 shared strings, 4 SMS variants), 55 in `auth-email` (9 keys × 4 scalars + 17 body paragraphs + 2 shared), 57 on watchOS (55 simple + one plural's two categories). Subject-pronoun elision with third-person verbs throughout, per § 755. Where `values-b+pt+PT/strings.xml` and `locales/pt-PT.ts` differ the wrist wins, because it was curated and the web catalogue was rule-transformed and still carries leftovers: `palavra-passe`, not the web catalogue's 29 surviving `senha`. `link` is kept over `ligação` in the other direction, because web uses it 78 times to `ligação`'s 15 and a second vocabulary would be worse than an imperfect one. `registado` / `guardar` / `eliminar` / `contacto` / `definições` / `telemóvel` / `em direto` / `sapatilhas` throughout; "A CORRER" and "Em pausa" on the wrist, taken verbatim from Wear OS.

**Verification.** Go: 746 tests, 0 failures (`GOTOOLCHAIN=auto go test ./...`; the workstation's local toolchain is 1.25.12 against a `go.mod` requiring 1.26.6). Edge Functions: 518 passed, 0 failed, 23 ignored over the whole `supabase/functions/` tree — run as `deno test` directly, never through the shared local stack. watchOS: the parity script green at 56 strings × 7 locales with both declaration sites agreeing; `actionlint` clean, `check_ci_diagnostics.mjs` and `check_toolchain_pins.mjs` both green.

**What this does not claim.** The pt-PT copy is **model-authored and not natively reviewed**, exactly as § 755's was; the existing native-review box is widened to name these catalogues rather than ticked. And **nothing here is Mac-verified**: the xcstrings edit is JSON that `python3` re-parses and the plist/pbxproj edits are one line each, but no Xcode has compiled the catalog, no simulator has rendered a pt-PT wrist, and `test-watch-ios` cannot run on this workstation. § 755's Wear OS work was verified by a real Gradle run; the watchOS half of this one is verified only to the rung the tooling allows.
## 762. "47 production handlers" was the count of non-test modules, the one file that reported no errors was the one typed against `any`, and 81 was a floor rather than a total

**Decided 2026-08-27.** [§ 757](#757) exempted the Supabase Edge Functions from the repo-root coverage guard and said outright that the exemption was not a claim something else covered them. This closes that. `deno check` now runs over the whole tree in the `edge-functions` job, and the tree that had never been type-checked came back with **81 errors**, which is now **0**.

**The filing's count was right and its label was wrong.** "85 tracked `.ts` files, 47 of them production handlers" — the 85 and the 47 both reconcile exactly (47 non-test, 38 test), but 47 is the count of **non-test modules**, not of handlers. Eleven of them are shared library modules under `_shared/` with no HTTP surface at all, and the rest are the `lib.ts` / `handler.ts` / `paging.ts` halves the tests exist to exercise. The number of **deployed functions is 16**, one `index.ts` per directory, of which `config.toml` names seven (those needing `verify_jwt = false`). That matters for how the finding reads: sixteen internet-facing entrypoints is the alarming number and it is smaller than the one filed, while the tier's real size — the thing a typecheck has to cover — is the 85.

**81 over the tree, 80 over the non-test half: tests carried exactly one.** That single error is the argument against exempting them, not for it. It was a `walkPages` callback in `export-data/stream_section.test.ts` written as `(r) => seen.push(r.id)` — an arrow returning `Array.prototype.push`'s new length where the signature says `void | Promise<void>`. Harmless here, and precisely the class that is not harmless when the callback's return value is what the code under test branches on. A test that does not typecheck is as free to assert something impossible as any other module, so the lane checks all 85.

**One omission, repeated sixteen times.** Every `createClient` call was made without the `Database` generic, so the client resolved to `SupabaseClient<any>`, `.from('x')` resolved to `never`, and every column read, insert and update in the tier was checked against nothing: 39 of the 81 are `TS2339`, "property does not exist on type 'never'". The `_shared` helpers compounded it — `supabase: ReturnType<typeof createClient>` captures the DEFAULT generic instantiation, which is not what a real `createClient(url, key)` call returns, so passing a real client to one was the other 32 (`TS2345`). Two symptoms, one cause, and the fix is one line per call site. There is no second generated artifact: `_shared/database.ts` re-exports `apps/web/src/lib/database.types.ts` across the tree boundary, which is the single committed output of `gen:types` and already carries a CI drift check. A copy generated into `apps/backend` would need a second drift check and would rot between them. Every re-export is `export type`, so the specifier is erased before the CLI bundles a function and nothing crosses the boundary at runtime — which is load-bearing, since that file has a runtime `Constants` export that would otherwise be dragged into sixteen deploy bundles.

**Service-role and user-scoped clients are the same type, and the pair that looked like it needed two was the pair that proved it.** Nothing about privilege is expressible here: the two differ only in which key and which `Authorization` header built them, and RLS is enforced by Postgres at request time. So there is one alias, `DbClient`, and a parameter carrying it says nothing about what the caller may read — the parameter *name* does, as it already did before any of these were typed.

**The one file that reported zero errors was the one covered by `any`.** `delete-account/index.ts` — the GDPR Art 17 handler, thirteen client parameters — was clean at base because it annotated them as bare `SupabaseClient`, which is `SupabaseClient<any, …>`. It looked like the best-typed file in the tree and was the least checked one. Typing it properly surfaced a real defect immediately: `ThirdPartyOutcomes` was declared as an `interface`, and TypeScript gives an object-literal **type alias** an implicit index signature while an interface gets none, so the record was not assignable to the `deletion_audit_log.third_party_outcomes` jsonb column it is written into. This is § 757's own shape again — a thing that appeared covered because of an accident of declaration rather than a declaration.

**81 was a floor.** A `never` collapse hides everything downstream of it, so binding the generic *revealed* 20 further errors, six of them in five files that had reported none at all (`clip-public-track`, `delete-account`, `parkrun-import`, `race-results-import`, `revenuecat-webhook`). Anyone budgeting off the filed number would have been budgeting off the errors the first error was tall enough to conceal.

**Seven were more than type-level.**

- **`strava-import` validated one value and ran on another.** The bound check read `body.lookbackDays` off the untyped request bag; `handleSync` then read it again through `?? 90`. Nothing tied them, and the only thing rejecting a JSON `null` was `Number.isInteger` sitting first in the `||` chain — reorder that chain so a bound comes first (the natural edit) and `null` reaches `backfill`, where `null * 86400_000` is 0, the lookback window collapses to this instant, and the sync reports success having imported nothing. Both handlers now take validated locals, pinned by a new `strava-import/wiring.test.ts` in the `delete-account` source-grep idiom. **The runtime today was safe** — `Number.isInteger(null)` is `false`, measured, so the 400 fires — and saying otherwise would overstate it; what was wrong is that the safety was an accident of clause order that the compiler could not see and a reviewer had no reason to preserve.
- **`clip-public-track` read a nullable owner off a view and used it twice.** `public_runs` is a view, and Postgres cannot carry `runs.user_id`'s NOT NULL through one, so the generated row type says `string | null`. A null would have built a Storage path reading `null/<id>.json.gz` and then handed a null owner to `clip_track_for_user`, whose argument is NOT NULL — the second failure landing *after* the track had been downloaded and decompressed in memory. It now fails closed to the same 404 the missing-row branch gives.
- **`race-results-import` spread a jsonb column into an object literal.** The enrich path merged `existing.metadata` with `...`, and the column can legally hold an array or a scalar as well as an object; spreading a string splats its characters in as numeric keys. Guarded with both halves of the check, because `typeof x === 'object'` is true for an array — [§ 662](#662)'s lesson, in a new place.
- **`_shared/strava`'s `gzipBytes` promised a width its own first line would throw on.** A bare `Uint8Array` is backed by `ArrayBufferLike`, `SharedArrayBuffer` included, and neither `Response` nor `Blob` accepts a view onto shared memory. Narrowed to `Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>`, which is what every caller already passes — and the narrowing let a `(globalThis as any).CompressionStream` become the real global, removing an `any` rather than adding one.
- **`strava-import`'s `backfill` declared a return type its body contradicted.** `rate_limited` was in the object and not in the type. An excess property is a compile-time complaint, not a runtime strip, so the response body has always carried the flag; the type had simply gone stale. (No client reads it — filed below.)
- **`events-connect-onboard` cast a nullable column to `string | undefined`.** `stripe_connect_account_id` is nullable, and the cast erased exactly the value the read can return.
- **`_shared/strava`'s embedded-best table was keyed by `string`.** The four keys are `runs` columns, so they are now typed as such: a typo there used to be a write PostgREST rejects at runtime, and is now a compile error.

**Moving the client type broke a hand-written list, so the guard now walks the graph.** `_shared/rate_limit.ts` held one of the two `?target=deno` supabase-js imports [§ 699](#699) requires on `clip-public-track`'s module graph, and that import has moved behind `_shared/database.ts`. `offline_worker_boot_guard.test.ts` named the two files by hand and would have gone on asserting over a file with no supabase-js import at all while the module that had inherited the obligation was named nowhere. It now walks the probe function's whole local module graph, and was proved to trip by removing `?target=deno` from `database.ts` and watching it report that file by name.
