**The lane derives its file set, and a second guard runs that same expression.** The predecessor step in this very job was written as three hardcoded test paths and silently missed four `*.test.ts` files added afterwards; that is the failure mode to design against, not a hypothetical. So `scripts/edge_functions_typecheck_coverage.test.mjs` does not restate what should be checked — it reads `ci.yml`, lifts the step's own `files=$(…)` line out of it, runs THAT, and compares the result with every Deno-compilable file git reports under the tree. The two cannot disagree, because there is only one of them. Both failure modes were exercised: a `.mts` dropped into `_shared/` is named (the `-name '*.ts'` selector walks past it), and rewriting the step to name paths fails on the missing derivation. It also asserts the typecheck runs **before** the Supabase stack starts — it needs no database, and behind a Docker pull a stack that fails to come up would take the verdict with it, which is `parity-types`' own reason for hoisting its source-only guards.

**`edge-functions` joins `parity-types` in `DIAGNOSING_JOBS`.** Adding a typecheck to it makes five unrelated things — a dependency prefetch, the typecheck, a live function-host boot, an integration suite and a unit suite — share one job name, which is exactly the condition [`check_ci_diagnostics.mjs`](../../scripts/check_ci_diagnostics.mjs) rule 2 exists for. The two test steps had no `::error::` of their own and now do. Registering a second job also caught two assertions in that guard's own suite that had the registry's size written into them as `1`; both now count off the registry.

**Verification.** `deno check` over the tree: **81 before, 0 after**, both computed at this commit. `deno test --allow-all --no-check supabase/functions/`: **520 passed, 0 failed, 23 ignored**, against a 518/0/23 baseline — the two added are the new wiring test, and nothing regressed. The same suite **with** checking is identical. `deno cache --no-check` over the whole tree followed by `deno check --deny-import` completes, so the lane still never reaches the network on a warm cache; the one new `deno.lock` line is `@types/boolbase`, a cheerio declaration nothing had previously needed to resolve. `actionlint`, `check_ci_diagnostics.mjs` (15 self-diagnosing steps across 2 bundled jobs), its 11 unit tests, `tsconfig_coverage.test.mjs` (5), the new coverage guard (3) and `check_doc_checkboxes.mjs` all green.

**What this does not claim.** Nothing here was run against the deployed functions or a live Supabase; the evidence is the type-checker, the pure-helper suite and the source-grep guards. And the typecheck's reach stops at the Stripe SDK: `Stripe.Account` resolves to `any` through the esm.sh specifier all four payment functions import, so every Stripe call in the tier is still unchecked — filed rather than fixed, because closing it means changing how that dependency is resolved, not annotating a call site.

**The lane needs a `node_modules` on disk, which is why it provisions one.** The four Stripe functions import `https://esm.sh/stripe@17.5.0?target=deno`, and those declarations reference the node types — so `deno check` aborts with `Could not find "@types/node" in a node_modules folder` before reading a single file, and the `edge-functions` job installs no npm dependencies. `deno install` provisions it from the ROOT `package.json`'s own `@types/node`, which [§ 757](#757) had added a day earlier for the repo-root `tsc` root; no `setup-node` and no workspace install is involved. It writes an npm specifier map into `deno.lock` in the runner's checkout, which is committed nowhere and fails no check — `sync_deno_lock.mjs` reads only the `workspace` section, and that section is untouched. Reproduced both ways before landing: with `node_modules` deleted the check fails on exactly that error, and passes after the new step.

**A cross-tier source guard could not see the new call shape.** `security_guards.test.ts` pins that `revenuecat-webhook` verifies its HMAC *before* constructing the service-role client — the webhook is the only legitimate writer of `subscription_tier`, so the ordering is a privilege boundary. It located the call with `/createClient\s*\(/`, which `createClient<Database>(` does not match, so the guard stopped finding the call at all. It failed loudly, which is what its `!== -1` assertion exists to produce; the lesson is that an ordering guard one line narrower would have gone quiet instead, and a source guard that greps for a call shape has to admit the type argument.

## 763. Three of the four write-locked tables held a wider INSERT than UPDATE, and the one that mattered was a live forgery path rather than the unwritable column the filing predicted

**Decided 2026-08-27.** [#789](https://github.com/Absence0760/project-running/issues/789) filed the write-side companion to [§ 759](#759): "four tables carry column-level INSERT/UPDATE for `authenticated`; a column added there is silently *unwritable* (42501 on a PATCH), and three of the four still hold a table-level INSERT beside a column-scoped UPDATE." **The two counts are right, the headline defect has never fired, and the aside at the end of the sentence is the one that was live on `main`.**

**What the catalogue actually says.** Four tables hold a column-level write grant, and only for `authenticated` — `anon` holds none, so the write side is *not* the read side's "both roles identical" shape. Only **one** of the four (`event_attendees`, `20270520_001`) column-scopes **INSERT**; the other three column-scope UPDATE alone. So the filed defect is only unconditionally true on that one table: on `achievements`, `challenge_participants` and `coach_messages` a new column would have been **insertable and not updatable** — write-once by accident, a POST that succeeds and a PATCH that 42501s, which is a stranger failure than the one described. And it has never happened: no column has been added to any of the four since its lockdown landed, measured across all 434 migrations. It is a latent risk worth pinning, not a present bug.

**The asymmetry is real on three tables and exploitable on one.** A table grant implies every column, so a column-scoped UPDATE locks nothing while the same client holds a wider INSERT on a table it may also DELETE from — [§ 584](#584)'s finding, closed for `event_attendees` by `20270520_001`. Whether it *bites* depends on RLS, which the filing did not check and which splits the three cleanly:

* **`achievements` — inert.** The table has no permissive INSERT policy and no permissive DELETE policy at all, so both grants are dead: measured under the owner's own JWT, the INSERT raises `42501 new row violates row-level security policy` and the DELETE silently affects zero rows. Column-scoping the INSERT here, as the filing implies, would have been a no-op.
* **`coach_messages` — half inert.** `coach_messages_owner_insert`'s `WITH CHECK` confines a client to `role = 'user'`, so assistant-turn forgery was already blocked and stays blocked. What was reachable is narrower: the client chose its own `id` and its own `created_at`, against a lockdown whose stated purpose (`20260518_001`) is "the auditability of the conversation log".
* **`challenge_participants` — live.** "users join visible challenges" and "users leave their own challenge" are both own-row verbs, so `completed_at` — the column `20270209_001`'s header reserves for `recompute_challenge_completion` and that `challenge_participants_completed_lockdown_test` pins against a direct UPDATE — was writable in two statements. Verified under the participant's own JWT: the UPDATE raises `42501`, then `delete from challenge_participants where challenge_id = <mine>` followed by an INSERT carrying `completed_at = now()` succeeds. `joined_at`, omitted from the UPDATE grant by the same header, was backdatable the same way. The existing pin asserted the refusal that held while the row sat still and said nothing about the row being replaced.

**The fifth defect was not filed at all, and it is the one the read side had already argued about.** [§ 759](#759)'s fourth assertion is that `anon` and `authenticated` are held identical, because they diverged once for eleven weeks and a divergence is a hole on the wider side. Swept across every column of every public table and every DML verb, there is exactly **one** place in the schema where `anon` holds a privilege `authenticated` lacks: `coach_messages`, table-level **UPDATE**, against `authenticated`'s column-scoped `(archived_at, reaction)`. `20260518_001` revoked the table grant from `authenticated` only; `20270408_001`, whose header says it was "generated from the canonical fully-migrated schema", faithfully version-controlled the leftover. It is inert — the owner policy reads `auth.uid() = user_id` and `anon`'s is null — but that is RLS covering for a grant, which is the same argument § 759 refused to accept on the read side.

**So `20270616_001` is three narrow changes and one redundant one.** Column-scope `challenge_participants`' INSERT to the three columns both clients actually send (`joinChallenge` in `core/data.ts` and `social_service.dart` each post `{challenge_id, user_id, team_club_id}`), so leaving and rejoining now resets `completed_at` and `joined_at` — which is what leaving and rejoining means. Revoke `anon`'s `coach_messages` UPDATE. Column-scope `coach_messages`' INSERT to `(user_id, plan_id, role, content)`, the four the only client insert site sends; the assistant turn is written by the secret-key client in `coach/handler.ts` and is service_role. And revoke `achievements`' client INSERT + DELETE outright — provably behaviour-neutral, and the same "stating an invariant at the privilege layer is cheaper than re-deriving it" § 584 used for its partial unique index. The redundancy has a second purpose: with it, no table in the write registry hands a client an INSERT surface it has not thought about, so the class guard below needs no per-table exemption.

**Online safety is not ceremony here, it is absence.** Measured on this Postgres: a `revoke insert on public.achievements from anon` inside an open transaction holds `AccessShareLock` on `pg_class` and its indexes and **nothing at all on the target relation**. GRANT and REVOKE update a catalogue tuple; there is no scan and no rewrite, so none of `migration_locks.md`'s online-DDL machinery applies.

**`column_grant_write_lockdown_registry_test` is the write-side sibling, and it is six assertions rather than four because the write side has two failure modes pointing opposite ways.** It pins the withheld INSERT/UPDATE map per role with a reason per column — the § 759 direction, since pinning the granted set does not move when a column arrives ungranted; it fails when a table outside the registry acquires the per-column write shape; it fails when a locked table regains a table-level grant on the verb it locks; it fails when `anon` holds any column privilege `authenticated` lacks; **it fails when a column is insertable-but-not-updatable and not registered write-once with the reason writing it once is safe** — the § 584 class, stated as a schema-wide invariant rather than a fact about four tables; and it checks the one exemption the fifth assertion leans on (`global_segment_efforts`, genuinely append-only, no UPDATE policy and no UPDATE grant) rather than trusting it, so the exemption cannot go stale silently.

**The guard earned its place on its first run and again on its second.** Its first execution failed assertion 1 on `coach_messages.archived_at` and `.reaction`, which the new INSERT carve-out had withheld without anyone writing down that a turn is neither archived nor reacted-to at the moment it is written — the exact drift the registry exists to catch, caught against a migration written minutes earlier. Then the first draft of the new `challenge_participants` pin was **vacuous** in § 741's sense: it inserted `completed_at` against a challenge id that did not exist, so the `WITH CHECK`'s `is_challenge_visible` raised the same `42501` and the assertion passed before the fix as happily as after it. The committed form performs the exploit's own DELETE first, which both makes the re-INSERT otherwise valid — same visible challenge, same `auth.uid()`, no primary-key collision — and leaves the absent column grant as the only thing that can refuse it. It fails against `main` and passes against the migration, checked both ways. Seven probes, each rolled back, trip all six registry assertions by name; five of the six fire alone on at least one probe, and assertion 3 co-fires with 1 and 5 because regaining a table-level UPDATE necessarily empties the withheld set and makes every registered write-once column updatable.

**One consequence for `achievements_test`.** Revoking DELETE changes an observable behaviour: the bare `delete from achievements` the test used to run, which RLS answered with zero rows affected, now raises `42501` and would abort the pgtap transaction. The test now asserts both refusals by SQLSTATE. That the refusal moved a layer earlier is the point — an RLS-only refusal on DELETE affected zero rows *without raising*, so a future permissive DELETE policy would have re-opened a DELETE + re-INSERT path onto every column the `is_public` grant withholds, and nothing would have said so.

## 764. The bundled job was filed as a two-line registry edit and the registry was the defect; the "one non-hermetic step" was five call sites of a binary this repo installed nowhere

Two #789 entries about CI tooling misdescribing itself, both partly wrong, and wrong in the direction that made them look smaller than they were.

**The `parity-matrix` filing had the count right and the fix backwards.** It said the job bundles *four* unrelated guards — it does: `check_parity_matrix.dart`, `check_parity_ios_column.mjs`, `check_parity_pair_registry.mjs`, `check_doc_checkboxes.mjs`. It said adding the job to `DIAGNOSING_JOBS` was "a two-line change" blocked only until "the job's first step gains an `::error::` — the other three steps already have one." **Two of the four had none.** The pair-registry step, and the Dart matrix check, which was **unnamed** — and an unnamed `run:` step was outside the rule entirely, so the shortest way to satisfy `check_ci_diagnostics.mjs` had always been to delete a step's name. The job's own comment listed three of its four scripts and called them "these two guards" throughout; the job's *name* listed three of four.

**Adding the entry would have closed one instance of a class with three members.** The registry is hand-kept, and a hand-kept list of bundled jobs is a list that does not know when a job joins the class. Derived instead: a job that runs **two or more of this repo's own guards** is bundled by that fact. Measured over the committed workflows, that is five jobs, and the registry named two of them. The three it never named: `parity-matrix` (four guards, two undiagnosed — filed, deferred twice), **`workflow-lint` (five guards, *zero* diagnosed)** and **env-isolation's `unit` (two, zero)**; `pgtap-rls` diagnosed two of its three steps. Seven steps in all, none of which any filing mentioned but the first. `DIAGNOSING_JOBS` survives for the one bundle the derivation cannot see — `edge-functions` runs `deno test`, not a guard script — and a listed job that no longer exists still fails rather than reading nothing.

**Bundled over split, and the measurement is the reason.** Splitting `parity-matrix` into four separately-named jobs makes each guard visible in the checks list, at four runners and four checkout+setup pairs where there was one; GitHub bills a job by the minute, rounded up, so three seconds of `node` costs the same as a minute of it. The job's own comment already priced the Flutter setup as the only real cost, which is true and is an argument for splitting the Dart guard off — but it is not the deciding one. **Each split job needs its own line in the `CI gate` aggregator's `needs:` list, and an omitted line is worse than the problem being solved**: the gate passes when every job it needs passed *or was skipped*, so a job outside the list has a red that blocks nothing and reads as one more green row among thirty. Splitting trades an unlabelled failure for the risk of an invisible one, once per split, forever. A per-step `::error::` costs six lines and says the same thing the split job's name would have.

**So the gate's `needs:` list is now enforced too** (rule 3 in the same guard): every job in `ci.yml` is named there, and a `needs:` entry naming no job fails as well, since a deleted job leaves a dependency the aggregator will never hear from. Nothing had ever checked this; the list was complete by hand, over 28 jobs, in a file where a job is added far more often than the bottom of it is re-read. Proved to trip by deleting `- twin-parity` and watching it report that job by name. Parsing the job keys had to be scoped to the top-level `jobs:` mapping — `on:` holds two-space keys of its own, and the first version demanded the gate wait for `push` and `pull_request`.

**The `tsx` filing's premise reproduced exactly and its boundary was wrong twice.** `npm run test:unit` from a clean `npm ci` tree exits `127: tsx: command not found` — confirmed in an isolated checkout, not inferred. But the entry called the CI step "the one step in this job that is not hermetic", and it is not: `parity-types` also pulls a Deno runtime, the Supabase CLI and a Docker stack over the network. What is unique to `npx tsx` is not that it reaches the network but that it reaches it **for an unpinned package with no lockfile entry and no integrity hash** — third-party code chosen at test time, executing against this checkout. And the entry named one call site; there are **five**. `cross-client-roundtrip` runs `npx tsx` four more times, each the Node read-half of a round-trip assertion. The declaration that fixes one fixes all five.

**`tsx` was declared by nothing, and one manifest mentioned it.** `vite` lists it as an *optional peer* at `^4.8.1`, which installs no copy — so a guard asking "does some package.json mention tsx" would have passed on the day the suite was fetching it off the registry. Node 24 cannot stand in for it either: `node --test` on a web unit test fails outright, because type stripping does not rewrite the extensionless relative imports the tree is written with. Declared as an `apps/web` devDependency, and **the addition moves no other resolution** — comparing the resolved `name@version` multiset across both lockfiles before and after, the only new entry is `tsx@4.23.12`; every other line of the `package-lock.json` diff is npm re-hoisting the same versions. The CI step now runs `npm run test:unit`, so the command CI runs and the command its own diagnosis tells a reader to reproduce with are one string rather than two that drifted.

**A guard so the next one fails loudly.** `scripts/check_workflow_binaries.mjs` refuses any binary a workflow hands a package runner (`npx`, `npm exec`, `pnpm exec`, the `dlx` family) unless a package this repo declares provides it — the same species of hazard `check_toolchain_pins.mjs` already refuses for an action pinned to a mutable tag. The binary→package table is explicit because the mapping cannot be read without an install and `workflow-lint` has none, so an unmapped name **fails** rather than being skipped, and a mapped name no workflow uses fails rather than rotting into prose. It reads comments and `echo`'d reproduce lines like any other text, since a diagnosis telling someone to run `npx foo` makes the same claim the command does — which is the half that was wrong here. Tokens that cannot be a command name (`<bin>` in a template, the `/` between alternatives in a sentence) are prose; a binary an expression decides at run time is neither, and is reported.

**Verification.** Clean-tree reproduce: an isolated copy of the worktree, `npm ci`, then `npm run test:unit` from `apps/web` — **4332 of 4333 pass**, the single failure being `decisions_numbering_guard.test.ts`, which shells out to `git` in a tree copied without `.git`; it passes in the worktree. `check_ci_diagnostics.mjs` reports 31 self-diagnosing steps across 5 derived + 2 listed bundled jobs and the gate waiting for all 28 other jobs, with 22 unit tests; `check_workflow_binaries.mjs` reports 16 invocations of 3 binaries across 25 workflow and composite-action files, with 14; `check_toolchain_pins.mjs`, `check_pnpm_overrides.mjs` (6 overrides intact across both lockfiles), `check_script_types`, `check:tsconfig-coverage`, `check_root_scripts.mjs` and the three `parity-matrix` Node guards all green. Both workflow files parse.

**What this does not close.** The rule's subject is the named `run:` steps plus every guard step named or not, so an unnamed step that runs a *non-guard* check in a bundled job is still exempt — `workflow-lint`'s actionlint invocation was exactly that, and is named and diagnosed here by hand rather than by the rule. Widening it further would demand an `::error::` from `npm ci` and `go install`, and an allowlist of setup verbs is another hand-kept list of the kind this entry replaced.

## 765. The declarations were never missing — esm.sh renames the module they declare, TypeScript matches ambient declarations by literal specifier text, and the obvious guard against the collapse is satisfied by the collapse

**Decided 2026-08-27.** [§ 762](#762) closed the Edge Function typecheck and said outright where its reach stopped: `Stripe.Account` resolved to `any` through the esm.sh specifier the payment functions import, so every Stripe call in the tier was checked against nothing. This closes that. The tree was at **0 errors** before; binding the declarations put it at **2**, both genuine; it is at **0** again.

**The probe reproduced exactly, and the diagnosis under it was wrong.** `declare const a: Stripe.Account; const bad: number = a.id;` type-checks, as filed — and so does `declare const nope: Stripe.ThisTypeDoesNotExistAtAll`, which says the whole module is `any` rather than some field being loose. But the filing's account of *why* ("closing it means changing how that dependency is resolved", with a different esm.sh variant, an `npm:` specifier or a hand-written declaration as the candidates) does not survive contact with the graph. **The declarations are served, fetched and error-free.** esm.sh advertises them on the module's `x-typescript-types` header, Deno follows it, and `deno info --json` shows all ~450 of stripe's `.d.ts` files resolved as `Dts` modules with no error on any of them. Nothing needed to be resolved differently.

**What is broken is ambient-declaration matching, not resolution.** esm.sh rewrites stripe's own `declare module 'stripe'` to `declare module 'https://esm.sh/stripe@17.5.0/types/index.d.ts'` — the declaration file's own URL. TypeScript matches an ambient module declaration against the **literal text** of an import specifier, not against what the specifier resolves to. A module importing `https://esm.sh/stripe@17.5.0?target=deno` therefore matches no ambient declaration; the file it does resolve to has no top-level exports of its own, since everything lives inside that block; and Deno's compiler host yields `any` for it silently rather than the "file is not a module" tsc would report. Importing the URL **literally** binds the whole SDK — measured, the same probe then fails with `Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'`. So the fix is a `@ts-types` directive pointing at a three-line declaration file whose own import is that literal string: `_shared/stripe.ts` plus `_shared/stripe_types.d.ts`, and every payment function imports Stripe from there. **No runtime byte changes** — the specifier still carries `?target=deno` per [§ 699](#699), a declaration file is erased before anything is bundled, `deno.lock` is untouched, and `deno check --deny-import` still completes on a warm cache. Both alternatives the filing named would have been worse: an `npm:` specifier re-arms exactly the boot-time registry dependency § 699 spent a round diagnosing, and a hand-written declaration for "the handful of shapes we read" is a hand-maintained approximation of a 450-file SDK that would drift the first time a param was added.

**Nor did it want measuring against a live test-mode key.** The filed entry said the change "wants measuring against a live test-mode key" because these are the sign-off-gated functions. It is entirely type-level; no key, live or test, is involved in any of it.

**Stripe was the only dependency in the tier with this shape, and that was measured rather than assumed.** One probe file importing all seven of the tree's remote dependencies and assigning each to a `number`: `@supabase/supabase-js` at both the default and `?target=deno`, `deno.land/x/zipjs`, `deno.land/x/sentry`, `esm.sh/cheerio` and `deno.land/std/assert` all produced a `TS2322` naming a real type. Stripe produced nothing. Six of seven were fine; cheerio is the instructive contrast, because it is also an esm.sh package and its declaration entry is an ordinary module with real exports, so it binds the ordinary way.

**"All four payment functions" undercounts the Stripe boundary by one, and the one it misses is the inbound half.** `stripe-events-webhook` is 607 lines of `index.ts` and 278 of `lib.ts` — it verifies Stripe's HMAC by hand and parses Stripe's event payloads as `Record<string, unknown>`. It imports no SDK, so it had no declarations to lose and it is absent from the filing; but it is the function that writes order status, seats attendees and releases capacity, and a reader would conclude the Stripe surface is four functions wide. It stays hand-typed **deliberately**: § 699 measured `?target=deno` at 228 KB -> 2.4 MB per eszip, and this is the function Stripe itself calls with retries on timeout, so a 10x cold-boot cost for a type-only benefit is the wrong trade on the inbound path. Filed rather than done, with the reason.

**Two errors fell out, and they are § 762's own finding in a new place.** `CheckoutSessionMetadata` and `DonationCheckoutMetadata` were `interface`s. TypeScript gives an object-literal **type alias** an implicit index signature and an interface none, so neither was assignable to Stripe's `MetadataParam` (`{ [name: string]: string | number | null }`) — exactly what § 762 hit on `delete-account`'s `ThirdPartyOutcomes` against a jsonb column. Both are type aliases now; the values were always four strings. `events-connect-onboard` also carried a comment-documented workaround — `let account: { id: string }` with three lines explaining that the SDK resolves to `any` so the field had to be annotated by hand or the `any` would widen `accountId` back out of `string | null`. It is `let account: Stripe.Account` now. Two was not a floor: the check was re-run after fixing and nothing new appeared, and a `new Stripe('k').accounts` probe injected into each of the four files errors in each, so the checker is demonstrably live in all of them rather than merely quiet.

**Binding the declarations does not finish the boundary, because what reaches a Stripe call is not a fresh object literal.** The params helpers are deliberately Stripe-free — `events-checkout`'s is imported by `stripe-events-webhook`, which must not grow that polyfill tree — so `create` is handed a function **return**, and TypeScript runs no excess-property check on one. Measured with the declarations fully bound: a `defualt_currency` field added to `AccountCreateParams` passed `deno check` without a word, and would have come back from Stripe as `Received unknown parameter` — a 502 for every host trying to onboard. `AssertNoUnknownParamKeys<UnknownParamKeys<Shape, Params>>` at each call site puts the key names back under the compiler; four deliberate typos were injected and each was reported by name. This is [§ 762](#762)'s untyped-column-name-table lesson at the other end of the same tier.

**The obvious guard against a future collapse is satisfied by the collapse, which is why the one shipped is negative.** Pinning "this must not be `any`" invites `type IsAny<T> = 0 extends 1 & T ? true : false` plus an `extends false` constraint. Over this import the conditional resolves to `any` itself, and `any` satisfies every constraint — so it was written, the `@ts-types` directive was deleted to test it, and it reported **nothing**. Every assignability test has that property in both directions. Only a negative test discriminates: `Account.id` is a string, so constraining it to `number` must fail, and a `@ts-expect-error` over that assertion turns into a loud `TS2578 Unused '@ts-expect-error' directive` naming `_shared/stripe.ts` the moment the declarations stop binding. Proved by deleting the directive and watching it fire.

**Two guards, because neither can see what the other sees.** A collapse back to `any` changes no import text, so no source grep can find it — that half is the compile-time assertion above, carried by the existing `deno check` lane. A **new** function importing the URL directly produces no type error anywhere, so no compiler can find it — that half is `_shared/stripe_boundary.test.ts`, which also pins that the runtime specifier and the declaration specifier name the same stripe version (two strings, one package, and a bump that touches one types the tier against a version it does not run) and that both halves of the compile-time guard are still present. Every assertion in it was proved to fail against a deliberately broken tree, including the vacuity case: a test asserts that something still imports the boundary, so the file cannot go on passing over a tier the Stripe functions have left.

**Verification.** `deno check` over the tree, the `edge-functions` lane's own expression: **0 before, 2 with the declarations bound, 0 after**, all three at this commit. `deno test --no-check --allow-read --allow-env supabase/functions/`: **524 passed, 0 failed, 23 ignored** against § 762's 520/0/23 baseline — the four added are the new boundary guard, nothing regressed. `deno check --deny-import` completes, so the lane still reaches no network on a warm cache, and `deno.lock` is byte-identical (the declaration URLs were already in the graph via the types header; `deno install` was not run and no npm specifier map was written). `npm run sync:deno-lock:check`, `actionlint`, `check_ci_diagnostics.mjs` (16 self-diagnosing steps across 2 bundled jobs) and `scripts/edge_functions_typecheck_coverage.test.mjs` (3) green. The bundle question was measured rather than reasoned about: `deno info` on `events-checkout/index.ts` reports **582 modules / 7.42 MB before, 585 / 7.59 MB after** — the declaration tree was already in the graph at base, pulled by the types header, so this adds three modules rather than 450, and the only new module with any runtime existence is a re-export.

**What this does not claim.** Nothing was run against Stripe, in test mode or otherwise; the evidence is the type-checker, the pure-helper suite and the source guards. The compiler now agrees the params are well-formed and the responses are read correctly — it cannot say the *semantics* are right, and one such question is filed below (a destination-charge refund clawing back the application fee without reversing the transfer). And the warm-cache step ahead of the lane still runs `deno cache --no-check`, which does not walk the declaration graph, so on a cold `deno.lock` the typecheck fetches those ~450 files from esm.sh outside the retry wrapper that exists for exactly that hazard — unchanged by this entry, and filed.

## 766. The undeclared flag named one of four ways the Strava walk stops short, and the report — not the truncation — is what loses the runs

[§ 762](#762) filed `strava-import`'s `rate_limited` as a field the response has always carried and no client declares, to be closed with "one field on the result type plus a line of copy in six catalogues". The premise held. The scope did not, in the direction that matters: **`rate_limited` names one of four ways `backfill` stops short of the end of the lookback window, and the other three had no field at all.** The page loop has five exits — a page shorter than `per_page` and an empty page are the end of the window; a 429/503 sets `rateLimited`; a non-2xx `break`s silently; a body that is not an array `break`s silently; and `page > 20` (1000 activities) `break`s silently. Declaring the flag and stopping would have made a throttled sync honest and left the other three still reporting a truncated import as a finished one.

**Nothing is lost by the truncation. It is lost by the report.** The obvious second defect to look for was an advanced cursor, and there is none: `after=` is derived from `Date.now() - lookbackDays * 86400_000` on every call, `integrations.sync_cursor` is written by nothing in the repo (it appears only in the export column list), and `last_sync_at` is read by nothing but the two integration tiles. A re-sync therefore re-walks the same window and the un-imported activities are still fetchable — **until they age past `lookbackDays`.** That is 90 by default and neither client offers a way to raise it: web's `syncStrava(lookbackDays = 90)` has no caller that passes anything, and `ApiClient.syncStrava` the same. So the loss is real but deferred, and its cause is the sentence: a runner told "Strava sync complete. 40 new" does not sync again, and ninety days later the rest is unreachable. A false "complete" is a data loss on a 90-day fuse.

`last_sync_at` was the second sentence saying it. The stamp ran unconditionally after the loop, so a walk that fetched two pages of twenty and then hit a 429 left the tile reading "Last synced just now" — a claim that survives the toast the runner dismissed. It is now inside `if (complete)`, which also makes the column mean what its name says: the moment the whole window was last walked. A truncated repeat sync keeps the previous, true value; a first connect that never completed leaves it null, which both tiles already render as "waiting for first sync".

**The clients grade the response rather than casting it.** Web held two `data as StravaSyncResult` casts, which is not a check — the interface listed four fields and neither call site read any of them. `parseStravaSyncResult` (`apps/web/src/lib/integrations/strava_sync_result.ts`) and its Dart twin (`packages/core_models/lib/src/strava_sync_result.dart`, registered as the `strava_sync_result` parity pair) fail closed: only an explicit `complete === true` earns the success copy, and an unrecognised shape, an absent field or an embedded `error` reads as partial. A count is a non-negative integer or it is 0, rather than a malformed value the banner would then state as fact.

That direction is **deliberately the opposite** of `cloud_export_helpers`' `cloudExportShortfall`, which treats an absent `complete` as no shortfall. The reasoning there is sound and does not transfer: that response comes from either of two transports, one of which may be an older deployment, and warning on every export would be its own dishonesty. Here there is one transport, shipped from this repo alongside its callers, and the costs are not symmetric — a false "partial" costs one extra click, a false "complete" costs the runs.

**The result does not join the `import_failures` vocabulary, and the word is all that is shared.** `ImportFailureLog` records **per-activity** failures inside a client-side archive walk: every entry names an activity that was seen and refused, with a reason and a log-safe detail. A truncated page walk produces no such entry — the activities it did not fetch were never seen, so there is nothing to name. Reusing `ImportFailureReason` would have meant inventing a per-activity record for activities that never reached a client. `rate_limited` stays the word for the same condition in both places; the record does not.

The survey the filing invited came back clean in the other direction: `strava-import` is the only importer with this shape. `parkrun-import` fetches one results page and returns a non-2xx loudly rather than looping. The two web bulk importers walk a local archive with no remote pagination, throw on the 500 MB size cap, and report the per-activity photo cap as an aggregate — the truncation class does not exist for them.

**The mobile leg carried a third defect nobody had filed: it dropped `failed`.** `ApiClient.syncStrava` returned `Future<Map<String, dynamic>>` and the screen read `imported` and `skipped` off it, so a run Strava served that we could not ingest was invisible on the phone while web has reported it since that toast was written. Both methods now return the graded result, and the banner gained the with-failed form web already had.

**Coverage.** The parser is pinned on both platforms (12 mirror tests each), including that a whole `double` is a count on the Dart side — JSON has one number type and `Number.isInteger(12.0)` is true, so rejecting it would be a divergence rather than a stricter contract. Four Flutter widget tests drive the real screen through a fake client for the throttled, otherwise-truncated, finished and finished-with-failures cases. The Edge Function itself has no handler-level suite and gains none: it needs a live Supabase and a real Strava grant. What guards it is the source-grep idiom its own `wiring.test.ts` already uses — exactly two exits may set `complete = true`, the return shape carries the field, and the `last_sync_at` stamp sits inside the `if (complete)`.

## 767. The word was in 47 places, not 42, and the two the filing could not count were the two that decided whether a blanket rule was safe

**Decided 2026-08-27.** [followups.md](../product/followups.md) carried the one box [§ 760](#760-the-rename-the-box-asked-for-is-one-the-tool-forbids-and-the-catalogue-it-was-about-turned-out-to-be-three-tenths-finished-on-a-corpus-that-had-never-been-mined-for-the-auth-block) filed rather than guessed: the European catalogues say `padrão` where European Portuguese says `predefinição`, "42 call sites", "at least two meaning *pattern*". Closed. The filing's judgement was right and every one of its numbers was low.

**47 occurrences, not 42 — and the gap is a counting method, not a stale round.** `padrão` was counted per matching LINE and in lower case. Web holds **26** occurrences across 25 lines (`onboarding.step5Hint` says it twice) and the phone **21**, so the two component figures § 760 recorded — 22 and 20 — were each one short of the lines and further short of the occurrences. The two that a case-sensitive grep walks past turned out to matter twice over: `live.statTimer` and `liveSpectatorStatTimer` say `Cronômetro`, capitalised, and were missed by this round's own manual pass too. The guard, which is case-insensitive, named them.

**44 of the 47 mean the pre-set value; three do not, and they are not the same three.** Each site was read against its English source in `en.ts` / `app_en.arb` rather than swept. Two are *pattern* — `loadRamp.meaning_high` and `loadRampMeaningHigh`, "the pattern most associated with injury", the pair § 760 had already found on the phone. The third is neither *pattern* nor *default*: `dash.prAgeGradeTitle` is "the world **standard** for your age and sex", a sense the filing did not anticipate and which reads correctly as `padrão` in Portugal exactly as *pattern* does. So the filing's "at least two" was a floor in the direction it named and short by a whole third sense.

**`predefinição`, one word, not two.** European software says both `predefinição` and `por omissão`, and the honest reason to pick one is [§ 761](#761-three-normalizers-folded-every-pt-tag-to-brazilian-four-surfaces-were-filed-and-the-count-was-right-for-the-wrong-reason-and-the-guard-that-could-have-caught-it-ran-nowhere)'s own: a second vocabulary is worse than an imperfect one. § 760 had already named `predefinição` when it filed the box, so the choice was made where it belonged, before the word had 44 sites depending on it.

**Gender is what a word swap gets wrong, one round after the same lesson.** `padrão` is masculine and `predefinição` is feminine, so the agreement reaches past the noun in both directions and four strings carry pronouns bound to it — `onboarding.step5Hint`'s `substituí-lo`, `runEditor.makePublicHint`'s `alterá-lo`, and `onboardingPrivacyBody` / `setupPrivacyHint` which each carry two. § 760 recorded this for `tela` → `ecrã` and `academia` → `ginásio`; it is the same defect a `sed` would have shipped here.

**The guard could not be a deny-list, so it is the inverse of one.** § 760's tag-vs-content scan holds words the other variant does not use **at all**, and its own comment says why: a frequency rule needs a threshold and a threshold is a number nobody can defend. `padrão` fails that test — Portugal really does use it — which is precisely why § 760 declined to touch it and filed instead. So the direction is inverted: **the word is banned and the sites meaning the other sense are named**, each with its English source in a comment. That makes the ambiguity cost something to reintroduce. A new string saying `padrão` fails and forces the per-site decision, where a deny-list entry could only ever have been answered by dropping the word and blinding the scan everywhere else.

**The allowlist fails loudly rather than going quiet.** An allowlist that names a key the catalogue no longer has, or one that no longer says the word, is covering nothing while still reading as a decision — [§ 762](#762-47-production-handlers-was-the-count-of-non-test-modules-the-one-file-that-reported-no-errors-was-the-one-typed-against-any-and-81-was-a-floor-rather-than-a-total)'s lesson about a source guard whose pattern stops matching. Both halves assert every named site still exists and still says the word, and both were tripped on purpose in both directions before landing.

**Reading 47 sites found the class they sit in, which is the point of reading them.** Thirty more sites across the two catalogues, each a Brazilian form a derivation had carried in: the **ô/ê-for-ó/é proparoxytones** (`cronómetro`, `oxigénio`, `autónomo`), which is the class the deny-list already held `quilômetro` and `gênero` from — one word at a time, twice, without the class ever being named; the postposed **`demais`** intensifier fronted to `demasiado`, which § 755's own corpus had as `rápido demais` → `demasiado depressa` and applied to one phrase rather than to the construction; `planilha`, `todo mundo`, a `liberar` whose sibling key already said `desbloquear`, and the one `Pulou` § 760's `pular` → `saltar` rule reached in the catalogue it was not run over. All four proparoxytones are on the deny-list now, with `planilha`, `usuário`, `deletar` and `esporte` beside them, so the class is guarded rather than the instances.

**And one more casualty of § 755's elision rule, in the third shape it has taken.** § 760 found the rule deleting `você` where it was the verb's **object**. `planNewRecent5kWarning` reads "**Até si confirmar**" — here the pronoun was not deleted but replaced by a stressed oblique standing as a **subject**, which no Portuguese allows. Its own web twin says "Até confirmar" and is correct, so the pair disagreed on a sentence that is ungrammatical on one side.

**Half the surfaces shipping this locale had no lexical guard at all.** The web scan reads `lib/i18n/locales/` and the mobile twin reads `lib/l10n/`, so the Wear OS string set and the watchOS String Catalog — both of which ship pt-PT — were covered by nothing. Both measure **clean**, which is the reason to guard them now rather than the reason not to: § 755's wrist set and § 761's watchOS set were written in European Portuguese directly, and the defect this whole arc is about is a later derivation from Brazilian quietly undoing that. The scan is cross-tier, the shape § 761's `delete-account` guard already uses against the Go worker's catalogue, and each reader asserts it found strings before it asserts they are clean.

**Verification.** Web: 26 `padrão` occurrences before, 2 after, both allowlisted; `locale_reach` + `messages_parity` + `locale` 27 passed / 0 failed; `npm run check` 0 errors over 2,427 files. Mobile: 21 before, 1 after; `architecture_guards_test.dart` 210 passed / 0 failed and `l10n_parity_test.dart` 37 passed / 0 failed; `flutter gen-l10n` regenerated, `flutter analyze` 0 warnings and 0 errors, and the iOS twin byte-identical on `lib/` and `test/`. `pt-PT.ts` now differs from Brazilian on **1,430 of 5,056 keys, 28.28%** (was 27.70%) and `app_pt.arb` on **1,183 of 3,795, 31.17%** (was 30.69%). Each new guard was proved to trip: a planted Brazilian default and a stale allowlist entry on both platforms, plus a planted word on each watch surface and a wrist file its reader can no longer parse.

**What this does not claim.** The wording is **model-authored and not natively reviewed**, so the native-review box is widened rather than ticked, and two things are left in it deliberately rather than guessed. `longão` — Brazilian running slang for the long run, 7 web keys and 5 phone keys — is community vocabulary rather than dictionary vocabulary, and getting the Portuguese register wrong across twelve sites is worse than leaving one word Brazilian. And the phone still addresses its reader **two ways**: 36 `teu`/`tua` occurrences survive in `app_pt.arb` against **zero** in `pt-PT.ts`, the residue of the mixed register § 755 recorded and § 760 unified only inside the voice cues, where a spoken coach could not be left doing it. Which register a Portuguese app should use is exactly a native speaker's call, and it is now measured rather than merely noted. Nothing here was touched on the wrist or the watch, so no Mac verification arises for this change.

## 768. `sync_cursor` really was written by nothing, and the walk had two more exits than § 766 counted — the two that also threw the counts away

**Decided 2026-08-28.** Three filings, one defect from three angles: neither client could raise `lookbackDays` above 90; the 20-page cap told the runner to sync again when a re-sync re-walked the same window; and `handleConnect`'s `if (!code)` was unreachable. [§ 766](#766-the-undeclared-flag-named-one-of-four-ways-the-strava-walk-stops-short-and-the-report--not-the-truncation--is-what-loses-the-runs) shipped the honest *report* of a truncated walk; this is the honest *recovery* from one. Every measurable claim in all three filings held. What they were missing was two more exits and a second dead branch.

**The filings, measured.** `integrations.sync_cursor` is written by nothing: it appears in the initial-schema DDL, two export column lists (`export-data/backup_spec.ts`, `job_worker/internal/supabase.go`), the two generated type files and four doc lines — no writer, no reader. `after=` was `Math.floor((Date.now() - lookbackDays * 86400_000) / 1000)`, recomputed on every call. `lookbackDays` had exactly two call sites, `syncStrava()` on `/settings/integrations` and `api.syncStrava()` on the Strava tile, and **neither passed an argument**. And `code` reaches `handleConnect` only through a top level that has already rejected a non-string or an empty one, so `if (!code) return missing_code` could not fire.

**Seven exits, not five, and § 766 could not have counted the two it missed — they are not `break`s.** Six `break` statements leave the page loop: two claim the end of the window (an empty page, a short page) and four truncate (429/503, a non-2xx, a body that is JSON but not an array, the cap). § 766 counted those correctly, collapsing the two end-of-window exits, hence "five exits, four truncating". But `await fetch(url, …)` rejects on DNS, TLS and a dropped connection, and `await resp.json()` rejects on an HTML error page from anything sitting in front of Strava — the realistic shape of a bad gateway, and the reason the array check § 766 did count only ever fired on the rarer half of that case. Both propagated out of `backfill`, past `handleSync`, into `withSentry`, which answers **500 `internal_error`**. Measured on the first run of the new suite: **7 passed, 2 failed**, the two failures being exactly these. So the two exits `complete` could not describe are the only two that also discard `imported` / `skipped` / `failed` — the activities are in the database and absent from the report, and the runner is told the sync failed outright. Both now `break` with `complete` false, like every other truncation.

**The cursor is a window, not a page number.** A truncated walk stores `{"v":1,"from","after","before"}` in epoch seconds — the slice of Strava's list still to fetch — and the next sync resumes it. Page numbers would have been the obvious cursor and are the wrong one: they are only stable while the underlying list is, and a resume that restarts at page 1 with a narrowed window is stable by construction. A cursor that would **not** narrow the window is not written at all, because a resume making no progress loops a runner between two syncs forever; a truncation that got nowhere therefore writes nothing, leaving a cursor it could not advance intact for the next attempt.

**`from` exists because the first resume rule was backwards, and the test said so.** The obvious rule — honour a stored cursor when the caller's requested floor does not reach further back than the cursor's `after` — refuses **every same-lookback re-sync there is**. `after=` is recomputed from the clock, so the frontier of a truncated 90-day walk is always *newer* than the floor the next 90-day walk asks for, and the comparison rejects it every time. The cursor therefore carries the oldest instant the **job** covers, separately from the oldest still to fetch, and containment is tested against that. A runner widening `lookbackDays` reaches past `from`, the cursor is ignored, and the wider walk subsumes its remainder anyway.

**The walk direction is measured off the page rather than assumed.** Strava returns the activity list oldest-first when `after` is set and newest-first otherwise, and which end of the walked span is the frontier depends entirely on which. That is a documented upstream behaviour this repo cannot verify from here, so `extendWalkedSpan` reads it off the page it just fetched — one comparison of the first and last `start_date` — and `nextWalkWindow` moves the floor up or the ceiling down accordingly. Under the newest-first reading the resume excludes activities created since the truncation, which the live `strava-webhook` already ingests; the cursor clears when the window finishes and the next sync covers them regardless.

**Measured end to end: the cap is now escapable.** Against a simulated 1,250-activity window, the first sync spends 20 fetches, reports `complete: false` / `resumable: true` and records a cursor; the second starts past the 1,000th activity, spends 6 fetches (five full pages plus the empty one that ends the window), reports `complete: true` and clears the cursor. That is the whole content of the second filing: "sync again to finish" is now an instruction that can succeed.

**`resumable` is a separate claim from `complete`, fail-closed in the same direction.** Only an explicit `true` earns it, it is never true alongside `complete` (a finished window subsumes any point inside it), and an embedded `error` forces `complete` false without dragging the resume point down with it — a walk that recorded one still has it. Both surfaces use it to choose between "syncing again picks up where it stopped" and "recorded no restart point", which is the difference between an instruction and a hope.

**The default lookback stays at 90, and the control is what changes.** Strava's per-user budget is 100 requests per 15 minutes and the walk spends one per 50 activities, so raising the default would make every routine sync several times heavier for history the runner already has — the filing said this and it is right. Web gets a select beside **Sync now** (90 days / 6 months / a year); mobile gets a **Sync older history…** item in the tile menu opening a picker, with the plain **Sync now** left at 90 so the common path stays one tap. The three windows and the maximum live in the `strava_sync_result` pair beside the fields that grade the answer, because what a client may ask for and what it may believe about the reply are one contract; a web guard pins the maximum to the function's own `400 invalid_lookback_days` bound, making it a third rail like `nearby`'s.

**A truncation is a state of the connection, not a moment.** Both platforms said it once, in a toast or a top banner, and the window is measured from now — so the record of "there is more to fetch" has to outlive the thing the runner dismisses, or the rest ages out unnoticed. It is now a note on the card and on the tile until a walk reaches the end of the window.

**The second dead branch, and the one adjacent branch that is reachable.** `handleConnect`'s `if (!code)` was the filed one. The trailing `unknown_action` after the three action `if`s is dead for the same reason one level up — the top level has already narrowed `action` to the three-value union — so the dispatch is now a `switch` the compiler proves exhaustive, which cannot grow a fourth unreachable arm. The adjacent branch worth checking is `handleConnect`'s `'<missing>'` log arm: it **is** reachable, because the top level accepts an empty `redirect_uri` string where it rejects an empty `code`, and it is correct — `parseRedirectAllowlist` drops blanks, so an empty claim can never match. Left as found.

**The mobile callback was not inert where it mattered.** Section S recorded `threkir://strava-callback` as absent from the committed dev allowlist and "inert locally because `STRAVA_CLIENT_ID` is empty, so documented rather than changed". True of `.env.development`. It was also absent from **`.env.example`**, which is the file an operator copies to configure production, where a whole-string comparison against a list carrying only the web callback answers every in-app connect with 400 `invalid_redirect_uri`. Both now carry it, pinned by a guard reading `kStravaCallbackUri` out of the Dart client so moving the scheme moves the guard.

**Coverage, and the reason there is any.** `backfill` lived inside `index.ts` behind a module-level `Deno.serve`, so no test could reach it without binding a port — which is why the page walk had never been exercised at all. It is now `strava-import/backfill.ts` with a stubbed `fetch` and a hand-rolled client: 22 Deno tests over the seven exits, the cursor parser's fail-closed refusals, both narrowing directions, the non-narrowing refusal, the ignore-a-wider-request rule, and the two-sync cap escape. `wiring.test.ts` keeps the source-grep guards and gains four more.

**No migration.** The column has existed since `20260405_001`, is already in both generated type files and is already in the Art 20 export, so writing it needed neither DDL nor a regeneration.

**Verification.** Deno: 550 passed / 0 failed / 23 ignored over the whole functions tree; `deno check` clean on all five `strava-import` modules. Web: 4,352 unit tests passing (4,347 before), `svelte-check` 0 errors over 2,429 files, `check:e2e-types` clean. Mobile: `flutter analyze` 0 warnings / 0 errors, `settings_integrations_strava_partial_test.dart` 8 passing (4 before), `architecture_guards_test.dart` 247 and `l10n_parity_test.dart` passing, iOS twin byte-identical on `lib/` and `test/`. Dart: `strava_sync_result_test.dart` 16 passing. Registry, compliance-drift and doc-checkbox guards all green. Three Playwright tests added to `integrations-connected.spec.ts` and one stale assertion in it corrected — the connected-card spec asserted the literal "last 90 days" the note no longer says.

## 769. `refund_application_fee` is not a claw-back — it pays the host our cut, and sent without `reverse_transfer` it made every cancellation cost the platform the whole ticket

**Decided 2026-08-28.** [§ 765](#765) closed the Stripe typecheck and filed what the compiler cannot see: `events-cancel` created its refund with `refund_application_fee: true` and no `reverse_transfer`. This closes that, and three more money flows the same read surfaced. Nothing here was run against Stripe in any mode.

**The filing held on the fault and was backwards on the mechanism, which changes the arithmetic by a factor of forty.** The charge type is a genuine destination charge — measured from the code that CREATES it, not from the refund: `buildCheckoutSessionParams` sets `payment_intent_data.transfer_data.destination` plus `application_fee_amount`, and `buildDonationSessionParams` does the same. So `reverse_transfer` is the right instrument, as filed. But the filing (and the code comment, and `club_events.md`) read `refund_application_fee: true` as *"the platform fee is clawed back"*. It is the opposite: Stripe's own words are *"by default the platform account keeps the funds from the application fee. To push the application fee funds back to the connected account, set the `refund_application_fee` parameter to `true`."* Sending it **alone** did not decline our fee — it paid the fee **to the host**, on top of the ticket they already kept, because *"by default the destination account keeps the funds that were transferred to it, leaving the platform account to cover the negative balance from the refund."* On a cancelled $50 class at 250 bps the platform was debited **$50.00** and then transferred a further **$1.25**; the host netted **$50.00** for a class nobody attended. The filing described the loss as "the class fee"; it was the whole ticket, plus our own margin, on every cancellation. Stripe is explicit that the half-and-half state is not a configuration at all: *"If you refund the application fee for a destination charge, you must also reverse the transfer."* Both flags now go, and a full refund nets every party to zero less Stripe's processing fee, which is never returned.

**The params moved into a helper so the guard § 765 built could reach them, because this was the one money-MOVING call without it.** All three other Stripe calls carry `AssertNoUnknownParamKeys`; the refund was a bare object literal at the call site. It now goes through `buildRefundParams` with the alias declared against `Stripe.RefundCreateParams` — and the alias was proved live rather than assumed, by adding `reverse_transfers` and watching `deno check` report `TS2344: Type '"reverse_transfers"' does not satisfy the constraint 'never'`. That is the exact failure this call is most exposed to: Stripe silently drops an unknown parameter's intent and answers `Received unknown parameter`, so a typo'd reversal flag restores precisely the bug, and only a compiler can see it.

**A second money bug was sitting in the same function, wired end to end and dead at the last link.** `20270522_001` widened the buyer's `event_orders` UPDATE policy to `('paid', 'partially_refunded')`, `events-cancel` widened its order query to match, and both carry comments saying a partially-refunded registration must remain cancelable "or it can be neither attended nor cancelled". `cancelAction` still returned `'noop'` for it — and a test *pinned* that, listing `partially_refunded` beside `refunded`/`canceled`/`failed` as terminal. So the buyer reached the EF, got `{ok: true, action: 'noop'}`, and the web handler's ternary — which distinguishes only `refund_initiated` from everything else — showed them **"Reservation released"**. No refund, no seat freed, a success toast. A partial refund is not the buyer giving up their place; it is money coming back on a place they kept, so it now decides exactly as `paid` does. The `refund_initiated_at` stamp and its rollback were separately keyed to `.eq('status', 'paid')`, which for such an order matches zero rows and reports no error — they CAS on the status read, the shape the webhook's own refund arm already uses.

**Third: a partial refund on a donation erased the whole donation from a charity's public thermometer.** `fundraiser_totals` sums `amount_cents` filtered on `status = 'paid'` (`20270213_001`), and `donationStatusTransition` flipped `paid -> refunded` on any `charge.refunded`, partial or not — the event ledger had grown a partial branch in `20270521_001`'s companion change and the donation ledger, five lines below it in the same file, had not. A $5 goodwill refund on a $500 donation therefore removed **$500** from the total. The donations table has no `partially_refunded` state and no refunded-amount column, so neither available answer is exact; leaving the status alone overstates by the $5 that came back, flipping it understates by the $495 that did not, and only the first is also **true about the status**. Take the smaller and truer error, log the gap, and let the completing refund still move it on. Recording the amount properly needs a column plus a change to `fundraiser_totals`, which needs a type regeneration this branch was not permitted to run; filed. The scope argument **defaults** to `'full'`, so the call site is load-bearing and a source guard pins that `index.ts` passes it — forgetting to would restore the old behaviour with the lib test still green.

**Fourth, and not fixed on purpose: the host is not the merchant of record, and four places said they were.** `buildCheckoutSessionParams`' comment, `buildAccountCreateParams`' comment, `club_events.md § Money movement`, and `/terms` §6 all state that the destination charge makes the host merchant of record. Naming the settlement merchant is `on_behalf_of`, which no call site sends; Stripe: *"If `on_behalf_of` is omitted, the platform is the business of record for the payment."* The parenthetical in `club_events.md` — "they own refunds, chargebacks, and the tax relationship" — is wrong on each: the platform issues the refunds with its own key, and *"For destination charges, with or without `on_behalf_of`, Stripe debits dispute amounts and fees from your platform account."* This is **not** a typo to patch in silently. Sending `on_behalf_of` moves the settlement currency, the fee structure and the identity on the buyer's card statement, and it contradicts or vindicates a buyer-facing contract in `/terms` §6 depending which way it goes — an owner-and-counsel call, and one that is **required** rather than optional for a host outside the platform's region, which `buildAccountCreateParams` already accepts a `country` for. The comments and the engineering doc now state what the code does; the choice is a ticked-or-not item on a new pre-deploy checklist in `club_events.md § Refunds`.

**Fifth, also filed rather than built: `donations-checkout`'s idempotency key cannot do what it claims.** It is derived from a donation id minted by `crypto.randomUUID()` **inside the request**, so no later invocation can resolve to the same row; the key covers the SDK's retry of one HTTP request and nothing more, where its comment claimed "a retried EF call (same row) reuses the same Stripe session". A donor double-click opens two sessions against two pending rows. The unpaid one lapses to `canceled` on `checkout.session.expired`, but a donor who completes both is charged twice. `events-checkout` avoids this with `resolveHold`; a donation has no seat to hold and repeat giving is legitimate, so imposing the same dedupe is a product decision, not an obvious fix.

**Compliance gates prod, not code.** These functions are gated on owner + CISO + counsel sign-off ([§ 139](#139)) and fail closed at `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` unset (503). The whole path is written and the gate is unchanged; what the sign-off gets is a checklist of five money questions in `club_events.md § Refunds`, not a stub. Two of them cannot be answered from here at all: whether a transfer reversal against a host already paid out should be allowed to leave their account negative (`controller.losses.payments`, `debit_negative_balances`), and the standing hazard that a refund issued from the Stripe **dashboard** reverses nothing unless the operator ticks the box — the webhook processes such a refund identically, so no code change can defend against it and it is a runbook item.

**Verification.** `deno check` over the whole functions tree — the `edge-functions` lane's own `find` expression — passes; the injected-typo probe above fails it by name. `deno test --no-check --allow-read --allow-env supabase/functions/`: **535 passed, 0 failed, 23 ignored**, against § 765's 524/0/23 baseline; the eleven added are five new pure assertions and four source guards across `events-cancel/wiring.test.ts` (new) and `stripe-events-webhook/wiring.test.ts`, plus two donation-transition cases. **Every new test was proved to fail against `HEAD` rather than assumed to.** `git show HEAD:…/events-cancel/lib.ts` into a scratch tree, with the new suite's `partially_refunded` assertion beside it: `AssertionError: Values are not strictly equal` pre-fix, `ok` post-fix, same test file both times. The same method on the donation transition (`AssertionError` pre-fix, `ok` post-fix) and on both wiring guards (3 of 3 failed against `HEAD`'s `events-cancel/index.ts`; the donation-scope guard failed against `HEAD`'s webhook `index.ts` while its three siblings passed, so the file is not failing wholesale). One trap was hit and worked around rather than reported as proof: running the *whole* new `lib.test.ts` against the old `lib.ts` dies at import on the missing `buildRefundParams` export, which fails for the wrong reason — the isolated assertion above is what actually discriminates.

**What this does not claim.** No Stripe key, live or test, was used, requested or written. Every claim about Stripe's behaviour is quoted from its published documentation, not observed: the flow of funds, the `reverse_transfer` / `refund_application_fee` coupling, `on_behalf_of`'s effect on the settlement merchant, and dispute liability on destination charges. The refund round-trip stays **UNVERIFIED** exactly as § 187 left it, and this entry does not change that — it changes what the request will contain when someone finally runs it. Nor is the reversal's own failure mode measured: a connected account already paid out has nothing to reverse against, and whether Stripe permits the negative balance or refuses the refund outright decides whether this change can strand a buyer who is owed money. That is the first item on the checklist and it needs operator `sk_test_` keys, not more reading.

## 770. Four guards that misread their own input: the one filed as failing "in the safe direction" passes a blocking lock on `runs`, and the widening nobody had measured is either 0 steps or 89 depending on which of two readings you take

**Decided 2026-08-28.** Four #789 entries, all describing the same defect: a guard that parses its input with a regex or a naive split and therefore reports confidently about text it never actually read. Three held and were worse than filed in the same direction — each fails in the direction the filing said it could not — and the fourth dissolved on measurement.

**The `;` split is not a cosmetic fragmentation, and it is not safe.** `check_migration_online_safety.mjs` stripped comments with two regexes and split on every `;`. Over the 435 committed migrations that turns **3441 statements into 7366 fragments**: 504 dollar-quoted function bodies carry 3540 semicolons between them, so more than half of what the guard graded was never a statement. The filing said it "fails in the safe direction (a loud false positive)". It does not. `stripSqlComments` ate `--` to end of line before knowing whether it opened a comment, so a statement whose *literal* contains one loses its own terminator and is glued to the next line — and if that line carries `not valid`, the blocking `ADD CONSTRAINT … CHECK` in front of it is vouched for by a constraint it has nothing to do with. That reads a bare `ADD CONSTRAINT` on `runs` as clean, which is precisely the downtime [`migration_locks.md`](../backend/migration_locks.md) exists to prevent and precisely the defect [§ 757](#757) found and fixed one layer up. The shape is **not hypothetical in this repo**: `20270518_001` line 33 carries `-- the ` inside a `comment on index … is '…'` literal. A third variant needs no comment at all — `check (state <> 'not valid')` hands the escape hatch to a statement that does not take it.

Fixed with a lexer rather than a wider regex, because the regex was never the problem: `apps/backend/scripts/sql_lex.mjs` tracks line comments, **nested** block comments (Postgres nests them), `'…'` with `''` and E-string backslash escapes, `"…"` identifiers and `$tag$…$tag$` bodies, splits at genuine top-level semicolons, and **throws on anything unterminated** rather than consuming to end of file — SQL the lexer cannot read is SQL a guard must not report a verdict about, and `scanMigrations` names the file rather than skipping it. Literals are blanked for the scan so their contents cannot vote. Measured over every committed migration **with the cutoff ignored: not one file changes verdict**; 27 change only the text the message quotes.

**The new-Edge-Function detector was wrong 22 times out of 28.** `check_compliance_drift.mjs` decided a function was new from `/^@@.*\+1\b/m`, which matches `@@ -1,3 +1,4 @@` — a comment added to the top of a file that has been there a year — exactly as readily as `@@ -0,0 +1,120 @@`. Filed as a sibling of the first, "on an advisory check", which understates it: measured over the last 2000 commits there are **109 touches of a `functions/*/index.ts`, 6 of them genuinely new, and the detector fired 28 times — 22 false positives, 0 false negatives**. The most recent is `d67ab6fdf`, the commit before this branch's base. git answers this exactly and is now asked (`--diff-filter=A`); a heuristic was never needed. Two more of the § 757 shape went with it: `git diff … -- ${path}` interpolated into a shell string splits a filename containing a space into two pathspecs and reads the diff of neither (now `execFileSync` with an argv array), and two per-file `catch { return '' }` swallows made a git failure read as an empty diff and disabled that file's rules while reporting a pass. **The reason nothing could see any of this is that the file had no exports and no tests**; the decisions are now pure functions over `{changed, added, diffFor}` with `main()` the only part that talks to git, and the suite pins the old detector's premise — the fixture it matched — beside the new verdict.

**The per-file cache-key match gives a green tick to the exact failure it was written for.** `check_toolchain_pins.mjs` compared every `defmt-print` cache key against the *first* install in the file. The filing said the cost was "an extra misleading line" and that per-job matching "needs step-boundary tracking for a shape the repo does not have today". Both halves are wrong. `ci.yml` has held **two** sim jobs since the day it was written (`sim-firmware`, `sim-scenarios`); they agree only by hand. With two jobs pinning different versions and each key correct for its own job, the guard reports the second job's correct key stale — that is the filed line. Mirror the arrangement, so job B's key names job A's version and therefore restores A's binary and lets B's `command -v defmt-print ||` win, and the guard prints **`[OK] cache key matches defmt-print 1.1.0`** over run 31623789083 repeating, the incident the file's own header records. And the step-boundary tracking already exists, tested, in the sibling guard: `parseSteps` in `check_ci_diagnostics.mjs`. The fix is an import and a line offset, not new machinery. A job that caches the binary and never installs it is now named too; an install present but not a valid pin stays silent, so the range error is not buried under a second line about its key.

**The widening nobody had measured is 0 or 89, and the filing described it as one thing.** [§ 764](#764) left rule 2 exempting an unnamed step that runs a non-guard check in a bundled job, and the followup proposed a cheap partial close — "treat an unnamed step whose command invokes any repo-local path as a check" — noting nobody had measured what it would catch. Measured: across the **6** bundled jobs there are **33** `run:` steps, **31** already in the subject, and the exempt set is **exactly 2** — `npm ci` in `parity-types` and the `go install` that fetches actionlint in `workflow-lint`. Both are setup, and § 764's motivating case, actionlint's *invocation*, is already a named diagnosed step. Neither names a repo-local path under any reading, so **the proposed widening newly catches 0**. The other implementation is not equivalent and is the one a reader would reach for, because `isGuardStep` is *also* what decides bundling: widening the predicate takes the bundled set from **6 jobs to 15** and the subject from **31 steps to 127**, of which **89** print no `::error::` today — `cp .env.example`, `npm run check --workspace=apps/web`, every "Parse version from tag" in every release workflow. One filing, two readings, 0 against 89.

So the rule is not widened. What was actually missing is that the blind spot was *invisible*: the guard reported 31 steps diagnosing themselves and said nothing about the ones it never asked, which is why the boundary lived in a paragraph and the followup had to ask someone to re-derive it. It now lists them as `[SKIP]` with the job and the command and counts them in the summary, so the set is on screen at every run. The real-tree test asserts no exempt step invokes anything from this repo — the property the widening was reaching for — without pinning a count that would rot.

**Membership was derived, and the class is not four guards — it is most of them.** § 764's lesson was that a hand-kept list of two became five when membership was derived instead. Applying the same move here: every one of this repo's **17** `check_*.mjs` guards was probed by running its own exported functions against a crafted input. Three were the filing. **Ten more carry a demonstrated misread**, one verified clean (`check_migration_versions.mjs`), and two were not probed. Every one of the ten is **latent** — each guard exits 0 on the committed tree, and each was checked for why:

- **`check_workflow_binaries.mjs`** drops a runner whose binary sits on the next physical line. `run: |` + `npx \` + `totally-unpinned-cli` parses to nothing at all — `binaryOf('\')` returns null and the caller `continue`s without a word, while the file's other invocations keep the anti-vacuity check quiet. The YAML folded scalar (`>-`) is the same hole. No committed workflow puts a binary on a continuation line.
- **`check_lambda_alias_sync.mjs`** takes the first `FUNCTIONS=(…)` in the file, non-globally. A sync script that sets the array per environment (`prod` gets two lambdas, `preview` one) certifies `osrm-proxy` as "synced and deployed" on a branch where nothing repoints it — issue #590 defect 2 verbatim. The committed script has exactly one flat array.
- **`check_ios_native_declarations.mjs`** guards `dartSources.length === 0` as a vacuous pass and has **no equivalent check on `swiftSources`**, whose collector swallows a `readdirSync` failure. Move `CalendarBridge.swift` out of `ios/Runner/` — an ordinary Xcode refactor — and both `NSCalendars…UsageDescription` rules stop enforcing silently.
- **`check_watch_ble_uuids.mjs`** reads UUIDs out of comments on **both** sides, so a stale UUID quoted in `ble.rs`'s module doc and one quoted in a Dart trailing comment can agree with each other while both live declarations have drifted — § 410's off-by-one-row bug passing the guard written to catch it.
- **`check_pgtap_refusal_assertions.mjs`** keys mutation verdicts by description string, so two assertions in one file sharing a description collapse last-writer-wins and a vacuous refusal is scored *killed* on its twin's verdict. Scanned: 0 duplicate descriptions across the committed pgtap tree.
- **`check_root_scripts.mjs`** tokenises shell on `(\S+)`, so it reads `--silent` as a script name, swallows a `;` into a directory name, and fails on a quoted `cd "apps/web"` — three false accusations at once, while missing the genuinely absent directory after the `;`. It also greps for the literal `pnpm -C`: switch to `pnpm --filter`, pnpm's own recommended workspace form, and it reports a pass having verified nothing. That is round 20's failure shape exactly.
- **`check_parity_pair_registry.mjs`** truncates the CLAUDE.md bullet at its first newline — deliberately, to separate it from the watch-port paragraph — so a soft wrap makes every pair named after it invisible to the very check that exists for § 604. The committed bullet is one 70,133-character line.
- **`check_parity_ios_column.mjs`**'s rule 2 needs `iOS` and a legend symbol on the same physical line, so a wrapped fourth statement defeats the check described as catching "the failure that happened". `parity.md` currently soft-wraps nothing.
- **`check_pnpm_overrides.mjs`** enforces a parent-scoped pin (`@sveltejs/kit>cookie`) against every copy of `cookie` in the tree, producing a false accusation about a copy the override never reached. It cannot fire today only because `package.json` happens to declare a bare pin beside the scoped one.
- **`apps/web/scripts/check_constraint_unions.mjs`** strips `--` before knowing whether it is inside a literal, so it can delete a `check (col in (…))` clause it exists to read. Re-parsed through the new lexer: **the same 68 `table.column` → value sets**, and its realistic failure is a loud `no CHECK constraint found` rather than a false pass.

None is fixed here, and that is a scope call rather than a judgement that they are fine. Three of the four filed items were understated in the same direction, so the presumption should be that these are too; each wants its own reproduction, its own pinning test, and — for the four with no test sibling and no lane that would run one — a CI step as well. They are filed individually with the input that produced the wrong output, so the next session reproduces rather than re-derives. What the sweep settles is the shape of the problem: this is not four guards with a parsing bug, it is a guard family written in regex against languages that have quoting, nesting, continuation and scope, and the two that were already **loud** about their blind spots (`check_migration_versions.mjs`, clean; `check_pgtap_refusal_assertions.mjs`, whose `codeMask`/`splitArgs` handle dollar-quoting and nested strings correctly) are the ones that had done the lexing.

**Verification.** `sql_lex` 14 new tests; `check_migration_online_safety` 16 → 20, the four new ones run against the pre-fix module at 0 passed / 4 failed; `check_compliance_drift` 0 → 8, with a side-by-side run of the old and new scripts over one scratch repo showing the old reporting a new Edge Function and the new reporting none; `check_toolchain_pins` 39 → 43, the three new ones at 0 passed / 3 failed pre-fix; `check_ci_diagnostics` 22 → 24, the exempt reporting absent pre-fix. `check_workflow_binaries` 14, `check_parity_pair_registry` 18, `tsconfig_coverage` 5 unchanged. `npm run check:script-types` clean, `actionlint -shellcheck= -pyflakes=` clean, all four guards exit 0 against the committed tree.

## 771. The seventh catalogue was never a seventh chunk, every non-English reader downloads two of them, and the emitted files a pattern rule would have had to classify carry no names at all
