It is the operator worklist: `select * from event_orders where status = 'refund_failed'`. Stripe's own instruction for a failed refund is to "arrange an alternative way to provide your customer with a refund", which is a human action on a payout rail this tier does not automate, so the state exists to be *queried*, not resolved by another webhook.

**The seat is deliberately not restored.** Re-seating would either oversell the class or take a seat back off someone who has already been told they are in, and it answers a question nobody asked: the buyer cancelled, they want their money, and a reinstated registration is not that. A wiring guard asserts the reversal handlers never write `event_attendees` and never `.delete()`.

**Reachable only from `refunded`, which is the asymmetry worth the paragraph.** `partially_refunded` is a **seat-bearing** status on both `enforce_paid_order_for_priced_event` and the buyer-cancel RLS policy (migration `20270522_001`), so moving a partly-refunded order out of it on a failure would take the roster entry and the cancel affordance away from a buyer who is still attending and lost nothing — the `20270522_001` bug, reintroduced from the other side. On donations the same arm is refused for a second reason: `fundraiser_totals` nets `amount_cents - refunded_cents` over the two live statuses, so sending a partly-refunded donation to the excluded `refund_failed` would drop the **whole** donation off the charity's total including the part that was never refunded, and the only alternative — subtracting this instalment from `refunded_cents` — is arithmetic on a running total, which is exactly what § 769 avoided so an at-least-once redelivery cannot double-apply. A failed partial refund is logged for reconciliation and the status stands. Understating what was raised is the smaller, safe lie.

**`refund_failed` is terminal against everything except the refund actually landing.** `refund_failed + charge.refunded (full) -> refunded`: somebody paid the buyer back another way and it worked, and a ledger stuck denying a refund that has happened is the same defect pointing the other way. A **partial** `charge.refunded` returns null instead, because `partially_refunded` would resurrect a seat-bearing status for an order with no attendee row left to bear it. Replay safety needs nothing new: the CAS matches the status that was read, so the second delivery reads `refund_failed` and the table returns null.

**What was deliberately not built.** No re-seat, no waitlist bump, no automated retry refund, and no `refund_failed_at` column — `refunded_at` already carries when the refund was recorded and the `console.error` carries the Refund id and `failure_reason`, which is the same operator signal shape the oversold branch beside it already uses. No pgtap: the local Supabase stack is shared across worktrees and a `db reset` would clobber another session's schema, so writing pgtap I could not run would be shipping an unexecuted spec. The CHECK widening is instead covered by `check_constraint_unions.mjs` (which reads the migration and the TS union and fails on drift in either direction) and by CI's stack start, and the migration was applied and rolled back against the live local database to confirm both constraints take the new value.

**Verification.** `deno test --no-check --allow-read --allow-env supabase/functions/` — **616 passed, 0 failed, 23 ignored** (581 before this change and § 788's round; 20 new cases here across `lib.test.ts` and `wiring.test.ts`). `deno check` over all 55 modules exits 0, and the new `AssertAssignable<Stripe.Refund, RefundSource>` was proved live by retyping `status` to `number` and watching TS2344 name both types — which also proves the SDK declarations still bind rather than collapsing to `any` (§ 765). `check_edge_function_test_vacuity.mjs`: **616 killed, 0 survived**, exemption list still empty. Five targeted mutations were run to prove the new assertions reach the new code rather than riding the blanket operator: admitting `succeeded` into the reversed set kills 2, letting `partially_refunded` reverse kills 2, deleting the dispatcher's `refundReversed` gate kills 1, adding a seat delete to the reversal handler kills 1, and typo'ing `refund.failed` kills 3. `check_migration_versions.mjs`, `check_migration_online_safety.mjs` and `check_constraint_unions.mjs` all pass.

## 790. The persisted grouping key was four hand-written copies of an expression whose meaning is the database's locale provider's opinion — and the half of the filing that was wrong was wrong in the safe direction

The `#789` sweep filed the exercise-name key as "seven live SQL functions" disagreeing with two clients in two ways. The count is **four**, by replay: `gym_exercise_records` (`20261224_001`), `gym_exercise_set_history` and `gym_exercise_set_history_batch` (both last written by `20270525_001`), and `gym_workout_summaries` (`20270510_001`). Three of the six migrations the filing names — `20261225_001`, `20261231_001`, `20270323_001` — hold definitions a later `create function` replaced, which is the reading error § 787 exists to record. A fifth function, `gym_exercise_names`, does carry a bare `btrim` but is deliberately case- and spelling-preserving (it feeds the autocomplete datalist, not the grouping), so it is not in this class and was left alone.

**Gap (a) held exactly as filed.** `btrim(text)` with no second argument strips U+0020 and nothing else, so a name carrying any other edge whitespace kept it through the trim and the `\s+` pass then converted it into a leading or trailing SPACE. Measured: `<TAB>Bench Press` normalised to `" bench press"` server-side and `"bench press"` on both clients.

**Gap (b) was wrong on three of the four characters it named, and wrong in the direction that made the filing understate the problem.** It claimed Postgres `\s` "excludes U+00A0, U+202F, U+2007 and U+FEFF under every common ctype". Measured against the live stack — PostgreSQL 17.6, `datlocprovider = 'i'`, ICU `en-US` — `\s` **matches** U+00A0, U+2007 and U+202F. Only U+FEFF is genuinely excluded, and U+FEFF is not Unicode `White_Space` at all. The filing also missed that ICU's `\s` matches U+001C–U+001F, which neither client folds.

**What is actually wrong is one layer deeper than either gap, and neither gap describes it.** `\s` is `[[:space:]]`, and past ASCII its membership is decided by the collation, not by Unicode. The same expression, on the same database, answers differently depending on which collation the argument carries: `chr(160) ~ '\s'` is `true` under the database default and `false` under `collate "en_US.utf8"`. So the four copies did not merely disagree with the clients — **they disagreed with themselves across deployments**, and a persisted grouping key whose value is a function of the server's locale provider is not a key. That is the finding that decides the fix: the canonical class is written by explicit code point, so no provider can move it, and `public.normalise_exercise_name` (migration `20270623000001`) is that class written once for the SQL rail with the four RPCs calling it.

**The anchor is the CLIENT definition, even though SQL is the rail that persists.** The brief suggested SQL as the natural anchor because `exercise_key` is stored — but nothing in SQL ever *writes* that column. Both persisted keys (`gym_routine_exercises.exercise_key`, `exercises.name_key`) are stamped client-side by `normaliseExerciseName`, and the SQL functions only re-derive a key from `gym_sets.exercise_name` at read time. The persisting rail is therefore the clients, and theirs is also the correct definition: Unicode `White_Space` plus U+FEFF, trimmed properly. Moving SQL onto it changed no client behaviour at all — the two client edits are the same class respelled from `\t\n\v\f\r` to `U+0009-U+000D` so one parser can read all three rails.

**No backfill was needed, and one shipped anyway.** Locally: 4 `gym_routine_exercises` rows and 43 `exercises` rows, **0 diverged** from the canonical derivation. That is what the writers predict — every call site stamps `normaliseExerciseName(<the name it stores>)`, and the clone RPCs copy an existing pair rather than deriving a new one — and the client rule is unchanged by this migration, so a conforming client's key already equals the canonical value. But "every client build that ever wrote a row conformed" is a claim about history that a migration cannot verify, and a wrong grouping key silently splits a lifter's history rather than failing, so the migration carries an idempotent batched pass whose predicate matches only rows that already disagree. On a clean database it updates nothing.

**The invariant is the database's now.** Two CHECK constraints (`gym_routine_exercises_exercise_key_canonical`, `exercises_name_key_canonical`) assert the stored key equals `normalise_exercise_name(<its own name>)`, added `NOT VALID` and validated in a second pass per `migration_locks.md`. Neither table is in the guard's high-volume set, so the online form is ceremony rather than safety here — it costs nothing and is the house pattern. The constraints are safe against already-shipped clients precisely because the client rule did not move.

**The two-sided pin was ASCII-only, which is why nothing saw this for the life of the key.** `gym_workout_summaries.test.ts` and `gym_workout_summaries_test.sql` run one fixture through the TS `RunningPrTracker` and through the RPC, and every name in it was plain ASCII. Two surgical edits inside `w2` — whose expected answer stays "no PR, one exercise" — fix that without moving an expected value, an ordering or a plan count: its Bench set is tab-prefixed, and its whitespace-only name is a TAB rather than a space. Under the old rule the first made `w2` a brand-new exercise on the SQL side (and a first sighting is a PR on all three metrics, so `w2` joined that side's `is_pr` set and not the TS side's), and the second made `w2`'s `exercise_count` read 2 server-side against 1 in TS.

**Verification, and the vacuity check that shaped the new suite.** `normalise_exercise_name_test.sql` is 15 assertions; its first draft had two that did not discriminate on an ICU database (NBSP folds there under the old rule too), so the fixture was rebuilt around the tab and U+FEFF cases, which split the bucket under **both** providers. Replaying the old expression against the final fixture inside a rolled-back transaction moves five of the six: `session_count` 1 against the expected 4, distinct exercises 3 against 1, `gym_exercise_set_history` 2 rows against 4, `normalised_name` `" bench press"` against `"bench press"`, and `w4.is_pr` **true** against the expected false — the false PR badge, demonstrated. The sixth is the deliberate positive control (`w2` is a genuine 60→80 kg jump and still reads as a PR), so the false-expectations cannot be passing because everything is false. Both client suites go 21 → 22 tests in lockstep. The registry entry is mutation-verified: dropping U+200A from the web class alone makes `check_shared_constants.mjs` name the code point and both rails that disagree.

**The constraint's own grant was the one thing this change got wrong, and it was caught by testing the write rather than by reading the DDL.** A CHECK constraint that names a function ACL-checks that function against the role performing the INSERT — the same trap § 746 records one layer over, inside a SECURITY INVOKER body. Granted to `authenticated` alone (which is what the four RPCs need), every **service_role** write to `gym_routine_exercises` or `exercises` failed with `42501 permission denied for function normalise_exercise_name`, and service_role is exactly how the Playwright gym fixtures insert their routines. The grant list for a function behind a CHECK is decided by who WRITES the table, not by who calls the RPCs that read it. `anon` stays off it: RLS lets it write neither table, and a CHECK is only ever evaluated on a write. Two pgtap assertions now pin the privilege set and the service_role insert itself, so the omission cannot return silently.

**One thing measured and deliberately not changed.** `lower()` is collation-dependent too, and the key has always used it. Postgres `lower(U+0130)` on this stack returns `i` + U+0307, which is exactly what JS and Dart `toLowerCase()` return, so the one case worth checking agrees. The whitespace half is now provider-independent; the case-folding half is not, and making it so would mean not using `lower()` at all. Filed rather than done.

**Found on the integration branch, and it is § 781's shape one object class over.**
The migration's grant block revoked EXECUTE `from public` and named `anon` only in a
comment saying it was "deliberately absent". It was not absent: on a fresh `db reset`
`pg_proc.proacl` carried `anon=X`. Supabase ships an `alter default privileges` for the
`postgres` role in schema `public` granting EXECUTE on every new function to `anon`,
`authenticated` and `service_role`, so a function created by a migration arrives with an
**explicit** anon grant, and revoking PUBLIC leaves it standing — exactly the reason
§ 781 gave for a column-level `revoke select` being a no-op while the role holds the
table-level grant. The 31 migrations that already write `from public, anon` are the
house form, and this one now matches them. `normalise_exercise_name_test.sql`'s
fourteenth assertion is what caught it, on the integrated tree rather than on the
branch, because the branch had not been reset against the merged migration set.

**The class is 83 functions wide and is filed, not fixed here.** Measured against the
live catalog: of the 242 functions in `public`, 186 carry `anon=X`, and **83 of those
appear in a migration that explicitly revoked them `from public`** — `claim_next_job`,
`block_user`, `coach_roster_summary`, `enforce_create_rate_limit` and
`admin_unhide_target` among them. Each of those revokes states an intent that has never
held. Whether any is reachable in a way that matters depends on that function's own
`auth.uid()` check and on RLS beneath it, so closing it is 83 separate judgements plus
the guard that would keep them — a round of its own, not a line in this one.

## 791. The CHECK-constraint guard read one file of one client: 41 columns of 67, no Dart at all, and a `>=` that 26 uncovered columns satisfied

**Decided 2026-08-29.** [§ 787](#787) built the sibling registry for constants with more than one home and recorded that this guard's `PAIRS` array "covered 34 of 68". Both halves of that sentence needed re-measuring, and both were close but not right.

**The counts, filed against measured.** The filing said `check_constraint_unions.mjs` covers **41 of 68** set-shaped CHECK columns. 41 is exact — the array held 41 entries and 41 distinct `table.column` keys. 68 is the raw replay total and **67 is the live one**: `runs.kind` was defined by `20261204_001` and its column dropped by `20261206_001`, so replaying every migration leaves a phantom the filing itself noticed one clause later ("a CHECK on a column later DROPPED leaves a phantom entry … harmless only because its pair was deleted from `PAIRS` by hand"). A coverage rule counting it would demand a registry entry for a column no client can ever write, so the guard now reads the generated `database.types.ts` for the live column set and excludes phantoms — and *fails* when the registry names one, which is what "by hand" was standing in for. The filing said **eleven** client unions live outside `types.ts`; measured, **37 declarations across 23 files** do. It said **nineteen** Dart enums / const lists enumerate a CHECK-constrained set, and its own enumeration lists twenty; measured, **29** do — it missed `nutrition_totals.dart`'s `mealSlots`, `run_stats.dart`'s `_pbBracketLabels`, `export_job.dart`'s `_statusTokens`, `recurrence.dart`'s `RecurrenceFreq`, `recap_screen.dart`'s `RecapPeriod`, `preferences.dart`'s `DistanceUnit`, and all three of `routine_builder_sheet.dart`'s option lists. The registry now holds **67 columns and 121 client rails — 87 web, 34 Dart — across 46 files**.

**The registry is keyed on the column, not on a union name, and that is the change.** `{ tableColumn, tsUnion }` could only ever describe one client rail, which is why widening it to a second file was not an edit but a redesign. An entry is now `{ tableColumn, clients: [...] }`, and a rail declares its **shape** rather than having one inferred: a TS union, a const string array, an object-key map, a record list plus the field to read, or a Dart enum read as snake_case (`activityCount` → `activity_count`). Five shapes because five shapes exist in the tree — `personal_records.distance` is enumerated *only* as three `Record<string, …>` maps and two Dart `<String, …>` maps, and `route_markers.kind` only as a list of specs. A `Record<Union, X>` icon or label map is deliberately **not** registered: TypeScript already makes it exhaustive, and registering the compiler's own work would be noise. That asymmetry is the reason the Dart half matters most — Dart has no analogue, so every Dart list is unguarded by construction.

**Coverage is now an obligation, enforced in the guard rather than in a doc.** A live set-shaped CHECK column with no entry fails. An entry naming a column `database.types.ts` no longer has fails. A column registered twice fails. A column that no client enumerates is registered with an empty `clients` list **and a `note` saying why** — an entry with neither fails, so "nobody spells this one out" is recorded as a decision instead of read as an oversight. **15 of the 67 are that shape**: the queue vocabulary the Go worker drains, the per-stage erasure results only the delete-account SQL writes, the platform each client stamps for itself, and four whose values are spelled as *inline* unions on a row type or a function parameter with no name to register.

**The two tolerated deltas are declared per rail and checked for staleness.** `data_export_jobs.status` carries `none` and `stalled` on all four of its rails — the first means "no job on record", the second "running past its own deadline"; the column can hold neither. Both are declared as `allowExtra`, and the guard fails if the client ever drops one (a stale exemption silently widens the guard) or if the CHECK ever *admits* one (the exemption is then a lie). `allowMissing` is the mirror for a deliberately narrower client. Nothing is exempted wholesale: a THIRD client-only status still fails.

**No drift was found, and that is the honest result rather than a disappointing one.** Every one of the 121 rails agrees with its CHECK today, which is what the filing predicted ("All agree with their CHECK today"). The near-match sweep that produced the registry also surfaced nine declarations that *look* like a drifted copy and are not — `pace_segments.ts`'s `ActivityKind` omits `stroller`, `age_grade.ts`'s `AgeGradeSex` and `segments.ts`'s `SegmentGenderFilter` omit `prefer_not_to_say`, `checkpoint_projection`'s `RunnerStatus` trades `dns` for `racing`, three surface/kind *filters* add an `any`/`all` sentinel. None is a copy of the column's vocabulary; each is a narrower or wider concept that happens to overlap, and registering them would have manufactured drift where there is none.

**The boundary with § 787's registry is the rails, not the subject.** `check_shared_constants.mjs` also carries a `runs.source` entry, and it is not a duplicate: it compares the column's CHECK against the SQL functions that *filter* on it, where this guard compares the same CHECK against the client declarations that *enumerate* it. Nothing is registered twice, and the ci.yml comment between the two steps now says which is which — a class split across two registries with no stated seam is the defect § 787 recorded, and it applies to its own sibling.

**Two defects in the guard's own first draft, both found by running it rather than by reasoning about it.** The extractor missed `static const _wearAreas = [...]` (a Dart class member — the declaration keyword is not first) and reported `ReportDialog.svelte`'s `REASONS` as absent, because its inline record type annotation `{ value: ReportReason; label: MessageKey }[]` carries `;` field separators and the walk to the `=` stopped at the first one. Both would have read as "this vocabulary was deleted" rather than as a guard bug, which is the failure mode § 770 and § 774 catalogued. **A third was found by a unit test written for it**: `topLevelChunks` skips comments when deciding where to *split*, but the chunk it returns still contains them, so a list carrying `// 'ghost' was removed` above its last entry read `ghost` as a live member **and lost the entry underneath it** — a guard that both invents a value the CHECK has never admitted and reports a real one as absent. Comments are now blanked inside each extracted region, and never over a whole file: a `//` inside a regex literal is not a comment and this walker cannot tell.

**A fourth failure mode was closed before it could fire.** The registry keys on a declaration *name*, and `personal_records.distance`'s two web rails were locals called `labels` and `order` inside a ten-thousand-line `data.ts`. A future `const order` added anywhere above them would have made the guard read the wrong literal and pass vacuously. `findInitializers` now returns every match and the extractor **throws on more than one**, and the two locals are renamed `PR_BRACKET_LABELS` / `PR_BRACKET_ORDER` so the registry entry is unambiguous by construction rather than by luck.

**Dart rails name `mobile_android` only, and the suite pins the premise instead of trusting it.** `lib/` is byte-identical to `mobile_ios` ([§ 39](#39)), so a second path per rail would be a copy of a copy — but a test now asserts every registered Dart file has a byte-identical iOS twin, so the day that invariant breaks this guard says so rather than certifying half a client.

**Verification.** The guard exits 0 over the committed tree with **136 OK lines** (121 rails + 15 no-client columns). Its suite is **33 cases, all passing**, and its coverage case asserts `registry == live columns` as an ordered equality — the `checks.size >= PAIRS.length` it replaces is satisfied by a registry covering 41 of 67, and was. Proved by mutation, fourteen of them, each reverted: a value added to a TS union, removed from a const array, removed from an object-key map, renamed in a record list, added to a Dart enum, removed from a Dart const list, removed from a Dart key map, renamed in a Dart record list — all eight caught, naming the file and the declaration. Widening `routes.surface` in its migration fails **all three** of its rails including the Dart one, which is the case the filing says nothing caught. A new `check (brand in (…))` on a live column fails as unregistered; a registered declaration renamed fails as missing; a stale `allowExtra` fails as stale; registering `runs.kind` fails as a dropped column; an empty `clients` with no note fails; a column registered twice fails; a second declaration of a registered name fails as ambiguous. `node --test apps/web/scripts/*.test.mjs` 76 passed, `node --test scripts/*.test.mjs` 473 passed, `tsc -p apps/web/tsconfig.node.json` clean, and the full web unit suite `tsx --test 'src/**/*.test.ts'` 4335 passed after the `data.ts` rename. No migration was written and no Supabase stack was started.

## 792. Four inputs could hand the runner a raw postgres error, and the class needed a containment guard rather than an equality one

**Decided 2026-08-29.** [§ 787](#787) built `check_shared_constants.mjs` for a value with more than one home where one home is not TypeScript, and filed three items it did not close. This entry closes them. The three filings named eight numbers between them; **six were right, two were not, and the two wrong ones were both in the direction of understating the defect.**

**What was measured.** Every bound was resolved by replaying all 441 migrations rather than by reading the migration each filing cited — the discipline [§ 787](#787) records, after a re-issued function body silently dropped a value for three months. `body_metrics.weight_kg > 0 and <= 500`, `gym_routine_sets.target_percent_1rm > 0 and <= 200`, `recipes.servings >= 1`, `club_posts.body <= 4096`, `events.description <= 2000`, `training_plans.name <= 120` and `user_profiles.parkrun_number <= 32` are all exactly as filed, each defined once and never re-issued. The eleven `enforce_create_rate_limit` call sites carry exactly the eleven ceilings the filing lists, and the eleven buckets are one-to-one with them. **Two corrections.** There is no `checkpoint_health` table — the weigh-in column is `checkpoint_crossings.body_weight_kg`, `between 20 and 400`, and `checkpoint_health` is the name of a *retention function*. And `user_profiles.parkrun_number` is not "30 on web": the web field carries **no cap at all**, so the one rail the filing scored as merely conservative was the rail with a reachable `23514`. The `maxlength="30"` it found on that page belongs to the runner handle, a different column.

**Four reachable raw errors, not one.** The filing named one; sweeping the class found four, and dropped one it had named. (1) **Settings › Preferences**, both fields. `min`/`max` on those inputs are decorative — the card saves from a button's `onclick`, not a form submit, so the browser's constraint validation never runs, which is the trap issue #677 already hit in the onboarding wizard and which made the height field's existing `max="300"` worth nothing. A typed 600 kg *or* 500 cm went straight to a `23514`. The filing's other half — that `min="0"` admits exactly 0 against a `> 0` CHECK — is **not** reachable there: the save path already coerces a non-positive value to null. (2) **The race-board weigh-in**, on both platforms, with no ceiling at all against a 20..400 column; and its web label read the unit off the **distance** preference while `parseWeight` read it off the **weight** preference, so a km/lbs runner was told "kg" and parsed as lbs. (3) **Recipe servings on mobile**, `parseTypedDecimal(...) ?? 1`, where a typed `0` is `0.0` and not null — the column's floor is 1. The web twin was already clamped. (4) **The parkrun number on web**, uncapped against 32. Meanwhile `gym_routine_sets.target_percent_1rm`, which the filing lists as "unbounded on the client", **has no client input surface at all** — no editor on either platform writes it, so there is nothing to bound.

**`numeric(p, s)` is the same defect wearing a different SQLSTATE.** `recipes.servings` has a floor in its CHECK and no ceiling, so the filing reads as if only the low end is reachable. But the column is `numeric(5,1)`, and a mistyped `9` is a `22003` rather than a `23514` — equally raw, equally unactionable. The guard therefore treats the precision declaration as a bound like any other, and a client with no ceiling against a column that has one from either source fails.

**The registry is the client module, not a list in the guard.** `core/column_limits.ts` and `column_limits.dart` are keyed by `<table>.<column>`, so the key *is* the locator: the guard splits it, resolves that column's live CHECKs by replay, intersects them with the precision ceiling, and proves the client's bound sits inside. Nothing in `check_shared_constants.mjs` holds a copy of any number, which is the property § 787 states about itself and the reason the entry could not simply be a fourth row in `REGISTRY` — **that comparison asks whether every home says the same thing, and this one is not symmetric.** A client capped below its column is conservative and correct; capped above, or not capped, it is the defect. So the bounds check is a second registry with a containment comparison, and the two clients are still compared to each other for equality, because one number per field is the other half of the contract.

**One number per field, for the four caps that had three.** `club_posts.body` (1200 on four surfaces, 4096 in the column), `events.description` (1000 vs 2000) and `training_plans.name` (80 vs 120) are **deliberately** stricter and stay where they are: a club post is a notice board, a plan name is a header, and nothing suggests a runner has wanted more. What changes is that each is now written once instead of at nine call sites, and the containment is checked. `user_profiles.parkrun_number` is the one that moves. Its two rails held 32 / (none) / 20, and 20 is below every number involved — a 25-character id typed fine on the web and was silently truncated on the phone. Both rails are now the column's own 32: a parkrun athlete id is `A` plus digits and approaches neither bound, so there is no product reason to be stricter, and being stricter is what broke it.

**A weight bound has to be converted, and the rounding is directional.** The body-weight field is typed in the reader's unit and stored in kilograms, so a range stated in kg names numbers the field never shows. `weightBoundsIn` / `WeightFormat.boundsIn` convert it, rounding the floor **up** and the ceiling **down**: 20 kg is 44.09 lb, and a displayed floor of 44 would advertise a value (19.96 kg) that the real kilogram gate then refuses. Both suites pin exactly that. The onboarding wizard's hard-coded 44 / 550 — which were cosmetic, because its own gate is in kilograms — now come from the same call.

**The rate-limit ceilings gain a second home worth reading.** They had three: the SQL call site, two client doc comments, and prose in `api_database.md`. Nothing compared them, and a comment nothing reads is what the filing was about. So the two comments no longer state the numbers, and `api_database.md` gains a **bucket table** the guard parses — anchored on the backticked bucket name, so it reads the row it means rather than the third number on a line. The guard also refuses something the prose could not express: **one bucket debited with two different ceilings**, which `check_rate_limit` cannot represent because it keys the counter by bucket alone. That is not hypothetical — `create_report` has had four call sites over time and `clone_gym_routine_template` two; today each bucket resolves to one live site, and the guard is what keeps it that way.

**Verification.** `node scripts/check_shared_constants.mjs` reports 7 registered constants and 29 checks, green. Its suite is 44 tests, 15 of them new, and the guard is proved by mutation in eight directions: a cap raised above its CHECK, a range leaving the CHECK at the top, the same at the exclusive bottom, the two clients disagreeing on one field, a field bounded on one client only, a client module the extractor can no longer read (reported as blindness, not agreement), a doc row stating a ceiling the SQL does not enforce, and a bucket the SQL raises that the table omits. Each fails with the field named; each passes again when reverted. Web: 4,323 `tsx --test` cases pass, `svelte-check` reports 0 errors over 2,441 files, `tsc -p tsconfig.scripts.json` exits 0, and a new Playwright case pins the preferences gate. Mobile: `column_limits_test.dart` (9), `settings_body_metrics_screen_test.dart` (11, two new — one pinning the lbs range as 44.1..551.1), `checkpoint_checkin_screen_test.dart` and `nutrition_screen_test.dart` all pass; `dart analyze` adds no warning or error; `diff -r` is clean between the twins. `nutrition/recipes.spec.ts` fails on this branch and on `main` alike, for an unrelated reason filed below: the recipe is built from *today's* food log, and whether a seed row falls in the browser's UTC "today" depends on the hour the suite is run.

**CodeQL found two high alerts in this round's own new guards, and both were real.**
`findInitializers` escaped `$` and nothing else, so any other metacharacter reaching the
pattern changed what the guard matched rather than failing — a `.` matches any character
and would certify the wrong list. It now refuses a non-identifier outright and escapes
the whole set anyway. And `rustVectors`' `(?:[0-9a-fA-F]+|\\\s*)+` nested two
quantifiers over overlapping input: **measured at 703 ms for a 24-character
unterminated hex run**, which is minutes by 32 characters and a hung CI job on any Rust
file the guard could not parse. The branches are now disjoint on their first character,
so the match is linear and the language is unchanged. Both are pinned by tests. Neither
ships to a user — these are build-time guards reading repo files — but a guard that can
hang CI or silently match the wrong declaration is the same class of defect the guards
exist to catch, and § 786 and § 788 both record that proving a guard finds its own
first-draft bugs.

## 793. The watch's golden wire vectors were pinned twice and compared never, and the two docs that read as contracts about the radio were both wrong

**Decided 2026-08-29.** [§ 787](#787)'s shared-constant sweep filed two watch-rail items. Both were real; both were also wrong about their own scope, in the direction that mattered.

**The filing said five wire formats. There are six, and the one it left out is the only one that carries a run.** `CRS1` / `WKT1` / `RBK1` / `SCR1` / `SET1` are the phone→watch pushes; `TRK1` is the run blob that goes the other way, pinned by three firmware goldens and five phone ones, and it is the format a divergence actually costs a finished run. **The filing also said "every golden vector exists twice". One did not**: `settings.rs`'s `golden_vector_auto_lap_only` had no phone counterpart at all. v7 and v8 shipped without single-field vectors on the phone rail, so both `flags3` fields were pinned there only inside the 196-byte all-fields golden, where a layout error hides behind its neighbours' offsets. It has one now, and the two rails agree.

**Measured before anything was built: the rails agree today, all seventeen pairs of them.** No live divergence. That is the finding a guard is for — the pins were correct and nothing had checked, which is the state § 641's `turn_cues` was in right up until it wasn't.

**The enforcement is a script, and the reason is that no suite can see both rails.** `cargo test` runs from `apps/custom_watch` against a `no_std` crate and cannot open a Dart file; `flutter test` runs from `apps/mobile_android` and cannot open a Rust one; the Swift, Kotlin and Monkey C rails in the same filing can read neither. A committed fixture both suites loaded would cross those boundaries but be **weaker**, not stronger: two rails each recomputing a vector from their own encoder and a third party comparing the two pins is two independent computations plus an equality, where a fixture is one number both rails read back. So `scripts/check_watch_wire_vectors.mjs` parses the vector out of both sources and compares — the same shape `check_watch_ble_uuids.mjs` already has, for the same reason (§ 410 / § 416), wired into a `watch-wire-vectors` job in the `CI gate` aggregator's `needs:` list.

**Both registries are closed, because an open one is the § 641 defect wearing a registry's clothes.** Every `#[test] fn *golden*` under `apps/custom_watch` must be a registered pair or carry a written reason for having no phone counterpart — and a "rail-local" vector whose bytes turn up on the phone rail anyway is a hard error, since that is the registry lying. The phone sweep runs the same rule in reverse, over the test files that carry one of the magics **the firmware itself declares** (parsed out of the `*_MAGIC: [u8; 4] = *b"…"` constants, so a seventh format drags its own test file in without anyone widening a list). A phone vector that is neither registered nor **byte-identical to one that is** fails: that is what holds `sim_watch_screen_test.dart`'s third copy of the run blob to the registered one without a row of its own.

**A second registry covers the values restated on more than one rail, which is the rest of the same filing.** The five wire versions and six frame caps (Rust ↔ Dart); the Apple-Watch 512-point route budget across `apple_watch_route_bridge.dart` ↔ `ArmedRoute.swift` ↔ `WatchIngestBridge.swift`, which had three prose "must match" cross-references and no test at all; the 40 m / 20 m off-route hysteresis across Rust, Dart, Swift and Kotlin; and the Minetti fit plus its clamp, flat cost and segment window across Rust, Dart, TypeScript and Monkey C. The re-arm row is the fussy one and deliberately so: three rails **derive** it as half the threshold and Wear OS writes `20` out, so the reader resolves the derivation and **refuses a rail that has stopped deriving** rather than reading a fresh literal as agreement. `ble.rs`'s `LINK_SERVICE_UUID: u128` — the third copy of the service UUID, the one the scan response advertises, whose own comment asked for byte-for-byte equality — went into `check_watch_ble_uuids.mjs` instead, where the other two copies already live; its grouping is ignored, because the literal's underscores landing on the dash positions is a coincidence rather than a rule.

**Proved by mutation, eight ways.** A firmware-only `SETTINGS_VERSION` bump, a one-byte nudge of the firmware `CRS1` golden, a phone-only nudge of the new auto-lap golden, a phone-only route budget, a Wear-OS-only off-route threshold, a sign flip on one Minetti coefficient in the Garmin field, a new firmware golden nobody registered, and a drifted third copy of the run blob: each fails, and the tree passes. **The guard's own unit tests caught a defect in its first draft** — a prose assert message made of nothing but hex letters and spaces (`"deadbeef cafe decade"`) read as a byte vector, so whitespace is now accepted only immediately after a `\` line continuation. A related limitation shaped the sweep rather than being papered over: `comment_strip.mjs` does not track Dart `${…}` interpolation, so three importer tests cannot be blanked at all. None of them mentions a magic, so none is swept — and a file that **does** mention one and still cannot be lexed is a hard error, never a skip, on the rule `sql_lex.mjs` already states: a guard must not report a verdict about source it could not read.

**The doc filing was right twice and understated both times.** `firmware.md` said the GATT service carries "seven" characteristics; `ble.rs` declares nine (`roadbook` and `push_status`). The same stale seven was in four more places the filing did not name — `roadmap.md`, `privacy.md` (where it is a security claim), `quality_standards.md` and `local_testing.md`. `watch_settings.dart`'s comment said "the firmware still decodes v1-v7 frames"; `decode` accepts **v3 through v8**, so the sentence was wrong at both ends — v1 and v2 have been refused since the CRC became mandatory, and v8 is the version the phone itself stamps. Two more of the class turned up in `firmware.md` alone: it said the watch "records runs locally to LittleFS", when tier 1 has no filesystem at all (four 4 KiB internal-flash slots, 253 records), and it named `off_route_alert.dart` as the phone-side twin of the 40 m / 20 m thresholds — that module is the *escalation to a trusted contact* and deliberately fires at 75 m after 90 s, so a reader following the reference would have found a different number and no way to know which was the contract. The real twin is `run_screen.dart`'s `_offRouteThresholdMetres`, and it is now one of the four rails the guard compares. The class sweep found four more the filing did not: `local_testing.md` had BTN3 walking "seven rows" of the §351 settings menu against `MENU_ITEMS = 8`; `roadmap.md` had the `SET1` v7 row saying "v1–v6 still decode" and three stale counts against a `Page` enum that is now 41 built-ins plus four composed seats and a `face::Metric` catalogue that is now 40; and `settings_menu.rs` priced the per-page mask at "33 checkboxes" against 45 pages, which is now written count-free so it cannot rot again. `tier1_log.md`'s § 374 entry claimed `decode` accepts "v1–v7", and that one was wrong the day it was written — v1 and v2 had been withdrawn at § 403, before v7 landed — so it carries a bracketed correction rather than a rewrite. The remaining counts in `tier1_log.md` and in § 377's own ADR text are left alone: those were true when they were written, and this log rewrites no history.

**Verification.** `node scripts/check_watch_wire_vectors.mjs` exits **0** over 38 lines — 17 vector pairs compared byte-for-byte, the third copy of the run blob held to one of them, and 20 constant rows agreeing across 2, 3 or 4 rails — and its 21 unit tests pass. `node scripts/check_watch_ble_uuids.mjs` exits 0 on **11** UUIDs (10 pairs plus the advertised u128) with its suite at 20 → **24** tests; `comment_strip.test.mjs` still passes its 9. `cargo test --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu -p watch_core`: **2349** lib tests plus the property suites, 0 failed. `flutter test test/watch_settings_test.dart`: **38** passing, unchanged in count — the auto-lap golden is a new expectation inside the existing rung test, not a new case — and `dart analyze` over the two changed Dart files reports only the three pre-existing package-import infos. `diff -r` is clean on both twin trees. `tsc -p tsconfig.scripts.json` exits 0 over the two new `.mjs` files and `tsconfig_coverage.test.mjs` still passes, so they are inside a tsc program. `actionlint` is clean and `check_ci_diagnostics.mjs` accepts the new `watch-wire-vectors` job — both of its steps carry their own `::error::`, because a job running a second guard is a bundled one by that fact — and reports `ci-gate` waiting on all **29**. `check_shared_constants.mjs` and `check_parity_pair_registry.mjs` are untouched and still pass. **No hardware and no simulator ran**, so nothing here moves any claim past *host-tested* on `quality_standards.md`'s ladder: the guard proves the two encoders agree about bytes, not that either has ever driven a radio.

## 794. The page ring was drawn by hand beside the chain it draws, and it had been wrong since § 376

**Decided 2026-08-30.** [§ 793](#793)'s doc sweep found this and [#829](https://github.com/Absence0760/project-running/pull/829) built the guard for it; that PR turned out to be a second, independent integration of round 25 and was closed as superseded by [#828](https://github.com/Absence0760/project-running/pull/828), which is on `main`. Everything else in it exists on `main` already under different filenames. This one thing does not, and it is the half worth keeping, because it is the only piece of round 25 that caught a live defect nothing else was watching.

**`docs/custom_watch/navigation.md`'s page-cycle diagram is `page.rs`'s own `next()` chain drawn out by hand, and the two had disagreed since the storm page landed.** The drawn ring stepped `SUN --> WPT`; the firmware steps `SUN --> BARO --> WPT`. `BARO` — [§ 376](#376)'s storm watch — was declared, reachable on the wrist, and absent from the canonical drawing of the ring BTN3 walks, and the prose above the diagram called the closing run a trio where the firmware walks four.

**That is not the cosmetic class of doc drift.** The `Page` declaration order **is** the bit order of the 64-bit `SET1` pages mask the phone pushes, so a reader deriving a bit position by counting round the drawn ring gets every page after the gap off by one — and the page the runner asked to see is the one that goes missing.

**The guard compares edges in both directions, not counts.** `scripts/check_watch_page_ring.mjs` reads the `next()` chain out of `page.rs` and the mermaid block out of `navigation.md` and reports a declared edge that is not drawn *and* a drawn edge the wrist does not take, because an invented edge is as wrong as an omitted one. It is a set comparison rather than an order comparison because the flowchart has subgraphs and cluster edges and is not one line. A count would not have caught this: the diagram named 45 pages either way.

**CodeQL raises one high alert against it, and it is a false positive.** `js/bad-tag-filter` reads the `\s*-->\s*` split as an HTML-comment terminator and asks why `--!>` is not also matched. Nothing here parses HTML — `-->` is mermaid's edge arrow and the input is a repo-committed `.md` — so widening the pattern would split on a sequence mermaid never emits. The alert is dismissed through the code-scanning API, which is the only thing that suppresses anything; the `codeql[js/bad-tag-filter]` marker at the split carries the reasoning beside the code and says in as many words that it does not suppress on its own.

**Verification.** Against `main`'s tree the guard exits **1** naming all three disagreements (`SUN --> BARO` and `BARO --> WPT` declared-but-undrawn, `SUN --> WPT` drawn-but-not-declared); with the diagram corrected it exits **0** — `the page ring agrees edge for edge: 45 edge(s) over 45 page(s)`. Its 8 unit tests pass, including the § 376 defect reproduced on a fixture, a drawn edge the firmware does not take, a chained `A --> B --> C` line read as two edges, a mermaid comment line ignored, a missing anchor throwing rather than passing, and an empty parse throwing rather than passing vacuously. The two new steps sit in the existing `watch-wire-vectors` job, which is already in `ci-gate`'s `needs:` list and already bundled, so both print their own `::error::`; `node scripts/check_ci_diagnostics.mjs` exits 0 reporting 48 self-diagnosing steps and `ci-gate` waiting on all **29** jobs, and `actionlint` is clean.

## 795. Route-design preferences in the graph-cycle sidecar are soft edge weights plus a ranking term — they can bias a loop but never deny one, and elevation-aware is deferred for want of a DEM, not for want of code

The `#789` filing said the remaining route-design preferences (scenic / park-adjacency, cul-de-sac mode, multi-objective ranking) needed the v3 graph search "where we own the edges + scoring". The code said something narrower and more useful: the sidecar owned the edges only in the sense that it *walked* them — `internal/graph/build.go` parsed foot-permitted ways out of the PBF and threw every tag away, and the graph stored `lat/lng/edgeHead/edgeTo/edgeLen` and nothing else. There was nothing to weight. So the first piece is attribution: one packed byte per directed edge holding a road-class bucket (arterial / residential-ish / foot-first) and a green flag, deliberately a `[]uint8` and not a struct, on the same footprint argument the package doc already makes for dropping the OSM node id. Green space is collected in the *same* way pass rather than a second one (the file is already streaming every way) and rasterised into a coarse occupancy grid on the spatial index's own 200 m cells; an edge is green when its midpoint lands in a green cell, which is also how a footpath through a park earns the flag. A closed way's raster rows are filled between that way's own extremes, because boundary-only rasterising leaves the middle of any park larger than a cell unmarked — capped at ~10 km of span so one national-forest polygon cannot blanket an extract, and the fill is convex per row, so it over-marks a concave park's bays. That is the right direction to be wrong in: the result is a soft weight, so over-inclusion makes a few extra edges cheap while under-inclusion silently makes the feature not work. The green coordinates are released before the builder allocates, which is the run's peak.

Three constraints shaped the rest, all of them things the code could have got wrong quietly. **Weights are soft only** — every multiplier is finite and strictly positive, never an edge removal, because a hard filter can disconnect a buildable neighbourhood into "no loop" and the fallback then serves a *worse* route than the unbiased search would. **A preference never denies a route**: if the weighted search clears nothing over the spur floor the whole search repeats unweighted and that loop is served with `preferenceApplied` omitted, mirroring the web handler's existing round_trip rule — and an unhonoured ask must never read as honoured, which is why the field is absent rather than echoed back. Worth recording that the retry is cheap insurance and not a common path: the reuse penalty (×8) dwarfs every preference multiplier (≤1.8), so a far point that yields a clean loop unweighted essentially always yields one weighted. The suite therefore pins the *outcome* — a preference never returns nil where the plain search returns a loop, across three fixtures and five targets — rather than pretending to exercise a branch that a connected graph struggles to reach. **True length still comes from geometry**: Dijkstra now returns real metres alongside the weighted cost, because the far-point picker sizes candidates against the loop the runner asked for and a weighted cost is no longer a measure of that; `PrefNone` skips the multiply entirely, so the unpreferenced search is bit-identical to the one that shipped.

Cul-de-sac mode is the design's deliberate exception and it inverts the *ranking*, not the shape score. Dead ends are found structurally (the shortest walk to a degree-1 node touching neither the loop nor an arterial — the dead ends worth running down hang off neighbourhood streets) and spliced in as out-and-backs, capped at four per loop, 250 m one way and a fifth of the target in total, and only ever added to a loop running short, since a stub credits distance and cannot shorten anything. The stub length is then credited at a weight sized to roughly cancel the isoperimetric penalty the spur incurs — a loop that grows by a fraction `f` with no new area keeps only `1/(1+f)²` of its score — so a runner who asks for dead ends is not served a loop ranked below itself for having them. But the spur floor still applies to the served geometry: an augmentation that would drop the loop under it is walked back a stub at a time, because a cul-de-sac loop is still a loop.

The selection rewrite is the piece most able to regress something invisible. The old two-branch rule (in-band → roundest, else closest-to-target) is now one weighted score over distance error, `areaEfficiency` and the preference share, pinned against a verbatim copy of the old selector over 800,000 random candidate sets spanning the whole accepted target range. That corpus caught a real divergence and it is worth naming: the old comparator used a 1e-9 tolerance on its leading objective, which makes it **non-transitive**, so no scalar score can reproduce it in general — and a manufactured pair of loops equidistant from target to the last bit was being separated by float noise instead of by shape. The fix is to snap the leading objective to that same 1e-9 grid before the tie-break rides underneath it, which restores agreement and is, unlike the original, a total order. The two preference weights are stated in each branch's own currency: a fully preferred loop may buy half of the roundness scale while the field is judged on shape (every candidate has already cleared the spur floor, so trading our aesthetic proxy for the roads the runner explicitly asked for is the right trade), but only one band's width of distance error while it is judged on distance, because a preference must not serve a length nobody asked for.

**Elevation-aware is deferred for want of data, and the filing's "needs v3" framing was wrong about it.** The blocker is not the search: GraphHopper is booted with no `graph.elevation.provider` (`apps/job_worker/graphhopper/config.yml` lines 5 and 13-15, and the "No elevation" note in `apps/job_worker/deployment.md`), and the sidecar's own PBF parse keeps only `lat`/`lng` per node because an OSM extract carries no terrain to keep. A grade-weighted edge cost would have nothing behind it, and fabricating a grade signal would be worse than not offering the preference — so `elevation` is absent from the wire vocabulary rather than accepted and ignored. Unblocking it costs a **DEM as a deploy input**: an SRTM/Copernicus tile set mounted on the sidecar's Fly volume beside the PBF, sampled per node at build time into a per-edge grade alongside the existing attribution byte, plus the disk and RAM for it on both engines. That is a deploy-shaped change, not a code-shaped one, which is why it is recorded here rather than half-built.
**Four corrections found reviewing this before it merged, and the first was a live regression in the DEFAULT generator.** Both branches of the new score added a `1e-12` tie-break to a term of a different magnitude — out of band to a number of **metres**, in band on top of a constant `1000` — so float rounding annihilated it. Measured against a verbatim copy of the old selector, the out-of-band tie-break vanished above a ~4.5 km target (0.3 % of candidate sets diverging at 4,500 m, rising to ~5.5 % at 100 km), and the in-band one collapsed 151 distinct distance-errors onto **two** distinct scores, keeping the farther loop in 12 of 30 equal-roundness pairs. The pin drew its targets from `[500, 4500)` while the handler accepts up to 100 km, so it certified the one stretch that could not fail and stopped exactly at the onset — a pin whose corpus is narrower than the input range is not a pin. Both branches now score on an O(1) scale (in band on the roundness scale, out of band strictly below it), which retires the `1000` bonus entirely since every candidate has already cleared the spur floor, and the corpus is 800,000 sets across the whole accepted range in four shapes. **A `cul_de_sac` ask reported itself applied when no spur was spliced** — its ask is binary and observable, unlike the two gradients, so it is now gated on the stub length the code already had. **The builder retained both node-id sets across its own peak allocation**: `ws.green` was released with a comment explaining that liveness is per variable rather than per field, and the same reasoning applied unremarked to `ws.refs` and `ws.greenRefs` — 289 MB against 0.4 MB at 5M ids per map, on a 4 GB machine. **And the tests asserted against the constants they claimed to pin**: raising all three cul-de-sac caps 3-12x left the suite green, as did neutering every tag-to-attribution decision in the builder, which no test reached at all because both decisions were bare expressions inside a loop only a PBF can drive.

## 796. A road-design preference was a downgrade off the durable generator, and it advertised itself as honoured whatever happened

**Decided (2026-08-30, issue #789 § F / `followups.md:149`).** The filing described the remaining route-design work as "scenic/park-adjacency, elevation-aware, cul-de-sac mode, and the multi-objective post-hoc ranking" — four features on top of a shipped "quiet roads" toggle. The defect underneath was structural and unlisted: `handleGenerate` skipped the graph-cycle sidecar entirely whenever a preference was set (`if (config.graphCycleUrl && !req.preference)`), so a runner who ticked "quiet roads" was silently moved off the v3 graph search — the durable generator, the one that traces the neighbourhood loop geometry cannot find — and onto a custom-model `round_trip`. The preference was, in practice, a switch that traded route quality for road class. The sidecar now honours preferences on its own weighted search, so the preference rides the chain instead: graph-cycle first carrying it, `round_trip` under a custom model only as the fallback it already was. The never-deny retry stays exactly as it was and is not negotiable — one plain race when the preferred race comes up empty — because a preference is an enhancement layered on the route, and the route is the contract; the same reasoning that made it necessary when the engine could reject a custom model makes it necessary when a weighting can starve a search.

**What the 200 body now says, and why the ask is never the evidence.** The response carries `preferenceApplied`, taken only from the serving engine's own verdict — the sidecar reports what its weighted search actually delivered and reports nothing when its unweighted retry is what found the loop, and the `round_trip` path claims a preference only when GraphHopper could express it as a model *and* the preferred race is what produced the served candidates. Echoing `req.preference` back would have been free and wrong: every one of those paths can serve a loop that ignores the ask, so a client repeating the ask would tell the runner their quiet route was quiet on no evidence at all. Omission is the honest answer, and the surface is expected to say so.

**`cul_de_sac` has no GraphHopper expression and never will.** "Permit a capped number of short stubs into quiet dead-ends" is a claim about the shape of the assembled loop, not about any edge in isolation, and no encoded value marks a dead end — so `buildCustomModel` returns null for it and `round_trip` runs plain. Only a search that builds the loop can honour it. `scenic` is expressible but only as a proxy: this engine declares just the foot-profile encoded values (`graph.encoded_values` in `apps/job_worker/graphhopper/config.yml`) and imports no elevation at all, and OSM land use is not an encoded value in any build, so park adjacency and per-edge grade belong to the sidecar, which owns the extract. Both models therefore spend nothing but `road_class`, pinned by a test — naming an encoded value the engine lacks fails the whole request rather than the one clause, and the never-deny retry would have hidden that as a preference silently doing nothing. **Elevation-aware is not in the vocabulary for the same reason** and the filing's four-item list is three: there is no elevation on this rail to be aware of.

**The selector gained no ranking term, because there is nothing on this rail for one to rank.** The first draft added `1 + 0.25 x share` to `pickBestLoop`'s in-band score, justified on the pool being mixed by construction — the sidecar measuring a share and `round_trip` measuring none. **The pool is never mixed.** `pickBestLoop` has one production call site and its argument is the `round_trip` candidate list; the sidecar's loop is returned to the caller before selection is reached, so no candidate carrying a share can ever enter it. The term returned exactly 1 for every input it could ever see, and the comment asserting otherwise was the kind of false rationale that outlives the code it explains. It is deleted, along with the share's parse and its ride onto the candidate — an unreachable branch with a confident comment is worse than an absent one. **The multi-objective ranking the filing asks for lives in the sidecar**, the only component that enumerates several candidate loops and knows each one's share; that this rail has no such choice to make is the finding, not a gap. What the web side does keep is the sidecar's *verdict*, which is consumed.
**Never-deny has a second edge, and the sidecar's own decoder is what opens it.** `decodeBody` uses `DisallowUnknownFields`, so a sidecar deployed before this change answers **400** to a request carrying `preference` — which is precisely why the handler skipped it. The Lambda and the sidecar deploy separately, so that skew is an ordinary window, and in it the caught error read as an outage: on a deploy with a `round_trip` fallback the request degraded quietly, but on a graph-cycle-only deploy the same request returned **502**, the alarm-driving status, with the preference as the sole reason a buildable route was denied — the identical request without one returned 200. A sidecar that ANSWERED and refused is now retried once without the preference, which is why `GraphCycleError` carries the status: a refusal can be retried differently, an unreachable host cannot, and retrying a dead host only doubles the wait before the honest 502. **A second waste in the same shape:** the round_trip never-deny retry was gated on the preference alone, but `cul_de_sac` has no custom model, so its first race was already the plain one and the retry re-sent a byte-identical race — doubling a fan-out of up to 32 upstream fetches exactly when the engine is failing. Both retries are now gated on the thing that actually differs.

## 797. Three route-design preferences that are mutually exclusive on the wire get one single-choice control, and the page reports the preference the server applied rather than the one the runner asked for

`/routes/new` shipped the cheap half of the route-design preference set as a
lone "Quiet roads (avoid highways)" checkbox, whose only job was to turn
`preference: 'quiet'` on the `POST /api/routes/generate` body on and off. Widening
the vocabulary to `'quiet' | 'scenic' | 'cul_de_sac'` does not widen the wire: the
body carries at most ONE preference, so three checkboxes would let a runner
express a state the request cannot represent and leave the page to silently
discard two of them. The control is therefore a four-option radio group —
the three preferences plus an explicit "No preference" that sends no field at
all — built from native `<input type="radio">` inside `<label>`s under a
`role="radiogroup"`, the same idiom `RunEditor`, `EventEditor` and
`RouteMarkerEditor` already use. Native radios are what buy the accessibility:
one tab stop for the group, arrow keys to move the selection, and a real
checked state, none of which a `div` with `role="radio"` has without hand-rolled
roving focus. Each option's hint moved out of the `title=` tooltip the checkbox
carried — a tooltip is not reachable by keyboard and is not announced — and into
visible text inside the label, so every reader gets it.

The second half is honesty about the result. A preference is an enhancement the
generator may decline: the handler races the preference-aware request and, if
that yields nothing, retries the whole race without it, and a request that never
reaches the server at all (point-to-point, an unconfigured endpoint, an engine
outage) falls through to the in-browser heuristic, which honours no preference
whatsoever. Before this the runner saw the same rendered loop either way. The
200 body's additive `preferenceApplied` is now read in `RouteBuilder`, which
grades it against the preference it SENT rather than re-listing the union —
so an absent field, an unknown token and a heuristic fallback all resolve
identically to "not applied" — and hands the page a nullable applied value on
every generation that produced a route. The page compares it to the ask it
captured at call time (not to the live control, which the runner may have
changed mid-generation) and, on a mismatch, states that the loop was generated
without the preference. Fail-closed is the point: a deployment predating the
field sends nothing, and reading nothing as success would make the note
disappear exactly where it is most needed. The same resolution fixed a
pre-existing gap in the AI route assistant, which listed `avoidHighways` in its
"applied" summary while never touching the control or the request — the parsed
`preference` now drives the control, with `avoidHighways` mapping onto `'quiet'`
when nothing narrower came back.
**Two corrections found reviewing this before it merged.** The not-applied note was a `role="status"` region mounted by the same `{#if}` that put its text inside it — the exact shape [§ 736](#736-a-live-region-only-announces-what-changes-while-it-is-already-mounted) settled five days earlier: a live region announces changes made *inside* it, not its own arrival, so the one message on the page whose entire job is disclosure was announced to nobody. It is now permanently mounted with only its text changing, carrying a bare `aria-live` for the same reason § 736 chose one. And the message called the result a **loop** while the first case it exists for is point-to-point, where the button itself says "route" and the server is never reached at all — so all seven catalogues now name a route, in the wording each already uses for one. The AI summary's label lookup also became a `Record` keyed by the union: an if-chain ending in a fall-through would render a fourth preference under the last branch's label, stating as fact a preference the runner never asked for.

## 798. The route assistant's preference is a whitelisted vocabulary like shape and surface, and `avoidHighways` survives beside it because it answers a different question

The NL route box could extract a distance, a shape, a surface and an avoid-highways flag, but the generator's road-design preference — the thing that decides whether the loop is biased onto residential streets, toward parks and water, or into dead-end spurs — was reachable only from the manual "Quiet roads" checkbox. So the one field that makes a plain-English request more expressive than the slider was the one field the assistant could not fill. `RouteConstraints` now carries `preference: RoutePreference | null`, validated in `constraints.ts` against a `ReadonlySet` exactly as `shape` and `surface` are: the model may emit `quiet`, `scenic` or `cul_de_sac` and nothing else, and any other token — a hallucination, a case variant, a hyphenated spelling, an object — is dropped rather than forwarded. The vocabulary is owned by `generate/graphhopper.ts`, not by this module, so the set is typed on construction (`new Set<RoutePreference>([...])`) and a value the generator later drops from the union fails the build here instead of reaching it as a token it cannot route. Unlike every other field, the absence is carried as `null` rather than filled with a default: the others default to something the runner would plausibly have picked anyway (5 km, a loop, roads), whereas defaulting a preference would silently bias every generated route toward a design nobody asked for.

`avoidHighways` stays on the object beside it, and is not folded into `quiet`, because the two answer different questions to different consumers. `avoidHighways` is the boolean the `/routes/new` form's own checkbox is bound to and the flag the applied-summary line reports; `preference` is the enum the generate body carries into the GraphHopper custom model. Collapsing them would either make the summary unable to say "avoiding main roads" without inspecting an enum, or make the enum unable to express `scenic` and `cul_de_sac` at all — both of which are preferences that have nothing to say about highways. What they must not do is disagree, so the derivation is one-directional and precedence is fixed: an explicit `preference` from the model wins outright; failing that, `avoid_highways === true` derives `quiet` (it is the same ask, and `quiet` is what implements it); failing that, a `trail` surface derives `scenic`. The stated road constraint outranks the surface inference when both hold, because "avoid main roads" is something the runner said and a trail surface is something we inferred a preference from. `cul_de_sac` is never derived at any precedence — it inverts part of the loop score by design (`graph_cycle_loop_generation.md` § Extension), so inferring it from a request that did not ask would hand a runner a route built out of dead-end spurs. A derived value records `preference` in `assumptions`, which is what the review panel shows as "we assumed this"; landing on `null` records nothing, because nothing was assumed — telling a runner we assumed a preference we did not set is the same dishonesty from the other direction.

One thing the filing suspected and the code did not bear out: `surface` is extracted **and consumed** — `/routes/new` maps it onto the builder's road/trail mode. The field that is extracted and only *displayed* is `avoidHighways`, which the NL path reports in the applied summary without ever setting the page's `quietRoads` state, so a request to avoid main roads is acknowledged and then not honoured. That gap is on the page, not on the extractor, and closing it is what the returned `preference` exists for.

## 799. `revoke ... from public` and `revoke ... from anon` each withhold a function on one Postgres image and neither on both — so the class the filing named is real, the measurement that "disproved" it was taken on the wrong database, and four functions were open

The followup said Supabase ships an `alter default privileges` for the `postgres` role in `public` granting EXECUTE on every new function to `anon`, `authenticated` and `service_role`, so a function arrives with an **explicit** anon grant that revoking PUBLIC cannot reach — § 781's column-revoke no-op one object class over — and that 83 functions were in that state.

**The first measurement said the opposite, and it was taken on an image the filing was not about.** Probed on this workstation (Supabase CLI 2.109.1) in rolled-back transactions: a function created in `public` by `postgres` comes up with `proacl` NULL, which is Postgres's *built-in* default of owner plus `PUBLIC`; `revoke execute ... from public` materialises `{postgres=X/postgres}` and `has_function_privilege('anon', …)` goes false; `revoke execute ... from anon` materialises `{=X/postgres,postgres=X/postgres}` and leaves it **true**. The `pg_default_acl` row that grants anon by name belongs to `supabase_admin`, which creates none of our functions; the `postgres` row is `{postgres=X/postgres}`. So on *this* image the filing is inverted — `from public` is the statement that works and `from anon` is the one that withholds nothing.

**Two shipped pgtap suites prove CI's image is the other one, and CI is what prod resembles.** `coach_roster_summary_test` asserts `throws_ok(..., 'not authenticated')` for `set local role anon` — it expects anon to be *admitted by the ACL* and refused by the body, and `coach_roster_summary` was only ever revoked `from public`. `donations_status_lock_test` calls `fundraiser_totals` as `service_role`, which no migration ever granted. Both pass on CI (`supabase/setup-cli` pinned to `2.84.2` in `ci.yml`) and both fail on a current workstation with `permission denied for function`. That is only possible if CI's image grants anon/authenticated/service_role **by name** at create time. No pgtap assertion anywhere contradicts it: every test claiming anon *cannot* execute something (`try_consume_strava_quota`, `notify_data_export_ready`, `delete_notifications`, `is_blocked_either_way`) names `anon` in its revoke, so it holds on either image.

**The conclusion is neither the filing's nor the first correction's: neither single-grantee revoke is portable, and only naming both is.** `revoke execute ... from public, anon` removes the PUBLIC entry where there is one and the anon entry where there is one. 31 migrations already write it; it is the house form, and this ADR is why.

**Replaying all 444 migrations against the catalogue, with one rule swapped, sizes both worlds.** Under this image's rule the replay reproduces the live catalogue exactly — 117 anon-executable predicted, 117 measured, zero over- and zero under-predictions — so the model is trustworthy; under CI's rule the same model gives **183 of 242 anon-executable, 105 non-trigger, 81 of them SECURITY DEFINER**, against the filing's 186. The filing was right, for the environment that matters. Its "83" was a count of migrations naming a function in a `from public` revoke, and only 17 of those are anon-executable here — but 54 more functions are anon-executable on CI and prod than on this workstation.

**Triage rule.** 66 of the anon-executable functions return `trigger`, and no grant makes those callable (`select notify_run_kudos()` raises 0A000 for every role), so they are inert. Of the callable remainder, 33 carry an explicit `grant execute ... to anon` from the migration that created them and have a named logged-out caller — the public share, spectator, discovery and fundraiser surfaces. The rest were graded by what an anonymous caller actually gets, measured as `set local role anon`, which is what PostgREST does for a request bearing the publishable key: **SECURITY DEFINER and answering** is the sharp end, **SECURITY DEFINER but raising on a null `auth.uid()`** is a failed intent and not a hole, and **SECURITY INVOKER over RLS** reads zero rows.

**Four were repaired, in `20270625000001`.** `enqueue_run_rematch` is the one place in 444 migrations where `revoke ... from anon` stands alone, written under the comment "Authed users only"; `segment_leaderboard_tiered` was withheld from anon by `20260830_001` as a stated audit fix and handed straight back by `20261022_001`, because `drop function` + `create function` re-issues the image default and nothing re-emitted the revoke — the failure mode a replay of migration *text* cannot flag, since no migration is wrong on its own words. Neither was exploitable: both bodies raise 42501 on a null `auth.uid()` before reading or writing, which is exactly why nothing noticed for eight months and a year respectively. The other two answered rather than refusing. `cleanup_stale_rate_limits()` returned 0 to an anonymous caller, and its whole body is `delete from rate_limits where window_start < now() - interval '24 hours'` — an anonymous `POST /rest/v1/rpc/cleanup_stale_rate_limits` cleared every elapsed rate-limit window, defeating every throttle in the app. Its three siblings were already `{postgres, service_role}`, and three later migrations cite this one **by name** as the reference for that pattern while it was the only member of the family nobody had locked down. `refresh_gym_workout_totals(uuid)` returned void: a SECURITY DEFINER write to `gym_workouts` for any workout id with RLS bypassed, idempotent because it recomputes from `gym_sets`, and reachable only by an anonymous caller who has no business there.

**What was deliberately left anon-callable, and the surface that justifies it.** The 33 explicit grants stay: `public_profile_by_id` and `public_recap_by_id` back every `/share/*` lookup and the logged-out `/live/[id]`; `clip_route_for_viewer`, `route_markers_for_viewer`, `route_conditions_for_viewer`, `public_run_gear`, `run_engagement_counts` back the public run and route pages; `heatmap_points_in_bbox`, `clubs_in_bbox`, `discoverable_routes_in_bbox`, `nearby_routes`, `routes_within_box`, `search_public_routes`, `search_clubs`, `search_public_events`, `search_race_listings`, `browse_public_challenges`, `popular_route_tags` back logged-out discovery; `fundraiser_totals` / `fundraiser_feed` / `fundraiser_anchor_visible` the public fundraiser page; `challenge_leaderboard`, `global_segment_leaderboard`, `segment_effort_ranks`, `global_segment_effort_ranks` the public boards (§ 746); `confirm_safety_contact_by_token` lets a trusted contact confirm from an emailed link with no account at all. Three more are load-bearing inside definitions rather than at a call site: `is_public_route_by_id` and `is_public_event_by_id` are named by the `public_runs` view, `is_public_club_by_id` by `public_routes`, and `is_event_visible` by the `checkpoint_crossings`, `event_checkpoints` and `event_pricing` SELECT policies, all `to public`.

**`is_challenge_visible` is the one where withholding would have been the bug.** Two `challenge_participants` policies are `to public` and name it, anon holds SELECT on that table, and a policy expression is ACL-checked against the *querying* role — so revoking it turns an anonymous read of a public challenge's participants from 9 rows into `42501: permission denied for function is_challenge_visible`. Measured both ways before the decision. It is § 746's trap exactly, and it is why this round revoked four functions rather than sweeping a class: the reference graph has to be read per function.

**The class is not closed, and the unclosed half is the serious one.** On CI's and prod's image, **21 SECURITY DEFINER functions with no in-body auth check at all** are anon-executable, because their migrations wrote `revoke ... from public` without naming anon: the job-queue API (`claim_next_job` returns a queued job's payload and burns an attempt, `finish_job` marks any job succeeded or failed, `defer_job` reschedules it — draining the queue kills map-matching, exports and every notification email), the four `cleanup_stale_*` sweeps, the three `enqueue_*` mail batches (an anonymous caller can fire a weekly-digest send), `clear_device_token` / `clear_push_subscription`, `auto_hide_target` (an anonymous content takedown), `mark_attendance`, and the `find_*_jobs` / `jobs_*_summary` payload readers. A catalogue scan says 20 of the 21 are named by no policy, view, constraint or SECURITY INVOKER function, so adding `, anon` to their existing revoke is inert on this image and the fix on the other; the exception is `_run_comment_parent_is_top_level`, which a `run_comments` INSERT policy `to public` names. That sweep is deliberately **not** in `20270625000001` — it cannot be verified against the image it is for from this workstation, and the four repaired here were each verified live. It is the next round.

**Verification.** `supabase db reset` + `supabase test db --local`: 264 files, 2234 assertions; `anon_execute_registry_test.sql` passes 6/6, and the only two failures are `coach_roster_summary_test` #10 and `donations_status_lock_test`, which fail identically on the untouched tree (baselined by removing the migration and the test and re-running) and are the image divergence this ADR is about. `check_migration_versions.mjs` reports 444 unique version keys; `check_migration_online_safety.mjs` passes (a GRANT/REVOKE takes no lock on any relation, so no online-DDL machinery applies); both pgtap refusal-assertion guards pass, 168 assertions mutation-checked with 5 expected survivors. `npm run gen:types` and `dart run scripts/gen_dart_models.dart` both move nothing, which is what a grant-only migration should do. The new test pins the **rule** rather than the statements: that a fresh `public` function is anon-executable before any grant statement, that at least one single-grantee revoke fails to withhold it — whichever one depends on the image — and that naming both always does, so an image change is a loud failure here instead of a silent re-reading of every `revoke` in the tree.

**The sweep the previous paragraph deferred landed in `20270626000001`, and it found a second class the guard cannot see.** Replaying the 444 migrations before it, under the workstation's rule, reproduces the live catalogue exactly — 264 of 264 functions, zero over- and zero under-predictions — so the same model's CI-rule answer of 198 anon-executable is trustworthy. Subtracting the 46 that carry a deliberate `grant execute ... to anon` and the 80 that return `trigger` leaves **72 callable functions anon held EXECUTE on for no stated reason**: 57 SECURITY DEFINER, 15 SECURITY INVOKER. 71 were withheld; one was deliberately kept. **Only 54 of the 72 have a malformed revoke anywhere in history.** The other **18 were never revoked from anything** — their migration wrote `grant execute ... to authenticated` and stopped — so no statement is wrong for a statement-shaped scan to flag, while on Cloud they arrive with the create-time anon grant and are as open as the rest. `increment_coach_usage(uuid)`, `get_coach_usage(uuid)` and `public_run_counts(uuid[])` take the target user id as a parameter and are in that 18; so are `is_pro`, `dm_threads`, `redeem_coach_invite`, `personal_records`, `weekly_mileage` and `routes_intersecting_track`. The reverse error is in the same report: `enqueue_run_rematch` and `segment_leaderboard_tiered` still carry a malformed statement in history and are already closed, because this ADR's own migration re-issued them. **A replay of migration text answers "was a statement written badly"; only a replay of the resulting ACL answers "is the function open".** Against the 69 routines a statement-shaped replay names, the two sets differ by 18 in one direction — open and unflagged — and 15 in the other, those being the 13 trigger-returning entries no grant can make reachable plus the 2 already closed.
