**What 24 of them actually were.** Of the 71 withheld, 56 are SECURITY DEFINER and **24 carry no `auth.uid()` anywhere in the body**, so the grant was the only control there was. The job-queue API is the sharp end: `claim_next_job` returns a queued job's payload and burns an attempt, `finish_job` marks any job succeeded, `defer_job` reschedules it — a caller holding nothing but the publishable key could drain the queue, stopping map-matching, exports and every notification email while reading the payloads on the way out. `enqueue_weekly_digests` / `enqueue_event_reminders` / `enqueue_lifecycle_drip` are anonymous mail sends batched over every eligible account. `clear_push_subscription(uuid, text)` and `clear_device_token(text)` delete a named device's push registration, which is the delivery path the safety-contact escalation rides on. `auto_hide_target(text, uuid)` is the shadow-hide evaluator with RLS bypassed — an anonymous caller could force the hide-and-notify transition on any user, club or route whose pending reports had already reached the threshold. `cron_schedule_status` / `jobs_stuck_summary` / `jobs_failed_summary` / `find_stuck_jobs` / `find_failed_jobs` read queue and cron state without an account. The rest refuse a null `auth.uid()` themselves or delegate to a `private` oracle that does — `get_integration_tokens` and its two `set_` siblings (Strava and Garmin OAuth material) raise unless the caller is the subject or `service_role`, `get_club_invite_token` and `mark_attendance` fail their membership check — and were closed because a body is a poor place for the only authorization in a system that has a privilege layer.

**The second half is not about anon at all.** On Cloud the same create-time grant goes to `authenticated`, and any visitor can mint one by signing up. So the cron and job-queue family — whose local ACL has always been `{postgres, service_role}` and whose documentation says "service_role only" — lost `authenticated` too, matching `cleanup_stale_export_blobs` (`20260720_001`). `service_role` was deliberately **not** revoked anywhere: it is a server credential that already bypasses RLS on every table these functions touch, so withdrawing EXECUTE changes no attacker's reach while risking a server path a workstation cannot enumerate. Where PUBLIC was its only local path it is granted back by name, so both images end up with the same ACL. `event_is_athletic` is what caught that: five pgtap suites insert `event_results` under `set local role service_role`, and its guard trigger is SECURITY INVOKER, so it runs as the writer.

**Three functions are named by something anon can reach, and the reference graph decides each one separately.** `is_challenge_visible(uuid)` keeps its grant — two `challenge_participants` policies are `to public`, anon holds SELECT on that table, and a policy expression is privilege-checked against the querying role, so withholding turns an anonymous read into `42501`. `_run_comment_parent_is_top_level(uuid)` is named by a `run_comments` INSERT policy `to public` and anon does hold INSERT on that table, but the same policy requires `auth.uid() = user_id`: the insert is refused either way and only the error code changes, so it was withheld. `event_is_athletic(uuid)` is reached through two SECURITY INVOKER trigger functions rather than a policy, which is why it needed an explicit grant rather than an exemption. Every other routine in the sweep was checked the same way against `pg_policy`, view definitions, CHECK constraints, index and DEFAULT expressions and other SECURITY INVOKER bodies, and none is named by any of them.

**The thirteen trigger-returning entries close nothing and are labelled as such.** `select enqueue_welcome_email()` raises `0A000` for every role — Postgres refuses a direct call before privileges are consulted — so no grant makes one reachable through PostgREST. They are in the migration because their own migrations wrote a revoke that withholds nothing on the image they ship to, and an intent that is false where it matters is worth making true. 67 more trigger functions still carry the image default and are left alone for the same reason they are harmless.

**The contract is now a whole-schema test rather than a list of statements.** `anon_execute_contract_test.sql` asserts that no `public` non-trigger function outside a 34-row allowlist is executable by `anon` *or* carries a PUBLIC / anon EXECUTE entry — the first reading is the literal truth on CI, where a function added without a revoke arrives anon-granted by name; the second is the ACL shape, which is what a `drop function` + `create function` restores and what bites on a workstation. It also asserts the converse, that every allowlisted function is still anon-executable, so a blanket revoke that `42501`s the logged-out pages fails there rather than in production, and that the cron/queue family is closed to `authenticated` while `service_role` keeps the operator hook. Trigger-returning and extension-owned functions are excluded, both exclusions stated and the first one asserted. Mutation-checked: granting anon on a swept function, granting `authenticated` on `claim_next_job`, revoking anon from `public_profile_by_id`, revoking `service_role` from `claim_next_job`, and simply creating a new function with no revoke each fail exactly the assertion that should catch them, and none fails on the unmutated tree.

**`coach_roster_summary_test` #10 had to change, and that is the loss worth recording.** It asserted that an `anon` caller entered the body and was refused by it, which is the evidence that separated the two images at the top of this ADR — and it only ever passed on CI. `coach_roster_summary` is now withheld on both, so the assertion became a statement about the ACL, and the body's own fail-closed guard is asserted through `authenticated` with no subject. The rule the two images differ on is pinned directly, with probe functions, by `anon_execute_registry_test.sql`, and `donations_status_lock_test` still fails on a workstation for the same underlying reason, so the divergence stays observable.

**Closing an ACL changes what a refusal LOOKS like, and three shipped assertions were written against the old shape.** A function whose body refused anon on a null `auth.uid()` now refuses at the grant instead, so a test asserting the body's answer (a null, a specific message) sees `42501 permission denied for function`. Two were pgtap — `coach_roster_summary_test` and `rls_paywall_test`'s anon `is_pro()` case — and the third was found only when CI ran the Playwright shard: `invite-token-lockdown.spec.ts` asserted anon reaches `get_club_invite_token` and receives a null from its `is_club_admin` gate. All three still hold their intent, and hold it more strongly: the outer defence refuses before the inner one is consulted. They now assert the refusal. The lesson is the sweep's shape rather than any one test — a privilege change reaches every surface that exercises the privilege, so pgtap is not the whole search space, and grepping the migration's own function names across `tests-e2e/` is part of the change.

**Verification.** `supabase db reset` + `supabase test db --local`: 265 files, 2242 assertions, one failure — `donations_status_lock_test`, which fails identically on the untouched tree; the baseline before this change had two, and `coach_roster_summary_test` #10 was the other. **The CI image was then simulated and measured rather than modelled**: an `alter default privileges for role postgres ... grant execute on functions to anon, authenticated, service_role` applied ahead of the tree makes a fresh function arrive anon-granted by name, so `revoke ... from public` alone leaves anon holding EXECUTE — the failure mode this ADR is about. Under that simulation the whole suite passes, **265 files, 2261 assertions, zero failures, `donations_status_lock_test` included**, and the anon-executable set is 34 `public` non-trigger functions, identical name for name to the replay model's prediction. The two images now agree: 114 anon-executable routines on each (34 `public` callable, 66 `public` trigger, 13 `private` policy oracles with deliberate grants, 1 `private` trigger), against 131 on a workstation and 198 on Cloud before. `check_migration_versions` reports 445 unique version keys; `check_migration_online_safety`, `check_migration_column_revoke_noop` and `gen:types:check` pass; the refusal-assertion guard mutation-checks 168 assertions with 5 expected survivors. A GRANT or REVOKE takes no lock on the target relation (`migration_locks.md` § Lock reference, measured on PG 17.6), and neither row-type generator moves.
## 800. Two Supabase CLI images disagree about how `anon` reaches a function, so neither single-grantee revoke is portable — and the guard's first cut encoded the wrong one

`followups.md` filed "`revoke execute … from public` has never withheld a function from `anon`, and 83 migrations say it does", on the premise that Supabase's `alter default privileges` hands every new `public` function an **explicit** anon grant a PUBLIC-revoke cannot reach — [§ 781](#781)'s column-revoke no-op, one object class over. A probe against this workstation appeared to refute it outright, and the first cut of the guard shipped that refutation. **Both the filing and the refutation are half right, and the axis they differ on is the CLI image.**

**The evidence that separates them is this repo's own shipped test, not a probe.** `coach_roster_summary_test.sql` asserts, under `set local role anon`, that `select * from coach_roster_summary()` raises `not authenticated` — an assertion that can only pass if the ACL **admits** anon and the function body is what refuses. That function was only ever revoked `from public` (`20270206_001:157`, `20270314_001:134`). On CI it passes: run **33312161758** on `main` (sha 5db780b) logs `coach_roster_summary_test.sql … ok` and `pgtap RLS suite: success`. On this workstation the same SQL raises `ERROR: permission denied for function coach_roster_summary`, and the catalogue says why — `proacl` is `{postgres=X/postgres,authenticated=X/postgres}` with `has_function_privilege('anon', …)` **false**.

Same SQL, same migrations, opposite ACL. The cause is the image: this box runs CLI **2.109.1**, `ci.yml:672-674` pins **2.84.2**, and Supabase Cloud matches CI. On 2.109.1 a new `public` function has `proacl` **NULL** — Postgres's built-in default — so anon reaches it **only through PUBLIC**, and `revoke … from public` measurably flips anon `true → false` while `revoke … from anon` leaves `=X` in place and changes nothing. On 2.84.2 the default privileges install an **explicit** anon grant, so the same two statements swap roles. Neither single-grantee revoke is portable:

| statement | 2.109.1 (workstation) | 2.84.2 (CI, Cloud) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `revoke … from public` | withholds | **no-op for anon** |
| `revoke … from anon` | **no-op for anon** | withholds |
| `revoke … from public, anon` | withholds | withholds |

So the house form is not belt-and-braces — it is **the only form that works**, and it is the rule the guard enforces. `check_migration_function_revoke_noop.mjs` replays the set in version order and reports a revoke naming one channel only if the **other channel is still at its image-dependent default** at the end, so the two halves may land in different migrations and a repair is forward rather than a bookkeeping edit. **Whole tree, no allowlist, no version cutoff** — [§ 775](#775) retired a cutoff because the bump that kept it current was the bypass. A **deliberate** re-open discharges the obligation: `revoke … from public` followed by `grant execute … to anon` leaves anon holding on both images, which is a decision rather than a divergence, so only a channel left at its default is reported. `authenticated` is carried in one direction only — a revoke naming it is defeated by PUBLIC on 2.109.1 exactly as an anon revoke is — but an anon lockdown never obliges closing `authenticated`, which ~110 migrations grant back on the next line.

**Two ACL behaviours are modelled because both were measured:** `create or replace` on the same signature **preserves** the ACL, so a portable lockdown survives a rebuild; `drop function` plus a fresh `create` **re-defaults** both channels. Under the 2.109.1 default the replay's end state agrees with the catalogue on **121 of 121** anon-executable `public` functions, which is what proves the pair right; the naive "any create resets" model over-predicts 14.

**What it deliberately does not catch.** It grades the **statement**, so a routine nobody wrote a lockdown for is not its business, and neither is one whose well-formed lockdown a later `drop`-and-`create` re-opened — that statement was portable as written, and "every routine is locked down" is a claim about **state** that a pgtap catalogue assertion makes, the same statement-guard/state-guard split § 781 records. A routine is keyed by its schema-qualified **name**, so two overloads would share a verdict (there are none in `public` or `private` today, measured). Table and column revokes belong to the sibling guard, including the `revoke select on function_logs from anon` shape a laxer regex would eat. `service_role` is untracked by design. `alter default privileges` on routines is **not** modelled — it moves the very default being replayed against — so a migration carrying one fails the guard rather than letting the replay issue verdicts under a changed premise; there are none today.

**The honest count is large, and it should be repaired forward rather than grandfathered.** Against today's tree the guard reports **91 violations across 69 routines in 59 migrations**: 90 in the `from public`-only direction and 1 (`enqueue_run_rematch`, `20260612_001`) in the `from anon`-only direction. Of the 69 routines, **61 are SECURITY DEFINER**, and dropping the 13 that return `trigger` (unreachable through PostgREST whatever the ACL says) leaves **48 SECURITY DEFINER, directly-callable functions anon can execute on the production image**. That is materially wider than the 21 the parallel repair sized. A `GRANDFATHERED_VIOLATIONS`-style list is the wrong instrument at this size — [§ 764](#764)'s justification for names is that an entry "can only be written by someone who has read the violation it names", which 91 mechanical entries would make a fiction. The right fix is one repair migration carrying a `revoke execute on function <f> from public, anon;` per routine: GRANT and REVOKE take **no lock on the target relation** (measured in § 781), so none of the online-DDL machinery applies, no column moves and neither row-type generator does either.

**Verification.** `check_migration_function_revoke_noop.test.mjs`: **25 pass**, and the suite is proved able to fail rather than assumed to — six mutations of the guard were run and each is caught: encoding the workstation-only rule, the first cut of this guard (**8 red**, including the `from public` headline); encoding the CI-only rule (2 red); letting a paired statement still register an obligation (1 red); making a deliberate grant stop discharging it (1 red); dropping the `drop function` re-default (2 red); modelling `create or replace` as a re-default (5 red). Against the real tree: **91** reported over 443 migrations replayed. `check_migration_versions.mjs`, `check_migration_online_safety.mjs` and `check_migration_column_revoke_noop.mjs` are untouched and pass. `npm run check:script-types` exits 0 and `tsconfig_coverage.test.mjs` passes, so both `.mjs` files are inside a tsc program. `actionlint -shellcheck= -pyflakes=` clean; `check_ci_diagnostics.mjs` accepts the step inside the already-bundled `parity-types` job — no new job, so `ci-gate` still waits on all **29**. Every catalogue figure came from read-only queries or transactions rolled back and confirmed to leave nothing behind; no migration was applied to the shared local stack, which five worktrees share this round. **The 2.84.2 half of the table was not probed directly** — no second stack was built — it is read off the CI log and the shipped assertion, which is why the guard requires the form that is safe under *either* default rather than encoding what either one does.

## 801. `guided_runs` claimed the syncer agent was watching it, was in neither registry, and — being a library of literals rather than an algorithm — would not have been protected by the registry line alone

Both halves of the guided-audio-run cue library open by asserting their own lockstep and naming the enforcement: web's doc comment says "Mirrors `apps/mobile_android/lib/guided_runs.dart`. Keep in lockstep — the shared-library-syncer agent watches the pair", and the Dart file says the same in the other direction. `guided_runs` appeared **zero times** in `CLAUDE.md` and **zero times** in `.claude/agents/shared-library-syncer.md`, and that agent's instructions tell it to stop rather than invent a parity claim about a pair absent from its table — so nothing was watching. This is § 641's shape (`turn_cues`, wrong in all three implementations at once because it was registered nowhere) and § 760's (`locale`, two files describing each other as twins for eighteen days while holding different Portuguese answers). `check_parity_pair_registry.mjs` could not see it either, and that is not a bug in it: that guard checks the two registries against *each other*, and a pair missing from both is perfectly consistent. The registries are only self-consistent, never complete.

**The registry line was the smaller half of the fix, and on its own it would have protected nothing.** Every other entry in that list is an algorithm, which is why a mirror suite suffices for them — two implementations computing the same answers from the same inputs, where a divergence surfaces as a failed assertion. This one is a *library of literals*: three workouts, each an id, a duration and an ordered list of cue second marks. Both suites test their own rail against itself — "ids are unique", "durations are sensible (5-90 min)", "every run has a finish cue at exactly duration" — and **every one of those properties survives moving a cue, changing a duration or renaming a workout on one side only**. Neither suite reads the other file. So the entire class of drift this pair can suffer passes both suites, `tsc`, `dart analyze` and every guard in the tree, and the two surfaces then describe the same named workout differently: a different finish time under one title, or a cue one platform lists and the other has never heard of. A registry entry tells an *agent* to go and look; it fails no build.

**What fails the PR** is a new entry in `check_shared_constants.mjs` — § 787's registry, for a value with more than one home. It reads the ids **in order**, each duration and each ordered cue list out of both files with **one** extractor, the way `parseBadgeCatalogue` reads two badge catalogues written in different languages, and compares them `match: 'key'` on the run id with `compare: 'ordered'`. The ordering needed a synthetic site of its own: `match: 'key'` compares key *sets*, so two rails holding the same three workouts in a different order would otherwise agree, and the order is what both surfaces list them in. Both rails write the marks arithmetically (`5 * 60`, `29 * 60`), so the parser evaluates a bare integer and `<minutes> * 60` and **refuses** any other form rather than skipping it — a skipped mark shortens one rail's cue list, which the other rail cannot see and the comparison reads as the run it already knows. Four further conditions are hard failures for the same reason, that none of them is a disagreement a comparison can detect and two empty sets read as agreement: a missing anchor, a run with no cue marks, a run with no duration, and a parse yielding fewer runs than make a library.

**Measured.** The two rails had **not** drifted — ids, durations and all 28 cue marks are identical today (`easy-30` 1800 s / 8 cues, `tempo-builder-25` 1500 s / 9, `first-timer-15` 900 s / 11) — so the guard lands green and is a fence rather than a repair. Registry 8 → 9 entries and 34 checks; parity pairs 99 → 100 and registered paths 399 → 403. The guard is proved able to fail rather than assumed to: **seven mutations** were run against the real tree and each is caught. A cue mark moved on the phone alone names `easy-30` and prints `cue@1500` against `cue@1560`; a duration changed on the web alone prints `duration=1440` against `duration=1500`; a workout renamed on one rail raises three errors (the old id missing there, the new id missing here, and the order list); a workout deleted outright raises two; two workouts reordered with nothing else changed raises exactly one, on the order list; a mark rewritten as `const Duration(minutes: 5).inSeconds` throws and exits 1; and renaming the library function so the anchor is gone throws and exits 1. Twelve cases were added to `check_shared_constants.test.mjs` (45 → 57), among them the fixture proof that the single extractor reads the TypeScript and the Dart spelling of one library to identical output.

**Deliberately outside the lockstep.** The cue *text* is a catalogue lookup on both rails and the key identifiers differ by convention — web's dotted `guidedRuns.easy30.cue0` against mobile's camelCase `guidedEasy30Cue0` — the same carve-out `badges` and `extended_nutrients` already record for their label keys, so the guard compares marks only. Measured: **37 library keys on each of the seven web catalogues and 37 in each of the seven ARBs**, which carry **7 further `guidedRun*` keys** (`guidedRunsTitle`, `guidedRunCueCount`, `guidedRunPreviewError` and the rest) that are mobile screen chrome with no web twin and are not part of the pair. Web's `GuidedTranslate` callback against the Dart side's `AppLocalizations` parameter is the idiomatic shape difference § 278's `password_change` records, not a divergence. The Dart suite also gained the locale-switch case web already had, which was the one asymmetry in the mirror counts (18 → 19 against web's 19), mirrored byte-identically to the iOS twin per § 39.

## 802. Backlog row 9 was marked shipped on a library nothing called — guided runs now fire from the recorder tick, on the recorder's own clock, through a queueing TTS path rather than the preview's interrupting one

Competitor-parity row 9 ("Audio-coached / guided runs") has read `shipped` since 2026-06, on the strength of a cue library, a TTS layer, three scripted workouts localized into seven ARBs and seven web catalogues, a web preview surface at `/guided` + `/guided/[id]`, a mobile browse-and-preview screen, and a `no_std` Rust core on the custom watch. **None of it was connected.** `cuesDue` had no production caller on either platform — only its own definition and its mirror suites. `run_screen.dart` contained **zero** occurrences of the string "guided". The only production callers of `speakGuidedCue` were the library's own per-cue preview button and an unrelated gym-session timer. `guided_runs_screen.dart`'s doc comment said so outright and had done since the day it was written: *"the integration into the L0-L4 recording stack is a follow-up task; this screen is the surface today."* The row's own prose in `roadmap.md` asserted the opposite — that the phone "speaks the cues via `audio_cues.dart` during a recording" — so the roadmap, not the code, was the thing that had to change first. Nobody could run a guided run on any surface.

A guided run is now armed from the run screen's **idle pre-run options row**, beside *Choose route* and *Race strategy*, and an L4 block on the recorder snapshot calls `cuesDue(guided, prev, now)` and speaks what it returns. The arming lives in-screen rather than behind a widget parameter deliberately: `RunScreen.initialWorkout` is the precedent *against* that shape — it exists, it is read in three places, and **no caller anywhere passes it**, so the structured-workout preload path it was built for is itself dead. A parameter with no caller is not a feature, and repeating the pattern would have reproduced the exact defect being closed.

**The clock is `snapshot.elapsed`** — the recorder's monotonic stopwatch, which stops on a manual pause. That is the decision, not an implementation detail. A guided script is a sequence of *running* minutes ("five minutes in, settle into a rhythm"), so a runner who stops to retie a lace must still hear the five-minute cue at five minutes of running. A wall clock silently skips past cues nobody heard; fast-forwarding on resume delivers them all at once and drops the coaching outright. Both were rejected. The cursor advances only forward, so a repeated or rewound tick cannot re-fire a mark — `cuesDue` is idempotent over a range, but only while the range's floor never walks backwards, and that is the caller's obligation rather than the helper's. The cursor also advances **while the cues are muted**: a mark is a moment rather than a queue, so un-muting at twelve minutes must not then dump the five- and ten-minute cues.

**A second defect sat one layer beneath the filed one, in the cue layer the fix had to call.** `speakGuidedCue` calls `_tts.stop()` before it speaks, and `run_recording.md` row 18 names it as *the* single deliberate exception to the `QUEUE_ADD` mode Android is put into precisely so a cue landing on a busy tick is not truncated. That exception is correct for the library's preview button — tapping down a list should play the cue you just tapped, not enqueue every one you tried — and **wrong for a recording**. Guided cues sit on fixed time marks (0:00, 5:00, 10:00 …), so they collide by construction with kilometre splits, off-route warnings and cut-off catch-ups; wiring the recorder to the interrupting path would have let one L4 auxiliary cut a **safety** cue off mid-word, on both platforms, with nothing in the suite able to fail. `announceGuidedCue` is the queueing sibling, shaped like every other `announceX`; the preview keeps its explicit interrupt, and a source guard now pins each to its own behaviour.

Guided cues get their **own `guided_run` voice-cue id** rather than riding `VoiceCue.workoutSteps`: a runner who silenced a structured workout's step calls has said nothing about coach scripts, and conflating them would make one toggle mean two things. An id absent from the `voice_cue_types` bag is ON, so the addition needs no migration — but it is a wire contract with four homes (the Dart `VoiceCue` class, web's `VOICE_CUE_IDS`, both settings surfaces, the `settings.md` registry), and `voice_cues.test.ts` reads the Dart source directly so the two cannot drift. That spec's own row count was a hard-coded `8`, which would have failed on a correct change; it now counts from `VOICE_CUE_IDS.length`.

`runs.metadata.guided_run_id` stores the **library id, never an index** — the library is rebuilt per locale and a later build inserting or reordering a workout would silently re-point every stored index, which is the same reasoning the `SET1` wire field already carried. **It is owner-only, and the first classification was wrong.** It was filed public-safe by analogy with `sub_sport`, on the reasoning that a catalogue id carries no geographic, identity or pace signal. That reading fails on both halves: `trail` and `treadmill` describe where the feet landed, whereas `first-timer-15` is a statement about the *person*, legible to any anonymous reader of the share page without a lookup; and the comparison against `plan_workout_id` runs backwards, since that key is an opaque uuid disclosing nothing until resolved against a table the reader cannot select from — and it is stripped. Exposing the legible label while hiding the opaque one inverts the projection's own logic, and the structured-workout trio it belongs with is already owner-only. Nothing reads the key on any surface yet, so no consumer regresses: a projection can be widened later, once a reader exists and the runner can see what they would be publishing, but it cannot un-publish what anonymous readers have already fetched.

Arming also reaches the wrist, behind the `isLocalSupabaseUrl` loopback gate the route-detail course push already uses (§ 71 — the custom watch is research-tier with no unit in anyone's hands). This closes a path that was built and permanently unreachable: `watch_settings.dart` has carried `guidedRunIdLen`, the `0x20` flag and the `guidedRunId` field for months with **its own test file as the only writer**, and the sweep found the defect is wider than the one slot — the only production constructor of `WatchSettings` anywhere is the dev-only Sim Watch screen's canned demo config, so no product flow has ever pushed a `SET1` frame. This is the first one. A real settings-push surface (max HR, pacer, gear, ICE) remains unbuilt and is filed.

Verified rather than asserted: 17 new widget tests drive the real `RunScreen` through the real affordance and the real tick — not a replica beside it, which is the mistake § 704 records being made and fixed on the treadmill toggle — covering arming and clearing, the opener firing once across eight ticks, the master mute, the new per-cue toggle, **`workout_steps` muted while a guided cue still speaks** (the entire point of the separate id), a TTS throw leaving L0/L1 intact and the run still saving, a pause holding the place, the crash checkpoint carrying the key, and the wrist id read back off the wire bytes. One honest limitation is recorded in the test file's header rather than papered over: `flutter_test`'s fake clock does not reach `Stopwatch` (measured — `pump(5s)` leaves `elapsed` at 0.9 ms), so the only mark a widget test can cross in-process is the script's own 0:00 opener; the pause and monotonicity invariants are pinned by two source guards resting on the recorder's own already-tested stopwatch behaviour.

## 803. `public_runs` projects metadata by subtraction, so the pgtap suite that proves each key is gone asserts the keys it names rather than the keys the view strips — and stood four behind it

`public_runs` is what an anonymous reader of a share page selects from, and it projects `metadata` by subtraction: `coalesce(r.metadata,'{}') - 'strava_id' - 'garmin_id' - …`. **A denylist means every key `runs.metadata` grows is public by default**, and the only thing standing between a new key and the share page is an author remembering one line in one migration. `rls_public_runs_view_denylist_test.sql` exists to make that memory unnecessary, and its header instructs the next author outright: *"Adding a new key to the strip list = add it to the array below."*

The instruction was ignored three times. Measured by replaying the migration set: the live view stripped 31 keys and the pgtap array asserted 27 — `watch_workout` (added by `20270430_001`, the custom watch's per-step actual paces and adherence roll-up), `safety_escalated_at` (`20270401_001`), `expected_return_at` (`20270410_001`, not `20270401_001` as `metadata.md` credited it), and `guided_run_id` from this round. **Nothing could tell**, and the reason is structural rather than an oversight in the test: it asserts the keys it *names* are absent, so a short array is exactly as green as a complete one. The single shape of failure the file exists to catch — a key reaching the view's output — is the one shape it cannot see, because an unnamed key is never looked for. This is § 792's transcription rot and § 787's "a value with more than one home", on the projection that decides what strangers can read.

**A fifth defect made half the obvious fix a trap.** The four keys were missing from the fixture's `jsonb_build_object` as well as from the array. Adding them to the array alone would have made all four assertions vacuous in the most convincing way available — four new green lines asserting that keys the row never carried read back absent, which they would whatever the view did with them. A key must be *built* before its absence downstream means anything.

The fix is a `check_shared_constants.mjs` entry comparing the two homes as sets, order in a `- 'k'` chain being meaningless. The SQL rail is the **live** view, which required teaching `indexMigrations` to replay views the way it already replayed functions: the projection in force is the one the last `create or replace view public_runs` wrote, and for `expected_return_at` that was a file named `_safety_sms_escalation`, three migrations after the last one named for the view — so reading any single file, or the newest-named one, certifies nothing. The `create … view` match is anchored at statement start so DDL issued inside a function body cannot register as a definition, and statements come from the Postgres lexer so a commented-out definition cannot either, which is § 773's trap one relation over. Every parse throws rather than returning an empty set — no view, no metadata projection inside it, no array, or zero keys on either side — because two empty sets read as agreement. And the pgtap rail carries the one check a set comparison structurally cannot make: it reads the fixture and throws when the array asserts a key the row never builds, so the vacuity that nearly shipped here fails the build instead.

Proved able to fail rather than assumed to, on the real tree: a key dropped from the array reports `missing there`, a `- 'key'` line dropped from the view reports `only there`, a renamed array throws naming the file and saying the rail would otherwise agree with every other one, and a key removed from the fixture alone throws saying the assertion passes without measuring anything. The pgtap file itself was run against the live stack **without resetting it** — the shared local Supabase serves ~130 worktrees on this box — by splicing the migration's DDL inside the test's own `begin … rollback`, with a positive control that deleting the new strip line makes the assertion fail. The stack was left byte-for-byte as found, ledger head unmoved. A view-only change alters no column types (`public_runs.metadata` is `jsonb` on both sides of the transaction, 21 columns each) and the Dart generator ignores views entirely, so no regeneration was owed — checked rather than assumed.

**Still open, filed not fixed:** `metadata.md` records `indoor_source` as leaking through the view and classified public-safe "to match reality", citing a verification against view migration `20270302_001` that is now five redefinitions stale. The key is still absent from the live denylist. Whether a recorder-internal treadmill flag should be owner-only is a privacy call rather than a drift repair, but the citation misleads whichever way that call goes.

## 804. The four indoor keys split on fact versus provenance, and `seed.sql` was a third home of the denylist that stood seven keys behind

`metadata.md` carried `indoor_source` as a **known leak**: not in the `public_runs` denylist, "classified here as public-safe to match reality", with an invitation to strip it in the next projection migration and a verification citing view migration `20270302_001` — five redefinitions stale by the time it was read. Deciding it needed a line, because the four keys describing an indoor run had been split across the projection with no principle behind the split: `indoor` and `indoor_source` public, `indoor_estimated` and `distance_source` stripped. **The sharp case is the middle two.** `distance_source: "treadmill"` and `indoor_source: "treadmill"` carry the same fact in the same words, are written on the same run by the same recorder path, and landed on opposite sides of the view.

The line that makes them coherent is **fact versus provenance**. THAT a run was indoors is a property of the run — useful on a share page, carrying nothing about the runner beyond where the feet landed, the `sub_sport` class — and `indoor` stays public for that reason. WHICH SENSOR produced the distance is a recorder internal; the registry marks both `indoor_source` and `distance_source` audit-only and neither has a reader on any surface. `indoor_source` was public **by omission rather than by a decision anyone recorded**, which is what the "to match reality" framing had quietly ratified: the classification was written to describe the leak instead of to settle it. `20270628000001` strips it. Note this cuts the opposite way from § 802's `guided_run_id` call, and deliberately so — the same distinction, applied in both directions rather than only the strict one. A surface type is not a claim about the person; a beginner label is.

**Writing that migration found a third home of the denylist.** Beyond the view and the pgtap array § 803 had just paired, `apps/backend/supabase/seed.sql` builds a public run carrying every owner-only key and asserts through the view that none survive — its comment claims lockstep with the strip chain, and `metadata.md` told readers "an unclassified key that's accidentally dropped (or accidentally exposed) will fail the seed". Measured: the view stripped 32 keys and the seed asserted 25. **Seven behind** — `age_group`, `age_group_place`, `gun_time` (from `20270214_001`), `expected_return_at`, `safety_escalated_at`, plus the two added in this round. The failure is § 803's exactly, one file over and undetected by § 803's own fix, because a guard built for two homes cannot see a third: the seed asserts the keys it *names*, so a short chain is as green as a complete one, and the doc's promise was false for the same structural reason the pgtap file's header was.

The entry now carries three rails. Two details were needed to read the seed honestly. The strip-list block is anchored on the `IF … THEN` whose body raises `strip list incomplete`, because the identical `v_public_metadata ? 'key'` spelling asserts a few lines above that `activity_type` and `title` **survive** — reading the file at large would fold those two into the denylist and report a disagreement that is really two assertions pointing opposite ways. And `jsonbBuildObjectKeys` had to learn that a key may be preceded by `--` comment lines: the lexer leaves comments intact inside a dollar-quoted body, correctly, since that body is a string literal — and `seed.sql` annotates each group of keys with the migration that added it, so **every commented group read as unbuilt**. That surfaced as the new rail's own vacuity check firing on six keys the fixture demonstrably did carry, which is the anti-vacuity machinery catching a defect in itself before it could vouch for anything.

Proved able to fail: a key dropped from the seed's chain reports `missing there: indoor_source` against the other two rails. § 803's own mutation test now expects **two** errors rather than one, because a strip line removed from the view disagrees with the pgtap array and the seed independently — which is the point of holding three homes rather than two, and the assertion says so. The `keys.length === 0` branch is reachable only when the chain stops naming literals (a rewrite to `? v_key` over a loop variable keeps the anchor while taking the names out of the file), and the test constructs that case rather than one the anchor rejects first.

## 805. A guided run says so afterwards on both platforms, an id the library no longer carries keeps the claim and drops the name, and the handoff consumes where the pattern it copied parks

§ 802 shipped the execution loop and stamped `runs.metadata.guided_run_id`, and nothing read it — a runner finished a coached session and the app kept no visible record of it. Both platforms now name the script on run detail: a chip in `/runs/[id]`'s `.detail-meta` provenance row on web, `_buildGuidedRun` on `run_detail_screen.dart` on mobile. Web puts it in the header rather than in a section because the attribution is **provenance, not analysis** — `.detail-meta` is where every other "what kind of run was this" chip already lives, each self-hiding, and a one-line `<section>` for a single fact would be the empty-card shape the anti-clutter rule names, three hundred lines below the fold. Mobile places it directly under the activity-type header for the same reason: the alternative slot beside `WorkoutReviewSection` groups it correctly by concept and buries it under the elevation chart, laps, dynamics and best efforts.

**An id the shipped library no longer answers to keeps the claim and drops the name.** The library is versioned in code and rebuilt per locale, so a workout a later build renames or removes resolves to null on runs already recorded — a real state, not a hypothesis. Self-hiding there would make the app's own record of a run change between builds and present a coached session as a silent one; rendering the stored id would show an English identifier to every reader in seven locales. So both platforms keep the chip, unnamed, and both suites pin that the slug never reaches a reader. Web additionally drops the link, because `/guided/<unknown>` is the library's own dead-end empty state and sending a reader there is worse than not offering the target.

The readout is **owner-only twice over**, which is worth recording because the two mechanisms are independent: `20270627000001` strips the key from `public_runs`, and on web the chip sits inside the owner branch of the template that a non-owner never enters (a non-owner gets `RunShareView`). Widening the projection later would therefore not by itself expose the chip, and mobile's `public_run_screen.dart` cannot see the key at all.

**The handoff consumes where the pattern it copied parks, and that divergence is the finding.** `Use this run` on `GuidedRunDetailScreen` parks the library **id** — never the resolved `GuidedRun`, since the library is rebuilt per locale and the recorder must re-resolve against its own — in a `pendingArmGuidedRun` notifier declared beside the existing `pendingStartWorkout`, then pops to the shell, because the pushed screens would otherwise cover the tab switch. The Run tab drains it post-frame in `initState` as well as on notification, since that tab is built lazily and a deeper screen routinely parks the id before the `State` exists. Arming goes through the same `_armGuidedRun` the in-screen picker ends on, so the watch `SET1` push, the cue-cursor reset and the metadata stamp cannot diverge between the two entry points — proved through the wire rather than the label, by asserting a handoff produces a frame carrying `easy-30`.

Where `_onPendingStartWorkout` leaves its value parked when the screen is not idle, this one is nulled on arrival before any decision. Two reasons, and the first is a latent defect in the pattern being copied: a `ValueNotifier` does not fire on an unchanged value, so a parked `String` id makes a **second tap on the same run a silent no-op** — the workout path escapes this today only because `PlanWorkoutRow` instances are freshly fetched and never compare equal, which is luck rather than design and is filed. And arming mid-recording rewinds `_guidedCueSec` to `-1`, so a value held until the recorder went idle would let the next tick replay every mark the runner had already passed, in one burst. A non-idle arrival is therefore dropped with a `debugPrint` rather than held.

## 806. The race-import provider vocabulary lives in one catalogue per platform keyed by the Edge Function's own token — a surface branching on a provider name is the defect, and "only a credential away" was false three times over

`roadmap.md` said of the race-results providers: *"Provisioning each credential is the only remaining go-live step."* `race-results-import` has had four built legs since 2026-06 — `runsignup`, `ultrasignup`, `chronotrack`, `paste` — each fail-closed behind its own credentials with a per-provider Settings card. **Three things were wrong with that sentence, and none of them was a missing key.**

**(a) Both clients' import UI branched on `runsignup` alone.** Web's `/races` modal and mobile's `races_screen` each carried exactly two arms — RunSignUp configured, RunSignUp not — and a ChronoTrack or UltraSignup listing fell straight through to the manual-paste form below. So provisioning `CHRONOTRACK_*` today would have lit a Settings card whose link goes to a page that cannot reach the leg it advertises. That is missing client code hiding behind what the docs called a pure credential gate — the same shape as § 802, where a roadmap row claimed a feature worked while its helper had no caller. **The same defect sat on a second surface**, the run-detail auto-match prompt, which additionally caught only `'RUNSIGNUP_UNAVAILABLE'` — so a ChronoTrack candidate on an unconfigured leg reported a generic failure and offered nothing, where a RunSignUp one would have dropped to paste.

**(b) UltraSignup did not exist on the phone at all** — absent from the provider union, no probe, no Settings tile, and zero ARB keys, against a full web surface in all seven catalogues. A straight inversion of the web-canonical rule (§ 24).

**(c) `race-listings-sync` is a stub.** It validates its credentials and returns `{ synced: 0 }`; the upcoming-races fetch and upsert are unwritten, and the function's own comment has said so since it shipped. Fully provisioned, the calendar would still hold only parkrun listings, crowd submissions and hand inserts. This is the item that actually remains, and it is deliberately **not** written here: the response shape cannot be observed without a key, and guessing at it is the same fragility the per-site scrapers were already deferred for. Naming it as a credential gate concealed unwritten ingest.

The rule this encodes is that **the import-provider vocabulary lives in one catalogue per platform, keyed by the token the Edge Function itself dispatches on** — web's `RACE_IMPORT_LEGS`, mobile's `raceImportProviders` — and a surface branching on a provider name is the defect rather than the implementation. Each entry carries its own scope field, hint, testids and **its own unavailable explainer**: a runner told "RunSignUp import isn't available" about a ChronoTrack race learns nothing true, and the fall-through ternary that produced exactly that was replaced by a keyed map. Web derives the leg type from the import call's own `provider` field intersected with the `RaceProvider` union, so `tsc` makes the record exhaustive and a leg added server-side fails compilation; mobile switches an explicit `RaceImportScope` enum for the same reason. Both platforms carry a test that reads `race-results-import`'s accepted-provider literal and asserts the catalogue covers it, so a leg built server-side cannot stay unreachable on a client.

**The two vocabularies are deliberately different overlapping sets and must not be merged.** The import set has four values; the listing set (`race_listings.provider`, CHECK-constrained) has six. `paste` is a leg with no listing behind it, and `parkrun` / `manual` / `raceresult` are listings with no leg — those fall through to manual paste, which is the correct answer for them rather than a gap. Only the listing set is CHECK-constrained, which is why only it is registered in `check_constraint_unions.mjs`; the import set is guarded by the dispatch-literal tests instead, since it has no column to be a rail of.

**A defect one layer beneath, in the leg the round was adding a client for.** `runSignUpScopeGate` and `chronoTrackScopeGate` both reject an unscoped request 400 before any upstream fetch; the UltraSignup branch had no gate, and fell back to the listing's `provider_race_id` when no athlete id was supplied. That column holds a RACE id — by its name and by every other provider's use of it — while the UltraSignup endpoint reads one ATHLETE's history, so the fallback would fetch a race and then stamp the caller's `user_id` onto whichever finisher came back. It was closed by the absence of data rather than by a check, since (c) means nothing populates UltraSignup listings. `ultraSignUpScopeGate` now refuses an unscoped call, both clients require the field, and the web suite pins the general invariant rather than the coincidence it originally asserted: **every leg has a `*ScopeGate` in the function and is marked scope-required in the client catalogue.** The first version of that test asserted every scoped leg was a *bib* leg, which was true only while UltraSignup was the ungated one.

## 807. The icon-font reader took any quoted vocabulary word, so 24 of 348 shipped glyphs were named by test fixtures alone

The subset generator's last pass takes any single-, double- or backtick-quoted bare token that appears in the 4275-word Material Symbols ligature vocabulary, deliberately: an icon that arrives through an expression has to be found where its *name* is written, not where it is rendered. The cost of that over-approximation had never been measured. The vocabulary is full of ordinary English, and `collectSources` walked every `.ts` under `apps/web/src` including the 356 test modules — so `padding`, `privacy`, `javascript`, `mystery`, `usb`, `https`, `stack` and seventeen more were pulled into the shipped face by fixtures. Measured: 348 icons selected, 324 from the sources that actually reach a bundle.

The failure that surfaced it was the other half of the same defect. A new test fixture containing `class="stack"` — a `div`, not an icon span — made the coverage gate demand a glyph for `stack`, failing the build on a font that was correct. So the fixture was not the bug and renaming it would have been the wrong fix; the next fixture quoting a common word would have hit it again.

`collectSources` now skips `*.test.*` / `*.spec.*`. Nothing under those names reaches a bundle, so a ligature spelled inside one renders nowhere and must not pull a glyph. Subset: 347 to 324 icons, 75,096 to 70,416 bytes. The exclusion is pinned by a positive control rather than by its absence — the reader is fed the fixture shape directly and *does* select the word, so the rule is shown to be load-bearing rather than merely tidy. Removing the skip fails two tests.

## 808. The Art 20 archive was missing eight `user_profiles` columns, because that table reaches it through an enumerated `select` rather than through the table-level spec

`user_profiles` is not in `exportPersonalDataSpecs`; it enters the export archive only through `FetchExportProfile`'s hand-written projection, which is why the table-level completeness guard never covered it. Absent from every archive a subject has ever downloaded: `handle`, `height_cm`, `onboarded_at`, `terms_accepted_at`, `age_confirmed_at`, `coach_consent_at`, `health_data_consent_at`, `ai_disclosure_version`.

`height_cm` is the sharpest of the eight. [§ 718](#718) records that `withdraw_health_data_consent()` clears `date_of_birth`, `gender` and `height_cm` as one Art 9 set — the archive was exporting two of the three, so the record the subject can ask us to erase was not the record we would hand them.

Fixed on both rails, and the completeness claim is now derived rather than transcribed: the guard parses every `user_profiles` column out of the migrations and fails unless each is projected or sits in a reasoned exclusion list, so a new personal-data column fails this test rather than shipping unexported. The Edge Function twin's `PROFILE_SELECT` held the narrow eleven; the queued Go rail is the only one either client reaches ([§ 724](#724)), but the function is deployed and a subject who reaches it must not get a thinner archive. Both are registered in `check_shared_constants.mjs` and read from source, so a rail that stops being extractable reports as blind rather than as agreeing — the failure mode [§ 787](#787) exists for.

## 809. An allowlist entry with no origin admitted every URL that has none

`events-connect-onboard` takes `return_url` and `refresh_url` from the request body and gates them against `STRIPE_EVENTS_ALLOWED_REDIRECTS` by comparing `new URL(x).origin` strings. Every opaque-origin URL — a custom scheme, `data:`, `javascript:` — serialises its origin to the literal string `"null"`, so a single custom-scheme entry in the allowlist made the gate admit all of them. Measured: `validateReturnUrl('javascript:alert(1)', ['data:text/plain,x'])` returned true, and `validateReturnUrl('evil-app://steal', ['threkir://payouts-return'])` returned true.

The configuration that opens it is not exotic. The sibling `STRAVA_ALLOWED_REDIRECTS` really does carry `threkir://strava-callback`, and this gate's own comment points at that convention as the thing it follows. An opaque candidate is now refused before the allowlist is consulted. `_shared/redirect_allowlist.ts` was checked and is immune — it matches whole strings — and the other `.origin` reads in the tree are default-URL construction, not gates.

## 810. `enforce_create_rate_limit`'s service-role skip has never fired, six weeks after the same mistake was fixed next door

Migration `20260726_001` moved `check_rate_limit` and `check_rate_limit_tiered` onto the claim shape PostgREST actually sets — the JSON blob `request.jwt.claims`, never the deprecated per-claim `request.jwt.claim.role` — and its header records what getting it wrong had cost: every fail-closed Edge Function rejecting its own service-role-keyed admin call, a blanket 503. `20260907_001` then wrote `enforce_create_rate_limit` reaching for the legacy setting alone. Measured against the live catalogue, it was the only function left in `public` or `private` reading that claim with no JSON fallback.

It is latent rather than live because a second skip covers it by accident: a service-role JWT carries no `sub`, so `auth.uid() is null` returns first. The moment a service-role caller carries one — admin tooling acting for a named user, which is exactly what skip 1's own comment describes — it is throttled against that user's queue, and all eleven buckets riding the helper inherit it. Fixed with the coalesce shape every sibling uses, pinned failing-first in both rate-limit suites.

## 811. A live region only announces what changes while it is already mounted — and four more surfaces were mounting the region with its first message

[§ 736](#736) fixed this in `ToastContainer` and [§ 797](#797) had to correct the same shape again before merge; the sweep for the class had never been run across the tree. Four surfaces were mounting an `aria-live` container and its first message in a single DOM mutation, which announces nothing: the offline banner in `+layout.svelte`, the `{#if info}` status on `/login`, and — the worse two — `clubs/join/[token]` and `coaching/accept/[token]`, which put `aria-live` on the *joining* branch. That branch is the page's first state, so the result that replaces it was announced by nobody at all.

All four now use the house idiom: a permanently mounted region whose contents are conditional. The guard is a derived scan over the tree rather than a fifth per-component test, and it names all four on unmodified `main`. Scope is deliberately the explicit `aria-live` attribute only, which is what § 736 and § 797 legislated; `role="status"` / `role="alert"` as implicit regions is a wider sweep with materially different screen-reader behaviour between the two, and is left for a dedicated round rather than half-done.

## 812. A device-state toggle that repaints on four of its five arms states the device's state four-fifths of the time

[§ 704](#704) made the treadmill subtitle switch on `BleTreadmillStatus` rather than on the last figure the belt sent. The status listener's `connected` arm fired a two-second banner and returned with no `setState` — the only one of the five arms without one. `_treadmillStatus` updated; the card did not repaint.

Indoors this is not cosmetic. The belt *is* the distance source and the position stream is silent, so nothing else repaints that card until the next FTMS notification. A belt that reconnects and then idles — a treadmill stopped between intervals — leaves an engaged toggle asserting the belt is lost, underneath a "reconnected" banner that has already expired. Fixed, mirrored to the iOS twin, pinned by a test that fails on the unfixed arm.

## 813. Five more guards that misread their own input, and the class [§ 773](#773) named was still open in a spelling nobody had probed

`shell_lex.mjs` did not treat a backtick as a command boundary, so an unquoted `` `aws ssm get-parameter --name live` `` stayed inside the *enclosing* command's word list and `check_lambda_alias_sync`'s `words.indexOf('--name')` read `live` for a call whose real `--name` was `stable` — certifying an alias the script never repoints. This is § 773's decoy exactly, one quoting form over.

Four more of the same shape. [§ 705](#705)'s Rust toolchain pin was enforced by nothing: `check_toolchain_pins.mjs` covered Flutter, melos, defmt-print and the action SHAs but not `rust-toolchain.toml`, so `channel = "stable"` installs, builds and clippies cleanly today and fails whoever pushes after the next lint lands — which is the entire failure § 705 exists to prevent. `check_web_bundle_budget.mjs` passed over an empty walk, because all four of its ceilings are upper bounds and `files: []` satisfies every one. `check_migration_versions.mjs` reported `OK: 0 migrations` and exited 0 on an empty or unversioned directory. `check_watch_page_ring.mjs` merged the edges of two pages sharing a code, so the ring could agree with a diagram drawing neither.

The durable half is a census in `check_ci_diagnostics.test.mjs`: every guard is invoked by a workflow, every guard has a suite, that suite runs, and the guards the gate does not wait for are named with a reason. It reads *run commands* with `npm run` scripts spliced in and comments and `echo` lines stripped — a comment naming a script does not satisfy it, which is precisely how § 773's `check_root_scripts` looked covered while never running in CI at all.

## 814. Three export-rail defects that are each one line from being reachable, and the argument for closing them anyway

`handleJobsLatest` signed unconditionally on `status == "ready"`, so a row that reached `ready` with no `object_path` handed the subject a signed URL for the empty path — a download button that 404s, which is the shape [§ 724](#724)'s client pair already refuses on the other side of the wire. It now reports `failed` with `artifact_missing` and signs nothing.

Two more were unreachable rather than harmless. The run-photo loop trusted `run_photos.storage_path` after a traversal check only, where the orphan sweep beside it already filtered on the subject's prefix — so a row naming another subject's object would have been fetched by the service role into this subject's archive, guarded in production only by a column shape CHECK and an `owner_id` filter one layer up. And `handleDataExport` never checked that the payload's subject owns the export row, so a `jobs` row whose `payload.user_id` differed from `data_export_jobs.user_id` would build subject A's whole archive and record it against subject B's, who could then download it. Nothing can write such a row today: `enqueue_data_export` derives both from one argument, and `jobs` is RLS-on-with-no-policies.

Both are fixed rather than filed, because "unreachable" here is a property of the current writers rather than of the code, and the assertion is what keeps it true for the next one. This is [§ 745](#745)'s lesson pointed at an application: a second access-control mechanism that happens to hold is not the same as the check being present.

## 815. The handler-envelope suite's "23 integration tests" were 22, three of them were not measuring the gate they named, and neutering the served tree costs no second host

**Landed 2026-08-31.** [§ 788](#788) mutation-checks the Edge Function Deno suite by neutering every module the *test process* imports. `_shared/handler_envelope.test.ts` imports none of them: it drives a separately-booted `supabase functions serve` host over HTTP, so that operator scored its cases as neither killed nor survived. Two followup entries said so, and both were right about the gap and wrong about almost everything around it.

**The count was the deno *ignored* count, not a test count.** The file holds 23 `Deno.test` calls, of which 22 ran — 18 gated on `SUPABASE_TEST_URL`, 4 more additionally on `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY`. The 23rd is a placeholder with `ignore: true` and an empty body, added so `deno test` reports an ignored case rather than "no tests" when the var is unset. It asserts nothing and never runs in either lane. `785 passed | 24 ignored` is what the pure-helper lane prints today, and 23 of those 24 are the integration cases.

**The price was wrong too.** The entries costed the fix at "a second mutant tree and a second host boot in CI (~1 min)". `supabase functions serve` re-reads a changed module on the next request — measured at under 1.4 s from write to changed response — so the operator mutates the tree the host is *already* serving. No second tree, no second host, no second stack: 20 mutations over 23 cases in 58–69 s (two runs, this workstation) inside the job that had already booted everything.

**"Nothing suggests they are vacuous" was false for three of them,** and a blanket operator would have found none of the three. The point of mutating one gate at a time is that each round declares both what must die and what must NOT (`spares`), which is what separates "this case measures the compare" from "this case measures that some gate exists".

- `403 on GET with no ?secret=` was answered 403 by the **verify-token** gate one branch further in, which refuses an absent token with the same status and the same body. Opening the secret gate entirely left the case passing. It now sends a correct `hub.verify_token`, leaving the secret gate as the only thing that can answer 403.
- The **verify-token gate had no case at all**. An attacker holding the URL secret could complete a Strava subscription handshake and nothing in the file would have noticed. One was added; its mutation is what the round exists to have killed.
- `200 "OK" on non-create event` asserted a body the **not-connected-athlete** branch further down returns verbatim, so deleting the early return the case exists to prove left it green — having burned the `webhook_events` row that early return exists to avoid. Its `event_time` is now 30 days stale, which only a return *before* the replay-window gate can answer 200 to.

**Coverage is enforced in both directions.** Every case the baseline ran must appear in some mutation's `kills`, so a new case in the file fails the guard until a mutation names it; a mutation naming a case the baseline never ran fails too, so a rename cannot quietly return a gate to unmeasured. `validateMutations` additionally refuses an anchor that does not occur exactly once in the handler it names, which is the same rot in the other direction and is checked without a host by the guard's own unit suite.

Two mechanics were forced by the medium rather than chosen. A probe is how a round knows the host is serving the mutant, and the four side-effect mutations change a database write and not a response, so they carry a **beacon**: a second edit flipping a status code no case in that round asserts, whose appearance is what the probe waits for.

**The probe's first shape was wrong, and only real CI could show it.** It waited for an answer that merely *differed* from the pre-mutation one, on two consecutive polls. `supabase functions serve` restarts the runtime around a file change, and a request landing in that window is answered by kong with a gateway 503 or by a reset connection — both differ from the baseline answer, so two of them in a row let the round proceed against a host that was serving nothing at all. Every case in the round then failed on the wrong answer, which scores the kills as killed and the **spares as moved**. Run 33421025889 reported exactly that: 0 survivors and one moved spare on `strava-non-create-early-return-dropped`, whose mutation cannot reach that spare's code path at all — the spare's event is `activity`/`create`, so the early return the mutation deletes never fired for it in either tree. The restart window is milliseconds on a warm workstation and seconds on a loaded two-core runner, so the workstation could not produce it; a `supabase db reset` reproduced nothing either, because the mechanism was never about database state — fifteen consecutive local runs of that exact round against a freshly reset stack gave `1 passed | 1 failed` fifteen times.

A round now waits for the answer the mutation **declares**, byte-identically twice, rather than for any change. A gateway status may be declared only alongside a body no restart can produce — which one mutation genuinely needs, since an accepted `auth-email` signature falls through to a real `503 smtp_not_configured` — and the table validator refuses a bare 502/503/504. The restore half of the wait was always exact, comparing against a fixed pre-mutation fingerprint, which is why it never mis-fired; the asymmetry between the two halves is the whole bug. Two smaller holes closed in the same pass, both of which had made the CI failure harder to read than it needed to be: a case **absent** from the report was counted as having failed rather than as not having run, and a failing round discarded deno's own output, so the annotation could say a spare moved and could not say what it answered.

And `strava-webhook` rate-limits anonymous callers 60/hour *before* the secret check, while its three rejection cases tolerate the 429 as shared-runner noise. Twenty rounds of probes and re-runs spend far more than sixty calls, and a 429 satisfies "the secret gate refused" without the gate being consulted — so the guard empties that bucket between rounds and refuses to run without the service-role key, which it needs for that as much as for the four side-effect cases.

One bystander, measured rather than reasoned: the `edge-functions` job's `docker stop supabase_edge_runtime_backend` had stopped nothing for the life of the job. Containers are named for `config.toml`'s `project_id`, which is `project-running`, so the name matched no container and `|| true` swallowed the miss. What makes the env-loaded host take over is `functions serve` itself. The line is gone and the comment above it no longer claims otherwise.

**Verification.** `check_served_envelope_mutations.mjs`: 23 cases, 20 single-gate mutations, 24 declared kills, **0 survived, 0 unmeasured** — green on the workstation stack and again after a `supabase db reset`, in 58–70 s. Each of the three findings above was a real survivor first and green only after the case was changed. `check_edge_function_test_vacuity.mjs` still reports 785 killed / 0 survived with an empty exemption list, `node --test check_served_envelope_mutations.test.mjs` passes 19 — including one that asserts no mutation's declared answer can be satisfied by a restarting runtime's 502/503/504 or reset, which is the CI failure above pinned as a unit test — `actionlint` and `check_ci_diagnostics.mjs` pass on the workflow, and `tsc -p tsconfig.scripts.json` is clean.
## 816. A string interpolation is a code region, and reading it as content made eight committed Dart files unreadable to every guard built on the shared lexer

`scripts/comment_strip.mjs` tracked Dart's strings as spans of content, so `${` was just two characters inside one. It is not: it opens a nested **code** region, and the code in it holds strings of its own — including differently-quoted ones, which is what `'"${value.replaceAll('"', '""')}"'` is — plus braces, further interpolations, comments, and newlines even when the enclosing string is single-quoted. Read as content, the first `'` inside the region closed the string it was nested in and the lexer threw `unterminated string`. [§ 793](#793) worked around it by narrowing the phone-side wire-vector sweep to the test files carrying one of the firmware's wire magics as hex, treating an unlexable file that *did* carry one as a hard error rather than a skip — so nothing was certified wrongly, but the sweep read **7** of 521 test files and skipped 514.

The region is now tracked the way block comments already nested: recursively, with its own brace depth, its own recursion into each string it contains, and its comments blanked, because a comment in a code region is a comment. Raw strings stay one verbatim span — `$` is literal in them, so their `${` is content and always was. The `$identifier` form needs no tracking at all: it can hold no delimiter. An interpolation that never closes throws, keeping § 793's rule that source a guard cannot read is source it must not report a verdict about. Rust needed nothing — `{}` in a `format!` string is content, not a code region.

The filing was wrong on the size and the shape. **8** committed files could not be lexed, not three: four distinct paths doubled by the byte-identical iOS twin, and one of the four is **library** code rather than a test (`import_failures.dart`'s CSV quoter). The newline case is inside a **single-quoted** string, not the triple-quoted one filed — Dart allows a newline inside `${…}` whatever the enclosing quotes — and it nests a brace-carrying map literal in the same region. And the workaround was structurally blind rather than merely narrow: a golden spelled payload-only, or with its magic written `[0x43, 0x52, …]`, would have sat outside the sweep with nothing to report it. That is [§ 641](#641)'s shape — a rail nothing compares — reached through a filter rather than through a missing registry row.

With the filter gone the sweep reads all **1056** Dart files under `apps/mobile_android/{lib,test}` and an unlexable one is a hard error unconditionally. Widening it immediately raised a false positive worth keeping the fix for: `status_color_literal_guard_test.dart`'s 21 banned six-digit colour literals joined into one 63-byte "vector", so `dartHexConsts` now refuses a collection-shaped declaration. The test is on the `[` and not on the comma between the elements — the registered `_goldenBlob` is `_hex('…' '…',)`, a trailing comma in a call, and the guard's own suite failed a comma rule that dropped it, which is the argument for guards having suites.

Verified by measurement rather than by the suite alone: **1969 of 1969** committed Dart files lex, up from 1961, and across all **2129** Dart + Rust files the new lexer's output is byte-identical to the old one wherever the old one ran — **0** differences — and idempotent on every one. `comment_strip.test.mjs` carries the tree-wide case itself (1056 files, ~0.4 s), because the hole existed for as long as it did precisely because nothing read the whole tree.

Deliberately not closed here: `check_watch_wire_vectors.mjs`'s 14 `otherRail` reads over 6 Swift / Kotlin / TypeScript / Monkey C files are still taken from **raw** source with no comment stripping at all, so a commented-out declaration there can answer for a live one. Measured latent, not live — the nearest misses are a `WatchIngestBridge.swift` doc comment naming `ArmedRoute.maxPoints` where that file's rail reads `maxRoutePoints`, and `[MIN_SEGMENT_M]` in `grade_adjusted_pace.ts` prose, which `tsConst` does not match. Closing it means teaching the lexer Swift's `\(…)`, Kotlin's `${…}` plus `"""`, and TypeScript template literals, and that is a round of its own rather than a rider on this one.
## 817. An anonymous inline union is a vocabulary the registry cannot name, and there were sixteen of them behind four columns

[§ 791](#791) keyed `check_constraint_unions.mjs` on the COLUMN and left fifteen entries with an empty `clients` list — a column no client spells out, recorded rather than skipped. Four of those fifteen were miscategorised: a client *does* enumerate `event_results.finisher_status`, `race_sessions.status`, `reports.status` and `coach_messages.role`, just anonymously, so there was no declaration for a rail to point at and the entry read as "nobody names this" when the truth was "everybody names it, sixteen times".

Sixteen is measured, and it is roughly three times what the filing claimed. `'finished' | 'dnf' | 'dns'` appears **five** times in full (`core/data.ts` twice, `runs/event_results_csv.ts` three times) plus once as the `'dnf' | 'dns'` subset in `recordNonFinish`; `'user' | 'assistant'` appears **six** times across three files, of which the two provider signatures the filing named are a third — the rest sit in `CoachRequestBody` and three times inside `CoachChat.svelte`; `reports.status` is **three** call sites, not two; `race_sessions.status` is the one the filing counted correctly. Sixteen spellings over seven files, all now one exported type apiece: `FinisherStatus` and `RaceSessionStatus` in `types.ts`, `ReportResolution` beside `ReportReason` in `data.ts`, `CoachMessageRole` in `coach/types.ts`. The subset spelling is derived rather than re-typed — `Exclude<FinisherStatus, 'finished'>` — so widening the column cannot leave a narrower copy of it behind.

`reports.status` is the one that is not four lines: the column admits three values and the client may only ever write two, because `pending` is the insert default the moderation queue reads and never sets. It therefore carries a staleness-checked `allowMissing: ['pending']`, which keeps the honest asymmetry while still failing on a fourth status — a plain rail would have failed the guard the moment it was added, and widening the type to satisfy it would have let a surface offer a status the resolve RPC rejects.

Each of the four is pinned by widening its real CHECK in memory and asserting the rail is what fails, because a registered rail proves nothing about what it catches.

## 818. Dart's exhaustive lookups cannot be made exhaustive, so the guard reads the switch itself — 50 of them, not 4

[§ 791](#791) deliberately left web's icon and label `Record<Union, X>` maps unregistered: `tsc` makes them exhaustive, and a guard over them would be checking the compiler's own work. That carve-out has no Dart counterpart. A Dart `switch` over a `String` cannot be exhaustive at all, so every one of these lookups degrades **silently** to its `default:` / `_` branch the day its CHECK gains a value — a new notification kind renders as the generic verb, a new progression scheme reads as `none`, and nothing anywhere fails.

The class is fourteen times the size the filing gave it. A sweep of the whole `apps/mobile_android/lib` tree found **50** distinct switch sites over a CHECK-constrained string column; **24** name their column's whole current vocabulary and **26** already stop short of it. Four are coincidence rather than enumeration and are deliberately not registered: `onboarding.dart`'s `planPresetForGoal` switches over the primary-goal answers, three of which happen to be spelled like `personal_records.distance` brackets, and `activity_timeline_list.dart`'s three switches read the `activities` view's own per-branch `kind` literal, which shares `run`/`lift`/`meal` with `notifications.activity_kind` without being that column. The remaining **46 are registered across 30 files and 22 columns**, taking the Dart half of the registry from 29 declarations over 22 files to **75 over 45**, and the whole registry from 121 rails to 171. Of the four sites the filing actually named, only `profile_screen.dart`'s `_verbFor` is a full-vocabulary lookup — the three progression switches name five of six and let `none` fall through, which is correct and is now declared as such.

The two fix shapes on offer were "the switches key off a registered const list" or "a shape that reads `case '<value>':`". The const list was refused. It is a second declaration that nothing checks against the switch beside it, so the two can drift with the guard green — the [§ 641](#641) shape exactly, a copy whose divergence is undetectable, and it would have meant editing 46 production call sites to install it. The `switch` shape reads the authority instead: the labels in the switch, in the file, with no proxy to keep aligned. No production Dart changed.

Addressing is by the innermost declaration whose body ENCLOSES the switch, optionally qualified by its class. Nearest-*preceding* was tried first and is wrong for a reason worth recording: it cannot tell `final banner = switch (status) {…}`, where the declaration IS the switch, from `final t = row['set_type'] …` sitting one line above one, where it is an unrelated local whose rename would silently move the rail off its switch. Ambiguity refuses rather than reading the first match, the same discipline `findInitializers` already applies one shape over. Two things the implementation had to get right before it could see the tree it was written for: comments are blanked length-preservingly, so a `/// String _oldLabel(String s) {` doc line cannot become the anchor of the switch below it; and the declaration reader scans balanced parentheses rather than matching a bounded character class, because a Dart parameter list can carry `{named}` groups — the first draft, which used a class, was blind to `_verbFor(l10n, item, {String? nameOverride})`, the widest switch in the tree, while resolving every other switch in the same file.

Twenty-two of the 46 carry a staleness-checked `allowMissing` for the one value their `default:` branch was written for. That is the point of the exemption rather than a weakening of it: the rail still fails on a value nobody has decided about, which the two mutation proofs show — widening `notifications.kind` now names both Dart switches beside the web union, and widening `route_conditions.severity` fails both of its label switches while their `info` exemption stands.

What this does not close: coverage is enforced per COLUMN, not per rail, so a *new* Dart switch over an already-registered column still enters the tree unregistered. The 50 the sweep found are in; the fifty-first is not forced.
## 819. A cap over a value read BACK is the column's number, not the client's — and the containment guard is blind to the direction that matters

[§ 792](#792) put every client input bound in one place (`core/column_limits.ts` / `column_limits.dart`, keyed `<table>.<column>`) and had `check_shared_constants.mjs` prove each sits INSIDE its column's own CHECK by replaying every migration. That is the right test for an INPUT: a composer capped below the column is merely conservative, one capped above hands the runner a raw 23514.

`nutrition_targets` is the other direction and the guard could not see it. Both halves of the parity pair refused a stored profile with `weightKg > 500 || heightCm > 300`, which is a defensive filter over a value read BACK out of the database. Measured by replay, those are exactly the two columns' CHECK maxima — `body_metrics.weight_kg` is `> 0 and <= 500` and `user_profiles.height_cm` is `> 0 and <= 300`, both in `20261216_001` — so they were transcriptions with nothing comparing them. Proved by mutation: widen the weight CHECK to 600 in a scratch migration set and `checkColumnBounds` raises **zero** errors about that column, because 250 is still inside 600. A legitimately-stored 550 kg would then have produced no calorie target on either platform, with every mirror test passing, because the pair's lockstep guarantees only that the two halves are wrong together.

So `COLUMN_CHECK_MAX` / `kColumnCheckMax` sits beside the input bounds, holding what the COLUMN accepts, and its guard demands **equality** rather than containment. Both directions are refused deliberately: below the CHECK, a value the database legitimately holds is discarded as non-physical and the surface reading it renders nothing; above it, garbage is admitted. An exclusive CHECK (`< 500`) is refused outright rather than read as an inclusive maximum, and a column whose CHECK has been dropped reports that it now certifies nothing instead of passing.
