Three things the filing had wrong or did not reach.

**The mirror-test count was 34; it is 36** — 18 web, 18 Dart, now 19 each. Small, but the figure was the filing's evidence for "with every test passing" and it was not computed.

**`ageYears > 120` is not a third DB cap.** There is no age column: age is derived from `date_of_birth`, which no CHECK bounds. It stays a stated plausible-human ceiling — but it was written twice in the same file on both platforms (`ageFromDob`'s range test and the filter), and is now `MAX_AGE_YEARS` / `maxAgeYears`, named once.

**`column_limits`' own comment on `user_profiles.height_cm` said "The column allows anything above 0."** It does not; it caps at 300, and the registered client bound of 300 is EQUAL to it, not narrower. That sentence was written by § 792 itself, in the file whose whole purpose is that a number the database owns is not transcribed — which is the argument for the guard reading the CHECK rather than for a comment describing it.

The Health Connect importer, filed as "same shape, unregistered", is worse than unregistered: its "sane 30–300 kg" disagreed with the registered bound in **both** directions. 300 is above the 250 the body-metrics field offers, so an import could seed a body weight the runner then could not re-save; 30 is above the 20 floor, so a legitimately light runner's real sample was discarded as noise. It reads `withinColumnLimit('body_metrics.weight_kg', …)` now.

Knowingly left: `apps/custom_watch/core/src/nutrition_targets.rs` carries the same two literals. It is a one-way research-tier port outside the enforced lockstep ([§ 24](#24)) with no database in reach, so it keeps its numbers and a comment naming where they come from.

## 820. A label may not name a unit the value beside it does not use, and the key may not either

The mobile weigh-in field's label key was `checkpointWeighInWeightKg` — "Body weight (kg)" in all seven catalogues — beside a `suffixText` carrying `WeightFormat.label(activeWeightUnit)`. The filing called this cosmetic on the grounds that the suffix is authoritative. It is not cosmetic: a runner on lbs read **"Body weight (kg)"** with an **"lbs"** suffix, two units in one `InputDecoration`, one of them wrong. The label names no unit now, in every locale, and the key says so.

A sweep of both platforms for the class — every ARB key whose name encodes a unit, every English value carrying a unit token, each cross-checked against whether its call site renders through a preference — found **two** contradictions, no key-only cases, and about thirty-five benign fixed-unit labels. The second was `prefsSplitIntervalDefaultSubtitle`: "Default (1 km for running, 5 km for cycling)", shown on the split-interval row whenever no override is set. `ActivityType.splitIntervalMetresFor` returns **1 mi / 5 mi** in imperial, deliberately and with a comment recording why — an imperial runner expects to be told when they pass a MILE, and defaulting everyone to a kilometre fired their splits at 0.6, 1.2, 1.9 mi. So the row named the wrong unit for exactly the runners the unit-aware default exists for. It takes the two intervals as placeholders now.

Worth recording because it is the same defect twice with opposite provenance: the weigh-in label was written before its suffix, the split-interval subtitle was left behind when the value under it was fixed. Neither is caught by a scan for hardcoded English — both strings are translated into all seven languages, and each translation faithfully carries the wrong unit. The pins are therefore per-surface rather than global: a widget test reading the rendered `InputDecoration` under a lbs preference, a widget test reading the subtitle under a mi preference, and a source guard that parses all seven catalogues so a translator restoring "(kg)" in one language alone fails the PR.

The web half of the same weigh-in already resolved this the other way, interpolating the real unit into the string (`"Body weight ({unit})"`). Both are honest; they differ because the mobile field has a suffix slot and the web one does not.
## 821. A store's atomic write is only atomic against itself — the wipe that deletes its temp file, and the delete it overtakes

`writeStringAtomic` has given every in-flight write its own `.tmp` sibling since the helper was born, so two writes to one file cannot collide on a temp path. That is the whole of what it promises, and it was read as more: nothing ordered two *operations* over an `OfflineSyncStore` directory against each other.

Two interleavings, both measured. `clear()` — the sign-out wipe — deletes EVERY file in the store's directory, deliberately, because a filename filter can only approximate "nothing of the prior user survives" ([§ 313](#313)). That includes the `.tmp` of a write still in flight, whose `rename` then fails with a `PathNotFoundException` naming a temp path its caller has never heard of. The second is silent and worse: a delete that overtakes an in-flight write to the same id removes `<id>.json`, the write's rename then puts it back, and `rowsById` says the row is gone while the file sits on disk for the next cold-load to resurrect. No exception anywhere.

Every directory-mutating entry point now runs on one serial chain. Three things about its shape are load-bearing. It is **whole-directory, not per-id**: `clear`, `rewriteAll`, `loadAll` and the index flush all touch files a per-id lock does not name, so per-id exclusion would have left each of them racing a row write. It is keyed on the **directory, not the instance**, because the interleaving that matters is between two instances — `offline_store_wipe.dart` builds a throwaway store per screen-owned type precisely because all instances of a type share one directory, so a per-instance chain would have left its `clear()` free to race the live screen's write; the cross-instance case is pinned separately and fails on a per-instance chain. And the chain never becomes an error future: one failed write must not reject every write queued behind it.

A separate isolate remains out of reach of any in-process lock. That is not a new gap — `kAtomicOrphanMinAge` already exists because the background-sync isolate runs its own store instances over the same directories.

## 822. Four gates that all failed closed, in two idioms, across five call sites — and why that was still worth changing

Filed as three mobile dotenv gates missing the try/catch their sibling has. Measured, none of the three was what it was filed as. `offRouteEscalationEnabled` and `adaptiveFitnessGateEnabled` are pure `String? → bool` parsers that never touch dotenv and cannot throw; the reads live at their call sites, and all five of those already guarded — three with `try/catch`, two with `dotenv.isInitialized &&`, which are exactly equivalent because `NotInitializedError` is the only thing `dotenv.env` throws. `_weighInGate` has carried its `try/catch` since the screen shipped.

What was true underneath is not the guard but the *binding*. Key plus guard was spelled at five sites in two idioms, two of them duplicates of each other, and two of them private top-level getters inside screen files — so "does this gate fail closed" was a question about five call sites rather than about one module, and the two private ones could not be asserted about at all. The test the filing asked for was unwritable against the code as it stood.

So each flag now has one binding module holding its key const, its guarded gate, and nothing else — `off_route_flag.dart`, `adaptive_fitness_flag.dart`, `weigh_in_flag.dart`, beside the `nearby_flag.dart` that already had this shape and mirroring web's own `*_flag.ts` layer. The parse stays in the parity-pair file it belongs to, so [§ 709](#709)'s single accepted-affirmative set is untouched. Two guards keep it: all four gates answer `false` against an uninitialised dotenv (with an affirmative case beside it, or the group would pass against four gates hard-wired off), and a gate key read literally anywhere but its own module fails the suite — which is the only thing that stops a sixth caller re-spelling the read in whichever idiom it copies.

## 823. A refund is a thing with an identity, and modelling it as a delta folded into a parent column is why a failed PARTIAL refund had nowhere to live

**Filed:** § 789 built `refund_failed` and deliberately refused to move `partially_refunded` on either ledger. The follow-up entry recorded the cost: "the money discrepancy exists **only** in a `console.error`; `event_orders` carries no refunded amount at all, and `donations.refunded_cents` keeps stating an instalment that came back to us." It proposed a per-refund child row keyed on the Stripe Refund id — "idempotent by construction, would let `refunded_cents` be *derived* rather than accumulated, and would give the partial case the same worklist the full case now has."

**The headline is exactly right and reproduces.** Both reversal handlers end a failed partial the same way: a `console.error` naming the row and the refund, then `Response.json({ ok: true, skipped: 'no_transition' })`. No write. And the only other trace is `webhook_events`, whose three columns are `(provider, event_id, received_at)` — no type, no payload, no ledger — so there is genuinely nothing in the database that relates the delivery to money. `event_orders`' `CREATE TABLE` (`20261229_001`) confirms the second half: `amount_cents`, `platform_fee_cents`, `refunded_at`, and no refunded amount at all.

**But `refunded_cents` was never accumulated, and the sentence that says it was is the load-bearing error in the filing.** `refundedCentsOfCharge` returns Stripe's own **cumulative** `charge.amount_refunded` (or, on a full refund, the donation's own `amount_cents`), and the webhook's CAS carries `.lte('refunded_cents', refundedCents)` so a delivery reporting a smaller total than the ledger already holds cannot walk it back. There is no `+=` in the path. The column is a **monotone latch on an externally-computed running total** — which is precisely what made it idempotent under § 769, and precisely what makes a failure unrepresentable: a latch has no downward direction. So the choice was never accumulate-versus-derive. It was *mirror an external total* versus *sum a local set*.

**And summing the local set is the one thing that had to be refused.** The two event families carry different objects. `charge.refunded` carries a **Charge**: it states the cumulative amount and carries no refund id, so no child row can be keyed off it. Only the refund-lifecycle trio (`refund.failed` / `refund.updated` / `charge.refund.updated`) carries a **Refund**. A refund that succeeds instantly and emits no lifecycle event therefore produces no child row at all — and *which* of these events an endpoint receives is dashboard configuration this repo cannot read, which § 789 measured and is why it handles both API eras rather than assuming one. Deriving `refunded_cents` from an incomplete set would count a succeeded refund with no row as money the charity kept: a bounded understatement traded for an **unbounded overstatement**, on a public charity thermometer. The filing's stated benefit was the one part of it that could not be built.

**So the child rows are the authority for reversals only, and the correction is strictly additive.** `payment_refunds` (migration `20270630000001`) holds one row per Stripe Refund, `stripe_refund_id` unique, exactly one parent (two nullable FKs plus a CHECK, so both sides keep real referential integrity where an untyped `(entity_type, entity_id)` would keep neither), the refund's own status from Stripe's five-value vocabulary, and its amount. `fundraiser_totals` and `fundraiser_feed` then report `amount_cents - refunded_cents + least(reversed, refunded_cents)`, where `reversed` is the sum of that donation's `failed` / `canceled` children. A reversed refund's amount is **already inside** `refunded_cents`, because `charge.refunded` fired when the refund was created — so adding it back is not new arithmetic on a running total, it is a second, separate total summed from rows that cannot be counted twice. The `least(…)` clamp keeps the whole expression inside `[0, amount_cents]` whatever a child row says. Fail-closed in the right direction throughout: a reversal we never hear about leaves § 789's "smaller, safe lie" exactly as it was.

**The idempotency proof is the schema, not the caller.** Three deliveries of one Refund upsert onto one unique key and the thermometer does not move — pinned by asserting the **total** rather than the row count, because the total is what a double-apply corrupts. That is the property the arithmetic § 789 refused could not have had: `refunded_cents -= amount` moves once per delivery. Out-of-order delivery is handled in the database rather than in the handler: `lock_payment_refund_writes` **latches a terminal status**, so a benign `refund.updated` carrying `pending` arriving after the `refund.failed` that settled the refund cannot un-say it — the same shape as the `.lte` CAS beside it, for the same reason (the wire is at-least-once and unordered).

**`refunded_cents` therefore stays a maintained mirror, and nothing new joins `derived_state.md`.** That file is the registry of trigger-maintained caches with an authoritative local recompute; `refunded_cents`' authority is Stripe, and the reversal sum is computed at read time inside the two thermometer functions over an indexed child table rather than cached anywhere. A cache column for it would be a third figure to drift.

**Two more places the filing understated itself.** "The same worklist the full case now has" is too modest: `select * from event_orders where status = 'refund_failed'` names the order but no amount, because the table has none — so even for a **full** failure an operator had to go to Stripe to learn what to pay back. `select * from payment_refunds where status in ('failed','canceled')` answers for both ledgers, both scopes, with the figure. And "a schema change, not a webhook arm" is a schema change **and** a webhook arm: nothing was writing a Refund id anywhere, so the row had to be recorded before the reversal gate and for every status — recording only the reversals would leave a failure with no sibling instalment to read it against.

**Fail-closed at both boundaries the CHECK creates.** `Stripe.Refund.status` is declared `string | null` by the SDK (§ 789), so a status this build has never heard of would reach the insert as a plain string and 23514 into an endless Stripe retry on an event that changed nothing: `knownRefundStatus` records **nothing** instead, which reproduces the pre-table behaviour exactly. `failure_reason` is third-party text under a 120-character cap (`free_text_caps_test` derives its population from the catalogue, and Stripe's longest documented reason, `charge_for_pending_refund_disputed`, is 34) and is **truncated** rather than refused — a clipped reason is still the reason, where dropping the row would lose the money discrepancy over a cosmetic field.

**RLS.** No permissive policy of any kind and `revoke all on public.payment_refunds from anon, authenticated` — the `20270621_001` lockdown taken at table level rather than as a column re-grant, because there is no client read path to serve: the payer sees the net figure `fundraiser_feed` already projects, and an operator reads it under the service role. That puts the table on `role_grant_matrix_test`'s service-role-only allow-list beside `app_quota`, `deletion_audit_log` and `data_export_jobs`, and it deliberately creates no column ACL, so `column_grant_lockdown_registry_test` owes it no entry. No new SECURITY DEFINER function is added, so no new instance of the `revoke execute … from public` trap: the only new function is a trigger function, which `anon_execute_contract_test` excludes by return type and which pins `search_path`. `fundraiser_totals` / `fundraiser_feed` are `create or replace`d, which preserves their ACL.

**Online safety.** `CREATE TABLE` locks nothing that exists; a new relation has no rows, so its CHECKs and its unique index are written single-step and the online two-step would be ceremony over zero rows. The two FKs are declared inline on the empty child rather than added later, because `ADD … FOREIGN KEY` takes a lock on the **referenced** table either way and `NOT VALID` would only skip a scan of nothing. There is no backfill and there cannot be one: a refund predating this migration emitted its lifecycle event before there was anywhere to put it, and synthesising rows from `refunded_cents` would fabricate refund ids. `create or replace function` takes only an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on the `pg_proc` row.

**What was deliberately not built.** No `refunded_cents` on `event_orders` — the child row carries the amount for both ledgers and a second copy on the parent would be the drift this entry exists to avoid. No status move on `partially_refunded`: § 789's two refusals both still hold, and this change does not touch them. No `refund.created` subscription: it would improve child-row coverage but cannot be *relied* on for the same dashboard-configuration reason, and a correction that is right only when an endpoint is configured a particular way is worse than one that is always additive. And no buyer-facing surface for the state — that is the sibling open follow-up, still open.

**Verification.** `deno test --no-check --allow-read --allow-env supabase/functions/stripe-events-webhook/` — **140 passed, 0 failed** (131 before, 9 new: 5 in `lib.test.ts`, 4 in `wiring.test.ts`; three existing `readRefund` shape assertions were widened for the new `amount`). `deno check` on the two changed modules exits 0, which is also what re-proves `AssertAssignable<Stripe.Refund, RefundSource>` still binds with `amount: number` added. `check_edge_function_test_vacuity.mjs`: **794 killed, 0 survived**, exemption list still empty. `payment_refund_ledger_test.sql` is **21 pgtap assertions**, run green against the live local stack; `check_pgtap_refusal_assertions.mjs` reports 179 refusal assertions across 273 files with **no unexplained survivors**. `check_constraint_unions.mjs`, `check_migration_online_safety.mjs`, `check_migration_versions.mjs`, `check_migration_column_revoke_noop.mjs` and `check_migration_function_revoke_noop.mjs` all pass; the constraint-union entry is the registry's **first Edge Function rail**, because the webhook's `REFUND_STATUSES` is a real third rail of that CHECK and not merely a private copy. `npm run gen:types` was run and committed; `dart run scripts/gen_dart_models.dart` produces **no diff**, because the generator emits from an explicit table allow-list and `payment_refunds` is deliberately not on it — a Dart row class for a table no client role may read would be unreachable by construction.
## 825. A refund that failed had an operator worklist and no reader — and the surface that reaches BOTH ledgers is a notification, not a badge

**Filed as** "a badge + copy on the event-detail order block (web, then the mobile twin per § 24), and the decision of whether the buyer is emailed". Three of those four clauses did not survive measurement.

**The event page's problem is not that the badge is missing — it is that the block the badge belongs in cannot draw.** `/clubs/[slug]/events/[id]` renders every order state inside `{:else if regState === 'already_registered'}`, and `regState` comes from `registrationOpen(..., viewerHasPaidSlot)`, where `viewerHasPaidSlot` is the *attendee* row, not the order. § 789 deliberately does not restore the seat, so a `refund_failed` buyer has no attendee row, `regState` is `open`, and the page was offering them a fresh **Register · $X** button while holding money it owed them. Adding a branch to the registered block would have rendered for nobody. The banner therefore sits outside it — and outside the `!isPast && pricing` gate too, because money we still owe does not stop being owed once the class has happened, and that gate is why a past event showed nothing at all.

**The donation ledger is not "equally silent"; it has no donor-facing surface to be silent on.** `donations` carries **no client SELECT policy** (`20270213_001`, re-cut by `20270621_001`), so a direct read by the donor returns zero rows, and there is no `my_donations` RPC, no `/donations` route and no mobile screen — a donor cannot read their own donation row anywhere, in any state, today. "The same is true of the donation ledger" understates it in one direction and misdescribes it in the other: nothing renders a wrong status there because nothing renders a status there.

**And there is no mobile twin to write.** Mobile has no paid-registration surface at all — `event_detail_screen.dart` does not contain the strings `price`, `paid` or `stripe`, and `parity.md`'s claim of a "read-only price + Register on the web handoff" is not in the source. Paid registration is staged for P3 (`club_events.md § Slice P`). Mirroring a banner about an order onto a screen that has never mentioned payment would be an orphan, and building the P3 read surface to hang it on is a different slice.

**So the email decision is made in the affirmative, and the shape it takes answers the mobile question too.** The buyer cancelled and left; they are not coming back to the event page, and an in-app-only notice is a leaf falling in a forest. What is added is a **`refund_failed` notification kind** (migration `20270701000001`) rather than a `jobs.kind` of its own, because the `notifications` AFTER-INSERT fan-out already turns one row into the inbox entry, the email, the web push and the native push in all seven locales — a bespoke `lifecycle_email` template would reach exactly one of those four and skip the inbox, which is the **only one of them mobile renders**. One row is also the only thing that can reach a donor at all, given the paragraph above: the notification carries the whole sentence rather than pointing at a ledger they cannot see. `email.md`'s existing rails do the rest — `importantKinds` (so the default `important` mode delivers it), `pathForKind`, `notificationLinkFor`, `_verbFor` on both clients.

**It gets no `kindMutePrefKey` entry.** `data_export_ready` has one because the three-mode channel setting is too blunt for a notice about your own data-rights request. A per-kind opt-out of being told we are still holding your money is not a control anyone benefits from having; `email_notifications = off` still silences it, which is the fail-closed property that matters and the one a per-kind key can never override.

**The two ledgers give the kind two shapes, and the null one is the interesting half.** An event order carries `event_id` + `event_instance_start`, so the CTA lands on the page whose banner says the same thing at length. A donation carries neither — and `eventPath`'s own fallback is `/clubs`, which would answer "we still have your money" with a club directory, so that arm goes to the inbox instead, where the message already is. On web `notificationLinkFor` returns null for it and the row renders as plain text.

**An anonymous donation is a limit, recorded rather than papered over.** `donations.donor_user_id` is nullable and null means a donor who was never signed in: there is no account to put an inbox row on and this rail cannot reach them. The trigger guards on it rather than letting the INSERT raise 23502 — a not-null violation inside the webhook's own `UPDATE` would abort the transaction and roll the ledger move back with it, turning a missing notification into a ledger that never records the failure. Their only contact point is the address they gave Stripe, which this database does not hold, so they remain a § 789 worklist item.

**The transition is the dedupe, so there is no `notified_at` column.** Both triggers are `after update of status ... when (old.status is distinct from new.status and new.status = 'refund_failed')`. The webhook CASes against the status it read, so a redelivered Stripe event updates no row and fires nothing; the `when` clause is the second belt, against a later touch of the same row for some other reason. This is `email.md`'s own rule for recurring transactional mail — the enqueue trigger's transition guard is the dedupe — and it is why `data_export_ready`'s `notified_at` stamp has no analogue here: an export job is announced from a *worker* that can retry, a ledger status moves once.

**The CTA is `billing@threkir.com`, which `/terms` § 5 already names** ("Contact the same address with any other refund request"). Stripe's instruction for a failed refund is to "arrange an alternative way to provide your customer with a refund"; naming the address that arranges it is the difference between a status and a next step. The **host** is deliberately not the contact: `buildCheckoutSessionParams` does not send `on_behalf_of`, so the platform is the business of record for the payment ([§ 769](#769)), and pointing the buyer at the host would be sending them to someone who cannot pay them back.

**Verification.** The migration was applied and rolled back against the live local database, and both arms were exercised in that transaction before the pgtap was written: the order transition announces once, a later touch of the same row announces nothing, a signed-in donor is told with no FK attached, and an anonymous donation still moves to `refund_failed` while announcing nothing. `refund_failed_notification_test.sql` — **15 of 15 pass** against the real database. Four of those fifteen are the grant lockdown: trigger firing uses the owner's rights, so the EXECUTE grant a new function inherits from `public` is vestigial, and on a SECURITY DEFINER function it is the shape `20261123_001` swept off the three social notify triggers — both are revoked and pinned the way `rls_definer_hygiene_pt3_test.sql` pins those three. `check_constraint_unions.mjs` names three rails for `notifications.kind` and failed on the mobile `_verbFor` until it was added; `notification_kind_coverage.test.ts`, `messages_parity.test.ts`, `notification_copy_guard_test.go` and `notification_link_guard_test.go` all pass. `go test ./internal/` passes (the copy guard reads the TS union, and `TestRenderNotificationEmail_AllKinds` failed on the missing render case until it was written). `svelte-check` is 0 errors. Two Flutter widget tests render the row rather than grepping for `case 'refund_failed':`, which the existing source guard would pass on an arm returning an empty string. `order_status_copy_guard.test.ts` reads both ledgers' CHECK out of the newest migration to restate it and fails if the page names a status the ledger cannot hold — proved in both directions by renaming the literal to `refund_reversed` and watching both cases fail. `event-self-cancel.spec.ts` runs **3 of 3 green** against the local stack, the new case seating no attendee row because that is the shape the ledger actually produces. The web unit suite is **4456 passed, 0 failed** (`coach/handler.test.ts` excluded — it hangs without a Supabase URL of its own), and `dart analyze` reports **0 warnings and 0 errors** over `mobile_android` (3428 infos, the documented baseline).

**Postscript (CI, PR #845): the banner starved the event title, and `toBeVisible` was the wrong assertion for it.** The Playwright case passed locally and failed in CI, deterministically, with the `<h1>` in the DOM on all 17 polls and hidden on all 17. The cause was not the fixture and not timing. `.hero` is `grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr) minmax(16rem, auto)`: the title column's min is genuinely **0**, and an `auto` max track is sized to its content's **max-content** width — the longest line with no wrapping. The banner's body copy is a 125-character sentence whose max-content is **868px**, so the side rail took 816px of a 944px hero and left the title **38.06px** on macOS and exactly **0** on CI's wider Linux font metrics, where an empty bounding box reads as `hidden`. Both sibling cases passed in CI precisely because neither renders the banner, which is the evidence that isolated it.

**Two things follow, and the second is the one worth keeping.** The fix is to bound the rail — `minmax(16rem, 22rem)` — rather than to shorten the copy, because shortening it would leave the next long string in `.hero-side` free to do the same thing; the skeleton beside it (`.skel-hero`) had bounded its own rail at `minmax(14rem, 18rem)` all along, and the real hero only escaped because everything that had ever lived in the side column was short. Measured after: title **502px**, rail pinned at 352px, and the register box's own 284px max-content is under the cap so the two shipped states are unchanged. And the regression guard is a **width** assertion, not `toBeVisible()` — at 38px the heading was "visible" and completely unreadable, so visibility was never the property that broke. Proved in both directions: reverting the one CSS declaration fails the new assertion naming the measured `38.0625`.

## 826. The API version a webhook endpoint is pinned to is unreadable from the repo, but every delivery states it

**Filed** as "record the endpoint's pinned API version somewhere a future reader can check it against `2024-10-28.acacia`", beside adding the three refund events to the pre-deploy checklist. The checklist half is done in `club_events.md`. The recording half had a better answer than a doc line.

[§ 789](#789) handled all three refund-lifecycle events because "a webhook endpoint's delivery version is dashboard configuration this repo cannot read". That is true at *build* time and false at *run* time: every Stripe event payload carries `api_version`, which is the version the endpoint is pinned to. `parseStripeEventEnvelope` dropped it, so the one place the answer was available was thrown away on arrival.

It is now carried on the envelope and graded by `refundEventsApiEra`, and the refund branch logs the verdict beside the raw value. A `legacy` line means the endpoint predates `2024-10-28.acacia` and is receiving only the deprecated `charge.refund.updated`; `modern` means the other two reach it. Both are logged rather than only the anomaly, because an operator checking "is my endpoint configured right" needs a line to find, and an absent warning is indistinguishable from a branch that never ran.

**Three details are deliberate.** The version is **optional in the parse** — a delivery that omitted it reads as null rather than being rejected, because no handler branches on it and dropping a real money event over a diagnostic field is the more expensive failure. The comparison is on the **ISO date prefix only**: a Stripe version is `YYYY-MM-DD` optionally followed by `.name`, the date orders lexicographically, and the suffix is a label rather than an ordinal — a whole-string compare would rank `2024-10-28.acacia` against a same-day `.zebra` by spelling. And an unparseable version claims **`unknown`, never `modern`**: reporting the modern era for a value we could not read would restore precisely the assumption this exists to remove, and both are pinned by test.

**What this does not do.** It cannot tell anyone whether the endpoint's `enabled_events` list actually includes the three events — an event that is not enabled is never delivered, so there is nothing to log, and the failure mode stays exactly the silent one § 789 was written to close. That is unreachable from here in any form and is a checklist item, now written down beside the `sk_test_` / `ca_` / `whsec_` key items rather than living only in an ADR paragraph.

**Verification.** `deno test --no-check --allow-read --allow-env supabase/functions/` — **788 passed, 0 failed, 24 ignored** (784 before; 4 new cases across `lib.test.ts` and `wiring.test.ts`). `check_edge_function_test_vacuity.mjs`: **788 killed, 0 survived**, exemption list still empty. `deno check` over the three touched modules exits 0.
## 827. The function-revoke class was already closed when its round opened, so the round became a verification — and the filing's arithmetic is wrong in three places while its one reassurance is inverted

`followups.md` filed "`revoke execute … from public` has never withheld a function from `anon`, and 83 migrations say it does" as **a round of its own**. By the time that round opened the class had already been repaired on the round-26 integration branch: `20270625000001` and `20270626000001` land the revocations, `check_migration_function_revoke_noop.mjs` is the statement guard, `anon_execute_contract_test.sql` and `anon_execute_registry_test.sql` are the state guards, and [§ 799](#799) + [§ 800](#800) record the reasoning. Re-deriving that would have produced a second opinion nobody needed. **The useful thing left was to check it from the outside** — to reproduce every number independently and see whether the repair actually holds — plus the two documentary gaps the filing named that the repair did not fill.

**Every figure in § 799 and § 800 reproduces exactly.** Replaying the tree with the three post-sweep migrations withheld reports **91** violating statements over **69** routines in **59** migrations, split **90** `from public`-only and **1** `from anon`-only (`enqueue_run_rematch`). The 69 are 68 in `public` plus `private.enforce_consent`, which is why a `"public\.…"` scan finds 68 and the ADR says 69. Classified against the live catalogue: **61 SECURITY DEFINER**, 8 SECURITY INVOKER, 13 returning `trigger`, leaving **48 SECURITY DEFINER directly-callable**. Against the repaired tree: **242** functions in `public`, **82** returning `trigger`, **100** anon-executable, of which **34** are non-trigger — name for name the contract test's allowlist. The guard reports **448 migrations replayed, zero violations**; its suite is **25 pass**; the two pgtap suites are **6/6 and 6/6**, run through `psql` with `pgtap` created transiently and dropped afterwards rather than through `supabase test db`, because the local stack is shared.

**Three of the filing's four numbers are wrong, and the fourth is exact.** `242` is right. **`83`** is a count of nothing measurable — not routines (69), not migrations (59), not statements (91). **`31`** is **33** on the `revoke execute on function … from public, anon` reading at the pre-fix commit, 41 counting the `revoke all` spelling, and **48** on today's tree (36 + 12); the doc had version-controlled the filing's figure, and it is now computed. **`186`** was never true of the image the probe ran on — 117 there — and is approximately the CI/Cloud figure, where § 799's replay model says 183. That the filing's headline count was right only for the environment it was not measured in is the whole reason § 800 exists.

**The reassurance is the serious error, not the arithmetic.** The filing framed the work as low-stakes — *"most are SECURITY INVOKER with RLS beneath, so the stated intent failing is not automatically a reachable hole"* — and **61 of 69 are SECURITY DEFINER**, which bypasses RLS by definition, so for 88 % of the set the EXECUTE grant was not a second line of defence behind RLS but the only line there was. 24 of those carried no `auth.uid()` anywhere in the body. A filing's own severity estimate is an input to whether the round happens at all, and this one argued for deferring the round that found an anonymous `POST /rest/v1/rpc/cleanup_stale_rate_limits` clearing every elapsed rate-limit window.

**The repair holds against the image it is for, and the reason is one line of a test rather than a simulation.** The workstation cannot run the CI image, so a direct probe of the production posture is not available here. It is not needed: `anon_execute_contract_test.sql`'s second assertion excludes a function from the clean set when `proacl is null` **as well as** when an `aclexplode` row grants PUBLIC or `anon`. A NULL `proacl` is the workstation default and the CI image's explicit-anon-grant shape is the other; a function that no migration ever revoked fails that assertion on either. This is what closes the 18 routines § 799 found that carry no malformed statement anywhere in history — the ones a statement replay is structurally unable to see — and it is why the state guard is not redundant with the statement guard.

**The one live regression risk since the sweep was checked.** `20270629000001` re-creates `enforce_create_rate_limit`, a function the filing names, three migrations after the sweep. It uses `create or replace`, which preserves the ACL, and it restates `revoke execute … from public, anon, authenticated` anyway so the withholding survives a future drop-and-create. The guard agrees; the contract test still passes.

**Guard re-proved by mutation, in both directions, rather than trusted.** A scratch migration creating a function and revoking `from public` alone exits 1 with an `::error file=…::` naming the file, the routine, the statement and the repair; the same with `from anon` alone exits 1 naming the other channel; `from public, anon` exits 0 at 449 migrations replayed. The scratch file was removed and the tree confirmed clean. CI wiring was checked rather than assumed: the guard and its suite run as two self-diagnosing `if ! …; then echo "::error::…"; exit 1; fi` steps inside the already-bundled `parity-types` job, and `check_ci_diagnostics.mjs` reports 51 self-diagnosing steps across 9 derived + 2 listed bundled jobs with `ci-gate` waiting on all **29** — no new job, so [§ 764](#764)'s two obligations are already discharged.

**What this round actually changed.** Nothing in the schema, no migration, no client code — the posture was correct on arrival. Two documentary gaps the repair left: `conventions.md` had no house rule at all for this, and now carries *A revoke names every channel the grantee can reach the object through*, which generalises the column case ([§ 781](#781)) and the function case into one rule plus the three corollaries they share — a `drop` takes the ACL with it, a statement guard and a state guard are different guards and a no-op revoke needs both, and a privilege change reaches every surface that exercises the privilege (pgtap is not the whole search space; `invite-token-lockdown.spec.ts` was found only by CI). And `api_database.md`'s "31 migrations already write the `from public, anon` form" is now the computed 48 with the guard named beside it.

**What is left open.** Nothing in this class that this workstation can close. The residual is the one § 800 already states: the 2.84.2 half of the image table is read off a CI log and a shipped assertion rather than probed directly, so the *first* proof that prod's ACL matches the model will be CI running `anon_execute_contract_test.sql` on this branch. That test is designed to be the loud failure if it does not.
## 828. Every store directory gets one order, and the recording path is deliberately outside it

[§ 821](#821) serialised `OfflineSyncStore` and swept the rest of the tree, filing what it found: twelve atomic-write call sites in the two file stores it did not take, plus two more in `watch_ingest_queue.dart`. Both stores carry the same shape, and both were measured before anything was changed.

The route store's outcome is the one the filing named and it is worse than a resurrection. `save` writes the file and *then* rebuilds `_routes`, so a `delete` that lands during the write's `await` removes `<id>.json`, the rename puts it back, and the save re-inserts the row — memory and disk **agree** on a route the user asked to delete, a cold load agrees too, and no exception is raised anywhere. The run store does the same and additionally re-writes the index the delete had just pruned. `OfflineSyncStore`'s version at least left the two disagreeing, which a reload could resolve.

The sidecars were the half nobody had filed, and on the route store they are the more serious one. `route_owner_tags.json` is read-modify-write and `_ownerTagsTouched` is cleared by whichever write lands first, so eight overlapping `save` calls left as few as **two of eight** routes tagged. An untagged route is visible to — and drainable into the cloud account of — every other account on the device, which is the direction `_persistOwnerTags`' own doc calls unrecoverable. It reproduced on roughly one run in three, which is exactly why nothing had noticed it. `watch_ingest_queue.dart` has one racy pair too, and it reproduces every time: both `main.dart` call sites fire `setLastKnownOwner` unawaited, so a sign-out landing on a sign-in put a delete and an atomic write over `last_owner.txt` in flight together and the next cold start hydrated a stamp the store had been told to forget.

§ 821's chain fits, so it was lifted into `serialiseStoreWrite` in `core_models` beside `atomic_io.dart` rather than copied, and `OfflineSyncStore` moved onto it in the same round. One thing had to be added. § 821's six entry points could each name a private unchained body; the two file stores have around thirty that share `_persistIndex` / `_persistSyncedIds` / `_persistOwnerTags`, and a helper that queues behind its own caller deadlocks with no error and no completion. So the chain is **re-entrant on its own key**: a nested call runs inline. That is not a convenience — on the recording stack a write that never lands is strictly worse than the race being closed, and a deadlock is the one failure mode a serialisation primitive can introduce that the code it replaced could not.

The recording path is the constraint that makes this different from § 821, and the answer is that it is **not on the chain at all**. `saveInProgress` / `clearInProgress` / `loadInProgress` own `in_progress.json`, which no chained operation reads, writes, deletes or sweeps, and `_inFlightSave` already makes overlapping ticks mutually exclusive with a deliberate skip-don't-queue policy (the cursor has not advanced, so a skipped tick's waypoints go out with the next one). Their pinning test holds the store's chain open *forever* through a `Completer` that is never completed, and asserts a tick still appends, recovers, and clears while a chained `save` sits queued behind the gate. The same reasoning admits `watch_ingest_queue`'s `enqueue` and `drain`: an enqueue's path is a fresh uuid nothing else names, and a drain awaits `api.saveRun` per file, so chaining it would be the one thing that puts a watch payload's write behind a stalled network upload. Nothing with unbounded latency — no network call, no untimed lock — is inside a chained body, which is what makes queueing behind one safe.

## 829. The sidecar `FileLock` excluded nothing, because a POSIX record lock is owned by the process

Both file stores held `FileLock.blockingExclusive` over their sidecar read-modify-writes, documented as the cross-isolate half: *"`background_sync.dart` runs a second store over this directory, so a read-modify-write needs the lock or two interleaved merges still drop the later writer's work."* The reasoning is right and the mechanism does not implement it.

Measured, twice. Two `RandomAccessFile` handles on one path in one Dart process both acquire `FileLock.blockingExclusive` immediately and run concurrently; so do two handles opened from two *isolates* of one process. That is POSIX `fcntl` record-lock semantics — the lock is owned by the process, and a second request from the same process replaces rather than blocks. WorkManager's `callbackDispatcher` runs in a second Flutter engine in the **same** Android process, so the one writer the lock named is precisely the one it could never exclude. Against a second store instance in the foreground isolate it did nothing either.

So it went, rather than being kept beside the new chain. Two locking schemes in one file is how the next race gets written, and this one was not merely inert: `blockingExclusive` has no timeout, so keeping it would have put an unbounded wait inside a chained body on the L0/L1 recording stack in exchange for exclusion it does not provide. What actually survives an interleaved isolate is the merge-never-replace in every sidecar writer, which is unchanged and is the real defence; a lock only ever narrowed the window. An arch guard fails the suite if either store spells `FileLock` in code again.

The residue is swept. Each lock file was created lazily and never deleted, so an install carries one zero-byte `<sidecar>.json.lock` per sidecar that no store listing names — `sweepAtomicWriteOrphans` only knew about `.tmp`. It is now `sweepStoreScratchFiles` and drops both: `.tmp` still behind `kAtomicOrphanMinAge`, because a concurrent writer may own one, and `.lock` outright, because nothing writes one any more.
## 830. The case half of the exercise key was collation-dependent at 1 code point between providers and 1,406 under `C` — and the two CLIENTS, which nothing was comparing, disagreed at 466

**Decided 2026-08-31.** [§ 790](#790) closed the whitespace half of `public.normalise_exercise_name` by naming its class code point by code point, measured that `lower()` carried the same defect, and filed it: "`lower()` is collation-dependent too, and the key has always used it. Postgres `lower(U+0130)` on this stack returns `i` + U+0307, which is exactly what JS and Dart `toLowerCase()` return, so the one case worth checking agrees."

**Half of that sentence is wrong, and it is the half about the clients.** Measured over every one of the 1,112,063 assignable code points: Postgres ICU returns `i` + U+0307 and **JS agrees**, but Dart returns a bare `i`. Dart's `toLowerCase()` implements Unicode SIMPLE case mapping from an older table; JS's is full mapping from a newer one. They disagree at **466 code points** — U+0130, U+037F, six Cyrillic Extended-B letters, 135 in the Cherokee / Unified-Canadian range, 49 in Latin Extended-D/E, 7 Glagolitic and Coptic, and 267 in the supplementary planes. That is a divergence between the two halves of a **registered parity pair**, and no rail could see it: the registry compared the whitespace class and nothing else, and each client suite tested its own answer against itself.

**It is reachable, and § 790's own CHECK constraints are what made it loud.** `gym_routine_exercises.exercise_key` and `exercises.name_key` are stamped client-side and held to `exercise_key = normalise_exercise_name(exercise_name)`. Measured against the live stack: for the name `İtme`, web writes `i` + U+0307 + `tme` and the ICU server derives the same, so the CHECK passes; mobile writes `itme` and it does not — **23514 on a legitimate save**, for any of the 412 code points where Dart's table and the server's disagree. Before § 790 the same divergence was a silent bucket split instead.

**The collation measurement, which is what the filing was actually about.** `lower()` answers with the collation of its argument, so the answer moved with the deployment. Over all 1,112,063 code points, ICU `en-US` against: libc `en_US.utf8` **1** (U+0130); ICU `tr-TR` **2**, and one of them is **U+0049** — `lower('I')` is U+0131 on a Turkish database, so every "Incline Press" re-keys; ICU `lt-LT` **3** (U+00CC, U+00CD, U+0128); `C` and `C.utf8` **1,406**, since those fold ASCII and nothing else. A per-code-point sweep cannot see the sixth: ICU applies Unicode's contextual Final_Sigma rule and libc does not, so `lower('ΟΔΟΣ')` ends in U+03C2 on one provider and U+03C3 on the other.

**The durable fix was measured and deferred, which is the load-bearing judgement here.** Naming a case-mapping table the way § 790 named the whitespace class means the 1,488 code points carrying a non-identity simple lowercase mapping — exactly one of which, U+0130, is 1:many, so the rest fit `translate()`. Measured: `translate()` over that table costs **60 µs** a call against **0.34 µs** for `lower()` (200,000 calls: 12.0 s against 0.068 s), because Postgres scans the `from` string once per input character. The four RPCs re-derive the key once per `gym_sets` row, so a 15,000-set history pays **~1.9 s of pure folding** per `gym_workout_summaries` call. An ASCII fast path brings ASCII names back to 2.3 µs and leaves non-ASCII names at 62 µs — it taxes precisely the population the table exists to protect. That cost is removable, but only by persisting the key on `gym_sets` so nothing re-derives it at read time, which is a change to the shape of the highest-volume gym table. Filed as the successor, with the dependency named.

**What shipped instead closes the whole of the filed defect for 0.13 µs.** `collate "und-x-icu"` — the ICU root locale, present on every ICU-enabled server, carrying no language tailoring by definition, and outranking the argument's own collation. Re-measured under all six collations, across every code point and across a 10,031-string context corpus (each cased code point alone, ASCII-flanked, doubled, and followed by a combining acute): **zero** disagreement, where the old derivation disagreed on 14 / 24 / 10 / 9,849 of those strings under `tr-TR` / `lt-LT` / libc / `C`. Cost 0.47 µs against 0.34 µs, and unchanged for non-ASCII input.

**Two folds are named by code point on all three rails**, because the pin fixes the server and the clients still disagree with each other. U+0130 folds to a bare `i` **before** the lowercase — its Unicode simple mapping, what Dart and libc already return, and the only 1:many unconditional lowercase mapping there is, so removing it leaves every remaining fold 1:1. U+03C2 folds to U+03C3 **after**, collapsing Final_Sigma in both directions so a Greek lifter's all-caps spelling meets their lower-case one. Those are the two reachable in a Latin or Greek exercise name. Recomputed after them, the residual is 465 between the two clients, 410 between Dart and the server, 55 between JS and the server — Cherokee, Vithkuqi, Garay, Medefaidrin and their neighbours — and is filed rather than fixed. Both folds are registered in `check_shared_constants.mjs` as a third entry beside the whitespace class, mutation-verified: pointing the Dart post-fold at itself makes the guard name the code point and both rails that disagree.

**An ASCII-only fold was considered and rejected on a measurement**, not on taste. It is the one option that is trivially identical on three rails forever — and 397 code points between U+00C0 and U+052F fold identically on all three rails **today**, every one of which it would stop folding. "Überzüge" and "überzüge" are one bucket now; under an ASCII fold they are two. A fix that splits a German lifter's history to close a Turkish edge case is the § 790 defect pointing the other way.

**Residual, stated rather than implied.** The ICU version linked into the server can still move the answer across a major upgrade, and so can each client runtime's own table — the pin removes the *collation* dependence the followup named, not the *version* one. A server built `--without-icu` has no `und-x-icu` and the migration fails at `create function`, which is loud and fail-closed. The two CHECK constraints are dropped and re-added `NOT VALID` then `VALIDATE`d rather than left alone: their expression is unchanged, so Postgres keeps `convalidated` true when the function underneath moves, and every stored row would carry a claim nothing had re-checked. 0 of 47 stored keys diverged locally under either derivation, and the batched backfill ran anyway for § 790's reason.

## 831. The autocomplete grouped on the spelling while claiming only to preserve it, and the filing's model of the fix was a misreading of the sibling it cited

**Decided 2026-08-31.** `gym_exercise_names` feeds the gym editor's datalist and is deliberately case- and spelling-preserving, which is why [§ 790](#790) left it on a bare `btrim` when it moved the other four RPCs onto `normalise_exercise_name`. But preserving the spelling and **grouping by** the spelling are different decisions, and the function made both with one expression. `btrim(text)` with no second argument strips U+0020 alone, so a name pasted with a leading tab was its own suggestion — visually identical to the clean one, differing by an invisible character, inserting a name that keys to the same exercise — and a case variant was a third. The editor is where the stray character gets typed a second time.

**Grouping is the canonical key now; display is chosen from the group.** `uses` is the count over the group, so the number beside a suggestion is how often the LIFT was logged rather than how often one spelling of it was, and the blank-name filter moves onto the key for the reason § 790 gave (`btrim(coalesce(name,'')) <> ''` counted a lone tab as an exercise named " ").

**The filing's justification was wrong in a way worth recording.** It proposed picking the most-used spelling "as `gym_exercise_records` already does with its `array_agg(display order by started_at desc, display)`". Read, that expression picks the most **recent** spelling. The idiom is reused; the ordering is not. Most-used is right for a list already ordered by use count — the suggestion a lifter accepts then reproduces their own commonest spelling rather than whichever one they typed last — with ties broken most-recent then by the spelling, so the answer is a total order. The pgtap fixture makes the two rules disagree (the most-used spelling is the older one) so the assertion fails under the sibling's ordering rather than passing under both; verified by mutating the `order by`, which also surfaced the tab-prefixed spelling as the answer.

**Two RPCs now resolve the same question by different rules, and that is filed rather than settled.** Unifying them changes a shipped records surface, and the better rule is genuinely arguable there: a lifter who renamed "DB Bench" to "Dumbbell Bench Press" wants the new name on a records page and, for a while, the old one in an autocomplete they have used a hundred times.

**One thing deliberately not fixed.** A group whose ONLY spelling carries edge whitespace still displays it. Trimming the display would mean a fourth hand-written copy of the whitespace class — the defect § 790 exists to have removed — and the filed complaint was the duplicate suggestion, not the invisible character on its own.

## 832. Seven defects in the Edge Function tier, six of them where a guard existed but the value that reached it was the wrong one

A round measuring the `#789` work in `apps/backend/supabase/functions/**` found seven live defects. Six share one shape: the refusal was written, tested and correct, and the argument handed to it was not.

**The paid class that could never be sold twice.** `events-checkout` graded the sales window on `event.starts_at` while pricing, capacity, the cancelled-occurrence guard and `events-cancel`'s refund cutoff all resolved per `instance_start`. `events.starts_at` is the SERIES row, so for a recurring class every occurrence after the first was `sales_closed` from the moment the first one began — the `gym-class-instructor` and `yoga-pilates-instructor` personas' entire revenue path, refused with a 409 that names the right reason for the wrong week. The web client sends `next_instance_start`, so this was reachable from the shipped UI on the second week of any recurring paid event.

**The lifetime subscriber a monthly renewal downgraded.** `mapEventToTier` declines to knock a `lifetime` holder down to `pro`, and `lib.test.ts` proved it — supplying `currentTier` itself. The handler resolved `currentTier` only for the deactivating types and `PRODUCT_CHANGE`, on the reasoning that "other activating events always grant at least pro". That is wrong in exactly one direction: lifetime outranks pro. A lifetime owner carrying a parallel monthly subscription got a `RENEWAL` every month, each of which reached the mapper with `currentTier: null`, wrote `pro` over `lifetime`, and left the guard unreachable for four of the five activating types. The monthly's eventual `EXPIRATION` then read `pro` and wrote `free`. The read is now taken for every event that can move the tier; one extra `user_profiles` select per webhook is not a price worth a lost lifetime entitlement.

**Three refusals that were unreachable.** `clip-public-track` ran `DecompressionStream` + `JSON.parse` outside its try, so a stored blob that would not decode threw past the handler into `withSentry`'s 500 and the `!Array.isArray(points)` 502 below it was dead code for precisely the input it names. `export-data`'s `decodeTrack` promised `TrackPoint[]` and returned whatever `JSON.parse` produced, so an object reached `buildGpx`'s `for…of` — and the caller's `track.length < 2` guard is false for `undefined`, so the TypeError escaped the per-run `catch` that exists to tolerate one bad blob and failed the WHOLE export. `revenuecat-webhook` parsed `{}` into `undefined` and threw on the first field read: a 500, which RevenueCat retries for three days, on a payload that can never succeed.

**The archive that was not XML.** `buildGpx` escaped the title and interpolated `startedAt`, each point's `ts`, and `lat`/`lng`/`ele`/`bpm` raw — the last four into quoted attributes, out of a track that is `JSON.parse` of a blob with no schema between it and the renderer. The Go twin (`buildGpxDoc`) escapes all three text fields and cannot reach the numeric case at all, because its decode types them as `float64`. The Deno side now escapes the same three and drops a point it cannot place rather than closing an attribute with it.

**And one that was only a coercion.** `race-listings-sync` read any unrecognised `provider` as RunSignUp, so a caller naming a provider this function has never heard of got RunSignUp's credential gate: a 503 today and a `synced: 0` success once the key lands. Its sibling `race-results-import` answers 400 `unknown_provider` and its comment names this the same class of bug as claiming an unconfigured leg is configured.

Four further fail-closed gaps were closed in the same round without a live exploit behind any of them: `validateFreshness` returned `ok` for a non-finite stamp (both comparisons against NaN are false, so the replay window opened for anything unparseable — both live callers happen to type-check first, which is why nothing noticed); `isValidTimestamptz` admitted year `0000`, which ISO 8601 uses for 1 BC and Postgres rejects outright, so the gate that exists to turn a cast failure into a 400 passed it through to a 22008; `computeApplicationFeeCents` returned `NaN` for a non-finite input straight into `application_fee_amount`; and `verifyStripeSignature` accepted `t=1700000000junk` because `parseInt` stops at the first character it cannot read — harmless in itself, since any other integer breaks the HMAC, but it left the parse and the signed payload disagreeing about what `t` was, so a regression that signed the header TEXT would have been invisible to every test.

## 833. A rate-limit bucket key that accepted any bare word, and a test that pinned it that way

`trustedClientIp` validated the trusted header against `/^[0-9a-f:]+$/` for the IPv6 branch, which is satisfied by `a`, `deadbeef`, and 45 letters — so any token a caller sent minted a window of its own, and a rate limit that resets on demand is not one. The design's real defence is that the header is overwritten by the edge on every request, and that defence is intact; but the value check is what the docstring claims to be doing ("a single, plausible IP literal"), and it was not doing it.

The tell was in the suite rather than the source: `rate_limit_invariants.test.ts` measured "the length bound is 45 characters, the longest IPv6 text form" using 45 letters — a value that is not an address — and it had to, because the hex-only class could not accept a single real 45-character IPv6 literal. The longest text form is `ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:ffff:255.255.255.255`, whose IPv4-mapped tail carries dots the class excluded. So the bound named an address family the check could not admit, and was pinned with a string the check should not have admitted.

The fix requires a colon for the v6 branch and puts `.` in the class, which closes the bare-word case and admits the form the bound is named for. It is deliberately NOT a full IPv6 parser: a hand-rolled one is its own bug surface, and strictness buys nothing against a caller who can set the header at all — they would simply supply valid addresses. The property worth having is that a value which is not an address does not get a window; that is now stated, with both address families as positive controls beside it.

## 834. The Art 20 export's renderers had no behavioural test because they could not be imported

`csvRow`, `csvEscape`, `buildGpx`, `xmlEscape` and the two Storage-path assertions lived inside `export-data/index.ts`, which runs `Deno.serve` at import — so `wiring.test.ts` could only grep their call sites as text and no test had ever called them. `decode_track.ts` had already been split out of the same file for exactly this reason and says so in its header. They now live in `export-data/render.ts` on the same terms.

The split is what made § 832's GPX escaping defect visible and is what a regression would now hit: the CSV column count against the row's field count (an added header with no matching value shifts every later field for the whole export, silently), a title carrying comma / quote / CR / LF surviving a round trip through a real RFC 4180 splitter, and `canonicalTrackUrl` / `canonicalHrUrl` refusing each near-miss a corrupt or legacy row could carry — including each other's suffix, since the two must not be interchangeable or the hr sweep downloads the track and files it under `hr/`.

## 835. The envelope on every Edge Function response had no test, and the request it forwards has to be the raw one

`withSentry` wraps all sixteen functions and nothing measured it. Two of its properties are load-bearing. A handler's own `Response` must reach the caller unaltered — including a deliberate 4xx, because every fail-closed refusal the rest of the suite measures is a non-2xx that an envelope treating it as a failure would collapse into one opaque 500. And a THROWN error must not reach the caller at all: the message is where a PostgREST `details` string, a Storage path or a row value would travel, and `clip-public-track` reaches this envelope on an anonymous request. The body is a constant, the message goes to the operator log only, and both halves are now stated with the other as its control — a silent 500 is the opposite failure and would satisfy a test that only checked the body.

The third property is the one a refactor is most likely to break: the wrapper must `await` inside its own `try` (a bare `return handler(req)` catches the synchronous throw and leaks the rejected promise) and must hand the ORIGINAL request through, since the HMAC paths verify over the raw bytes and a consumed or rebuilt body would break every webhook while every stubbed test still passed.

## 836. A money row's identity is a column too, and the lock that listed fourteen of them did not list that one

`lock_event_order_status` has said in its own comment since `20270303_001` that "a non-service-role UPDATE may touch ONLY `refund_initiated_at`", and implemented that as `old.<col> is distinct from new.<col>` over fourteen columns plus a separate `status` check. `event_orders` has sixteen. The two it did not name are `refund_initiated_at`, deliberately, and `id`, not. That matters on this table and on no other payment table, because `event_orders` is the only one carrying a permissive client UPDATE policy — "buyer initiates refund on own paid order", `using (buyer_user_id = auth.uid() and status in ('paid','partially_refunded'))` with the same WITH CHECK — while `20270408_001` grants `authenticated` UPDATE on every column. Measured on the local stack as the buyer's own JWT with RLS in force, before the fix: the refund stamp updates one row, and so does `update event_orders set id = <any uuid> where id = <mine>`. The WITH CHECK still holds — `buyer_user_id` and `status` are untouched — and the two foreign keys that reference the row (`event_attendees.order_id`, and since `20270630000001` the refund ledger's `payment_refunds.event_order_id`) are `on update no action`, so they refuse the rewrite only once such a child exists. Before a seat is taken or a refund is recorded, the id moves freely. The cost is auditability rather than money: the id is what `events-checkout` writes into the Stripe session's `metadata.order_id`, what it hands back to the client, and what `handleNotPaid` resolves an expiry delivery by — so after a rewrite an expired session's soft reservation is never released (the handler answers `skipped: unknown_order`) and a reconciliation of Stripe's records against this ledger finds a charge whose order has vanished. The same round made it worse by making that id the join key of a second ledger.

The fix is not a fifteenth column name, because the shape is the defect. An enumeration of what may *not* change is a denylist, and every column added afterwards is client-writable until somebody remembers to extend it — which is exactly how `refund_initiated_at` had to be hand-added when `20270303_001` opened the one legitimate write, and exactly how `id` was missed on the way past. `20270702000001` rewrites both money-ledger locks as allowlists over the whole row: the two row images must be equal once the permitted columns are removed from each, `to_jsonb(new) - 'refund_initiated_at' is distinct from to_jsonb(old) - 'refund_initiated_at'`. A new column is locked the moment it exists. `donations` gets the same treatment with an empty allowlist — its header has claimed "the donation webhook is the sole writer" since `20270213_001` while the trigger checked `status` and, from `20270620_001`, `refunded_cents`, leaving `amount_cents` (the numerator of `fundraiser_totals`), `paid_at`, `platform_fee_cents` and `client_request_id` to RLS alone. That half is inert today and is being stated rather than changed: `pg_policy` has zero rows for `public.donations`, so a client UPDATE matches nothing and never reaches the trigger. It stops being inert the first time anyone adds a donor-edits-their-message policy.

`payment_ledger_write_allowlist_test.sql` measures it in the direction that catches the recurrence rather than the instance. It probes every `event_orders` column but the stamp, one at a time, with a type-correct value distinct from the fixture's — and separately asserts that the probe list COVERS the live column set, so a column added to the table fails this file until it is probed here too. Two more assertions exist because the first one is otherwise cheap to satisfy: that every probe actually ran (an empty result table would report no writable columns just as convincingly), and that the row still carries the figures the webhook wrote. Run against the pre-fix trigger definitions the file turns four assertions red; run against the fix, eleven green.

## 837. Every grant registry in the suite filters `relkind in ('r','p')`, and nine of the twelve public views execute as their owner

The three class guards that decide what a client may touch — `column_grant_lockdown_registry_test` (SELECT), `column_grant_write_lockdown_registry_test` (INSERT/UPDATE), and `role_grant_matrix_test` — each restrict their population to ordinary and partitioned TABLES. A view is outside all three by construction, and that is not the harmless omission it looks like: a single-FROM, no-aggregate view is auto-updatable, and only three of the twelve views in `public` carry `security_invoker`. The other nine — `public_runs`, `public_routes`, `public_profiles`, `public_food_log`, `public_gym_*`, `public_race_listings` — execute as `postgres`, which has BYPASSRLS, so an INSERT grant reaching `anon` on `public_runs` is a write into `runs` past every policy on it. `20260626_001` records the security-invoker choice deliberately; what nothing recorded is that the choice makes the view's grant list load-bearing. The only thing standing there today is a `revoke all … grant select` pair that each strip migration re-emits by hand — three times in the #789 round alone — and one `activities` INSERT assertion in `activities_view_windowed_test`. `view_client_write_grant_test.sql` makes it the class: no view or materialized view in `public` grants `anon` or `authenticated` any write verb, over a population asserted non-empty and beside a positive control that both roles still hold SELECT, so an empty write set reads as a withholding rather than as an empty catalogue. Measured: granting `insert on public_runs to anon` turns it red. `service_role` is deliberately outside the assertion — the workstation CLI image and CI's pinned 2.84.2 disagree about default privileges on views, so a `service_role` reading there proves nothing about production.

The same file's sibling closes a narrower gap in the same shape. `public_runs` is re-emitted in full on every strip migration, each header claiming "same column list as the previous", and the two things measuring that claim were a `hasnt_column(track_url)` and a metadata-denylist sweep — so a re-emit carrying a new base column through was caught for exactly two names out of the table. Worse, `route_id` and `event_id` are projected through `is_public_route_by_id` / `is_public_event_by_id`, and `public_helpers_shadow_hidden_test` exercises both helpers as bare functions rather than through the view: dropping the `event_id` wrapper and selecting `r.event_id` raw passed every shipped assertion, which is measured — the mutation turns only the two new assertions red. `public_runs_projection_test.sql` pins the projection with `columns_are` (which fails on a missing column as loudly as on an added one, so it carries its own positive control) and moves ONE run row between a public and a private anchor for each conditional column, so the null is a withholding rather than a link the row never had; the shadow-hidden branch of each helper is measured separately, because a re-emit naming the older `is_route_visible_to` would drop exactly that half.

## 838. Two shipped tests asserted the service-role skip fires and neither could say what made it fire

`enforce_create_rate_limit` reads a role from two claim sources — the legacy `request.jwt.claim.role` setting and the `role` key of the `request.jwt.claims` blob — and `20270629000001` added the second because `20260907_001` had only the first, so skip 1 was dead code on every current PostgREST deployment for two years. What made that survivable, and undetectable, is that skip 2 covered the same callers by accident: a service-role JWT usually carries no `sub`, so `auth.uid()` is null and the next line returns. Both shipped assertions of the skip — `create_rate_limits_test` and `direct_message_rate_limit_test` — set `set local role service_role` AND a `role` key in the JSON blob in the same statement, so they cannot separate the three candidate sources. Measured: a body whose only change is an added `current_setting('role')` fallback passes both files with zero failures while making a session that merely RUNS as `service_role`, presenting no such claim, skip the throttle.

`create_rate_limit_claim_source_test.sql` drives each source alone against an already-spent bucket, so an assertion that the write LANDS is a statement about the skip rather than about the window having room. The fail-closed direction is the point: a session running as `service_role` whose JWT does not say so is throttled, because PostgREST derives the claim from the key that was presented and the session role is not evidence of anything. Beside it, the two arms of the coalesce measured one at a time (blob-only with the legacy setting explicitly empty, legacy-only under a plain `authenticated` session), a role claim naming something *else* — without which a body skipping on any non-empty role claim would pass both arms and be wide open — and the unparseable-blob case, which aborts the write with 22P02 rather than resolving to no role. That last one is pinned as fail-closed on purpose: a body that swallowed the parse error would fall through to `v_role = ''` and hand the caller whatever the remaining skips allow.

## 839. The Art 20 export surface was asserted to have a size limit and a mime list, and never to have the right ones

`storage_bucket_privacy_test` proves the `exports` bucket exists, is private, carries no `storage.objects` policies, has SOME `file_size_limit`, has SOME `allowed_mime_types`, and is bigger than `runs`. None of those is a value. A regression to a 26 MB cap — back inside the range `20270602_001` was written to escape, where a full-history archive was truncated to "on the order of tens of runs" — satisfies `exports.file_size_limit > runs.file_size_limit`, and a mime list widened to `text/html` satisfies `allowed_mime_types is not null`. The photo buckets are the same shape one door along: `20270622000002` narrowed three of them to the strippable set because § 557 settled that an image we cannot strip is an image we do not accept, and the only thing measuring it is `check_shared_constants.mjs` reading the migration TEXT — a different claim from what the applied `storage.buckets` row says, and blind to a console edit or a bucket that storage-api created with its own defaults. The word `heic` does not appear anywhere in the pgtap suite.

`export_surface_contract_test.sql` pins the values, and pins the mime lists in BOTH directions with an array-length assertion beside them, because `@>` alone passes a bucket narrowed to `['image/png']` (which breaks every JPEG upload) and `<@` alone passes an empty list. It then asserts `data_export_jobs` on both of the rails `20270603_001` deliberately gave it — RLS with no policies AND no client grant, so "a policy added by mistake later still cannot open a client read path" — where `role_grant_matrix_test` names the table only to EXCLUDE it from its readability catch-all, so a later `grant select … to authenticated` is invisible there. The 64-character `error_code` cap is measured at 64 and 65 (the column is a machine token; a raw upstream error string carries paths and addresses into a durable row), the one-in-flight partial unique index is measured in both directions (a second in-flight row refused, a terminal-status row admitted, which is what makes it partial rather than one-row-per-user), and the Art 17 cascade the table comment claims is driven rather than read.

The sweep is driven too, and that is the assertion with the most reach: `cleanup_stale_export_blobs` is COMPOSED — it deletes the objects and then calls `expire_stale_export_jobs` — so a `ready` row cannot outlive the object it points at. `data_export_jobs_test` calls the expiry directly, so deleting the `perform` leaves that file green while production stops expiring rows. The fixture stages four objects (a stale archive in the new bucket, a stale one at the LEGACY `runs/{uid}/exports/` prefix, a fresh archive, and an unrelated track), and the assertion names the two survivors rather than counting the deletions. One environment note is baked in: storage-api carries a `protect_objects_delete` trigger refusing a direct DELETE from `storage.objects` outside the Storage API, so the test sets its escape GUC. **This paragraph originally said that was a no-op on CI's pinned 2.84.2 image "which does not have the trigger", and that the risk was a forward one if Supabase Cloud ever shipped it. Both halves were wrong and neither was measured** — corrected the same day by measuring the images rather than assuming them (CLI 2.84.2 starts `storage-api:v1.44.11`, 2.109.1 starts `v1.62.5`, and `0055-prevent-direct-deletes.sql` is present in both). The trigger is `FOR EACH STATEMENT`, so it raises with zero matching rows: the nightly sweep has been failing on every run, and because the DELETE precedes `expire_stale_export_jobs`, no job row was expired either. The GUC this fixture sets was load-bearing on CI, not decorative. The sweep itself is repaired in the round that measured this; what remains open is the deeper question this note gestured at — that it is deleting rows rather than objects in the first place.

## 840. The refund ledger's only writer held its privileges by inheritance, and the image that grants them has already changed once

`20270630000001` created `payment_refunds` and wrote exactly one privilege statement: `revoke all on public.payment_refunds from anon, authenticated`. Nothing granted anything to `service_role`, which is the sole writer — `recordPaymentRefund` in `stripe-events-webhook` upserts every `refund.created` / `refund.updated` / `refund.failed` delivery through it. That works because Supabase's `alter default privileges` for `postgres` grants every DML verb to anon, authenticated AND service_role by name, so a fresh table arrives with service_role already holding them and the revoke strips only the two client roles. `20270603_001` did not rely on that for `data_export_jobs`: it argues in its own header that "a new table inherits nothing" and then writes the grant out. The sibling one round later did not.

Inheriting a privilege is not the same as having it, and this is not a hypothetical: `20270625000001` already measured the same default moving underneath this schema in the other direction. The workstation CLI's current image (2.109.1) ships a `postgres` default ACL of `{postgres=X/postgres}`, and on it `payment_refunds` lands as `service_role=Dxtm/postgres` — TRUNCATE, REFERENCES, TRIGGER, MAINTAIN and none of SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. It is the ONLY base table in `public` that service_role cannot fully read and write there, which is exactly what `global_segment_grants_test`'s "a table shipped with no grants at all fails HERE" assertion says, and it takes `payment_refund_ledger_test` down at its first fixture insert. What that image demonstrates about the deployed one is the point: if the default ever reaches it, `recordPaymentRefund` logs the upsert failure and returns 500, so Stripe retries the delivery indefinitely while every refund goes unrecorded — and `fundraiser_totals` computes what the charity KEPT from the `failed`/`canceled` children in that same table, so the thermometer silently reverts to counting a bounced refund as money returned. `20270702000002` states the grant. It is a no-op against Supabase Cloud and CI's pinned 2.84.2, and a repair everywhere else; `payment_refund_ledger_test` gains the pair that has to hold together — the writer keeps everything, the clients keep nothing.

Two of this branch's three local pgtap failures were that one omission. The third, `donations_status_lock_test`, is the function-side analogue and is deliberately left alone, on a measurement rather than on effort: about a hundred functions in `public` are unexecutable by `service_role` on the newer image, because `revoke … from public` withholds nothing where there is no PUBLIC entry and the by-name default is what was granting them. Two grants close that file completely — verified, it then runs 19/19 locally — but the reason not to write them is that the class carries no production risk at all. Every RPC any server-side caller invokes under the service key (`check_rate_limit`, `check_rate_limit_tiered`, `get_integration_tokens`, `set_integration_tokens`, `set_integration_tokens_cas`, `delete_user_integration_secrets`, `delete_user_provider_secrets` — the Edge Functions and the Go worker between them) already holds an explicit EXECUTE grant on both images. `fundraiser_totals` and `fundraiser_feed` are reached only by the web client as anon or authenticated, so their absence from service_role is a test-fixture inconvenience and nothing else — which is exactly what separates them from `payment_refunds`, where the missing privilege was on the sole writer's own path. It stays the documented environmental failure the previous round recorded.
